'The whole base knows her': Service dog helps autistic IDF soldier thrive in classified Air Force role
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:24:48 UTC
04:24:48 KST

Pvt. A., 18, and her service dog have become well known in the Israeli Air Force’s Special Air Forces Wing, known as Wing 7. Everyone on base already knows Vali, the third service dog to complete basic training at the Mahane Alon base in the Galilee.
Pvt. A. serves in a classified role with Vali at her side as part of the IDF’s “Titkadmu” program, a unique enlistment track designed to integrate young men and women on the autism spectrum into military service.
From the first day of basic training, commanders made it clear to the company that Vali was a service dog with a job to do and was not to be touched or disturbed.
During formations, the dog sat or lay quietly, and at the basic training graduation ceremony she synchronized herself with A.’s movements, sitting at attention and lying down at rest.
“She took part in all the marches, including a night march, as well as field and camouflage exercises,” A. said. “The other girls in the company welcomed Vali with great enthusiasm and a lot of respect for her role.”
Maj. H. said the IDF’s attitude toward service dogs has evolved over time, particularly as awareness has grown of their importance for soldiers with disabilities.
Israel’s Equal Rights for Persons with Disabilities Law enshrines the right to bring service dogs into public places, and their use was later expanded to support people with post-traumatic stress disorder and autism.
“The trend increased significantly after October 7,” Maj. H. said. “Although A. was not allowed to bring the dog into the dining hall during basic training, at her permanent base Vali integrated very well and became part of the unit’s daily life. There are several career soldiers, including a lieutenant colonel, who serve with assistance dogs, as well as reservists with PTSD who come with their dogs.”
The road to Wing 7 was long and filled with bureaucracy.
“I arrived at the recruitment office with a regular first-call notice. Of course, I came with the dog,” A. said. “When they asked why I had a dog, I explained that she was a service dog because I have anxiety attacks. About half an hour later, the head of the mental health section came and said they don’t enlist soldiers with service dogs.
“At that moment, I insisted on going through the first-call process. The mental health officer gave me an exemption on the spot, and that is how I began the volunteer process and joined the ‘Titkadmu’ track.”
Pvt. A. eventually reached Maj. H., who told her he would support her.
“He said he thinks service dogs can help a great many people, and that he sees this especially with reservists, and he thinks it is a great idea,” she said.
In the end, Pvt. A. enlisted together with Vali and went through induction and basic training with her.
“The commander at the induction center asked to take a picture of Vali wearing an Air Force beret. So somewhere there is a picture of her with the beret,” she said with a smile.
Now, when A. sleeps at her permanent base, Vali sleeps beside her in her crate.
“The whole base knows Vali and says hello to her. She contributes to the atmosphere and helps reduce tension. I know there is a lot of work being done to encourage enlistment with service dogs.
“There are reservists with service dogs, with levels of experience and knowledge that no one else has, who are able to continue in their roles because of the dogs. The dog also helps the other soldiers in the unit.”
Vali’s training began when Pvt. A. was just 16. Dana Wilker, owner of a training and instruction center for assistance dogs, trained her.
“Service dogs work with and accompany the people who rely on them for about eight to 10 years,” Wilker said. “That is a significant period of time, especially for someone who received the dog at age 16, with so many changes and so much growing up.”
Wilker, who also researches the cognition of working dogs, said: “Over these years, I saw A. open up and, with impressive inner strength, help herself develop and move forward.
“During training, the dogs undergo intensive exposure to a wide range of situations intended to prepare them for anything, including loud noises and unusual smells, until the dog is able to remain calm and continue working and carrying out tasks for the person it assists even in unusual situations.
“That was the case, for example, over the past month, when Vali accompanied A. throughout basic training.
“Vali and A. demonstrated to the military system that it is both possible and worthwhile to integrate and enlist soldiers who are accompanied by assistance dogs.”

Lina Altawell
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
 Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the UN General Assembly on Thursday before a largely empty hall after delegations from several countries walked out in protest because of Israel's genocidal war against the Gaza Strip, as large demonstrations took place across New York.
Delegations left the General Assembly hall as Netanyahu took the podium, protesting the premier, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Before Netanyahu's speech, large crowds demonstrated near UN headquarters and elsewhere in New York, against his appearance and accusing him of committing "genocide" in Gaza.
The protests included anti-Zionist Orthodox Jews carrying signs describing Netanyahu as a "war criminal," as well as American and Israeli Jewish opposition groups and Western and Palestinian organizations opposing the genocidal war.
The Yedioth Ahronoth Israeli newspaper said that "large crowds" left the hall immediately after Netanyahu took the podium, before he began speaking.
Israel's Channel 12 also published an image showing most seats in the hall empty.
Netanyahu has been wanted by the ICC since 2024.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, the Israeli genocidal war on Gaza has killed more than 73,000 and injured over 175,000 Palestinians, most of whom are children and women, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
Israel has also destroyed 90% of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure, while the UN has estimated the cost of reconstruction at about $70 billion.

Xi and Trump discuss AI cooperation (VIDEOS)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:20:46 UTC
04:20:46 KST

Xi and Trump discuss AI cooperation (VIDEOS)
US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, have discussed cooperation on artificial intelligence during talks in Washington, stressing the technology’s growing global importance.
The meeting came as the two countries compete for leadership in AI while negotiating over advanced chips and critical materials, which became key bargaining points in their trade dispute last year.
Welcoming Xi to the White House for a state visit, Trump said the talks would cover security, technology and “superintelligence” – his new term for AI.
“The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come,” the US president said.
Xi said China and the US “bear a historic responsibility to promote human development and progress.”
“Both China and the United States are leading nations in artificial intelligence; we have both the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the well-being of the people,” the Chinese president said.
Beijing and Washington stand to benefit from cooperation and lose from confrontation, Xi added, stressing that competition between the two countries should be a “race” rather than a fight “in which one either wins or loses.”
Earlier this month, Trump singled out China as Washington’s main rival in the AI race, declaring that “whoever wins AI, wins.”
Technology has increasingly become a source of friction between the two powers. Washington restricted exports of advanced chips to China last year before later allowing some sales to resume in exchange for a 15% share of the revenue. Beijing, meanwhile, imposed export controls on several rare earths and restricted their supply for foreign military use.
China has agreed to suspend some of the restrictions for a year following a Trump-Xi meeting in South Korea last October.
Ahead of Thursday’s summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Washington and Beijing had agreed to extend their tariff truce by another two months. The arrangement has kept tariffs well below the peaks reached during last year’s trade war, when US duties on Chinese imports climbed as high as 145% and Beijing’s levies on American goods reached 125%.

Unknown

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Deputy Secretary of the Russian Security Council, Army General Oleg Salyukov warned Yerevan of the disappointment that US "security guarantees" may bring.
"If Yerevan chooses American security guarantees, this will definitely entail possible disappointment with the results obtained," he told reporters.
Salyukov noted that "the events related to the transfer of Nagorno-Karabakh under Azerbaijan’s jurisdiction were largely the result of the policy pursued by the Armenian leadership that came to power as a result of the so-called Velvet Revolution of 2018." "However, the results of these events were used by the Armenian leadership not as an incentive to work on mistakes, but as a pretext for public statements about the ineffectiveness of military-technical cooperation with Russia and Armenia’s participation in the Collective Security Treaty Organization, which, in our view, is completely unfounded and short-sighted," the Russian Security Council deputy secretary stressed.
He recalled that cooperation between Russia and Armenia "in the military sphere after the formation of the Commonwealth of Independent States and the establishment of the Collective Security Treaty Organization structures was carried out on the principle of common military and economic security across the entire range of areas, with unified standards for building armed forces, including military training."
"Armenia’s armed forces are currently 90% equipped with Russian weapons and possess the most advanced Russian weapons systems, including Iskander tactical ballistic missile systems, Tor-M2 air defense systems, Su-30SM aircraft and advanced armored vehicles. Most of the officer corps of Armenia’s armed forces are graduates of Soviet and Russian military educational institutions," Salyukov cited as examples.
"As for the Collective Security Treaty Organization. Mr. [Armenian Prime Minister Nikol] Pashinyan regularly says that he has no objection to Armenia being expelled from the Collective Security Treaty Organization. Russia, meanwhile, has already proven more than once in the new century that, provided mutual agreements are observed, it is a security guarantor for the countries participating in the Collective Security Treaty Organization," the Russian Security Council deputy secretary stressed.

Zelensky says the ‘spirit of Anchorage’ concessions are no longer on the negotiating table. He credits Ukraine’s battlefield position.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:18:59 UTC
04:18:59 KST

Zelensky says the ‘spirit of Anchorage’ concessions are no longer on the negotiating table. He credits Ukraine’s battlefield position.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the “Anchorage agreements,” which included Russia’s demands for recognition of its sovereignty over occupied territories, are no longer on the negotiating table. He spoke at a meeting with representatives of the Ukrainian community in the U.S.
The talks have shifted away from Ukrainian neutrality and recognition of Russian sovereignty over occupied territories, Zelensky said.
He said Ukraine’s armed forces played the biggest role in that shift and that the situation on the front gives Ukraine room to reject Moscow’s demands.
“We control the situation on the battlefield today. It’s hard for us, but the Russians aren’t making any major advances. Where they are advancing, Russia is paying a very high price in human lives — hundreds, thousands of them,” Zelensky said.
The phrase “spirit of Anchorage” emerged after Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump met in Alaska on August 15, 2025. Russian officials began using it to refer to what they said were agreements reached there. In February 2026, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Russia had accepted U.S. proposals on Ukraine after the Alaska summit, but Washington itself was now unprepared to accept them. He later said that “the spirit of Anchorage is evaporating.”
Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Ukrainian president’s office, has said that, by “the spirit of Anchorage,” Russia means ending the war on terms under which the international community would recognize Russian sovereignty over Crimea, the Donetsk and Luhansk regions, and the Russian-occupied parts of the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions.

French president says he warned Trump diesel export ban would raise prices, calls move ‘bad’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:17:34 UTC
04:17:34 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç, Necva Taştan Sevinç
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday he had warned US President Donald Trump that a possible US ban on diesel exports would raise fuel prices, calling the move a “bad” decision.
“We are not directly dependent” on American oil, Macron told French broadcasters TF1 and France 2.
He added that such a decision “would raise prices.”
“I told him that this decision would be bad,” Macron said, referring to his meeting with Trump at the UN General Assembly earlier this week.
Macron also said France is taking steps to prevent fuel shortages amid disruptions to energy supplies linked to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.
“We are doing everything to avoid fuel shortages,” he said, adding that France has replenished its gas stocks and also has oil reserves.
He said France would continue securing fuel supplies in the coming weeks and would convene G7 countries to assess whether strategic reserves should again be released to ease pressure on the market.
“We will look at whether, at that time, it is necessary to release stocks again to ease the market,” Macron said.
Macron also announced the deployment of French military resources to protect a key energy site in Saudi Arabia.
“We will send military resources, soldiers, radar, defense systems to protect this site,” he said.
The comments come as the US considers restrictions on diesel exports amid record-high fuel prices. Trump said Tuesday he supported the idea of restricting diesel exports, while US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Wednesday that an outright ban would not work and could in fact push up gasoline and jet fuel prices.
Possible Russian attack
Macron said it was possible that France could face an attempted Russian attack similar to last month’s incident at Leipzig airport, while denying a report saying that the CIA had warned French intelligence services of a possible Russian drone attack on southern France.
“The CIA did not inform the French secret services” of such a threat, he said. “But we are facing a worrying situation,” he added, saying an attack “could happen.”
Macron said Russia is carrying out an increasing number of “hostile and sometimes criminal acts” against European countries and that there have been “several indications” of renewed Russian mobilization.
Spanish daily El Mundo reported Wednesday, citing sources familiar with an alleged CIA alert, that several European governments had been warned of a possible Russian drone operation targeting Spain, France, or Italy; the report has not been independently confirmed.

CNN, MS NOW, Politico allowed back in White House after judge’s order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:13:51 UTC
04:13:51 KST

CNN, MS NOW, Politico allowed back in White House after judge’s order
- A federal judge ruled that President Trump's ban on CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House likely violated their constitutional due process rights, ordering their access to be restored.
- The White House accused these outlets of spreading falsehoods and leaking sensitive national security information, but the judge doubted these claims motivated the ban.
- Top US broadcasters paused White House pool coverage in solidarity, emphasising the public's right to independent and accurate government information without media restrictions.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back into the White House on Sept 24, six days after being banned by President Donald Trump, after a federal judge ordered that the journalists have their access restored.
District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled overnight that revoking the White House press credentials of the three media outlets “likely violated their constitutional due process rights.”
Reporters for CNN, MS NOW and Politico who attempted to return to the White House early on Sept 24 ahead of a visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping were initially turned away by the Secret Service but were allowed in later around midday.
Journalists from other outlets surrounded CNN’s tent on the White House driveway and filmed reporter Betsy Klein as she reported live following her return.
“Welcome back,” several journalists said.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico had requested an urgent court hearing on Sept 24 after their reporters were initially barred from the White House despite the judge’s order.
In his ruling, Kelly took issue with how the White House went about expelling the three news organisations.
“The ‘general rule’ is that ‘individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them’ of a constitutionally protected interest,” the judge said.
Trump has long attacked media that have aired critical coverage of him, repeatedly blasting the press as the “enemy of the people.”
The Republican president barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House on Sept 18 for distributing what he called “fake news” and “fiction and lies.”
They filed a joint lawsuit asking for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.
Ahead of the ruling, the Department of Justice had argued that Trump can “control reporters’ access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office.”
“Access to the White House is a privilege – not a right,” it said.
National security?
The White House Press Office accused CNN in a letter to the cable news outlet of “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information,” with similar accusations leveled against MS NOW and Politico.
The letter to CNN cited several stories about the US-Iran war and a story on Trump’s plans to build a military bunker below the planned East Wing ballroom which allegedly “disclosed ‘top-secret’ construction details.”
Kelly, who was appointed by Trump during his first term, appeared unconvinced.
“The Court is sceptical – at least on this record – that Defendants’ interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes,” the judge said.
In a rare move, the top five US broadcasters said that they were halting pool coverage of the White House – where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day – in solidarity with CNN.
“The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting,” ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said. AFP

Ed Miliband meets Iran’s foreign minister as Tehran gives US ultimatum on strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:13:06 UTC
04:13:06 KST

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has met his Iranian counterpart, Abbas Araghchi, for the first time in New York amid warnings from senior Iranian security officials that the US has four to five days to respond to its conditions for reopening the strait of Hormuz.
The previously unknown apparent deadline was specified by Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of the supreme national security council, in a TV interview on Wednesday evening, and it is unclear what action Tehran will take if the US does not respond to Iran’s preconditions for reopening the vital waterway.
A faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday.
Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond.
Rezaei, a recently promoted hardliner, said Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and Araghchi had flown to New York to convey Iran’s internally agreed terms, not to negotiate new ones. “There has been no discussion whatsoever that these conditions should change, that a new condition should be removed or added,” he said.
The big change appears to be that Tehran now insists Washington act first. “Talk is enough. Negotiations are enough. Now we must act,” Rezaei said.
He warned that if the US did “not fulfil the conditions, we will neither open the strait of Hormuz nor is there any negotiation on the table”.
Rezaei said the seven conditions must be implemented “completely and all at once”, adding that the US had been given “four or five days” to do so. After that, he said, Iran would determine its “next step”, without specifying what that would entail.
The meeting between Miliband and Araghchi, one of an exhaustive round of bilaterals undertaken by the Iranian foreign minister, is the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers for a year and the first exchange since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries.
Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen.
He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to the British couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment in Tehran.
Overall, European diplomats have not sensed a US-Iran breakthrough in New York.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, also said it would be wrong to characterise the Witkoff talks with Iran as a major breakthrough. It is understood that Araghchi, speaking largely through a Qatari mediator, set out to him the seven preconditions to be met before it is willing to reopen the strait, including the lifting of US sanctions and an end to war on all fronts, a reference to Israeli military activity in south Lebanon.
Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis.
Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: “If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.”
Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to “the US bully” with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks.
He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases.
Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: “We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from the United Nations podium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.”

China's Xi urges US, Iran return to negotiations as Trump hails 'great meeting'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:12:50 UTC
04:12:50 KST

During a closed-door meeting at the White House with US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping urged the US and Iran to return to dialogue to end their war, as Trump hailed the meeting as "great".
China has "always maintained that the sovereignty and security of all countries should be respected" and has played a constructive role in easing tensions and encouraging negotiations, Xi said on Thursday, according to state-run Xinhua news agency.
He expressed China’s support for the US and Iran returning to the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding and voiced hope that both sides would return as soon as possible to resolve their differences through negotiations, reach a comprehensive agreement, including on the nuclear issue, and achieve peace.
After the US and Israel launched the war against Iran on February 28, Pakistan helped secure a ceasefire on April 8 and later hosted more than 20 hours of talks between American and Iranian officials in Islamabad.
Following weeks of mediation, Pakistan and Qatar helped secure the June 18 deal, which provided the two sides with a framework and 60 days to negotiate a longer-term agreement aimed at ending the war.
However, the two sides soon resumed retaliatory strikes, with tensions continuing.
Xi also urged the US to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’” and handle the Taiwan question “prudently” to lay a solid foundation for bilateral strategic cooperation and relations.
Beijing’s position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity is “crystal clear", he said.
China considers Taiwan a breakaway province, while Taipei has insisted on its independence since 1949.
Xi also said that building a constructive China-US relationship based on strategic stability is not an expedient measure nor something that can be achieved overnight, additionally calling for translating the new vision of a constructive bilateral relationship of strategic stability into action.
‘Great meeting’
Trump said he and Xi had a "great meeting".
Trump made the comments to reporters in response to shouted questions before the two boarded the Marine One helicopter on the White House grounds for a brief tour.
Trump also said Xi “has great interest in granite. He likes granite.”
“He’s an expert on stone aside from many other things. And he loves good granite,” he added.
The Chinese president left the White House after the bilateral talks but was expected to return later with his wife, Peng Liyuan, for a state dinner.
Meanwhile, First Lady Melania Trump took Peng on a tour of the National Museum of Asian Art while Trump and Xi held talks.
Xi arrived Wednesday for a three-day state visit to the US, his first in more than a decade.
He is the first Chinese leader to make two state visits to the US since the two countries established diplomatic relations in 1979.
Then-US President Barack Obama hosted Xi for his first state visit in 2015.
Xi’s current visit comes after he hosted Trump for a state visit in May, when the two sides agreed on a “new vision of building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability".

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Netanyahu calls genocide allegations 'the greatest lie of the century'
The Israeli prime minister said allegations of genocide in Gaza leveled at Israel by various world leaders or groups were false.
"It will take time for the world to acknowledge what is so plain to see. That Hamas used Palestinian civilians as human shields. That it used hospitals, schools, mosques as terrorist command posts. That it sold much of the food we let into Gaza," Netanyahu alleged.
"And while Hamas did everything possible to keep Palestinians in harm's way — often at gunpoint — Israel did everything possible to get them out of harm's way," he said, listing measures like warnings to civilians.
"I want to ask you a question: what genocidal regime gives a million polio vaccinations to the enemy's population? What genocidal regime enables the distribution of 2 million tons of food into Gaza? Accusing Israel of genocide is the greatest lie of the century," he said.
He also called out New York's "antisemitic" mayor, Zohran Mamdani, as one of the people spreading this message. He said that since Mamdani's election "many Jews no longer feel safe in New York."
Netanyahu said the "simple truth" was not that Israel committed genocide but that it prevented one, saying "that's exactly what Mr. Mamdani's Hamas buddies would have done to us if we had not stopped them."
Netanyahu says he 'drew a red line' on same podium 14 years ago
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began his speech with a reference to his notorious General Assembly appearance in 2012, when he stood with illustrated graphics depicting how near to creating a nuclear bomb he thought Iran was.
"Ladies and gentlemen, 14 years ago I stood on this podium and I drew a red line," he said. "I vowed to prevent Iran's murderous dictatorship from developing atomic bombs. Nuclear weapons that could destroy the state of Israel, nuclear weapons that could threaten the whole world. That's exactly what we did."
Netanyahu said that while it was "very hard" to devastate Iran's nuclear facilities, he said it was "one of the easiest decisions" he'd had to make as prime minister, "because if we hadn't done it, we'd all be dead."
Iran contends that its nuclear program was for peaceful purposes like electricity generation, a claim that Israel and the US dispute.
Netanyahu also referred to Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa's call for Israel to pull back its forces in the Golan Heights border area, addressing al-Sharaa and saying "you should know that the Jews have been in the Golan Heights since the days of Moses," referring to the Old Testament prophet thought to have lived more than 3,000 years ago.
Delegates leave the chamber in large group as Netanyahu enters
As Israeli Prime Minster Benjamin Netanyahu's turn to speak at the UN General Assembly came, a large number of delegates from various countries stood up and left the chamber to cheers and jeering.
Only after repeated appeals for calm was it possible for him to begin his address.
"Before I begin, just a quick announcement: if there any other moral cowards who have not yet left this hall, please do so now. Thank you very much," Netanyahu said.
He returned to the issue of the walkout later when discussing his decision to target Iran and its nuclear capabilities.
"Now do you want to hear the ultimate irony? In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall. In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran's nukes," he claimed, saying "it's hard to imagine more mind-blowing hypocrisy."
Protesters had also gathered outside the building in New York ahead of Netanyahu's address. Some were arrested by police. A Democratic nominee for New York's 10th congressional district in November's midterm elections, Brad Lander, also joined the demonstrators, albeit wearing a suit and tie rather than a slogan-laden T-shirt.
READ: Nigeria and US sign mining deal
On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the United States agreed to increase American investiment in the West African nation's mining sector.
Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced the deal on Thursday, a day after he signed the framework deal with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.
"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value. We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses," Alake said.
Read more about the US-Nigeria mining agreement.
Abbas calls for saving two-state solution and Palestinian self-determination
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas used his remarks to implore nations to support the two-state solution, saying his people seek a non-militarized, democratic Palestinian state that can exist alongside Israel in peace.
He said the first step to preserving the idea of such a solution is to protect the lands upon which a future Palestinian state would be based, as well as protecting those people who have lived upon them for generations.
Abbas underscored the fact that the Palestinian people would not be displaced by "military occupation, nor settlement expansion, annexation, nor settler terrorism."
He further said that "no lasting security can be built upon the occupation of another people and the denial of its legitimate rights," adding that the Palestinians have their own plans for an independent state and emphasizing the need to end the Israeli occupation in order to negotiate a solution.
This plan, Abbas said, is based on protecting Palestinians from displacement, preserving their lands, democratically renewing political institutions and building a new sovereign Palestinian state — with east Jerusalem as its capital.
All of this, he said, would be carried out with a "commitment to international law" and the right to exercise self-determination with the aim of achieving security and peace with Israel to, "pave the way to regional integration, cooperation, prosperity and security for everyone."
Abbas concluded his remarks by thanking those 160 nations whom he said have recognized Palestinian statehood, calling for its inclusion in the United Nations.
Palestinian leader Abbas blasts US and Israel in General Assembly
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, addressing those gathered at the UNGA via video because the US State Department refused to allow the Palestinian delegation into the country, has rejected Washington's approach as "unlawful and punitive."
Abbas described the denial of visas as a US failure to live up to its responsibility as the host nation of the international body.
Abbas quickly pivoted to blast Israel's "genocidal war" in Gaza, as well as the sanctioned "ethnic cleansing" perpetrated by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Saying that Israeli violations of international law put the two-state solution at grave risk, Abbas described the situation in Gaza, the West Bank and east Jerusalem as part of a "malicious colonial scheme" and warned of a "new Nakba."
He also referenced attacks on Muslim and Christian religious sites by radical Jews as having the potential to transform the current security situation into a wider religiously fueled conflict.
Not only Middle East, rising sea level threat also on slate for day 3 meetings
Beyond AI and the headline-grabbing conflict in the Middle East, the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday will discuss another pressing issue that impacts the world’s citizens — rising sea levels.
A high-level meeting is slated to begin at 10:00 a.m. (1400 GMT) on Thursday as swelling seas redraw coastlines and pose existential risks for islanders and those who live in low-lying areas near the shores of the world's oceans and seas.
The UN says nearly 900 million people live in such areas, adding that another one million could be impacted by mid-century.
Rising sea levels, says the UN, threaten not only land but also livelihoods and even the existence of entire nations. In the words of UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, "Rising seas are sinking futures."
Israeli and Palestinian leaders set to address UNGA on day 3
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas are both expected to address members of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) on Thursday, with the issue of the Middle East writ large on the day 3 agenda.
Netanyahu, who is increasingly unpopular at home and abroad, will not meet with US officials or Arab leaders during his stay. His office cited a "tight schedule" as the reason, listing as many as nine meetings during his visit, including with the presidents of Argentina and Bolivia, the vice president of Colombia and the prime minister of Papua New Guinea.
The increasingly isolated Israeli leader's Palestinian counterpart, President Mahmoud Abbas, will also address the General Assembly. Abbas, however, will do so via video, as the US State Department refused to issue him an entry visa.
The broader subjects of Gaza's future and Palestinian statehood will also be topics of discussion. The UK will convene a meeting on Gaza's current and future status, and Saudi Arabia and Norway will host a ministerial meeting to hash out plans for the implementation of the so-called "two-state solution."
That's a wrap on Day 2 of the UNGA
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russian President Vladimir Putin for the ongoing war between the countries, calling him "patient zero."
The Ukrainian leader also announced new defense deals with Finland and Australia.
Elsewhere, Syrian leader Ahmed al-Sharaa called for the Israeli occupation of the Golan Heights to end, saying the territory belongs to Syria.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also addressed Israel, calling for what he described as the "genocide" in Gaza to stop.
This comes ahead of a speech by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the UN General Assembly on Thursday.
'Too much power in too few hands' — AI leaders warn about technology dangers
Besides world leaders, top bosses at AI companies also addressed the UN about dangers concerning artificial intelligence.
AI executives spoke to the UN Security Council and urged international cooperation on the hotly debated technology.
Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, highlighted two big risks with AI.
"First, we could lose control of the future to AI. The risk is that it moves so fast that people can no longer follow what's happening or intervene when needed," he said, adding that such a scenario would be "terrible."
Second, he said AI systems "could concentrate too much power in too few hands." "No one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their worldview on everyone else."
Anthropic boss Dario Amodei used the platform to call for a ban on the use of AI in the development of biological weapons, describing AI as the most crucial global security issue facing the world.
"If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," he said.
Amodei also urged global standards for testing new AI models.
Spain PM Pedro Sanchez calls for reforming the UN Security Council
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchezcalled for reforming the UN Security Council so that "all of the regions in the world" would be fairly represented.
Sanchez quoted the UN Charter, saying "no country should be a judge in its own case, no matter how powerful they are."
The Spanish leader continued to condemn the "genocide that (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu is still perpetrating in Gaza," while pointing to Madrid's sanctions against Russia as an example of his government's willingness to take action against countries whose conduct violates the UN Charter.
Ebola outbreak 'major' test for country, Congo's PM tells UNGA
Congolese Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka described the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo as a "major test" for the country.
"For the DRC, fighting this epidemic is an absolute priority. After having contained 16 previous outbreaks, the DRC is mobilizing recognized scientific and operational expertise. And thanks to national mobilization and the support of our
partners, the response has recently begun producing tangible results," she told the UN General Assembly.
As of 22 September 2026, Congo reported a total of 7, 773 confirmed cases, including 3,759 related deaths. A total of 839 patients are hospitalized in isolation.
Venezuela to hold elections, Rodriguez tells UNGA
Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, delivered her first address to the UN General Assembly since coming to power, promising her country would hold elections when the nation's people determine the "right moment."
"I want to make this very clear at this General Assembly: there will be elections in Venezuela," Rodriguez said, adding that her country "has initiated the process of democratic transformation for its rebirth" following two blows this year.
First, "strangulation of its internal political life and the heightened confrontation with the United States" and second, the earthquakes on June 24 that caused the deaths of more than 6,500 people.
Rodriguez took power after the US toppled the then-president Nicolas Maduro in January.
Rodríguez briefly met US President Donald Trump at the UN General Assembly as well.
Ukrainian foreign minister met with Iranian delegation on the sidelines of UNGA
DW's US Correspondent Misha Komadovsky reported that the Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Sybiah earlier in the day told a UN Security Council meeting that Ukraine was ready for an immediate and complete ceasefire without preconditions, if Moscow did too.
German FM calls on Iran to end Hormuz blockage
In a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called on Iran to end its closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
"It is up to Iran to engage constructively in negotiations and to loosen its stranglehold," Wadephul told journalists ahead of the meeting.
Wadephul also urged Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to engage seriously and credibly in sustainable negotiations with the US and neighboring states in the region, sources in the German delegation were cited by the DPA news agency as saying.
"There must now be an overall willingness to compromise in order to bring about a solution to the deadlocked conflict in the region," Wadephul was quoted as saying.
He stressed the readiness of Germany and the so-called E3, which also includes France and the United Kingdom, to support mediation efforts.
Wadephul also stressed in the talks the need for Iran and militias it supports in the region, namely Yemen's Houthi rebels, to halt attacks on civilian ships. He added that Berlin expects free transit through the Strait of Hormuz to be restored immediately, stressing the rejection of any fees for passage through the critical waterway.
"Not only the Gulf States, but large parts of Asia, Africa and also Europe are suffering under this blockade," Wadephul said.
He added that Germany welcomes renewed talks between the US and Iran on the sidelines of the General Assembly, adding that he planned to speak to his counterparts from Jordan, Pakistan, Iraq and Oman.

Türkiye's Fidan chairs OIC meeting, highlights Gaza and regional conflicts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:06:07 UTC
04:06:07 KST

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has chaired the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) Foreign Ministers’ Annual Coordination Meeting in New York, Turkish diplomatic sources said.
Thursday’s meeting was held on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly as Türkiye holds the rotating chairmanship of the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers.
In his address, Fidan discussed Israel’s ongoing genocidal war in Gaza, as well as its occupation and annexation activities across Palestine and attacks on Syria and Lebanon, according to the sources.
He also addressed developments affecting the wider Islamic world, including the situations in Iran, Yemen, Libya, Sudan and Somalia.
Fidan stressed the importance of the OIC’s role in protecting the rights of Muslim minorities and communities.
Türkiye holds OIC chairmanship
Held annually during UN General Assembly week, the coordination meeting provides a platform for foreign ministers from OIC member states to exchange views alongside the organisation’s annual Council of Foreign Ministers meeting.
The Council of Foreign Ministers normally meets once a year but can also convene extraordinary sessions to address major issues affecting the Islamic world.
Türkiye assumed the rotating chairmanship after hosting the 51st session of the Council of Foreign Ministers in Istanbul on June 21-22, 2025, under the theme “The OIC in a Transforming World”.
Türkiye previously hosted Council of Foreign Ministers meetings in 1976, 1991 and 2004.

Italy bans burqas, niqabs in schools, caps pupils with poor Italian skills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:04:22 UTC
04:04:22 KST

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's cabinet adopted a decree law on Thursday banning burqas and niqabs in schools and capping the number of students with a poor command of Italian per class.
The measure comes amid wider restrictions on Muslim women’s religious attire across Europe, which rights groups and Muslim communities have criticised as discriminatory and as limiting freedom of religion and expression.
According to Meloni, the decree introduces "a 30 percent cap on the number of students in a class who do not have an adequate command of Italian, more tools for learning our language, and a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools,"
If a child seriously struggles to integrate at school, social services will be called and the parents will be obliged to attend free Italian lessons.
Failure to comply will be punished with a fine of up to $1,140 (1,000 euros).
Italy is a frontline country for migration and integration is a hot campaign issue ahead of next year's general election.
Save the Children warned that forcing children to change schools or enrol in a different institution from their peers simply because of their nationality or limited proficiency in Italian would "create 'first-class' and 'second-class' students".
But Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said, "inadequate language proficiency... hinders educational progress".
"Parental participation in their child's educational path is fundamental for academic success", he told journalists.
Valditara said there were 34,000 school classes in Italy in which over 30 percent of the students are foreign.
But most of those would be not be affected by the new law, which targets new arrivals rather than those born in Italy or who attended kindergarten.
The 30 percent limit on the number of foreign students per class was established in a ministerial memorandum in 2010.
But the limit was flexible, and could be raised in cases involving foreign students with adequate language skills, such as foreign students born in Italy, or lowered when foreign students have a poor command of Italian.
‘New witch hunt at expense of children’
Opposition leader Elly Schlein accused the government of "a new witch hunt at the expense of children".
The burqa ban was "a matter of security", Meloni said in a television interview after the cabinet meeting.
"When a woman—or worse, a young girl—is forced to cover her face, she is being denied fundamental rights and the very integration that is so often loudly championed," she said.
A crackdown on the use of burqas in schools was called for in July by the National Future (FN) party.
The FN, which is not part of the governing coalition, is further to the right than Meloni's and has emerged as a major challenger, rising sharply in the polls since launching in February.

Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski at high-level week of 81st UN General Assembly in New York
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
21:03:53 CEST
04:03:53 KST

Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski at high-level week of 81st UN General Assembly in New York
24.09.2026
Over 30 meetings with world leaders, participation in the general debate and a UN Security Council session were the highlights of Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski's visit to New York. On 21-24 September, the head of Polish diplomacy took part in events related to the high-level week of the UN General Assembly's 81st session.
“Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all,” is the theme of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. The issue of change, particularly in the context of security and the development of artificial intelligence, was raised not only during the general debate but also in bilateral meetings.
Deputy Prime Minister Sikorski carried out a busy schedule of meetings, during which he presented Poland’s position on the most important challenges to international security and the future of multilateral cooperation. The minister consistently highlighted the significance of defending the principles of the UN Charter and international law, the need for effective multilateralism and for continued support for Ukraine in the face of Russian aggression.
In its statements, the Polish delegation attached particular importance to respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity of states and to accountability for international law violations—principles, which form the foundation of a stable international order. An important aspect of Polish activity was also dialogue with countries of the Global South and presenting the consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.
During a UN Security Council session on Ukraine, Minister Sikorski directly addressed Russia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergey Lavrov, setting the record straight regarding the Russian foreign minister’s lies and explaining the reasons for Russian escalation. The head of Polish diplomacy pointed out that
After more than four years of a senseless colonial war, Vladimir Putin has achieved nothing. He is running out of troops and resources and needs a pretext to mobilize. His unnecessary war has killed or wounded one and a half million Russians. Millions of Ukrainians and other Europeans are increasingly in danger. At any moment, Putin might try to provoke a NATO country and spread the war further, as we have heard from others
- said Minister Sikorski.
The head of the Polish MFA addressed Russian politicians:
To the representatives of the Russian Federation, I have this to say: You have been trying to conquer Donbas for over twelve years and Kyiv for over four. You have been stopped by heroic Ukraine, a country with one tenth of Russia’s GDP. But Poland has almost half of your GDP. Europe has ten times your GDP and NATO has 25 times your GDP. You can still kill a lot more people, but you cannot win. You can stop this imperial war of choice at any time
- said the head of Polish diplomacy.
During the UN high-level week meetings, Minister Sikorski talked with NATO’s Secretary Mark Rutte and took part in the meeting of foreign ministers of Poland, Germany, France, and the United Kingdom with foreign ministers of Australia, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea on the security of Europe and the Indo-Pacific. He also took part in the Visegrád Group foreign ministers’ meeting with the foreign minister of India. Traditionally, an informal meeting of the EU heads of diplomacy (FAC) was held. Minister Sikorski also met with US Senators Jeanne Shaheen and Ruben Gallego and attended a ministerial meeting on ensuring accountability for Ukraine.
Moreover, his schedule included a series of bilateral meetings with representatives of other countries, senior UN officials, and representatives of various sectors, including Polish diaspora start-ups and venture capital investors.
Deputy Prime Minister Sikorski met with top diplomats from: Peru, Nepal, Greenland, India, Kazakhstan, Egypt, Mauritania, the United Arab Emirates, and Jordan. Additionally, on behalf of EU High Representative Kaja Kallas, the head of Polish diplomacy held consultations with the foreign minister of Cameroon.
During the meetings, Minister Sikorski stressed the need to further increase international support for Ukraine. He also pointed out the importance of developing a joint vision of an international order based on respect for all countries’ rights and capable of responding to the Russian threat.

Trump's FDA nominee Heidi Overton affirms MMR vaccine and mifepristone are safe at crucial Senate hearing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:03:39 UTC
04:03:39 KST

On Thursday President Donald Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration appeared before lawmakers for a crucial Senate confirmation hearing in which she repeatedly distanced herself from the president’s false statements about drugs and vaccines but declined to say the president was ever wrong.
Heidi Overton, a physician who currently serves as a White House aide, told lawmakers at the hearing that the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine is both safe and effective, as are all other vaccines that are currently recommended by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. When questioned about the abortion drug mifepristone, she said the medication has met FDA safety and efficacy standards. She also said that she has seen no evidence that the use of Tylenol during pregnancy causes autism. All of that puts her at odds with the president.
Still, when asked if she believes it’s possible for the president to be wrong about something, Overton refused to answer directly, saying only that he “sets the policy directions, but he works with all of his advisers to get the best information.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Trump nominated Overton to head up the FDA in August, just a week after she stood behind the president as he signed an executive order aimed at altering the childhood vaccine schedule. That order called for the MMR vaccine to be broken into three separate shots. During the signing ceremony, the president claimed, without evidence, that the vaccine can be “lethal” to children.
During Thursday’s hearing, Overton said the shot remains the best available tool for combating the ongoing measles outbreaks that have been linked to the deaths of at least four Americans so far this year. Overton also acknowledged the ample evidence showing the combined shot is safe and effective. And she pointed out that no drug company currently produces separate mumps, measles and rubella vaccines for commercial use and that it could be years before any might become available or approved by the FDA.
“Anything new to the market would take time to develop, but that option was for the president’s decision, and he wanted to provide an option to Americans that, right now, are getting zero vaccinations after COVID,” she said.
As noted, Overton was also asked about the abortion drug mifepristone, which is subject to an ongoing FDA safety review despite more than 100 studies showing the drug is both safe and effective. In 2023 Overton wrote in a policy position for the right-wing America First Policy Institute that the drug is “dangerous to women.”
However, she declined on Thursday to say what her plans would be for the drug if her nomination is approved, saying that the FDA will continue to examine the post-market safety of all medications.
Overton’s nomination has been criticized by abortion rights groups. In a statement released Thursday, Reproductive Freedom for All President and CEO Mini Timmaraju said Overton has “one of the most alarming anti-abortion records of any FDA nominee to date and is entirely unfit to serve as a leader in public health."
“Senators who vote to confirm Overton will be choosing Trump over their own constituents, and voters will remember that in November,” Timmaraju said.
If approved, Overton laid out one major priority for the FDA: cracking down on illicit e-cigarette products. However, she defended the agency’s recent decision to approve several flavored vape products, which have been criticized as appealing to minors, saying they can be effective at helping adults to quit cigarettes.

Mona got a scan while on holiday. It uncovered what had gone undetected for months
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:03:38 UTC
04:03:38 KST

IN BRIEF:
- Pancreatic cancer is common but symptoms can be easily missed.
- Researchers say more funding is needed for better patient outcomes.
When Mona Thind went for a gastrointestinal scan in late 2024, she'd known something wasn't right for months.
At 52, she had been told by doctors that the pain she felt around her ribs and upset stomach was likely caused by constipation or poor diet, easily treated by upping her fluid intake.
Months later, the pain returned, and as she was setting off for a holiday to Byron Bay in northern NSW, her father raised concerns.
"As I was walking out of his house, he said to me, 'My heart tells me we should do a scan ... I feel it in my gut'," Mona told SBS News.
At the time, she recalled, she laughed about it, thinking he was a typical overprotective father.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
But at the upper gastrointestinal scan in Byron Bay, she knew the sonographer had found something.
"I saw the look on her face," Mona said. "I came home, and everything happened."
Mona had pancreatic cancer. In the 15 months that followed, she underwent six rounds of chemotherapy and major surgery, gruelling treatment which she pushed through.
"When I was first diagnosed, I didn't cry," she said. "I wasn't sad every day; I just went, this is what it is."
But on the day she was congratulated for beating cancer, she "fell apart" for the first time.
"My dad promised me that he would be there for every chemo treatment for me. And he died on my last chemotherapy day. He was there for every single treatment," she said.
"He was my pillar of strength."
A major disease, commonly undetected
Pancreatic cancer is the eighth most commonly diagnosed cancer in Australia.
It occurs when malignant cells develop in parts of the pancreas, and it's estimated that one in 70 people will be diagnosed with the disease by the age of 85, according to the Cancer Council.
Senior researcher at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research's Cox Lab, Dr Amelia Parker, says it's also one of the most understudied and complex cancers to treat.
"For pancreatic cancer, less than 13 per cent of patients will survive at five years, and part of the reason for that is that a lot of the symptoms associated with early-stage pancreatic cancer are largely vague or not readily diagnosed," she told SBS News.
"This means that patients often aren't seeking medical help until the cancer is much more advanced."
Like other cancers, once pancreatic cancer has spread to other parts of the body, it is much more difficult to treat, leading to lower survival rates.
"We're working very hard to improve our detection of those cancers so that patients who have that disease are diagnosed earlier and have all of the most effective treatments available to them," Parker said.
Parker believes research gaps driven by dwindling investment directly impact patient outcomes.
"There has been less investment in research funding historically. And that's really hampered our efforts to both understand the disease and use that understanding to develop new and better treatments."
She said her research was making "real strides" in improving understanding of the disease, and she hoped it would translate into better outcomes for patients.
"But for that to happen, for there to be innovations in treatment, we really need to invest in funding," she said, adding that funding for cancer research was "highly competitive".
"There's more research out there that would make a difference," she said.
Kerry Strydom, CEO of the Australian Cancer Research Foundation, hopes to change that.
"I'm absolutely convinced that funding is the way that we will advance breakthroughs," she told SBS News.
"You've seen how the pace of technology improvements has accelerated over the last few years — we need to get those tools, that equipment, the latest technology, into the hands of our scientists, and I'm convinced that it'll get us closer to a world free from the burden of cancer.
"It's really important that we continue to back brilliant researchers so that they can turn their promising ideas into breakthroughs."
Hope for future advancements
In August, the US Food and Drug Administration approved a new oral prescription medication, daraxonrasib, sold under the brand name Rasonque, for previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer.
Parker from the Garvan Institute says that this marks a significant step forward for people diagnosed with one of the toughest common cancers.
"We work closely with our international colleagues to make sure that Australian patients could potentially have access to the same quality of care as in other parts of the world."
But Parker's ambition was clear: "My overall hope is that we'll be able to develop new treatments that will mean a cancer diagnosis is not one that's met with a lot of fear and uncertainty, that it's easily treatable and patients can look forward to a very long life ahead of them."
"So in many ways, I hope that maybe I'm out of a job in the future," she said.
Mona is hopeful that more funding for cancer research in Australia and abroad will pave the way for new treatments.
"It's very important to get that research so that we can treat people," she said.
"But what it really translates to is hope ... It's that birthday that you would have missed because there's no treatment, that trip you would put off because you may not be here.
"It's not just about the treatment; it's what you're giving back to the patients and their families and their friends."

'Spinning out of control': What came before OpenAI’s Medicare hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:03:31 UTC
04:03:31 KST

IN BRIEF
- The Australian government says an OpenAI agent "scaled the fence" of a Medicare portal, accessing statistics but no patient records.
- One of the first known AI hacking incidents is known as the Hugging Face attack.
Just as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman finished warning the world about the dangers of AI at the United Nations, news broke closer to home: one of his company's own agents had broken into an Australian government portal.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that in June an agent linked to the ChatGPT developer gained unauthorised access to the public–facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal.
Both OpenAI and the Australian government have said no personal information was accessed during the breach.
But the nature of the incident has raised some concerns.
According to Albanese, the hack occurred after OpenAI's research team utilised an internal model to conduct internet-based research on public spending in medicine.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"There's an AI agent looking for information, asking questions. There were blocks clearly, which were coming back telling the AI agent, no. The AI agent found a way around those blocks. Didn't accept no for an answer," Albanese said.
"One of the issues here is we could not find precedent for this. But others, there may be, but not that we're aware of."
Dominic Meagher, a research fellow at ANU's Crawford School of Public Policy, told SBS News that while "this particular incident hasn't made me feel panic, but it does reinforce what we've heard from a few other recent incidents".
He likened AI to "a car spinning out of control."
"This isn't someone trying to do something. This is a piece of technology that isn't behaving the way we expected. It's doing what it was told, and it's operating in its environment according to the laws of physics.
"I don't think there's any way that we're going to avoid some bizarre things happening in the next few years ... How we manage all this is going to be really important."
This is the first known case of an AI agent hacking into a government portal — but it is only part of a pattern of various AI models going rogue and hacking different networks with different intentions, on several occasions.
The Hugging Face attack
One of the most infamous AI hacking incidents is known as the Hugging Face attack, with some describing it as the first time AI escaped human control.
In July, about 700 OpenAI models that were under development started breaching internal company tools, gained access to the internet and eventually hacked Hugging Face, an online library for AI models.
Later, the Reuters news agency reported that Hugging Face was not the only target and that the models had also hacked into other companies.
"These AI models have really been selectively evolved rather than coded, which is why they don't always behave in the way you're expecting," Meagher said.
"It's quite a tricky thing that people are working on. It raises a whole lot of interesting questions that I think are unresolved."
Anthropic hacking incidents
In late July, just weeks after the Hugging Face attacks were announced, Anthropic, developer of Claude AI, announced that while its models were being tested by an Israeli start-up, Irregular, they had accidentally connected online and hacked three companies in January.
At the time, Claude said in a statement that "these are three isolated incidents and were not part of a controlled, experimental comparison. We must therefore be cautious about drawing conclusions from them".
Later this month, they confirmed a fourth company was also hacked during the time.
A 'similar behaviour by Meta'
In August, Meta joined the chain, with the company announcing that one of its AI models hacked another company during a cybersecurity test.
The company announced at the time that its model "exploited a security vulnerability in a third-party service, in a manner similar to previously reported instances with other companies".
Hacking a gym class
During the same time, Andrew Bird, an Australian working with OpenClaw, a popular AI agent software that runs through the Claude service, reported another AI hack incident — this time targeting a gym.
He asked the agent to book him a gym class; the class was booked out, but the AI agent found a solution: it kicked someone off the waiting list and added Bird's name.
"This is a case where [the AI agent] did what he was asked to do, but not what he [Bird] wanted, because that's an impolite way of behaving. And clearly the gym didn't intend for that to be available," Meagher said.
"But he [Bird] didn't specify not to do that because why would he? It would never have occurred to him that that was an option."
Google hacks
Google announced last week that its model Gemini hacked into three companies during a test of its cyber-security in May.
During the hacks, Gemini found public information online and guessed credentials to access three websites it thought were within the scope of its test, Heather Adkins, Google's vice president of security engineering, said in a statement.
In one case, the Gemini model guessed passwords until it gained access to a protected system. In the other two cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that let it access protected systems, according to the Wall Street Journal, which first reported the news on Friday.

====================================================================================================

Dmitry Glukhovsky’s new novel ‘Registration,’ about Russians seeking to cash in on the war, has been called an émigré’s rebuke to those who stayed behind. Is that fair?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:02:15 UTC
04:02:15 KST

Dmitry Glukhovsky’s new novel ‘Registration,’ about Russians seeking to cash in on the war, has been called an émigré’s rebuke to those who stayed behind. Is that fair?
On September 17, Dmitry Glukhovsky posted his new novel, “Registratsiya” (“Registration”), online for free. Set in wartime Russia in the 2020s, it follows the pregnant girlfriend of a contract soldier as she tries to marry him as quickly as possible to qualify for benefits. The book is still stirring debate on social media. Many readers fault Glukhovsky, who has lived outside Russia since 2022, for judging those who stayed so harshly while he himself is relatively safe. Literary critic Liza Birger examines whom Glukhovsky condemns, and why.
Warning: This article, like Glukhovsky’s novel, contains profanity.
In 1920, Nadezhda Teffi published the story “Ke fer?” (“What to Do?”) in the first issue of the Parisian émigré newspaper Posledniye Novosti. Amid snippets of Parisian conversation, she described a bewildered Russian general emerging onto the Place de la Concorde and repeating: “All this, gentlemen, is very well, of course. Very well indeed. But que faire? What do we do?”
More than a century later, Glukhovsky has written “Registration,” in which “What do we do?” again becomes the prevailing tone — merciless and deeply bitter. Beyond the painful bewilderment of the present day, there is real horror here, too: the story of an ordinary person turning into a monster.
Monsters have long been Glukhovsky’s central subject, well before he himself was cast as one in the eyes of Russian society: in October 2022, he was added to the “foreign agents” registry, and in 2023, he was sentenced in absentia to eight years in a penal colony for an antiwar Telegram post. No one has done more to find Stephen King–style everyday horror in Russian life.
Mutants inhabit a future subway system in “Metro 2033” (2002) — and, as history has shown, that was hardly the worst way things could turn out. In “Sumerki” (“Twilight,” 2007), an ancient Mayan curse creeps from the jungles of the Yucatán into a Moscow translator’s apartment. In “Tekst” (“Text,” 2017), the source of horror turns out to be an ordinary narcotics officer’s phone. And in “Post” (“The Outpost,” 2019–2021), madness crosses a bridge over the Volga, spread by the words of a “demonic prayer.” The only way to escape is to puncture your own eardrums — much as with Russian propaganda. The monsters almost always come from outside, while Moscow remains the center of the world — as though Glukhovsky cannot imagine it as a source of evil, though today we might argue otherwise. What frightens him much more is the horror and despair of the rest of Russia.
Stephen King wrote that a plot is a fossil waiting to be dug up, and that “we make up horrors to help us cope with the real ones.” Glukhovsky has found that in present-day Russia, there is no need to dig: monsters are literally around the corner. In this new world, we have to protect ourselves from ourselves above all.
“Registration” opens with a sketch of seemingly peaceful life in Vologda. Tatyana, whose son Sasha is a contract soldier, is getting their new apartment in order. While he is at the front, she uses his pay to cover the mortgage. Meanwhile, Sasha’s girlfriend Ulyana, a massage therapist at a small salon, vapes a strawberry-flavored e-cigarette with a friend (“Kristina laughed melon, Ulyana strawberry”) and dreams of the future: she has just learned that she is pregnant with Sasha’s child.
The opening pages are the novel’s best. Here Glukhovsky still has the energy to write beautifully: “Things grew orderly; things grew clean. Life was finally doing what Tatyana told it to. It obeyed her puffy, crimson hands, as if scalded, smoothing itself down and lining up in rows.” Later, horror displaces that beauty. Sasha, it turns out, has gone missing in the war. When he is found in a Moscow hospital without his legs, his mother and girlfriend begin fighting over the benefits while he is still alive.
So Ulyana travels from Vologda to Moscow. She urgently wants to marry Sasha because, with a child, she is entitled to two-thirds of the benefits. They face delays in registering their marriage, and someone demands a bribe. In Moscow, she stays with her aunt and uncle, Marina and Maksim, members of the city’s intelligentsia. Maksim runs a small bookstore beyond the Third Ring Road. He boldly keeps books by “foreign agents” on the shelves — until activists show up with prosecutors — reads Meduza through a VPN, and tries to keep his composure. Marina runs a decorating agency and takes contracts from the mayor’s office. To keep her business, she reluctantly puts portraits of “heroes of the special military operation” on bus stops for May 9. Their family has “crawled away” from the war. Their son Kirill has already gone to Georgia via the Verkhny Lars border crossing and come back because “it gets a little old,” and he keeps partying happily despite the draft summons hanging over him.
Bringing Moscow intellectuals and a massage therapist from Vologda together feels rather contrived. In real life, they are probably farther apart than the émigré writer is from his characters. But the contrivance lets Glukhovsky show a cross-section of society and leave no one in the story unstained. Émigrés come in for just as much criticism. Consider Kirill’s speech about how Muscovites brought Tbilisi “the best Moscow had to offer — matcha lattes, kink parties, and dog-walking services,” yet the Georgian capital still cannot measure up to the Russian one. Or Maksim’s school friend Mitya, who calls from Israel and says that once they dig all the “little Arabs” out of the tunnels in Gaza, there will be peace. “Isn’t that the same as what’s happening back home?” Maksim asks.
But gathering everyone in one place and giving each a line so no one remains innocent has a downside. For Glukhovsky, the world that willingly yields to evil and adjusts to it is, above all, a world of women. He does more than show how people adapt to evil: again and again, he shows women doing it faster and better. The picture is strange. Men started the war and men fight it, yet in Glukhovsky’s novel, it is mostly women who adapt to it, bargain, and inform on others. Women send men to war, too. And women are first in line for the benefits it brings.
Hi, I’m Vladislav Gorin.
I’m the host of Meduza’s daily Russian-language news podcast. This summer, the Russian authorities opened a criminal case against me — not for committing a crime, but for telling the truth about Russia and its war against Ukraine.
Because the Kremlin has branded me a criminal, I can’t go home. I also can’t safely travel to countries like Turkey — even though it’s a NATO member — because I could be arrested and extradited to Russia. I can’t even renew my passport at the consulate anymore.
None of this is going to stop me. I know there are hundreds of thousands of people in Russia who don’t want this war and who still believe in freedom and democracy, and they deserve access to independent journalism. Please support Meduza so I can keep reaching them.
Maksim, ever ready to discuss morality, “sniffed at it but ate anyway” — not always realizing that Marina’s city contracts largely supported the family. Eventually, he gives in, too, and takes books by his beloved “foreign agents” off the shelves: “Bykov and Ulitskaya gazed up at him from the box like kittens peering from the bottom of a bucket on their way to be drowned.” Sasha was a kind boy who felt sorry for slugs as a child. He went to war so no one, “not the cops, not anyone,” could “treat him like shit” anymore. But it is never entirely clear whether that was his own idea or whether his mother sent him to earn money. At the end, Tatyana remembers taking him to the military enlistment office and watching him look at her from the bus “as though it were a prank, as though any moment they’d call the whole thing off and let him go home for lunch.”
Men are “easy to transport by train,” Ulyana thinks when she sees a group of uniformed men of different ages at the station. “You can fit a lot in at once.” Tatyana’s husband Vitalya does little but grunt and wait for a drink to ease his hangover, and no one listens even when he tries to say something. In her fight for the benefits, Ulyana learns to use AI to write denunciations to the FSB and demands that her marriage to the dying Sasha be registered immediately. In the final scene, her transformation into a monster is complete.
“We’ll wait it out, we’ll sit tight, we’ll outlast them for sure. That one died, and this one will die too…” members of the underground scrawl on ads around the city in an act of covert defiance. “But will the people who make it through be the same people who hoped to wait it out?” Maksim wonders. That may be the most complete summary of “Registration.” The book is not really about the marriage registration Ulyana is pursuing. It is an urgent attempt to register — to record — the reality of waiting out the war, waiting for who knows what.
Nothing ages faster than language, which Glukhovsky has always treated as a key to making his work feel current and true to life. Yet his attempts to capture it do not always succeed. Tatyana’s Vologda habit of clearly pronouncing unstressed o’s, sayings like “dick-cunt-Dzhigurda,” and the endless Dovlatov and Bulgakov quotes Maksim seems to use in place of his own words already sound like relics of another time. “Registration” keeps reminding us that its events are happening right now — yet by the end, that “now” sounds a little like “yesterday.”
The decision to post the novel online seems driven by a need to join a conversation before it is too late, though that conversation is nearly over already. Glukhovsky himself tries not to see a divide between “those who left” and “those who stayed” — or, more precisely, any fundamental difference between them. But judging by readers’ first reactions, people inside Russia see the novel as an accusation, and an unfair one, precisely because they no longer recognize their country in this portrait.
Still, the novel should not be read as an accusation or a hatchet job. That is not what “Registration” is about. It is an émigré writer’s attempt to imagine life on the other side of Russia’s border. Is it hard to write a novel about Russia in the 2020s from afar? No harder than writing one about the 19th century or the year 2033. Besides, writers rarely leave home anyway; being away from the thick of events is perfectly normal for them. Whatever else it is, Glukhovsky wrote “Registration” to record and understand what is happening, not to condemn. The book is merciless to everyone, not just the so-called “stayers.” In interviews and essays, Glukhovsky often says “we,” repeating that evil can be found in each of us and that our defeat is collective.
That is also the subject of his book “My. Dnevnik padeniya” (“We: Diary of a Fall”), published by Vidim Books in 2024. It collects columns and essays dating back to 2012, along with retrospective commentary in which he sees them as telling the story of a catastrophe. “Registration,” too, is about any of “us” who tries to wait it out, look away, or somehow come to terms with the new reality. Estudio Zero shapes pink Mexican co-living complex after sound wave

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
