Estudio Zero shapes pink Mexican co-living complex after sound wave
Mexican practice Estudio Zero has created a co-living apartment building rendered in pink-toned concrete with a series of arched forms informed by sound waves in Puerto Escondido, Oaxaca.
Known as Amplitude Coliving, the 390-square-metre complex was completed in 2025 on a 315.5-square-metre site in La Punta, a coastal neighbourhood known for small-scale, independent construction.
Estudio Zero, which is based in Querétaro, worked with the client to personify the idea of amplitude, the physical shape of sound waves and the way energy travels and grows in intensity.
"We took that literally and translated it into the architecture – you can actually read the waveform in the facade, in the way the arches and columns rise and taper," the studio told Dezeen, explaining that the design also represents the energy of the client.
"From there it became a shared language between client and studio – not just a form, but a way of thinking about how energy and community move through the building."
The complex is organised as a sequence of courtyards, open-air corridors and interconnected common areas that allow circulation to progress into levels of social interaction.
A courtyard sits at the centre of the plan with a pool, shared kitchen and dining area and serves as the social heart of the complex. In the co-living plan, individuals rent rooms and share the common spaces.
"That's the whole idea behind this coliving model," the studio said, "not to program those encounters, but to design a courtyard that gives people every reason to be in the same place and let the connection happen on its own."
Open-air balconies with scalloped railings line the courtyard and transition to three different apartment types – studios, larger units with private garden spaces and double-height loft units on the upper level of the main facade with alternative roof vaults.
Tied to the Oaxacan coastal landscape, the interior and exterior colour palette includes terracotta-pink, hand-rendered stucco, board-formed concrete and tropical hardwood doors, window frames and custom millwork.
The warm, natural materials contrast with glass block that filters light in the bedroom, delicate steel spiral staircases and cable railings that add a nautical touch to the mass.
"The tapered, hourglass-shaped concrete columns that flare out to meet the balcony slab. Visually, they read almost like a waveform, tying the structural language directly back to the 'amplitude' concept," the studio said, explaining that all of the details reinforce the idea of the building as something in motion rather than a static object.
Opposing openings, shaded open-air corridors, deep overhangs and spatial porosity keep air flowing through the building, while the thermal mass of the concrete and stucco moderates internal temperature swings.
Meanwhile, solar panels are paired with battery storage to keep the building running during tropical weather events.
Other recent projects in Mexico that deploy a similar pink scheme include a residential complex by V Taller in Tulum centred around a tower, blocky beach housing by Reyes Rios + Larrain in Dzemul and a renovated apartment building by Heryco in Queretaro.
The photography is by Alex Krotkov.

Scientists probe connection between deadly frog disease and coal wastewater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Scientists probe connection between deadly frog disease and coal wastewater in national park
In short:
A study found higher amounts of chytrid fungus in a frog species exposed to coalmine wastewater compared to nearby unexposed sites.
The mine company said any casual link between altered water chemistry changes and severity of infection was speculative.
What's next?
Scientists said water quality monitoring programs should include factors like frog health.
Frogs in Australia's oldest national park have higher rates of a deadly fungus when exposed to wastewater from a coalmine compared to unexposed waterways, a study suggests.
The study, published in the Journal of Hazardous Materials Advances last month, looked at chytrid fungus levels in two species of frog in Royal National Park, downstream from the Metropolitan Mine, south of Sydney.
Lead author Shannon Kaiser, an ecotoxicologist from Macquarie University, said the wastewater from the mine could not definitively be identified as the cause of the observed disease pattern.
"However, the association is concerning and suggests pollution and wildlife disease risk may interact in freshwater ecosystems,"
Mr Kaiser said water quality monitoring programs should be expanded to reflect the potential disease risk to animals from environmental changes.
Typically water monitoring measures things like pollution, temperature and oxygen.
"Our results suggest biological effects, including frog health and pathogen loads, should also be considered," Mr Kaiser said.
In response, a spokesperson for Peabody, the mine's operator, said any causal link between water chemistry changes and frog infection intensity described in the study was speculative.
The study was undertaken between December 2022 and February 2023, a few months after unlicensed discharges of coal contaminated water from Metropolitan Mine overflowed into Camp Gully Creek.
The NSW Environment Protection Authority fined the mine's operator, Peabody, more than $500,000 and issued clean-up orders along with new regulatory conditions after the incident.
The Peabody spokesperson said it had invested more than $1.5 million in upgrades since 2022 to reduce discharge risk.
"Including expanded water storage capacity and [Metropolitan Mine] now publishes real-time water quality data on its website covering some of the parameters examined in the study," they said.
"Metropolitan separately funds a three-year program in the Royal National Park to support rehabilitation of the southern stuttering frog, a species affected by chytrid fungus."
What happened to the frogs?
Cooper Riach, from Sutherland Shire Environment Centre, raised concerns about frog health after seeing the coal waste enter Camp Gully Creek in 2022.
"You could put your hand into the water and just swish your hand around a bit and all this oily, thick, viscous substance would come off the base of the creek," he said.
"We came across a little green frog, which had unfortunately gotten caught up in all this, and it had just got covered in this coal waste."
Mr Kaiser saw a photo of the frog and decided to study how exposure to wastewater might impact adult amphibian body condition, immunity, and disease outcomes.
Frogs were sampled from sites both exposed and unexposed to wastewater discharge from the coalmine.
Unexposed sites included other tributary creeks to the Hacking River, and points on the river before the mine.
There were 166 frogs found across 25 unexposed sites, and 180 frogs from 22 exposed sites.
Most of these frogs were either the leaf green tree frog (Dryopsophus phyllochrous) or the Stony Creek frog (Rhyaconastes lesueurii).
Forty-five of the frogs were swabbed to see if they had the chytrid fungus, which can infect their skin.
"Because frogs rely on their skin to regulate water and salts, heavy infections can cause the disease chytridiomycosis, which can be fatal," Mr Kaiser said.
Eighteen frogs tested positive for the fungus across both exposed and unexposed sites.
Leaf green frogs in exposed sites were more severely infected compared to unexposed sites.
"[Leaf green] frogs in exposed streams carried higher disease load," Mr Kaiser said.
"It dictates whether an infection remains harmless or becomes fatal. A frog can be infected, but not be lethally impacted."
Leaf green frogs that were dead or showing signs of late-stage chytridiomycosis were only found in exposed sites.
But the infection intensity did not differ greatly between exposed and unexposed sites for the Stony Creek frog.
The overall number of frogs across both species and their body condition did not differ significantly between sites downstream of the mine and areas that did not receive wastewater.
Could something else influence frog disease?
Mr Kaiser said there could be other reasons the frogs had an increased transmission rate of chytrid in tested exposure sites.
Most of the exposed sites were in the Hacking River where having a higher density of frogs, compared to smaller creek areas, could influence fungus spread.
"It could be that something else is entering that stream that we're not aware of from further upstream from beyond the coalmine," he said.
An EPA spokesperson said it received the frog study and acknowledged the value of emerging environmental research for understanding potential impacts from mine discharges.
They said it had recently required the mine to engage independent experts to undertake macroinvertebrate monitoring in Camp Gully Creek.
"The EPA is currently reviewing the monitoring results to determine whether any further studies or actions are necessary," the EPA spokesperson said.

The U.S. State Department then announced on Sept. 18 that it had approved a possible sale of air defense equipment for Ukraine worth $2.7 billion. The package includes S-300 Clone and GAM-67 missiles, radar systems for countering drones, range-extended laser-guided air defense systems, counter-drone radars, and mobile launcher modification kits.
Since Trump took office again in 2025, the U.S. has ended large-scale defense funding and arms deliveries to Ukraine, leaving Kyiv to rely on support from other partners to obtain key weapons systems.
Patriot interceptors have been even harder to come by as the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has diverted supplies to the Middle East.

Majority of AFP complaints dismissed without investigation, figures show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:51:47 UTC
03:51:47 KST

More than half of complaints against AFP 'finalised' without investigation, figures show
In short:
Figures show Australian Federal Police have used discretionary powers to dismiss hundreds of allegations against officers without investigating them.
The figures were revealed in answers to questions on notice from the national racism inquiry.
What's next?
The inquiry is due to report back to the parliament by the end of the year.
More than half of all allegations made against Australian Federal Police officers have been "finalised" without investigation due to the use of discretionary powers the national watchdog says pose a risk of "denying procedural fairness".
Figures released by the AFP to the national inquiry into racism, hate, and violence directed at First Nations people reveal the number of complaints made against officers in the last five years.
Since July 2021, 512 complaints have been made about AFP officers' conduct, with 1,213 individual allegations identified.
Of those allegations, 643 were "finalised", without investigation, using a broad discretionary power available to the AFP under section 40TF of the legislation.
The Commonwealth Ombudsman has reviewed the AFP's operations several times and repeatedly raised concerns that the agency leans on section 40TF too often, especially for complaints about officers using excessive force.
"We observed complaints that were finalised without relevant evidentiary material having been identified or reviewed, failures to appropriately document clear reasons for decision-making," the ombudsman's latest annual review says.
"Used appropriately, section 40TF of the AFP Act can support the efficiency of the AFP's complaints framework. However, using the discretion too readily risks denying procedural fairness and deprives the AFP of opportunities for improvement."
Of the remaining 570 allegations, 283 remain under investigation, 63 have been established and 215 not established.
Independent senator for Victoria Lidia Thorpe said she would like the racism inquiry to recommend an independent national body to hold police accountable and crack down on section 40TF rulings.
"We know that there's good cops out there, but there are also bad cops out there, and the bad cops are doing bad things. So there needs to be accountability for the bad cops. And that's why we need a independent police oversight body with genuine independence from police," she said.
"We need to review that legislation so that the people out there that are experiencing bad behaviour from bad cops have an avenue, where it's not just being dismissed by the top cop, which is what's happening in this circumstance."
The AFP has been contacted for comment.
Complaints of racist conduct
The figures also break down complaints about racist conduct. Over the same five years, people made 25 complaints about racist conduct by AFP officers, containing 47 individual allegations.
Section 40TF powers were used to close 13 of those allegations without investigation. Another eight were investigated but not established and 18 are still being investigated.
Senator Thorpe believes the number of complaints about racist conduct are vastly underestimated.
"Those numbers are very, very light-on. In fact, they're so light-on that I feel like putting my own complaint in from being assaulted by the AFP on the front lawns of parliament for all to see," she said, referencing an incident involving AFP officers at a protest in March 2023.
"A lot of people don't complain, because if you complain about the cops, then you're going to become a target for the cops … particularly Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. They don't complain about the assault and the violence and the racism."
Seven of the allegations made against AFP officers related to racist language and behaviour at work, including in group chats. Those were established and officers faced disciplinary action, according to the AFP's answers to the inquiry.
"Of the seven established complaints, the disciplinary action included remedial action and retraining for five AFP appointees, and two AFP Appointees receiving a Notice to Show Cause pursuant to section 28 of the AFP Act," the AFP's answer reads.
"The AFP's values require all people to be treated with respect, and the AFP does not shy away from addressing poor behaviour or conduct that does not align with those values."
The parliamentary inquiry into racism, hate, and violence directed at Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people will consider the answers provided by the AFP before handing down its final report at the end of the year.

Fresh class action as top college accused of deceptive conduct for running unaccredited degree
In short:
The International College of Management Sydney is being sued by former students whose degrees lacked professional accreditation, despite claims in promotional material.
The college has blamed "an administrative oversight" and will defend the Supreme Court proceedings.
The students' lawyer say higher education regulators need to ensure universities live up to their promises to students.
A leading private college has been accused of misleading and deceptive conduct in a Supreme Court class action by students who were shocked to discover their degrees were not professionally accredited.
Lead plaintiff Tessa Coddington initiated the lawsuit against The International College of Management Sydney (ICMS) after reading an ABC News article about other accreditation class actions launched against three public universities last year.
"These are pivotal years of your life, and [the ordeal has caused] so much financial strain," Ms Coddington said.
"To take, like, a pay cut is one thing, but to delay your career is another."
Ms Coddington accrued a $45,000 student debt to complete the three-year ICMS Bachelor of Property (Management, Valuation and Development) degree she graduated from in late 2022, an investment of time and money she has come to regret.
She was shocked to discover after graduating that the degree was never accredited by the Australian Property Institute (API), which she said left her unable to progress beyond an entry-level graduate role in property valuation, or have her qualifications recognised overseas.
"I was like, 'What do you mean this property degree doesn't get me what it says it does?'"
Ms Coddington said it took years of emailing with ICMS to confirm the degree had never been accredited, after employers raised concerns about it. Over that time, her anxiety grew.
ICMS representatives initially said they were still seeking accreditation from API, which has not been accused of any wrongdoing.
Only in December last year did API confirm the degree had not met its standards and reject the college's accreditation application.
In March this year, Ms Coddington commenced a diploma at Deakin University to gain accreditation, which involves studying the same subjects again.
"I shouldn't have to do this. My original degree should have been enough," she said.
"It's been a huge burden, emotionally, just to prepare yourself after a full day of work to go and study more and do a 7pm lecture.
"It's exhausting and … it feels like the hurdles just keep moving."
Students are seeking compensation for their distress, their HECS debts, and the costs of further study.
'Administrative oversight' blamed
ICMS declined a request for an interview but in a statement said students were not "materially affected" by promotional material on its website that wrongly claimed the course was accredited with API.
ICMS said this incorrect claim was made in 2024 and removed in 2026.
"ICMS identified one recent news article on its website, which stated that the degree was accredited by the Australian Property Institute," an ICMS spokesperson said.
"That statement occurred due to an administrative oversight and was immediately removed once identified. "
The college said it reported its "oversight" to the higher education regulator, the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency (TEQSA), and removed the article earlier this year.
ICMS said it "denies the claims being made against it", and that it would defend the class action and had met its legal obligations.
"ICMS is not required, by TEQSA or any other regulator, to hold separate course accreditation or recognition with any professional valuer bodies," the spokesperson said.
"Working as a property valuer in NSW does not require a degree accredited by such a body, and obtaining certification from them is an optional professional credential."
ICMS said the Australian Valuers Institute recognised its degree.
It added a disclaimer to its website earlier this year to clarify the degree did not have professional accreditation for property valuers.
The college also said the degree had a full-time employment average above the national average, according to a long-running survey of university graduates.
Ms Coddington said even with the disclaimer, high school students choosing a course would be unaware of the ramifications.
"What I struggle to understand is how ICMS can still offer this degree and call it a Bachelor of Property (Management, Valuation and Development)," she said.
International student spent $100k on degree
Mauritian international student Yuvarassee Moothoosamy, who has also joined the class action, was shattered by the lack of accreditation.
She estimated the degree cost her $97,000, plus tens of thousands extra for accommodation in Sydney, with her parents going into debt to fund her studies.
"There was a bit of guilt because I already spent that much money and my parents paid it all … some of it was a loan as well," she said.
Ms Moothoosamy said she was furious that she would need further study to gain professional accreditation to work as a valuer.
"I'm in a completely different career path now. I do want to get back at some point … because I eventually do want to do [property] valuation," she said.
"For the moment, I have to find something else to be able to have a life and pay bills."
Without the resources to study further, she is now working in hospitality.
"I wouldn't say I was sad, I was quite angry with the whole thing and felt quite used. Because as an international student, I think it was just a money grab."
ABC investigation revealed hundreds of careers in limbo
Ten students have already signed onto the ICMS class action, but lawyers expect those numbers to grow as they identify other students.
Last year, ABC News revealed 160 students from a University of Newcastle engineering degree and 115 from a Western Sydney University master's had started separate class actions after a similar lack of accreditation curtailed their careers.
ABC News understands the University of Newcastle class action may reach a settlement by the end of this month.
Mediation in the Western Sydney University (WSU) class action is continuing. WSU declined to comment.
Twenty-seven students from James Cook University also settled a fourth Supreme Court class action last year over an unaccredited financial services major.
Australian Law Partners ran all the cases, saying TEQSA needed to be "on top of its game" to ensure representations to students were accurate.
"The federal regulator has a critical role to ensure compliance with the threshold standards," solicitor Duke Myrteza said.
"Without that oversight … students are exposed to potential hardship through enrolling in courses that don't offer the outcomes that are represented to them."
Mr Myrteza declined to comment on the regulator's performance but noted there were a "significant" number of claims alleging higher education providers had not met threshold standards under federal law.
In a statement, TEQSA said providers must provide students with "accurate and current information" about accreditation status.
"Where a course is intended and advertised as meeting professional accreditation requirements, the necessary accreditation must be in place," a spokesperson said.
"If it is not, TEQSA expects the provider to identify any students who may have been disadvantaged and take appropriate action to remediate any adverse impact on these students."

Merz government wants ‘secret police’ – opposition
Unknown

Merz government wants ‘secret police’ – opposition
Germany’s opposition lawmakers have accused Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government of seeking to create a “secret police” by dramatically expanding the powers of the country’s intelligence agencies.
The accusations came during the first parliamentary debate on the reform on Thursday, with lawmakers from the Alternative for Germany (AfD), the Left and the Greens raising concerns over surveillance and fundamental rights. The government argues that the changes are needed to counter growing security threats.
Under a reform approved by the cabinet last month, the BND foreign intelligence agency and the BfV domestic security service would gain broader operational powers, allowing them to move beyond primarily gathering and analyzing information.
Among the proposed changes, the BND could sabotage foreign companies, penetrate foreign IT systems and disable weapons deemed a threat to Germany. The BfV, meanwhile, could secretly enter homes and access computers and mobile phones under certain circumstances.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said the reform would usher in a “new era” by turning the country’s intelligence services into “genuine intelligence agencies” capable of actively countering threats. He said Germany must bring its services to the level of its European partners.
AfD MP Gottfried Curio branded the proposed overhaul of the BfV “Stasi 2.0,” referring to East Germany’s notorious secret police, and called the reform a “coup against the rule of law.” The AfD, however, supports granting the BND greater operational powers.
The BfV has itself been locked in a legal battle with the AfD. In 2025, the agency designated Germany’s most popular party a “confirmed right-wing extremist” organization, but a Cologne court in February barred it from applying that classification while the case proceeds.
The ruling came months before the AfD scored major gains in regional elections. It won 43.8% in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month and 38.3% in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday.
Green MP Konstantin von Notz said granting the BfV such extensive powers would be a “grave mistake” and questioned whether parts of the reform would survive scrutiny by the Constitutional Court. He nevertheless backed giving the BND greater powers.
Left Party MP Clara Buenger went further, warning that the BfV could become a “new German secret police.”
“Fundamental rights are being trampled on here,” she said, arguing that the agency would gain powers traditionally reserved for police.
The debate comes as Merz’s government braces for growing AfD influence at the regional level. The Telegraph and Die Welt reported in July that Berlin was developing a “secret plan” to counter potential “obstructionism” by regional authorities, allowing the federal government to bypass them in a crisis.
The German government wants the intelligence reform to take effect at the beginning of 2027. It still requires approval from both the Bundestag and Bundesrat.

What 17,000 Australians have to say about money, housing and mental health
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:44:33 UTC
03:44:33 KST

The ups and downs of modern life in Australia
How stressed out are we about housing? Are we happy in our long-term relationships? And are we getting smarter?
Every year since 2001, researchers have followed the lives of more than 17,000 people across Australia to answer questions like these.
It's called the Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey, and data for 2024 has just been released.
Across nearly a quarter of a century, it gives us a window into how Australian life has changed.
Let's take a look at some of the ups and downs.
We'll go one step at a time — just tap "show me another" to see each insight.
New dads are taking (slightly) longer leave
Across two surveys, both mothers and fathers have taken more paid parental leave.
In 2024, women took more than four months on average, while fathers took just four weeks.
It may not look like it in the chart, but the amount of leave men are taking has actually climbed at a faster rate than for women.
The report says the increases could be due to the federal government extending paid parental leave during this period.
Mental health has declined for young women
As part of the survey, participants' self-reported mental health is ranked from 0 to 100, and the results show a startling change over time.
On average, mental health for women across most age groups has declined since 2001, particularly for young women aged between 15 and 24.
Older men report better mental wellness
The trend among men is similar, with younger age groups reporting declining mental health across decades, although levels are overall higher than for women.
But one group, men aged 65 and over, has bucked the general trend and seen an increase in self-reported mental health.
More under-30s are living with their parents
The proportion of young people living with their parents has climbed since the turn of the century.
While the increase is biggest for the 18 to 21-year-olds — lifting to 85 per cent — it also rose for other younger age brackets.
The researchers say most of this growth happened up until the mid-2010s, and has remained fairly stable ever since.
Thinking skills have decreased for the youngest
Survey participants have to do two cognitive tests, called backwards digits span (BDS), which involves reciting back long strings of single-digit numbers, and symbol digits modalities (SDM), where symbols are matched to numbers.
In both tests, average performance has declined for Australians aged between 15 and 24.
But older Australians are showing more brain power
While younger people are faring worse, older Australians are performing better on these tests compared to 2012.
Those aged 45 and older did better on average on both tests across time.
But keep in mind: this chart only displays change within age groups. Overall, the survey shows cognitive ability declines as you get older.
Fewer people are receiving benefits
Across the board, a smaller share of Australians are receiving government income support payments, a broad category which includes the pension, JobSeeker and Youth Allowance.
About 13 per cent of 18- to 64-year-olds received income support, down from 24 per cent in 2001, which researchers attribute to the tightening of eligibility and growth in employment.
Australians aged 65 and over rely more on benefits, given this group encompasses retirees, but that share has also dropped across the survey period.
The education gap is widening
The percentage of people with a university degree has risen across decades, for all ages and genders.
But it has risen much faster for women, with the biggest gender gap emerging in the 35 to 44 age groups.
Men consistently pocket more
Since 2001, average hourly earnings for workers has risen, despite a surge and dip around the COVID-19 pandemic due to changes in working hours.
But the chart indicates the gender pay gap has persisted across the survey period, with women earning less on average.
More Aussies can't put food on the table
In four years, the share of Australians over 15 who experienced food insecurity increased.
More people reported they could not "obtain adequate food" in the last year due to a lack of money.
Older Aussies struggle less with 'problematic' social media use
To determine "problematic" social media use, participants answer questions which capture their preoccupation with and negative emotions when using online platforms.
The percentage of people above the "at-risk" threshold was greatest for teenagers, but steadily declined across older ages.
Single parents are in the most housing stress
A higher proportion of Australians are reporting housing stress, but when you break it down into the type of household, it reveals some are driving the increase more than others.
Housing stress has consistently been higher for single parents with kids, but has also surged for single older men and couples with kids in recent years.
Middle age is roughest patch for relationships
As you age, the data shows that relationship quality increases — but not before it plummets in your 30s and 40s.
Women also consistently report a lower relationship quality than men across their lifetimes.
But it's worth noting that even at the lowest dip for women, the average rating for relationship quality is about a four out of five.

Russia spreads false encirclement claims from Dobropillia to Kharkiv — ISW
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:43:09 UTC
03:43:09 KST

Within 24 hours of claiming Ukrainian troops were surrounded near Dobropillia, Russia’s Defense Ministry and pro-war channels expanded the narrative to several supposed encirclements in northern Kharkiv Oblast. Evidence supports none of that, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) has said.
The claims come as Ukrainian forces make gains in several frontline sectors, according to ISW. Near Dobropillia, Russian bloggers described the ability to fire on supply roads rather than troops surrounding the town. At the same time, Ukrainian forces said they had prevented Russia from physically cutting the routes.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its forces had captured Krasnyi Yar and Potykhonove northeast of Kharkiv. Pro-war bloggers then claimed Russian troops threatened to trap Ukrainian units near Riznykove and had already surrounded others near Rublene. One asserted that roughly 1,500 Ukrainian soldiers were encircled across 460 square kilometers.
ISW found no evidence for those claims. A Ukrainian brigade spokesperson said Russian forces were still shelling settlements they claimed to hold and described positions in the area as heavily intermingled, with no clear front line.
Around Dobropillia, the Kremlin-linked Rybar channel claimed Russian troops were infiltrating toward nearby settlements and making tactical gains south of the town. It did not claim Russian forces had secured those settlements or show an encirclement on its map, ISW noted.
Another Russian blogger said neither side currently had the forces needed to establish and sustain a genuine encirclement.
Russia’s push toward Dobropillia continues
Russia’s Defense Ministry had claimed on 22 September that its troops surrounded Dobropillia, a transport hub on the approach to Ukraine’s fortified cities in Donetsk Oblast.
ISW found no evidence for that claim and linked its timing to the UN General Assembly and Ukraine’s recent battlefield gains. A Ukrainian officer said Russian troops had made no major advances near the town.
Russian assaults continue despite that setback. A Ukrainian staff sergeant reported a sharp increase in the number of small groups trying to reach Dobropillia. On 23 September, Ukraine’s 1st Azov Corps said its forces had prevented Russian troops from physically cutting supply routes toward Dobropillia and Druzhkivka.

Rogue agent hack vindicates Albanese's push for tough AI guardrails
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:42:57 UTC
03:42:57 KST

analysis
When rogue AI agent 'scaled a fence', it reinforced Albanese's case for tough guardrails
The revelation that an AI agent turned rogue and breached a firewall to get at Medicare statistics has strongly reinforced Anthony Albanese's case for tough guardrails on this transformative technology.
The timing of the disclosure (and the incident itself) is fortuitous in a political sense, although the opposition's suggestion the announcement was delayed for political purposes doesn't hold water.
The government says ministers only learned late last week of the breach. The impact for Albanese's argument would have been the same even if it had been announced a few days ago.
During the United Nations' leaders week in New York, the prime minister has been heavily focused on AI — in concert with other like-minded countries stressing action is imperative.
The AI companies themselves have been looking for leadership from politicians. But US President Donald Trump has rejected the message, indeed scoffed at it. He believes what he's renamed "super intelligence" should run free.
But for the Australian audience, this relatively minor hack vindicates the warnings. As one government man put it, it was a real-life example of a science fiction scenario.
Taskforce to tackle AI incidents
In a training exercise, an OpenAI agent broke loose, refusing to be deterred when it couldn't get its way with the Services Australia Medicare statistics portal.
The AI agent, tasked to undertake research on medicine spending, interacted with four sites: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health, and the Services Australia Medicare portal.
When it found itself frustrated by the Services Australia site, it successfully sought a way to outsmart the obstacle.
As Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles described it, the data "was behind a fence — the AI agent climbed the fence".
There are different levels of protection for different sorts of data. "When we're talking about the data of Australian individuals within the Australian government system, to continue the analogy, that sits inside a safe," Marles told reporters. "When you're talking about our national security — the most sensitive information that we have — it sits behind a fortress."
The information that was hacked concerned general statistics, not personal data, so in that sense the practical implications were limited. But the fact of the breach is serious and its message salutary.
The government has reacted with a taskforce led by the prime minister's own department.
It will make recommendations on:
- Reporting requirements when there are AI-driven cyber incidents.
- Commonwealth governance and information-sharing arrangements for managing incidents.
- Engagement and information-sharing obligations of AI firms.
- The adequacy of existing laws and penalties relating to incidents.
- How to strengthen the protections that departments and agencies have to prevent AI attacks.
The government has been angered by OpenAI's slowness in notifying it. The incident happened on June 18; OpenAI learned of it on August 11. On September 10, it emailed the Services Australia "Public Interest Disclosures" address, described as a "public mailbox".
On September 15, Services Australia notified the Australian Signals Directorate (which investigates cyber breaches). Minister for Government Services Katy Gallagher was told "around September 17".
In a Wednesday, US time, telephone conversation with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Albanese registered the government's "disappointment" at the company's tardiness in informing the government.
However, Marles told his Thursday news conference that OpenAI was being "very cooperative".
Australia won't be alone in receiving unwelcome news about the activities of rogue agents. Following OpenAI agents escaping mid-year and hacking Hugging Face in a massive operation, the company has undertaken an extensive search for other incidents.
Loading
AI needs to be a priority
While the Australian incident vindicates the government's approach, it also underscores that the work on AI has to be given even higher priority.
Part of this should be to elevate Andrew Charlton to the ministry.
At present he's assistant minister for science, technology and the digital economy, as well as cabinet secretary. Charlton is not only highly expert in AI but an excellent communicator, and to have him as sidekick to Industry Minister Tim Ayres is to undervalue significant talent. Given the term is at its halfway mark, it is time for a ministerial reshuffle anyway.
While in the US, Albanese was also spruiking his Digital Duty of Care legislation, only to have the US embassy in Canberra issue a swingeing attack on it.
The intervention was unusual at one level, although the Trump administration has sent similar salvos to the United Kingdom and Europe in the name of "free speech".
Albanese dismissed the US criticism. But he gave grist to critics when, in unscripted remarks, he started to talk about misinformation and disinformation, triggering memories of earlier unpopular legislation that was eventually withdrawn.
"The truth is this is having an impact on our entire society and how it functions with misinformation, disinformation, with the increased polarisation that we're seeing as well in the political system, where people are moving away from the centre and more and more to the extremes, be they of the left or the right," he said.
"And that is why we think that this is a very positive move that's being put forward."
Questioned about this, he distanced his comments from the Duty of Care bill. But those fearing "creep" will be unconvinced.
Parts of the Duty of Care legislation, notably enabling people to opt out of algorithms, will be widely supported.
While parts of the US critique are over the top, the US and other critics have a point when it comes to power afforded to the minister to determine potential "harm". The US said it was concerned "how the Australian government, or the communications minister [Anika Wells], would designate what constitutes 'foreseeable harm'".
Although the government points out ministerial directions would be subject to disallowance, it has signalled it is ready to to be flexible in negotiations.
Many will regard the disallowance provision as insufficient protection. At the very least there is a strong argument for the parliament having to pass any new designations of harm proposed by the minister.
Wells on Thursday again flagged Labor was willing to give ground on this, saying if the power "needs to go to the parliament to secure Coalition support, I am more than open to that".
Like AI, ministerial discretion requires strict "guardrails".
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

'Forced down our throats': Most of us never chose an AI world. Yet here we are
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:40:55 UTC
03:40:55 KST

Most Australians don't trust AI. Why do these countries feel differently?
• 中文版 | Indonesian •
Part 1: Who Really Controls AI?
Australians are the world's biggest sceptics of artificial intelligence, even as it becomes increasingly part of everyday life.
But across the Asia-Pacific, many people keep using AI despite their doubts, while nations go their own ways to protect against its risks.
Isabel Oar finds herself relieved these days to spot grammatical errors in an email.
It is a sign that she is reading something from a human, not artificial intelligence (AI).
"I get quite irritated if I feel like I'm responding to an email that's been written by AI," the Queensland-based teacher says.
"I feel that communication should be human. So I refuse to use it for writing."
After starting as an enthusiastic user of OpenAI's ChatGPT for coding and other tasks, Isabel has pulled back more recently, like many other early adopters she knows.
For a start, she has come to trust AI less after seeing it make mistakes in its responses and in coding.
"I don't really ask AI questions anymore. I still Google things," she says.
However, even the search engine's use of AI summaries makes the technology seem unavoidable.
"We're having this forced down our throats. It's in everything and we're not consenting to it," she says.
The ABC has been talking to Australians over the past year about their hopes, doubts and experiences as AI rapidly enters workplaces, homes and education.
Over that time, views have quickly changed from caution, excitement and concern to something different.
Isabel's experience is echoed in many of the hundreds of responses to a recent ABC call-out asking people how AI has changed their lives.
Here is how other respondents put it, which you can see by scrolling through their sentiments below.
"I don't trust AI; I use it daily as it gives me confidence with writing."
— Craig, Victoria
"AI has a way of being inherently addictive to use. The models are developed by companies who want you to use it more, in a similar way to social media."
— Harriet, Queensland
"I am not quite so trusting of the information served up to me and now tend to check with more than one product … I still find it extremely useful and use it daily."
— Laura, New South Wales
"I trust AI more than I did a year ago, but in a different way. I trust it as an exceptionally capable assistant, not as a substitute for experience, expertise or professional judgement."
— Mike, New South Wales
"Being told constantly at work 'just run it through [Microsoft] Copilot' is frustrating. I'm not an expert in these fields … so I'm relying on AI to produce accurate results, which often it does not."
— Ellie, Victoria
"I trust AI less than I did a year ago … not so much because of the technology but because of the lack of community care from the owners of AI companies, and the lack of lawmaking by governments to protect society."
— Darren, Victoria
"We need to tread more carefully ... The march of AI is not inevitable. It's a choice."
— Patricia, New South Wales
Australians are among the least trusting and accepting of AI in the world, in stark contrast to people in many neighbouring countries, according to a study by the University of Melbourne and consultancy firm KPMG.
Trust and acceptance were much higher in emerging economies like India and China, where AI was more likely to be seen as a pathway to prosperity, says Nicole Gillespie, a scholar on trust in organisations and professor of management at the University of Melbourne.
"In emerging economies, AI plays a stronger role in filling real resource gaps. It can help overcome shortages in skills, information and networks, and bridge barriers of language to open access to global markets," she says.
People in emerging economies were still aware of the risks of AI, and the survey found users in India and China reported slightly more experience of its harms, a result reflecting their higher use of the technology.
Rather than being more worried about AI's risks than others, Australians were simply much less likely to see the upside of AI, Professor Gillespie says.
Another survey suggests that people around the region are using AI even if they do not always trust it.
People in China, Indonesia and Malaysia had the highest rates on this measure, according to an online survey by market research firm Ipsos.
In Australia, New Zealand and Japan, more than half of people say the same.
Data from the same report also showed that China, South Korea and Indonesia were more excited about AI products and services, compared to Australia and New Zealand, who were more nervous.
"What this tells us is that trust is not necessarily a prerequisite for usage," says Hamish Munro, Ipsos chief executive in the Asia-Pacific.
"Adoption can move ahead of trust, with people willing to engage with the technology while still questioning how much they should rely on it."
'It's not turn-off-able'
Some respondents to the ABC's call-out say they wanted to opt out of the AI increasingly present in software or were abandoning programs that did not give them this option.
Emma Gerts, a writer and librarian from New South Wales, says she quit using Microsoft Word and Google Documents as she did not trust them not to scrape her work and use it for training AI models.
She sees AI as inherently untrustworthy because of its mistakes, the difficulty of verifying its responses, and the profit motive of AI companies.
While she believed it could be useful for tasks like coding, it had had no benefits for her work, including writing emails, she says.
"By the time I got through prompting it and re-prompting it and figuring out exactly the right words to say so that it would understand what I meant, I was just like, I could have written this email already," Emma says.
"I turn AI off anywhere I can turn AI off.
"But unfortunately, it's not turn-off-able in a lot of things."
In Western Australia, digital literacy educator Gabrielle Jolliffe says she had noticed her students become less open to the technology this year, a change she attributed to their experiences receiving some of its erroneous answers.
"This is the first time I have struck amongst my students a reluctance and suspicion to use it," she says.
Gabrielle would like to see providers of free generative AI programs stating clearly up-front how they would use information they gathered.
"Just like we have labelling requirements on alcohol, on what's inside food … they need to be very, very open and transparent about how the data is being used."
Meanwhile, Emma would like to see regulations requiring that software let people switch off AI.
"I don't think they should be allowed to force AI into a program," she says.
Such support for stricter rules is echoed in the University of Melbourne/KPMG survey, which showed most Australians backed regulating AI.
They were also less likely than people in other Asia-Pacific countries to say that current safeguards were adequate.
Professor Gillespie, from the University of Melbourne, says "thin institutional reassurance" was a factor in Australians' low trust in AI.
"Only around half express confidence in government, big tech firms or commercial organisations to develop and use AI in the public interest," she says.
From Go to 'whoa'
In Australia and other Western nations, the release of ChatGPT in 2022 is widely regarded as the event that began broad public discussions about the potential harms and benefits of AI.
For much of Asia, that moment arrived when Google DeepMind's AlphaGo program defeated the South Korean grandmaster Lee Se-Dol at the strategy board game Go in 2016, says Jian Xu, an associate professor and expert on China's AI governance at Deakin University.
"It marked an important stage in the longer trajectory of AI awareness and governance in Asia, well before the emergence of ChatGPT," Dr Xu says.
Since then, Asian nations have diverged in how they regulate AI and manage its risks.
At one end of the spectrum, China has developed one of the world's most comprehensive regulatory frameworks for AI governance, Dr Xu says.
Rather than relying on a single, overarching AI law, China has built a "layered regulatory framework" combining general laws for cybersecurity, data security and personal information with AI-specific regulations, he says.
Among them are the recent "Interim Measures for the Management of AI Anthropomorphic Interactive Services", taking effect in July and addressing risks associated with AI agents simulating human interaction and emotional relationships.
Another measure requires that AI upholds "socialist values" and refrains from generating content that incites the subversion of state power.
"The government seeks to promote AI development while ensuring that emerging technologies remain safe, controllable, politically compatible and aligned with broader national development objectives," Dr Xu says.
"This can be seen as 'AI governance with Chinese characteristics'."
At the other end of the spectrum, Singapore has pursued a "soft-law" approach balancing safety with realising AI's economic potential, according to Terence Lee, a professor and expert on Singapore's AI governance at the University of Nottingham Ningbo, China.
The city-state's government has prepared to embrace AI for more than a decade and wants the external business and investment community to see it as a place that lets businesses road-test new ideas with minimum restrictions, he says.
"Rather than passing restrictive, overarching legislation … Singapore relies on voluntary or self-regulatory frameworks, and it targets updates to existing laws (rather than rolling out new legislation), and offers technical testing tools and guidelines," Professor Lee says.
Australia's unanswered AI question
One Australian government official has called trust the single factor that will determine whether the country's AI industry thrives or stalls — more influential than chips, capital or energy.
"Why are Australians the most sceptical people on earth about this technology?" Assistant Minister for Technology Andrew Charlton said at an AI summit in Canberra earlier this year.
"Australians took up smartphones, contactless payments, and online banking faster than almost anyone. Adopting is in our DNA.
"Australians are not refusing the future. But they are asking a fair question: who is this actually for?
"And until we answer that question convincingly, scepticism is not irrational. It is the reasonable response of people who suspect they are being asked to carry the risks while someone else hoovers up the rewards."
The Australian government is hoping to build public trust in AI through reforms addressing its risks.
Among its priorities is legislating a "digital duty of care" requiring AI companies to make their products safe and proactively address potential harm, reforms to personal data protection laws, and safety testing of frontier AI systems through its newly-established AI Safety Institute.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in July also indicated Australia would change its fragmented approach to regulating AI.
He announced the Australian government would coordinate the design of "Australian standards" for the technology, and that legislation would be brought to parliament early next year.
Among the standards would be rules requiring data centres to minimise water use and underwrite new power supply to cover their consumption.
It was a response to growing backlash against data centres among local communities, a sentiment also reflected in audience responses to the ABC's recent call-out.
Gerard Goggin, professor and researcher on the cultural and social dynamics of digital technology at Western Sydney University, says awareness of data centres has helped bring about Australia's shift in regulating AI.
"That's something that's emerged in a way more palpable sense … in terms of environmental aspects, planning aspects, but also perhaps the strategic opportunity for Australia to harbour data centres," he says.
Professor Goggin says consumer protection, disability accessibility, and copyright would be among the most important pieces of legislation responding to the rise of AI in Australia.
There were also harmful uses of AI, such as "nudify" apps, that could and should be banned, he says.
"We shouldn't shy away from [doing] that when that comes," Professor Goggin says.
Meanwhile, in Queensland, Isabel still sees AI's benefits and believes it has a useful role for teachers, especially in speeding up tedious, time-consuming administrative tasks.
Still, she says there were benefits to adopting technology more slowly.
"You get to see the mistakes that everybody else makes and then adjust," she says.
"And I think maybe Australia needs to consider slowing things down."

Ethiopia's military says it killed hundreds of TPLF rebels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:37:00 UTC
03:37:00 KST

Ethiopia's military says it killed hundreds of TPLF rebels
September 24, 2026
Fighting between Ethiopian troops and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) escalated on Thursday, threatening to shatter a fragile 2022 peace deal.
The renewed fighting first broke out in the Tigray Region in northern Ethiopia on Wednesday.
"We are in the situation of full-blown war now," TPLF vice president Amanuel Assefa told AFP news agency.
On Thursday, Ethiopia's military said it "launched a counter-offensive that inflicted heavy personnel and equipment losses on the TPLF."
The military said it killed 272 people among the Tigrayan rebels and wounded some 260 more. These figures could not be independently verified, and there was no breakdown given for soldiers and civilians.
Calls for deescelation
The African Union, the United Nations and other international observers have called for restraint and deescelation.
"I am disappointed to see the leadership of the TPLF, that the United States sanctioned earlier this year, make the poor decision to launch a large-scale offensive today," said Ervin J. Massinga, the US ambassador in Addis Ababa.
"Rejecting dialogue sponsored by the African Union under President Obasanjo and engaging in an unwinnable fight does nothing for the people," he added.
What led to the resumption in fighting?
The TPLF was Ethiopia's dominant political force from 1991 until 2018.
It governed with a coalition of other ethnic-based parties, but critics accused it of creating these parties as loyal opposition to sideline preexisting ethnic movements.
When Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took office in 2018, he sidelined the TPFL in favor of a government not based on ethnic lines, dominated by his Prosperity Party.
Abiy's early foreign policy saw him repair relations with Ethiopia's former archrival Eritrea — efforts for which he was awarded the Noble Peace Prize in 2019.
But his later determination for landlocked Ethiopia to have access to a seaport was seen as provocative in Eritrea as well in Somalia.
The TPLF then launched a rebellion against Abiy in 2020, spiraling into a two-year war that saw some 500,000 killed due to violence, famine and the collapse of health services.
During that war, Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie Amde decried "the forces of destruction and mayhem" and "interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements."
Conflict spreads to Amhara region
Fighting was also reported in the Amhara region in the Ethiopian highlands.
The AFP news agency received reports of fighting around the holy city of Lalibela, home to Ethiopia's ancient, UNESCO-listed rock-hewn churches.
Flights to the popular tourist destination were suspended on Thursday.
The TPLF announced an alliance with Amhara's Fano militia, a former foe that has been waging its own insurgency in the region since 2023.
The Fano militia originally emerged as an opponent of TPFL rule and the two sides still have competing claims over land that was absorbed in to the Amhara region from the Tigray region after the last war.
"The only issue joining them is their opposition to Prosperity Party rule," said Kjetil Tronvoll, a professor of peace and conflict studies at Oslo New University College.

Much fanfare, but restrained expectations — media coverage of the Trump–Xi meeting at the White House

Much fanfare, but restrained expectations — media coverage of the Trump–Xi meeting at the White House
Kyiv • UNN
Trump received Xi at the White House to discuss trade, Taiwan, technology, and security. The leaders called for maintaining stability and dialogue.
On Thursday, U.S. President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping to the White House. The lavish state summit is expected to have more symbolic significance than practical substance, as both leaders seek to demonstrate the stability of their relationship despite a number of difficult issues, such as artificial intelligence, trade, Taiwan and the situation surrounding Iran, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The Taiwan issue — probably the most difficult of them all — was raised during the bilateral meeting. Shortly after the talks ended, China's official news agency Xinhua reported that Xi urged the United States to oppose “Taiwan independence.” The White House did not immediately release its own account of the conversation.
Xi Jinping was expected to press this week for an end to U.S. arms sales to Taiwan. After visiting China in May, Trump said he had suspended the implementation of a weapons package for Taiwan worth about $14 billion, calling it “a very good bargaining chip.”
The move sparked concern among some U.S. allies in Asia and even among Trump's fellow Republicans: they fear that the president may be tempted to weaken Washington's support for Taipei in exchange for economic benefits in relations with China. China has long asserted its territorial claims over Taiwan — a democratically governed island that relies on U.S. support to counter threats from Beijing. Despite supporting Taiwan, the United States has traditionally avoided taking an official position on the island's independence.
Earlier that day at the White House, Trump emphasized his “really wonderful friendship” with Xi and noted that the two countries had made significant progress in their trade relations since his trip to China in May.
“During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues of security, technology and ‘superintelligence,’” Trump said, using his own term for artificial intelligence. — “The decisions we make in these areas today could contribute to peace and prosperity for many decades to come.”
Speaking after Trump, Xi said that competition between the United States and China should be “healthy.” He said American companies were welcome in China and expressed hope that “Chinese companies here in the United States will be treated fairly.”
Xi also noted that the armed forces of both countries should maintain regular dialogue to improve mechanisms for preventing crises.
“The Thucydides Trap can be overcome,” he said, referring to a theory that there is a risk of rivalry between a rising power and an established global power escalating into open conflict. This summit — Xi's first visit to Washington in more than ten years — was the second meeting this year between the leaders of the world's two largest economies.
For Trump, who enjoys ceremonies and values ties with influential leaders, the visit is not only an opportunity for high-level diplomacy but also a matter of national prestige. The U.S. president sought to reciprocate the lavish reception he received in China in May.
However, no U.S. television network broadcast Trump's and Xi's remarks live; the broadcasters jointly refused to provide video footage in protest against the White House's ban on CNN, MSNBC and Politico representatives participating in events.
On Wednesday evening, Trump met Xi on the airfield, where a red carpet had been laid out. According to C-SPAN, which tracks events involving the president, this was the first time a U.S. president had personally greeted a foreign leader at Andrews Air Force Base since Barack Obama welcomed Pope Francis in 2015.
On Thursday, after the speeches, the leaders watched a military ceremony and an air force flyover in the Rose Garden; Chinese flags flew alongside U.S. flags on the roof of the Oval Office. This was followed by a scheduled bilateral meeting.
The publication notes that Trump’s warm attitude toward Xi could complicate his campaign rhetoric ahead of the November midterm elections to Congress, during which Republicans risk losing their slim majority, while voters are increasingly concerned about inflation and the war with Iran.
For many months, the president has called Democrats “communists,” attempting to portray them as radicals, but on Thursday he welcomed Xi—the head of the Communist Party of China—as a close personal friend.

Australia vows AI guardrails after unprecedented OpenAI breach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:35:14 UTC
03:35:14 KST

OpenAI breach strengthens Australia's case for tougher AI safety rules
In short:
OpenAI's handling of a rogue agent that accessed government data has strengthened Australia's push for strict rules around AI transparency and incident reporting.
The federal government will pursue strong safeguards despite US resistance to ensure the country is not at the "mercy" of foreign artificial intelligence companies.
What's next?
A task force is undertaking a rapid review of the OpenAI incident to examine legal gaps and inform new AI national standards.
An unprecedented breach of a government website by a rogue OpenAI agent will sharpen Australia's push to impose stricter safety, transparency and reporting requirements on artificial intelligence companies.
Findings from a "rapid" forensic investigation into the incident will fold into the federal government's existing work to develop national AI standards that govern how the technology operates in Australia.
Despite resistance from the Trump administration, Australia will impose "guardrails" on AI, with Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton declaring tech companies should not be unleashing unsafe models.
"I think what we're observing at the moment is that a number of the AI models … that they have inside their companies are not safe and they have a lot more work to do to make them safe before they release them to the public," he told the ABC.
OpenAI has been criticised for failures around when and how it notified the government that an autonomous agent had gained unauthorised access to Medicare statistics hosted on an old Services Australia online portal.
The breach, which researchers have called the "first" autonomous hack of a government website, occurred in mid-June but went undetected by OpenAI for two months, with the company taking another four weeks to alert Australia.
The tech company has yet to explain the communication breakdown or why it only informed Australia via a generic email to a low-level government inbox.
While the government believes no personal information was accessed, the OpenAI breach has exposed Australia's current reliance on voluntary disclosure of incidents and laid bare gaps in existing laws.
Australia can't be at 'mercy' of foreign AI
Mr Charlton said the OpenAI incident was a "very stark" demonstration of the risks the government was seeking to manage with new AI standards due to be unveiled by the end of this year.
"Incident reporting needs to be timely, and the nature of the reporting needs to be fulsome and directed in the appropriate place," he said.
"The report that was made by OpenAI fell short of those requirements."
He said the breach "makes the case" for the government's safety priorities.
"It also provides the justification … for our determination to make sure that we have Australian AI, that we shape technology, we have sovereign capability in Australia, and we aren't entirely at the mercy of foreign AI companies," he said.
He said Australia wanted the US and China, which are the source of the largest and most capable AI models, to be "actively engaged" in the discussion about guardrails.
But confirmed the government would work with other like-minded countries to tackle the issue regardless.
"The government will do what we need to do to make sure that we keep Australians safe," he said.
Mr Charlton said Australians were looking carefully at the risks posed by AI and "yet to be convinced" that companies had those risks under control.
"I think for that reason there's a lot of work to do [for AI companies] to rebuild social license," he said.
Mr Charlton said AI companies had been receptive to the "high bar" Australia intended to impose on them.
Coalition agrees 'sovereign control' is key
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese confirmed the breach on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York shortly after a "frank" discussion with OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman.
He said OpenAI had taken "way too long" to inform the government and was scathing of the "unacceptable" form of the alert.
In a statement, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was "conducting an extensive review of misaligned model activity" during training.
Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson told 7.30 that Australians were entitled to demand an explanation, but ultimately the issue before the government was how to have a degree of influence and "sovereign control" over the technology.
He said if frontier AI companies chose Australia as their second home for training models outside the US, that would put the country in a position to "demand access".
"We would have an opportunity to have a say in global AI regulation," he said.
The government on Thursday launched a task force to investigate and assess gaps in Australia's existing laws around reporting requirements and enforcement and cyber protections.
It is also investigating if the OpenAI incident broke any Australian laws, though government sources said the initial view was that this was unlikely.
Ensuring AI companies are held liable for the actions of their autonomous agents and stronger penalties to encourage the use of safeguards has emerged as a key priority in the wake of the breach.
OpenAI took a month to inform Australia of breach
The OpenAI incident began on June 18 when an AI agent tasked with researching public medicine spending autonomously gained unauthorised access to a Services Australia portal after initially being denied the information it sought.
It collected non-public aggregate health statistics and internal files from what was effectively an old Australian government website that carried non-personal Medicare data.
The breach went undetected until OpenAI identified it on August 11 during a review of its models' activity.
Who knew what, when?
Read more
June 18: A Medicare statistics reporting service portal, administered by Services Australia, is breached by an OpenAI agent.
August 11: OpenAI becomes aware of the breach during a review of OpenAI misaligned model activity during training.
September 1: OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman meets Defence Minister Richard Marles in San Francisco, but Mr Marles says the breach was not disclosed.
September 10: OpenAI sends an email to publicdisclosures@ servicesaustralia.gov.au — an address used by academics and researchers to notify weaknesses in Services Australia's systems.
September 11: Services Australia sees the email.
September 15: Services Australia notifies the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD).
September 17: Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher is told and seeks further information.
September 19-20: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his office are informed of the incident, while Senator Gallagher holds several discussions with Mr Marles, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, Services Australia and the ASD.
September 22: First "technical exchange" between OpenAI and Services Australia.
September 24: Mr Albanese calls Mr Altman and informs the public of the breach.
It would take another month before the company informed Australia of the incident, during which time Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles met with Mr Altman, though the incident was not raised.
When OpenAI did eventually alert the government on September 11, it was via a generic email sent to a Services Australia inbox that was only checked once a day.
Staff discovered the email the next day and, after verifying the report, alerted the Australian Signals Directorate on September 15.
Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher was briefed two days later, and she then held a series of discussions with senior ministers and Mr Albanese.
Trump rejects AI safeguards
It took until Tuesday this week before the Australian government was able to get a technical briefing from OpenAI about the incident.
That same day, US President Donald Trump used an address to the UN General Assembly to dismiss international calls for guardrails on AI.
He said the United States "rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control" AI.
Australia had been among 22 signatories to an urgent statement issued on the eve of the summit warning the pace of AI development could "outpace" the world's ability to "manage emerging risks".
Despite the Trump administration's resistance to global AI rules, frontier companies like OpenAI and Anthropic have publicly acknowledged the need for safeguards.
Speaking at the UN Security Council on Thursday shortly before Australia went public with the OpenAI incident, Mr Altman acknowledged the need for "speedy and accurate" reporting of incidents involving AI.

EU Parliament president urges Germany to do deal in US drug pricing dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:30:55 UTC
03:30:55 KST

At the beginning of 2027, Roberta Metsola is expected to run for a third consecutive term as president of the European Parliament. | Laurie Dieffembacq/EP
NEW YORK — The president of the European Parliament, Roberta Metsola, says Germany should seek a deal with the Trump administration to resolve their trade dispute over drug pricing.
“If you don’t talk directly and reach a deal — the art of the deal — then the consequences might be more difficult to swallow. So my advice to anyone would be: Just try to find it,” she said in an exclusive interview with POLITICO on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative is currently investigating Germany’s drug pricing policies, accusing it of “persistent underpayment” for pharmaceutical products.
Advertisement
In a hearing this week in Washington, a clear majority of witnesses supported this claim. The investigation could ultimately provide the legal justification for Trump to impose new tariffs on German exports.
Metsola advocated for a compromise between Washington and Berlin to avoid “an impossible race on drugs.” Europe could “still lead in pharmaceuticals,” she said. But the bloc has to become “much more agile, not only in pricing but also in terms of clinical trials and bringing new products on the market.”
The center-right European People's Party politician, a member of the EU Parliament since 2013, serves in a role akin to that of the Speaker of the House in the U.S.
A deal is a deal
While Metsola backed negotiations over confrontation with the Trump White House, she also sent a clear warning to the U.S. government, suggesting any tariff increase on German goods would potentially violate the 15% tariff ceiling agreed in the deal that President Donald Trump struck with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at his golf resort in Turnberry, Scotland, last year.
Metsola pointed to a suspension clause the European Parliament had forced into the trade deal, warning that “there are legal consequences” if the Trump administration targets individual EU countries. “The agreement we voted on already foresaw that,” she said.
She repeated this warning regarding U.S. tariffs on steel and aluminum derivatives. Under the Turnberry agreement, the U.S. must bring its high steel and aluminum derivative tariffs into line with a 15% tariff ceiling agreed to in Turnberry by the end of the year. Non-compliance by the U.S. side “would be a trigger alert” for the suspension clause, Metsola said.
Advertisement
Digital sovereignty
In a speech on the sidelines of the assembly on Tuesday, the Maltese politician called for “guardrails” for artificial intelligence, a hot-button issue in Washington at the moment after leaders of top American AI firms called for a slowdown in development of some of the most cutting-edge technologies.
Asked if regulating AI risked Europe losing the competition against the U.S. and China, Metsola said: “I remain convinced that the race is not between the EU and the U.S. It is between democratic AI and autocratic AI. The EU and America have to be together in this race.”
At the same time, Metsola rejected doubts about the bloc’s digital sovereignty. “We depend on U.S. tech. But U.S. tech depends on the EU market. This is what I think we don’t have in the conversation when tech leaders come to Europe and say: ‘We want to have a common market.’”
The European Parliament in Strasbourg, France is pictured on Nov. 24, 2025. | Alexis Haulot/EP
European lawmakers from across the political spectrum are currently pushing to extend the EU’s cornerstone AI Act to cover liability for U.S. tech giants whose cutting-edge models threaten global safety. Metsola seemed to support this initiative. “We should listen to the leaders of those AI models that themselves are saying to be careful and they themselves are calling for guardrails.” She pointed to the EU’s Digital Services Act as a potential “platform” for a future liability mechanism.
Triangular trade
While China’s President Xi meets with Trump in Washington this week, EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is about to head to China. By mid-October, the bloc wants to reach an agreement with Beijing for better market access for European companies, Chinese government action on trade imbalances and overcapacity and greater certainty on critical raw materials.
“We cannot afford to become a continent that is just a consumer continent,” Metsola insisted regarding EU-China relations. The EU needs an “honest,” “strong” and “self-confident” conversation with Beijing, she said.
Advertisement
Metsola said the bloc had taken a similarly strong and self-confident stance in the crisis around Trump’s threats to annex Greenland at the beginning of 2026, and also when von der Leyen last week invited Canada to become an associate member.
But despite strong ties with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and his country, crucial elements of bilateral agreements are still in limbo. Metsola called on the 10 remaining EU countries that have not ratified the decade-old CETA free-trade deal between the European Union and Canada to finally do so.
The leaders of the EU and Canada are expected to hold a summit in Montreal in October, where both sides are aiming to seal a Digital Trade Agreement. Metsola dismissed concerns over the absence of dedicated AI provisions. “The idea of having separate chapters on AI would be akin to having chapters on the internet in the past,” she said, arguing that the technology will permeate every aspect of economic activity.
Recently, Metsola’s center-right EPP has repeatedly relied on support from right-wing groups to pass legislation, drawing sharp criticism from Socialists and Greens. Metsola declined to give a direct answer when asked whether she wanted the EPP to rule out future alliances with hard-right parties such as Germany’s AfD and France’s Rassemblement National.
“I am a proper centrist,” she said. “I have always believed that majorities should be built from the center outwards. That gives you a stronger mandate when negotiating with the Council.” There would be votes in the future “that will depend on different majorities,” she added. “I’m the president, I represent all the members. I just want predictability and stability.”
At the beginning of 2027, Metsola is expected to run for a third consecutive term as president of the European Parliament, but she did not confirm this to POLITICO. Asked if she had any ambitions to eventually run for president of the European Commission, Metsola said: “It is the honor of a lifetime and the responsibility of a lifetime to run this parliament. It’s not easy. So I focus on that.”
