Sun, sand and headphones: new show extols ocean's healing power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Sea Stories celebrates ocean's transformative force at Newcastle's New Annual festival
In the pre-dawn half-light, people sit in chairs and on picnic blankets on the sand of Dixon Park beach in the coastal city of Newcastle.
Wearing headphones and gazing at the ocean, they are there for Sea Stories, an immersive aural work created by Melbourne theatre-maker Roslyn Oades for Newcastle's New Annual festival.
Each morning during the week-long festival, this communal listening experience unfolds as the sun slowly rises above the horizon.
"Everyone is watching the ocean … listening to this score that's designed to synchronise with the stages of sunrise," Oades tells ABC Arts.
A meditative blend of music, sound and storytelling, Sea Stories features the voices of a diverse selection of people — among them a retired coal miner, an Afghan refugee and a Paralympian — who share a love of the water.
"All the stories are about transformative experiences with the ocean," Oades says.
"It's a love-letter to the power of water, which people in Newcastle know a lot about."
Watching the coast wake up
The first iteration of Sea Stories appeared at Festival 2018 during the Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast.
Creating that work was a revelation for Oades, a self-described night owl who was surprised by the scene she encountered when she rose early to witness the beach come to life.
"It's so busy at that time," she says. "There were surfers pre-dawn and then the people with rowboats come out and the lifeguards are there and people are walking.
"It's like watching the East Coast wake up."
When New Annual director Tory Loudon invited Oades to make a Newcastle version of the work, she jumped at the chance.
"It's so wonderful as an artist to be able to revisit and refine a concept," Oades says.
Conscious of not being a local, Oades recruited associate artist Janie Gibson, a Novocastrian theatre-maker whose work Meet Me at the Baths appeared at the 2025 New Annual festival, to work on the project.
The pair had previously worked together, when Gibson performed in a 2008 production of Stories of Love and Hate, Oades's work about the Cronulla riots.
Oades entrusted Gibson with the crucial task of finding the right people to speak to and conducting the interviews, which Oades describes as a "very targeted" process.
She also partnered with sound designers Michael Toisuta and Bob Scott, the latter working with Oades on several audio projects over the years, including The Nightline, which had a recent run at Melbourne's Malthouse Theatre, and The Enormous Radio, set to premiere at the 2026 Melbourne Fringe.
Local musician Christopher Sutherland, who performs as Abhaya Sky, provided the title music.
Oades emphasises the collaborative nature of her work.
"I really believe there's no such thing as a genius in the arts," she says.
"It takes a village to make a work, no matter what the marketing tells you. It's very much a team effort."
Stories of resilience
Sea Stories features the firsthand accounts of six people demonstrating, in different ways, the transformative power of water.
Two years after her leg was amputated following a fall from a fifth-storey balcony, Monique Murphy won a silver medal swimming for Australia at the 2016 Rio Paralympics.
"Swimming helped her find herself again," Oades says.
The first time Afghan refugee Arwin Arwin saw the ocean, he was boarding a boat to come to Australia.
"He couldn't even swim or have a life jacket. He had to tie himself to a mast," Oades says. "Now he sits on the coast and looks back at the ocean."
Coal miner Joe Clayton started ocean swim club Newcastle Sandrays seven years ago.
"His story is about the power of community — you just keep turning up," Oades says. "He created this whole beautiful swimming group."
The work opens with Jeanette Lacey, a palliative care nurse at John Hunter Hospital who found herself struggling in her role.
Worn down by the hospital system and considering a career change, she made an appointment to see a psychologist.
While she waited for the appointment, she cast around for other potential strategies to improve her mental health.
She landed on ocean swimming, setting herself a challenge to swim in the ocean every day for a month.
It was no small undertaking for Lacey, who had always feared the water.
But much to her surprise, she soon conquered her fear. "She became completely addicted," Oades says.
By the time the scheduled appointment came around, Lacey found she didn't need it.
"The ocean had helped her reset," Oades says.
"She actually loves working with dying people. She's really good at it. It's just the hospital system was really hard.
"But because she can now swim every morning, she's able to carry on with that work rather than quitting."
Healing from grief
The work also features the story of Ken Lambert, whose wife, former ABC presenter Jill Emberson, died from ovarian cancer in 2019.
"His story is one of healing," Oades says.
In the wake of Emberson's death, Lambert began going on what he called "grief runs" early in the morning.
"He'd run and then watch the sunrise and go home," Oades says.
One morning, his run took him to the Bogey Hole, an ocean bath built by convicts in 1819. Struck by the beautiful dawn scene before him, he dived into the water.
It was a restorative experience, and the Bogey Hole soon became a regular stop on his running route.
"He gradually started putting his life back together," Oades says.
"He joined a ukulele group and then he invited all those people to come to the Bogey Hole, too."
The group soon created a set of quasi-religious rituals to accompany their visits to the scenic swimming spot, making small offerings to the ocean and initiating new members in an irreverent ceremony involving silver hotpants and a swim.
"[His life] could never be the same without his love of Jill but he's found this other loving community," Oades says.
In the final story, Awabakal man Peter Gillam reflects on the paintings of Joseph Lycett, a convict artist who was jailed for forgery in Newcastle in 1815.
Lycett's paintings of the local Awabakal people were some of the first by a European artist depicting traditional Indigenous cultural practices.
"[Gillam] talks about them as being like a family album … putting back the missing pieces of the story of the Awabakal people," Oades says.
"He is also working with Elders to … revive language and he shares some beautiful words in Awabakal about the ocean.
"It's such a special Newcastle story to have woven in there."
Sea Stories is at New Annual from September 25 to October 2.

Monochrome magic to the allure of aluminium: The art of portraiture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

From aluminium to oils, how do you cut through on Portrait Artist of the Year?
From early Roman-Egyptian portraits to the modern-day selfie, people seem to have an enduring fascination with the human face.
"We are, by nature, really geared as humans towards recognising faces, and fascinated by them," says Robert Wellington, associate professor of Art History at Australian National University and a judge on ABC iview's Portrait Artist of the Year.
"It's a very human thing."
But what draws us to this art form and its many incarnations over the years?
We spoke to the semifinalists of Portrait Artist of the Year to find out.
Thomas Readett
Age: 33
Location: Adelaide, South Australia
Occupation: Mural artist
Medium: Oil and spray can
Thomas likes to work big. The Ngarrindjeri artist, born and raised on Kaurna country, specialises in large-scale murals and portraiture.
Playing with 3D illusions and conceptual spacing, Thomas also primarily works in monochrome. He trained using oil painting, but now mixes paints with aerosol. For his most special portraits, he uses a black paint made from peach pits that he says adds depth to the shade.
"One of the challenging things about working in monochrome is that you've got less to work with to capture the same amount of expression in your sitter, to capture the story," he says.
"You're restricting yourself … but for me it's what I really enjoy, that challenge of trying to capture the essence of somebody just using two colours."
A singer in a nu metal band called Falter, Thomas likes to blast heavy music when he paints.
Rendering a portrait of comedian, TV personality and writer John Safran in his heat, Thomas impressed the judges with his ability to combine the flair of street art with classical painting techniques.
"I'm loving the mash-up in Thomas's portrait," says judge and director of the National Portrait Gallery, Bree Pickering.
"It's giving me a little bit of a 90s poster vibe. But at the same time, the way that he's playing with light around the clouds is really harking back to an era of old portraiture."
Sidney Speirs
Age: 22
Location: Bathurst, NSW
Occupation: Optical assistant
Medium: Oil and acrylic paint
When Sidney saw how much art therapy helped her brothers, who both have autism, the born-and-raised Bathurst woman knew what she wanted to do.
While currently working as an optical assistant and painting in her spare time, her dream is to one day become an art therapist.
Her entry into PAOTY was the first time she'd completed a self-portrait, something she says was an "awkward but freeing experience".
"There was a freedom that came with viewing myself simply as a subject and not something to judge or improve upon," she says.
"To really lean into my fears and challenge them I chose to paint myself without makeup, in a position that isn't designed to flatter, but to show a piece of who I am."
Sidney's bright, photo-realist style impressed the judges, particularly that she renders her portraits without a grid, just using free drawing — something they say shows "an incredible level of skill".
"I'm reminded of the pop artist James Rosenquist and the way that he used these skills and tricks to show us something that looks like a photograph," says judge and art historian Robert Wellington.
"I wondered how this was made, I thought it might be airbrushing, but I look more closely and you can actually see the fine brush strokes. It's quite a feat."
Liz Gridley
Age: 37
Location: Melbourne, VIC
Occupation: Artist and art shop sales assistant
Medium: Oils on aluminium
Liz was working as a graphic designer in the city and hating it when she and her husband moved to regional Victoria for his work.
But the lower cost of living meant she could also spend more time on her art. She worked hard on developing a style she describes as "surreal realist – realism with some kookiness!"
A self-proclaimed gamer and pop culture nerd, Liz does live drawings at conventions, as well as working in an art supply store.
Using aluminium as a canvas is a shining point of difference in Liz’s work.
"Working on the aluminium gives it a very lovely glossy reflective surface," explains judge and award-winning artist Abdul Abdullah.
"When you apply paint to aluminium it creates beautiful transitions between colours. It's a really fun thing to do but it's hard, and Liz handled it really well."
Liz has had regular solo exhibitions and won many awards for her art, including the 2025 Summer Exhibition Winner at the Victorian Artists Society.
Winning her PAOTY heat with her luminous portrait of athlete Nedd Brockmann and his dog, Liz said the experience was "an adventure".
"I just got a quest!" she laughs.
"I'm so excited I get to paint again."
Jenny McCracken
Age: 59
Location: Central Coast, NSW
Occupation: Muralist, 3D illusionist, teacher
Medium: Acrylic paint
Jenny has been a working artist for more than 30 years, after failing art school, twice. Starting off designing menu boards for restaurants, she has gone on to dabble in murals, portraits, wildlife arts, 3D pavement art, trompe l'oeil (trick of the eye) paintings and sculptures.
She gets involved in her work; when she was a finalist in the 2000 Moran Portrait Prize, she built a brick wall for her painting to go on.
"I am a self-described art tart, 'cause I'll paint most things," she says.
After three decades in Melbourne, Jenny moved to a small NSW town in the bush, which has inspired her to focus more on being an "art-ivist", focusing on biodiversity and the environment.
Jenny won her heat with a charming portrait of Ellie Cole, incorporating the Paralympic swimmer's prosthetic leg with the teddy bear she brought as her special object.
Judge Bree Pickering says Jenny's work "just gives us this real moment of delight and deep storytelling".
Harley Kirkwood
Age: 47
Location: Newcastle, NSW
Occupation: Tattoo artist
Medium: Oils
Harley has never entered an art competition before, but his portrait work is known around the world.
He is a renowned tattooist, making his name in some of Hollywood's most iconic studios.
"Portrait tattoos are obviously very important to people," Harley explains, "Not many people go out and get a portrait of someone they don't like."
Despite his success, the self-taught painter has dreams of leaving his job in the tattoo studio and working full-time as an artist.
Judge Bree Pickering says his experience is obvious in his quick, detailed portraits.
"What we see from Harley is an ability to look at his sitter, draw things out and then just very simple flourishes that give us a lot of character in the painting."
He draws inspiration from his two kids, who write him notes and leave little drawings on his easel: "They give me a little bit of love to look at while I paint."
He was sure to bring some of the most special ones along to his PAOTY heat, where he dazzled the judges with his "accomplished" portrait of Baker Boy.
Jasmine 'Jazz' Lancaster Merton
Age: 17
Location: North Sydney, NSW
Occupation: High school student
Medium: Oil, wax, coloured pencil
The only art lessons that teenage artist Jazz has received are those in the classroom at her Northern Sydney high school.
The youngest competitor in this season of PAOTY, the 17-year-old has always adored drawing. She particularly loves drawing hands, saying they're her favourite feature on a person.
But the young artist is no stranger to competition: in 2025, Jazz won the Young Archie award with her self-portrait, 'My Name is Jazz'.
She uses both oil paints and coloured pencils, leaning into the pencils when she wants to work more quickly. It also allows her to play with cross-hatching and texture.
"I think that texture is always better than perfection and can create a greater sense of personality and detail in an artwork," she says, and the judges agreed, selecting her portrait of singer Casey Donovan as the winner of her heat.
"This is a young person that knows who they are as an artist and is just going to keep on developing," judge Bree Pickering says of Jazz.
In her final year of high school, Jazz hopes to continue studying art and work towards her first solo exhibition.
We've got a story for you. Stream the new season of Portrait Artist of the Year on ABC iview or watch Sundays at 7:30pm on ABC TV.

====================================================================================================

The start-up is just the excuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:29:42 UTC
03:29:42 KST

‘The start-up isn’t the goal,” said Gadi Bahat, founding director of the Leaders program at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. “The people are.”
It’s a deceptively simple distinction, but one that has shaped the program since its inception six years ago.
While many academic entrepreneurship initiatives operate as accelerators, bringing students together around promising business ideas in the hope of producing the next successful start-up, the Leaders program takes a different route. It operates as part of the university’s Yazamut 360 center, led by Dana Gavish and Prof. Carmel Sofer, whose joint vision has helped position entrepreneurship as a strategic pillar at BGU.
“We looked at the traditional model and said not every student wants to become a start-up founder,” Bahat recalled.
“Entrepreneurship is much more than creating companies. It’s a way of thinking, a mindset. It’s leadership combined with personal resilience. These are skills and personal qualities that today’s world demands, whether you launch a start-up or not.”
That philosophy has produced dozens of graduates who have carried those skills into industry, research, and the public sector.
It has also led to socially minded start-ups like ANNIE. Founded by Leaders alumni Ofek Eliasko, Idan Mizrahi, and Tal Ben-Lulu, the venture aims to improve the treatment of trauma casualties by connecting first responders, field medics, and hospitals through a real-time monitoring platform.
Like the Leaders program, the company’s origins are less about technology than about people.
“We didn’t focus on building a technological product,” Eliasko said. “We became passionate about solving a real human challenge.”
Bahat, in turn, never intended to work in academia. An electronics engineer with an MBA, he spent decades in Israel’s hi-tech industry, serving in senior executive positions at companies such as Comverse and Alvarion before leading two start-ups of his own.
Then came an unexpected phone call. A former colleague, BGU’s Sofer, asked him to step in for what was supposed to be a temporary assignment.
“I came for a few months, and I fell in love,” he laughed.
The value lies in doing
“We don’t teach entrepreneurship through theory,” Bahat explained. “We teach everything through practice.” 
That practical experience unfolds as what Bahat described as an entrepreneurial journey built on three pillars: entrepreneurial knowledge, personal skills, and hands-on work.
Students are divided into teams and asked to build start-ups together. But unlike a traditional accelerator, success is measured less by the company’s future than by the individual’s development.
“The start-up is the learning tool,” Bahat explained. “Students encounter obstacle after obstacle. Every time they overcome one, they’re building an entrepreneurial mindset.”
Only later, while completing his master’s thesis, did Bahat discover the academic terminology describing what he had intuitively built.
“It’s called incidental learning,” he said. “Students come to learn entrepreneurship, but along the way, they leave with far more and acquire a completely complementary set of skills.”
Those skills range from negotiation and public speaking to resilience and what Bahat calls “entrepreneurial agency,” the confidence and ability to drive change independently.
“You’re the engine,” he said. “That’s exactly what the market is looking for.”
That philosophy would eventually help shape one of the program’s most ambitious ventures. Eliasko and Mizrahi first met through Leaders, though their company took shape elsewhere.
Amid the war and the mass-casualty events that followed, Eliasko experienced an event that would eventually become the foundation of ANNIE.
“We witnessed a highly complicated medical evacuation following a mass casualty event,” he recalled. “Tragically, one person died, while another recovered.”
What he observed stayed with him long afterward. “As we later examined what had happened, it became clear that there were significant gaps in the way trauma casualties are managed and evacuated in the field.”
Rather than accepting those failures as inevitable, the pair began asking what technology could do differently.
The result became ANNIE – a platform combining wearable hardware and software that can monitor critical vital signs in real time and transmit them continuously from the point of injury through emergency dispatch centers and eventually to hospitals. 
Its ambition reaches beyond traditional emergency medicine.
“Our vision is for ANNIE to become as common as defibrillators,” Eliasko said. “Every rescue team, every disaster response unit, every emergency situation should have access to it. Ultimately, we want to integrate into existing emergency systems, not only in Israel but everywhere.”
Neither founder believes the company would exist without Leaders. “We actually built the foundations of ANNIE during the program,” Eliasko said.
“Leaders gave us a place to begin before we entered the real world.” Mizrahi agreed, arguing that the most valuable lessons had little to do with business models or investment pitches. “It challenged us professionally, but even more mentally,” he said.
Students were encouraged to leave the classroom, interview strangers, test assumptions, and, above all, make mistakes.
“Bahat always said, ‘Go wild,’” Mizrahi recalled. “‘There are no limits; take it wherever you want.’ We made plenty of mistakes, but we also succeeded.”
Some of the most lasting lessons had nothing to do with entrepreneurship.
“The academic degree doesn’t teach you how to stand in front of an audience in English,” Mizrahi said. “It doesn’t teach resilience. It doesn’t teach you how to communicate under pressure.”
Perhaps even more important were the relationships.
“We had incredible mentors,” Mizrahi noted, recalling his personal mentor, Yoram Yaacovi, a former Microsoft executive.
Beyond the BA
When asked how they fared once the program concluded, Mizrahi laughed. “Who says Leaders is over? Bahat still gets phone calls from us in the middle of the night.”
For the latter, those conversations are part of the program. “Students tell us this was one of the strongest experiences they’ve ever had,” he said. “And six years later they’re still using the tools.”
This ongoing connection is formalized through the Leaders Alumni Association. Upon completing the program, graduates join an exclusive, growing network of hundreds of alumni who hold highly sought-after positions across a wide range of industries. Through dedicated networking events and gatherings, the association ensures that the community continues to thrive, offering lifelong professional value, support, and collaboration opportunities long after the academic year ends.
This relationship has also shaped the program itself. Early cohorts were given almost complete independence, but after it proved overwhelming, changes were made so that every team is paired with alumni mentors.
“We threw them into the deep end,” Bahat admitted. “It was too much.”
Reflecting less on entrepreneurship than on humility, Bahat asserted that he has learned an enormous amount from his students. “If you’re open enough and humble enough, younger people will teach you far more than you expect.”
Eliasko offered similar advice to future participants. “Leaders is only a taste of the real world,” he said. “Push yourselves. Stay up late. Take yourselves to the limit. That’s where the real growth happens.”
Mizrahi is even more succinct. “It’s a place where you’re allowed to dream,” he said. “More importantly, it’s a place where you’re expected to make those dreams happen.”
Today, the program has also evolved alongside technology, with artificial intelligence becoming a growing part of the curriculum, and next year each student team will develop its own AI agents as collaborative teammates throughout the program.
Even so, those changes serve the same underlying objective. “The methodology changes; the person remains at the center,” Bahat said.
For a university program that insists start-ups are merely a means to an end, the emergence of ANNIE may seem like a remarkable success story. Bahat would probably disagree. The company, after all, is only evidence that the real experiment worked. The real product of Leaders isn’t a start-up, but the people capable of building one.
This article was written in cooperation with Ben-Gurion University.

Latvian DM tells 'Post': Israeli weapons are top-notch, I support its right to self-defense
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:29:40 UTC
03:29:40 KST

Israeli weapons are top-notch, and it has the right to self-defense, Latvian Defense Minister Raivis Melnis told The Jerusalem Post in an exclusive interview on Thursday.
Latvia currently faces a significant threat from drones spilling into its territory as a result of the Ukraine-Russia War.
Against the backdrop of the upcoming elections, with Latvia's general elections scheduled for October 3, 2026, the visit carries considerable weight; according to Israeli defense sources, Melnis has already said during the visit that Latvia is open not only to dialogue but also to action.
Latvia's key areas of interest were expected to be air defense and counter-drone systems.
During the visit, Melnis met with Defense Minister Israel Katz, Director-General Amir Baram, and top Israeli defense industry companies such as Rafael, Elbit, and Israel Aerospace Industries.
Melnis told the Post that Latvia is looking into "loitering systems and air defense systems" among other defense products.
Latvia looks to buy Iron Dome system
One system Latvia is exploring is Iron Dome, a top system for shooting down drones, such as those used by Russia, though to date the country has relied on a collective European security air defense architecture.
Another set of systems Latvia is exploring are anti-ballistic missile systems, where it is looking at a "wide spectrum" of options.
There have been reports that Israeli systems besides the Arrow can shoot down certain kinds of ballistic missiles, and those systems are much cheaper than the Arrow for smaller countries like Latvia.
He said they had "initiated those discussions, but we need to move fast. There is strong intent, and it would be very positive to get certain" air defense systems.
"We hope we will get these systems soon. Israeli systems are battle-proven, very high-end systems that have shown reliability during three years of war. Israeli companies provide systems for defending Israel, but also have the capacity to produce for different foreign partners. Israel has developed a really strong military industry," he noted.
Asked if moving fast meant three to five years, since many defense systems can even take 10 years to develop, he responded, "I hope it will take much less time than three years from the decision to the delivery. I hope for a much shorter time."
Next, he was asked whether he met with Israeli officials to obtain cyber-AI defense products to cope with the increasingly threatening cyber-AI attack posture facing the world.
According to Melnis, obtaining such AI defense products was not on the list of goals for this specific visit, "but our experts are looking at different additional new technologies to improve cyber capabilities."
He mainly focused on discussing the purchase of "loitering munitions [kamikaze drones], artillery, and radar systems." He said some Israeli products in this area are unmatched elsewhere.
Further, he said he would send additional Latvian military experts to learn more.
Moreover, he said he wanted to "learn from Israel's experience about how to protect borders, including from drones, missiles, proxy forces, and in cyberspace."
He affirmed that "Israeli advice and guidance, based on its battle experience, was very unique."
Melnis said he told Katz that the only two countries that have wide-ranging battlefield experience are Israel and Ukraine.
He added that Israel's experience in the defense arena went back decades, beyond even the intense last three years.
In addition, Melnis said the visit has "a political perspective. Our president and other officials have visited Israel. This deepens our political cooperation. We strongly support Israel's right to self-defense."
"We condemn Iranian attacks on Israel and support Israel's defense of its country and its people. Iran is an enemy not just for Israel, but also for the region, and for our friends in Ukraine where Iran is supporting Russia," he added.
Despite the NAZA film harming Israel's reputation across the globe, Melnis said that he wanted to "show solidarity – it is an honor to be here," adding he has not yet seen the film.
While the EU is boycotting Israel's settlements, Latvia wants to expand economic cooperation and friendship with Israel.
Melnis took office in May 2026, following the resignation of his predecessor generally presumed to be related to drone incursions into Latvian territory.
His visit follows two previous visits to Israel by the Head of Latvia's Procurement Department.
In recent years, according to foreign sources, Latvia has purchased Israeli arms and cyberware in several deals including Rafael's Spike missiles, worth around 200 million euros, Elbit's UT30 turret system,t and several contracts reportedly worth more than 600,000 euros to buy Cellebrite’s phone-hacking equipment and software.

IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir on Thursday called the arrival of Israel’s sixth submarine, the INS Drakon, a major step in strengthening the IDF’s capabilities during a ceremony at Haifa's naval base.
“Even these days, our eyes are open toward what is happening in Iran and among its proxies. The Iranian regime is hurt and wounded, but has not learned to change its intentions,” Zamir said at the ceremony.
“With the integration of the INS Drakon into the Navy, the Navy reaches improved maritime readiness and new heights in its capabilities and operational strength: more covert, farther-reaching, deeper and more lethal.”
Zamir added that Israel’s recent military achievements were “unprecedented,” citing operations against senior figures, strengthened defensive readiness, improved deterrence and expanded operational capabilities.
Herzog: 'INS Drakon' is a new chapter for Israel's Navy
President Isaac Herzog said the vessel represented a glimpse into the future of the Navy, and added that the submarine fleet would expand Israel's operational capabilities.
“Today, as we receive the INS Drakon into the ranks of the Navy, we look for a moment into the future,” Herzog said.
“The Drakon submarine joining the Navy today, like the additional submarines that will arrive after it, together reflect the bright future of the Navy. A future that means innovation, a future that means broader operational capabilities, a future that means immense power available to the State of Israel, more than ever before.
"Power that we will be able to use, and will not hesitate to use when necessary, even thousands of kilometers from Israel’s borders.”
Herzog said that in recent years, the Navy sailors and many others involved in the project had worked at the Kiel naval base in Germany.
“Over the past two years, Israeli Navy soldiers and many others connected to this enormous project worked at the Kiel port on German soil. Another almost unimaginable symbol,” he said.
“Eighty-one years since the terrible Holocaust, the nation-state of the Jewish people is building together with Germany the crown jewel of global defense engineering. At the same time, the State of Israel is not only importing security equipment from Germany, but is also exporting advanced defense systems to it, thereby contributing to the defense of all of Europe.”
Herzog thanked Zamir, Defense Minister Israel Katz, Ministry of Defense Director General Maj.-Gen. (res.) Amir Baram, Navy commanders and soldiers, and representatives of the German government and Thyssenkrupp for their roles in bringing the submarine into service.
Addressing the submarine crews, Herzog praised their work and said the arrival of the Drakon marked a new chapter in Israel’s naval capabilities.
“Above all, I want to thank you, the submarine fighters under the command of Cmdr. O. Two years of training and long weeks at sea have brought you here as heralds of a new chapter in Israel’s maritime strength,” he said.
“We hold in our hearts, with appreciation and pride, the memory of the 69 members of the Dakar crew, and send a comforting embrace to their families.”
He told the Drakon’s crew that the human element remained the decisive factor despite the submarine’s advanced technology.
“Today, when the Drakon submarine is entrusted to you, the fighters of the submarine flotilla, among the finest sons and daughters of Israeli society in all its diversity, we remember one clear principle: the person determines. The person operating the machine, whether it is the most advanced and expensive machine, is the one who will always bring victory and the ability to complete the mission in full,” Herzog said.
Herzog also referred to the legacy of the INS Dakar submarine, which disappeared in 1968 and whose crew of 69 sailors were lost.
“Even at this ceremony, especially at this ceremony, we remember well the painful journey of the Dakar submarine, whose name not only serves as inspiration for the Drakon submarine, but also represents the immense courage and strength of spirit that characterized its crew,” Herzog said.

Former England soccer star Wayne Rooney says grandma was Polish Jew during Auschwitz visit

2026-09-24
18:28:56 UTC
03:28:56 KST

Wayne Rooney, the former English soccer star, revealed that his maternal grandmother was a Polish Jew during a family visit to Auschwitz.
Speaking in his Disney+ documentary, The Real Rooneys, Rooney explained that he "recently found out my mum's mum, my nan, her family was Polish Jews."
“Technically, if that’s true, you’re actually Jewish,” a producer called from off camera. Judaism is passed down maternally, and given Rooney's heritage comes from his "mum's mum," the former soccer player is considered Jewish by Halacha (Jewish law).
"I'm Catholic, but I've always asked questions like, 'Why aren't we Jewish?'" Rooney responded.
He explained that his mother told him that his great-grandmother had fled Poland for Liverpool, adding that they thought her original surname was Greenburg.
The Rooneys visit Auschwitz at their 10-year-old's request
The announcement came during a family trip to Poland, where the family aimed to learn more about World War II for their son's school project.
“Kit really wanted to go,” Rooney's wife, Coleen, told the Guardian when asked whose idea the trip had been.
Rooney added, “It’s really important to learn about history, good and bad. Sometimes with your kids, you only want to tell them the good stuff, and I don’t think that’s good for them."
"I've watched a lot of documentaries on it, and you just wouldn't think human beings could do that to other human beings. It's crazy," he told his taxi driver on the way to the concentration camp.
Although his sons hadn't been to Auschwitz before, Rooney himself had visited with his England teammates during the 2012 Euros, which were held in Poland and Ukraine.
Jewish organizations respond to Rooney's announcement
Rooney could usurp Nick Blackman, the Blackburn Rovers player who is officially recognized as the first English-born Jewish player in the UK's Premier League.
Blackman debuted in 2009 while Rooney, who has subsequently discovered his Jewish heritage, debuted for Everton in 2002.
Blackman played for Israel's Maccabi Tel Aviv towards the twilight of his career.
However, Campaign Against Antisemitism (CAA), a UK-based charity dedicated to exposing and countering anti-Jewish hate, felt that Rooney's newfound history had bigger implications. In a statement on X/Twitter, CAA commented that "this news is a reminder that the idea that Jewish people are not sporty is a myth laced with antisemitic tropes about Jewish physical weakness."
"In fact, before the Second World War, Jewish people were at the pinnacle of European sport across a range of disciplines, including football," it added.
"It is taking time to rebuild that culture from the ashes of the Holocaust, and educate about how Jewish people and people with Jewish heritage have contributed, and continue to contribute to the world of sport."

Poet, author Yehuda Atlas passed away at age 89, Sourasky Medical Center announces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:28:52 UTC
03:28:52 KST

The Israeli author and poet Yehuda Atlas died on Thursday at the age of 89, Sourasky Medical Center's Ichilov Hospital in Tel Aviv announced.
"Yehuda was an eternal child until his last moments. In his life, he acted and worked for people out of emotion and a desire to help. He was an editor, children's writer, and translator, and in his last years he wrote about children at risk out of a sense of mission. May his memory be blessed," read the statement.
Atlas, one of the most recognizable and beloved authors in Hebrew children's literature, left behind a work that became an integral part of the childhood of several generations in Israel.
His most recognizable book, And This Child Is Me (Vehayeled Haze Hu Any), was published in 1977 and introduced readers the a child's world in simple, direct, everyday language as he grapples with parents, friends, shame, love, jealousy, and frustration.
In an interview with Walla Culture, Atlas revealed the principles of his writing: "I write briefly, simply, understandably, and to tell the truth."
An inflation in children's books
In the same interview, Atlas said that he believed there was an "inflation" in children's books, criticizing books that he described as trying to be too educational or therapeutic.
"Everything in our lives is a long process, and by the time you get close to describing the problem, you're at the end of the book," he said.
This is a developing story.

No More ‘Trump Avenue’: Canada’s Capital Moves to Rename Street Amid Tense Trade War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:27:50 UTC
03:27:50 KST

Ottawa's City Council voted unanimously on Wednesday to remove President Donald Trump’s name from a residential street in the Canadian capital amid an increasingly hostile trade war.
The motion to rename “Trump Avenue” in the city’s Central Park neighborhood was brought forward by River Ward councillor Riley Brockington on Sept. 9 and swiftly received support from other local officials. “I don't like the idea of anything that's named for Donald Trump, who's demonstrated hostility towards Canada,” Ottawa Mayor Mark Sutcliffe said at a news conference after the vote.
The move symbolizes the strained relations between the two countries, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney goes head-to-head with the Trump Administration in a trade standoff. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect on Sept. 8, matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. after negotiations collapsed last month. Trump’s repeated threats to annex Canada and his insistence on referring to it as the “51st state” have significantly contributed to the tensions.
The streets in Ottawa’s Central Park neighborhood were named after New York City institutions in the late 1990s and early 2000s, when Trump was primarily known for his businesses and real estate ventures, long before his political aspirations came to fruition.
Brockington said a consultation with local residents will now follow, with alternative names proposed for “Trump Avenue” ahead of a vote.
“I could speak at great length why I believe, strongly, it is time to rename ‘Trump Avenue,’ but I don't want to give a platform anymore to the person who is on the current street sign blades,” Brockington said. “I do believe this is about a new beginning, and I want this to be a community-led process where the community ultimately will select and recommend to City Council what that new name will be.”
In a statement to TIME, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly referred to the name change as a “meaningless gesture” and said “these local governments should do right by the citizens they serve, thank President Trump for defending their country, and make a good deal to benefit Canadian and American citizens alike.”
TIME has reached out to Ottawa's City Council for comment.
The vote to cut the street name comes after President Trump recently pushed through controversial renaming efforts of his own.
In late August, he signed an Executive Order renaming Lake Ontario, which borders the Canadian province of Ontario and the U.S. state of New York, as “Lake America.” The order applies to U.S. federal references of the lake and does not determine how Canada—or others—refer to the body of water. Several lawmakers across both countries have rejected the new moniker.
Thomas Juneau, a professor of public and international affairs at the University of Ottawa, says the street name change in Ottawa is “illustrative of the mood” of Canadians.
“Polls have repeatedly [shown] how extremely unpopular Trump is, and how his targeting of Canada on trade, and his trolling on social media, have made him and the U.S. unpopular,” he tells TIME.
A poll by Politico, conducted Sept. 13-15, found that 83% of Canadians thought it was wrong for Trump to impose tariffs on their country, while 71% backed Carney’s retaliatory tariffs. Another poll, conducted by Abacus Data between Sept. 4-9, found that 82% of Canadians had a negative impression of Trump.
Carney says he studied risk of U.S.-led military action amid annexation threats
In a new interview, Carney admitted he had prepared over the past 12 months or so for the “extreme tail risk” that Trump might order military action against Canada, amid the U.S. President’s repeated mentions of his desire to annex the country.
“I think you have a responsibility in these roles to look at extreme tail risk,” Carney told the New York Times. “That’s just risk management. That’s not a base case, but it would be irresponsible not to” prepare.
Juneau says the “risk of American military intervention against Canada is extremely low,” but reasons that just because Canada “shouldn't take [Trump’s] threat literally, it doesn't mean they shouldn't take it seriously.”
In an April 2025 interview with TIME, Trump denied he was “trolling” when discussing annexation. “We’re taking care of their military. We're taking care of every aspect of their lives… We don't need anything from Canada. And I say the only way this thing really works is for Canada to become a state,” he argued.
Carney, in line with other Canadian officials, has vehemently pushed back against the idea, stressing that Canada is “not for sale.” In June, after Trump revived talk of his ambitions to annex Canada, Ontario Premier Doug Ford simply stated “Canada will never be the 51st state.”
Despite the tensions, Carney said he and Trump have spoken “frequently” since trade talks collapsed last month. However, there is no clear path toward an end to the trade standoff.
“Trump is actively trying to choke off the Canadian economy," says Juneau, noting that a key sticking point in trade negotiations, according to Carney, has been Washington's efforts to restrict Canada’s ability to negotiate trade deals abroad.
Canada seeks international alliances to remove reliance on U.S.
The U.S. accounted for 72.5% of Canadian merchandise exports in 2025, according to the country’s annual trade report, making it Canada's largest trading partner by a wide margin.
Canada and the U.S. are also deeply integrated through defense arrangements, including their membership in NATO and the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD)—a bilateral defense and national security arrangement involving the shared defense of the continent.
Amid the strained relations with the Trump Administration, Carney has sought to diversify Canada’s trade and security alliances to reduce its reliance on the U.S.
“The weaponization of that interdependence by the U.S. makes [Canada] extremely vulnerable in a way that pretty much nobody else is,” insists Juneau, pointing to the urgency of Carney’s task.
The Canadian government has set itself a goal is to “double non-U.S. exports in the next decade” as it seeks to expand trade with other markets.
In January, Carney met Chinese President Xi Jinping to forge what he called a “new strategic partnership” to end Canada's economic reliance on the American market.
Canada is also currently in negotiations with India as it seeks to negotiate a new comprehensive economic partnership agreement with Delhi, and is in talks for a free trade agreement with the Philippines.
The diversification efforts extend into defensive measures. At the E.U.-Canada summit in June 2025, Canada established a new Security and Defense Partnership with the bloc. Canada later became the first non-European country to participate in the "Security Action for Europe” (SAFE) instrument, which provides low-interest loans to help member states purchase military and defense equipment.
Canada is seeking to further strengthen ties overseas by becoming the European Union’s first “associate member”—a goal European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has vowed to help make a reality. The proposed arrangement, the details of which have yet to be ironed out, would likely deepen cooperation on matters including trade, defense, AI, and Arctic security.
Carney made his pledge to E.U. lawmakers when he addressed the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Sept. 17. Touting closer ties with the bloc, he said “Europe and Canada are stronger together” and insisted "we are not fair-weather allies, we believe that our prosperity grows when it is shared."
Juneau warns that despite Carney’s current push to diversify trade and defense away from the U.S., the results of these deals may take a long time to truly stand up, as "in practice, diversifying trade and security relationships is measured in years and decades."

Russian Finance Ministry sets Hormuz opening scenario for $50/bbl oil price in budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:26:37 UTC
03:26:37 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Setting the base oil price in the budget at $50 per barrel means that the Russian Ministry of Finance is already factoring an open Strait of Hormuz scenario into its forecast, Igor Yushkov, an expert from the Financial University and the National Energy Security Fund, told TASS.
"The Ministry of Finance has taken a very conservative approach to assessing future oil and gas revenues, making it a bet on stability," the expert noted. "Essentially, the Ministry of Finance is now factoring in a Strait of Hormuz opening scenario to ensure it does not depend on this factor," he said.
The global oil market was highly volatile in 2026, Yushkov said. In January, the price of Russian Urals crude stood at $41 per barrel, but in March, following the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, it jumped to $77, after which prices fluctuated sharply amid Middle East instability.
The ministry in this connection is deliberately budgeting a rather low oil price to mitigate the risks of unexpected deficits and the need to revise the budget throughout the year, the expert added.

Average household utility rates in Russia are expected to rise 11% in July 2027, up from the 8.7% increase authorities previously projected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:22:27 UTC
03:22:27 KST

Average household utility rates in Russia are expected to rise 11% in July 2027, up from the 8.7% increase authorities previously projected
Russia’s Economic Development Ministry forecasts an average 11% increase in utility rates on July 1, 2027. It projects average increases of 8.6% on July 1, 2028, and 7.6% on July 1, 2029.
The figures are higher than the ministry’s earlier projections of 8.7% for 2027, 7.1% for 2028, and 6.1% for 2029, according to Faridaily. The ministry attributed the revisions to rising inflation and larger projected increases in gas and electricity rates.
The planned average utility rate increase of 9.9% on October 1, 2026, remains unchanged.
Shortly after the State Duma elections ended on September 20, Russian authorities announced plans to raise taxes. The Finance Ministry proposed taxing passive income, such as interest on bank deposits and dividends, at 13–22%, up from the current 13–15%. It also proposed immediately applying the maximum 22% value-added tax (VAT) rate to purchases from foreign online stores, though a phased increase had previously been discussed. A third proposal would impose a 100-ruble fee on parcels from abroad worth up to 200 euros, which are currently exempt from customs duties.

One dead after security forces open fire during Ebola burial in Congo, sources say
Sept 24 - One person was killed and several others wounded after security forces fired shots to contain unrest during the burial of a suspected Ebola victim in northeastern Congo on Thursday, two sources said.
• The incident occurred at Katula-Paida cemetery in Beni, a city in North Kivu province, which has recently seen a surge in Ebola infections.
• The burial team was preparing to bury the body in line with Ebola safety procedures when residents demanded to see the deceased, questioning whether the person had died of Ebola, according to a member of the Ebola response team in the city.
• Tensions escalated and security forces escorting the burial team opened fire as they sought to contain the unrest, the source said.
• At least one person was killed and several others were injured, according to the response team member and a health official who asked to remain anonymous.
• Investigations are underway to establish the full toll and circumstances of the incidents, two health officials said.
• The incident is the latest in a series of attacks on burial teams and other Ebola responders, underscoring persistent mistrust among the population.
• The outbreak, declared on May 15, has infected 7,820 people and killed 3,779, according to government data released on Wednesday. REUTERS

Russian-linked software sold to US government as CEO allegedly hid Russian control – two now arrested
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:20:08 UTC
03:20:08 KST

The US has arrested the CEO of Virginia-based digital forensics company Oxygen Forensics and a Russian national over allegations that they concealed the company’s Russian ownership and the fact that its software was developed in Russia while selling it to US government agencies, according to the US Justice Department.
The case highlights a potential route through which Russian-linked networks could seek access to sensitive US institutions: concealing Russian ownership and influence behind seemingly legitimate American companies.
Lee Reiber, 55, and Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov, 52, are charged with conspiracy to commit wire fraud. The US Justice Department alleges that five Russian nationals, including Davydov, owned and controlled Oxygen Forensics through a Cyprus-based holding company, while its software was developed by a team in Russia.
Software sold to US government agencies
According to the criminal complaint, Oxygen Forensics presented itself to US agencies as an independent American company with no foreign ownership or control.
The company sold digital forensic software used to recover and analyze data from electronic devices to the US Department of War and three Department of Homeland Security components: the Secret Service’s National Computer Forensics Institute, Homeland Security Investigations, and the DHS Office of Inspector General.
The National Computer Forensics Institute awarded Oxygen Forensics a five-year contract in September 2024. The award file included a certification from Reiber stating that the company had no immediate or highest-level owner, according to the affidavit.
The Justice Department alleges that this was false. The Russian owners allegedly continued to make significant company decisions, set Reiber’s compensation, control payments and retain signatory authority over bank accounts after their names were removed from public corporate filings.
Russian software development allegedly concealed
The complaint says the same five Russian nationals also owned a Russian company founded by Davydov in 2000, previously known as Oxygen Software and now called MKO Systems.
According to the affidavit, the Russian company developed the software used by Oxygen Forensics, with developers working in Russia under Davydov’s direction. MKO Systems also sold its software in Russia under different product names to customers that reportedly included the Federal Security Service (FSB), the Russian Investigative Committee and the Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs.
After the US expanded sanctions against Russia in 2022 following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Russian owners allegedly agreed with Reiber to conceal both the company’s ownership and its Russian development operations.
Reiber was installed as CEO, president and chairman in March 2022, while the Russian owners were removed from the company’s public filings, according to the Justice Department.
The complaint alleges that the arrangement did not end the Russian owners’ control. One of them was later appointed to the company’s board using a Turkish identity, according to the affidavit.
OSINT investigators had traced Russian software links
Militarnyi separately reported that OSINT investigators from InformNapalm had previously traced corporate and technological links between Oxygen Forensics and Russia’s Oxygen Software, now known as MKO Systems.
According to Militarnyi, the Russian company’s products were supplied to Russian security and law-enforcement agencies, including the FSB and Ministry of Internal Affairs. The investigation traced a common corporate and technological origin between the Russian and US software ecosystems.
CEO allegedly denied Russian involvement
The Justice Department says Reiber repeatedly certified to US authorities that the company had no foreign ownership or control.
In March 2026, he allegedly told DHS personnel that no Russian was involved in developing Oxygen Forensics’ software and that no one in Russia had access to its development environment. Days later, he published a statement saying the company had no development presence in any restricted jurisdiction.
The complaint alleges that the software was in fact written and managed by a team in Russia, using a cloud environment administered by one of the Russian owners.
The affidavit also describes a November 2023 exchange in which Reiber allegedly told the Russian owners that public reporting about the company’s Russian connections could jeopardize a pending US government contract.
Arrests and seizures
Reiber was arrested in Idaho on 20 September and released on bond after appearing in federal court. Davydov was arrested the same day at London Heathrow Airport before boarding a flight to Istanbul. The US says it will seek his extradition.
Separately, a federal judge authorized the seizure of Oxygen Forensics’ corporate bank accounts, around 57 domains and other cyber infrastructure allegedly used in the scheme. The domains and related infrastructure were seized on 20 September.
The case is being investigated by the US Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, with assistance from the Department of War Office of Inspector General’s Defense Criminal Investigative Service.
Each could face up to 20 years in federal prison if convicted.

Ethiopian army says 272 Tigrayan fighters killed as conflict escalates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:19:03 UTC
03:19:03 KST

Ethiopian army says 272 Tigrayan fighters killed in Amhara
Tigray People’s Liberation Front says in a ‘situation of full-blown war’ with Ethiopia’s government.
Ethiopia’s army says it has killed at least 272 fighters from the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) in a counter-offensive in the country’s northwest Amhara region.
The Ethiopian National Defence Force said on Thursday that another 260 Tigrayan fighters were wounded and several were captured.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Can Ethiopia’s seven-group rebel alliance challenge Abiy Ahmed?
- list 2 of 3Ethiopia warns of ‘destruction’ as Tigray rebels launch offensive
- list 3 of 3Fighting widens across Ethiopia as Tigray clashes escalate
“Government forces launched a counter-offensive that inflicted heavy personnel and equipment losses on the TPLF” after the group and its allies attacked several areas of North Wollo, a region of Amhara that borders Tigray, the army said in a statement on Facebook.
The intensification came days after TPLF and six other armed groups from across Ethiopia announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, which committed itself to removing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government.
The coalition brought together the newly-formed Amhara Fano National Movement, the Oromo Liberation Army and other movements from the Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz regional states.
‘Full-blown war’
“We are in the situation of full-blown war now,” TPLF Vice President Amanuel Assefa told AFP news agency on Thursday.
He confirmed that Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside local armed groups in Afar and Amhara.
The alliance marks a striking realignment that had been almost a year in the making, bringing together armed groups with very different histories and grievances against the central government, including forces with histories of conflict among themselves.
In a statement issued as the fighting widened on Wednesday, the alliance said the federal government was attacking its forces on several fronts and presented their response as part of the broader struggle that had brought the coalition together.
Meanwhile, the escalation has disrupted air travel, as Tigrayan forces seized three local airports in the region.
Flights to Lalibela, a UNESCO-listed site in Amhara known for its medieval rock-hewn churches, were suspended on Thursday, according to Reuters news agency.
AFP also received reports of fighting around Lalibela, causing its airport to close. The area has often been targeted by the Fano, a local armed group that is now operating alongside the TPLF.
Wider regional rivalries
TPLF last went to war with the Ethiopian federal government in 2020, leading to a devastating two-year conflict that ended with a peace deal in 2022.
In his address at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, Ethiopia’s President Taye Atske-Selassie Amde blamed the escalation on “the forces of destruction and mayhem” and “interference in our internal affairs by adversarial elements”.
He said Ethiopia had exercised “immense restraint” and made progress with its neighbours.
Analysts say the Tigray rebels have support from Eritrea, which fears landlocked Ethiopia is planning to invade its territory to gain access to the Red Sea.
The TPLF’s Assefa told AFP “we have no information about Eritrea’s plan”. Asked if they would request Eritrean intervention, he said: “Not yet.”
Ethiopia’s domestic conflicts are becoming harder to separate from wider rivalries in the Horn of Africa, particularly Addis Ababa’s deteriorating relationship with Eritrea and Sudan’s civil war.
Sudan’s army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan has visited Asmara twice since July for talks with Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki, while Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) commander Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, known as Hemedti, reportedly visited Addis Ababa in late August.

Ukraine war latest: Russia takes aim at Ukraine's internet infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:15:55 UTC
03:15:55 KST

Key developments on Sept. 24:
- Russia puts Ukraine's internet in its sights as attacks on Kyiv infrastructure intensify
- Polish Deputy PM says Starlink station fire possibly Russian sabotage
- Denmark warns Russia could escalate hybrid attacks against NATO in coming months
- Ukrainian drones attack Russia's Rostov Oblast, Krasnodar Krai, allegedly targeting oil depots
Russian strikes have hit multiple data centers and internet providers in Kyiv over the past two days, disrupting service for around 100,000 households as Moscow expands its attacks on Ukraine's internet infrastructure.
Ukraine's Digital Transformation Ministry said around 100,000 households in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast experienced internet problems following the Sept. 23 drone attack, as specialists worked to assess the damage and restore stable service.
"This is the beginning of a phase where, since September, they have started taking it out systematically," Anatolii Frolenkov, a representative of the 1-IX internet exchange point, told the Kyiv Independent.
Frolenkov added that attacks on Ukraine's communications infrastructure are not new, pointing to earlier strikes on energy and telecommunications networks. But the recent escalation of attacks on data centers and communication nodes marks a shift in intensity, he said.
Several providers reported direct damage to their infrastructure. UTELS reported damage to a Kyiv data center housing its core equipment, leaving it without power, while Pavutyna said one of its data centers was hit, causing outages for some customers.
Crazy Network said a strike damaged a central internet traffic exchange in Kyiv, disrupting internet and telephone services in the capital and in Vinnytsia and Khmelnytskyi oblasts.
The disruption continued into Sept. 24. Kyiv-based provider Etherlink said an attack damaged its main network node, knocking some customers offline and forcing the company to relocate the core of its network.
Other companies reported more extensive losses. Hosting provider MiroHost said the data center in Ukraine that housed its infrastructure was destroyed in the attack, company founder Oleksandr Olshansky told dev.ua. Around 90-95% of MiroHost customers use infrastructure outside Ukraine and were unaffected, he added.
CityHost also said equipment it stored at a Kyiv data center had been destroyed, disrupting some of its services.

Polish Deputy PM says Starlink station fire possibly Russian sabotage
A fire at a Starlink ground station in Poland may have been a deliberate attempt to disrupt internet access used by Ukrainian forces at the front, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told reporters on Sept. 24.
Gawkowski said there were indications that the fire at the station in Wola Krobowska, in Poland's Masovian Voivodeship, on the evening of Sept. 23, may have been an attempt to disrupt its operations.
The station is operated by the state-owned telecommunications company Exatel and serves as an internet hub that carries traffic through Poland, including to Ukraine, Gawkowski said.
He suggested Russia could be behind the incident, describing it as potentially part of Moscow's hybrid warfare. Polish authorities have not concluded their investigation into the incident.
He said a disruption could affect internet access for the Ukrainian military, potentially depriving Ukrainian forces of communications at the front.
On top of allowing flawless high-speed communications between combat positions and command posts, Starlink internet, when mounted on drones, allows for an almost unjammable connection not constrained by the limits of traditional radio antennas.
Over 2026, Ukrainian forces have found increasing success using Starlink-enabled drones over Russian-occupied territory, most notably in the "middle-strike" range (50-200 kilometers from the front line), where Russian logistics routes have been devastated by Ukrainian attacks.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk separately said on Sept. 24 that the circumstances of the fire "do not look good," while cautioning that it was too early to determine whether the incident was sabotage or an accident, Polish news agency PAP reported.

Denmark warns Russia could escalate hybrid attacks against NATO in coming months
Russia is likely to intensify its hybrid campaign against NATO and Western countries in the coming months, carrying out more frequent attacks with potentially greater consequences, Denmark's military intelligence service warned on Sept. 24.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said Russia had become increasingly willing to take risks as the security situation in Europe deteriorates.
"Russia will intensify its hybrid war by carrying out more frequent attacks against the West and NATO, with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past," the agency said in its latest threat assessment.
The attacks could include destructive cyber operations targeting critical infrastructure as well as sabotage carrying a significant risk of casualties, according to the assessment.
DDIS also warned of a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia, even while the war in Ukraine continues.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia's part" and could take place "in the coming months," the agency said.
Such an attack could involve isolated drone or missile strikes against infrastructure supporting Ukraine, with Russia potentially claiming that the weapons crossed into NATO territory because of Ukrainian electronic warfare, according to the assessment.
DDIS also said Russia could stage a false-flag attack using Ukrainian-made drones or deploy a limited number of troops, potentially without national insignia, into a NATO country bordering Russia.
At the same time, DDIS assessed that Russian President Vladimir Putin remains unlikely to compromise on Moscow's core war aims and may see the next several years as a "window of opportunity" before European military capabilities grow significantly stronger.
Despite the increased risk of escalation, DDIS said it saw no indication that Russia was preparing a full-scale invasion of a NATO country. Such an invasion remains "highly unlikely," according to the assessment, although the agency said it could not be ruled out entirely.
The intelligence service estimated that Russia would need at least six months to prepare the forces required for an invasion.

Ukrainian drones attack Russia's Rostov Oblast, Krasnodar Krai, allegedly targeting oil depots
Ukrainian drones allegedly targeted oil depots in Russia's Rostov Oblast and Krasnodar Krai overnight on Sept. 24, according to local authorities.
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that Russian air defenses intercepted and destroyed 40 Ukrainian drones over several Russian regions, including Rostov Oblast, Krasnodar Krai, and occupied Crimea, overnight on Sept. 24.
Rostov Oblast Governor Yury Slyusar claimed Russian air defenses intercepted Ukrainian drones over Taganrog and the Kagalnitsky and Neklinovsky districts.
According to Slyusar, falling drone debris damaged administrative buildings at an oil depot in Kagalnitsky district, but there were no casualties or fire.
Additionally, Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ said on Sept. 24 that an oil depot in the settlement of Novotitarovskaya in neighboring Krasnodar Krai also caught fire following a drone attack.
Russian state-controlled media TASS claimed that a fire broke out on the premises of "a facility" after debris from a drone fell in the Dinsky district of Krasnodar Krai. No injuries were reported.
Ukraine has not commented on the strikes, and the Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claims.

Man from Tyumen jailed for 8 years for leaving $3.50 worth of Stars under banned Telegram posts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:14:15 UTC
03:14:15 KST

The Central District Military Court in Yekaterinburg has sentenced a Tyumen resident to eight years in a maximum-security penal colony over paid reactions (“Stars”) that he left under posts on Telegram channels. As Mediazona reports, 57-year-old Mikhail Antonovich was found guilty of financing terrorism (Article 205.1, Part 1.1 of the Russian Criminal Code), which carries a sentence of 8 to 15 years.
This is the first known conviction involving the use of Telegram Stars, though media outlets had previously reported on other cases that were opened over Stars.
According to the case file, Antonovich, who was detained in December 2025, had left Stars under posts on the channels NEVZOROV, BEREZOVIEW (Taras Berezovets) WAR IN UKRAINE, Nakipelo Michael Nacke, and Sasha Shpak Official. Investigators counted 130 Stars with a total value of 292.99 rubles $3.50.
As the Memorial Human Rights Group reports, investigators consider these channels to be involved in “propaganda of terrorism and media support for the terrorist organizations the Freedom of Russia Legion, the Russian Volunteer Corps, and the Azov Brigade, including organizing financing channels for the purchase of weapons and subsequent drone strikes on Russian territory, as well as organizing terrorist attacks on Russian soil. The content of the channels indicates that funds, including the virtual currency Telegram Stars, are monetized and subsequently directed toward financing the activities of the aforementioned terrorist organizations.”
On Sept. 22, 2026, Memorial published an appeal to Telegram founder Pavel Durov asking him to make paid reactions in the messenger anonymous and to take other measures to protect users from persecution by the Russian state.

A fire at a Starlink ground station in Poland may have been a deliberate attempt to disrupt internet access used by Ukrainian forces at the front, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told reporters on Sept. 24.
Gawkowski said there were indications that the fire at the station in Wola Krobowska, in Poland's Masovian Voivodeship, on the evening of Sept. 23, may have been an attempt to disrupt its operations.
The station is operated by the state-owned telecommunications company Exatel and serves as an internet hub that carries traffic through Poland, including to Ukraine, Gawkowski said.
He suggested Russia could be behind the incident, describing it as potentially part of Moscow's hybrid warfare. Polish authorities have not concluded their investigation into the incident.
He said a disruption could affect internet access for the Ukrainian military, potentially depriving Ukrainian forces of communications at the front.
On top of allowing flawless high-speed communications between combat positions and command posts, Starlink internet, when mounted on drones, allows for an almost unjammable connection not constrained by the limits of traditional radio antennas.
Over 2026, Ukrainian forces have found increasing success using Starlink-enabled drones over Russian-occupied territory, most notably in the "middle-strike" range (50-200 kilometers from the front line), where Russian logistics routes have been devastated by Ukrainian attacks.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk separately said on Sept. 24 that the circumstances of the fire "do not look good," while cautioning that it was too early to determine whether the incident was sabotage or an accident, Polish news agency PAP reported.
The Starlink incident came as Poland temporarily evacuated border crossings with Ukraine on Sept. 24 during a Russian attack near the Polish border.
Tusk said Poland evacuated the border crossings in Hrubieszow and Dorohusk as Russia attacked Ukraine near the Polish border, PAP reported. The crossings were later reopened.
Polish border guards said the crossings in Dorohusk and nearby Zosin were evacuated twice on Sept. 24. The first evacuation began at around 3 a.m., while a second evacuation took place around 11:30 a.m. and lasted about 30 minutes, Polish broadcaster TVP reported.
Poland's Government Security Center also issued alerts for residents in the Lublin and Podkarpackie regions amid the Russian attacks.
"The escalation of actions of the Russian Federation is becoming a fact, and its examples are getting closer and closer to our borders," Tusk said in a briefing with defense officials. "What can be expected is that the next weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions from the Russian side. Unfortunately, we cannot rule out that this escalation will also concern our territory."
Russia launched drones overnight at western Ukraine on Sept. 12, striking a gas station near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk border crossing and a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train just 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Polish border.
Poland's deputy permanent representative to the U.N., Michal Miarka, said on Aug. 24 that Russian aggression in Ukraine poses a serious threat to neighboring states, as evident in recent airspace violations of the Polish, Romanian, and Latvian airspace.
The diplomat pointed to a Russian cruise missile crashing in Poland's Lublin province after traveling about 90 kilometers (55 miles) into Polish territory during a mass strike against Ukraine on July 30.
Countries in Ukraine's neighborhood have increasingly felt the impact of the war as Russian drones and missiles have repeatedly entered Romanian, Moldovan, and Polish territory.

Ukraine Pushes EU to Sanction Russian Billionaires Vladimir Lisin and Vladimir Potanin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:13:41 UTC
03:13:41 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine Pushes EU to Sanction Russian Billionaires Vladimir Lisin and Vladimir Potanin
Ukraine is urging the European Union to impose sanctions on Russian billionaires Vladimir Lisin and Vladimir Potanin, Politico reported on September 24.
Kyiv argues that targeting their massive steel and nickel enterprises is a necessary step to restrict Russia’s war economy.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The push from Ukraine comes shortly after EU envoys agreed to remove prominent Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the bloc’s sanctions list just days prior.
According to Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the commissioner advising Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on sanctions policy, the EU created a “risky precedent” with those removals, but could win back credibility by listing Lisin and Potanin.
Vlasiuk told Politico’s Playbook that Lisin and Potanin control major companies—NLMK and Nornickel, respectively—that are highly beneficial to the Russian war economy. Including them in the next batch of individual sanctions would effectively cut their enterprises off from trading in the EU.
“Everyone is aware about these guys but avoiding any action against them,” Vlasiuk stated. “But now arguably there is leverage to push this forward.”
To date, the sheer size of the businesses owned by the two billionaires and their substantial footprints in Europe have kept them off the sanctions list, Politico noted.
Lisin’s steel company, NLMK, operates processing facilities in the Belgian region of Wallonia, which led the Belgian government to oppose his listing. The company also maintains production sites in Strasbourg, France; Verona, Italy; and Frederiksvaerk, Denmark.
Politico reported that, similarly, Potanin has avoided sanctions due to Europe’s dependency on Russian nickel and palladium, particularly within the automotive industry, which has enabled him to continue growing his empire during the war.
Vlasiuk linked the hesitation over Lisin and Potanin to broader frustrations within the bloc, pointing to the ongoing debate over whether to sanction Aughinish Alumina, an Irish exporter that supplies Russia.
“It’s always the same story. You can have 20 countries for whom [sanctioning] is an obvious decision and one who opposes,” Vlasiuk told Politico. “These alumina exports should really be banned. It’s obvious for us, and we have plenty of ideas for what to do next.”
Lisin’s camp has strongly pushed back against Kyiv’s proposal. In a statement provided to Politico’s Playbook, a spokesperson for the billionaire denied any involvement with Russia’s war effort.
“This information campaign is unfair competition, where the sanctions-related agenda is leveraged as a way of pressure to eliminate a competitor from the market and to inflict further substantial harm on the European economy,” the spokesperson wrote.
“It is well established and has long been recognized that neither Mr. Lisin nor NLMK cooperate with the enterprises of the Russian military-industrial complex. NLMK manufactures exclusively civilian products,” they continued.
Representatives for Potanin did not immediately reply to Politico’s request for comment regarding the proposed sanctions.
On September 23, 51 UN member states issued a joint statement ahead of a UN Security Council meeting urging Russia to agree to a “full, immediate, and unconditional ceasefire” in Ukraine, a commitment Kyiv already accepted in March 2025.
In response, Russia launched a massive 10-hour, overnight assault on September 24, firing 227 aerial targets at Ukraine, including 219 drones and seven missiles. The barrage triggered air raid sirens across Kyiv for virtually the entire day, killing multiple people, injuring dozens, and damaging civilian infrastructure including a maternity hospital, residential buildings, and the historic “Shaiba” market.

Russian military marketplace Roy.Market, launched amid strikes on Wildberries and Ozon warehouses, is tied to former President Dmitry Medvedev and his son’s circle, investigation finds

Russian military marketplace Roy.Market, launched amid strikes on Wildberries and Ozon warehouses, is tied to former President Dmitry Medvedev and his son’s circle, investigation finds
Roy.Market, a Russian marketplace for military personnel whose launch was announced in mid-August, has ties to people close to Dmitry Medvedev, a former Russian president and prime minister who is now deputy chair of the Security Council, the outlet Vot Tak reports.
Roy.Market bills itself as a marketplace for dual-use goods. Buyers and sellers must request access and fill out a form.
The Center for Unmanned Systems and Technologies (TsBST) launched the marketplace. The center was founded by United Russia, PSB — a key bank for Russia’s Defense Ministry — and the Nasha Pravda foundation, which was created at Medvedev’s initiative.
Nasha Pravda was founded by the Dar and Gradislava foundations, which featured in Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK) investigations into Medvedev’s assets. FBK claimed the foundations had been created solely to manage the former president’s property. An estate in Plyos that FBK described as Medvedev’s secret country home was registered in the foundations’ names.
Medvedev’s son Ilya also has ties to Nasha Pravda. In early 2025, he helped hand over a shipment of goods from the foundation to Russian troops. Until recently, Roy.Market was headed by Ivan Koptenko, a classmate and friend of the younger Medvedev. Roy.Market’s developers call the elder Medvedev the “inspiration” behind the marketplace.
In the summer of 2026, the Ukrainian military began striking warehouses belonging to Wildberries and Ozon, Russia’s largest marketplaces. Kyiv said the marketplaces served as an unofficial supply channel for Russian troops.
