UN chief asks to tackle root causes of sea-level rise by capping emissions
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
02:12:18 CST
03:12:18 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Thursday called for efforts to tackle the root causes of sea-level rise, primarily by capping greenhouse gas emissions.
"Any overshoot of the 1.5-degree limit (on man-made global temperature increase) must be as small and short as possible. Global emissions must peak immediately, and fall 60 percent by 2035," he told a high-level meeting on sea-level rise.
"We must triple renewable energy, double energy efficiency, slash methane emissions, halt and reverse deforestation, and transition away from fossil fuels -- fast and fairly," he said. "The G20 (Group of 20) must lead, and COP31 (UN Climate Change Conference) in Türkiye must deliver."
Guterres also stressed the importance of protecting people from rising waters -- by embedding sea-level rise resilience in national adaptation plans, development budgets, infrastructure and land-use decisions; and drawing on science, data, and the knowledge of indigenous peoples and local communities.
Around 770 million people live less than 5 meters above the high-tide line. Without significant adaptation and mitigation, the risks facing coastal cities and communities could increase tenfold by 2100, he said.
Sea-level rise is a threat multiplier. It batters economies, trade, infrastructure, and food systems; erases cultural heritage and identity; fuels instability; and it threatens the territorial integrity of some nations, he said.
Guterres also called for closing legal gaps.
The International Court of Justice and the International Law Commission stated that continued statehood is possible, even if territory is lost. States have called for maritime zones and boundaries to be preserved as coastlines shift. People's rights do not disappear because their homes do. And those people must be protected, he said.
"We need legal clarity consistent with the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea -- and international cooperation is essential to reach the arrangements that affected states and local communities deserve," he said.
Rising seas are sinking futures. In 2024, the global sea level rose almost 6 mm, the highest annual increase ever recorded. And the pace is accelerating.
According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, even in the best-case scenario, sea levels are projected to rise by as much as half a meter by century's end. Without drastic emissions cuts, that rise could reach a meter. Meanwhile, Greenland and West Antarctica are losing ice faster, risking irreversible change, Guterres said.
Sea-level rise is measured in millimeters. But its toll is measured in millions of shattered lives, uprooted communities, and stolen futures. Those on the front lines must be front and center in every decision, he said. "We cannot allow countries and cultures to vanish beneath the waves -- or leave the aspirations of billions dead in the water. The SOS has gone out. The world must answer." ■

EU sanctions former RT France chief Xenia Fedorova over pro-Russian propaganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:12:16 UTC
03:12:16 KST

The Council of the European Union confirmed the Russian commentator had been added to its sanctions list on Thursday. In France, she had already faced an expulsion order and an asset freeze, both of which she challenged.
Former RT France chief Xenia Fedorova has been placed under EU sanctions over her alleged role in spreading pro-Kremlin narratives, further complicating her efforts to return to French media.
The Council of the European Union added Fedorova to its sanctions list on Thursday, accusing her of being "active in the dissemination of pro-Russian narratives in France and the Union in the context of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine".
The decision extends measures already imposed by France against Fedorova, who has become a prominent media figure on outlets associated with conservative billionaire Vincent Bolloré.
Under the EU sanctions, Fedorova faces an asset freeze across all 27 member states. EU individuals and entities are prohibited from making funds available to her, restricting her ability to receive payments, including a salary.
She is also subject to a travel ban preventing her from entering or transiting through EU territory.
According to the document, published on Thursday in the EU’s Official Journal and seen by Euronews, Fedorova is accused of relaying "narratives aligned with those promoted by the Russian authorities".
"In particular, Xenia Fedorova has portrayed Western and European support for Ukraine as prolonging the war, presented Russia as seeking peace while portraying Europe as pursuing confrontation, questioned established accounts concerning the unlawful transfer and deportation of Ukrainian children, and disseminated narratives portraying European and NATO policies as threats to European security," the document further stated.
In its decision, the EU noted that Fedorova had regularly appeared on French media outlets, including CNews, Europe 1 and Le Journal du Dimanche (JDD), following the suspension of RT's broadcasting activities.
According to the Council, these appearances allowed her to continue spreading pro-Russian narratives to a wide audience in France.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot welcomed the agreement on Wednesday during a press briefing at the United Nations in New York, a day before the sanctions were formally announced.
Barrot welcomed the EU's decision to extend measures already introduced by France to all 27 member states.
Following Thursday's announcement, he said France and the EU would continue to counter Russia's alleged destabilisation activities.
"France, like the European Union, will continue to thwart the destabilisation activities carried out by Russia on our soil," he said.
"Our determination is absolute: those who think they can conduct hostile operations against our democracy with impunity will face the consequences".
The French Foreign Ministry subsequently confirmed that France and Germany had jointly proposed Fedorova's inclusion on the sanctions list, describing her as an "active Russian influence agent in France".
French authorities warn against Fedorova's return to broadcasting
Fedorova, who previously headed RT France, has been subject to a French deportation order and asset freeze since late July.
At the time, French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said her behaviour undermined France's fundamental interests and that her presence in the country constituted a serious and immediate threat to public order.
Fedorova's lawyer subsequently said she had been abroad on holiday when she learned of the measures. She has not been seen in France since.
However, there were indications that media outlets associated with Bolloré were exploring ways for her to resume appearances from outside France.
On 10 September, Nuñez warned CNews that it could face "criminal sanctions" if Fedorova returned to its broadcasts from abroad.
In a letter to French audiovisual regulator Arcom, reported by Le Monde and AFP, the minister argued that allowing her to appear remotely could "facilitate the interference operations she is accused of".
Fedorova has challenged the French deportation order in court and has regularly addressed French authorities on X.
She has not yet publicly commented on the latest EU sanctions.

scars left by bears ripple through these japanese cedar surfboards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:10:43 UTC
03:10:43 KST

In the forests of Keihoku, north of central Kyoto, Asian black bears sometimes strip bark from cedar and cypress trees, leaving long wounds across their trunks. The behavior is known as kumahagi. As the trees continue to grow, new tissue forms around the damaged area and the wood develops warped, irregular grain. For foresters, those marks can sharply reduce the timber’s commercial value. Kyoto City says damaged trees are often chipped for fuel or left in the mountains.
Those scars are exactly what drew the people behind the BEARS WOOD PROJECT to the material. Launched in 2022 by Kyoto’s Tsutsumi Asakichi Urushi with foresters and woodworkers in Keihoku, the project uses timber whose value has fallen after bear damage. On the wooden surfboards produced through its siita brand, the altered grain moves straight through the finished surface. Cedar shaped into a long, curved board is coated in glossy urushi, making the marks left in the forest even easier to see.
images via Tsutsumi Asakichi Urushi
takuya tsutsumi brings urushi onto the surfboard
At the center of the project is Takuya Tsutsumi, fourth-generation head of Tsutsumi Asakichi Urushi, the Kyoto lacquer shop founded by his family in 1909. The company has spent more than a century refining urushi, the natural resin traditionally used across Japanese craft as a coating and adhesive. Tsutsumi joined the family business in 2004 and has since taken the material onto bicycles, skateboards and surfboards, objects that place lacquer well beyond the formats usually associated with the craft.
For siita, Tsutsumi works with wooden surfboard shaper Rodrigo Matsuda, who has been making wooden boards for close to two decades. Matsuda shapes the timber in Keihoku, while Tsutsumi handles the urushi finish. Their workshop sits beside the Katsura River inside a converted century-old farm shed. Temperature and humidity affect the viscosity and sheen of urushi as it is worked, so Tsutsumi adjusts the process according to the conditions of each session.
a new use for a damaged tree
The forestry problem behind the boards extends beyond their unusual appearance. Kyoto Prefecture describes kumahagi as bears peeling bark from species including cedar and cypress before biting into the exposed wood. The prefecture identifies the damage as a significant issue for forestry, while acknowledging that aspects of why and when the behavior occurs remain unresolved.
Tsutsumi describes the BEARS WOOD PROJECT as an attempt to keep that damaged timber economically useful. Rather than selecting only the clean sections of a trunk, the collaborators work with areas that have grown unevenly around the wound. He says the group asks foresters to cut the affected trees on the condition that the timber is purchased at a proper price. The scar becomes an economic question as much as an aesthetic one. A feature that once lowered the value of the wood becomes the detail that distinguishes one board from another.
from the mountains of kyoto to the water
Keihoku has supplied timber to Kyoto since the establishment of Heian-kyo more than a thousand years ago. The siita workshop sits within that long timber landscape, using local cedar alongside other woods such as paulownia. Its reference point comes from much farther away: the alaia, the finless wooden surfboards ridden in Hawaii before the arrival of modern foam and fiberglass construction. Tsutsumi’s earlier experiments with lacquered alaia eventually developed into siita, which formally launched in 2023.
There is a strange sequence embedded in each of the bear-scarred boards. A bear marks the tree first. The cedar spends years growing around the wound before Matsuda begins shaping it, and Tsutsumi eventually covers the surface in layers of urushi. Beneath the lacquer, the forest is still legible. The finish seals the distorted grain in plain sight to turn an interruption in the tree’s growth into the board’s most recognizable feature.

Twelve-country group, including Türkiye, opposes new permanent seats in UNSC reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:08:16 UTC
03:08:16 KST

The Uniting for Consensus group has reiterated its opposition to creating new permanent seats on the UN Security Council, calling instead for an expansion of elected membership, including longer-term rotational seats.
The group, comprising Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, Italy, Malta, Mexico, Pakistan, South Korea, San Marino, Spain and Türkiye, issued a joint statement on Thursday during the high-level week of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
“Our shared goal is to work for a more representative, democratic, transparent, accountable, and effective Council, capable of responding to today’s global challenges,” the statement said.
The group said expanding elected membership would “contribute to the maintenance of international peace and security while preserving the principle of sovereign equality.”
“Such expansion would be the fairest and most democratic way to address Africa’s historical underrepresentation,” as well as that of other underrepresented regions, including Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the Caribbean, it said.
The group “reiterates its opposition to the creation of new permanent seats,” according to the statement.
It also reaffirmed its support for the Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) process, calling it “the only legitimate and inclusive platform led by Member States to discuss Security Council reform.”
“The path forward must be based on dialogue, flexibility, and compromise,” the statement said, calling for the reform process to address the “five sets of interconnected issues” and seek “the broadest possible political consensus.”
On the veto, the group said it supported its abolition but called for immediate steps to limit its use in specific circumstances.
“While supporting the abolition of the veto … we should act jointly immediately to move towards its limitation in specific circumstances, including but not limited to mass atrocities and war crimes,” it said.
The statement cited the Franco-Mexican Initiative and the ACT Code of Conduct as existing initiatives aimed at limiting the use of the veto.
The group said it was ready to work with the UN General Assembly president, future IGN co-presidents and all member states during the 81st session to advance comprehensive Security Council reform.

Big tech hands in its DSA censorship reports to the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:08:00 UTC
03:08:00 KST

Big tech hands in its DSA censorship reports to the EU
The EU has published a wide range of reports detailing what social media companies like TikTok and Meta are doing to comply with its Digital Services Act (DSA). The reports detail the extreme censorship needed to stay on Brussels’ good side.
Under the European Commission’s “voluntary Code of Conduct on Disinformation,” the largest online platforms operating in the EU are required to submit biannual reports explaining their efforts to combat so-called “disinformation.” Although adherence to the code is described as “voluntary,” those who do not comply are subject to fines under the DSA, which came into force in 2023.
The commission published reports by Meta, TikTok, Google, Twitch, and more than two dozen other platforms on Wednesday. Each report spans hundreds of pages, and details the speech restrictions and censorship policies put in place at the behest of the EU.
These include restrictions on political speech surrounding elections, which the EU has mandated in every major European vote since 2024, under the pretext of fighting “Russian interference.” According to documents released by the US House Judiciary Committee earlier this year, these measures have almost always been used “to disadvantage conservative or populist political parties.”
In its report, TikTok admitted that it removed more than half a million posts concerning elections in Bulgaria, Cyprus, Denmark, Hungary, Malta, Portugal, and Slovenia this year. RT has covered the EU’s efforts to interfere in the Bulgarian and Hungarian elections in depth, and found that TikTok came under particularly intense pressure from Brussels, after its failure to implement sufficiently draconian restrictions during Romania’s presidential election in 2024.
Each report is hundreds of pages long, and every major social media company admitted that they now defer to EU-approved “fact-checkers” to police content on their platforms. Meta explained that it now automatically down-ranks content flagged by fact-checkers, while YouTube stated that it has trained AI models to pre-emptively remove content it thinks would fall foul of these groups.
Multiple reports specify that the platforms themselves must pay the fact-checkers’ salary. These fact-checkers flagged more than 14 million posts on Facebook in the first six months of this year alone.
Every social media platform devoted a chapter in its report to the Russia-Ukraine conflict, with Facebook noting that all posts on the conflict are subject to monitoring for “disinformation and misinformation” by pro-EU fact-checkers.
Russian media outlets are banned from Facebook, while Ukrainian outlets are free to operate, and Kiev is permitted to fundraise on the platform.
Despite mentioning “disinformation” more than a dozen times, the DSA does not define the term.

Ukraine put robots where its soldiers used to die clearing mines—and lost none
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:04:28 UTC
03:04:28 KST

Ukraine's Third Army Corps says it became the first military unit in the world to use ground robots for mine clearance inside a live offensive, sending the machines ahead of its infantry into the deadliest sectors to keep soldiers out of the line of fire, Censor.NET reported. The corps built the capability from nothing during its Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive in Donetsk Oblast.
Keeping soldiers alive has become the organizing principle of how Ukraine fights, and handing the jobs most likely to kill them to ground robots is how an army that refuses to treat its people as expendable defends the line.
Robots cleared 30 km of routes in two nights
On the Shandryholove axis, the robots cleared 30 kilometers of routes in two nights—work that two companies of sappers would have needed a full week to finish. The corps reported no losses among its sappers there. Announcing the operation's second phase, corps commander Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi said protecting personnel drives how his troops plan and fight:
"People often ask, but what about our losses? My answer: we minimize them by every possible means. In assault operations, drones and ground robots always move ahead of the infantry," he said.
Robots clear most of the mines and mine Russian routes in return
The corps says it built the system from scratch and scaled it from a single squad up to the entire corps, arguing that manual clearing would be impossible across open terrain swept by fire. Ground robots now lift roughly 60% of the anti-personnel mines in its area of responsibility. They also work in reverse, remotely mining Russian advance routes—one crew can lay up to 200 meters a day, cutting off enemy reserves. The same machines carry frontline logistics, evacuating the wounded and hauling in provisions and equipment.
Operation Vivaldi continues in Donetsk Oblast, where the corps recently air-dropped robots behind Russian lines. Its advance has disrupted Russia's plan to encircle the fortified belt of Donetsk cities. In the second phase, the Third Army Corps liberated Shandryholove and Derylove and took full control of Drobysheve. Across the operation's first two phases, it has retaken 125 square kilometers.

TeachPhilosophy101, a free and helpful collection of resources and ideas for teaching philosophy, has recently been updated.
Its materials cover course planning, how to use class time, student assessment, challenges, and much more.
TeachPhilosophy101 was created by John Immerwahr (Villanova) and previously revamped by Erin Tarver (Emory). Recently David Sackris (Arapahoe Community College) took over as editor of the site, making further changes and adding additional resources.
Some of those new resources come by way of an arrangement with the Philosophy Documentation Center and the journal, Teaching Philosophy, to provide free access to any articles in the journal that are linked to on the TeachPhilosophy101 site.
It’s very much worth checking out.
And if you’d like to contribute materials or ideas for TeachPhilosophy101 , email Professor Sackris.

The 5 Best Strength Exercises for People Over 50
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:03:27 UTC
03:03:27 KST

Some changes famously accompany aging. For some people, it gets harder to hear in crowded places; for others, reading a menu in dim light gets trickier. But not everyone knows to expect a loss of muscle mass. Starting around age 30, people lose 3-5% of their lean muscle per decade. For most people, this decline isn’t noticeable until around age 60, when it might start to make daily activities more difficult.
One of the most effective ways to combat muscle loss is to build and protect the muscle you already have through strength training. Not only will that help you avoid frailty and falls, but it can also keep you moving with ease through your daily activities.
When people ask Charlie Grundas, a certified personal trainer and owner of We, The Collective Fitness in Chicago, why it’s important to strength train after 50, he has an easy reply: “Do you ever want there to be a time where you can’t get off the toilet?” he says. “I don't think there should ever be [a time when] you drop something on the floor, and you're like, ‘Well, forget it, I don't own that anymore.’”
You also start losing bone density as you age, and strength training builds healthy bones, which helps prevent falls and fractures. Plus, the muscle you build may offer some insulating protection if you do stumble, says Will Hewitt, certified personal trainer and director of training at Flight House Fitness in Charlestown, Mass.
Strength training can help at any age, whether you want to keep improving in your athletic pursuits, be able to pick up grandchildren, or simply bring your groceries inside in one trip, Grundas says. It’s OK to start with just a few exercises and just a few sets and repetitions: anywhere from one to three sets of six to 15 repetitions is beneficial, according to the American College of Sports Medicine. What’s most important is that you do it—ideally at least twice a week.
It’s always a good idea to get the green light from your doctor before starting any new exercise routine. You might also consider working with a fitness professional, like a certified personal trainer or certified strength and conditioning specialist, if you’re new to strength training at this stage of life or if you’ve had any injuries or surgery. A professional can help you modify movements and swap out equipment that might feel better for your particular circumstances, Hewitt says.
They can also help encourage you to try activities you might think you “shouldn’t” do in your 50s and beyond. “Your days of doing an 18-inch box jump may be over, and that's a hard pill to swallow, but let's do a six-inch box, and maybe six months from now, we'll be doing 12 inches,” he says. “It's just like eating your vegetables: You just have to keep doing it, and you'll be better for it.”
Here are some of the best strength-training exercises he and others recommend you try as you get older, plus how to do them with proper form.
A squat is the movement required to stand up from sitting down, which is something you’ll want to be able to do your whole life long, Grundas says. This particular variation works your quads, hamstrings, glutes, and core, and it’s approachable for people of all fitness levels, Hewitt says. Holding a weight at your chest can help you keep your chest up, and keeping a wide stance can help you squat more deeply, according to the National Academy of Sports Medicine.
How to do it
- Start standing with your feet slightly wider than shoulder-width apart, toes pointing slightly out, holding a dumbbell (cupping one end like it’s a heavy goblet) or kettlebell at your chest with both hands.
- Push your hips back and bend your knees to lower your body until your thighs are parallel to the floor or as far as you can comfortably go, keeping the weight close to your chest and your elbows inside your knees.
- Press through your feet to return to the starting position.
- Complete all repetitions, aiming for six to 15.
Modify it
You can work all the same muscles by doing a step-down instead. Standing on a stair, start to walk down, and as soon as your heel touches the lower step, press through your standing leg and return both feet to the higher stair, Grundas says. Repeat, alternating feet with each repetition.
At the end of the weekly yoga class he teaches, Grundas challenges his class to stand up from the floor without using their hands. This works many different lower-body muscles and your core, in addition to helping you maintain your mobility and your balance. A 2026 European Journal of Preventive Cardiology study found people who could sit down and stand up from the floor without using their hands or other body parts for support had a four times lower risk of death over the study period compared to people who required more support.
How to do it
- Start standing barefoot on the floor.
- Sit down cross-legged on the floor using as little support from your hands or legs as possible.
- Stand up, once again using as little support as possible.
- Complete all repetitions, aiming for three to five.
Modify it
Use your hands or legs as needed to help you sit and stand. Keep practicing, aiming to be able to do the movement with less help.
If you’re able to sit and rise without support, challenge yourself with a Turkish get-up instead, Grundas says.
This movement can help you maintain your ability to put dishes away on the highest shelf in your kitchen or stow your suitcase in the overhead compartment on a plane, Grundas says.
How to do it
- Start sitting on a bench or a sturdy piece of furniture with your feet planted on the floor, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your shoulders with your elbows bent and your palms facing forward.
- Press both dumbbells overhead until your arms are straight but not locked.
- Pause briefly, then lower the dumbbells to return to the starting position.
- Complete all repetitions, aiming for six to 15.
Modify it
If you need something a little easier, use light weights to do a lateral raise, Grundas suggests:
- Start standing with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand by your sides, palms facing your body.
- Keeping your arms straight and your shoulders back and down, slowly lift the dumbbells up and out to your sides until the dumbbells are level with your shoulders.
- Slowly lower the dumbbells back to the starting position.
- Complete all repetitions, aiming for six to 15.
If you’re ready for a more challenging move, try a bench press, he says:
- Lie on your back on a flat bench with your feet flat on the floor holding a barbell with your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart.
- Press the bar up until your arms are straight, but don’t lock your elbows.
- Slowly lower the bar with control until you’re just about at your chest.
- Complete all repetitions, aiming for six to 15.
Grundas recommends a modified deadlift to help you maintain your ability to pick something up off the ground.
How to do it
- Stand on one foot with the toes of your other foot on the floor slightly behind your heel, like you’re in a staggered “kickstand” position. Keep most of your weight in your standing leg and a slight bend in that knee. Hold a dumbbell or kettlebell in your opposite hand.
- Keeping that slight bend in your standing knee, push your hips back and lower the weight in front of your leg until you feel a stretch in the back of your thigh.
- Pause briefly, then press through your standing foot to return to the starting position.
- Complete all repetitions, aiming for six to 15, then repeat on the other side.
Modify it
Try it without any weight at first to get used to the movement. Once you feel comfortable in the kickstand position, you can try a single-leg Romanian deadlift, where you extend your kickstand leg straight behind you instead. You can also lift heavier weight with both feet on the floor in the traditional Romanian deadlift position.
Core exercises help improve balance, which can ward off falls, Hewitt says. Your core muscles also include your pelvic floor, so strengthening these muscles can help prevent bladder and bowel issues that become more common with age.
How to do it
- Start on your hands and knees on the floor.
- Press through your palms and toes to lift your knees a few inches off of the floor.
- Keep your back flat and hips level as you hold this position for 10 to 60 seconds.
Modify it
Elevate your hands on a sturdy bench, step, or couch to make this a little easier.
Once you get comfortable holding this position, make it a little more challenging by lifting one hand off the floor at a time and tapping it to the opposite shoulder or holding one arm and the opposite leg in the air for several seconds, Hewitt says. You can also crawl forward and backward in this position without letting your knees touch the floor.

New study reveals that fluctuating—not just intense—brain signals play a hidden role in overeating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:00:42 UTC
03:00:42 KST

A recent study found that people with higher body mass index and tendencies toward disinhibited eating experience more fluctuating brain responses to food rewards. The findings, published in Translational Psychiatry, suggest that inconsistent reward signals in the brain may play a role in overweight and overeating. Meanwhile, individuals with binge eating disorder showed specific inconsistencies in how much they consciously desired food from moment to moment.
Binge eating disorder involves recurrent episodes of eating large quantities of food while experiencing a loss of control. People with this condition frequently experience high rates of overweight and obesity. Previous research into eating disorders has primarily focused on the average strength of brain signals when people encounter food cues.
One major psychological theory suggests that repeated exposure to highly rewarding foods sensitizes the brain’s motivational pathways. Over time, this sensitization could cause food cues to trigger heightened arousal and cravings. However, hunger and satiety naturally fluctuate.
If eating for pleasure repeatedly overrides the body’s natural fullness signals, a person’s response to food might become highly variable rather than uniformly strong. Instead of just looking at average brain activity, researchers suspected that fluctuations in these signals from moment to moment might better explain erratic eating patterns. To test this idea, cognitive neuroscientist Nils B. Kroemer, psychology researcher Mechteld M. van den Hoek Ostende, and their colleagues at the University of Tübingen in Germany investigated whether variability in reward processing is higher in people with binge eating disorder.
The researchers focused on the nucleus accumbens, a region deep in the brain that plays a central role in processing rewards, anticipating pleasure, and driving motivation. They also looked at the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a brain area involved in cognitive control, impulse regulation, and weighing the costs and benefits of a potential action.
The researchers recruited 79 women for the study. The sample included 35 participants diagnosed with binge eating disorder, 21 with subsyndromal binge eating disorder who experienced less frequent episodes, and 23 control participants with no history of binge eating. The groups were matched so that their average body mass index was similar, allowing the researchers to separate the effects of the eating disorder from the effects of body weight.
During the first session, participants completed a behavioral experiment called a grip force effort allocation task. They were asked to squeeze a specialized handgrip device to earn either monetary rewards or small snack foods. The researchers calibrated the task to each person’s maximum grip strength.
This calibration ensured that the relative effort required was identical for everyone, regardless of their baseline physical fitness. In some trials, the required effort was explicitly shown on a screen, making the physical cost obvious. In other trials, the difficulty was hidden to create uncertainty.
After each round, participants rated how much they subjectively wanted the reward and how much effort they felt they had exerted. The points earned during the task were later exchanged for actual cash or snack calories. This allowed the researchers to quantify the physical effort participants would exert for a specific prize.
The researchers found that participants with binge eating disorder showed higher variability in their trial-by-trial ratings of wanting food. Their conscious desire for the food fluctuated widely from one moment to the next, especially during the uncertain trials. This high variability in subjective desire was not seen when they played for money.
However, their actual physical effort to obtain the rewards did not vary in the same way. The researchers noted that this disconnect might mean people with binge eating disorder rely more on external cues or habitual responses to decide how much effort to expend. This could cause their physical behavior to remain steady even while their internal feelings of desire fluctuate.
For the second phase of the study, 59 of the women returned to the laboratory after an overnight fast. They completed a similar version of the handgrip task while lying inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging scanner. This machine tracks blood flow in the brain, providing an indirect measure of neural activity in real time.
The researchers specifically measured the brain’s activity during the anticipation phase, which occurred exactly when the participants first saw the reward cue but before they started squeezing the handgrip. They calculated how much the neural signals in the nucleus accumbens and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex fluctuated across the trials.
Trial-by-trial fluctuations in the nucleus accumbens were positively associated with a higher body mass index. Across all groups, participants with higher body weight exhibited more variable reward signals in this brain region. Participants who reported higher levels of disinhibited eating on a standard eating behavior questionnaire also displayed greater variability in the nucleus accumbens.
The researchers found a similar pattern in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. A higher body mass index was linked to more fluctuating activity in this cognitive control region. To ensure these fluctuations were not just random brain noise, the researchers checked control regions in the temporal lobe that are not involved in reward processing.
Those control regions did not show the same variability, indicating the effect was specific to the reward and control centers. The results for binge eating disorder specifically were less definitive. While participants with the disorder showed slightly elevated variability in the nucleus accumbens compared to the control group, the evidence was not statistically significant.
The highly variable brain responses were more closely tied to overall body weight and a general tendency to eat without restraint, rather than a clinical diagnosis of the eating disorder. The study’s design includes several limitations that affect how the results can be applied. The research only included female participants, meaning the observed patterns might not generalize to men.
Sex hormones can influence eating behaviors and reward processing, which the study could not account for. The laboratory setting also tightly controlled when participants ate and minimized changes in their mood. Real-world binge eating episodes are often triggered by shifting emotional states and metabolic changes, which the sterile experimental environment was designed to eliminate.
Additionally, the researchers did not measure actual food consumption during the experiment. The study measured the willingness to work for food and the brain’s anticipation of it, rather than how much participants actually ate. Future studies tracking daily food intake would be needed to link these fluctuating brain signals directly to binge eating episodes.
Finally, slight head movements inside a brain scanner can sometimes look like variable neural activity. People with higher body weight sometimes move slightly more in scanners. While the researchers used mathematical models to correct for head movement, imaging experts often view residual motion artifacts as a potential complication in imaging research.
The study, “Obesity is associated with greater variability of reward signals in the nucleus accumbens,” was authored by Mechteld M. van den Hoek Ostende, Anne Kühnel, Monja P. Neuser, Thomas Dresler, Jennifer Svaldi, and Nils B. Kroemer.

The EU announced it will use December’s G20 summit in Miami to condemn Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, regardless of whether Russian President Vladimir Putin accepts Washington’s invitation to attend.
Commission deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill said the bloc has used every G20 meeting since 2022 to condemn the war and call for its end, Euronews reported. He said the same approach will continue “irrespective of the participants at any G20 meeting.”

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The G20 is a key forum for addressing existing and emerging global challenges. Some of which have been created precisely by Russia’s war against Ukraine,” Gill said on Thursday.
“I also recall that Russia is escalating attacks on Ukrainian civilians as we speak. July and August were the deadliest months since the war started,” he continued.
The meeting is represented by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council António Costa, and comprises of a total of 19 countries alongside the EU and the African Union.
EU’s Kallas criticized the invitation
“Trump’s inviting Putin to the G20 was very hard to hear, because considering that even a few days ago, there were Russian intelligence officers charged for murders of Americans on American soil” EU foreign policy Kaja Kallas said.
“So, my question is, do these intelligence officers operate, you know, alone, or do they get orders from Vladimir Putin? And I can tell you, they get orders from President Putin,” she added.
Ukraine Opens Second EU Negotiating Cluster as Reform Delivery Shapes Further Accession Progress, KSE Institute Says
Kallas was referring to an indictment unsealed by the US Justice Department on Sept. 15, which charged five people linked to Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). Three of them were also charged with hired murder conspiracy.
According to Radio Liberty, the defendants include a former FSB colonel Kirill Khrameyev and his son, Yury, identified as a suspected FSB officer, alongside three other men who were hired to surveil and kill a prominent Russian dissident.
Russia declined to comment until “credible evidence” emerges.
EU already divided by the invitation
French far-right presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen welcomed Putin’s G20 invitation on Thursday.
Speaking to Politico on the same day, the National Rally leader said France could no longer provide financial aid to Ukraine under her leadership, though it could continue training Ukrainian troops and supplying the country with military support.
She also rejected claims that France is already at war with Russia and reiterated her wish for France to leave NATO after Russia’s war against Ukraine ends.
Her remarks come as Russian disinformation campaigns target possible contenders in the April 2027 elections with deepfakes, fabricated media reports and false claims.
Kremlin’s mixed signals
The Kremlin welcomed the US invitation, on Wednesday, only to walk back its statement on Thursday by saying it was too early to talk about it.
“It is premature to talk about this for now, a decision has not yet been made,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told journalists, according to Russian news agency Interfax.
On Sept. 12, he framed the meeting between Putin and Zelensky at the G20 summit in Miami as “impossible,” reiterating Moscow’s position that the two leaders could only meet in Moscow.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the invitation on Wednesday, after meeting Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York.
On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump met with President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the same summit, where he said Putin was willing to meet. “He’d like to see the war end,” he added.
Putin, however, has yet to accept any of Zelensky’s repeated invitations to meet in person and did not attend this year’s UNGA, where Lavrov represented Russia instead.
While Zelensky reiterated he is ready to meet the Russian President directly, urging the US to organize trilateral talks, Putin consistently avoids direct meetings.
Before Thursday‘s latest remarks, Lavrov said that the Kremlin will not pause its “special military operation” even during negotiations.
On Sept. 18, Putin accused Kyiv of sabotaging peace efforts, claiming that Ukrainian officials “speak of peace” while “doing everything to ensure” it doesn’t happen.
Three days later, Peskov said there had been no progress in negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine, but Moscow hoped trilateral talks involving the US would resume.
Meanwhile, any diplomatic momentum has repeatedly been followed by heavier Russian attacks.

From Zelensky to Pezeshkian, five speeches that stood out at this year’s U.N. General Assembly debate
United Nations meetings on September 23 generated an unusually large number of headlines. Heads of state addressed the annual General Assembly debate at U.N. headquarters in New York, and the Security Council met there as well. Below are excerpts from some of the remarks that drew the most press attention: speeches by the presidents of Ukraine, Iran, and Argentina, plus an indirect exchange between the Russian and Polish foreign ministers over Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Volodymyr Zelensky, president of Ukraine
To add another thousand square kilometers, Putin is paying with 248 people for every kilometer… […] And we know that Putin recently once again promised representatives from the American President that he would seize our Donetsk region. And he said he needs just a few more months…
This is probably the 17th or 18th time in 5 years that he has made this promise. It is always the same: “Just a few, a few more months”…
And then he moves the deadline again. […] Something always seems to stop Putin from simply saying: “That’s it. Enough. Peace.”
Something always stops him from admitting that 17 million square kilometers of his own territory — internationally recognized by all of you — should be enough for this man. […] He is “patient zero” — the one from whom this idea of war keeps spreading further. […] The more freedom Putin has to act – the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else.
That is why “patient zero” must be stopped.
Sergey Lavrov, Russia’s foreign minister
Russia — and President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly confirmed this — is prepared to negotiate to achieve precisely such a lasting and just peace. […] But having learned from bitter experience, we will not pause the special military operation during negotiations, regardless of their format. When President Donald Trump said that Greenland could very well become part of the United States, a U.N. spokesperson was asked at a press conference what he thought about it. He replied: “The issue must be resolved on the basis of international law, the U.N. Charter, the principle of Denmark’s territorial integrity, and the right of Greenland’s population to self-determination.”
At a press conference on January 29 of this year, António Guterres was asked: “Does the right to self-determination also apply to Crimea and Donbas?” The secretary-general replied (I am compelled to quote him in full): “We have had some very interesting discussions on this subject. There are two principles. One is the territorial integrity of states. The other is the self-determination of peoples. But the self-determination of peoples entails a whole series of requirements, given the way this principle was formulated. And after a very careful study by our Office of Legal Affairs, our position is that the principle of self-determination does not apply to the situations in Crimea and Donbas. Therefore, in this situation, the principle of territorial integrity prevails.” If anyone understood any of that, I envy you.
As we can see, Greenland is neither Crimea nor Donbas, and “never the twain shall meet.” We eagerly await the next episode in this “series.” It will be interesting to hear the Secretariat’s response to possible questions from journalists about the plans of Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland.
Radosław Sikorski, Poland’s foreign minister
After more than four years of a senseless colonial war, Vladimir Putin has achieved nothing. He is running out of troops and resources and needs a pretext to mobilize. […] At any moment, Putin might try to provoke a NATO country and spread the war further, as we have heard from others.

That is, it became a useless organization whose only purpose is to feed a caste of parasites — hopelessly arrogant people disguised as well-intentioned bureaucrats. During the pandemic, agencies under this organization placed themselves above scientific evidence and the sovereignty of nations, promoting forced lockdown policies around the world that destroyed jobs, ruined the education of an entire generation of children, and cost millions of people their lives as they died alone, without basic medical care. That is why I tell you: when it comes to artificial intelligence, Argentina will put itself at the forefront of freedom. We have the critical minerals, the energy, the talent, and the capacity to compete at every link in that value chain, and we want to be the most competitive place in the world to develop it, with a cutting-edge legal framework, a commitment not to regulate preemptively, a commitment not to regulate preemptively, limited liability for companies that operate with AI agents, and tax benefits.

Democratic lawmakers accuse Trump administration of interference in Brazilian elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:56:06 UTC
02:56:06 KST

A group of 31 Democratic members of the US Congress has sent a letter to the secretary of state, Marco Rubio, criticising the Trump administration over “an apparent effort to interfere with, and potentially undermine” Brazil’s elections.
Latin America’s largest country will hold the first round of its presidential election on 4 October, with polls showing a technical tie between the incumbent leftist president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro.
In the letter sent to Rubio on Thursday, 30 members of the House of Representatives and the senator Bernie Sanders listed a series of measures the US government took that they interpret as attempts to secure a victory for Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
They wrote that those actions “reflect a broader and deeply troubling pattern of interference by the Trump administration in recent electoral processes across Latin America”, citing the recent midterm elections in Argentina and presidential elections in Honduras and Colombia.
In July, a group of 11 Democratic members of Congress sent a similar letter arguing that Trump was trying to interfere in Colombia’s election in favour of the far-right millionaire and former lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella, who went on to win the second round.
In Thursday’s letter, the lawmakers wrote that US officials under Trump have engaged in a “sustained, multifaceted campaign of interference and destabilization in Brazil”.
They noted that when Trump imposed his first tariffs on Brazil last year, he made clear that one reason was Bolsonaro’s trial over his attempt to stage a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula. The former president was ultimately convicted and, unable to run because he is under house arrest, named his son to take his place.
They also cited new tariffs that Trump imposed on Brazil in July under section 301 of US trade law, as well as plans by the US government to send two officials to Brazil to “cast doubt on the integrity of the country’s voting system, considered by many experts to be among the most reliable in the world”. The Lula administration ultimately denied the US delegation visas.
The Brazilian president has repeatedly complained that Trump is trying to interfere in Brazil’s elections and, in his speech opening the UN general assembly this week, said, without naming anyone: “We will not allow the enemies of democracy, internal or external, to act against the will of the people.”
In the letter sent to Rubio on Friday, the Democratic lawmakers wrote that “rather than helping defend Brazilian democracy”, the US is “acting as an agent of interference and destabilization – using diplomatic, economic and political pressure in ways that risk weakening the country’s democratic institutions, undermining confidence in Brazil’s electoral process, and inflicting further damage on our relationship with a strategic US ally and trading partner”.
They asked Rubio if Trump’s administration would commit to respecting Brazil’s electoral process and requested a response by 1 October.
The state department has not yet responded to a request for comment.

Italy passes ban on burqas in schools, cap on foreign students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:55:39 UTC
02:55:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Italy bans burqas in schools, caps numbers of foreign students per class
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's cabinet adopted a decree law Thursday banning burqas and niqabs in schools and capping the number of students with a poor command of Italian per class.
It introduces "A 30 percent cap on the number of students in a class who do not have an adequate command of Italian, more tools for learning our language, and a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools," Meloni wrote on social media.
If a child seriously struggles to integrate at school, social services will be called and the parents will be obliged to attend free Italian lessons.
Failure to comply will be punished with a fine of up to 1,000 euros ($1,140).
Italy is a frontline country for migration and integration is a hot campaign issue ahead of next year's general election.
Save the Children warned forcing children to change schools or enrol in a different institution from their peers simply because of their nationality or limited proficiency in Italian would "create 'first-class' and 'second-class' students."
But Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said "inadequate language proficiency... hinders educational progress."
"Parental participation in their child's educational path is fundamental for academic success", he told journalists.
Valditara said there were 34,000 school classes in Italy in which over 30 percent of the students are foreign.
But most of those would be not be affected by the new law, which targets new arrivals rather than those born in Italy or who attended kindergarten.
The 30 percent limit on the number of foreign students per class was established in a ministerial memorandum in 2010.
But the limit was flexible, and could be raised in cases involving foreign students with adequate language skills, such as foreign students born in Italy, or lowered when foreign students have a poor command of Italian.
Opposition leader Elly Schlein accused the government of "a new witch hunt at the expense of children."
The burqa ban was "a matter of security", Meloni said in a television interview after the cabinet meeting.
"When a woman -- or worse, a young girl -- is forced to cover her face, she is being denied fundamental rights and the very integration that is so often loudly championed," she said.
A crackdown on the use of burqas in schools was called for in July by the National Future (FN) party.
The FN, which is not part of the governing coalition, is further to the right than Meloni's and has emerged as a major challenger, rising sharply in the polls since launching in February.

Le Pen, Mélenchon, Attal : les temps forts du sommet Playbook Paris Live de POLITICO

PARIS — Trois candidats à l’élection présidentielle se sont succédé sur le plateau du premier sommet Playbook Paris Live de POLITICO, non sans s’interpeller et se donner quelques coups de griffe. Eux à l’Elysée, continuent-ils d’aider l’Ukraine face à la Russie ? Quelle mesure prendre pour faire face à la flambée des prix des carburants ? Faut-il ralentir ou accélérer le développement de l’intelligence artificielle ? Le point sur leurs déclarations.
GABRIEL ATTAL
L’ancien Premier ministre a ouvert le bal de nos interviews. Candidat depuis le 22 mai, il peine à s’imposer comme le représentant du bloc central, face à son rival Edouard Philippe, qui fait la course en tête dans les intentions de vote.
1. Sur l’Europe et l’Ukraine
Advertisement
Aucune hésitation possible pour le candidat Renaissance : la France doit continuer de soutenir financièrement l’Ukraine. “Ce n’est pas une opération humanitaire. [...] C’est un investissement pour notre sécurité, pour le quotidien des Français”, a-t-il martelé. Faut-il aller envoyer nos avions protéger le ciel ukrainien ? “Je pense qu’il ne faut pas l’exclure [...] si ça répond à une demande des Ukrainiens.” Une demande qui ne lui “semble pas être d’une clarté totale aujourd’hui”. Et “si ça se fait en coopération avec d’autres nations”, a-t-il précisé.
Interrogé sur la contribution française à l’Union européenne, que son ancien collègue au gouvernement Bruno Le Maire propose de baisser de 5 milliards d’euros, Gabriel Attal répond par la négative ! “Ça ne me satisfait pas”, a-t-il réagi. Toutefois, il s’est montré ouvert à ce que, “éventuellement”, les amendes payées par les géants du numérique puissent servir de “manière transitoire” à réduire la dîme versée par les Etats membres.
2. Sur l’intelligence artificielle
L’ex-ministre de l’Education nationale a fait de l’IA l’un de ses quatre chantiers prioritaires. S’il entend les craintes actuelles autour de son développement, il rejette l’idée de faire une pause pour en limiter les risques. Il prône la création d’une “régulation sans ralentir le rythme de développement de l’IA en mettant en place une organisation internationale”, sur le modèle de l’Agence internationale de l’énergie atomique.
Pour soutenir les entreprises européennes, Gabriel Attal mise également sur son concept d’“Etats-Unis d’Europe” et sur la commande publique.
3. Sur les finances publiques
Advertisement
Gabriel Attal s’est montré prudent sur le projet de loi de finances pour 2027, attendant d’avoir la copie de Sébastien Lecornu entre les mains. Interrogé sur le risque d’une censure du gouvernement et les signaux envoyés par le Premier ministre en direction du Rassemblement national, il a estimé qu’on ne “peut pas faire confiance au RN [...] et à LFI”. “Marine Le Pen ne regarde que son intérêt politique du moment dans les décisions qu’elle prend, et pas l’intérêt de la France”, a-t-il taclé, invitant l’exécutif à chercher à discuter “avec ceux qui sont entre la LFI et le RN”.
Lui président, il prévoit de mettre en place un plan de 150 milliards d’euros d’économies sur cinq ans, avec un gros effort sur les dépenses sociales. Une “base”, car il “faudra probablement aller plus loin”, a-t-il reconnu. Face au spectre d’une crise de la dette, Gabriel Attal, qui s’est entretenu mercredi avec plusieurs économistes (Xavier Jaravel, Natacha Valla ou encore Olivier Blanchard), a annoncé qu’il préparait “un plan de secours au cas où la situation se dégraderait à très court terme”. Il devrait aussi dévoiler prochainement la suppression “d’une strate” dans le mille-feuille territorial.
MARINE LE PEN
La candidate RN, qui postule pour la quatrième fois à l’élection suprême, est, pour l’instant, l’ultrafavorite de cette élection présidentielle.
1. Sur l’Europe et l’Ukraine
L’aide à Kyiv ? Il faut y renoncer, a martelé Marine Le Pen : “Nous ne pouvons plus aider financièrement l’Ukraine.” Pour la candidate du Rassemblement national (RN), la France, étant donné sa situation budgétaire, “n’a plus les moyens” de soutenir le pays face à l’agression russe. “Il faudra peut-être trouver d’autres formes de financement”, a-t-elle avancé, sans plus de détails.
Si la députée du Pas-de-Calais reconnaît “un risque d’escalade” dans le conflit, à la lumière des récentes actions hostiles menées par Moscou, elle refuse de faire un lien entre la sécurité de la France et la défense de l’Ukraine, estimant que “le sujet n’est pas là”.
Advertisement
La candidate souhaite toujours retirer la France du commandement intégré de l’Otan, mais elle ne le fera pas tant que la guerre menée par la Russie en Ukraine fera rage. “Ce n’est pas le moment de prendre des mesures en ce sens, mais, bien sûr, ma volonté de le faire reste intacte”, a-t-elle déclaré.
2. Sur le budget
C’est aussi parce que la situation financière de la France l’inquiète que Marine Le Pen veut qu’un budget soit adopté au Parlement. “Une crise obligataire peut se déclencher du jour au lendemain”, a-t-elle alerté. Mais aussi parce que l’élection présidentielle se tient l’an prochain, “une lumière au bout du couloir”, a estimé la candidate.
Interrogée sur sa volonté, ou non, de censurer le gouvernement de Sébastien Lecornu, “MLP” a reconnu que c’était “différent” par rapport à l’année dernière. Son objectif : “Faire en sorte que [le budget] soit le moins imparfait possible”, pour éviter à tout prix une loi spéciale, qui deviendrait nécessaire si les textes budgétaires ne sont pas adoptés avant la fin de l’année. Car elle ne pourrait plus, alors, rectifier les mesures votées en 2026 avant l’examen d’un nouveau projet de loi de finances, pour 2028.
La candidate du RN a annoncé qu’elle présenterait la trajectoire budgétaire de son éventuel quinquennat le 6 octobre — dont “125 milliards d’économies” sur cinq ans.
3. Sur le climat
Advertisement
Alors que la France est frappée depuis plusieurs mois par des épisodes caniculaires, conséquences du dérèglement climatique, Marine Le Pen est revenue sur ses propos relativisant la crédibilité des scénarios du Giec, référence scientifique mondiale sur le climat.
Assurant que le réchauffement climatique “n’est absolument contesté par personne”, elle a estimé que certaines “hypothèses [du Giec] sont optimistes”, d’autres, “plus alarmistes”.

Candidat lui aussi pour la quatrième fois à l’élection présidentielle, le leader Insoumis défend une politique de non-alignement sur la scène internationale.
1. Sur l’Otan et le G20
Malgré l’intensification de la guerre hybride russe en France, Jean-Luc Mélenchon a réaffirmé qu’il était en faveur d’une sortie de l’Otan. Le candidat Insoumis a affirmé que, “quand on a affaire à quelqu’un comme Trump, c’est une affaire de dignité aussi”, pointant que l’Alliance ne pouvait pas dépendre de la seule bonne volonté du président américain.
Interpellé sur l’invitation lancée par Donald Trump à Vladimir Poutine de venir au G20 à Miami, en décembre, Jean-Luc Mélenchon a botté en touche. “Je ne suis pas le bon client, j’ai toujours condamné ce machin [le G20]. Moi, je connais l’Organisation [...] des Nations unies”, a-t-il justifié.
Advertisement

Le leader Insoumis s’est inquiété de l’ambition de l’Allemagne de construire la plus grande armée conventionnelle d’Europe. Republican Panic Sets In Over Prospects of a Massive Blue Wave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:54:29 UTC
02:54:29 KST

The DC Brief
Twice A Week
Essential context on the people, politics, and issues driving Washington.
With less than six weeks to go until Election Day, the sentiment among Republicans is shifting from nervous to fatalistic, as a pileup of bad news has many convinced they are heading toward an electoral disaster.
The warning signs are coming in quickly from across the map—much on it from red states where President Trump won comfortably just two years ago. Outside groups backing the GOP are now spending in the millions on Senate races in once-safe territories like Nebraska and Kansas; South Carolina, Mississippi, South Dakota, and Arkansas are all drawing renewed attention amid fears of a historically massive blue wave.
At a closed-door briefing on Wednesday with his caucus, Republican Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina delivered a particularly grim message: 2026 is not going to look anything like 2024. As leader of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, Senate Republicans’ official campaign arm, Scott is tasked with deciding how to dole out a sizable warchest in the final weeks of the midterms. To wit, he told his fellow Republican Senators that the NRSC’s top priorities are now almost entirely defense, as they scramble to avoid losing GOP-held seats in Texas, Iowa, Maine, and Alaska. They are also still investing to flip Democratic seats in Michigan and New Hampshire—where some recent polls show Democrats Abdul El-Sayed and Chris Pappas with small leads over Republicans Mike Rogers and John E. Sununu.
Notably absent from this plan were North Carolina and Georgia—two Senate seats Republicans were touting as major targets last year. Now some are writing those off as all but won by Democrats Roy Cooper and Jon Ossoff. An operative familiar with Scott’s thinking stressed that the NRSC’s strategy remains fluid until Election Day and noted that outside groups could still step in to back up their candidates in those states.
A day earlier in Iowa, which Trump won in 2024 by 13 points, state lawmakers received an even starker warning. Radio host Steve Deace, a real player in conservative circles there and a loyal Trump ally, told his followers on Wednesday afternoon that “Iowa House Republicans were informed by their own pollsters that if you are in a +15 district you’re within the margin for error, if you’re in a +10 district you’re underwater, and that this might end being an even worse midterm environment than 2006.”
Iowa Republicans on the ballot are not being subtle about their efforts to put some distance between their fortunes and the MAGA Movement. Rep. Zach Nunn voted last week to curb Trump’s deeply unpopular war against Iran—a month after campaigning with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who is running that war. Rep. Ashley Hinson, the GOP nominee for the open Senate seat, is running ads touting her work with Democrats, not her endorsement from Trump.
As Deace noted, “If the environment is this bad in my home state, where Trump has been the most popular political figure over the last decade, I can’t imagine where it is everywhere else.”
There’s similar scrambling in Texas, where a super PAC blessed by Senate Majority Leader John Thune is now on track to spend more than $100 million, an add on of $35 million to the $65 million the group had already booked in advertising to boost Ken Paxton’s bid against James Talarico. The total price tag for keeping the Senate seat is on track to approach $200 million just on the GOP side.
It’s little better for House Republicans. Between their official campaign arm, allied outside organizations, and the candidates themselves, there is a massive $485 million well of ad reservations between Aug. 1 and Election Day—and that’s just in districts Trump won, according to a Politico analysis.
Even Speaker Mike Johnson has grown frustrated with Trump and his constant introduction of tumult in the political ether. During his Sept. 13 appearance on NBC’s Meet the Press, Johnson appeared obviously annoyed as he kept getting asked about Trump’s fresh promise to send every American adult a $5,000 check if Republicans keep their House and Senate majorities. “I guess we’re going to spend the whole segment talking about this one issue,” Johnson said. “I want to talk about what we’ve actually done and not ideas on the table.”
It’s a common frustration across the party as gas prices—diesel especially—seem to know no limits, a war in Iran grinds toward its eighth month, and Russia’s war with Ukraine continues despite Trump’s promises to end it on “day one.” With all those drags on their ticket, Republicans have struggled to impress upon voters bragging points like the lowest crime rate in 126 years and declining prescription drug costs, or passing a massive tax cut.
The dynamic has left Republican strategists deeply frustrated. They have plenty of cash, succeeded (for the most part) in recruiting solid candidates, and are facing an opposition party that has spent much of the year fighting its own coalitions. Yet the environment still seems to be trending bluer than anyone anticipated.
A simmering fear is that the trendlines may get even worse in the coming weeks. As one Republican strategist told me this week, Election Day cannot come quickly enough.

'No eligible elector will be left behind': Goa CEO clarifies on 97 missing voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:52:42 UTC
02:52:42 KST

NEW DELHI: The Office of the Chief Electoral Officer of Goa on Thursday clarified the controversy surrounding 97 voters who were not included in the final electoral roll published in February 2026, saying the cases were subsequently processed through house-to-house visits and that many of the voters have since been enrolled.In a press note shared on X, the CEO's office said the 97 cases were separately processed by Booth Level Officers (BLOs) for completion of Form 6, the application used for inclusion of names in the electoral roll.
"Many have since been enrolled, while the remaining cases are being processed," the office said, adding that no eligible elector would be left out.The clarification comes amid a controversy over the exclusion of the 97 voters following Goa's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
What happened to 97 voters
According to an Indian Express report, the 97 voters had initially been flagged during the SIR process for what the Election Commission described as "logical discrepancies" in the electoral database.These discrepancies could arise from issues such as mismatches while linking an elector to parents or grandparents in older electoral rolls.The affected voters were subsequently given an opportunity to submit documents and objections.
In Goa, 649 electors came forward, following which Electoral Registration Officers (EROs) and Assistant EROs examined their cases. Officials found 97 cases where the earlier decisions needed to be reversed and the voters were eligible for inclusion.
However, the final electoral roll published on February 21, 2026, did not include the 97 names.
Software row at centre of controversy
The issue subsequently drew attention to the Election Commission's ECINet electoral-roll software.According to an Indian Express investigation, the Goa CEO's office sent eight communications between February 11 and 17 seeking a rollback or reversion facility that would allow the earlier deletion decisions to be reversed.The controversy has also triggered criticism from opposition parties, which have questioned the functioning and centralisation of the electoral-roll system.

Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

AI Arrived at the Worst Possible Moment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:49:04 UTC
02:49:04 KST

AI is not arriving in a world capable of receiving it. Instead, it is coming into a world that has spent the last two decades systematically dismantling the very foundations that would allow us to deploy such a powerful technology responsibly. Institutional authority, shared truth, and information integrity have been battered. We are building the most sophisticated cognitive technology in human history atop the most fractured trust landscape in modern memory.
If you wanted to design the worst possible moment for AI to emerge, you might create a moment like this one.
From post-truth to post-trust
A decade ago, we worried about living in a “post-truth” world. Oxford Dictionaries selected “post-truth” as its Word of the Year in 2016, defining it as circumstances in which objective facts are less influential in shaping public opinion than appeals to emotion and personal belief. Post-truth describes a world where facts still exist but are often overshadowed by emotional narratives.
What we are experiencing now goes deeper. I call this the “post-trust era:” a world where the very mechanisms that allow us to establish trust have broken down. It is not just that emotions sometimes trump facts. It is that we have lost shared foundations for deciding what counts as a fact in the first place.
Look at what has happened to our information ecosystem over the past two decades. We moved from a world in which truth was curated by editors, printed by presses, and distributed by a small number of recognizable intermediaries, to a world in which anyone can publish, amplify, distort, or fabricate. Data exploded, and social media fragmented audiences. Algorithms began optimizing for clicks, engagement, and sensationalism. The incentives shifted from accuracy to attention: virality over veracity, outrage over nuance, speed over scrutiny.
The numbers tell their own story. Nearly 8 in 10 people get directed to their news primarily through algorithmic systems such as social feeds, search engines, and aggregators, effectively outsourcing their information diet to systems they neither understand nor fully trust. In the United States, trust in the federal government has fallen from over 70% in the late 1950s to under 20% today. Confidence in mass media has dropped: fewer than one-third of Americans express even a “fair amount” of trust. Religious institutions, financial systems, healthcare organizations, and even science itself have seen trust erode.
Post-truth describes a distortion in how people weigh facts and feelings. Post-trust describes a deeper fracture: the loss of shared procedures for determining what is real.
When the first photographs appeared in the 1830s, people marveled at their fidelity. For nearly two centuries, seeing was believing. A picture was not perfect, but it was evidence.
In early 2023, an AI-generated image of Pope Francis wearing a stylish white puffer jacket spread across social media platforms. It was compelling because it sat in a narrow band between familiar and unexpected. The photo’s style, posture, and lighting borrowed credibility from decades of real photography. Many accepted it as real before they had time to question it.
Within two years, AI-generated images, voices, and video had become so pervasive and so convincing that the question was no longer “can you spot the fake?” but “can you trust anything you see?”
The ability to fabricate convincing “evidence” at scale has arrived just as our information ecosystem is most fragmented. Research from Duke and NYU shows that exposing people to opposing political views on social media can increase polarization rather than reduce it. A landmark study in Science found that false news spreads significantly faster and more widely than trustworthy news online. Neuroimaging research suggests that when people encounter information challenging their political beliefs, brain regions associated with negative emotion light up, while confirmatory information activates reward pathways. We are not only divided about facts. We are wired to process confirming and disconfirming information through different cognitive channels altogether.
That is the substrate into which AI arrives: a world where information is abundant, but trust is scarce, where consensus reality has splintered, and where the mechanisms for establishing shared truth have broken down.
A different kind of intelligence
Into this fractured substrate arrives something genuinely new. Not just another tool, but the first technology in history whose core competence is cognition.
Past technologies extended our capabilities while remaining subordinate to human thought. The printing press amplified the words we chose to print. Electricity transformed the energy we decided to harness. Combustion engines replaced the muscle power we used, and computers executed calculations we programmed. The internet distributed the messages we wrote.
AI breaks that pattern. It no longer merely executes tasks. It generates arguments, synthesizes information, makes recommendations, and produces creative work that feels, at a human level, like someone else’s thoughts. A single model can write an essay, summarize a legal transcript, translate a medical note, draft code, plan a marketing campaign, and compose music.
At the heart of most of these systems is an architecture that learns by predicting what comes next, a word, pixel, or token, in a sequence. These models do not know “truth” in the way humans understand it. They discover patterns, frequencies, and correlations in whatever data they are given.
And here is where the timing becomes critical: the data they are given is generated in a post-trust world.
AI is trained on our news stories, our social media feeds, our digitized books, our biased archives, our polarized debates, our conspiracy theories, our scientific breakthroughs, and our misinformation. It absorbs not only our knowledge but our distortions. It learns not only our facts but also our conflicts about those facts.
The result is a strange mirror. AI reflects us to ourselves, refracted through statistical patterns and scaled by computation. It gives us answers we cannot easily audit, based on training data we cannot thoroughly inspect, optimized for objectives we do not always control.
A new kind of cognitive infrastructure is emerging at the precise moment our social infrastructure for trust is under strain.
Excerpted from The Trust Code with permission from Tiffany Xingyu Wang.

Ukraine Opens Second EU Negotiating Cluster as Reform Delivery Shapes Further Accession Progress, KSE Institute Says

Ukraine Opens Its Second Negotiating Cluster, but Further EU Accession Progress Depends on Reform Delivery – KSE Institute
In Q3 2026, Ukraine continued to advance in its EU accession negotiations. On July 14, Cluster VI, “External Relations,” was formally opened, becoming the second open cluster. As of September 16, two of six negotiating clusters and seven of 33 chapters had been opened. At the same time, measurable progress in negotiations and legislation contrasted with slower delivery on rule-of-law commitments, according to KSE Institute’s Ukraine EU Accession Tracker for Q3 2026.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Hungary did not approve the opening of Cluster II, “Internal Market,” and Cluster III, “Competitiveness & Inclusive Growth.” Following the July government change, nine Ukraine Facility-linked bills were removed from the Verkhovna Rada’s agenda; seven have since returned, while two still have no replacement. The new government nevertheless remains committed to opening all six negotiating clusters and completing negotiations by the end of 2027.
Progress on rule-of-law commitments remains slow. Only one of the ten points in the Kachka–Kos plan has been fully completed. Six of the 11 priority laws identified by EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos have been adopted and signed, while two more are awaiting signature. Reforms concerning NEURC independence, state-aid control, and the restoration of civil-service competitions remain incomplete.
Putin Envoy Heads to New York as Washington Renews Ukraine Diplomacy Effort
Two of the EU’s three financing tracks are conditional on reform delivery. The Macro-Financial Assistance track totals €8.35 billion, but the next €3.7 billion installment has been delayed until at least Q4 because some conditions were not met by August 31. Following the revision of the Ukraine Facility, its total payment envelope increased to €40.9 billion, with 27 new reform steps added.
As of mid-September, Ukraine had received €21.6 billion in seven Ukraine Facility installments, while €1.7 billion from previous payments had been withheld due to unmet commitments. The €28.3 billion Ukraine Support Loan for defence is not conditional on reforms; €8.4 billion has already been disbursed. The further pace of accession will increasingly depend on completing prosecution and anti-corruption reforms, key legislative changes, and the conditions tied to European financing.
