Ministry of Social Policy completes work on pension system reform bill
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:44:35 EEST
01:44:35 KST

Ukraine's Minister of Social Policy, Family and Unity, Denys Uliutin, held a meeting with World Bank representatives led by the new Regional Director for Human Development, Aparnaa Somanathan.
"The parties discussed the ongoing modernization of the social protection system, which the Ministry of Social Policy is implementing with partner support under the World Bank-funded SPIRIT project. Particular attention was paid to pension system reform," the ministry stated.
It was noted that the Ministry of Social Policy has finalized the relevant bill, notably in cooperation with World Bank partners.
"The primary goal is to ensure the new system is fiscally sustainable in the long term," the agency emphasized.
As earlier reported, in September 2023, then-Prime Minister Denys Shmyhal announced that a reform of the solidarity-based pension system would be carried out in 2024.
In October 2023, then-Minister of Social Policy Oksana Zholnovych stated that the government would prepare the entire infrastructure for a funded pension system by 2025, though if the war continued, its launch would only be possible after victory.
In September 2024, First Deputy Minister of Social Policy Daria Marchak (now Deputy Minister of Economy) reported that the reform of the solidarity-based pension system had been developed.
Meanwhile, Zholnovych stated that the ministry plans to implement the funded pension system starting in 2026 and projected the launch of the new solidarity-based pension system for July 2025.
In early January 2025, Shmyhal announced plans to introduce basic social assistance and adopt legislation on a funded pension system in Ukraine in 2025.
In January 2025, Zholnovych stated that the initial accumulation of funds under the funded pension system could begin in 2026.
In August 2025, Uliutin, the Minister of Social Policy, Family and Unity, announced that work was underway with international partners on a temporary financial instrument to preserve pension savings and protect them from the impact of inflation.
In October 2025, Uliutin stated that introducing a mandatory funded pension system in Ukraine was premature at that time, as the financial market was not yet prepared to ensure the effective investment of such funds.
In November 2025, Uliutin announced that the ministry would complete the drafting of the pension reform bill by the end of December 2025.
In February 2026, Uliutin stated that he expected to finalize the pension reform work and submit the bill to the Verkhovna Rada in 2026. In his view, the current demographic situation and the state of the pension system were highly favorable for launching a comprehensive pension reform.
The government's action plan provides for the introduction of a voluntary funded pension system in 2027.

Settlers torch Palestinian cars amid West Bank raids, demolition
Unknown

2026-09-24
16:43:27 UTC

Breadcrumb
Settlers torch Palestinian cars amid West Bank raids, demolitions
Israeli settlers continued attacking Palestinians in the occupied West Bank on Thursday, following a night in which settlers torched cars, while international charity Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP) said Israeli raids and restrictions have prevented its staff from carrying out their work.
Israeli settlers wounded two Palestinians, leaving them with head injuries, in the village of Farkha, west of Salfit, on Thursday after attempting to steal a flock of sheep, the official Palestinian Wafa news agency reported.
The attacks came after settlers torched Palestinian-owned cars in the village of Atara, near Ramallah, overnight and sprayed graffiti calling for revenge following a car-ramming involving the son of Israel's ambassador to the US, Neria Leiter, on Wednesday.
Some of the graffiti read "Revenge Olga Alei Zahav Leiter", referring to the killing of Netanel Shakron, a resident of the Alei Zahav settlement who was shot dead on Sunday.
Other graffiti read "Qusra, wait for Thursday" and "Evacuations – we promised, we delivered", in an apparent reference to the village of Qusra, south of Nablus, which has been under siege by Israeli settlers and subjected to army restrictions since mid-August.
Thursday also marked the second consecutive day that Israeli forces continued to raze agricultural land in the village of Deir Nizam, in the central West Bank, while 17 apartments were also demolished.
The New Arab's West Bank correspondent, Naela Khalil, said the land being targeted is home to thousands of olive trees that are key to the livelihoods of Palestinians.
The head of the village council, Ramzi al-Araj, told The New Arab that the "bulldozing affects around 215 dunums of land located east of the village of Deir Nizam".
He described the operation as an example of "collective punishment", warning that its continuation could threaten the wider area and residents' livelihoods, particularly as the olive harvest season approaches.
In Beit Imrin, northwest of Nablus, Israeli forces bombed the home of Palestinian detainee Dawas Hassoun. Israeli authorities have accused Hassoun of killing a settler around a year and a half ago.
Israeli raid disrupts MAP work
According to MAP, Israeli forces carried out a raid earlier this month on the town of Biddu, northwest of Jerusalem, arresting at least 53 Palestinians.
In a statement shared with The New Arab, the organisation said one of its staff members had been prevented from working and that the raid had taken a physical and mental toll on them.
"The Israeli forces restricted movement, closed all the shops, bakeries and pharmacies, and harassed the citizens. They imposed a curfew that no one was allowed to leave their homes. They started firing tear gas and searched cars and houses. They entered a house in my village and turned it into a military post and an interrogation centre. They detained more than 50 men, interrogated them and beat them," the MAP staff member said.
They added that the town remained unsafe and vulnerable to Israeli attacks, which had prevented MAP from carrying out vital work, including medical check-ups, mental health services and the provision of medicine.
The latest developments come after Israeli ministers and members of parliament on Wednesday attended an event to inaugurate an illegal settlement built in an area from which Palestinian residents had been expelled.
The settlement, named Metzoke Eretz, is among 104 settlements legalised by the government during its last term.
Its outposts were built directly on registered privately owned Palestinian land.
The far-right Israeli minister Bezalel Smotrich attended the event, along with far-right MK Limor Son Har-Melech and Israeli media personality Yaakov Bardugo.
On Thursday, the Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission reported that Israeli authorities had approved the construction of 400 settlement units in the Karnei Shomron settlement, located on Palestinian land east of Qalqilya.
The commission said construction was set to begin on 23 November, marking a shift from the planning stage to the marketing and implementation phase.
Since the start of Israel's war on Gaza in 2023, there has been a surge in Israeli military raids and settler attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Guidance: Otterburn firing times
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:43:24 BST
01:43:24 KST

Otterburn firing times
Dates and times when Otterburn and Redesdale ranges and Bellshiel demolition range are being used for live firing.
Documents
Details
As seen in the Security Defence Review, the Army are at heightened readiness due to a new era of threat. This has placed greater demands on the Defence Training Estate across the UK, which is being used for training more regularly and at shorter notice.
As such, the firing time notifications published on Gov.UK have been standardised to show the daily timings for when live-firing is permitted on the UK DTE. This is a change from the previous method of showing when training bookings had been made in advance.
This to ensure safety of all users, as it is not possible to change Gov.UK notifications at short notice. Broadly, the only guaranteed safe times for access are before or after the firing times provided on this page, however there may be exceptional circumstances where extensions have been requested.
If you wish to use the DTE for recreation, please always refer to onsite safety warning signals to understand if the site is safe to access before doing so.
Your safety
Danger - When warning signals are displayed, regardless of the timings, do not cross the range boundary.
Warning signals are red flags by day and red lamps by night; range boundaries are marked by red and white poles.
Red flags and red lamps indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries.
Do not enter the danger area when in use, this could result in loss of life.
Do not touch any military debris, it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) via 0191 239 4261 or the police.
Learn more about accessing MOD training areas

Schlein calls schools decree shameful witch hunt at the expense of children
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:42:14 CEST
01:42:14 KST

Centre-left opposition Democratic
Party (PD) leader Elly Schlein on Thursday called a government
decree mandating a 30% cap on foreign pupils in Italian
classrooms and a burqa ban in Italian schools as a shameful
witch hunt at the expense of schoolchildren.
                                    
                                       
				"The outcome of today's Cabinet meeting confirms that the Meloni
government is living on another planet compared to the real
country," said Schlein.
                                    
                                       
				"Italian families are currently worried about the condition of
school buildings—with 68 collapses and 80,000 accidents in the
last year alone—and the more than 500 euros they must spend on
textbooks, all while Italian teachers' salaries remain among the
lowest in Europe.
                                    
                                       
				"Faced with all this, the government's response is to kick
foreign children out of classrooms.
                                    
                                       
				"Who do they think they are fooling?
"After four years of cuts and no serious investment in school
infrastructure, they are concocting a new witch hunt at the
expense of the youngest, singling them out as targets.
                                    
                                       
				"It is a shameful decree that attempts to mask the government's
inability to address the concrete problems facing public schools
behind a new ideological banner.
                                    
                                       
				"Schools are open to everyone, as our Constitution states."

====================================================================================================

Ambassador Cuculi on an official visit to Crete
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
18:42:12 CEST
01:42:12 KST

Ambassador Paolo Cuculi made an official visit to Crete, the largest Greek island, where he met with Governor Arnautakis, the mayor of Heraklion, Kalokairinos, and the CEO of the Heraklion Port Authority—managed by the Italian company Grimaldi – Papadakis. During the talks, the well-established synergies between Italy and Crete in the areas of trade, tourism, and culture were highlighted, particularly in light of the rich legacy left by the centuries-long Venetian presence on the island, with a view toward continuously strengthening ties with Italy and its territories.
                                    
                                       
				   Accompanied by Professor Greco of La Sapienza University, the Ambassador also visited the archaeological site of Phaistos, which will be added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2025, where Italian archaeologists have been conducting excavations for over a century under the coordination of the Italian Archaeological School of Athens (SAIA). The mission, currently led by Professor Pietro Militello of the University of Catania and coordinated by SAIA, brings together scholars from the CNR and the Universities of Bologna, Catania, Genoa, Rome “La Sapienza,” Salerno, Udine, Uninettuno, and Ca’ Foscari in Venice, in close coordination with Greek authorities.
                                    
                                       
				   The Ambassador then met with a large delegation from the Italian community residing on the island and presented the honor of Knight of the Order of the Star of Italy to the Honorary Vice Consul in Heraklion, Paolo Bartolozzi. As part of efforts to promote Italy’s artistic excellence throughout Greece, the visit concluded with a concert by the Caligo Quartet of the Carlo Felice Theater Foundation in Genoa, organized by the Embassy at the Heraklion Cultural Center, which was attended by a large audience of dignitaries, representatives from the business and cultural sectors, and members of the Italian community.
                                
ALL RIGHTS RESERVED © Copyright ANSA

Russian attack puts three countries on alert as drones enter Moldova and Romania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:40:43 UTC
01:40:43 KST

Moldova’s Defense Ministry reported four drone incursions, Romania’s Defense Ministry confirmed a drone crash, and Poland’s Operational Command scrambled fighters twice during Russia’s 24 September attack on Ukraine.
The strike wave forced Moldova to close part of its airspace, Romania to warn residents and launch F-16 fighter jets, and Poland to activate aircraft, air defenses, and radar. No casualties were reported in the two confirmed crashes, and Poland detected no incursion during its first deployment. Moldova has recorded dozens of Russian drone incursions this year.
The drones approached from Ukraine’s Vinnytsia, Odesa, and Chernivtsi oblasts, according to Moldova’s Defense Ministry. Authorities temporarily closed part of the country’s northern airspace.
Near Cernița in northern Moldova, one drone struck a tree, fell into a field beside a farm, and exploded, police said. No casualties were reported.
Investigators preliminarily identified the camera-equipped wreckage as a Gerbera, a low-cost Russian drone often used during attacks on Ukraine. Police said it was the first device of that type found in Moldova.
Police also reported a resident’s account of another explosion near Vadul Rașcov, but said they were still investigating the location.
Romanian radar first tracked an aerial target over Ukraine near the border before it entered northern Romania, the Defense Ministry said. Romania launched two F-16s and sent emergency alerts to residents’ phones in the area. The drone remained in Romanian airspace for about four minutes before crashing near Solca, the ministry said. Officials reported no casualties or damage and had not identified the drone’s origin.
Poland’s Operational Command launched fighters twice in response to Russian strikes on western Ukraine. The first Polish deployment ended around 08:00 with no airspace violation detected; the command announced a second at 09:07. It also activated ground-based air defenses and radar.
The incursions came amid a wider assault. Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 282 drones of various types, along with ballistic and other missiles, overnight into 24 September. Ukrainian officials reported detecting four drones over Chernivtsi Oblast, the Ukrainian region bordering Moldova and Romania, and shooting down three.
Moldova’s repeated airspace breaches
The latest incident followed several breaches in August. An unidentified drone exploded near Crocmaz on 9 August. Another object exploded near Talmaza on 17 August after Moldova briefly closed part of its airspace.
President Maia Sandu said Russian drones had entered Moldovan airspace 39 times in 2026, compared with 17 times throughout 2025. Moldova has portable air-defense weapons and electronic warfare equipment, but Sandu said these chiefly protect individual sites. Her government is working with partners to expand air-defense coverage and speed up threat warnings.

NATO strengthens intelligence sharing due to the threat from Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:39:45 EEST
01:39:45 KST

NATO strengthens intelligence sharing due to the threat from Russia
Kyiv • UNN
NATO is strengthening intelligence sharing following a series of incidents likely linked to Russia. The Alliance considers a limited attack unlikely, but possible.
NATO is increasing intelligence sharing in response to a wave of acts of sabotage and other incidents likely linked to Russia, but the Alliance must maintain "calm and confidence" in its ability to counter any threat from Moscow. A senior NATO commander told Reuters on Thursday, UNN reports.
Details
The statement by U.S. Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich came after Denmark's military intelligence service warned that Russia would likely intensify its hybrid war against the West in the coming months (the term encompasses a range of attacks that do not reach the level of a full-scale military assault).
The Danish service also said there was a "low but growing risk" that Moscow could launch a limited military attack on one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
"This is concerning," said Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, commenting on a series of incidents in recent weeks, including an attempted drone attack on Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport and a Russian vessel firing signal flares toward a Danish military helicopter.
"But we must remain calm and confident that we, as an Alliance — the most powerful alliance in history — have the tools and mechanisms necessary to manage these risks," he added.
The publication notes that Moscow has repeatedly denied involvement in hybrid warfare or sabotage operations in NATO countries, as well as any plans to stoke conflict.
In addition
Grynkewich gave Reuters a telephone interview on his way to the change-of-command ceremony at NATO headquarters in Norfolk, Virginia, where a British Army general is taking over the post from a U.S. Navy vice admiral.
Responding to a question about the risk of a limited Russian attack on NATO territory, Grynkewich emphasized the Alliance's readiness for such a scenario, noting that such a development was "unlikely, but cannot be ruled out."
Grynkewich rejected the suggestion that Russian dictator Vladimir Putin might see an opportunity to strike NATO because the United States had depleted a significant portion of its global stocks of long-range precision missiles during the war with Iran (according to people familiar with the data). "Absolutely not. He had better not try to do that while I am in command here," he said, adding that NATO has every capability to defend every inch of its territory.
"If we move beyond the current phase and see new threats emerge, I am confident that I already have the necessary authority to take measures to deter any aggression against the Alliance."
What else is worth knowing
The transfer of command in Norfolk to a European officer is part of a broader reorganization that meets the requirements of U.S. President Donald Trump: European countries must take on more responsibility for their own security. A European officer will also lead NATO's Allied Joint Force Command in Naples.
NATO's Allied Joint Force Command in Norfolk is responsible for operations in the Arctic and Northern Europe, as well as for protecting transatlantic supply routes.
Seeking to reassure European allies concerned about a review of the U.S. military presence on the continent, Grynkewich said Washington would continue to provide NATO with "critically important but more limited resources and capabilities" as Europeans assume a greater role.
He noted that regarding the number of U.S. troops that will remain in Europe and "which specific forces may be redeployed," "there is no predetermined decision." Currently, about 80,000 U.S. service members are stationed on the continent.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to withdraw from NATO — an organization dominated by the United States since its founding in 1949 — accusing Europeans of benefiting from security without making an adequate contribution.

Taiwan has redrawn the AI map
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:39:07 UTC
01:39:07 KST

Artificial intelligence (AI) is usually discussed as a technology story, but in Asia it has become a trade story, and nowhere is that more visible than in Taiwan. The nation has spent four decades mastering semiconductor manufacturing, and now finds itself at the center of the fastest redrawing of Asia’s trade map in a generation. What Taiwan does with that position, at home as much as abroad, would shape its economy for decades to come.
The scale of the shift is striking.
Intra-Asian trade in AI-enabling goods — the chips, components and equipment on which the technology runs — has roughly doubled since before the COVID-19 pandemic to nearly US$2 trillion last year, and AI-linked goods now account for about one-third of Asia’s total exports, close to twice their share a decade ago, HSBC Global Investment Research said.
Within that surge, Taiwan’s gains stand apart. Its share of global trade in the intermediate inputs that feed AI hardware has nearly doubled over the past decade, and about 80 percent of its exports now fall within the AI category, the highest concentration of any economy in Asia. Taiwan does not merely participate in the AI hardware economy; to a considerable extent, it is its center of gravity.
What has changed most in the past two years is not the scale of Taiwan’s role, but its geography. Taiwan’s trade with ASEAN in AI-enabling goods reached US$47.4 billion in the first quarter of this year, up 77 percent from a year earlier, and the bloc now takes about one-quarter of Taiwan’s exports, up sharply from just a few years ago.
The Singapore corridor illustrates the mechanics: Taiwanese exports to the city-state rose 160 percent year-on-year in the three months to May, lifting Taiwan from Singapore’s fourth-largest trading partner in 2024 to its largest last year, a shift underpinned by Taiwanese semiconductor firms whose investment into Singapore’s manufacturing sector has grown more than 10-fold compared with the late 2010s.
The counterpart to this southward tilt is a historic rebalancing away from China. Taiwan’s trade balance with China slipped into a deficit in July last year for the first time since 2002, followed by several months of deficit early this year, as export controls redirected advanced chip shipments toward the US. Nearshoring is adding a further channel, with Taiwan’s exports to Mexico nearly tripling last year as high-end hardware is assembled there for the US market.
Taiwan’s deepening trade deficit with South Korea, at a record high, tells a similar story of centrality rather than weakness. South Korean high-bandwidth memory flows into Taiwan’s advanced packaging facilities, where it is integrated into the AI servers and accelerators that ship onward to US customers, a complementarity that has made Taiwan South Korea’s fourth-largest export market. Taiwan sits at the point where the region’s most valuable inputs converge and its most valuable outputs depart.
The next phase of Taiwan’s AI story is being written at home. Global technology leaders including Amazon Web Services, Google and Nvidia have committed to cloud regions, data centers and research facilities in Taiwan, drawn by the density of the semiconductor ecosystem and the depth of the engineering talent around it. There is considerable room to grow: Taiwan’s own data center investment remains a small fraction of the US level relative to the size of its economy, which suggests that the domestic build-out has barely begun even as Taiwanese chips power data centers everywhere else.
The macroeconomic payoff is already substantial. HSBC expects Taiwan’s economy to be among the fastest-growing in the world this year, the fastest in Asia, with a current account surplus that ranks among the largest anywhere relative to the size of its economy. That surplus points to a further opportunity: As Asia’s AI infrastructure demand rises, the region’s savers might increasingly deploy capital at home rather than channelling it abroad, and few economies are better positioned than Taiwan — with its combination of export earnings, deep corporate balance sheets and expanding domestic investment pipeline — to convert hardware leadership into broader financial market development and wealth creation.
The risks that accompany this position deserve honest treatment. With four-fifths of exports tied to a single technology cycle, Taiwan is more exposed than any of its neighbors to a downturn in global AI capital spending, tighter export controls or sharp swings in semiconductor prices, and some of the current export strength might reflect front-loaded orders that normalize over time. Rising computer and component prices could also feed inflation pressures at home and across the region.
Yet concentration is the consequence of being indispensable. Taiwan spent four decades building the capabilities the AI era demands, and the same discipline applied to the next stage, diversifying its trade corridors, deepening its domestic digital infrastructure and putting its considerable savings in the transition would extend that indispensability well beyond the factory gate.
The world’s AI ambitions run through Taiwan. The task ahead is to ensure that Taiwan’s economy captures the full value of that position.
Adam Chen is CEO and head of banking at HSBC Taiwan.
Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Indeed, since 1979 it has been embedded in US law, with the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) charging the US with helping to improve the island’s ability to deter an attack from
Academia Historica director Chen Tsui-lien (陳翠蓮), speaking at the handover ceremony for her new role on Monday, said that when she accepted the position, she knew that her peaceful life as a history professor was a thing of the past, and that from now on she would have to “wear a helmet.” A specialist in Taiwan’s post-World War II history and the 228 Incident, she has been accused of being politically divisive. When Panama severed diplomatic relations with Taiwan and recognized China in 2017, Beijing achieved one of its most important diplomatic victories in Central America. However, nearly a decade later, Panama is demonstrating that diplomatic recognition does not necessarily eliminate Taiwan from a country’s political system. Panama and Taiwan had diplomatic relations for more than 100 years and the goodwill between the countries was displayed last week when Panama’s National Assembly established an interparliamentary exchange group with the Legislative Yuan. Photo: CNA

Ambling Changhua’s sumptuous cultural park
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:39:05 UTC
01:39:05 KST

Located a 40-minute drive south of Changhua City, the Cheng Mei Cultural Park (成美文化園) lies beyond a roadside verge of tall, thick trees.
A right turn follows a long allee flanked by manicured foliage, from the thick, burly heads of large bonsai trees to the crimped bark of Japanese black pine and lush Chinese juniper.
With many stony, tree-lined scenic pathways and towering coniferous and deciduous trees, visitors will find themselves meandering happily through a sprawling, artistically sculpted masterpiece.
Photo: Shane O’Reilly
This undulating 10-hectare private garden estate is all thanks to the prominent Wei Family (魏家), local food and drink magnates who founded this estate as a passion project of sorts.
After a massive magnitude 7.3 earthquake in September 1999 destroyed their 1885 ancestral home, they began a seven-year restoration plan in 2005, which was expanded to include these incredibly ornate gardens in honor of their parents and ancestors.
And as such, this handsomely renovated ancestral home is the architectural gem at the heart of everything here.
The Dream-Sowing Seed (播夢種子 / 播夢種籽), a tall, bulbous wood and steel installation, is located approximately 50m in from the entrance and serves as an in-and-out gateway from one garden trail to another.
A labyrinth of landmarks includes a prominent lake, ornamental pools replete with fat, mottled koi, mini waterfalls and a colossal 500-year-old Burmese Rosewood.
The meticulously pruned He-De Garden (和園) is home to a grove of impressive pine and cypress species as well as a pond and a traditional footbridge.
It’s all a sinuous, whimsical affair, wayfaring from billowing bushes to carefully crafted themed gardens and quaint cobblestone walkways.
Beautifully sheared, the topiary breathes an air of natural, flowery scents, a home to fluttering butterflies and dragonflies dancing and skimming water surfaces.
On hot summer days, visitors can recline in the underarm shade of many a knotted, gnarled tree from the comfort of a strategically placed bench or Adirondack chair.
Gravel avenues and babbling waterways run in tandem, while clearings open out to lavender patches or garden folly, their wood frames wound with the trellises of hanging plants.
Occasionally, banks of verdant shrubbery are broken by pops of color from Pink Cassia, Queen’s Wreath, and splashes of Ixora. However, much of this vibrancy will be lost between October and March.
ANCESTRAL HOME
Keeping much of its historical majesty intact, Chengmei Gongtang (成美公堂) unfolds as a layered, multi-winged, and rather angular red-brick, red-tile structure encompassing three courtyards.
Beyond the painstakingly preserved bedrooms and altar room, dozens of chambers are ideal as showrooms for what has become a traditional folk museum, with numerous interactive displays and educational spaces.
There’s even an air-conditioned, mahogany-furnished, high-wood-beam screening room with films on continuous playback, perfectly suited to relax, cool down and learn a little about the estate before venturing onward.

A 2022 paper in Materials, by Chen Wei-sheng (陳偉聖), Jian Guo-cai (簡國財) and Lee Cheng-han (李政翰), demonstrated selective extraction. It also identified unfinished work, including multistage processing and regenerating the extraction liquid. The experiment established a technical foundation, without claiming an industrial business. Taiwan upgrades S China Sea outpost patrol capacity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:39:04 UTC
01:39:04 KST

Taiwan has upgraded its maritime patrol capacity around the Pratas Islands (Dongsha Islands, 東沙群島) in the disputed South China Sea, including regularly sending larger ships there, the government said on Wednesday, responding to an increase in Chinese activities.
Lying roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong, the Taiwan-controlled Pratas Islands are seen by security experts as vulnerable to a Chinese attack due to their distance — more than 400km — from Taiwan.
In a statement late on Wednesday, the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) said its overall patrol and enforcement capacity in Pratas waters has been “comprehensively upgraded.”
Photo courtesy of the Coast Guard Administration
With the completion of a wharf project in July, a newly built 100-tonne-class patrol boat has been formally stationed at Pratas, “significantly enhancing nearshore patrol capabilities and immediate mobile response capacity,” it added.
Additionally, large patrol vessels are being regularly deployed to patrol waters around Pratas, demonstrating “strong multilayered deterrence and mobile enforcement capabilities,” it said.
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Chinese coast guard ships have increased their patrols near Pratas, the most recent of which happened earlier this month.
The CGA is in charge of security for Pratas, which also has an airstrip, but no permanent civilian population other than the military.
The CGA also said that it had confiscated nine Chinese fishing boats around Pratas since the start of this year and had repurposed them for reef patrol and marine conservation work.
The Pratas Islands are a national park with largely untouched reefs, given tourism is almost non-existent.
Taiwan’s other South China Sea outpost is Itu Aba (Taiping Island, 太平島) in the contested Spratly Islands (Nansha Islands, 南沙群島) in the southern part of the sea.

Housing market shows signs of stabilizing: poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:39:01 UTC
01:39:01 KST

Taiwan’s housing market has shown signs of stabilizing as consumers become less bearish on property prices, but tight mortgage lending is likely to keep any recovery in transactions modest, a survey released by Evertrust Rehouse Co (永慶房屋) on Wednesday showed.
The share of consumers expecting home prices to fall next quarter dropped to 28 percent this quarter from 36 percent in the previous quarter, while those expecting prices to remain unchanged rose to 43 percent from 37 percent and those anticipating prices to rise edged up 2 percentage points to 29 percent, the survey showed.
“The shift suggests housing sentiment is moving from outright pessimism toward stability rather than a broad-based return of bullish expectations,” Evertrust research manager Daniel Chen (陳賜傑) told a news conference in Taipei.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
The government’s new stimulus program for first-time homebuyers, which took effect last month, has become more targeted, with eligibility limited to applicants under 50 years old with annual income not exceeding NT$2 million (US$62,933).
That explains why about 65 percent of respondents supported the age limit, while 67 percent backed the income cap, Chen said.
The measures, along with the central bank’s selective credit controls, have helped drive investors out of the market, leaving demand from owner-occupiers as a dominant source of support, he said.
However, tighter mortgage lending remains a major constraint, Evertrust general manager Yeh Ling-chi (葉凌棋) said.
The median rate on first-home mortgages has risen to 2.6 percent, while rates on second-home loans have climbed to 2.9 percent, increases of 54 and 72 basis points respectively, Evertrust data showed.
Some lenders are also taking one to three months to review and disburse property loans amid strong demand for corporate financing, including from Taiwanese technology companies expanding overseas, Yeh said.
In some cases, borrowers are being pushed back to January next year, as banks prioritize developer-arranged property loans and affluent customers, he said.
“That is limiting the ability of buyers to transact even as housing sentiment improves,” Yeh said.
Evertrust expects existing-home transactions to edge higher in the fourth quarter, while prices remain broadly stable.
Housing transactions nationwide fell 2 percent in the first seven months of this year from a year earlier, although the pace of decline has continued to narrow amid a strong economy, Yeh said.
The recent easing of second-home lending rules could help revive demand, but continued credit restrictions are likely to limit the scale of any rebound, he said.
For the full year, housing transactions are expected to range between 256,000 and 267,000 units, representing a decline of 2 percent or an increase of 2 percent from last year, he added.

Foundation for Defense of Democracies China Program chair Matt Pottinger yesterday praised Taiwan for taking “creative and resilient” steps to maintain a secure communications environment.
He made the comment during a meeting with President William Lai (賴清德) at the Presidential Office in Taipei, his fourth visit since Lai took office in 2024.
Lai thanked the foundation for “taking concrete action to support Taiwan.”
Photo courtesy of the Presidential Office
He also referred to the Resilient Taiwan for Sustainable Democracy International Forum, held on Saturday last week by the Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Committee for the second consecutive year.
More than 500 experts and guests from Taiwan and abroad attended the forum, demonstrating “the spirit of solidarity and cooperation among democratic partners,” Lai said.
“When authoritarianism seeks to spread fear, democratic societies should spread confidence through resilience,” he said.
Lai thanked Pottinger for delivering the forum’s closing keynote, during which he said that “peace through strength is essential to maintaining Taiwan’s freedom and prosperity.”
Pottinger’s remarks were in line with Taiwan’s efforts to build resilience, Lai said, adding that “peace depends on strength, strength depends on resilience and resilience depends on unity.”
The delegation also helped conduct a tabletop exercise last week focused on bolstering communications resilience, which was extremely helpful, he said.
“Moving forward, Taiwan will continue to build diverse, decentralized communications systems with backup capabilities,” Lai said.
Pottinger, who previously served as US deputy national security adviser, thanked Lai for receiving the delegation and wished those present a happy Mid-Autumn Festival.
The delegation saw how Taiwan’s training has become more closely aligned with real-world conditions, Pottinger said, adding that practical resilience training involving a growing share of the population was a good way to build confidence and ultimately improve deterrence.
Cross-party support has also helped pass several defense budgets, he added.
The delegation was “deeply impressed by the creative and resilient steps the Taiwan team took to maintain a secure communications environment,” Pottinger said, adding that he looked forward to discussing more issues with Lai.

NZ calls China its most persistent cyberthreat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:59 UTC
01:38:59 KST

China is New Zealand’s most persistent and capable state-backed cyberthreat, as foreign actors targeted government agencies and organizations in sectors including health, education and information technology, the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said in a report released yesterday.
The center, part of the New Zealand intelligence community, said it had identified activity suspected to originate from foreign state actors that put sensitive New Zealand information at risk.
It linked suspected state-sponsored cyberactivity to actors from China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, according to its annual Cyber Threat Report.
Photo: Reuters
“Of these nations the People’s Republic of China is the most persistent and capable state actor undertaking cyberactivity in New Zealand,” the report said.
The assessment is the latest warning from a Western-aligned intelligence agency over alleged Chinese cyberespionage, which Beijing has routinely denied. It follows a report release last month by the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service that said that China was the only country New Zealand had detected conducting espionage “at scale.”
“China urges the relevant institution in New Zealand to stop spreading lies and creating conflict and to do more to foster mutual understanding and trust between China and New Zealand,” a Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson said when asked about the report.
“China always opposes and resolutely cracks down on hacking attacks in accordance with law,” they said during a regular briefing.
The cybersecurity report said that 86 of 369 cyberincidents deemed to be of potential national significance in the year to June had suspected links to state-sponsored actors.
The incidents included activity targeting government agencies, health and education organizations and information technology managed-service providers.
The agency warned that geopolitical competition was increasingly playing out in the South Pacific, where it was aware of state-backed cyberespionage targeting governments and infrastructure.
New Zealand has close family, cultural, political and economic ties across the Pacific, and such activity could affect citizens, businesses and civic institutions, it said.
State-backed actors were likely to target organizations that operate infrastructure or networks, provide essential public services or hold information that could offer a strategic advantage, the NCSC said.
It said that cyberespionage can be difficult to detect, with actors conducting reconnaissance and positioning access in systems over months or years before using it for intelligence gathering or disruption.
Long-running intrusions could lead to the compromise of operational technology and the loss of corporate and personal data, it said.

White House still blocking reporters despite court order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:59 UTC
01:38:59 KST

A US federal judge early yesterday temporarily blocked US President Donald Trump’s ban of three news outlets from the White House grounds, ordering that CNN, MS NOW and Politico must have their access restored. However, reporters for two of the outlets were denied entry hours after the ruling.
The back-and-forth is the latest in an extraordinary showdown between Trump and media outlets whose coverage he dislikes.
Trump first announced he was banning the outlets on Friday, assailing what he called “fake news,” and later saying that their reporting was a risk to national security. The outlets said in a joint lawsuit that the ban was a blatant free speech violation because it singled them out for the content of their coverage.
Photo: AP
In his late-night ruling, US District Judge Timothy Kelly ordered the White House to “immediately return, reinstate and restore” the three outlets’ access.
They had met the legal thresholds to obtain a temporary restraining order, in effect for 14 days, and were likely to succeed in showing that their press passes were revoked without due process, he said.
“This is a high bar, but plaintiffs have met it,” he wrote.
Kelly — whom Trump nominated in 2017 and who ordered a CNN journalist’s access restored in a similar case in 2018 — also said the government must have clear standards for conduct that would lead to revoking a press pass.
He called the standard of objectionable reporting outlined in letters that the White House sent the outlets “so vague it hardly does the trick.”
The judge also made clear he did not buy the administration’s argument that the news outlets’ reporting endangered national security, adding that Trump himself had not used that argument in the beginning, focusing solely on what he called negative coverage.
“Nothing in the record ... suggests that the revocation of plaintiffs’ hard passes was motivated by national security concerns,” he wrote.
The ruling came after Kelly heard arguments in an emergency hearing on Wednesday. Temporary restraining orders are typically designed to preserve the “status quo” pending a closer review of the case by the court.
However, a few hours after the ruling, a CNN reporter said she was denied entry to the White House compound. Politico said one of its reporters was also blocked.
The White House did not immediately respond to an e-mail requesting comment.
Attorney for the outlets Theodore Boutrous Jr argued in the hearing that there was an urgent need for renewed access, saying that the ban caused irreparable harm to the outlets at a time of momentous news events.
“We’re at war. We have world leaders coming to Washington,” he said.

Ethan Hawke leads a tense, Depression-era thriller in  ‘The Weight’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:58 UTC
01:38:58 KST

In April 1933, US president Franklin D. Roosevelt signed an executive order banning the hoarding of gold and requiring Americans to deliver excess quantities to a Federal Reserve Bank by that May. The policy isn’t the subject of much discussion in the tense and earthy thriller The Weight, but it does set the stage for a heist, in which a group of work camp prisoners are assembled for a dangerous, off-the-books gold smuggling job, with Ethan Hawke leading the charge.
Hawke plays Samuel Murphy, a single father to a young daughter, Penny (Avy Berry), who is struggling to make ends meet four years into the Great Depression. Murphy is smart, capable and honest, which does not necessarily benefit him or his daughter in these greedy and violent times. They return from church one day to find they’ve been evicted from their apartment. On the search for a new one, some toughs give them a hard time. But self-defense excuses only go so far when the agitator you’ve punched in the face is a police officer. Soon, Murphy is being shipped off to a work camp. If he’s not out in time, Penny will become a ward of the state.
With a raspy voice and a world-weary look, Murphy tries to keep to himself at the camp. But he can’t help but distinguish himself as a resourceful problem solver, and the warden, Clancy ( Russell Crowe ), takes notice. Clancy isn’t your run-of-the-mill sadistic, mustache-twirling kind of warden. He can seem even a little likable at times. But he’s also the one with all the power: It’s hard to know if he can be trusted even if he gives the workers the occasional day off. Still, when Clancy promises that if Murphy pulls off the gold job, he’ll sign papers to free Murphy so that he can reunite with Penny, he decides it’s a bet worth taking.
Photo: AP
So Murphy puts together a team of fellow prisoners: Singh (Avi Nash), Olson (Lucas Lynggaard Tonnesen) and Rankin (Austin Amelio) to help transport heavy gold bars from point A to B through the wet Oregon wilderness (played by Bavaria). There are also a few deeply suspicious and ornery guys who are working for the ones planning the operation, and a Native American woman, Anna (Julia Jones), who joins the trek as well. It’s a big group trying to stay under the radar on this white-knuckle journey, in which they have to figure out how to cross a broken rope bridge with the heavy gold (it involves a very stressful tossing and catching scheme) and ford a river to cover their tracks. No one is sure they can trust anyone in the group. And then there’s the wild card terror of the giggly lone vagrant looking for something to eat and wondering what exactly is in all those heavy-looking bags.
Hawke feels natural in this environment, clad in denim workwear that may have been standard issue at the time but also looks like something your average Brooklynite dad would wear. And he’s believable as the guy whose brain gets him out of more scrapes than his brawn.
The Weight comes from director Padraic McKinley and writers Matthew Chapman, Matthew Booi and Shelby Gaines, who keep the momentum going at a rousing and confident clip.
It is very much a “dad movie,” which isn’t, in this case, a bad or even limiting thing. More than a few people have compared it to something Clint Eastwood might have done at some point — just a solid, hearty, meat-and-potatoes kind of movie.

A 2022 paper in Materials, by Chen Wei-sheng (陳偉聖), Jian Guo-cai (簡國財) and Lee Cheng-han (李政翰), demonstrated selective extraction. It also identified unfinished work, including multistage processing and regenerating the extraction liquid. The experiment established a technical foundation, without claiming an industrial business. Motorcycle training to be boosted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:55 UTC
01:38:55 KST

Five hours of practical training would be added to motorcycle rider training courses from Jan. 1 next year, including three additional hours of on-road training, the Ministry of Transportation and Communications said on Wednesday, adding that pilot on-road motorcycle license tests in selected regions will also begin in October next year.
The ministry since January has been redesigning licensing in a bid to improve drivers’ skills.
Although attending a training course is not required prior to taking a motorcycle license test, the Highway Bureau provides subsidies to do so.
Photo: CNA
In the first six months of this year, 784 motorcyclists died within 30 days of being involved in a traffic incident, accounting for nearly 60 percent of total deaths in the category, ministry data showed.
Highway Bureau data showed that 59,912 people obtained government subsidies to take motorcycle training courses last year, up from 40,378 in 2024.
The training course for a regular motorcycle license consists of six hours of classroom instruction and 10 hours of practical training.
Proposed amendments to the Regulations Governing the Management of Private Motor Vehicle Driver Training Institutions (民營汽車駕駛人訓練機構管理辦法) announced on Wednesday would increase practical training hours for license applicants to 15, effective from Jan. 1 next year.
The five additional hours would be two hours of motorcycle handling skills at the training venue and three hours of on-road training to improve field of vision awareness, recognition of road conditions and the judgement of when to use headlights, the ministry said.
In addition to the increase in practical training hours, the ministry also announced that it would begin a trial in October next year to conduct on-road tests for motorcycle license applicants.
People would be eligible for a NT$1,300 subsidy after applying through a driving school, paying the course fee, completing the training and obtaining a license within the subsidy period, the Highway Bureau’s Web site said.
People who undergo post-test road-safety training are eligible for a NT$1,200 subsidy, while those who undergo pre-test road-driving training can receive NT$2,500, it said.

US lawmakers urge Trump to maintain arms sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:54 UTC
01:38:54 KST

Four US Senate Republicans as well as a bipartisan group of US representatives wrote letters to the White House on Wednesday calling on the administration to uphold US commitments to supply Taiwan with arms ahead of US President Donald Trump’s summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平).
Xi is expected to press Trump to halt Taiwan arms sales altogether during his three-day visit to Washington, sources briefed on the matter said.
The Chinese leader landed in Washington on Wednesday night and was after press time last night to hold talks with Trump.
Photo: Bloomberg
The Trump administration in December last year approved an US$11 billion arms package to Taiwan, the largest ever, but a second US$14 billion package has been on hold for months.
US senators Mitch McConnell, John Cornyn, Lisa Murkowski and Thom Tillis wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth expressing concern about more than US$15 billion in stalled national security assistance for Taiwan.
The letter cites the US Department of State’s failure to move ahead with US$300 million in foreign military financing the US Congress appropriated for Taiwan, the defense department’s failure to obligate US$1 billion and the administration’s decision to withhold approval for a US$14 billion package of foreign military sales.
“We are concerned by President Trump’s description of Taiwan as ‘a very good negotiating chip’ in engagements with Xi Jinping and the Chinese Communist Party,” the letter said.
“It is difficult to imagine how the United States might credibly project influence deterrence in the Indo-Pacific if the price of keeping up diplomatic appearances is denying our partners key deterrent capabilities,” it said.
The state and defense departments did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Rubio, speaking to reporters in New York, said the administration had to balance broader needs.
“I know everyone’s focused on Taiwan, but I want you to focus globally for a moment. If we sell you something, we don’t have it anymore. Now, we may be able to make it in the future, but we don’t have it right now,” he said.
“Anytime we do any sales — not to Taiwan, to anybody — it is always balanced against what are our own needs in different parts of the world and whether we can afford to sell something, because we may need it for ourselves. So that’s going through that process,” he added.
Trump’s fellow Republicans in Congress rarely question his administration’s actions publicly.
Three of the senators who signed Wednesday’s letter — McConnell, Cornyn and Tillis — are leaving the Senate at the end of this year, with only Murkowski remaining.
In a separate letter addressed to Trump, a bipartisan group of seven US representatives urged the president not to consult China on arms sales to Taiwan.
They commended the administration for its “record-breaking arms package for Taiwan” announced in December last year, saying that this package, alongside other steps taken to deepen bilateral military cooperation, is successfully helping deter Chinese aggression.
“Increasing Taiwan’s self-defense capabilities, including through additional arms sales, is essential to US security,” they wrote.
The letter also pressed Trump to demand the release of wrongfully detained US citizens in China, called for expanded bilateral law enforcement cooperation to combat the fentanyl crisis and urged Trump to hold Beijing accountable for its weaponization of critical mineral supply chains.
The signatories were US representatives Young Kim, Ami Bera, Aumua Amata Coleman Radewagen, Gabe Amo, James Moylan, Michael McCaul and Ryan Mackenzie.

Vouchers program lifts registration of pets, official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

A lottery for vouchers has helped increase the number of registered cats and dogs nationwide by 18,500, Animal Welfare Department Deputy Director Chen Chung-hsing (陳中興) said yesterday.
As of the end of last month, about 2.73 million cats and dogs had been registered by their owners, Chen said.
People completed registration for an additional 18,500 pets after the Ministry of Agriculture on Aug. 25 launched the vouchers draw, he said.
Photo: CNA
To enter the draw for the vouchers, people had to complete the registration of their cat or dog, or confirm a registration completed prior to the start of the voucher campaign, he said, with people limited to one entry each.
The Animal Protection Act (動物保護法) stipulates that owners can be fined NT$3,000 to NT$15,000 if they fail to register their cats or dogs aged four months or older.
Nearly 33,000 pet owners had entered the lottery as of Wednesday, Chen said.
Winners are eligible for one of 30,000 vouchers, as well as 100 pet health checkup reimbursement vouchers, the department said.
The NT$300 vouchers can be used to buy pet food or other supplies, or agricultural products at any of the 436 stores operated by collaborating businesses or associations, it said.
Winners of the checkup vouchers can take their dog or cat to a veterinary clinic for a health check or medical treatment, it said, adding that the voucher can be submitted to the department for up to a NT$3,000 reimbursement.
Lottery entries are open until Wednesday next week, it said.
The draw would be livestreamed on the YouTube channel of the ministry’s Animal Protection Information Network on Friday next week, it said.

Vessel donation to Manila would not harm fishers: OAC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

Ocean Affairs Council (OAC) Minister Kuan Bi-ling (管碧玲) on Wednesday said decommissioned coast guard vessels were given to the Philippines to enhance regional rescue capacity and would not affect Taiwanese fishers’ rights and benefits.
Kuan made the remarks after confirmation on Tuesday that a 500-tonne Coast Guard Administration (CGA) patrol and rescue vessel would be given to the Philippine Coast Guard.
The donation ceremony was reportedly done in Manila, but whether the vessel — previously numbered “CG123” and named Kinmen (金門) — has been handed over has yet to be confirmed.
Photo courtesy of the Ocean Affairs Council
China’s Taiwan Affairs Office (TAO) on Wednesday criticized the donation for “taking the side of the evildoer,” China Central Television reported.
TAO spokesperson Zhu Fenglian (朱鳳蓮) called for cross-strait cooperation on safeguarding territorial sovereignty for “the Chinese nation,” it reported.
Zhu criticized the donation for “increasing the risk of undermining Taiwanese fishermen’s rights and benefits,” as the Philippines and Japan had initiated maritime boundary negotiations involving waters east of Taiwan proper, it added.
Kuan on Wednesday in a Facebook post said the donation aimed to boost regional rescue capacity and maritime safety.
Taiwan has the right to cooperate with nearby countries and dismisses Beijing’s uninvited opinions, she said.
CGA authorities have long supported local fishery workers’ operations, Kuan said.
That included expelling Chinese vessels that trespass into Taiwanese waters, delivering life-saving medicines to fishers in distant waters, and helping with marine emergencies such as fishing boat grounding, fires on the ship or crew members overboard, she said.
Neighboring countries could more promptly help rescue a Taiwanese boat that encounters danger within their rescue zone if they are equipped with better vessels and rescue capabilities, Kuan said.
International maritime search and rescue is mutual assistance as well as a humanitarian action, Kuan said, adding that to boost a neighboring country’s rescue capacity would enhance Taiwanese fishers’ safety.
To establish a transparent, reliable regional maritime order, Taiwan has signed the Taiwan-Japan Fisheries Agreement, as well as the Agreement Concerning the Facilitation of Cooperation on Law Enforcement in Fisheries Matters with the Philippines, she said.
In contrast, China constitutes a more urgent risk to Taiwan’s fishers, Kuan said.
It arbitrarily conducts military drills around Taiwan, approaches and inspects Taiwanese vessels for so-called law enforcement, and detains Taiwanese boats and fishers for long periods without a transparent handling process, she said.
The donation’s agreements specify that the vessel must not be used in law enforcement against Taiwanese fishing boats, Kuan added.

A roadmap for the next UN secretary-general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:46 UTC
01:38:46 KST

Leading the UN has always been a balancing act, but the breakdown of the postwar global order has added a new dimension of complexity to the role. The next secretary-general, who is to take office next year, will fill the most prominent position in multilateral governance at a time when multilateralism is arguably at its nadir. To rebuild trust in international cooperation, the new leader must view this crisis for what it is: an unprecedented opportunity for fundamental reform.
Seven candidates are vying to replace Antonio Guterres, although the third UN Security Council straw poll has further narrowed the field (while indicating members’ willingness to respect the principle of regional rotation, according to which the next secretary-general will be from Latin America or the Caribbean). Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica and Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett of Guyana have emerged as the top two contenders, but the absence of a clear front-runner could encourage a late entrant.
Whoever is ultimately selected will need a transformative roadmap for the first 100 days — and beyond — to shape the UN’s trajectory and ensure that global governance is made fit for the 21st century. Cepei, the Bogota-based think tank that I head, has partnered with organizations around the world and convened regional consultations with leading academics, former diplomats, policymakers, practitioners and other stakeholders to reflect on the agenda and priorities of the next UN secretary-general and the future of UN leadership more broadly.
Illustration: Mountain People
These meetings show that expectations are high. Although the UN secretary-general’s independent powers are limited, an incumbent wields political capital, serves as the organization’s public voice, appoints senior officials and oversees management. So, the question becomes, how can the next secretary-general demonstrate leadership, credibility and direction in the first 100 days while operating within these limits?
For starters, the next secretary-general should focus on delivering consistent messaging and on using the largely predictable UN calendar to achieve some early wins. They should begin with political clarity, not thematic expansion; complete existing agendas, such as the Sustainable Development Goals and climate agreements; and shift the focus from proliferation to execution.
More fundamentally, the new head must also commit to making power more transparent; embed inclusion across the UN system; strengthen coordination with member states; and ensure that financing is aligned with governance.
That means rebuilding trust from within. When appointing the senior leadership team, the next secretary-general should select people who demonstrate political courage, independent judgement, discipline in setting priorities, a willingness to take risks and withstand criticism, and a renewed commitment to mediation.
Such leaders will be well-positioned in the long term to incentivize coordination, build coalitions that outlive their tenure, and pursue meaningful structural and organizational change backed by concrete accountability mechanisms.
Instilling a renewed sense of purpose in a workforce of about 120,000 people struggling with low morale and impossibly tight budgets will require a compelling diagnosis of the UN’s challenges, a vision for its future and priorities for action. The diagnosis should focus on political factors first and foremost, as many of its problems can be traced to choices made by member states, weakening consensus and shifting power relations. To be sure, this limits what institutional reform — or the secretary-general alone — can realistically achieve. But, more importantly, it suggests that the selection and transition agenda should address not only the expectations for the next secretary-general, but also what member states are prepared to provide in return.
The secretary-general will inherit the unfinished UN80 Initiative, which aims to improve efficiency, review implementation of the body’s mandates, and examine possible structural changes and program realignments. In the first 100 days, important decisions must be made about which parts of the reform agenda to continue, which to adjust, and which to abandon, while keeping in mind the need to avoid reform fatigue and ensure that the next phase is shaped and owned by member states.
At the country level, the secretary-general must also make difficult choices about activities the UN should no longer pursue, while improving delivery, localization and coordination. This requires greater clarity about where the UN adds value, focusing on its universal legitimacy, convening and norm-setting power, and, perhaps most importantly, mediation and “good offices.” The guiding principle should be differentiation, not withdrawal: continuing direct delivery where necessary while relying more deliberately on regional and national actors when they are better placed to act.
Lastly, to reduce the UN’s dependence on voluntary contributions and earmarked resources, often from a small number of major donors, the next secretary-general should begin engaging with member states to develop a more sustainable funding model. This means preparing to make strategic use of the organization’s existing levers of authority to align financing with governance, which would strengthen the system’s effectiveness and accountability. This could be accomplished by maximizing unearmarked voluntary funding and creating project-specific funding windows (where transaction costs do not distort governance), while also providing contributors with appropriate political recognition and greater transparency.
The new UN head’s broader agenda — restore peace, protect the most vulnerable, and convince the world to act on climate change and regulate artificial intelligence — represents a formidable challenge, especially as geopolitical upheaval impedes efforts to forge consensus or deliver long-term solutions. The UN has not adapted quickly enough to today’s multipolar reality in which influence is dispersed across many sites. Tokenistic engagement and negative narratives reinforce a sense of exclusion, deepening the legitimacy crisis.
However, the next secretary-general can change that trajectory. Although rebuilding legitimacy will not be easy or immediate, a leader who demonstrates strong management skills and a commitment to reform in the first 100 days will provide an important foundation on which to build a reinvigorated UN.
Philipp Schonrock is director of Cepei, a Bogota-based independent think tank that specializes in global governance and data and digitalization to accelerate sustainable development.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

Taiwan thanks countries for support at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:46 UTC
01:38:46 KST

Taiwan yesterday thanked eight European and Indo-Pacific countries for opposing unilateral changes to the “status quo” in the Taiwan Strait in a joint statement earlier this week, as well as three of Taiwan’s allies for speaking up for the nation’s participation in the UN at the body’s General Assembly in New York.
Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) welcomed the support and expressed his appreciation for the countries’ stance, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.
Foreign ministers and senior representatives of Australia, France, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, Poland, South Korea and the UK issued a statement on Tuesday after meeting on the sidelines of the General Assembly.
Photo: AFP
“We emphasize the importance of maintaining peace and stability in the Indo-Pacific. We encourage dialogue and oppose any unilateral attempts to change the status quo across the Taiwan Strait,” the representatives said.
The ministry said it welcomed the continued attention from the international community and like-minded partners to maintaining peace, stability and the “status quo.”
In the face of growing geopolitical and regional challenges, Taiwan would bolster its self-defense and societal resilience, while deepening cooperation with democratic partners, it said.
Three of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies — Paraguay, the Kingdom of Eswatini and Palau — on Wednesday pushed for Taiwan’s inclusion in the UN when their leaders addressed the General Assembly.
The ongoing crisis in the Middle East was already troubling, but there could be an even more serious crisis in Taiwan, Paraguayan President Santiago Pena said in his speech.
“If oil was the fuel of the 20th century, chips are the fuel of the 21st,” he said. “What is at stake in this potential conflict is significant: the very future of humanity.”
Taiwan’s exclusion is “a stain on the United Nations,” Pena said, reaffirming Paraguay’s support for the full and meaningful participation of Taiwan in the UN and its specialized agencies.
Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr said that his country chooses its partners “based on shared values of democracy, human rights and a rules-based international order.”
Those principles “underpin our friendship with Taiwan, a trusted partner that can contribute even more fully if given space to do so,” he said.
“We stand with like-minded partners in calling for the reversal of misinterpretations of rules and procedures that have constrained Taiwan’s meaningful participation in this body,” he added.
King Mswati III also expressed Eswatini’s support for Taiwan, which he said plays a vital role in global supply chains.
Taiwan “has much to contribute to the international community and can play a highly meaningful role in building a sustainable future for humanity,” he said.
President William Lai (賴清德) thanked the representatives in a Facebook post, writing that democratic unity is the only answer to global authoritarian expansion.
As a key link in global democratic and supply chains, Taiwan is keenly aware of its responsibilities, Lai said.
“We are not only on the front line of safeguarding freedom and democracy, but also a mature, responsible and trustworthy force for good in the international community,” he added.

Twins umpire MLB games together
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:44 UTC
01:38:44 KST

Tyler Jones umpired the first game of this week’s series between the Toronto Blue Jays and the Baltimore Orioles and was napping the next day when his brother Austin called and told him that the middle game of the series was rained out.
A doubleheader on Wednesday meant that Austin Jones — who in addition to being Tyler Jones’ identical twin is also an umpire — was on his way to Baltimore to work the games alongside his brother.
“This is something we’ve dreamed about forever,” Tyler Jones said. “We were told last year: ‘OK, if we can make it happen, we’ll make it happen.’ And it didn’t. The schedules didn’t align. Even this year we weren’t even sure if it was going to happen or not, and then it was kind of a shock.”
Photo: AP
The 31-year-old twins called both ends of Wednesday’s doubleheader, each won by Baltimore by a 4-2 score. Austin worked first base in the opener and Tyler was at second. Then they swapped for the nightcap — although the numbers on their uniforms were the only easy way to tell them apart.
The two are on a list of Triple-A call-up umpires who fill in at the big league level for injuries, illnesses, vacations and other reasons of absence. There are typically five umpires on a crew for a doubleheader instead of four, so Austin Jones was added.
Austin Jones umpired his first MLB game in 2024, Tyler Jones last year. They had worked a game together in the Gulf Coast League and the Arizona Fall League, but never in the majors.
“We talk to each other daily, especially about baseball and about everything, what we go through on a day-to-day basis, but to be able to live it together, and come to the ballpark and see him in the locker room and play cards with him before the game and share that experience was probably the best part,” Tyler Jones said.
Tyler Jones jokes that he got into umpiring because “I was a really bad baseball player.”
They both started young, working youth games and earning some money when they were in high school.
“We did umpire school together and we roomed together,” Austin Jones said. “We had never really lived on our own, we were 18 years old. So it was our first time out of the house, doing things on our own, and we said: ‘Man, if this is kind of what life in professional baseball is like, this is pretty cool.’”

The dangers that come with having Chinese IDs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:44 UTC
01:38:44 KST

China’s “united front” tactics against Taiwan have long gone beyond slogans and propaganda, gradually extending into identity, the economy and everyday life.
Recent media reports said that some people in Taiwan are suspected of acting as intermediaries, urging other Taiwanese to travel to China to apply for IDs. While such activities are ostensibly packaged as convenient services, in practice, they might be using the IDs to gradually draw Taiwanese into China’s governance.
Once an issue involves organized recruitment, repeated assistance with applications, or direction or exploitation by foreign forces, it is no longer simply a matter of cross-strait exchange — it is a warning sign that Taiwan’s national security defenses must be taken seriously.
Under Article 9-1 of the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (臺灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例), people of the Taiwan Area are prohibited from establishing a household registration in China or obtaining a Chinese passport. The Mainland Affairs Council has made it clear that Chinese ID cards and permanent resident certificates are subject to regulations governing household registration in China. Those who contravene these rules might lose their status as residents of Taiwan and the rights that come with it.
Since the legal red lines have long been clearly established, no one should be allowed to exploit gaps in public knowledge by packaging something with such severe legal consequences as a “document application service” or a “business convenience.” This raises concerns about the involvement of organized recruitment, exchanges of benefits or foreign intervention. If those being recruited include active-duty military or law enforcement personnel, civil servants, defense technology workers or others in sensitive fields, this issue cannot simply be treated as an individual choice regarding one’s identity. When one’s identity is intertwined with public authority, classified information and key positions, a personal risk can become a major vulnerability for the system.
Furthermore, national security defenses cannot wait until classified information has been leaked or an organized network has already taken shape before scrambling to patch the gaps. Any organized solicitation or agency work should not be investigated merely by asking whether it is a “private activity,” but by tracing who is providing the funding, resources and directives behind it. Only then can Taiwan ensure normal cross-strait exchanges while safeguarding national security.
An ID card might appear to be a personal choice, but behind it lie questions of identity verification, legal jurisdiction and national security. What needs to be severed is not normal exchanges between people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait, but local networks that exploit Taiwan’s openness and freedom to build bridges and clear a path for foreign infiltration from within.
Yeh Yu-cheng is a secretary at the Pingtung County Public Health Bureau.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen
Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Indeed, since 1979 it has been embedded in US law, with the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) charging the US with helping to improve the island’s ability to deter an attack from

2-year sentences sought for Chinese men who illegally sailed to Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:38:43 UTC
01:38:43 KST

Prosecutors on Thursday indicted two Chinese nationals for illegally entering Taiwan after sailing across the Taiwan Strait on a rubber dinghy, recommending that each be sentenced to two years in prison.
The case came to light on Aug. 10, when an unidentified user on Threads wrote that a fisherman had found a rubber dinghy on a beach near Taipei Port in July, which they initially thought belonged to another fisherman.
After inspecting the vessel more closely the next day, however, the fisherman found life vests, Chinese-made fuel containers, and rolls of toilet paper with writing in Simplified Chinese, and reported the case to law enforcement, the user wrote.
Photo: CNA
After learning of the incident on July 24, the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) launched an investigation, and ultimately detained two male Chinese nationals, surnamed Luan (欒) and Yu (于), at Chaoyang Forest Park in Taoyuan on July 30.
The two men were turned over to the Shilin District Prosecutors Office, which received court permission to hold the men in incommunicado detention on Aug. 3.
In an indictment filed Thursday, prosecutors said Luan and Yu had set out by car from Qingdao, Shandong Province on July 19, and later purchased an outboard motor for their raft in Jinhua, Zhejiang Province.
On July 22, the two men launched their raft from the shoreline outside Fuzhou, Fujian Province at 4 or 5 a.m., crossing the Taiwan Strait and reaching the Taipei Port’s northern jetty around 2 a.m. on July 23.
After illegally entering Taiwan, Luan and Yu traveled to locations in New Taipei, Taipei, Hsinchu, Taichung and Taoyuan, before being arrested by Coast Guard investigators on July 30, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors said they had based their indictment on suspect and witness statements, cell phone data, surveillance video footage, and DNA analysis. They charged both Luan and Yu with violations of the Immigration Act and the Cross-Strait Act.
In light of the "substantive harm" Luan and Yu’s actions caused to Taiwan’s border control, coastal defense security and public order -- as well as the "severe public anxiety" aroused by their case -- prosecutors requested that both men be sentenced to two years in prison.
The indictment’s strong language likely referred to public criticism the Coast Guard received for failing to detect the men’s raft, which led the agency’s director to apologize on Aug. 11, one day after the incident became public.

Responses from mayoral candidates for Taipei and New Taipei City invited to attend a series of forums hosted by a coalition of youth and student organizations next month have been mixed, the groups said yesterday.
Four candidates seeking to represent Kaohsiung and Hsinchu City have already announced their intention to attend after receiving an invite, they said.
In the second round, the coalition invited candidates running in Taipei and New Taipei City, the coalition said.
Photo: Lo Kuo-chia, Taipei Times
Su Chiao-hui (蘇巧慧), the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) candidate for New Taipei City mayor, accepted, while her opponent, the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) Lee Shu-chuan (李四川), declined due to scheduling conflicts, they said.
The Taiwan Engagement Association for Youths, National Students’ Union of Taiwan, Taiwan Youth Association for Democracy, EdYouth, and student associations from National Taiwan University, Fu Jen Catholic University, National Tsinghua University, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University and National Sun Yat-sen University are among the events’ organizers.
They expressed regret that Lee would not attend, saying that they would be fair and impartial to the participating candidates.
The coalition on the same day sent invitations to Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) of the KMT, who is running for re-election, and his DPP challenger, Puma Shen (沈柏楊), but they have yet to respond, the coalition said.
The first set of forums would be held in Hsinchu and Kaohsiung, while the second would be in Taipei and New Taipei City, they said.
Candidates taking part in the forum may elaborate on their platforms and are expected to take questions from members of youth groups specializing in certain fields and the general audience, they added.
Lee’s campaign said his office has been in close contact with the groups.
The forum was too close to the final stretch before the elections, a campaign spokesperson said.
On Tuesday, Lee attended a forum hosted by a National Taipei University Department of Public Administration and Policy student association, they said.
“Lee is keenly interested in hearing the voices of young Taiwanese and will continue to engage in discussion with them,” they added.
