Russia ties family mortgage rates to the number of children. In Moscow, the rate for one-child families doubles to 12% on October 1.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:18:10 UTC
01:18:10 KST

Russia ties family mortgage rates to the number of children. In Moscow, the rate for one-child families doubles to 12% on October 1.
Russia’s Finance Ministry has revised the terms of its “Family Mortgage” program. Starting October 1, interest rates will depend on how many children a family has and where it lives.
Outside Moscow and St. Petersburg, annual rates will range from 10% for families with one child, with a loan limit of 6 million rubles, to 2% for families with five or more children, with a limit of 10 million rubles.
In Moscow, the Moscow region, St. Petersburg, and the Leningrad region, annual rates will range from 12% for families with one child, with a loan limit of 12 million rubles, to 4% for families with five or more children, with a limit of 18 million rubles.
Under the new terms, any family with at least one child under seven when the mortgage agreement is signed will be eligible.
For loans to build or finish building a house, or to buy land and then build a home on it, the rate will remain at 6%, regardless of the number of children or where the family lives.
The Finance Ministry said the changes would make the “Family Mortgage” program “better targeted and geared toward demographic goals.”
Previously, the program offered a flat 6% rate, with loan limits of 12 million rubles in Moscow, the Moscow region, St. Petersburg, and the Leningrad region, and 6 million rubles elsewhere. Borrowers had to make a 20% down payment.
Russia launched the “Family Mortgage” program in 2018. Kommersant reported in June 2026 that officials were discussing whether to vary the program’s interest rates and loan limits.

Foxtrot opens new store in Dnipro
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:17:26 EEST
01:17:26 KST

Omnichannel retailer Foxtrot on Thursday opened a new store in Dnipro at the MOST-city shopping and entertainment center, the company's press service said.
"We understand that today we cannot plan network development in the same way as several years ago. Security has become part of every decision – from the choice of locality and premises to the organization of work. But this does not mean that development is stopping. We simply define differently what a modern store in a large city should be, taking into account the risks of a frontline region," Foxtrot CEO Yuriy Polishchuk said.
The 700-square-meter store is the retailer's fourth location in the city and replaces its previous store at 2 Lamana Street. The press service said the move allowed the company to expand the range of key categories, add more brand zones and introduce an updated store format with key customer services.
Key features include an accessible service hub, brand zones of leading manufacturers and a broad premium-segment assortment. The store has two Apple brand zones and premium television lines from Hisense and Samsung. Large appliances are represented by Samsung, Bosch, Whirlpool and Hisense. Brand zones for small household appliances and beauty products include De'Longhi, Philips, Tefal and Braun.
As reported, at the beginning of September the retailer opened a renovated store in Kyiv at Gorodok Gallery shopping center. The company is also continuing to develop its online channels – the Foxtrot.ua online store and mobile application – and has a presence on three marketplaces: monomarket, ALLO and Kasta.
Foxtrot is one of Ukraine's largest omnichannel retail chains by number of stores and sales of electronics and household appliances. As of September 2026, the chain has 128 stores in 68 Ukrainian cities and continues to develop its omnichannel model.
According to Opendatabot, FTD-Retail LLC (Kyiv), which operates the chain, increased revenue by 28.7% in 2025 from 2024 to UAH 19 billion and increased net profit nearly fivefold, to UAH 35.2 million from UAH 6 million.
The founders of omnichannel retailer Foxtrot are Ukrainian businessmen Hennadiy Vykhodtsev and Valeriy Makovetsky.

Berezhna: Ukraine has about 11,000 libraries; many need to be reinterpretation
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:14:52 EEST
01:14:52 KST

Deputy Prime Minister for Humanitarian Policy and Minister of Culture Tetiana Berezhna believes that libraries should become more functional, multidisciplinary spaces.
"There are currently about 11,000 libraries in Ukraine; prior to the full-scale invasion, there were around 15,000. These are spaces that should actually play far more roles and hold much greater significance than merely providing Ukrainians with reading infrastructure. A library can become a space that transforms a person from a recipient of cultural services into an active participant in community life. Our grand vision is to turn libraries into multidisciplinary, highly functional spaces that go far beyond the traditional library model," Berezhna said in at the event dubbed "Unity in action: accessible cultural spaces as a foundation for community development" in Kyiv on Thursday
She noted that the government views libraries as places capable of uniting not only local residents but also those temporarily residing in the community, particularly veterans.
"We realize this is a very challenging task, as there are a great many libraries in Ukraine that require reimagining and transformation. Therefore, as a government, we acknowledge that we cannot handle this alone using state resources—we are open about this," the Deputy Prime Minister stated.
She recalled that the draft budget for the coming year includes "unprecedented" funding for the book sector. Specifically, for the first time in a long while, funds have been allocated for purchasing books for both public and school libraries.
Berezhna also confirmed that a support program for the book publishing sector would be implemented next year as part of the Thousand Springs(Tysiachovesna) initiative, which supports cultural products.
"We hope that members of parliament will support increasing the budget for books and book publishing," the Deputy Prime Minister emphasized.
Among other things, Berezhna announced the presentation of a concept for what libraries in Ukraine should look like, using two libraries—in Rohatyn (Ivano-Frankivsk region) and Bilohiria (Khmelnytsky region)—as examples under the Libraries for All donor-funded pilot initiative.
As earlier reported, the draft state budget for 2027 allocates UAH 100 million for replenishing library collections.
The reading strategy outlines plans for 2026–2028 to ensure access to books in communities lacking libraries or bookstores by developing mobile library services, such as bookmobiles.
In May 2023, Oleksandra Koval, head of the Ukrainian Book Institute (UBI), stated that there are 12,000 public libraries in Ukraine, of which only 3,000 to 4,000 are actively functioning. She also noted that libraries hold 160 million books, 52% of which were published before 1991.

Russia could launch limited attacks on NATO in coming months, escalating hybrid warfare without being ready for full-scale conflict, Denmark warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:13:49 UTC
01:13:49 KST

Russia is likely to intensify its hybrid war against the West, including more frequent sabotage and cyberattacks that could cause greater damage and casualties, Denmark’s Defence Intelligence Service (DDIS) said in a new assessment published on 24 September.
The assessment says Russia has become increasingly willing to take risks against European and NATO countries, even while its full-scale war against Ukraine continues. DDIS also assesses a low but growing risk of Russia carrying out a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia in the coming months.
Russia preparing to escalate hybrid attacks
DDIS said Russia’s hybrid attacks have increasingly shifted from attempts to create fear and weaken support for Ukraine toward efforts to directly disrupt Western assistance to Kyiv.
This includes sabotage targeting defense companies and railway transport carrying military equipment to Ukraine. The Danish intelligence service expects Russia to carry out such attacks more frequently and with greater consequences.
Future operations could include destructive cyberattacks capable of disrupting critical societal functions and sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties, according to the assessment.
DDIS also cited the foiled drone attack against Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany as an example of Russia’s growing willingness to conduct operations against targets in Europe. German authorities said the attack had been planned by Russia over several months.
Germany suspects Russian intelligence behind arson attack as hybrid warfare threat grows across Europe
Growing risk of a limited attack on NATO
The Danish intelligence service assesses that there is a low but growing risk Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia.
Such an attack could take the form of isolated long-range strikes against infrastructure supporting Ukraine. Russia could also use Ukrainian-made drones in a false-flag operation or deploy a limited number of troops, potentially without national insignia.
DDIS says Russia could attempt such an operation even while continuing its war against Ukraine and without having the forces needed for a regional war against NATO.
The purpose, according to the assessment, could be to divert European resources away from Ukraine and create divisions within NATO if Moscow believes the alliance would struggle to agree on a collective response.
Russia would likely try to ensure that any military attack remained below the threshold that would trigger a full NATO response. DDIS warns, however, that Russia may be uncertain about what would trigger such a response.
After CIA head’s visit to Moscow, Poland’s PM warns Russia is preparing to escalate war. He puts critical window at seven or eight months
No signs of an imminent Russian invasion
Despite the increased risk of limited attacks, DDIS says it sees no indications that Russia is preparing to invade one or more NATO countries.
The agency considers a full-scale Russian invasion of NATO “highly unlikely,” but says it cannot be ruled out. If Russia decided to launch such an invasion, DDIS estimates it would need at least six months to build up the necessary forces.
The intelligence service also says Russia would need several months to build up forces near a NATO border before a limited military deployment, making such preparations difficult to conceal.
Russian warship fires flares at Danish military helicopter as Moscow’s provocations escalate
Russia under pressure from Ukraine’s attacks
The assessment says Russia is currently under more pressure than at any other point in its war against Ukraine.
Ukraine’s sustained long-range strikes are causing increasing damage deep inside Russia, while Russian forces are suffering heavy losses for marginal territorial gains. Moscow is also facing economic pressure from military spending, international sanctions and Ukrainian strikes against Russian energy infrastructure.
DDIS assesses that there is no prospect of Russia achieving a major breakthrough in Ukraine over the next six months. At the same time, it says Putin is highly unlikely to compromise on his fundamental objectives in the war.
The agency says Russia believes Europe will develop a stronger independent military capability by 2030, which Moscow could view as an increasing threat. This could create what DDIS describes as a window of opportunity for Putin to attempt to change Europe’s security order.

In the Czech Republic, 16 houses dating back 7,000 years were found near a motorway
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
19:11:43 EEST
01:11:43 KST

In the Czech Republic, 16 houses dating back 7,000 years were found near a motorway
Kyiv • UNN
Archaeologists discovered a complex of dwellings belonging to the Linear Pottery culture. The finds include 1,879 domestic structures and 65 burials.
In the Czech Republic, while constructing a new high-speed highway, archaeologists came across an entire complex of ancient structures that expanded understanding of the settlement of this region by the first farmers. Arkeonews reports, as cited by UNN.
Details
According to archaeologists, these 16 ancient houses were built 7,000 years ago. It is also noted that these structures belonged to the Linear Pottery culture.
Some of the houses were up to 36 meters long, which may indicate enormous labor costs long before the emergence of the first cities.
Archaeologists also found storage pits for preserving crops, ovens for cooking and heating, and other objects related to everyday life.
In total, specialists documented 1,879 domestic features, 65 burials, and one human burial inside a domestic pit.

Archaeologists discovered 23 more ancient images of ships carved into the walls of a temple in Kition-Kathari, Cyprus.

Croatia approves Ukrainian Nord Stream suspect’s extradition to Germany despite Polish refusal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:11:08 UTC
01:11:08 KST

A court in Pula ruled that Ukrainian diving instructor Volodymyr Zhuravliov may be extradited to Germany over the September 2022 blasts that damaged the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany and caused major leaks in the Baltic Sea, RBC-Ukraine reported, citing his lawyers.
A Polish court refused to extradite Zhuravliov last year, but its ruling did not cancel Germany’s EU-wide arrest warrant. Croatia could therefore arrest him and decide Germany’s request for itself. The pipelines at the center of the case were built to carry Russian gas to Germany while bypassing Ukraine.
The firm Katerynchuk, Moor & Partners said it expected to receive the written ruling shortly and was preparing to challenge it in Croatia’s appellate court and before international judicial bodies. Zhuravliov also plans to announce an indefinite hunger strike. His lawyers said the Croatian court had disregarded the earlier Polish decision.
The Warsaw court refused to surrender Zhuravliov in October 2025, finding that the pipelines could be treated as a legitimate military target during an armed conflict. It released him from custody.
His Polish lawyer, Tymoteusz Paprocki, said Zhuravliov understood that the ruling applied only within Poland: under a European arrest warrant, the country where a suspect is arrested decides whether to send them to the country seeking them.
Germany amended the warrant in early September to add a war-crime classification, according to Zhuravliov’s lawyers. The change prompted the Croatian court to postpone an earlier hearing. The lawyers’ account of the amendment has not been independently confirmed.
How the Nord Stream case reached Croatia
Nord Stream 1 and 2 were built to carry Russian gas directly to Germany while bypassing Ukraine. Explosions on 26 September 2022 damaged three of their four lines; Nord Stream 2 had never entered service.
Germany issued a warrant for Zhuravliov in 2024. German prosecutors say he helped place explosives on the pipelines near Denmark’s Bornholm island. He denies involvement. Croatian police arrested him in Pula on 19 August 2026 under the European warrant.
Another Ukrainian suspect, Serhii Kuznietsov, was arrested in Italy in 2025 and later sent to Germany, where prosecutors have charged him over the explosions. He denies involvement. No court has established who ordered the attack.

NAZA to stream free after Israel threats against filmmakers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:11:06 UTC
01:11:06 KST

Breadcrumb
NAZA Gaza film to stream free after Israel threats against directors
Award-winning documentary NAZA will stream online for free following its worldwide release in November, giving audiences around the world access to the film about Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
NAZA, directed by Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, will be released in cinemas in more than 50 countries before streaming on the website of British newspaper The Guardian in November.
Announcing the decision on X on Thursday, Abraham said the documentary would be made available for free because of its "interest and public importance".
"…I and Rachel decided together with The Guardian that the film NAZA would be accessible online for free, without any time limit, so that every person can watch it and the soldiers' testimonies," Abraham wrote on X.
The Guardian said the film would be streamed "as part of the news organisation's commitment to the dissemination of independent journalism".
The film, shot on the rooftops of Tel Aviv, centres on Israel's use of AI in its genocidal war on Gaza, featuring testimony from 24 members of the Israeli military and intelligence services who spoke on condition of anonymity.
Its title comes from an Israeli military term used to refer to the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike.
The soldiers and intelligence personnel interviewed describe systems used to identify targets in Gaza and how strikes were approved despite the anticipated deaths of civilians, including children.
The documentary received a record-breaking 25-minute standing ovation at its premiere at the Venice Film Festival in September and went on to win the Special Jury Prize.
But the film's reception in Israel was markedly different, triggering a fierce campaign against Abraham and Szor from senior Israeli politicians, military figures and far-right activists.
Much of the backlash centred on the film's use of testimony from serving and former Israeli military and intelligence personnel to expose the systems behind attacks that have killed Palestinian civilians in Gaza.
Israeli officials accused the filmmakers of portraying Israeli soldiers as war criminals, while Culture Minister Miki Zohar accused them of "treason against the state". Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir threatened to use "every tool at our disposal" against it.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to pass legislation that would allow authorities to strip citizenship from Israelis who "smear" soldiers or "defame" the state.
The campaign soon extended beyond the filmmakers themselves to their families.
Dozens of far-right activists gathered outside the homes of the directors' families, including the home of Szor's parents, after messages circulated calling on activists to demonstrate there.
Some messages included explicit calls for violence, while one protester demanded the "death penalty for traitors" and called for the homes of the filmmakers' families to be demolished.
The threats prompted expressions of solidarity from Israeli human rights groups and members of the international film industry, who condemned the campaign against the directors and called for their safety and freedom of expression to be protected.
In 2025, Abraham and Szor won the Oscar for Best Documentary for No Other Land, along with their two Palestinian co-directors, Basel Adra and Hamdan Ballal.
That film, which documented Israeli settler violence and the displacement of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, also generated controversy in Israel.
Following the Oscar win, Ballal was brutally attacked by Israeli settlers.

Global gas prices continue to rise in 2026, but set to fall 40% by 2029 — ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:11:00 UTC
01:11:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Global gas prices continue to rise in 2026 due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, but are expected to decline by 40% by 2029 as LNG production increases, according to a document published on the Russian Economic Development Ministry’s website.
"Natural gas prices rose in 2025 amid a slowdown in Russian gas supplies to Europe and increased imports of more expensive LNG. In 2026, natural gas prices continue to rise amid a global drought, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, and damage to key LNG infrastructure in the Middle East," the document said.
However, prices are expected to decline by around 40% from 2025 levels by 2029, driven by the planned increase in global LNG production and the resumption of supplies from Persian Gulf countries, according to the forecast.
TASS previously reported, citing futures data from London’s ICE exchange and its own calculations, that the average gas price in Europe rose by 9% in 2025 to $422 per 1,000 cubic meters.
However, the average price since the beginning of this year stands at $598 per 1,000 cubic meters. The increase in gas prices has been driven by the ongoing Middle East conflict and record-low gas inventories in Europe ahead of the winter.
The average gas price in Europe stood at around $517 per 1,000 cubic meters in January 2025, up 53% year-on-year from 2024; $542 in February, up 88%; $467 in March, up 55%; $409 in April, up 28%; $412 in May, up 15%; $439 in June, up 14%; $410 in July, up 12%; $394 in August, down 10%; $393 in September, down 5.5%; $384 in October, down 16%; $368 in November, down 25%; and $334 in December, down 32%. In January 2026, the average price was $415 per 1,000 cubic meters, down 20% year-on-year from 2025; $396 in February, down 27%; $632 in March, up 35%; $544 in April, up 33%; $570 in May, up 39%; $534 in June, up 22%; $638 in July, up 55%; and $744 in August, up 89%.

TotalEnergies refused rescue aid during deadly Mozambique attack, inquest hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:09:46 UTC
01:09:46 KST

WINCHESTER, England — TotalEnergies refused fuel to helicopters evacuating civilians as Islamist militants overran the Mozambican town of Palma in 2021 and later denied British special forces use of its nearby construction site for a rescue mission, a British inquest heard this week.
The four-day hearing in Winchester was a coroner’s inquest, a British judicial proceeding to establish how and why Philip Mawer — a 58-year-old British construction contractor working on the French energy giant’s gas plant project — was killed by a rocket-propelled grenade while fleeing the assault.
The claims emerged in testimony and evidence presented during the hearing; the coroner did not, however, find that TotalEnergies’ decisions affected rescue efforts, saying Mawer’s security was the sole responsibility of his employer, a Dubai-based contractor, and the hotel at which he stayed.
Advertisement
Coroner Jason Pegg ruled on Thursday that Mawer was unlawfully killed by an unknown person, but accepted an argument by lawyers from TotalEnergies’ Mozambican subsidiary that the company had no legal duty of care to him because he was a subcontractor.
The testimony could carry consequences in France, where TotalEnergies faces two criminal complaints over its Mozambique operations, including an involuntary manslaughter case tied to the deaths of contractors during the Palma attack. A French investigating magistrate was appointed last year to examine that complaint.
“These hearings were crucial, crucial, crucial,” said Henri Thulliez, a French human rights lawyer who filed both criminal complaints in Paris and who was in Winchester to watch proceedings. “Finally, we have people talking under oath about what happened in Palma. It’s very important, and very rare when it comes to accountability for multinationals.”
Thulliez’s second complaint accuses TotalEnergies of complicity in war crimes and torture. It alleges the energy giant became an accomplice in a massacre — first reported by POLITICO — in which Mozambican soldiers brutalized, starved, suffocated, executed or disappeared around 200 men at the company's gatehouse from June to September 2021.
TotalEnergies has denied responsibility for the deaths during the ISIS attack, which killed 1,354 civilians, including 55 people working on the TotalEnergies project, according to a house-to-house survey carried out by POLITICO. In response to questions from POLITICO, it acknowledged in 2024 that “a small number” of project workers had been stationed outside its secure compound during the attack and exposed to the bloodbath.
In 2025, the company — through its subsidiary Mozambique LNG — told POLITICO it had no knowledge of the gatehouse killings, adding that its “extensive research” had “not identified any information nor evidence that would corroborate the allegations of severe abuses and torture.”
Advertisement
In response to a request for comment for this article, TotalEnergies referred POLITICO to its previous statements.
The coroner’s court heard that Mawer, country manager for Dubai-based contractor RA International, was in northern Mozambique helping build TotalEnergies’ gas project near Palma — an area that had been subject to Islamist attacks since 2017. By March 2021, rebels had cut land access to the project and the town.
TotalEnergies evacuated its own staff and allowed 700 Mozambican soldiers to deploy inside its fortified concession, while thousands of contractors and subcontractors remained in Palma, living in hotels protected by guards with wooden batons and protected around town by a few dozen soldiers and policemen. When militants attacked the town on March 24, Mawer took shelter in a hotel with 182 other people.
On March 26, after two days trapped at the hotel, Mawer fled in a convoy. A rocket-propelled grenade struck his vehicle, killing him.
The inquest heard that two members of Britain’s Special Air Service flew from Kenya to Mozambique intending to rescue Mawer. Francesca Wiley, a lawyer representing Mawer’s family, told the court that the SAS was denied permission to use TotalEnergies’ site. While debating their next move on March 27, the SAS were informed that Mawer was already dead.
The inquest also heard that TotalEnergies refused to supply fuel to helicopters operated by South African private military contractor Dyck Advisory Group, which was evacuating civilians from Palma. DAG chief Max Dyck said the lack of fuel limited the rescue effort. “Could we have saved a lot more people?” Dyck testified. “Definitely.”
Advertisement
TotalEnergies’ Mozambican subsidiary was represented by lawyer Adam Payter. He argued that Mawer was a subcontractor who was not formally under the company’s protection and for whom it had no evacuation plan.
Mawer’s brothers, Bill and Mark, accused TotalEnergies of abandoning him. “Why did Total refuse fuel and landing rights to the helicopter evacuation effort?” they said in a statement after the hearing. “Why was our brother allowed to die so close to a protected compound and a substantial military force?”
At the inquest, Detective Chief Inspector Patrick Allen of Britain’s SO15 counterterrorism command said a death toll of 1,402 was consistent with his unit’s own investigation. He also agreed with Mawer’s lawyer, Wiley, when she described the Palma assault as the “second biggest terror attack of all time, after 9/11.”

SC flags ‘false’ POCSO cases in marital disputes, bars immediate arrest of accused parent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:06:51 UTC
01:06:51 KST

Rape-murder of A law student: Petitioner Ameer-Ul-Islam seeking transfer from Viyyur Central Prison in Kerala to a jail in Assam
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Thursday laid down safeguards against the immediate arrest of a parent or family member accused under the POCSO Act when the alleged offence involves a child living under the same roof and there is a matrimonial dispute between the child's parents.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K V Viswanathan, flagging a rise in fakecases, said police should not act in haste in such cases and directed that, as a general rule, an expert in child and adolescent psychiatry or clinical psychology should evaluate the child before authorities decide whether there is sufficient reason to arrest the accused.The court said the safeguards were necessary in cases where allegations may be influenced by a strained relationship between the parents. It stressed that the measures do not dilute the seriousness of offences under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, but are intended to ensure that the power of arrest is exercised after considering all relevant circumstances.The court said immediate arrest should not take place when two conditions are present: a POCSO offence is alleged against a parent or family member living with the child, and a matrimonial dispute exists between the child's parents, whether or not the dispute is pending before a court.
The police officer receiving the complaint must verify whether such a matrimonial dispute exists, the court said. "When the above-stated threshold conditions are met, post the registration of an FIR, we are of the considered opinion that the investigating officer should not act in haste or take coercive actions in the form of arrest immediately," the bench added, as quoted by PTI.The verdict came in a matrimonial dispute involving an estranged Bengaluru couple. The wife had alleged that the child was sexually assaulted. The case was investigated by the CBI, which found the allegation to be false. The Supreme Court restored custody of the child to the father, taking into account the welfare of the minor.The court also directed the investigating officer or the Special Juvenile Police Unit to seek the services of an expert in child and adolescent psychiatry or clinical psychology, in consultation with the District Child Protection Unit or, where one is unavailable, the District Legal Services Authority, adding that the expert's evaluation must be conducted independently and without influence from either the parent or investigating authorities.After receiving the evaluation, investigators must consider the expert's opinion along with other evidence and circumstances before deciding whether there is "reason to believe" that the accused committed the offence and whether an arrest is warranted. The court said an exception could be made in cases where the material available is "palpable", allowing the investigating officer to dispense with an expert evaluation, but reasons for doing so must be recorded in writing.The bench also stressed that arrest is not automatically required merely because an offence is cognisable. The court said an arrest can cause "irreparable harm" to an accused parent or family member, particularly where the allegation later turns out to be unfounded.The Supreme Court also raised concerns about the consequences of allegations on children and their relationship with the accused parent."The trauma that a child is put through in the process and the accusation can damage the very fabric of the parent-child relationship," the bench said, adding that such a wound could leave an "indelible scar" on both the child and parent.The court also flagged what it described as an increase in false allegations in matrimonial disputes."What is alarming is that this tendency of making false accusations is on the rise," it said.The bench cautioned against parents being influenced by advisers during matrimonial disputes, saying that some may be driven by a "win at any cost" approach.
At the same time, the court said the safeguards were not a finding that allegations made in such circumstances are false. Investigating authorities must examine the allegations along with the surrounding circumstances and other evidence.
For complaints filed directly before a special court, the Supreme Court said an order taking cognisance and summoning an accused must demonstrate application of mind. The special court should also involve an expert in child and adolescent psychiatry or clinical psychology to evaluate the child and submit a report.
Trisha Mahajan is a journalist with The Times of India digital, with keen interest in covering business and corporate affairs. She also reports on key national and world developments and global news trends. A keen reader with a strong interest in storytelling that adds context, clarity, and depth to complex issues.

NATO steps up intelligence-sharing over Russia threat, top commander says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:06:50 UTC
01:06:50 KST

NATO steps up intelligence-sharing over Russia threat, top commander says
Sept 24 - NATO is stepping up intelligence-sharing in response to a wave of sabotage and other incidents apparently linked to Russia but should be "calm and confident" that it can handle any threat posed by Moscow, the alliance's top commander told Reuters on Thursday.
The comments by US Air Force General Alexus Grynkewich came after Denmark's defence intelligence service warned that Russia was likely to intensify a hybrid war — a term that covers a range of attacks below the level of a conventional military assault — against the West in the coming months.
The Danish service added there was "a low but growing risk" that Moscow might launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries that border Russia.
"It's concerning," Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, said of a string of incidents in recent weeks including an attempted drone attack at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport and a Russian ship firing flares towards a Danish military helicopter.
"But we should be calm and confident that we as an alliance, the most powerful alliance in history, have the tools that we need and have the mechanisms that we need in order to manage the risk here," he added.
Moscow has repeatedly denied any involvement in hybrid warfare or sabotage operations in NATO countries, or plotting any confrontation.
PUTIN BETTER NOT TRY ATTACK 'ON MY WATCH', GENERAL SAYS
Grynkewich was speaking in a phone interview with Reuters en route to a change-of-command ceremony at a NATO headquarters in Norfolk, Virginia, where a British army general is taking over from a US Navy vice admiral.
Asked about the risk of a limited Russian attack on NATO territory, Grynkewich stressed the alliance's readiness for any such contingency, saying such a development was "unlikely but something that we can't rule out".
Grynkewich dismissed suggestions that Russian President Vladimir Putin might see an opportunity to strike at NATO, given that the US has used up much of its global stockpile of highly accurate long-range missiles in the war with Iran, according to people familiar with the data.
"Absolutely not. He better not try it on my watch," he said, adding NATO was well positioned to defend every inch of its territory.
"If we proceed from the phase we're in and we start to see emerging threats, I'm confident that I have the authorities now that I need in order to take actions to deter any aggression against the alliance."
NATO IN MIDST OF CHANGE AS EUROPEANS TAKE GREATER ROLE
The handover of Norfolk to a European commander is part of a broader reshuffle in keeping with US President Donald Trump's demands that European nations take more responsibility for their own security. It will also see a European taking charge of NATO's Joint Force Command in Naples.
NATO's Joint Force Command Norfolk is responsible for operations in the Arctic and northern Europe as well as protecting transatlantic resupply routes.
Attempting to reassure European allies concerned about an ongoing review of US forces on the continent, Grynkewich said Washington would continue "to provide critical but more limited capabilities" to NATO as Europeans took on a greater role.
He said there was "no predetermined outcome" in terms of how many US troops would remain in Europe and "what the capabilities are that might relocate". About 80,000 US troops are currently based on the continent.
Trump has repeatedly threatened to leave NATO, which has been dominated by the US since its establishment in 1949, accusing Europeans of being free-riders on security. REUTERS

Delegates walkout as Netanyahu takes stage at UNGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:05:53 UTC
01:05:53 KST

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas said Israeli policies are threatening the "very life and existence" of his people in a prerecorded video shown at the UN General Assembly.
At the meeting of world leaders, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian rebuked US threats, stating that anyone attempting to bully the nation must understand that it is "ready for dialogue, diplomacy, and negotiations without accepting the language of force."
Iran-backed Houthis are continuing their advance against the Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen.
US Senate rejects resolution curbing Trump's Iran war powers
The US Senate on Thursday narrowly rejected a Democratic-led resolution aiming to stop the Iran war until hostilities are authorized by Congress.
The Senate voted 50 to 49 to reject the resolution, which had passed the House of Representatives in July. The vote was largely along party lines, with most of President Donald Trump's Republicans rejecting the measure and almost every Democrat voting for it.
France to send 'military means' to protect Saudi oil port
President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday France would send "military means" to help protect the key Saudi port of Yanbu for oil exports following attacks by Yemen's Houthis.
"We are going to send military assets, meaning soldiers, radars, and defence systems to protect this site," he said during an interview on the evening news.
Netanyahu: Genocide allegations 'biggest lie of the century'
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dismissed genocide allegations in Gaza as "the biggest lie of the century" during his UNGA speech.
Hundreds of human rights organisations and legal groups have described Israel's actions in Gaza as "genocide," including Amnesty International, Oxfam, and UNRWA.
At least 73,000 Palestinians have been killed by Israel in Gaza since October 2023, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
Netanyahu is wanted by the ICC for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu, who is wanted by the ICC for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity, claimed that Israel is "a country of law" in his speech at the UN General Assembly.
Later in his speech, Netanyahu pulled out a prop pager, saying “certainly Hezbollah remembers" them, referencing the 2024 attack that wounded almost thousands of people in Lebanon and Syria.
On 17 September 2024, thousands of pagers simultaneously exploded across Lebanon and parts of Syria, resulting in at least 39 deaths and 3,500 injuries in what was described as an unprecedented security breach within Hezbollah. Many of the victims were civilians and medical workers.
Netanyahu: Attacking Iran 'was one of the easiest decisions'
Israeli PM Netanyahu, who faces an ICC arrest warrant for alleged war crimes, says attacking Iran 'was one of the easiest decisions I've ever had to make.'
Netanyahu made the comments in his speech at the UN General Assembly. He also cited ancient Jewish presence in the Golan Heights as justification for Israel's occupation of the Syrian territory.
US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the nearly seven-month US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.
The talks face a big obstacle as neither side wants to be the first to surrender its leverage, according to comments to Reuters by two Iranian sources, two regional officials and two Western diplomatic sources, but behind Iran's stance is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation.
Trump says he and China's Xi had a 'great meeting'
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that he and Chinese President Xi Jinping had a "great meeting" after the two leaders met at the White House.
Trump made the comments to reporters in response to shouted questions before the two boarded the Marine One helicopter on the White House grounds for a brief tour.
Xi called for the United States and Iran to resolve "issues through negotiation as soon as possible," state news agency Xinhua reported after Trump gave his Chinese counterpart a lavish welcome in Washington.
Israel's Palestinian parties hit back over election ban
The Joint List of Israel's Palestinian parties has condemned its ban from the upcoming Knesset elections in October, telling The New Arab that the decisions are "based on racism" and reflect the "hypocrisy of those who claim to support democracy".
The Joint List, made up of Hadash, Ta'al and Balad, is one of two major Arab-Israeli political blocs representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, the other being the United Arab List (Ra'am), which was also barred from the election.
Both lists were barred by Israel's Central Elections Committee (CEC) on Wednesday, which also disqualified Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh and Hadash MK Ofer Cassif from running. The decisions are set to be challenged at the Supreme Court next week.
A spokesperson for the Joint List told The New Arab that it understood the bans "to be political decisions based on racism against Arab Palestinian citizens and anyone who opposes the Israeli occupation", adding that the list was the only alternative political force in Israel that opposed Israel's occupation of the Palestinian territories and respected international law.
Turkey has blocked the X account of a digital rights expert who heads Turkey's Freedom of Expression Association (IFOD), citing national security concerns, a watchdog said Thursday.
It was the latest in a string of closures of social media accounts that initially started with LGBTQ organisations on September 12 and has since spread.
The account of Yaman Akdeniz, a digital rights expert and an IFOD founder, was blocked to X users in Turkey "on grounds of protecting national security and public order", said EngelliWeb, which monitors Turkish internet censorship.
"My X account has been blocked and @GlobalAffairs withheld my account from Türkiye," wrote Akdeniz on X, in a post only visible with a VPN in Turkey, referring to the social media platform's global government affairs team.
Since September 12, Turkey has blocked hundreds of social media accounts in a crackdown that began with LGBTQ groups and has spread to journalists, media outlets, women's groups, human rights and media freedom advocates and beyond.
Abbas pledges first Palestine parliamentary vote in 20 years
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas reaffirmed plans to hold legislative elections on November 28, the first such vote in 20 years despite serious domestic doubts it will go ahead, as he seeks to advance internationally backed reforms.
Abbas, 90, used a pre-recorded video address to the UN General Assembly to condemn US restrictions on the Palestinian delegation's access to UN headquarters, calling them a breach of Washington's obligations as host nation.
"We have completed the national reform program to which we committed ourselves before our people and the international community," Abbas said in his remarks from Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06 after which Abbas' rival, Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists. Abbas this year decreed a presidential election would take place in 2027 but he has yet to set a date.
Gaza suffers world's worst ever economic crisis: UN
Gaza is suffering the world's worst economic crisis ever recorded, with nine in 10 businesses destroyed and hundreds of thousands of people unemployed, a top UN development agency warned on Thursday.
Israel's genocide has devastated the territory of two million people before a patchy ceasefire was announced in October 2025. At least 1,394 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began, with 4,839 injured -- according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
"The collapse of the economy of Gaza is the world's most severe economic crisis on record," said Pedro Manuel Moreno, acting secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD).
"It has wiped out decades of development and generated an acute economic crisis for its people," he told reporters in Geneva as the organisation released a new report.
The report also detailed an economic and financial crisis in the occupied West Bank, citing "reduced access to land and natural resources linked to (Israeli) settlement expansion".
British government provides £88 million in aid for Gaza
The British government on Thursday said it was providing an £88 million ($116.25 million) package of support for humanitarian relief and early recovery in Gaza.
The funding would help deliver health care, clean water, sanitation and hygiene services, waste management and protection support to people in Gaza and the West Bank, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said in a statement.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has landed in New York ahead of his UN speech, amid renewed calls for his arrest under an International Criminal Court warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.
Netanyahu has presided over Israel's genocidal war in Gaza, which has killed at least 75,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities, while Israeli settler and military violence has increased in the occupied West Bank.
The ICC fugitive is scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly in the early afternoon, local time, after his plane took off overnight from an airbase in southern Israel for security reasons, according to Israeli media.
Alongside his UN address, Netanyahu is expected to meet several world leaders during a trip that will last only a few hours on the ground, according to his office.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan expressed confidence Thursday that Ankara would regain access to the US F-35 fighter jet programme, saying he expected "concrete" steps from Washington to that end.
US President Donald Trump "expressed a positive willingness regarding Turkey's return to the F-35 programme," he told reporters before boarding the plane to return from the UN General Assembly in New York.
Turkey has long sought to resolve the long-running F-35 dispute with Washington and the Trump administration has also shown willingness to draw a line under the matter.
"We expect this willingness to now translate into concrete steps," Erdogan said [Getty]
US-seized tankers of Iranian oil are in Atlantic: tracker
Three Iran-linked oil tankers seized by the United States and carrying nearly six million barrels of Iranian crude oil were in the Atlantic Ocean on Thursday, tracking data indicated.
They did not have their destination marked on their transponders, but specialist website TankerTrackers said Wednesday on X that they were heading towards the United States.
"Nearly six million barrels (valued at nearly $600 million) of seized Iranian crude oil are quietly crossing the Atlantic Ocean towards the United States of America," the post said.
The tankers were seized after the US started a blockade of Iranian ports in retaliation for Iran's closing of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil exports from Gulf countries.
Israel policies threaten 'existence' of Palestinians: Abbas
Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas said at the UN on Thursday that Israeli policies no longer just jeopardized a two-state solution but were now threatening the "very life and existence" of his people.
"The danger is no longer limited to undermining the two-state solution and preventing the realization of the Palestinian state. It has now come to threaten the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland," Abbas said.

Both lists were barred by Israel's Central Elections Committee (CEC) on Wednesday, which also disqualified Balad leader Sami Abu Shehadeh and Hadash MK Ofer Cassif from running. The decisions are set to be challenged at the Supreme Court next week.
A spokesperson for the Joint List told The New Arab that it understood the bans "to be political decisions based on racism against Arab Palestinian citizens and anyone who opposes the Israeli occupation", adding that the list was the only alternative political force in Israel that opposed Israel's occupation of the Palestinian territories and respected international law.
Turkey has blocked the X account of a digital rights expert who heads Turkey's Freedom of Expression Association (IFOD), citing national security concerns, a watchdog said Thursday.
It was the latest in a string of closures of social media accounts that initially started with LGBTQ organisations on September 12 and has since spread.
The account of Yaman Akdeniz, a digital rights expert and an IFOD founder, was blocked to X users in Turkey "on grounds of protecting national security and public order", said EngelliWeb, which monitors Turkish internet censorship.
"My X account has been blocked and @GlobalAffairs withheld my account from Türkiye," wrote Akdeniz on X, in a post only visible with a VPN in Turkey, referring to the social media platform's global government affairs team.
Since September 12, Turkey has blocked hundreds of social media accounts in a crackdown that began with LGBTQ groups and has spread to journalists, media outlets, women's groups, human rights and media freedom advocates and beyond.
Abbas pledges first Palestine parliamentary vote in 20 years
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas reaffirmed plans to hold legislative elections on November 28, the first such vote in 20 years despite serious domestic doubts it will go ahead, as he seeks to advance internationally backed reforms.
Abbas, 90, used a pre-recorded video address to the UN General Assembly to condemn US restrictions on the Palestinian delegation's access to UN headquarters, calling them a breach of Washington's obligations as host nation.
"We have completed the national reform program to which we committed ourselves before our people and the international community," Abbas said in his remarks from Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06 after which Abbas' rival, Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists. Abbas this year decreed a presidential election would take place in 2027 but he has yet to set a date.
Gaza suffers world's worst ever economic crisis: UN
Gaza is suffering the world's worst economic crisis ever recorded, with nine in 10 businesses destroyed and hundreds of thousands of people unemployed, a top UN development agency warned on Thursday.
Israel's genocide has devastated the territory of two million people before a patchy ceasefire was announced in October 2025. At least 1,394 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began, with 4,839 injured -- according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
"The collapse of the economy of Gaza is the world's most severe economic crisis on record," said Pedro Manuel Moreno, acting secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD).
"It has wiped out decades of development and generated an acute economic crisis for its people," he told reporters in Geneva as the organisation released a new report.
The report also detailed an economic and financial crisis in the occupied West Bank, citing "reduced access to land and natural resources linked to (Israeli) settlement expansion".
British government provides £88 million in aid for Gaza
The British government on Thursday said it was providing an £88 million ($116.25 million) package of support for humanitarian relief and early recovery in Gaza.
The funding would help deliver health care, clean water, sanitation and hygiene services, waste management and protection support to people in Gaza and the West Bank, the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said in a statement.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has landed in New York ahead of his UN speech, amid renewed calls for his arrest under an International Criminal Court warrant over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.
Netanyahu has presided over Israel's genocidal war in Gaza, which has killed at least 75,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities, while Israeli settler and military violence has increased in the occupied West Bank.
The ICC fugitive is scheduled to address the United Nations General Assembly in the early afternoon, local time, after his plane took off overnight from an airbase in southern Israel for security reasons, according to Israeli media.
Alongside his UN address, Netanyahu is expected to meet several world leaders during a trip that will last only a few hours on the ground, according to his office.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan expressed confidence Thursday that Ankara would regain access to the US F-35 fighter jet programme, saying he expected "concrete" steps from Washington to that end.
US President Donald Trump "expressed a positive willingness regarding Turkey's return to the F-35 programme," he told reporters before boarding the plane to return from the UN General Assembly in New York.
Turkey has long sought to resolve the long-running F-35 dispute with Washington and the Trump administration has also shown willingness to draw a line under the matter.
"We expect this willingness to now translate into concrete steps," Erdogan said [Getty]
US-seized tankers of Iranian oil are in Atlantic: tracker
Three Iran-linked oil tankers seized by the United States and carrying nearly six million barrels of Iranian crude oil were in the Atlantic Ocean on Thursday, tracking data indicated.
They did not have their destination marked on their transponders, but specialist website TankerTrackers said Wednesday on X that they were heading towards the United States.
"Nearly six million barrels (valued at nearly $600 million) of seized Iranian crude oil are quietly crossing the Atlantic Ocean towards the United States of America," the post said.
The tankers were seized after the US started a blockade of Iranian ports in retaliation for Iran's closing of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway for oil exports from Gulf countries.
Israel policies threaten 'existence' of Palestinians: Abbas
Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas said at the UN on Thursday that Israeli policies no longer just jeopardized a two-state solution but were now threatening the "very life and existence" of his people.
"The danger is no longer limited to undermining the two-state solution and preventing the realization of the Palestinian state. It has now come to threaten the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland," Abbas said.

Russia could attack a Nato country within months, Danish intelligence says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:05:44 UTC
01:05:44 KST

Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services.
In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia.
The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland that local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”.
Krzysztof Gawkowski, the deputy prime minister of Poland, said the blaze, which broke out overnight in the Masovian voivodeship, had been “deliberately designed to disable the station”, disrupting internet access for a number of institutions, including the Ukrainian military.
Gawkowski said it had not been established who was responsible for the fire, but that “many signs suggest this aligns with Russia’s new doctrine of attack.
“While everything is operational today, we must recognise, as prime minister [Donald] Tusk recently noted, that this is an element of hybrid warfare,” he said.
Starlink has become a key part of Ukraine’s military communications, and the incident comes amid a spate of suspected Russian sabotage operations across European infrastructure supporting Ukraine.
Earlier this month, Germany publicly blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport, while a series of other incidents – including fires at drone factories and sabotage targeting rail infrastructure – have also been investigated for possible links to Moscow. Russia has denied involvement in such attacks.
In recent weeks, several European intelligence chiefs have warned that Russia may be preparing more assertive actions to test Nato countries’ commitment to supporting Ukraine, though officials differ over how imminent such a move may be.
Russia is expected to intensify its hybrid attacks against European countries with “greater consequences” for those targeted in the coming months, the Danes warned, including “destructive cyber-attacks that cripple societal functions as well as sabotage attacks that carry a high risk of casualties”.
A source familiar with Moscow’s thinking agreed that Russia was likely to step up its hybrid attacks.
“Russian military top command is convinced some Nato countries are directly involved in the war against Russia – not just by supplying Ukraine with weapons and intelligence, but by helping to guide missiles and drones,” the source said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“They therefore believe Nato is already waging a hybrid war against Russia, and that Russia has the right to respond in kind,” the source added.
“Hybrid attacks” are broad terms generally used to describe non-military tactics aimed at pressuring or destabilising an adversary, including cyber-attacks, sabotage and disinformation.
The aim of Russia’s actions would be to divert European resources away from supporting Ukraine, and deepen divisions within Nato if the alliance failed to agree on a collective response, the report added.
The service believes it remained “highly unlikely” that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a Nato country, but notably said it “cannot be ruled out”.
The Danish services said Russia could seek to test Nato’s article 5, which commits members to collective defence. They warned there was “a risk that Russia assesses that the Nato countries will not respond collectively”, particularly if Moscow believes the US is unable or unwilling to support its European allies in a potential war with Russia.
There have been ongoing jitters among Nato members over whether the alliance’s most powerful member, the US, would come to Europe’s defence under Donald Trump in the event of a Russian attack.
Questions over unity within Europe are also growing. Last week, Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, who has maintained close ties with the Kremlin, cast doubt on his country’s commitment to Nato’s collective defence principle, saying he did not want Slovakia drawn into a military conflict “because of some article 5”.
Speaking at the UN general assembly on Wednesday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that Russia continued to threaten countries beyond Ukraine, including Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states, while showing “no respect” for the sovereignty of countries in the south Caucasus and central Asia.
“The more freedom Putin has to act, the more dangerous the world becomes for everyone else,” he said.

Ukrainian suspect arrested after fatal stabbing at Polish abbey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:02:53 UTC
01:02:53 KST

A knife attack at a Catholic abbey in Poland left one person dead and four others injured. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the attack as a "horrific crime" and called for the perpetrator to be held accountable.
A Ukrainian man was arrested on Thursday after a knife attack at a Catholic abbey in southeastern Poland left one person dead and four others injured.
Police said the 31-year-old suspect attacked four men and a woman at the 17th-century abbey in Jarosław, around 30 kilometres from the Ukrainian border.
The attack took place at approximately 9:30 am, when police received reports of a stabbing.
Polish media identified the person killed as a priest. Police confirmed the death to AFP but did not verify the victim's identity.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the "murderer" would be "punished with the full severity of Polish law."
Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also addressed the attack in a post on X.
"Tragic events in Jarosław. A Ukrainian citizen was immediately detained by the police after an attack on five people. The services are investigating the motives and circumstances of the incident," he wrote.
According to prosecutors, the suspect had entered Poland from Germany and was travelling towards the Ukrainian border. Instead, he went to the abbey, where he allegedly took a knife from the kitchen and attacked clergy members and worshippers.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy condemned the attack, describing it as a "horrific crime."
"The perpetrator of this evil must bear full responsibility in accordance with the law," he said.
"We are shaken by this evil," Zelenskyy added. "Justice must be done."
Local newspaper Gazeta Jarosławska published photographs showing fire engines and police vehicles outside the monastery, with its entrance cordoned off.

Russian steel production to fall by 6% in 2026 — ministry forecast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:02:00 UTC
01:02:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. The Russian Economic Development Ministry expects pig iron production in Russia to decline by 4% to 48.5 mln metric tons in 2026, while steel production is projected to fall by 6% to 63.8 mln metric tons, according to a document published on the ministry’s website.
"In 2025, production indicators at metallurgical and pipe-making enterprises showed a downward trend due to weaker demand for metal products from major consumers on the domestic market," the document said.
By 2029, production of finished rolled ferrous metal products is expected to decline by 3.2% to 54.9 mln metric tons. Of the total finished rolled products, sheet metal production is projected to reach 26.4 mln metric tons by 2029, down 0.1% from 2025, while long product output is expected to total 28.5 mln metric tons, down 5.9% from 2025.
In non-ferrous metallurgy, production of major non-ferrous and precious metals showed mixed dynamics in 2025: precious metals production rose by 5%, aluminum production declined by 2.9%, copper production fell by 6.2%, while non-ferrous metal ore production increased by 7.1%.

Xi calls for 'candid, in-depth, continued dialogue' to deepen China-US cooperation at White House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:01:44 UTC
01:01:44 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for "trust," continued dialogue and "healthy competition" as US President Donald Trump hosted him at the White House.
Beijing and Washington should strengthen communication, Xi said on Thursday, stressing that despite differences in their "national conditions," the two countries can better understand each other, seek common ground, and build mutual trust through "candid, in-depth, and continued dialogue."
He encouraged strengthened contacts between Chinese and US government departments, including those overseeing foreign affairs, the economy, financial cooperation, law enforcement, and people-to-people exchanges.
He also voiced support for greater exchanges between the two countries' legislative bodies.
"We should coexist in peace," Xi said, adding that as two major countries they "stand to gain from cooperation and will both lose in confrontation."
Xi emphasised that China and the US do not need to avoid competition, but that it should be "healthy" and "kept within bounds." He called for "a race of catching up with each other," rather than a zero-sum "wrestling match in which one either wins or loses."
China and the US "must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation," he stressed, while calling for regular dialogue and improved mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention between their respective militaries.
"The Thucydides trap can be overcome," he said, referring to the risk of conflict between a rising power and an established one, a concept coming from US novelist Herman Wouk, referring to the ancient Greek historian.
Trump, meanwhile, said decisions made during his talks with Xi on security, technology and “superintelligence” — referring to artificial intelligence — could shape global stability for decades.
“During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and superintelligence. The decisions we make in these areas today can promote peace and prosperity for decades and decades to come,” Trump said.
He also said Washington and Beijing had been working to encourage a more balanced trading relationship, including greater market access for American farmers and ranchers.

Russian oil product exports expected to fall by 21.7% to 98.5 mln tons in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:01:08 UTC
01:01:08 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. The Russian Economic Development Ministry expects oil product exports to decline by 21.7% this year compared with 2025 to 98.5 mln metric tons, according to the baseline assumptions for Russia’s socioeconomic development in 2027 and the 2028-2029 planning period, which were reviewed by the government and published on the ministry’s website.
In 2025, Russia’s oil product exports actually totaled 125.8 mln metric tons, according to the Economic Development Ministry’s materials. Under the baseline scenario, oil product exports are projected at 98.5 mln metric tons in 2026, rising to 113.1 mln metric tons in 2027 and 134 mln metric tons in 2028 before edging down to 130 mln metric tons in 2029.
In its spring forecast, the Economic Development Ministry expected oil product exports to total 122.6 mln metric tons in 2026, 134 mln metric tons in both 2027 and 2028, and decline to 130 mln metric tons by 2029.
Under the Russian Economic Development Ministry’s updated conservative scenario, oil product exports could total 98.5 mln metric tons in 2026, 103.4 mln metric tons in 2027, 129.2 mln metric tons in 2028, and 130 mln metric tons in 2029.

Humor makes taboo words less distracting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:00:40 UTC
01:00:40 KST

Taboo words slowed people’s ability to identify font colors, but this distraction was reduced when the words were also funny, according to research published in Cognition & Emotion.
Taboo words—including profanity, insults, slurs, and sexual terms—can interfere with language processing. In the “taboo Stroop effect” (a variation of the standard Stroop effect, a psychological phenomenon where reading a word interferes with naming its ink color), people take longer to identify the font color of a taboo word than that of a neutral word. Researchers have generally attributed this delay to emotional arousal (a state of heightened physiological and psychological activity). Taboo words capture attention or make it harder to disengage from their meaning, leaving fewer attentional resources available for identifying their color.
However, taboo words are not exclusively offensive or unpleasant; some are also perceived as humorous. Because humor can itself be arousing but may help people shift attention more flexibly, Lise Abrams and colleagues examined whether humor would intensify or lessen the distracting effect of taboo words.
Experiment 1 involved 59 participants recruited via Prolific (an online platform used to recruit research subjects) after exclusions. Eligible participants were native English speakers living in the United States, between ages 18-29 years, and did not report color blindness, dyslexia, or ADHD. Participants saw 48 taboo and 48 neutral words, selected using previous nine-point ratings of tabooness, humor, and arousal. Each word appeared once in red, blue, green, and yellow, producing 384 randomly intermixed trials. Participants pressed one of four keys to identify the font color as quickly and accurately as possible, after completing color-key training and 40 practice trials. They also completed a demographic questionnaire.
Experiment 2 included 102 Prolific participants using the same eligibility criteria. The researchers selected 32 words divided into four groups based on the same nine-point norms: high-taboo/high-humor, high-taboo/low-humor, low-taboo/high-humor, and low-taboo/low-humor. The words were presented in separate blocks, along with neutral filler blocks, for a total of 256 trials. Participants again identified each word’s font color by keypress, and the researchers measured response time and accuracy.
In Experiment 1, participants identified the colors of taboo words more slowly than those of neutral words, demonstrating the taboo Stroop effect. This interference was strongest during the first set of trials and diminished with repeated exposure, suggesting that participants gradually became accustomed to the taboo words. Words rated as more taboo produced slower responses, but humor did not independently predict response speed or alter the effect of tabooness when taboo and neutral words were intermixed.
Experiment 2 again showed that taboo words slowed color identification. This time, however, humor changed the size of the effect: highly taboo words interfered with performance whether they were high or low in humor, but the interference was significantly smaller for the more humorous taboo words. Humor alone did not affect response times, suggesting that it did not simply make color identification easier; instead, it specifically reduced how strongly taboo content captured attention when words were presented in separate blocks.
The limited number of suitable words made it difficult to match the four word categories on characteristics such as emotional valence (the intrinsic positive or negative quality of a stimulus) and arousal. The young, US-based online sample and presentation of isolated words also limit how readily the findings can be generalized to other populations, cultures, or real-world language contexts.
Overall, the findings suggest that people’s responses to taboo language depend not only on how offensive a word is but also on whether it is funny, revealing a more complex relationship among humor, arousal, and attention.
The research, “When an F-bomb bonks your funny bone: humor attenuates the taboo Stroop effect,” was authored by Lise Abrams, Lori E. James, Maria-Elisabeth Lootus, and Meredith A. Shafto.

I am working individually — Dovbyk responded to accusations that he refused to play for the Ukrainian national team
Kyiv • UNN
Artem Dovbyk denied refusing the national team because of Bologna's priority. The forward is treating a hamstring injury and training individually.
Ukraine national team and Italian "Bologna" forward Artem Dovbyk rejected accusations that he does not want to play for the national team, stating that he has a minor injury and therefore is still training individually, reports UNN.
Details
On September 16, Ukraine national team head coach Andrea Maldera announced the Ukraine squad for the Nations League matches, which included, in particular, "Bologna" forward Artem Dovbyk.
However, the following day it became known that, due to injuries, Italian "Bologna" forward Artem Dovbyk and Zhytomyr "Polissya" midfielder Oleksandr Andrievskyi withdrew from the Ukraine football team squad.
Instead, Maldera called up two footballers from the reserve list: "Dynamo" midfielder Oleksandr Pikhalyonok and "Polissya" forward Ihor Krasnopir.
At the same time, on September 21, "Bologna" announced that Artem Dovbyk had returned to training with the team.
The Italian publication Corriere dello Sport reported today that Dovbyk had declined the call-up to the Ukraine national team.
In a comment to Tribuna.com, the Ukrainian said that the information that he was already training fully with the team was not entirely accurate.
Three days before the game against Torino, we spoke with Maldera because I had missed the game against Napoli. I explained to him what injury I had and said that I was preparing for the match against "Torino" and for the national team. But during the training session before the match, I tried to train with the team and realized that it was still too early. I called him and explained that I needed about another week to be fully ready. We jointly decided that I should heal the injury 100% and only then return. It is the back of the thigh. It is a different injury, not a recurrence as was written. Over the last few days, I have already started training with the team, but for now I only take part in the warm-up, and then work individually. Therefore, the information that I am already training fully with the team is not entirely accurate
Recall
Ukraine national team forward Artem Dovbyk will spend next season with Italian "Roma", having moved there on loan from Rome's "Roma".

West Bank herders use donkeys and trenches to move milk at night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:00:19 UTC
01:00:19 KST

Herders in the West Bank use donkeys to carry milk churns through an earthen trench before loading them onto a vehicle.
The journey takes place at night, with farmers helping the animals over the steep earthworks.
According to a farmer, access to the area has been restricted, making it difficult to transport milk and reach grazing land. He says there are no roads and that the trench has cut off their usual route, limiting the movement of people and vehicles.
The milk is eventually transferred to a truck, which leaves along a rough track.
They work at night because they fear being stopped or arrested if they enter the area during the day.

Google’s Gemini Can Now Make Calls for You on Pixel Phones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

Google has been trying to have its AI assistant make phone calls on your behalf for almost 10 years. Remember Duplex? It enabled the now-defunct Google Assistant to call restaurants and book tables. That service was shuttered a few years ago, but now comes round two, powered by modern large language models.
On Thursday, Google announced Call for Me, an experimental beta feature exclusive to its latest Pixel 11 smartphones in the US (and in English). Pixel 11 owners need a Gemini subscription and have to be enrolled in the Phone by Google app’s public beta. Google has instructions on how to participate here.
These calls are designed to reach businesses. Gemini can call your local hardware store to ask if they stock a specific tool, or chat with a barber to schedule a haircut. Just tell Gemini to make the call—it may ask you follow-up questions for more context—and the chatbot will introduce itself and can have a back-and-forth conversation to ensure your request is handled. If it runs into an automated phone menu, it can navigate it and even wait on hold. On your end, you can view a live transcript on the Pixel and take over at any point.
Google says it works best with businesses, but there are some establishments Gemini won't call, like emergency services. That said, you can ask Gemini to call specific numbers. For example, if your tattoo artist doesn't have much of a web presence, “Gemini will try to search for a phone number, but you may provide one as well,” a Google spokesperson tells WIRED. During these calls, the assistant's voice will be the same one used in Gemini Live interactions, even if your preferred Gemini voice has an accent.
Call for Me expands on Google’s suite of smart calling features on Pixels and Android. The Phone app can already screen incoming calls and block robocalls and telemarketers. Hold for Me lets the assistant listen for when the hold music ends and a live person is on the other end; it alerts you to pick up the phone when it’s finally your cue. Direct My Call can display the different choices in an automated phone menu before they’re spoken, so you can tap nine to reach a live person and skip the recorded voice reading out the whole list. It even has real-time Scam Detection, alerting you when it thinks the person on the other end is scamming you.
Voice assistants handling phone calls is a little more accepted today than back in the Duplex days. Call screening features abound—whether on a Pixel, Samsung, or iPhone, onboard assistants routinely intercept unknown callers to ask why they’re calling.
But these kinds of features—much like hyped-up AI translation features—can often fall short. Calls are unpredictable, and the person on the other end may hang up, assuming it’s just another spam call. What happens if Gemini doesn’t understand a person’s accent all that well? Will it trap the clerk in an endless loop of asking them to repeat themselves? And if the shop doesn’t have the tool you need, does the bot know how to bow out politely—or just cut the line?
“That is exactly what we want to continue testing,” the Google spokesperson says. “With this experiment, we look forward to users testing a variety of cases, so that we can continue to improve the feature across accents and noisy environments.” And yes, Google says Gemini will “politely” hang up if the business can't accommodate your needs.
It still points to a future where robots may take over these kinds of business phone calls altogether. Businesses are also experimenting with artificial-intelligence tools to interface with customers, like local California pizza chain Pizza My Heart, which lets you text its Jimmy the Surfer chatbot to order pizza.
It doesn’t seem too far off that you’ll ask your phone to call a restaurant, and the restaurant’s AI will answer. The machines are talking to each other, except they’re just debating whether you want the stuffed crust.
