New nuke sub leaves yard and heads to Scotland for trials
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:48:18 BST
00:48:18 KST

Cumbria Police closed Michaelson Road Bridge in Barrow-in-Furness on Thursday morning, working in collaboration with BAE Systems, and told residents a further message would be published once the crossing reopened.
The force confirmed the closure at 9am and said the bridge would remain shut while the operation was carried out. An updated statement issued later said: “Michaelson Road Bridge has now reopened. Thank you for your patience.” The closure ran until around 11.40am.
The UK Defence Journal understands that the operation covered the departure of a submarine from the yard, and that the boat involved was HMS Agamemnon, the sixth of the Astute class, with people gathering along the dockside to watch her leave.
Agamemnon was commissioned into the Royal Navy on 22 September last year at a ceremony in Devonshire Dock Hall attended by the King. Around 500 guests were present, and on the same day the King conferred Royal Port status on the town while steel was cut for HMS King George VI, the fourth and final Dreadnought-class submarine.
She completed a three-day trim dive shortly after commissioning, submerging to around 15 metres to confirm the integrity of the pressure hull and to establish her centre of gravity, with crew and engineers moving 16 tonnes of lead weights around the boat to simulate different loading conditions.
Steel was cut for Agamemnon in July 2013 and she was launched in October 2024, making her construction the longest of any nuclear submarine built for the Royal Navy, a delay attributed variously to the pandemic, the diversion of resources to begin the Dreadnought programme and the complexity of the Astute design.
Michaelson Road Bridge carries traffic across the entrance to Devonshire Dock, and closures of this kind are a familiar feature of submarine movements at the yard, with the bridge having to be swung clear before a boat of that size can pass out into Walney Channel.
At 7,400 tonnes and 97 metres, the Astute class carries Spearfish heavyweight torpedoes and Tomahawk Block IV land attack missiles, and the boats protect the deterrent submarines and the carrier strike group while also conducting surveillance and intelligence work. Seven were ordered, with the final submarine still under construction in the same hall.
Barrow remains the only facility in the United Kingdom with the infrastructure, site licence and resources to design and build British nuclear submarines, and the Defence Nuclear Enterprise annual update to Parliament published this month recorded that the workforce there has grown by more than 1,800 under the current government.
The yard is also preparing for the programmes that follow, with steel due to be cut on the first British SSN-AUKUS submarine in 2027 and the concept design completed earlier this year for SMITE2, a new submarine propulsion testing facility at the site.

Russian Rental Rush Hits Georgia, Serbia, Armenia—Kazakhstan’s Expected Wave Never Comes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:47:49 UTC
00:47:49 KST

- Category
- World
Russian Rental Rush Hits Georgia, Serbia, Armenia—Kazakhstan’s Expected Wave Never Comes
Russian demand for rental housing rose sharply in Georgia, Serbia, and Armenia in late summer 2026, according to real estate agents interviewed by Meduza, while agents in Kazakhstan reported no comparable increase.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Meduza reported the trend on September 24 after speaking with real estate agents in Tbilisi, Yerevan, Belgrade, Novi Sad, and Almaty. The outlet changed the agents’ names at their request.
Their accounts reflect individual market experience rather than comprehensive official arrival statistics.
According to Meduza, rumors of a possible new mobilization have circulated in Russia since the summer of 2026. Vladimir Putin has dismissed the reports as “nonsense” and said there is currently no need for another draft.
Russia’s two largest emigration waves since the full-scale invasion came in 2022, first in February and March and again after Putin announced a partial mobilization in September.
Georgia
Anna, a Russian realtor who has worked in Tbilisi for nine years, told Meduza that she has received up to five inquiries an hour since late July.
She said many new clients are younger than 30, arrive without firm plans, and have rental budgets of around $500.
Rents have so far increased by about $50–$100, Anna told the outlet. Apartments in major residential districts that could be rented for about $550 earlier this year are now being offered for $600–$700.
She expects some properties currently listed at $600–$700 to reach $900–$1,100 within several months if arrivals and demand continue to grow.
Irina, another Russian realtor working in Tbilisi, told Meduza that good listings now remain available for only a day or two.
Apartments that rented for $600–$700 a month a year ago are now going for $800–$900 a month, she said.
However, Irina expects demand to ease within three to four months.
She told Meduza that many clients plan to remain outside Russia for only two or three months before either returning or moving elsewhere in Europe.
Georgia’s Interior Ministry recorded about 1.5 million entries by Russian citizens during the first year of the full-scale war, Meduza reported.
Georgia’s national statistics service classified about 62,300 Russians as migrants, while more than 37,700 Russian citizens were living in the country in 2026.
Serbia
Meduza reported a similar rise in rental demand in Serbia.
Andrei, a Russian realtor working in Novi Sad, said he now receives several requests for long-term rental viewings each day, compared with periods earlier this year when he sometimes went a week without inquiries.
According to Andrei, individual apartments now attract lines of Russian applicants, with some prospective tenants offering above the asking price.
He linked the increase to rumors of a possible mobilization after Russia’s State Duma elections and to recurring internet disruptions in Russia.
Prices in Novi Sad have not risen significantly so far, Andrei told Meduza. Monthly rents there currently range from roughly $455 to $795, below the $909–$1,136 levels seen during the 2022 influx.
The situation in Belgrade is more pronounced. Petr, a realtor in the Serbian capital, told Meduza that “a lot of Russians” have been arriving since the second half of August and that he had not seen comparable demand since 2022.
Petr said rental prices in Belgrade have risen by about 20–30% since late July, with apartments in the city center now costing roughly $682–$1,136 per month.
He also said many landlords refuse on principle to rent to foreigners, partly out of concern that local students could struggle to find housing amid the increased demand.
Serbia’s Interior Ministry registered more than 140,000 Russian citizens between February 24 and November 2, 2022, according to data cited by Meduza.
Nearly 70,000 Russians obtained Serbian residence permits between 2022 and 2025.
Armenia
In Yerevan, Russian realtor Alexander told Meduza that demand began increasing in the second half of July, with August and September proving particularly active.
According to Alexander, rents in Yerevan have risen by roughly 30–50% since the beginning of the year.
A good two-room apartment in the city center now costs around $1,000 per month, compared with approximately $700 in the spring.
Kristina, another Yerevan realtor interviewed by Meduza, said inquiries for long-term rentals are now roughly twice the level seen during winter and spring.
Many prospective tenants contact her while they are still in Russia and preparing to relocate.
She also described a shift in the profile of arrivals.
Unlike the predominantly remote workers who relocated in 2022 with established jobs and budgets, more recent arrivals include people hoping to find work in the service sector, with some traveling using credit cards to cover their initial expenses, Meduza reported.
Armenia’s Migration Service reported in August 2024 that about 40,000 Russian citizens held legal residence rights or valid residence permits in the country.
Yerevan realtors interviewed by Meduza expect rents to peak in October, although they cautioned that longer-term price forecasts remain uncertain.
Kazakhstan
Kazakhstan has so far seen no comparable rental surge, according to Meduza’s interviews with realtors in Almaty.
The country recorded about 406,000 Russian entries in September 2022, but later tightened migration and residence rules.
Tamara, an Almaty realtor, told Meduza that Russian arrivals and departures currently appear largely normal, with no repeat of the demand seen four years ago.
Another Almaty agent, Dmitry, said local realtors had expected more Russians to arrive amid reports of fuel shortages and rumors of mobilization, but the anticipated increase did not materialize.
Russians once accounted for about 90% of his clients, he said, but now make up no more than roughly 10%.
Almaty housing prices have nevertheless increased by approximately 10–20% in recent months.
Dmitry attributed the rise to the start of the academic year and an influx of students, rather than to Russian arrivals, Meduza reported.
The reported demand follows a run of earlier warning signs.
In mid-July, searches for apartments in Yerevan reached 5,200 in a single week, exceeding the level recorded in the first week of the full-scale war in 2022, and rents in the Armenian capital had climbed by around 30% in three months.
By late August, more than 113,000 Russians had crossed into Georgia through the Verkhny Lars checkpoint in a single week, including over 20,000 on August 20 alone.

Ukrainians in UK fear cut to funds for Homes for Ukraine hosts could make them homeless
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:47:39 UTC
00:47:39 KST

Ukrainian refugees in the UK fear they could be left homeless after the government quietly axed 70% of funding for hosts of the Homes for Ukraine scheme, reducing monthly “thank you” payments to them from £350 to £100.
The scheme was launched after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and has provided support for 181,000 of the 234,000 Ukrainians who have since sought sanctuary in the UK.
Now the government has said it will cut the hosting payments and reduce contributions to local authorities, which are paid a sum for each arrival to meet the costs associated with delivering the programme.
A written statement to parliament from the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) on 15 September said funding would be reduced from £5,900 to £3,300. The changes will come into effect from 1 January 2027.
Tetiana, a 73-year-old Ukrainian refugee who has been hosted for two years and four months, said she was devastated to read the government’s letter circulated to hosts in the last few days informing them of the changes.
She said: “I feel that this financial change could impact on my host’s ability to host me. If the hosting comes to an end, I don’t know where I will go and how I can start again. I can’t work because of my age and because I have mobility problems.
“I fled from Kharkiv, which is close to the Russia frontline, so I can’t go back to Ukraine. I don’t know what I will do. I’m at a loss about what my options will be. This change has created a lot of uncertainty for me. I don’t know how I would be able to pay rent if hosting finishes for me.”
Nataliya Rumyantseva is hosting her mother, the first Ukrainian to arrive in the UK after the war started. She said the changes were likely to have a significant impact. “When refugees arrive here from Ukraine, they are shellshocked and need time to adapt and learn the language. If hosting changes to become a more commercial rental arrangement, I think that’s cruel.”
One host who lives in Greenwich said he did not know if he would be able to continue hosting because of the drop in payments. “I’ve been a sponsor since May 2022. I was dismayed to learn that thank you payments are reducing to just £100,” he said. “I lost my job within months of becoming a sponsor and these payments have become an absolute lifeline even though I did not volunteer for this scheme for the money. I genuinely worry about the consequences of this change for Ukrainians in the UK.”
One option the government proposes is that hosts can switch to landlord status and charge refugees rent.
A host who lives in Cardiff and is hosting a Ukrainian who has enrolled on a course of study said: “The situation feels like a cheap shot from the government. We, in good faith, opened our home to someone in need. That person, in good faith, planned for a life in the UK. And the government, in what seems like very bad faith, saw an easy way to claw money back from people who aren’t in a position to stop them.”
The government says it has so far provided more than £1.81bn for the scheme.
An MHCLG spokesperson said: “The UK’s commitment to supporting Ukrainians is unwavering and the Homes for Ukraine scheme remains open. As the scheme has evolved from an initial emergency response into a more established programme, these changes are designed to secure the scheme’s long-term future while maintaining support for sponsors, guests and councils.”

Russia Tests Molniya Strike Drones as “Flying Couriers” for Carrying Weapons and Food to Frontline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:47:36 UTC
00:47:36 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Tests Molniya Strike Drones as “Flying Couriers” for Carrying Weapons and Food to Frontline
Russian forces have begun experimenting with Molniya drones as a means of transporting weapons and supplies to frontline positions, according to footage released by the Sunstrike unmanned systems unit of Ukraine’s 82nd Separate Air Assault Brigade.
The footage published by the Ukrainian unit shows several configurations of the Russian drone carrying different types of cargo. In one instance, a rifle is attached to the aircraft, while another drone is shown carrying a package of supplies.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian defense outlet Militarnyi, the modifications suggest Russian forces are testing ways to expand the Molniya’s role beyond its primary use as a strike drone, potentially turning the platform into a lightweight logistics system capable of delivering supplies to troops on the battlefield.
Such a configuration could allow Russian troops to transport small loads to frontline positions without relying on personnel or conventional vehicles for the final stage of delivery.
However, there is currently no evidence that the use of Molniya drones for logistics has become a standard practice or is being employed on a large scale by Russian forces, Militarnyi noted.
The Molniya is a relatively basic Russian fixed-wing attack drone primarily used to deliver explosive payloads. It has a range of around 30 to 40 kilometers and can carry a warhead weighing up to seven kilograms. Modified versions of the drone have also been employed for reconnaissance and artillery fire correction.
The apparent experimentation with the Molniya comes as Russia continues to develop drones for operations against Ukrainian logistics. Trident Group CEO Yurii Humenchuk told RBC-Ukraine in an interview published on July 13 that Russia was working on a new category of medium-range strike drones intended to target Ukrainian supply routes.
According to Humenchuk, Russia is seeking a platform that would bridge the gap between relatively inexpensive Molniya drones and the larger, heavier Shahed-type attack UAVs.

Ukraine Hits Kasta and P-18 Radars Alongside Russian Attack Drone Facility
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:47:17 UTC
00:47:17 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Kasta and P-18 Radars Alongside Russian Attack Drone Facility
Ukrainian forces struck two Russian radar systems, a site used to store and launch attack drones, and a fuel depot during operations on September 23 and overnight into September 24, Ukraine’s General Staff reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, Ukrainian Defense Forces targeted a facility near the city of Donetsk that Russian troops used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones. The military said targeting infrastructure supporting Russian drone operations remains one of its priority areas of combat activity.
Ukrainian forces also struck two Russian radar stations in occupied Ukrainian territories. A 35N6 Kasta radar was targeted near Chekhohrad, formerly known as Novohrodivka, while a P-18 radar was hit near Yakymivka in the Zaporizhzhia region.
The Kasta 35N6 is a mobile two-coordinate radar designed to monitor airspace, detect aerial targets, and identify aircraft, including those operating at low altitudes. The system consists of antenna and electronic equipment, operational stations mounted on military trucks, backup power units, and a remote operator console that can be positioned up to 300 meters from the radar.
The P-18, meanwhile, is a Soviet-designed mobile early-warning radar operating in the VHF band. It is used to detect aerial targets, determine their range and direction, and relay the information to air defense units, according to the General Staff.
The latest strikes follow another Ukrainian operation against Russia’s radar capabilities several days earlier. On September 20 and overnight into September 21, Ukrainian forces targeted a Russian Kasta radar valued at at least $60 million, as well as a drone command post and an area where Russian personnel were concentrated.
Ukraine’s General Staff reported that the radar was hit near Pikuzy in the temporarily occupied Donetsk region. During the same operation, Ukrainian forces targeted a Russian drone command post near Dniproenerhiia in the temporarily occupied part of the region.

Eight attempted suicides during US aircraft carrier's extended mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:46:47 UTC
00:46:47 KST

Eight attempted suicides during US aircraft carrier's extended mission
WASHINGTON, Sept 24 - There were eight suicide attempts among US sailors on board the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group during its extended 286 consecutive-day deployment at sea, the Pentagon told a lawmaker in a written response to questions.
The nuclear-powered Lincoln, with roughly 5,000 personnel, was involved in the US naval blockade and combat operations in the war with Iran and — according to Democratic lawmakers — set a modern-day record for consecutive days at sea. The strike group consists of the carrier itself and several other warships.
In a letter to US Democratic Senator Kirsten Gillibrand dated September 22, Acting US Navy Secretary Hung Cao said that while there were no suicides during the deployments, there were a total of eight attempts on board the aircraft carrier and its accompanying vessels.
It was unclear how many individuals carried out the attempts.
"That this administration can find endless taxpayer dollars for bombs, ballrooms, and billionaires, but cannot take care of our service members, is completely unacceptable," said Gillibrand, who sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee.
Earlier this month the Abraham Lincoln and some of its supporting ships arrived at port in eastern Thailand after 286 days at sea, after having been deployed last November.
Typically naval deployments are for between six and nine months but can be extended during times of conflict. Mental health issues on long deployments have long plagued the US Navy. REUTERS

UK to Keep Sanctions on 2 Russian Oligarchs Despite EU Compromise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:46:42 UTC
00:46:42 KST

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham reportedly told President Volodymyr Zelensky that he disagreed with the EU’s decision to delist two Russian oligarchs closely connected to Russian President Vladimir Putin – Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman.
Burnham made the remarks during a private meeting with Zelensky on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, Sept. 23, citing sources familiar with the matter.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The UK intends to keep sanctions on the two men as they are linked to Moscow’s war effort, taking a step back from Brussels which removed Usmanov and Fridman from its blacklist on Tuesday.
The compromise ended weeks of deadlock among frustrated member states.
A compromise with two failed attempts behind it
Before formally making the decision, the EU ambassadors failed to agree on renewing the sanctions twice, after France joined Slovakia on Sept. 11 in demanding changes to the list of sanctioned individuals.
With talks stalled, the bloc extended the existing measures by one week on Sept. 14.
In return for delistment of Usmanov and Fridman, restrictions on the remaining entities and individuals, including asset freezes and travel bans, were extended for another three years instead of the usual six or 12 months.
According to Reuters on Tuesday, France and Luxembourg pushed for the removals. Media reports linked France’s position to two French nationals held in Azerbaijan, while Luxembourg reportedly sought Fridman’s delisting over his $16 billion arbitration claim against the country.
Ukraine Opens Second EU Negotiating Cluster as Reform Delivery Shapes Further Accession Progress, KSE Institute Says
Latvia and Estonia act nationally
As the EU sanctions require unanimity, Latvia initially blocked the deal.
Hours before the measures were set to expire at Tuesday midnight, Riga switched its diplomatic stance and lifted the veto.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs described the decision as a choice “between a bad one and a significantly worse one.”
Riga then imposed its own financial and entry restrictions on both men. The government also pledged to use all available legal tools to keep their funds in Latvia frozen.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said Tallinn “did not support this decision and abstained from the vote,” before signing a decree in New York placing Fridman and Usmanov under national sanctions. Estonia announced the decision on Thursday.
“Both men support Russia’s aggression against Ukraine, and I call on others to impose national sanctions against them too,” Tsahkna wrote in a statement on X.
Kyiv frames delistment as ‘suicidal and counterproductive’
Ukraine opposed the delistings from the start. As the deal emerged, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on Monday that the move would send the wrong signal to Moscow, exactly at the time when pressure needs to be increased.
On Tuesday, Zelensky met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on the sidelines of the UNGA in New York. Following the meeting, he said that “signals about lifting sanctions on certain Russian oligarchs appear suicidal and counterproductive,” particularly because air-raid alerts were sounding across Ukraine nationwide, even as the UN assembly met.
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, Zelensky’s adviser on sanctions policy, told Kyiv Post on Wednesday that the decision appeared “very strange,” given that the circumstances had not changed.
“Russia continues the war, and their [Fridman and Usmanov’s] ties with the Kremlin, which were among the grounds for sanctions, have not disappeared,” he said, warning that Russia was trying to fracture the unity of the EU and that the move must not become a new precedent.
He also said Kyiv would reiterate by proposing new sanctions on Russian oligarchs tied to Moscow’s military-industrial complex who had not yet been targeted.

Nigeria, US agree to increase mining investment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:46:00 UTC
00:46:00 KST

Nigeria, US agree to boost mining investment
September 24, 2026
Nigeria and the US have agreed to "deepen" American investment in the West African country's mining sector.
The deal was signed on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York City, Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced on Thursday.
"This is an important step in strengthening Nigeria-US cooperation around our mineral resources, valued at about $700 billion (€796 billion)," Alake said.
"The framework covers geological data and exploration, mineral development and processing, infrastructure, and technical capacity,"he added.
'We want more local processing'
Although known for its vast oil reserves, Nigeria is also home to deposits of lithium, gold, tin, gemstones, iron ore and phosphate.
Lithium, in particular, is in high demand globally as an essential component in the batteries are powering the green energy transition.
Alake said the agreement, which was signed on Wednesday, would be used to identify viable projects. He hinted that local jobs could be created by onshoring the refining of minerals, which until now have largely been exported as ore.
"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value," Alake said. "We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses."
However, these goals come as Nigeria's mining sector remains mired by safety concerns and environmental concerns.

FACTBOX: Economic Development Ministry’s forecast, oil prices, inflation, GDP
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:45:51 UTC
00:45:51 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Russia’s Economic Development Ministry has its year-end inflation forecast to 6.8%, Economic Development Minister Maxim Reshetnikov announced.
The ministry expects real household income to grow by 0.8% in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027. Russia's GDP growth in 2026 was raised to 0.6%.
In its updated forecast, the Economic Development Ministry set the price of Brent crude at $73 per barrel for 2027, with a projected decline to $66 by 2029.
TASS has summarized the key points of the ministry's forecast as presented by the minister.
Household income
- Consumer demand remains a driver of economic growth.
- The ministry expects a significant increase in consumer demand--by 4.1%--in 2026.
- The ministry projects real household income growth of 0.8% in 2026 and 1.5% in 2027.
- Growth is expected to accelerate to 2.8% by 2029.
- The historically low unemployment rate of 2.3% remains a limiting factor in the labor market.
Inflation
- The Economic Development Ministry expects inflation to return to the Central Bank's target of 4% by the end of 2027.
- The year-end inflation forecast has been raised to 6.8%.
- The ministry raised its GDP growth estimate for 2026 to 0.6%.
- The Economic Development Ministry also projects an acceleration in GDP growth from 1.4% to 2.4% during the 2027-2029 period.
Dollar exchange rate
- The average annual dollar exchange rate in 2026 is projected at 79.5 rubles.
- The Economic Development Ministry anticipates a gradual weakening of the ruble between 2027 and 2029.
- The ministry forecasts the dollar exchange rate at 86 rubles by the end of 2026, a figure that remains unchanged from the initial scenario assumptions.
Oil production and energy prices
- The Economic Development Ministry estimates Russia's oil production at 494 million tonnes in 2026, with a projected recovery to 500 million tonnes in 2027.
- The updated forecast sets the price of Brent crude at $73 per barrel for 2027, declining to $66 by 2029.
- The price forecast for Urals crude has been raised by $1-3, reflecting an assumption of a wider discount relative to Brent.
- The ministry expects the price of Urals crude to be $53 per barrel in 2027 and $51 by 2029.
- This is slightly above the $50 cut-off price established for 2027.
Investment
- The ministry’s investment forecast takes into account the higher interest rate trend projected by the Bank of Russia.
- A recovery-driven growth of 0.2% is expected to begin in 2027.
- The proposed budget framework creates room for easing monetary policy conditions and reviving investment activity in Russia.
- In its forecast, the Economic Development Ministry projects a return to investment growth in 2028-2029, reaching 2.5% and 3%, respectively.
Exports
- The Economic Development Ministry’s updated forecast takes into account reduced gas supplies to the EU, more moderate export growth to China, and LNG restrictions resulting from sanctions.
- Net exports are expected to contribute an average of approximately 0.2 percentage points annually to Russia's GDP growth over the next three years.

Interpol issues Red Notice for Uzbek banker who said he was kidnapped in Paris last year — on suspicion of organizing a separate kidnapping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:43:46 UTC
00:43:46 KST

Interpol has issued a Red Notice for Uzbek financier Kakhramonjon Olimov, who in the summer of 2025 claimed he had been kidnapped in Paris. A subsequent investigation by The Insider and L’Express found evidence suggesting the kidnapping of Olimov was staged. Then, last week, The Insider was the first to report that Olimov had been charged in a separate kidnapping case, with a source alleging that Olimov himself planned for the abduction of a business rival. Uzbekistan has ordered Olimov’s arrest, and Interpol has responded by placing the businessman on its international wanted list.
Olimov is the owner of Anorbank. According to the latest disclosed figures, he directly owns 52.36% of the bank, while another 47.06% is held by Netherlands-registered Bekamin B.V., which is also linked to Olimov.
After The Insider’s previous report, Anorbank said that the reports concerning Olimov were related to “personal matters” and had no connection to the bank’s capital, management, or operations. Uzbekistan’s central bank said at the time that Anorbank continued to operate normally and complied with required financial standards.
According to the court order authorizing his arrest in absentia, Uzbek authorities have charged Olimov under clauses “b” and “c” of Part 2 of Article 137 of Uzbekistan’s Criminal Code — kidnapping for financial gain or other motives, committed by a group acting in prior conspiracy. The charge carries a sentence of five to 10 years in prison.
In the summer of 2025, Olimov claimed he had been kidnapped in central Paris, taken to a villa near Nice, tortured, and ordered to pay $10 million. According to his account, he was released after paying $200,000 and signing an IOU for $5 million. However, a joint investigation by The Insider and L’Express found multiple inconsistencies in Olimov’s story: after his alleged release, the financier continued to exchange friendly messages with a man he had identified as one of the kidnappers, and his ticket back to Paris was paid for by that man’s driver.
According to a source who spoke to The Insider, investigators believe Olimov may have staged his own kidnapping in order to portray his former employer and adversary in a financial dispute, Batyr Rakhimov, as the organizer of the crime. On top of that, investigators allege that Olimov later used Uzbek security officials to arrange Rakhimov’s kidnapping in an effort to force him to drop financial claims against him. Rakhimov had previously demanded more than $200 million in compensation from Olimov for assets that he said came under his former subordinate’s control on terms that were highly unfavorable to him.
An Interpol Red Notice is a request to law enforcement authorities in member countries to locate a wanted person and provisionally detain them pending extradition or another legal procedure. It is not an international arrest warrant, as each country decides whether to detain the person based on its own laws.

What counts as ‘Made in Europe’? France, Germany and Spain are divided
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:43:11 UTC
00:43:11 KST

France wants a strict EU preference, Germany would include trading partners, while Spain is proposing a compromise as Brussels seeks to counter Chinese competition.
France, Germany and Spain are split over what should count as “Made in Europe”, as the EU prepares new rules designed to favour European industry amid growing competition from China.
The European Commission's proposed Industrial Accelerator Act would give European-made products, including cars, steel and green technologies, preferential treatment in public contracts.
But EU governments disagree over where Europe ends: France wants a strict EU preference, Germany wants to include trading partners, while Spain is proposing a compromise between the two.
Strict approach
France is pushing for a strict EU approach but Germany wants a more open model, allowing products made “with” Europe.
Berlin said in a position paper that rules of origin should be extended to the bloc’s trading partners, provided those countries grant European companies equivalent access in return.
This could include signatories to the WTO Agreement on Government Procurement (GPA), as well as countries with a free trade agreement or customs union with the EU.
“The Industrial Accelerator Act, from our point of view, must follow a principle – made with Europe,” German Minister for Economic Affairs Katherina Reiche said on Thursday ahead of a meeting of EU industry ministers. She added that countries such as Norway and Switzerland could be included, as well as “partner countries” like Canada, “which the Commission President has offered a particularly privileged partnership.”
Last week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed during her State of the Union speech that Canada be granted the status of “associate” member of the EU, as Ottawa seeks closer links with the Europeans amid a trade war with the US.
Bridging France and Germany
Spain has also issued a position paper, offering a compromise between the French and German approaches.
“We have made a proposal that establishes without a doubt the reinforcement of the European Union of the 27, as the specific area where it is necessary to reinforce the productive capacity in Europe,” Spain’s Industry Minister Jordi Hereu i Boher said.
He added: “But at the same time, I believe that we perfectly delimit what we call open strategic autonomy, in cooperation and in collaboration with other areas of the world and other countries.”
The paper proposes dividing the European preference into three groups: a core of the EU's 27 members; a second group including European Economic Area countries such as Norway and trusted partners that offer reciprocal access to public procurement; and a third covering countries with free trade agreements or customs unions with the EU, as well as signatories to the WTO Agreement on Government Procurement.
The third group could also include third countries producing components that are “critical” for the EU’s economic security, where this is justified by the “current lack of sufficient Union manufacturing capacity” or alternative sources of supply.
Italy, the EU's third largest economy, has yet to take a clear stance, with Minister for Enterprises Adolfo Urso on Thursday only saying he favoured a European preference open to “strategic partners.”
“We believe we need to start from the industrial base of the 27 member states, with an inclusive and balanced approach, both in terms of safeguarding industrial value chains and with regard to the strategic partners of our continent, whom we need to include in our industrial policy strategy,” he said.
Ireland, which holds the rotating EU Council presidency until the end of the year, hopes to broker a compromise among the 27 member states by December.

UNGA: Abbas blasts US and Israel, calls for Palestinian self-determination
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:41:00 UTC
00:41:00 KST

UNGA: Gaza dominates agenda as Abbas, Netanyahu speak
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 24, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's Prime Minister said attacking Iran was one of his 'easiest' decisions, as he had no real choice
- Many representatives walked out of the UN General Assembly ahead of Benjamin Netanyahu's speech
- Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas earlier urged nations to support the two-state solution, and sharply criticized Israel and the US
- The UK will host a meeting on the future of the Gaza Strip, while Saudi Arabia and Norway have called a ministerial meeting to discuss the implementation of the so-called two-state solution
- Beyond the Middle East, day 3 of the UNGA will address the problem that rising sea levels pose for low-lying islands and coastal regions
Read below for all the top headlines, videos and analyses on the 81 UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Netanyahu calls genocide allegations 'the greatest lie of the century'
The Israeli prime minister said allegations of genocide in Gaza leveled at Israel by various world leaders or groups were false.
"It will take time for the world to acknowledge what is so plain to see. That Hamas used Palestinian civilians as human shields. That it used hospitals, schools, mosques as terrorist command posts. That it sold much of the food we let into Gaza," Netanyahu alleged.
"And while Hamas did everything possible to keep Palestinians in harm's way — often at gunpoint — Israel did everything possible to get them out of harm's way," he said, listing measures like warnings to civilians.
"I want to ask you a question: what genocidal regime gives a million polio vaccinations to the enemy's population? What genocidal regime enables the distribution of 2 million tons of food into Gaza? Accusing Israel of genocide is the greatest lie of the century," he said.
He also called out New York's "antisemitic" mayor, Zohran Mamdani, as one of the people spreading this message. He said that since Mamdani's election "many Jews no longer feel safe in New York."
Netanyahu said the "simple truth" was not that Israel committed genocide but that it prevented one, saying "that's exactly what Mr. Mamdani's Hamas buddies would have done to us if we had not stopped them."
Netanyahu says he 'drew a red line' on same podium 14 years ago
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began his speech with a reference to his notorious General Assembly appearance in 2012, when he stood with illustrated graphics depicting how near to creating a nuclear bomb he thought Iran was.
"Ladies and gentlemen, 14 years ago I stood on this podium and I drew a red line," he said. "I vowed to prevent Iran's murderous dictatorship from developing atomic bombs. Nuclear weapons that could destroy the state of Israel, nuclear weapons that could threaten the whole world. That's exactly what we did."
Netanyahu said that while it was "very hard" to devastate Iran's nuclear facilities, he said it was "one of the easiest decisions" he'd had to make as prime minister, "because if we hadn't done it, we'd all be dead."
Iran contends that its nuclear program was for peaceful purposes like electricity generation, a claim that Israel and the US dispute.
Netanyahu also referred to Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa's call for Israel to pull back its forces in the Golan Heights border area, addressing al-Sharaa and saying "you should know that the Jews have been in the Golan Heights since the days of Moses," referring to the Old Testament prophet thought to have lived more than 3,000 years ago.
Delegates leave the chamber in large group as Netanyahu enters
As Israeli Prime Minster Benjamin Netanyahu's turn to speak at the UN General Assembly came, a large number of delegates from various countries stood up and left the chamber to cheers and jeering.
Only after repeated appeals for calm was it possible for him to begin his address.
"Before I begin, just a quick announcement: if there any other moral cowards who have not yet left this hall, please do so now. Thank you very much," Netanyahu said.
He returned to the issue of the walkout later when discussing his decision to target Iran and its nuclear capabilities.
"Now do you want to hear the ultimate irony? In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall. In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran's nukes," he claimed, saying "it's hard to imagine more mind-blowing hypocrisy."
Protesters had also gathered outside the building in New York ahead of Netanyahu's address. Some were arrested by police. A Democratic nominee for New York's 10th congressional district in November's midterm elections, Brad Lander, also joined the demonstrators, albeit wearing a suit and tie rather than a slogan-laden T-shirt.
READ: Nigeria and US sign mining deal
On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the United States agreed to increase American investiment in the West African nation's mining sector.
Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced the deal on Thursday, a day after he signed the framework deal with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.
"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value. We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses," Alake said.
Read more about the US-Nigeria mining agreement.
Abbas calls for saving two-state solution and Palestinian self-determination
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas used his remarks to implore nations to support the two-state solution, saying his people seek a non-militarized, democratic Palestinian state that can exist alongside Israel in peace.
He said the first step to preserving the idea of such a solution is to protect the lands upon which a future Palestinian state would be based, as well as protecting those people who have lived upon them for generations.
Abbas underscored the fact that the Palestinian people would not be displaced by "military occupation, nor settlement expansion, annexation, nor settler terrorism."
He further said that "no lasting security can be built upon the occupation of another people and the denial of its legitimate rights," adding that the Palestinians have their own plans for an independent state and emphasizing the need to end the Israeli occupation in order to negotiate a solution.
This plan, Abbas said, is based on protecting Palestinians from displacement, preserving their lands, democratically renewing political institutions and building a new sovereign Palestinian state — with east Jerusalem as its capital.
All of this, he said, would be carried out with a "commitment to international law" and the right to exercise self-determination with the aim of achieving security and peace with Israel to, "pave the way to regional integration, cooperation, prosperity and security for everyone."
Abbas concluded his remarks by thanking those 160 nations whom he said have recognized Palestinian statehood, calling for its inclusion in the United Nations.
Palestinian leader Abbas blasts US and Israel in General Assembly
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, addressing those gathered at the UNGA via video because the US State Department refused to allow the Palestinian delegation into the country, has rejected Washington's approach as "unlawful and punitive."
Abbas described the denial of visas as a US failure to live up to its responsibility as the host nation of the international body.
Abbas quickly pivoted to blast Israel's "genocidal war" in Gaza, as well as the sanctioned "ethnic cleansing" perpetrated by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Saying that Israeli violations of international law put the two-state solution at grave risk, Abbas described the situation in Gaza, the West Bank and east Jerusalem as part of a "malicious colonial scheme" and warned of a "new Nakba."
He also referenced attacks on Muslim and Christian religious sites by radical Jews as having the potential to transform the current security situation into a wider religiously fueled conflict.
Not only Middle East, rising sea level threat also on slate for day 3 meetings
Beyond AI and the headline-grabbing conflict in the Middle East, the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday will discuss another pressing issue that impacts the world’s citizens — rising sea levels.
A high-level meeting is slated to begin at 10:00 a.m. (1400 GMT) on Thursday as swelling seas redraw coastlines and pose existential risks for islanders and those who live in low-lying areas near the shores of the world's oceans and seas.
The UN says nearly 900 million people live in such areas, adding that another one million could be impacted by mid-century.
Rising sea levels, says the UN, threaten not only land but also livelihoods and even the existence of entire nations. In the words of UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, "Rising seas are sinking futures."
Israeli and Palestinian leaders set to address UNGA on day 3
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas are both expected to address members of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) on Thursday, with the issue of the Middle East writ large on the day 3 agenda.
Netanyahu, who is increasingly unpopular at home and abroad, will not meet with US officials or Arab leaders during his stay. His office cited a "tight schedule" as the reason, listing as many as nine meetings during his visit, including with the presidents of Argentina and Bolivia, the vice president of Colombia and the prime minister of Papua New Guinea.
The increasingly isolated Israeli leader's Palestinian counterpart, President Mahmoud Abbas, will also address the General Assembly. Abbas, however, will do so via video, as the US State Department refused to issue him an entry visa.
The broader subjects of Gaza's future and Palestinian statehood will also be topics of discussion. The UK will convene a meeting on Gaza's current and future status, and Saudi Arabia and Norway will host a ministerial meeting to hash out plans for the implementation of the so-called "two-state solution."
That's a wrap on Day 2 of the UNGA
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russian President Vladimir Putin for the ongoing war between the countries, calling him "patient zero."
The Ukrainian leader also announced new defense deals with Finland and Australia.
Elsewhere, Syrian leader Ahmed al-Sharaa called for the Israeli occupation of the Golan Heights to end, saying the territory belongs to Syria.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also addressed Israel, calling for what he described as the "genocide" in Gaza to stop.
This comes ahead of a speech by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the UN General Assembly on Thursday.
'Too much power in too few hands' — AI leaders warn about technology dangers
Besides world leaders, top bosses at AI companies also addressed the UN about dangers concerning artificial intelligence.
AI executives spoke to the UN Security Council and urged international cooperation on the hotly debated technology.
Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, highlighted two big risks with AI.
"First, we could lose control of the future to AI. The risk is that it moves so fast that people can no longer follow what's happening or intervene when needed," he said, adding that such a scenario would be "terrible."
Second, he said AI systems "could concentrate too much power in too few hands." "No one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their worldview on everyone else."
Anthropic boss Dario Amodei used the platform to call for a ban on the use of AI in the development of biological weapons, describing AI as the most crucial global security issue facing the world.
"If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," he said.
Amodei also urged global standards for testing new AI models.
Spain PM Pedro Sanchez calls for reforming the UN Security Council
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchezcalled for reforming the UN Security Council so that "all of the regions in the world" would be fairly represented.
Sanchez quoted the UN Charter, saying "no country should be a judge in its own case, no matter how powerful they are."
The Spanish leader continued to condemn the "genocide that (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu is still perpetrating in Gaza," while pointing to Madrid's sanctions against Russia as an example of his government's willingness to take action against countries whose conduct violates the UN Charter.
Ebola outbreak 'major' test for country, Congo's PM tells UNGA
Congolese Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka described the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo as a "major test" for the country.
"For the DRC, fighting this epidemic is an absolute priority. After having contained 16 previous outbreaks, the DRC is mobilizing recognized scientific and operational expertise. And thanks to national mobilization and the support of our
partners, the response has recently begun producing tangible results," she told the UN General Assembly.
As of 22 September 2026, Congo reported a total of 7, 773 confirmed cases, including 3,759 related deaths. A total of 839 patients are hospitalized in isolation.
Venezuela to hold elections, Rodriguez tells UNGA
Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, delivered her first address to the UN General Assembly since coming to power, promising her country would hold elections when the nation's people determine the "right moment."
"I want to make this very clear at this General Assembly: there will be elections in Venezuela," Rodriguez said, adding that her country "has initiated the process of democratic transformation for its rebirth" following two blows this year.
First, "strangulation of its internal political life and the heightened confrontation with the United States" and second, the earthquakes on June 24 that caused the deaths of more than 6,500 people.
Rodriguez took power after the US toppled the then-president Nicolas Maduro in January.
Rodríguez briefly met US President Donald Trump at the UN General Assembly as well.
Ukrainian foreign minister met with Iranian delegation on the sidelines of UNGA
DW's US Correspondent Misha Komadovsky reported that the Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Sybiah earlier in the day told a UN Security Council meeting that Ukraine was ready for an immediate and complete ceasefire without preconditions, if Moscow did too.
German FM calls on Iran to end Hormuz blockage
In a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called on Iran to end its closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
"It is up to Iran to engage constructively in negotiations and to loosen its stranglehold," Wadephul told journalists ahead of the meeting.
Wadephul also urged Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to engage seriously and credibly in sustainable negotiations with the US and neighboring states in the region, sources in the German delegation were cited by the DPA news agency as saying.
"There must now be an overall willingness to compromise in order to bring about a solution to the deadlocked conflict in the region," Wadephul was quoted as saying.
He stressed the readiness of Germany and the so-called E3, which also includes France and the United Kingdom, to support mediation efforts.
Wadephul also stressed in the talks the need for Iran and militias it supports in the region, namely Yemen's Houthi rebels, to halt attacks on civilian ships. He added that Berlin expects free transit through the Strait of Hormuz to be restored immediately, stressing the rejection of any fees for passage through the critical waterway.
"Not only the Gulf States, but large parts of Asia, Africa and also Europe are suffering under this blockade," Wadephul said.
He added that Germany welcomes renewed talks between the US and Iran on the sidelines of the General Assembly, adding that he planned to speak to his counterparts from Jordan, Pakistan, Iraq and Oman.

Russia concerned by use of satellites for interference in nations' affairs — MFA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:39:44 UTC
00:39:44 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Moscow views the growing use of communications satellites to interfere in the internal affairs of countries as an alarming trend and is advocating transparent regulation, Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Alimov said.
Speaking at the international forum "Partnership between the State, Business, and Civil Society in Ensuring International Information Security," Alimov highlighted what he described as the "problem of the illicit use of low-Earth-orbit satellite internet systems."
"There are well-known instances in which these technologies – ostensibly intended to provide convenient Internet access -have been used to interfere in the internal affairs of countries. This is undoubtedly an alarming trend," he said.
Moscow is advocating "transparent regulation of the use of such systems" and compliance by satellite operators with the national laws of the countries in which they operate.
"We are pursuing this work within the UN Security Council and the International Telecommunication Union," Alimov said.
He also highlighted challenges associated with the development of artificial intelligence.
"The use of this technology for malicious purposes poses a common threat to all states, requiring a collective approach at the international level," he said.
Alimov added that Russia is working to initiate negotiations on the safe and equitable use of artificial intelligence through specialized UN bodies and within the framework of the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, which was established this year and joined by Russia in July.

Erdogan outlines Türkiye's positions on UN reform, Gaza, Hormuz and defence ties in New York

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has outlined Türkiye’s positions on a wide range of regional and international issues, including reform of the United Nations, the Gaza crisis, tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, Black Sea security and Türkiye-US defence cooperation.
Speaking to journalists at Turkevi in New York on Wednesday, Erdogan also discussed the Terror-Free Türkiye process, relations with Iraq and Greece, the Development Road Project, climate change and Türkiye's preparations to host the COP31 climate summit in Antalya.
He said the UN system needed to become more representative, criticised the veto power of its five permanent members and called for a stronger General Assembly.
Erdogan also reiterated Türkiye's opposition to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, called for a return to negotiations between Iran and the US, and said Ankara was stepping up diplomatic efforts to revive the Black Sea grain corridor.
He said Türkiye expected the US to take concrete steps towards its return to the F-35 programme, while stressing that Ankara would continue developing its domestic defence capabilities, including the KAAN fighter jet.
Below is the full Q&A:
QUESTION: You published an article in Bloomberg in which you wrote that the United Nations needs reform and that this reform can no longer be postponed. This is not the first time you have said this, but in that article you also stressed that Türkiye is ready to play its part in reforming the United Nations.
As I understand it, you emphasised the idea of a regional United Nations, in which different regions have different problems and therefore require solutions tailored to their circumstances. What kind of UN do you envision, Mr President? What kind of UN would you like to see?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
First and foremost, we are talking about a United Nations in which the will of more than 190 countries is constrained by the veto power of five countries.
It is impossible for this unjust structure to maintain global stability and peace, remain faithful to the fundamental principles it upholds, and fulfil its promise to humanity.
The issue is not simply about Türkiye having a greater say. It is about Africa, Asia, Latin America, the Muslim world, Europe and all other regions being fairly represented in this global system through their own experiences and their own will.
That is why we say the veto mechanism should be abolished. We should move away from a United Nations model that protects only five members and towards a mechanism that embraces all members.
We should strengthen the General Assembly and make it more powerful and effective.
The new structure should be fairer, with elected members serving for defined periods and those seeking re-election having to regain the confidence of the international community.
The world's problems should be addressed and decisions made not by five members, but by all members.
Because the world no longer needs new walls; it needs new bridges.
QUESTION: You have delivered your 16th speech to the UN General Assembly. From your first speech until today, you have also been a voice for the oppressed and for the pursuit of a fairer world.
In your latest speech, you said, “As long as I live, I will continue to speak about these truths from this podium.”
Looking at the long journey from your first speech to today's address, and at where the world has reached today, how would you assess that journey?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
This journey has been one of standing firm.
When we first took to the podium of the UN General Assembly, whatever we said and wherever we stood, we remain, thankfully, in the same place today.
What has happened in Syria, Iraq, the Russia-Ukraine war, Africa, Myanmar and, most recently, Gaza has repeatedly demonstrated the truth of what I have been saying.
The foundations of the Russia-Ukraine war were laid in those years. Many issues in our region grew because of wrong steps taken at the time; sparks effectively turned into fires.
If the world had listened to what we were saying at the time and taken measures, so many lives would not have been lost.
If UN reform had been carried out in those years, preventing the conflicts and wars we see in our region and around the world today would not have been beyond our reach.
The fact that Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas was unable to attend the United Nations for two consecutive years is, in itself, an indication of how deeply injustice has become entrenched in the international system.
Our issue is not being against any country. Our issue is being against injustice.
We are happy that, from those days to today, we have always stood on the right side of history and have not taken a single step that would bring shame upon our nation.
Today, the world is moving towards the position we expressed from the very beginning.
QUESTION: Ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is declining sharply. The steep fall in the number of vessels passing through the region shows that the crisis is no longer just an issue concerning Iran, but has become a global energy and trade issue.
Does Türkiye have a concrete plan to bring the US and Iran towards a ceasefire? What are you proposing to the parties?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
The situation in the Strait of Hormuz shows that this is no longer simply an issue between Iran and the United States.
We have made our position on this matter very clear. We oppose the closure of the Strait of Hormuz to maritime traffic. Freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz must be protected.
Every tension in the Strait of Hormuz affects not only the countries of the region, but also Europe, Asia, energy markets, transport and the daily lives of millions of people.
The dramatic decline in commercial shipping in recent days clearly demonstrates the scale of the issue. The Strait is vital to global energy security and international trade.
Hormuz must be opened as a key to resolving problems through dialogue and negotiations.
We are telling all our interlocutors that we need to return to the negotiating table as soon as possible.
What needs to be opened are not new fronts, but new channels of diplomacy.
QUESTION:
While the world is focused on Hormuz, the war between Russia and Ukraine has also intensified again in the Black Sea. Attacks on commercial vessels have also increased again.
As a result, grain ships are waiting at ports. Could a new security mechanism similar to the Black Sea Grain Initiative, which was established through your efforts, be created and the corridor revived?
Are you hopeful following your discussions with the parties on this issue? Did this issue come up during your meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
The issue of security in the Black Sea is extremely important both for us and for our region.
The Black Sea is not a front in this war, and it must never become one.
In our talks with the parties, we are explaining in detail the need to restore the safety of navigation.
This would have two benefits: ensuring food security and preventing the war from spreading.
We have made it clear that we do not accept attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea, whoever carries them out, and that we expect the parties to act responsibly.
We have now stepped up our efforts to re-establish the grain corridor. We are also accelerating our diplomatic efforts to this end.
I raised the issue once again with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and the response I received from him was positive.
QUESTION: There are already various challenges at an early stage regarding the Mecca Defence Alliance. There is particularly some pressure on Saudi Arabia.
What would you like to say about the future of the alliance?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
The Mecca Defence Agreement is a strong step in the right direction.
If you undertake such an important initiative in such a challenging region, it is hardly surprising that you encounter some challenges.
If you say something new and demonstrate a new will, there will naturally be those who are uncomfortable with it.
We are not a state that was established yesterday. We are a state with enough experience not to be provoked or fall into traps.
I have no doubt that we will move forward more strongly once the institutionalisation efforts are completed.
The foundations have been laid for a platform that will produce regionally driven solutions to the region's problems.
We have all seen that those who come from outside and prescribe security solutions for our region often leave behind greater instability.
The sapling we have planted will soon grow and become a great tree.
We have confidence in our country and our nation, and we have confidence in our brothers and sisters.
QUESTION: Last year, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, there was a meeting attended by the Gulf countries, US President Donald Trump and yourself.
As an outcome of that meeting, Trump launched his Gaza plan in Sharm el Sheikh.
A similar meeting was held this year. You touched on part of this in your opening remarks, but will this second meeting produce an outcome soon, as the meeting in Sharm el Sheikh did?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
There can be no lasting peace in the Middle East without stopping the bloodshed in Gaza, making the ceasefire permanent and ensuring that Palestinians can have a dignified future in their own homeland.
The will that has emerged within the framework of the peace plan is important and valuable.
For lasting peace, tranquillity and stability in Gaza, almost everyone, including Hamas, has taken positive steps and expressed their desire for a solution.
However, Israel continues its aggression and is undermining peace.
The international community, led by the United States, must make Israel understand that it has to comply with this plan.
It is not enough simply to say, “Let the war in Gaza stop.”
We need to establish mechanisms that will prevent the war from starting again, accelerate the reconstruction of Gaza and guarantee the political future of the Palestinians.
The humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza remains there even as the world looks away.
I am talking about people struggling to survive among the ruins.
And this has not been happening for one day, one week, one month or one year, but for years.
This is an issue that concerns the shared conscience of humanity.
QUESTION: We also listened to your address to the UN General Assembly. We would particularly like to congratulate you on your messages regarding Gaza, which once again attracted considerable attention.
My question is about the F-35s.
US President Trump had made a commitment regarding the F-35s. However, months have passed and we see that there has still been no progress.
Could you give us an update on the situation?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
We also discussed this issue with Mr Trump at NATO.
He expressed a positive will regarding Türkiye's return to the F-35 programme.
We now expect this will to translate into concrete steps. We are continuing our contacts on this issue. I believe we will achieve a result.
My relationship with Mr Trump has also given momentum to Türkiye-US relations.
Cooperation between the two countries has made considerable progress compared with the previous administration.
I believe we will not stop here and will reach even more ambitious goals.
Of course, what is important for us is our domestic defence industry. This is extremely important to us.
We want to produce our own fighter aircraft, air defence systems and defence industry capabilities, particularly the KAAN.
Meanwhile, we also met with the British prime minister. Our efforts and work on the Eurofighter are continuing with them as well.
Türkiye has security requirements, defence needs and strategic objectives.
We will work towards our goals and, God willing, we will not take a step backwards.
QUESTION: I would like to ask for an update on the stage reached in the Terror-Free Türkiye process.
First of all, could you share the latest information with us on whether the organisation has entered the stage of laying down its arms?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
Terror-Free Türkiye is not a day-to-day issue for us.
This is about Türkiye overcoming a problem that has existed for nearly half a century.
As you know, the Turkish Grand National Assembly has established the legal framework. The relevant mechanisms have been established or are being established.
Our relevant institutions are on the ground and are carrying out the necessary monitoring.
For the framework law to be implemented, the organisation must actually lay down its arms and complete the disbandment process.
It is also clear how this will be determined and verified.
The process is moving forward step by step under the supervision of our relevant institutions.
Our parliament will also contribute to the process within the framework defined by the law, and Türkiye will, God willing, close the chapter on terrorism in unity and solidarity.
There are, of course, those who are trying to obstruct this process.
Those involved in the terrorism industry naturally do not want these chapters to be closed.
But we will not give them the opportunity they are waiting for.
As the People's Alliance and as the state, we are determined on this issue.
In short, we have received no indication of any problem.
The process is moving forward and, God willing, we will achieve the desired result before long.
QUESTION: Iraq's new Prime Minister Ali Zaidi visited Türkiye some time ago.
There have also been a number of developments between the two sides in both energy and the Development Road Project, which had been stalled for many years but is now gaining momentum.
How do you assess the positive atmosphere in relations between Ankara and Baghdad, both in terms of regional stability and perhaps stability within Türkiye?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
As you know, Prime Minister Ali Zaidi made his first visit to Ankara.
I can say that we have made a good start to the new era.
I believe we will develop relations between the two countries and achieve mutual gains.
Indeed, today we also met with Mr Ali Zaidi and his colleagues here at Turkevi.
As you know, the Iraqi government's authority will now prevail in the Sinjar region, where the PKK has been based in Iraq for a long time.
Today, we discussed with the Iraqi authorities how control of the area will be organised once it has been cleared of terrorism.
We also discussed the handover of Bashiqa.
With our neighbour Iraq, we now want to talk not about terrorism, but more about the Development Road, increasing our bilateral trade volume, stability, peace and prosperity.
The process is moving forward positively.
We have gained good momentum.
God willing, the outcome will also be positive.
QUESTION: Mr President, elections are approaching in Greece. There will be elections in May.
Once again, Türkiye is a major issue on the agenda.
You previously warned Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis against taking our bilateral disputes to other countries, but there are once again statements concerning the sale of F-35s and Türkiye's need to acquire F-35s.
Could this current course of events put the atmosphere of rapprochement and negotiations at risk?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
We have no intention of getting involved in the domestic politics of Greece or any of our other neighbours.
There may be elections in Greece, governments may change and opposition parties may change; these are not our concerns.
Our concerns are Türkiye's rights and security, and preserving peace and stability in the Aegean and the Eastern Mediterranean.
Let me make one thing very clear: Türkiye is not Greece's enemy. It is its neighbour and an ally under the NATO umbrella.
Relations between the two countries are too delicate and important to be turned into election material.
This is how we view these debates.
We are focused on our own agenda and are now attending to our own affairs.
QUESTION: Mr President, at the beginning of your speech you referred to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change.
What will Türkiye's main priorities be at COP31, which we will host in Antalya in November?
There are also demands from developing countries, particularly regarding climate finance.
What messages will you deliver on this issue?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
We simply cannot ignore the problems created by climate change.
This is extremely important to us.
At COP31, we will set out our measures and road maps, as well as what we plan to do to address the adverse effects of climate change in different parts of the world.
Indeed, in my speech at the United Nations today, I addressed not only the General Assembly but also climate change in a separate speech.
I also focused on these issues there.
The world is our home, and protecting it from pollution is our responsibility.
COP31 is not merely a climate conference; it is also a platform where developing countries can make their voices heard, set out their expectations and discuss concrete outcomes.
It is the responsibility of developed countries to stand by and support countries facing financial difficulties.
Combating climate change now requires action, not just words.
Disasters know no borders. Fires, floods and droughts do not distinguish between countries.
We, too, must remove borders when it comes to solving these problems.
I believe the COP31 summit we will hold in Antalya will be an important crossroads on this long journey.
QUESTION: If you allow me, I would like to ask the final question.
One of the main issues occupying the agenda in recent days is a situation known publicly as the “fund crisis”, which directly affects 455,000 investors.
The investigation is continuing. There have been detentions and arrests.
What message would you like to give investors, and could you give us some perspective on the road map ahead?
PRESIDENT ERDOGAN:
We are talking about a problem that has emerged in a limited area of the capital markets and in a certain number of funds.
In other words, there is no risk to our financial system or the Turkish economy.
Portraying this as a problem affecting the entire market would be unfair to the Turkish stock market.
All necessary steps are being taken and will continue to be taken within the principles of the capital markets and the framework of the law.
Our relevant institutions are pursuing the matter with determination.
Our judiciary has likewise launched a comprehensive investigation, and there have been a number of detentions and arrests.
I want everyone to know this: whoever is responsible will be held accountable before the law.
There should be not the slightest doubt about this.
Regardless of the circumstances, no one has the right to engage in a race to profit from the situation at the expense of others or to cause anxiety among our people.
Of course, given the nature of the capital markets, it is important that the process be conducted both transparently and with the utmost sensitivity.
That is also our instruction.
In addition, we will ensure that whatever measures are needed, including legal and administrative regulations, are implemented to prevent a similar problem from occurring again.

(China Economic Roundtable) Xinhua Headlines: From barbecue to immersive theater, diverse consumption scenarios bring new vitality to China's consumer market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:38:32 CST
00:38:32 KST

* Across China, consumers are increasingly seeking cultural experiences, leisure activities and services alongside goods, creating new opportunities for businesses to meet more diverse demand.
* China's National Bureau of Statistics began releasing the broader indicator of combined retail sales of consumer goods and services in June to provide a more complete picture of the changing consumption market.
* For local businesses, the changing demand is prompting efforts to turn temporary popularity into sustained consumption through improved services and more diverse experiences.
BEIJING, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- At a barbecue restaurant in Badaju Market in Zibo, east China's Shandong Province, the dining experience now extends beyond sizzling skewers and local delicacies to performances that introduce visitors to the city's history and culture.
"If visitors come just for the food, their visit is too short for them to get to know Zibo better," said Zheng Feng, who runs the restaurant.
The approach is part of a broader transformation at Badaju, a traditional neighborhood market that became an internet sensation in 2023. Since then, it has expanded its offerings to include cultural performances, handicrafts and creative products.
Over the past three years, the market has received more than 18 million visits annually on average, with over 430 merchants offering more than 100 business formats.
Across China, consumers are increasingly seeking cultural experiences, leisure activities and services alongside goods, creating new opportunities for businesses to meet more diverse demand.
In the first eight months of 2026, China's combined retail sales of consumer goods and services rose 2.5 percent year on year, with retail sales of services increasing 4.9 percent, compared with 1 percent growth in retail sales of goods, official data showed.
As incomes rise, service consumption is growing faster than goods consumption, a trend consistent with broader economic development, said Lin Jian, vice president of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation under the Ministry of Commerce, on China Economic Roundtable, an all-media talk show hosted by Xinhua News Agency.
Lin noted that per capita spending on services accounted for 46.1 percent of China's total per capita consumption expenditure in 2025, up 3.5 percentage points from 2020, and expected the share to surpass 50 percent during the 2026-2030 period.
China's National Bureau of Statistics began releasing the broader indicator of combined retail sales of consumer goods and services in June to provide a more complete picture of the changing consumption market.
For local businesses, the changing demand is prompting efforts to turn temporary popularity into sustained consumption through improved services and more diverse experiences.
Zhang Weihua, deputy head of Shandong's provincial culture and tourism department, said Badaju's continued appeal lies in its combination of consumer trust, local culture and interactive experiences.
The market has introduced clearer pricing, consumer complaint services and infrastructure improvements, while incorporating local cultural traditions into commercial activities and retaining its functions as a neighborhood market.
A similar change is taking shape in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, where small theaters and immersive performances are creating new spaces for cultural consumption.
At the city's Houhu Ximatou theater, an immersive street play titled "Changsha" takes audiences back to the 1990s, telling a story of friendship and entrepreneurship through scenes from the city's past.
Actors interact directly with audiences in recreated neighborhood settings, with some spectators even offering tissues to performers during emotional scenes, said Jin Xingzhou, an actor in the production.
Changsha had established 111 new performing arts venues by the end of June this year, with performances at these venues totaling 14,000 in the first six months and attracting 3.63 million audience visits, according to local cultural authorities.
Zhang Dandan, head of the Changsha New Consumption Research Institute, attributed the emergence of new consumption formats to changing consumer needs, which are driving innovation in products, services and business models.
At the national level, China's consumption expansion plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) calls for expanding service consumption, upgrading goods consumption, developing new consumption scenarios and improving the consumption environment.
The plan aims to boost China's total retail sales of consumer goods to around 60 trillion yuan (about 8.89 trillion U.S. dollars) by 2030. It also calls for expanding high-quality cultural and tourism offerings, improving the supply of performing arts products, and supporting the development of immersive and interactive venues for consumers.
Efforts similar to Zibo and Changsha are taking shape across China, with 50 cities participating in a national pilot program to develop new consumption formats, models and scenarios.
These cities have a combined resident population of over 480 million and account for more than half of China's total retail sales of consumer goods, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
As of early July, the pilot cities had collected proposals for more than 6,000 projects, with the potential to attract over 300 billion yuan in investment, the ministry said.
Lin said cities should develop distinctive consumption offerings based on their own cultural, ecological and industrial resources, supported by better services, consumption facilities and the business environment.
"Events attract consumers, supply turns interest into spending, and a supportive environment sustains long-term appeal," said Lin.
(Video reporters: Yang Shiyan and Zhao Jiale; Video editors: Yang Zeyi, Roger Lott, Zhao Xiaoqing and Hong Yan) ■
