Sexual objectification does not erase the perceived humanity of OnlyFans creators, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:00:34 UTC
00:00:34 KST

People who create content on the digital platform OnlyFans are heavily sexually objectified by observers, yet they are simultaneously viewed as capable individuals with free will. These findings challenge the traditional psychological assumption that sexually objectifying someone automatically strips them of their perceived autonomy and humanity. The research was recently published in The Journal of Social Psychology.
Sexual objectification occurs when a person is reduced to their body parts or physical appearance, primarily to satisfy the desires of others. Psychologists have observed that this reduction typically leads to dehumanization. When observers focus entirely on a target’s physical form, they tend to ignore the target’s internal states and mental capacities.
A primary casualty of this psychological process is agency, which is the capacity to think, plan, and act with intention. Prior research has consistently shown that sexually objectified women are viewed as passive and lacking the ability to make independent choices. This loss of perceived agency is a core component of dehumanization, effectively reducing a person to a mere tool for someone else’s gratification.
The rise of new digital media platforms has altered how people present themselves online. OnlyFans allows creators to share personalized explicit content directly with paying subscribers. Unlike traditional media, the creators retain control over their scheduling, content style, and pricing.
Researchers Chiara Pecini and Alessandra Sacino from the University of Genoa led a team to investigate whether the traditional rules of objectification apply in this modern digital environment. They wanted to know if observers can objectify a person while still recognizing that the person is actively orchestrating their own sexualization. The research team designed four distinct experiments to capture these social perceptions.
In the first experiment, 220 male participants reviewed fictitious survey responses supposedly written by a young woman. Half the men read a profile of a woman who actively used and enjoyed creating content on OnlyFans. The other half read about a woman who did not use the platform.
The researchers measured how much the men intended to sexually objectify the woman, alongside how much agency they attributed to her. The men reported higher intentions to sexually objectify the content creator compared to the woman not on the platform. However, the men did not rate the creator as having any less capacity to make choices or exercise self-control.
To see if this pattern held up against another highly sexualized role, the team conducted a second experiment with 253 men. This time, participants compared an OnlyFans creator to a motorsport umbrella girl, a traditional occupation where women stand alongside racecar drivers to shield them from the sun. The participants also viewed artificial intelligence-generated photos of the women in either highly sexualized or casual clothing.
The men reported higher intentions to sexually objectify the digital content creator than the umbrella girl. Despite this higher level of objectification, they attributed greater free will to the creator than to the umbrella girl. Whether the woman was pictured in sexualized or casual clothing produced results that were not statistically significant, suggesting the occupational role drove the perception.
The researchers then explored whether the creator’s financial success influenced how observers perceived their autonomy. In a third experiment involving 188 men and women, participants evaluated a creator who earned either a high monthly income of 4,000 euros or a low income of 120 euros. The photos again varied between casual and sexualized attire.
In this particular test, neither the income level nor the style of clothing altered the participants’ judgments. The differences in attributed free will across the groups were not statistically significant. The research team suspected that financial success alone might not communicate autonomy without understanding the creator’s personal motives.
A final experiment recruited 323 men and women to evaluate a creator’s profile based on a combination of income and their motivation for joining the platform. Some profiles stated the creator was intrinsically motivated, meaning she enjoyed showing off her body and feeling appreciated. Other profiles indicated an extrinsic motivation, stating she joined purely out of financial necessity.
The researchers evaluated self-determination, which is a specific facet of agency centered on a person’s ability to direct their own life free from external pressures. The participants rated the intrinsically motivated creator as having a higher level of self-determination than the extrinsically motivated one. A high income also slightly elevated the creator’s perceived self-determination.
Female participants were more sensitive to the motivation details than male participants. Women adjusted their ratings more sharply based on whether the creator enjoyed the work. Men tended to view the creators similarly regardless of their underlying motivations.
The results indicate a modern form of objectification where the target retains their perceived humanity and ability to choose. This attribution of agency can be a positive shift, but the researchers note it may rely on an illusion of total control. Once digital content is distributed, creators often lose the ability to dictate where their images end up, exposing them to nonconsensual sharing and harassment.
Observers who assume creators have complete autonomy might also engage in victim-blaming if that creator experiences online abuse. When society views these creators as entirely responsible for their sexualization, people might be less sympathetic when the creators face privacy violations. Fictional profiles in a controlled experiment also lack the interpersonal dynamics of a real digital exchange.
The participants in these experiments were familiar with the platform but were not active paying subscribers. Future studies will need to test whether people who regularly purchase explicit digital content perceive the creators differently. The researchers also hope to see if these attitudes apply to other forms of digital sex work.
The study, “Objects and Agents? Social Perception of OnlyFans Content Creators,” was authored by Chiara Pecini, Alessandra Sacino, Bianca Tallone, Roberta Rosa Valtorta, Gian Antonio Di Bernardo, and Luca Andrighetto.

TikTok drops appeal against £12.7m fine for not keeping under-13s off platform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:00:34 UTC
00:00:34 KST

TikTok will pay a £12.7m fine to the UK’s data watchdog after dropping an appeal against a ruling that it did not do enough to keep children below the age of 13 off the platform.
The video app was punished by the Information Commissioner’s Office in 2023 for inadequate checks of who was using the platform, and failing to remove underage users.
When issuing the fine the ICO said TikTok had done “very little, if anything” to address underage use of its service.
TikTok has a minimum user age of 13 but failure to enforce that limit resulted in up to 1.75 million UK children under 13 using the service in 2020, the ICO said. TikTok also failed to provide users with information about how their data was being collected and used, and neglected to obtain parental consent.
Emily Keaney, the ICO’s deputy commissioner, said: “Our successful action against TikTok shows how important it is for companies to have the right protections in place, including to prevent access by children who are not old enough to be using their services.”
Chinese-owned TikTok said it disagreed with the ruling but had decided to pay the fine because it related to a period between 2018 and 2020, after which it had implemented “many youth safety measures and policies”.
TikTok, which has more than 30m users in the UK, has also withdrawn an appeal against an ICO request for information about how its algorithm processes teenagers’ personal data – and how it serves potentially harmful content. The ICO said it would now resume the investigation.
At the time the fine was issued, the then information commissioner, John Edwards, told the Guardian that TikTok was “not doing enough” on multiple fronts.
“Our findings were that TikTok were not doing enough to prevent under-13s accessing their platform, they were not doing enough when they became aware of under-13s to get rid of them, and they were not doing enough to detect under-13s on there,” he said.
Age-checking measures at tech platforms will be at the vanguard of the government’s new under-16 age limit for accessing social media platforms, which comes into force next year.
The UK’s communications watchdog, Ofcom, has said “more action from the tech industry is needed” on enforcing age limits as the ban approaches. In Australia, which introduced a social media ban for under-16s last December, the eSafety commissioner has said a “substantial proportion” of under-16s in the country have kept their accounts, managed to create new ones or bypassed age-gating systems.

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Russia will consider the full range of circumstances when deciding on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s participation in the G20 summit, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov told reporters.
"We will consider the full range of circumstances related to the current situation. The president will, of course, personally make the relevant decisions. Meet the newest living cat species, the first described in 100 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Attention cat lovers: There’s an adorable new addition to the feline family tree.
Meet Leopardus tilcayo, a pint-size tiger cat discovered in Bolivia in the Yungas forests of the central Andes Mountains. L. tilcayo, reported September 17 in Current Biology, is the first new living cat species described and named by scientists in more than 100 years. The last one was the Uruguayan pampas cat (L. fasciatus), described in 1923.
L. tilcayo has a slender body, spotted fur and a ringed tail. It weighs roughly two kilograms, about as much as a two-month-old domestic kitten. For such a tiny cat, L. tilcayo has made a terrific splash, pouncing into headlines around the world. “I did not at all expect attention at this scale,” says Jonas Lescroart, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Lescroart and his colleagues hadn’t set out to discover a new species. They were looking to untangle one branch of the cat family tree. Until now, scientists didn’t have a good sense of how many tiger cat species existed. These small cats live in the tropical regions of the Americas and tend to look alike, Lescroart says.
The researchers analyzed the genetics of 38 species of the Leopardus genus, which includes tiger cats as well as more widely known animals like the ocelot. They expected to find two, three or even four distinct species of tiger cat. Instead, Lescroart and his colleagues’ analyses pointed to five separate species, including one that scientists had never before described: L. tilcayo.
The new species is based on two specimens: a female that was treated briefly for injuries at a sanctuary in Bolivia and released to the wild and a male that still lives at the sanctuary. His name is Tigrino. Lescroart’s colleague, Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, met Tigrino at the sanctuary and noticed that he looked a little different from the cats she expected to see in the region. Nogales-Ascarrunz, a cat conservationist and National Geographic Explorer, genetically tested Tigrino and then connected with Lescroart’s team to share data.
The researchers’ work suggests that there’s diversity hiding even among well-studied animals like cats. “I don’t know if you’ll have to wait another 100 years for a new species,” Lescroart says. Though at the moment, the team doesn’t have any other cryptic kitties on the radar.

Park Weave by Brendan David O'Mahony and Pablo de Lascurain Zambrano
"Research into 106 John Street identified Brunswick East's transition from a low-density residential and industrial suburb to a series of transit-oriented urban centres focused on public transport, walking and cycling.
"This change is driven by an increasing population of highly educated adults aged 25 to 39, who now comprise 44.9 per cent of residents.

EU sanctions Xenia Fedorova for brainwashing France with Russian propaganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:59:02 UTC
23:59:02 KST

The EU agreed to sanction the former head of the Kremlin media outlet RT France, Xenia Fedorova, on Sept. 24, for spreading pro-Russian narratives and supporting Moscow's hybrid war on Europe.
Fedorova ran RT France from 2017 until it was forced to shut down by EU sanctions.
Since then, she has "continued to disseminate in French media such as CNews, Europe 1, and Le JDNews, narratives aligned with those promoted by the Russian authorities," reads an EU press release announcing the sanctions.
"Our determination is total: those who think they can carry out hostile moves against our democracy with impunity will face consequences," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot wrote on social media as the new sanctions were adopted.
Fedorova portrayed European support for Ukraine as prolonging the war; presented Russia as seeking peace with a confrontational Europe; cast doubt on Russia's abduction of Ukrainian children; and portrayed European and NATO policies as threats to European security, reads the official EU sanctions listing.
French authorities also said that her "conduct undermines the fundamental interests of the state," and her continued presence on French territory "therefore constitutes a particularly serious and immediate threat to public order, in a July deportation order to Fedorova."
The sanctions mean that Fedorova's assets in Europe will be frozen, and EU citizens and companies are forbidden from making any funds or economic resources available to her.
Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) by propagandists such as Fedorova has become an increasingly important issue for EU policymakers as Russia steps up its hybrid war on Europe.
In addition to the 101 actors sanctioned so far by the EU for FIMI efforts, the bloc has partnered with Ukraine to analyze Russia's attempts to distort the information space; established a Hybrid Rapid Response Team to help third countries counter FIMI — most recently deployed in Armenia; and is setting up a Center for Democratic Resilience to protect democracy in the EU.
Concerns are high, especially for 2027, when many EU countries, including France, Spain, Italy, Poland, and Greece, are set to hold elections.
And the campaign for France's presidential election, not set to take place until April 18, 2027, is already underway, with candidates making support for Ukraine a key issue.

He started as a driver. Now he pilots Ukraine’s heavy strike drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:57:24 UTC
23:57:24 KST

A Ukrainian service member with the callsign Talisman learned to fly four heavy strike drone platforms and now switches between them when conditions demand it, the 808th Dnistrovska Separate Support Brigade reported on 23 September. Before joining the military, he worked in business.
He began his service in a unit in Rivne Oblast, in northwestern Ukraine, starting as a driver and later moving to battalion management tasks. He was then seconded to the 808th Brigade and eventually transferred to its roster permanently. It was there that he retrained as a heavy strike drone pilot.
Four platforms, one pilot
Heavy bombers were just coming into wide use when the unit was moved onto them. They trained for a week at the manufacturer, then practiced in the unit. Everyone started on the Vampire. After nearly a year on it, Talisman tried a second platform. "When you already have the base and the foundation, mastering another platform is much easier," he said.
Talisman now operates four platforms—the Vampire, a hexacopter with six motors, and three quadcopters: the Ares A1, the Heavy Shot, and the Magura Mini. Each type has its own characteristics—some are more resistant to jamming or navigation suppression than others, he said.
"I'd probably single out the Vampire and the Ares. The Vampire is more pleasant to operate, while the Ares is more resistant to various types of jamming. I've had situations where the Vampire wasn't working, and I continued carrying out missions on the Ares," Talisman said.
The Vampire is a six-rotor bomber built by Ukraine's SkyFall, originally codified with a range of up to 20 kilometers carrying up to 15 kilograms. The company says the current range is 35–40 kilometers. The Ares A1, built by Drones of Ukraine, has been in service since 2023 in strike, remote-mining, and resupply roles.
"The hardest thing is when there's no water. For a shower. Positions are all different: for some it's harder to get there, for some it's harder to work with drones. I have this thing—it's important to me that there's water," he said with a smile.
His crews have worked the Donetsk direction, near Lyman, in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, and later on tasks in Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts. In winter they drove in for the night and had to finish the task in that window, some faster and some slower depending on conditions and on Russian jamming, before the next crew took over. In warm weather they stay on position for four to seven days at a stretch, in crews of four or five.
His callsign came from his time serving alongside his fellow soldiers. "We had luck when I was with them. That's how they gave me this callsign," he said.
After the war, Talisman sees himself returning to civilian life. Before military service he was an entrepreneur and plans to go back to it.
Brigade tops remote-mining rating
In June 2026, the 808th Brigade topped Ukraine's DELTA remote-mining rating, which ranks units by how effectively they turn enemy approach routes into traps with drones.

OpenAI’s agent hacking Australia is a warning for governments everywhere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:56:42 UTC
23:56:42 KST

On Wednesday Australia’s prime minister revealed that one of OpenAI’s artificial intelligence agents hacked into a health care platform maintained by the nation’s government—and that OpenAI took months to inform the latter about the breach.
Should these kinds of events continue to occur—or if they’ve already happened without our current knowledge—they point to a need for stronger controls on private and sensitive data collected and stored by governments and other institutions. “This is a warning for governments and their [information technology] staff to bolster security,” says Rajesh Veeraraghavan, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service.
Addressing reporters at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City on Wednesday, Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese said, “The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files.” An investigation is underway as to whether other government systems were accessed, if any, he said.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The Australian government was alerted to the incident on September 10, but Albanese said the hack occurred months before, on June 18, when an internal OpenAI model was tasked with researching public health spending. OpenAI has said it became aware of the breach in August. According to the prime minister, the company proceeded to wait until that date in early September before it alerted the Australian government through a generic public e-mail—not through any official channel for cybersecurity reporting and disclosure. As a result, the government was further delayed in learning of the event, Albanese said.
“Early evidence here seems to suggest that there was, at best, some communication challenges,” says Michael Horowitz, a political science professor at the University of Pennsylvania.
The breach follows a series of hacks by models owned by leading U.S. AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Earlier on Wednesday U.S. tech leaders—including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman—stressed their concerns over the pace of AI development in an address to the U.N. Security Council. Illegally hacking a government platform to access records could prove a watershed moment for AI regulation. In his address to reporters, Albanese said the breach was “something that has precedence.”
Details are scant as to what kind of access and information the agent got in the Australian breach. Albanese said no personal information was exposed in the incident. OpenAI did not immediately respond for a request for comment from Scientific American.
Still, Veeraraghavan stresses that responsibility for such incidents should rest solely on the AI companies that made the involved agents. “OpenAI, in this case should be held responsible, even if the ‘intent’ to divulge information may not be clear,” he says.
In his briefing to reporters, Albanese expressed that Australia will take action to respond to the event. There will “be legal consequences,” he said. It’s not yet clear what those consequences will be, especially given that a legal case concerning this style of autonomous agent hacking has not been pursued in court yet.
It is perhaps a small relief that this incident happened to a close U.S. ally. “Australia wants OpenAI to be there, so they should be able to figure it out,” Horowitz says. But unless AI labs can learn how to test their models without allowing those models to escape, they may not keep getting so lucky.
Editor’s Note (9/24/26): This is a developing story and may be updated.

Spain’s housing crisis in spotlight with eviction of pensioner, 87
Thousands have protested in outrage at the eviction and a market widely denounced as unaffordable for renters and buyers
The eviction of an 87-year-old from her Madrid home has highlighted a political paralysis that has thwarted efforts to resolve Spain’s chronic housing crisis, fuelling debate before next year’s election.
Maricarmen Abascal’s 70-year stay at her home in upmarket central Madrid ended on Wednesday when she left escorted on a stretcher, flanked by protesters on one side and police on the other – a traumatic event broadcast live on TV.

Thousands protested in Madrid, Barcelona and elsewhere on Wednesday night in outrage at the eviction and a market widely denounced as unaffordable for renters and buyers – young and old alike.

Man, 105, being investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:55:51 UTC
23:55:51 KST

A 105-year-old man is under investigation on suspicion of being an accessory to multiple murders at a Nazi prisoner of war camp, German prosecutors have said.
The case, which is being handled by the public prosecutor’s office in Dortmund, centres on the Stalag 326 VI K camp in western Germany, in what is now the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
“The 105-year-old suspect is thought to have been a guard at the prisoner of war camp Stalag 326 VI K in the Senne region of western Germany,” prosecutors said in a statement. The man is “accused of being an accessory to multiple murders owing to his activities there”, they said.
The Senne camp housed between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by American troops.
The investigation is the result of an urgent last-minute scramble by the judiciary to prosecute alleged participants in the Nazi killing machine before they die. The judicial efforts stem in part from a recognition that many of the suspects who have escaped prosecution in the eight decades since the end of the second world war on the grounds that they were considered to have played an insignificant role were in fact integral to the implementation of the Hitler regime’s murderous aims.
A judicial precedent was set by the court case of John Demjanjuk, a former guard at the Nazi Sobibór death camp in occupied Poland, who was convicted in 2011 of being an accomplice to the murders of more than 28,000 Jews that took place in the time he worked there.
Prosecutors had sought Ukraine-born Demjanjuk’s extradition from his Ohio home to Germany for years, arguing that he was complicit in the crimes committed at Sobibór despite a lack of evidence that he had directly killed anyone.
Demjanjuk died aged 91 in March 2012 awaiting an appeal due to his age and frailty, which meant he did not go to prison.
The Demjanjuk case lowered the bar for proof of complicity, paving the way for other nonagenarians and more recently centenarians to stand trial.
The most prominent trial of recent years, and representative of what Hannah Arendt, a political theorist, described as a Schreibtischtäter (desk perpetrator, or bureaucratic mediator), was that of Irmgard Furchner, who worked at the Stutthof concentration camp between 1943 and 1945 as a secretary to the camp commandant. She was given a two-year suspended sentence for her role as an accessory to murder.
Her trial was, contrary to normal rules, filmed for historical purposes. Furchner made headlines after running away from her retirement home on the scheduled opening day of her trial.
Josef Schütz, a former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp north of Berlin, was sentenced for being an accomplice to murder to five years in prison in June 2022. He died the following year, aged 102.
In April last year an alleged former guard at Sachsenhausen died before he was able to face trial over charges of complicity in the murder of more than 3,300 people.
A separate investigation was opened last year by Dortmund prosecutors into a 100-year-old former guard at a PoW camp in Hemer, North Rhine-Westphalia, which also held mainly Soviet prisoners. He is suspected of participating in executions of prisoners between December 1943 and September 1944.
The new investigation was initiated by the Central Office for the Investigation of National Socialist Crimes in Ludwigsburg, in the southern state of Baden-Württemberg, which passed its preliminary investigation into the man to public prosecutors along with that of another former guard. The other suspect has since died, according to German media.
If the trial goes ahead, like other recent cases it is expected to throw light on the Stalag system in general and on Senne in particular, drawing survivors and historians to give evidence. Up to 5.7 million Soviet prisoners were held captivity in Germany. More than half did not survive.

Global digital trade hits 7.75 trillion USD with resilience: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
22:51:40 CST
23:51:40 KST

HANGZHOU, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- The global digital trade sector has demonstrated resilience amid multiple external pressures, with export value hitting 7.75 trillion U.S. dollars in 2025, a 7.1 percent year-on-year increase, according to a report released Thursday.
The export value accounted for 22.2 percent of total exports of global goods and services, up 2.6 percentage points from 2021, continuing to outpace total global trade growth, said the report titled "Global Digital Trade Development Report 2026" unveiled at the ongoing fifth Global Digital Trade Expo in Hangzhou, capital of east China's Zhejiang Province.
The report presents the scale and structure of global digital trade, technological transformation and innovative practices, while exploring future industry trends.
Digitally delivered trade exports reached approximately 5.26 trillion U.S. dollars, representing 67.9 percent of the total, with cloud infrastructure and artificial intelligence services leading the growth. Meanwhile, digitally ordered trade exports stood at 2.49 trillion U.S. dollars, according to the report.
For the first time, the report compiles 20 global digital trade innovation achievements from economies at different development stages, spanning diverse scenarios including AI empowerment, cross-border payments, green trade and digital intellectual property.
China's digitally deliverable service trade value expanded at an average annual rate of 11.2 percent between 2016 and 2025, outpacing the global average by 1.8 percentage points.
The fifth Global Digital Trade Expo, an event dedicated to promoting digital trade and industrial cooperation, is being held from Sept. 23 to 27.
The expo features 170,000 square meters of exhibition space, with international exhibitors accounting for over 20 percent of the total. The number of overseas pavilions has already exceeded the combined total of all previous editions.
According to a guideline on boosting reform and innovative development of digital trade released in November 2024, China expects the share of digitally deliverable service trade in total service trade to exceed 45 percent by 2029 and 50 percent by 2035. ■

NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China and South Korea set up a women's basketball semifinal showdown at the 2026 Asian Games after both teams advanced from the quarterfinals on Thursday.
South Korea opened the day with a 101-59 rout of Indonesia, building a 22-point halftime lead and placing six players in double figures.
South Korea shot 52 percent from 3-point range, making 15 of 29 attempts, and outrebounded Indonesia 41-27 while holding a 33-17 advantage in assists.
"Because we were the stronger team, our focus was on finding balance among all our players and improving our teamwork," said South Korea forward Kang Lee-seul, who finished with 11 points.

China endured a disappointing day in the 3x3 competition, with both its men's and women's teams eliminated in the quarterfinals.

Li Wenxia and Wang Yue scored five points apiece for China, with Zhang adding four and Sun Fengyi two. ■

Interview: China rising as global robotics powerhouse, industry leader says
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
22:51:08 CST
23:51:08 KST

BERLIN, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China is emerging as a global powerhouse in robotics, driven by the rapid adoption of robots across industries, a large and increasingly diverse domestic market and a national strategy supporting the development of robotics and artificial intelligence, said Susanne Bieller, Secretary General of the International Federation of Robotics (IFR).
"From our last visits to China, it was really impressive to see the speed of adoption and the interest across a broad range of industries, but also among people," Bieller told Xinhua in an exclusive interview on Tuesday, coinciding with the release of the IFR's latest World Robotics report.
The IFR, based in Frankfurt, Germany, represents robotics manufacturers and research institutes worldwide and provides industry data and analysis on the development of robotics. It publishes the World Robotics report annually, tracking global trends in industrial robot adoption.
According to the IFR's newly released World Robotics 2026 report, China installed 354,000 industrial robots in 2025, up 20 percent from the previous year and accounting for 59 percent of global installations. The figure was nearly 60,000 units higher than the previous annual record, further consolidating China's position as the world's largest market for industrial robots. Its vast manufacturing base continues to generate strong demand for robots across a wide range of applications.
Bieller said several factors were driving demand for robots in China, including industrial modernization, demographic changes and the country's industrial policy and national strategy for robotics.
"There are certain drivers for the demand for robots in China. First of all, the industrialization of the industry and the need for more technology to replace or encounter the demographic shift the country is facing in the years to come," she said.
"There is also the strong industrial policy and the national strategy for robotics, bringing robotics into the market in China. That's driving the demand, as it really looks into which application areas and industries need robots and how to best foster those industries to take up the technology."
Bieller said China's development of robotics was also closely linked to its broader effort to modernize its industrial system. "There is a well-thought-through strategy behind that, and companies are embracing the technology and looking into new ways to use new technologies, as we see from the humanoids right now," she said.
According to Bieller, the IFR sees China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) as placing greater emphasis on technological self-reliance, the modernization of traditional industries and the application of artificial intelligence in the physical world.
The Chinese industrial robot market also has considerable room for further growth. IFR projections indicate that the market could maintain average annual growth of around 5 percent to 10 percent through 2029.
China's domestic robot suppliers have also strengthened their position in the market. Their installations rose 15 percent in 2025 to 195,000 units. According to the latest IFR data, domestic suppliers accounted for about 55 percent of the Chinese market in 2025.
"Chinese companies have grown in competitiveness over the last decade, and the domestic share has increased dramatically," Bieller said. She noted that the growth was not confined to a small number of industries, with "huge opportunities" in sectors that have not invested as heavily in automation as automotive.
She cited logistics as one area with strong potential and said vehicles beyond passenger cars, as well as food, textiles and paper, could also see further growth in robot adoption. The characteristics of the Chinese market are also encouraging manufacturers to develop robots tailored to specific industrial needs, she said.
"Chinese companies have learned to develop robots that are just fit for the purpose," Bieller said, calling this a strength of Chinese suppliers in developing solutions tailored to specific markets and applications.
The development of China's robotics industry is also reflected in the changing role of manufacturing companies.
During a visit to Shenzhen in April, Bieller visited electric vehicle manufacturer XPeng's factory and saw robots being used in vehicle production. She said XPeng was also developing quadruped and humanoid robots.
"They are a customer of robots for their electric vehicle factory, but at the same time they are developing their own quadruped and humanoid robots," she said. ■

by sportswriter Li Jia
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 Asian Games witnessed a day where host nation Japan delivered historic breakthroughs, while China maintained its gold medal march on Thursday.
Japan ended China's quest for a ninth consecutive title in the men's table tennis team final following a narrow 3-2 win, clinching its first gold medal in the event since 1966.
The team tie was ultimately decided in the fifth match, where 19-year-old Wen Ruibo fell 3-1 to fellow teenager Sora Matsushima. Earlier in the contest, China faced strong resistance from Japan's Tomokazu Harimoto. Harimoto defeated Wen 3-1 and later swept Wang Chuqin 3-0 to level the overall score at 2-2.

China's young swimmers made waves as 19-year-old Zhang Zhanshuo claimed his sixth Asiad gold, winning the men's 800m freestyle in a Games-record 7:42.49. He then helped China win the men's 4x100m freestyle relay with an Asian-record 3:10.60, ahead of South Korea and Japan. China also dominated the women's 4x200m freestyle relay in 7:49.37, beating Japan by 10.16 seconds.
Wu Qingfeng won the women's 50m freestyle in a Games-record 23.98, missing the Asian record by just 0.01 seconds. Bahrain's Mikhail Arkhangelskiy won the men's 50m butterfly with an Asian-record 22.91, followed by Japan's Shoon Mitsunaga and China's Wang Changhao. This was also Bahrain's first gold at the Games.
Also in the pool, China beat Japan to win the women's water polo title.
China reclaimed the Asiad badminton women's team title with a 3-0 sweep of Japan, ending a gold-medal drought that spanned the last two editions of the Games. In the men's team final, China suffered a 3-2 defeat to Indonesia, missing out on the gold medal.
Out on the water, China claimed two golds and two silvers in the canoe sprint. In the women's kayak double 500m, Yin Mengdie and Yu Shimeng took gold with a time of 1:45.010, finishing 3.130 seconds ahead of Kazakhstan. Meanwhile, Ji Bowen and Wu Shengyue secured the men's canoe double 500m title in 1:40.741, beating Uzbekistan by 2.137 seconds. In rowing, China won nine out of 14 gold medals on offer.
China's Wu Zhifan and Liang Zhenglan finished 1-2 in the women's mountain bike cross-country. Since the event became an official Asian Games sport at Bangkok 1998, China has won all available gold medals in the women's cross-country.
Across other venues, Chinese shooters added two gold medals to the tally, winning the men's 10m air pistol team and the mixed skeet team.
In gymnastics, China's Qiu Qiyuan won the women's uneven bars, while Lan Xingyu topped the men's rings. In weightlifting, China's Yang Yang won the men's 60kg title, while He Yueji broke the men's 65kg snatch world record but settled for a silver.
In athletics, China's Huang Yingying and Li Yi took silver and bronze in the women's triple jump respectively. The gold medal went to Uzbekistan's Sharifa Davronova with a personal best of 14.35 meters.
China secured a 1-2 finish in men's discus throw, with Aduduaini Tuergong winning gold with 64.26m and Wu Nanjun taking silver with 61.58m.
Bahrain's Winfred Yavi claimed the women's 10,000m title in 32:39.18. ■

Why is Kosovo joining Gaza's International Stabilisation Force?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:50:29 UTC
23:50:29 KST

Breadcrumb
Why is Kosovo joining Gaza's International Stabilisation Force?
On 30 March, Kosovo’s government approved the deployment of Kosovo Security Forces personnel to Gaza as part of the proposed International Stabilisation Force (ISF) backed by the United States and envisioned under President Donald J. Trump’s peace plan.
Then on 7 September, Pristina formally signed an agreement to join the United Nations-mandated force, according to a statement posted on social media by the Board of Peace.
The decision places Kosovo at the centre of a wider international effort to establish security and support reconstruction in Gaza, while also raising questions about the mission’s role, its legal and political implications, and Kosovo’s ties with the United States and Israel.
Kosovo's strategic calculation
Kosovo’s decision to join the Board of Peace and the ISF underscores Pristina’s commitment to the United States. The small Muslim-majority Balkan state has long regarded Washington as its most important international partner.
This is particularly because of the US role in supporting Kosovo during and after the Kosovo War (1998–99) and in backing its independence, which the US under the George W. Bush administration formally recognised in February 2008 as one of the first countries in the world to do so.
But Dr Ramadan Ilazi, head of research at the Kosovar Centre for Security Studies (KCSS), said Kosovo’s decision should not be understood solely as an attempt to please Washington.
He described the motivation as a combination of principle, pragmatism, and strategic interest, arguing that Kosovo also wants to demonstrate that it can contribute to international security after more than two decades as a recipient of international assistance.
“There is now a strong desire to demonstrate that it can also be a contributor. Kosovo remains grateful for the international engagement that helped end the war in 1999, supported post-war reconstruction, and continues to provide security through KFOR. Participating in the ISF is therefore also a way of expressing solidarity and giving something back,” Dr Ilazi told The New Arab.
Lily Lynch, editor-in-chief of the Balkanist Magazine, holds that participating in Trump’s initiative sends a message that Kosovo’s relationship with the United States is intended to remain strong regardless of which political party controls the White House.
This is quite significant given concerns in Kosovo that a Trump administration could potentially be more accommodating toward Serbia.
“Kosovo decided to join the Board of Peace and [ISF] as a demonstration of its fidelity to the United States. The decision indicates that regardless of who is in the White House, Kosovo's commitment to its relationship with the United States is ironclad,” she told The New Arab.
“Some foreign policy commentators see Kosovo's existence as an independent state as a product of Clintonite foreign policy and liberal internationalism; there was concern among some in Kosovo that a Trump presidency would give Serbia an advantage,” added Lynch.
“But participation in the Board of Peace and ISF suggests that Kosovo wants to make clear that its commitment to a strong relationship with America transcends party politics.”
The Kosovo-Gaza comparison and its limits
Prime Minister Albin Kurti has framed the decision through Kosovo’s own experience with international peacekeeping. In announcing the government’s support for the deployment, Kurti pointed to the fact that Kosovo itself has benefited from international forces since 1999.
The analogy is also linked to the continued presence of NATO’s KFOR mission, which has provided security in Kosovo for more than two-and-a-half decades.
Lynch sees this as a deliberate attempt by Kurti to explain why Kosovo should now contribute to an international mission elsewhere, based on the argument that international forces helped provide security in Kosovo, and therefore Kosovo can now use its own experience and capabilities to assist another population.
Kosovo’s Security Forces have developed expertise in areas including search-and-rescue operations and demining, which policymakers in Pristina say could be relevant to the Gaza mission.
But the comparison between Kosovo and Gaza is also one of the most contested aspects of the decision because the circumstances surrounding NATO’s intervention in Kosovo and the proposed Gaza mission differ in fundamental ways.
In Kosovo, international intervention followed a war between Serbian forces and the Kosovo Albanian population and ultimately preceded Kosovo’s declaration of independence in 2008. Questions remain over whether Kosovo’s experience can straightforwardly serve as a model for the Gaza initiative. This distinction is important because Kurti’s comparison is not simply historical. It is also political.
Jelena Novakov, a Belgrade-based geopolitical analyst who writes for Kosovo Online, said the comparison is understandable given Kosovo’s own experience of conflict and international protection, but argued that it also contains a significant contradiction.
“For a young country that is still struggling with international recognition and, in a way, remains a recipient of international assistance through KFOR, this represents a significant demonstration of improved stability, even if largely symbolic,” she told The New Arab.
“What is debatable is the decision to participate in an initiative launched by the country that is largely responsible for the devastation in Gaza, after Kosovo itself experienced aggression,” Novakov added.
Dr Ilazi noted that Kosovo’s experience could provide a point of reference but cautioned against treating it as a model for Gaza.
“Kosovo and Gaza have different histories and political circumstances. Our experience cannot tell Palestinians what their future should look like. It can, however, remind us that people need both physical security and a say over how they are governed,” he said.
He also pointed to Kosovo’s own experience with international administration, arguing that this provided another lesson that could be relevant to the Gaza mission.
“We also know the frustrations of international administration, as we had our own share of that with [the United Nations Interim Administration Mission in Kosovo (UNMIK)], and these include decisions made far from the people affected, unclear accountability, and arrangements described as temporary that become very difficult to change. That experience is worth sharing too,” Dr Ilazi said.
Kurti appears to be carefully framing his message to reassure Kosovar Albanians who may be uneasy about Kosovo’s involvement in Trump’s Gaza initiative. With 4,600 KFOR troops stationed in Kosovo, at least as of earlier this year, the southeastern European country continues to depend on international peacekeeping troops.
“Kurti is trying to say, ‘international peacekeeping troops have helped keep us safe, so now we can use our own unique expertise to help others.’ Kurti is also undoubtedly trying to communicate Kosovo’s unique value to Trump’s putative peace effort. Of course, all of this would be far more meaningful if Trump’s plan for Gaza actually benefited the people of Gaza the way NATO helped Kosovar Albanians,” Lynch explained to The New Arab.
"I would say this is the main problem with Kurti's framing: He’s right that international forces helped the [Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA)] force Serbian troops out of Kosovo in 1999. This was a prerequisite for Kosovo’s eventual declaration of independence in 2008. That’s the difference here,” she noted.
“By Kurti’s own analogy, what’s happening with Trump's Gaza peace plan is much more akin to what would have happened in 1999 if NATO troops had helped Serbia retain control of Kosovo and had helped Serbian forces keep Albanians in submission.”
By invoking Kosovo’s experience with international protection, the country’s prime minister is presenting participation in the ISF as an extension of a principle that Kosovars know personally, which is the idea that international forces can provide security to a population emerging from conflict.
Whether that principle applies to Gaza, however, remains a matter of significant disagreement.
Between Palestinian sympathy and strategic necessity
The decision is also likely to be viewed through the lens of Kosovo’s domestic politics. With many citizens of Kosovo sympathetic to Palestinians, there is tension between public sentiment and Pristina’s strategic interests.
Kosovars who oppose Trump’s Gaza plan or support the Palestinian cause may nevertheless view participation as a necessary cost of maintaining the United States as Kosovo’s closest ally, which can be understood as a limitation faced by a small state.
Novakov said, however, that the issue has so far generated little sustained public debate in Kosovo. She attributed this partly to the country’s wider political and economic problems, including prolonged political instability, inflation, stalled negotiations with Belgrade and the EU, deteriorating relations with Washington, and the legal proceedings involving former KLA leaders.
“There is currently no large-scale public conversation about this issue in Kosovo,” Novakov told The New Arab. “There is support for Palestine among Kosovars, but the government’s alignment with the US is rarely raised as one of the main issues during demonstrations.”
Dr Ilazi cautioned against assuming that political support for the deployment necessarily translates into broad public support for every aspect of the mission. Although he stated that the parliament’s 89-0 vote on 17 April to approve the government’s earlier decision to deploy Kosovo’s forces to the ISF “shows broad political support for participation,” Dr Ilazi stressed that it does “not tell us how the public will respond to every task the mission might undertake, and I would avoid claiming a public majority without reliable polling.”
As he explained, much will depend on what people see unfolding in Gaza.
“Clearing unexploded ordnance, helping aid reach families and making neighbourhoods safer are contributions the government can explain clearly. Public confidence would be harder to sustain if Kosovo’s soldiers became associated with restricting Palestinian movement or protecting arrangements that leave people displaced,” Dr Ilazi told The New Arab.
Kosovo has relatively little ability to influence major international conflicts and may therefore prioritise maintaining relationships with powerful allies, chiefly Washington. The result is a complicated political position in which criticism of the Gaza policy can coexist with acceptance of Kosovo’s participation, according to Lynch.
“The majority of Albanians are sympathetic to Palestinians, though there are some very vocal Zionist Albanians as well. But even those who support Palestine and deplore Trump’s Gaza plan are likely to accept the Kosovo government's decision to participate as a necessary cost of keeping America as their closest ally. The prevailing thought in Kosovo is ‘we’re a small country, there’s not much we can do to shape major world events and distant conflicts, so we will accept this arrangement because this is what our closest ally wants,’” she told The New Arab.
For Novakov, the calculation is ultimately rooted in Kosovo’s continuing reliance on international support. Around 100 countries have yet to recognise Kosovo’s independence, including five European Union members (Cyprus, Greece, Romania, Slovakia, and Spain), while Russia and China remain opposed to its statehood.
With Brussels’ focus increasingly shifting towards Ukraine, she argues, maintaining a close relationship with Washington remains particularly important for Pristina.
Questions over responsibility and accountability
Beyond public opinion, the deployment raises questions about legal and reputational responsibility. There are valid concerns to raise about the possibility that Kosovo’s involvement could expose its personnel or government to scrutiny if the wider operation were associated with forced displacement, the consolidation of Israeli control over Gaza, or other conduct that violates international law.
Lynch argues that these concerns deserve particular attention because of Kosovo’s own experience with international justice and accountability. The recent conviction and 25-year sentence of former Kosovo political and military leader Hashim Thaçi on war crimes charges has already placed questions of wartime responsibility at the centre of public debate.
Against that background, participation in a controversial international operation could create additional scrutiny if Kosovar personnel became associated with actions later determined to be unlawful.
Dr Ilazi distinguished between the legal and reputational risks Kosovo could face.
“I would also separate legal responsibility from reputational damage. Establishing legal responsibility requires evidence about particular actions and circumstances. Public trust can be lost much earlier if a mission is seen as facilitating abuse or denying Palestinians control over their future,” he told The New Arab.
He also argued that Kosovo should establish clear limits on what its personnel can be asked to do.
“Those restrictions need to shape operational planning, with legal review, reporting to the Assembly and a credible option to suspend or withdraw the contingent. We should not leave individual soldiers to resolve political ambiguities that their government failed to address,” commented Dr Ilazi, who also argued that the perspectives of Palestinians themselves should receive greater attention in discussions about the force.
“One issue that deserves more attention is how Palestinians themselves view the force. Most discussions focus on Washington’s intentions and the calculations of contributing countries. Yet the people expected to live alongside this mission need meaningful influence over the arrangements it supports. From Kosovo’s experience, we should understand how much that matters,” he argued.
A new test for Kosovo's foreign policy
Ultimately, Kosovo’s decision to participate in the Gaza stabilisation effort highlights the difficult choices facing a small state whose security and international standing have been closely connected to the United States for many years.
For Kurti’s government, participation offers an opportunity to demonstrate continued commitment to Washington and to portray Kosovo as a country capable of contributing to international security rather than simply receiving international assistance.
At the same time, the decision places Kosovo between competing pressures, including domestic sympathy for Palestinians, its strategic partnership with the United States, questions about the nature of the Gaza mission, and concerns about legal and reputational consequences.
As the deployment moves forward, the central question will be whether Kosovo can maintain its strong relationship with Washington while avoiding becoming entangled in the contentious political and legal disputes surrounding Gaza.

9-year-old Israeli boy dies after rare brain-eating amoeba infection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:50:18 UTC
23:50:18 KST

A nine-year-old boy who was hospitalized earlier this month after contracting a rare infection caused by a brain-eating amoeba died on Thursday at Rambam Medical Center in northern Israel.
The boy, Baruch Neria from Pardes Hanna-Karkur, had been hospitalized in serious condition for about two weeks while under sedation and on a ventilator. According to the Health Ministry, an epidemiological investigation found that he had swum at Kursi Beach on the Sea of Galilee, a lake in northern Israel, a week before his hospitalization.
Neria's brain infection was caused by Naegleria fowleri, a microscopic amoeba found primarily in warm freshwater. In extremely rare cases, it can cause a severe central nervous system infection.
Only about 500 cases of infection have been documented worldwide, according to the Health Ministry, but the disease has a fatality rate of about 97 percent.
Three cases have been recorded in Israel in recent years. In July 2024, a 26-year-old man died and a 10-year-old boy was left in a vegetative state after exposure to the amoeba at a water park near the Sea of Galilee. In 2022, a resident of northern Israel died after becoming infected in a freshwater reservoir in the north.
Most infections occur in the United States, but the disease is rare even there: 31 cases were reported between 2012 and 2021, while 151 infections were reported between 1962 and 2020, of which only four patients survived.
Last week, a teenager from North Carolina and an eight-year-old girl from Louisiana died from infections caused by the amoeba.
Climate change could lead to an increase in infections, as the amoeba is surviving in places where it had not previously been observed. 
For example, an infection was reported in Minnesota, a relatively cool state where the amoeba would not ordinarily be expected to survive. Rising temperatures can also lower water levels in reservoirs, resulting in higher concentrations of the amoeba in the water and increasing the risk of infection.
How does infection occur?
Infection can occur when water containing the amoeba enters through the nose, allowing the amoeba to travel to the brain. The disease is not caused by drinking water and is not transmitted from person to person.
According to the Health Ministry, to reduce the risk when swimming in warm freshwater, people should avoid getting water into their noses as much as possible, particularly when jumping, diving or submerging their heads. They can close their nostrils or use a nose clip. They should also avoid digging into or stirring up the bottom in shallow water, where the amoeba may be present in higher concentrations.
When should you seek medical attention?
After exposure to warm freshwater, medical attention should be sought if symptoms such as fever, severe headache, nausea or vomiting develop. Symptoms such as a stiff neck (difficulty bending the neck forward), confusion, unusual drowsiness or altered consciousness require urgent medical attention.
The Health Ministry advises telling medical staff about any water exposure when seeking care. Although the disease is extremely rare, it can cause rapid deterioration.

Palestinian Authority Chairman Mahmoud Abbas addressed the United Nations General Assembly by prerecorded video Thursday after the United States denied him a visa to attend the annual gathering in New York for the second consecutive year.
Speaking from his office in Ramallah in the West Bank, Abbas opened his address by criticizing the Trump administration's decision and calling on Washington to reverse its restrictions on Palestinian officials.
“Preventing me from coming to address the General Assembly is a violation of UN procedures,” Abbas said. He called on the United States to “lift the sanctions and return to dialogue and respect” and to discussions aimed at advancing a two-state solution.
The General Assembly voted 152-3, with four abstentions, last week to allow Abbas to address the gathering remotely after he was denied entry. The United States, Israel and Paraguay opposed the measure.
Abbas used much of his speech to sharply condemn Israel's conduct in the Gaza Strip and West Bank.
“In Gaza, the Palestinian people are being subjected to killing, destruction, starvation, attempted displacement and a genocidal war that has created a major humanitarian catastrophe,” Abbas said.
Israel rejects accusations that its military campaign in Gaza constitutes genocide, saying it targets terrorist groups and operates in accordance with international law.
Abbas also accused Israel of accelerating settlement expansion in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, which Palestinians seek as the capital of a future state.
“Israel's policies, in violation of international law, are destroying the two-state solution,” Abbas said. “The danger is growing and threatens the existence of the Palestinian people on their land.”
He characterized Israeli policies in Gaza and the West Bank as a “colonial plot” intended to force Palestinians from their land and warned world leaders against allowing what he described as another Nakba, the Arabic term for “catastrophe” used by Palestinians to describe the mass displacement that accompanied Israel's establishment and the 1948 Arab-Israeli war.
“Do not allow violent gangs, with the approval of the Israeli army, to burn communities,” Abbas said, referring to attacks by extremist Israeli settlers in the West Bank.
Settler violence and settlement expansion have drawn growing international criticism. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said this week that settler violence was rising at an alarming rate and reiterated the UN's position that Israeli settlements in the West Bank violate international law. Israel disputes some international legal characterizations of the territory and says the status of settlements should be resolved through negotiations.
Barred from New York for second year
The U.S. State Department rejected Abbas' visa request for this year's General Assembly after taking the same step in 2025, again forcing the 90-year-old Palestinian leader to participate remotely.
The United States, as host country of the UN headquarters, generally has obligations to facilitate access for foreign delegations attending UN meetings, though Washington retains authority over visas and has imposed restrictions in some cases involving officials with whom it has serious disputes.
The Trump administration has accused the Palestinian Authority and Palestine Liberation Organization of undermining peace efforts, including through attempts to secure international recognition and pursue cases against Israel in international courts. Palestinian officials have rejected the U.S. restrictions.
The visa dispute comes as Abbas faces mounting pressure over the Palestinian Authority's political future and the question of who would govern Gaza under any long-term settlement of the conflict.
The Palestinian Authority exercises limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank under agreements reached with Israel in the 1990s. Hamas seized control of Gaza from Abbas' Fatah movement in 2007.
The Israeli-Palestinian conflict has again emerged as one of the dominant issues at this year's General Assembly, where a series of leaders have criticized Israel over Gaza, West Bank settlements and Palestinian statehood.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan used his address to condemn Israel's conduct in Gaza and urge greater international pressure on Israel while calling for broader recognition of a Palestinian state.
Other leaders, including Qatar's emir, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, have also accused Israel of genocide in Gaza. Israel has repeatedly rejected that charge, saying Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack and subsequent military operations are central to understanding the war and accusing critics of ignoring the threats it faces.
Abbas' address came hours before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was scheduled to speak before the General Assembly, setting up sharply contrasting presentations of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict from the two leaders.
Netanyahu is expected to defend Israel's conduct and address threats facing the country, including Iran, amid an unusually brief visit to New York and plans for protests surrounding his appearance.

Was Hitler behind niece's death? Documents raise questions about alibi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:49:50 UTC
23:49:50 KST

Hitler's possible role in niece's death under scrutiny after documents raise questions about alibi, report says
Newly unearthed records in a Munich archive have cast doubt on Adolf Hitler's whereabouts at the time of his niece's suspicious 1931 death, according to news magazine Der Spiegel.
Hitler's unusually close and controlling relationship with his niece, Geli Raubal, has long been the subject of speculation and rumor, and newspaper reports at the time suggested that Hitler may have played a role in her death.
Raubal died from a gunshot wound to the chest from a pistol belonging to Hitler, in what was officially determined to be a suicide.
According to the official account, Hitler's personal servant, Georg Winter, discovered the 23-year-old Raubal's body on the floor inside her locked room in Hitler's apartment in Munich on Sept. 19, 1931, a Saturday.
Hitler, who at the time was a prominent far-right extremist but had not yet seized power in Germany, was away in the city of Nuremberg that day, giving him what appeared to be a strong alibi.
But according to an article in Der Spiegel, historian Harald Sandner recently discovered documents in archives in Munich casting doubt on that account — and raising questions about whether Nazi sympathizers in the police may have falsified records to protect Hitler.
 Two death notices and an entry in an official local death registry all put the date of the discovery of Raubal's body to Sept. 18, a full day earlier, when Hitler was known to still have been in Munich.
 
Strange relationship
Hitler's relationship with Raubal, the daughter of his half-sister Angela Raubal, was the subject of intense speculation. Some contemporaries believed Hitler had been abusive or had pursued a sexual relationship with his relative.
Hitler reportedly strictly controlled nearly every aspect of Raubal's life after she moved to Munich in 1927.
She reportedly argued intensely with Hitler just before her death after Hitler refused to allow her to move to Vienna.
Sandner told the magazine the discrepancy in the documents over the date of Raubal's death may point toward a cover-up by the police, though there is no decisive proof.
Days after Raubal's death, a left-wing Munich newspaper reported Hitler had been in a heated argument with his niece, that injuries had been found on her body and that Nazi officials held crisis meetings regarding how to present the matter to the public.
Other newspapers suggested Hitler might have had Raubal killed — or killed her himself — though the Nazi leader publicly denied those allegations in a statement.

Trans activists accuse state gender committee of bias and obstruction

14:49:00 UTC
23:49:00 KST

Trans activists accuse state gender committee of bias and obstruction
Trans activists in Estonia have accused the state gender reassignment committee of obstruction and bias, and are demanding that the committee's chair be removed.
ETV show "Pealtnägija" heard both sides of the heated dispute; the gender reassignment committee (Riiklikku soovahetuskomisjon) says its critics represent a small but vocal minority.
Appearing in the "Pealtnägija" segment which aired this week were Karmen Ott, 22, and Stephanie-Emma Zorianska, 27, both from Harju County, and Sona Kravtšenko, 26, from Ida-Viru County. All three were born as boys but had felt since childhood that this gender assignment was not right for them.
The upbringing for all three and the struggles with gender identity which accompanied this could each make for a long story of its own, "Pealtnägija" reported, but suffice to say that Stephanie, who was born into challenging circumstances and grew up in a foster family, "came out" at around the age of 15; Karmen told her parents two years ago, while Sona, whose family is devout Jehovah's Witnesses, only revealed her identity to her family last summer.
All three appeared on "Pealtnägija" under their own names and were going public for the first time, with all its associated risks. These were particularly great for Sona. Not only has her mother not accepted that the person she calls her son in fact identifies as a trans woman, but the segment will likely be the first time many in the Jehovah's Witness congregation the family belongs to will have heard about the situation.
More than that, in giving the interview, Sona says she risks being shunned by the Jehovah's Witnesses, a socially conservative sect, and even of her mother no longer speaking to her. "I do hope she will, but that risk is very real. The possibility that I'll be thrown out of my home and no one will speak to me anymore is also a very real risk."
However, the reason Sona, Karmen and Stephanie are publicly sharing their journeys is much bigger than even these personal struggles, they say – and go all the way to the committee itself.
"I think this entire process, the way it works in Estonia, is so drawn out. It is long, it is humiliating, it weighs on people who are already having a hard time, because we are a minority in Estonia. And it is clear that the whole point of this committee is not to help people, but to fob them off and waste time and simply hide them away somewhere," Stephanie said.
To understand these accusations, a detour into history is needed. While during the Soviet era such issues were taboo or even punishable as a criminal offense, just before the turn of the millennium and a few years after Estonia had restored its independence, a medical expert committee on gender reassignment was established under the auspices of the Ministry of Social Affairs. This would investigate whether to permit a person to change their gender in terms of officialdom – for instance Estonian ID codes start with a "3" if the holder is male and "4" if female, if born in the 20th century; those born from 2000 onwards similarly have a "5" (male) or "6" (female) at the start of their ID code.
Initially, the rules set up required genetic testing to prove that a person was transgender, a document signed by the minister authorizing the start of medical intervention and, finally, if desired, another appearance before the commission to change the first digit of one's personal identification code.
The committee's work was suspended for a year in 2021, and its chair also changed. The rules were then also streamlined: A psychiatrist's diagnosis that the person is transgender and one meeting with the committee have since then been sufficient to decide this; also that decision is signed off on by the committee chair rather than the minister.
The committee consists of 11 doctors and other specialists. At least three, and usually four of these attend each and every meeting. The meetings are held on the premises of the West Tallinn Central Hospital.
According to the official statistics, the number of applications for gender transition has more than quadrupled in just the past five years: From 42 applications in 2020 to 177 last year. Compared with the situation 10 years ago, however, the committee's workload has increased tenfold during that time: A decade ago there were just nine recorded gender change applications.
The committee is chaired by long-serving gynecologist and fertility specialist Kai Haldre. According to Haldre, most applicants are young trans men, ie. women seeking to become men.
The rise was in line with trends elsewhere in the world, Haldre said. "We knew that in Western Europe and elsewhere there had been a sharp spike from around 2013-2015. Gender dysphoria among teenage girls had increased so sharply that wait lines suddenly appeared in many countries, and we were also told: You'll see, you'll end up with long waiting lists of several years," Haldre said.
There is no single explanation for why the increase has been so large. A separate question is how far social media has contributed to the rise in applications. Although the committee has upped the frequency of its meetings several times, it is still struggling with the volume of work. It has the capacity to meet with around 150 applicants a year, giving an average waiting time of two years. This very fact drew criticism from the gender equality commissioner in summer this year.
Karmen cited her own case, saying that in 2024 she realized she had to do something. "So what had happened was that I put my name down for the commission, sent a letter, and then they replied that my commission appointment should be sometime in 2027. That made me very disappointed in our health care system," she said. In the end, Karmen sought help from a foreign clinic which prescribed hormone therapy for her.
Formally speaking, the committee merely confirms the diagnosis of transsexualism which had been previously made by a psychiatrist, which carries the code F64.0 under the official classification, but in practice, in many respects, gender transition cannot be carried out in Estonia without it. For example, a doctor can prescribe the hormone therapy needed for gender reassignment independently, but confirmation from the committee is nevertheless generally required. In addition, without it the population register will not change a person's personal identification code from male to female or vice versa.
Karmen nevertheless got an available commission appointment unexpectedly this spring, as well as permission to begin treatment. Sona, however, was so disheartened by the lengthy wait time that she sought treatment on her own initiative too. Stephanie meanwhile had been turned down about a decade ago on the grounds she was still a minor then; she, too, has now been on the waiting list for a lengthy period of time.
"For some time I was writing to them every month, but the replies were along the lines of: 'look, we don't have time and we can't, and, essentially, stop writing to us'. You're sent running from one place to another, and then you realize that in their eyes you're not even a person at all. By law, these people are supposed to be the ones who help, but there is zero help from them. The whole process is humiliating," Stephanie said.
Added to the humiliation is the fact that Stephanie was attacked in the Mustamäe district of Tallinn last winter, due to her appearance. While traveling to work and having applied light makeup, she noticed a young man taking pictures of her on the bus. When Stephanie remarked that it was not pleasant to be taking pictures of people, she was violently assaulted, and suffered a broken tooth.
The investigation into the assault fizzled out, and no suspect was apprehended. In the wake of the attack, however, Karmen, Sona and Stephanie set up an initiative group with like-minded people, and at the start of summer sent the ministry an extremely extensive request for clarification; the content of this questionnaire sharply criticized the medical expert committee in its current guise, and, in a short period of time, garnered 400 signatures from transgender people and their supporters.
Karmen said the most troubling issue was that under the new regulation, the committee's only requirement is for gender identity issues, yet medical professionals have said the committee should green-light procedures such as hormone XXX therapy. "You don't need to go there for hormone therapy or any other medical procedures. In practice, however, nothing has changed, as doctors still require it. We know of one specific case where a doctor refused to prescribe hormone therapy to a patient out of fear that they could go to prison as a result," Karmen said.
In addition to the long waiting times, transgender people have charged the committee with humiliating transgender people by requiring a diagnosis which implies a psychiatric illness, basing its work on outdated scientific research and being ideologically biased.
Haldre's response was that patient groups tend to develop their own "mythologies." "I've sometimes said, half-jokingly, 'you know, I'll do anything you want, but bring me an article. Bring it and show me where the evidence base is'," Haldre said, adding that the core group, which consists primarily of young people, may not understand how the medicine works or the logic behind it.
Haldre, who has fought for women's abortion rights for decades, said the nucleus of the critics consists not only of young transgender people, but of people who often have complicated family backstories, not to mention strong views. For example, Stephanie bore a sign at this year's Tallinn Pride which effectively told the committee to go to hell. One anonymous letter from an activist, however, was so threatening that Haldre felt she had to contact the police.
Another source of frustration for activists is that since obtaining the necessary treatment via official channels takes years, many young people turn to foreign pharmaceutical intermediaries, or even run the risk of obtaining hormones on the black market.
At the same time, doctors say they never refuse to prescribe any medication simply out of small-mindedness.
"If medical intervention is needed, if an endocrinologist assumes such great responsibility, including, so to speak, with off-label drugs or medications which are not intended for this and have never been studied for it, then they need broader confirmation. That is also the case from the standpoint of medical ethics, not to mention surgery in this field," Haldre explained.
The same core group recently began calling themselves "Transrinne" ("Transfront"), which "Pealtnägija" said was a signal move. They have authored pages of analyses and appeals, suggesting that the committee and its chair are biased. Among other things, several activists secretly recorded their appointments with the committee, to demonstrate what they say are regressive and irrelevant questions being asked there. One of the clearer criticisms is that the committee does not follow World Health Organization (WHO) principles in determining whether someone is transgender. They also criticize Haldre for links to organizations that they consider transphobic.
What particularly offends those involved is that being transgender was historically speaking classified as a psychiatric disorder, and even to this day is classified under the code F64 in Estonia's system, denoting a disorder. Internationally, however, it is no longer considered a disorder – for instance in the U.S. gender identity disorder was struck off the American Psychiatric Association's diagnostic manual in 2013; WHO officially removed being transgender from its list of mental disorders at the start of 2022. According to Haldre, the classification issue in Estonia is an administrative one and not a regressive one.
"Pealtnägija" communicated with Haldre on a continual basis in preparation for its reportage, both by phone and in writing. Clearly disturbed by the accusations, Haldre repeatedly recalled that the committee's previous chair, Imre Rammul, had stepped down partly because of similar criticism. Social Affairs Minister Dr. Karmen Joller (Reform), who "Pealtnägija" asked for comment, also warned that doctors should not be attacked personally. "There are few competent specialists, and involving them is made more difficult by the fact that committee members have come under intense pressure," Joller said.
There is, however, one thing the parties agree on: that the regulations could be changed so that the committee would no longer have to consider whether or not to allow the first digit of a person's personal identification code to be changed. The gender equality commissioner, Christian Veske, said he supports this idea.
"To my mind, this is wholly problematic. A medical committee, as the name infers, should deal with health-related, medical procedures, as it were. To then give that medical committee an additional function, on which a transgender person's ability to bring their documents into line with their identity hinges, is a major issue for me, and I personally consider it unfair," Veske said.
