'I want to bring change and repair': Eisenkot lays out vision for Israel in first English interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:06:02 UTC
22:06:02 KST

Yashar party leader and former IDF chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot has emerged as the leading opposition candidate seeking to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of the October election.
Receiving rapid, widespread support at a crucial juncture, Eisenkot is well positioned to become the country’s next prime minister in the country’s first elections since the Oct. 7 Hamas attacks in 2023.
In his first in-depth interview to an English news outlet ahead of the elections, Eisenkot broke down to the Magazine his plans for the country as prime minister, what his security approach would be, and his stance on Oct. 7 failures – while also opening up on the loss of his son and two nephews who fell in battle during the Israel-Hamas War.
Eisenkot rose through the IDF’s Golani infantry brigade and was OC Northern Command, before serving as chief of staff from 2015 to 2019. His military career put him at the center of Israel’s confrontation with Iranian forces and their allies in Syria, a threat he identified in the interview as his foremost concern.
He entered politics in 2022 with Benny Gantz’s National Unity party. After Oct. 7, Eisenkot joined Netanyahu’s emergency government and sat as an observer in the war cabinet. He and Gantz left the government in June 2024. Eisenkot later broke with Gantz and founded Yashar, Hebrew for “straight” or “upright,” in September 2025.
A Channel 12 poll conducted Tuesday projected 23 seats for Yashar, 20 for the Likud, and 13 for Naftali Bennett’s B’Yachad. It gave Zionist parties opposed to Netanyahu 54 seats, short of the 61 needed for a Knesset majority without Arab parties. Eisenkot led Netanyahu, 41% to 38%, when respondents were asked who was better suited to be prime minister, though that difference is within the poll’s reported margin of error.
The numbers sharpen the question we put to him: How does he form a government while ruling out the Arab parties?
Eisenkot has presented himself as a unique candidate, offering a more reserved personality compared with the outgoing, outspoken figures who have dominated Israeli politics.
He arrived at The Jerusalem Post studio with the mannerisms that have come to characterize him, sitting at the edge of his seat and speaking calmly throughout the nearly hour-long interview.
Amid the countless theories and claims that there was a betrayal on Oct. 7, Eisenkot said that there was no possibility that this was the case.
“Unequivocally, there was no betrayal.... I know the people [and the system]. There is no chance that someone betrayed.”
Addressing Oct. 7 failures
“What there was, however, was deep negligence, arrogance, contempt, lack of professionalism – first of all by the military echelon, and afterward by the political echelon,” Eisenkot elaborated.
“And the most serious thing, in my view, is that all the cabinet ministers... are running again in the upcoming elections, except [then-defense minister Yoav] Gallant. This is inconceivable,” he said.
He told the Magazine that one of his top priorities would be to establish an official state commission of inquiry to probe government failures on Oct. 7.
“A state commission of inquiry must be established that will examine the last 10 years, from when I started my position,” he said.
Eisenkot himself became a bereaved father during the war, losing his son Gal two months into the war in Gaza. That same week, he lost a nephew, along with another nephew who fell in fighting a year later.
Speaking of his son, Eisenkot said, “The desire to contribute and do more for the country – there is no doubt that his fall... motivates me to act to be worthy of the heavy price that we paid, both as a country and as a family.
“He is with me every day,” he said.
Eisenkot's coalition redlines
Eisenkot also laid out some of his coalition redlines to the Magazine, saying that the two major Arab-led parties running – Ra’am and the Joint List – are not viable coalition partners.
“I decided that in the next government, I would see as a partner anyone who accepts Israel as a Jewish democratic state, the values of the Declaration of Independence, and the obligation of service.
“About a month ago, more or less, I understood that there is also a part of them [the Arab parties] that does not see Hamas as a terrorist organization.
“And I said that in the basic guidelines of the next government, it will be written that whoever does not accept that Hamas is a terrorist organization, that it needs to be dismantled and destroyed, will not be a partner in the next government.
“And therefore I do not see an Arab party that accepts my principles.”
When asked how he believes he could form a government when recent polling shows both blocs unable to form a coalition without the Arab parties, he said: “I believe the majority we receive will be much larger than what the polls currently show.
“We will continue working until the election to bring the opposition bloc to 63-64 mandates, together with my partners in the bloc, [B’Yachad leader Naftali] Bennett, [Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor] Liberman, and [The Democrats leader Yair] Golan.
“I said that I do not rule out any Zionist party. I see as a partner anyone who meets the four principles I have set.”
Regarding Ofer Winter, who chairs the right-wing People of Israel party that recently emerged, which has backed Netanyahu, Eisenkot said that “there is a contradiction in his positions.
“In the end, he [Winter] chooses to perpetuate the rule of the person who was in power on Oct. 7.
“He says he will go with whoever passes a conscription law, yet he chooses to go with someone who promoted draft evasion. I don’t see him joining any coalition.”
Stances regarding the West Bank
Eisenkot also spoke on his stance regarding Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who leads the far-right Religious Zionist Party and has strongly pushed to expand West Bank settlements.
“I will tell you a secret: I have family in Judea and Samaria, in [the West Bank settlement] Yakir, and some of them vote for him [Smotrich]. I therefore do not personally disqualify him.
“But Smotrich expresses highly problematic positions. I cannot accept his support for a draft-evasion law. He also called for refusal to serve.
“I am also deeply concerned by Judea and Samaria. Four years ago, Netanyahu took the Civil Administration and handed it to Smotrich, and took the police and handed it to [National Security Minister Itamar] Ben-Gvir.
“He undermined the [IDF] Central Command commander’s ability to exercise sovereignty and responsibility.”
When asked what he would do to change the situation in the West Bank, especially amid the spike in Jewish settler violence in the area, Eisenkot said that after entering office he would immediately “reverse” the situation and change who was in charge.
“The Civil Administration would return to military coordination, and police activity in Judea and Samaria would again be coordinated by the military command,” he said.
“Administrative orders would be restored against those who riot and harm the settlement enterprise. First and foremost, they harm the State of Israel,” Eisenkot continued.
When asked if he would consider firing the head of the Mossad, Roman Gofman, and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) Director David Zini, who are both Netanyahu appointments, Eisenkot said that while the two were “both very good commanders,” they were “incorrect appointments.”
“Now they have been appointed to positions. From here, it [the matter] will be examined through their performance,” he said.
One prime minister: Eisenkot nixes the idea of a rotation government
Eisenkot also ruled out the possibility of a rotation government, in which coalition partners would alternate serving as prime minister.
“I see one prime minister, whom the people decide on and elect, and he puts forward a work plan for four years, and he is prime minister for four years,” he elaborated.
Eisenkot also said that after the elections, the leader of the largest party should be the candidate for prime minister.
He said he had held that position before his rapid rise in the polls, when he was polling at “six seats, and Bennett had 26.”
The Yashar party leader said he had told Bennett and Liberman, “Let’s establish a clear rule: The head of the largest party is the candidate for prime minister.
“I have not changed my mind. They are the ones who changed their minds,” he added.
Change and repair: What would Eisenkot do differently from Gantz?
Comparisons have been drawn between Eisenkot and his former political partner Gantz, another former military chief once seen as one of Netanyahu’s strongest rivals, who has since lost public support.
When asked what would make him different from Gantz, Eisenkot paused and said: “I feel a very deep sense of commitment.
“If I believed someone else could defeat Netanyahu today, I would say that I should not run.
“The personal price I paid through the death of my son, two nephews, and the broader pain throughout the country give me a deep sense of mission.
“I want to bring change and repair. I do not want to say that someone appeared to me in a dream, but my inner feeling is that I now have the ability to defeat Netanyahu, bring Israel to a place representing 70% of its residents, and forge an alliance of those who serve.
“There is a commitment and a mission here to change things and return the country to normality. I look at my children, grandchildren, friends, and young people. I am doing this out of deep inner conviction. I do not have an obsession with becoming prime minister.”
Foreign affairs strategy and policies
Regarding his policies and strategy for foreign relations and defense, Eisenkot said his outlook is that “Israel is today facing the greatest strategic complexity since the establishment of the state.
“Therefore, difficult decisions are required, not simple ones, both externally and internally.
“The thing that concerns me most among the external threats is Iran.... My concern is that their lesson to us will be this: They have 440 kilograms of enriched uranium. They will put in centrifuges, and they will race to 90% and shock the world with the production of a nuclear explosive device.”
When asked if Israel had been able to achieve its military objectives throughout the current government’s term, Eisenkot had a direct response.
“No, unfortunately,” he said.
Elaborating further, Eisenkot continued that only “one of the war objectives was achieved: returning the hostages.
“Netanyahu initially opposed including that objective, and I forced it upon him on the ninth day of the war,” he added.
Eisenkot also said that he would invest in US-Israel relations, which he said he saw as crucial.
“I saw it from [former US president Joe] Biden to [US President Donald] Trump. These are special relations that are a necessity for Israel.
“The fact that Netanyahu, ‘Captain America,’” he said jokingly, “is bringing Israel to the lowest point in relations with American society.”
Eisenkot also said that he has not been in touch with Netanyahu during his campaign and after the establishment of his party.
When asked if he was in contact with US officials, Eisenkot responded directly, “The answer is yes. I won’t elaborate beyond that.”
He also expressed support for Trump’s actions in brokering the deal that secured the release of some of the hostages.
“But the most important thing is the peace among us. And that, in my view, is the biggest challenge for the government.”
“Peace, from Egypt to Jordan, is not something that can be taken for granted. We need to strengthen it and cultivate it.”
Dwelling with others: Israel's international standing
Asked how he believes he could improve Israel’s international standing, Eisenkot said that his approach would be different from Netanyahu’s stance, which he argued has put Israel into isolation.
He criticized Netanyahu for saying in 2025 that Israel needs to become a “super-Sparta.”
“We do not want to be ‘a people that dwells alone,’” he said, quoting the Bible.
“We need to be a strong country. And the challenge here is to be a strong Jewish state, a model state,” he added.
“The first steps require national agreement. The next government will have to make very difficult decisions. The first is a universal service law. Everyone must serve: haredim and Arabs. Arabs would perform National Service, while Bedouin service in the IDF would be expanded significantly.”
Drafting haredim
Regarding the issue of drafting haredim into the military amid the IDF’s severe manpower crisis, Eisenkot said that in addition to passing legislation to enforce haredi conscription, he would end the existing arrangement under which rabbis can grant exemptions through a lawyer.
Eisenkot said he would increase benefits for reservists and soldiers and revoke any state incentives granted to those who evade service.
Eisenkot has also called for a more “realistic plan” for drafting haredim into the IDF, under which 3% of haredim would be eligible for exemptions from service. He noted that this would be similar to exemptions currently granted to outstanding musicians and athletes.
This approach has drawn criticism from other opposition party leaders in the bloc who have called for no exemptions.
“Today, an annual cohort is approximately 70,000 people, so 3% is about 2,200.... Israel can permit that.
“At the height of the War of Independence, David Ben-Gurion refused to end the studies of 400 exceptional [Torah] scholars, saying, ‘Under no circumstances. We are a Jewish state.’
“I believe in that. I am not religious, but I grew up in a traditional family and have profound respect for Judaism and tradition.”
Eisenkot also said he would require all Israeli children to study through the state education system, which teaches core curriculum subjects such as math and English.
“Whoever is not in state education – secular, religious, haredi, Arab – will not receive funding from the state,” he said.
He said the reform of the country’s education system would take four years and involve putting “a lot of money into the education system in order to improve it.”
Eisenkot’s distinction for voters
When asked what makes him different from the other parties in the opposition bloc, he said that though he has respect for them, “I think what is different is the trust that the citizens of the country place in me.”
“Trust in my motives for wanting to become prime minister, my leadership, my experience, my responsibility, my personal example, and what I communicate to people.
“I believe I can create greater solidarity than any other prospective leader of Israel and rally the broadest possible public,” he said.■

Palestinian Elections: Gaza & West Bank youth launch independent list in rejection of factional politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:05:00 UTC
22:05:00 KST

A group of 25 young civil society figures from Gaza and the West Bank have formed an independent electoral list to contest the Palestinian legislative elections scheduled for November 28 — the first legislative vote in two decades — positioning themselves explicitly outside the factional politics that have dominated Palestinian public life since the Oslo era.
The list, currently unnamed, brings together doctors, engineers, journalists, human rights workers, and civil society professionals, aged 24 to 45. Its organizers say they are building something they believe is largely absent from Palestinian electoral politics: a youth-led platform centered on people’s immediate needs rather than partisan affiliation or political ideology. Its members — six are women, two have disabilities, one is Christian — reflect the diversity, inclusion, and independence of which the list boasts.
The initiative is led by Fadi al-Sheikh Youssef, 39, a media activist and civil society figure who attempted something similar in 2021, when Palestinian Authority (PA) President Mahmoud Abbas called for legislative elections before postponing them weeks before polling day, citing Israel’s refusal to allow voting in occupied East Jerusalem. Al-Sheikh Youssef’s 2021 list — called Hulum, or “Dream” — was approved by the Palestinian Central Elections Commission and prepared to contest the vote before the postponement ended the effort.
Now, with elections set for November 28 and the nomination period due to open on September 26, he’s trying again. The context, however, has changed dramatically.
Palestinians are heading to the polls — if the elections proceed at all — after nearly three years of facing Israel’s most aggressive attack on their presence in decades, amid international accusations of ethnic cleansing and genocide, even from its staunchest allies. According to the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics, 64 percent of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza are under 30. Most have never voted. Al-Sheikh Youssef’s list is, in part, addressed to them.
“Today, five years after we attempted to break into the Palestinian political establishment, we are returning with an independent youth list,” al-Sheikh Youssef told Mondoweiss. “We see an even greater need today for an independent youth body that does not belong to any political ideology.”
A platform built around daily life
Rather than putting forward a broad political platform, al-Sheikh Youssef says, the group is developing practical proposals to address problems facing young Palestinians, particularly in Gaza, including unemployment, economic marginalization, access to the labor market, health care, humanitarian relief, and the enormous social and economic burdens accumulated through years of war.
“We leave politics to the political parties,” al-Sheikh Youssef said. The group says it wants to explore digital employment opportunities, expand access to remote work, and create pathways for young Palestinians to enter the online labor market. Healthcare, humanitarian relief, rebuilding basic infrastructure — sewage and water systems, health services, education alternatives for primary school children, and adequate temporary shelter while Gaza awaits reconstruction — are also among its priorities.
Al-Sheikh Youssef previously founded the digital media organization Pal Plus, which he says was targeted and ultimately shut down by Israel. Living through Gaza’s genocide, he says, has given list members a firsthand understanding of the problems they are trying to address.
But they deliberately stop short of articulating a comprehensive political vision.
“Some people with strong partisan affiliations recognize the need for an independent civil list outside the ideological framework of Gaza’s existing parties,”al-Sheikh Youssef said. “A list that speaks to their needs, not their dreams.”
‘Young people representing themselves’
Among the list’s members is 38-year-old Amira Hamdan, a cultural and community activist who has worked with several cultural organizations, including the Tamer Institute for Community Education, where she was involved in child protection projects.
Hamdan says the list’s defining feature is that it seeks to identify young people’s priorities and develop solutions through them. She sees it as an experiment in civil governance that draws on the different professional experiences of its members. She also acknowledges that no electoral list can operate entirely outside of Palestinian politics, but says this one begins from a different starting point.
“Unlike traditional Palestinian electoral lists, this initiative does not begin with sweeping political slogans over issues such as Jerusalem, the 1967 borders, or the peace process,” Hamdan explains. “Its initial focus is on youth empowerment and practical problems such as conditions in displacement shelters.”
One of the group’s biggest challenges, Hamdan says, is building awareness among young Palestinians themselves. Members are trying to reach them through civil society organizations and their professional networks.
“We are betting on the young people we have worked alongside in different professional settings to vote for themselves and for those who represent them,” Hamdan said.
She acknowledges that members may lack extensive political experience but says they bring years of community work and project implementation experience and will acquire political experience along the way.
Muhammad Najm, 36, who works with nongovernmental organizations and was also a candidate on the Hulum list in 2021, says the group’s priorities begin with the basic infrastructure and services that sustain daily life in Gaza — sewage and water systems, rebuilding health services, finding alternatives for education, particularly for children in primary school, and developing adequate temporary shelter while Gaza awaits reconstruction.
“One of the list’s goals, he says, is to avoid becoming consumed by Palestine’s political turmoil to the point that the individual, and the individual’s basic needs, disappear from view,” he said.
Can daily life be separated from politics?
The list’s insistence on separating its civil program from the broader Palestinian political struggle, however, presents a fundamental challenge.
Many of the problems its candidates want to address, like rebuilding Gaza’s infrastructure, restoring health and education systems, and ensuring freedom of movement in the West Bank, cannot be resolved entirely through civil or municipal policy alone. They are shaped by the Israeli occupation, Palestinian political divisions, and the broader question of who governs Gaza and the occupied Palestinian territories.
The electoral process itself faces similar constraints.
The Central Elections Commission says it is preparing simultaneously for voting in the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza. But it has also acknowledged significant political and logistical challenges, particularly Israeli restrictions on movement and the question of holding elections in Jerusalem and Gaza. In Gaza, the commission has reopened offices, trained staff, begun assessing possible polling centers, and held meetings with political factions and civil society groups as it prepares for the November vote.
Those obstacles mean that even a list determined to concentrate on people’s daily lives would enter a legislature operating within a political environment that directly shapes many of those same needs.
Al-Sheikh Youssef, however, says the group does not expect to dominate the Palestinian political system. For him, winning even a limited number of seats would constitute an achievement.
The list is currently financed by its members and individual supporters. Al-Sheikh Youssef is seeking support from organizations that run youth empowerment programs, though he says such support need not take the form of money, but logistical resources and communication tools to publicize both the list and its proposed programs.
The objective, he says, “is to ensure that young Palestinians have an independent voice inside the Palestinian Legislative Council, even if that voice occupies only a handful of seats.”

Hurricane Polo brings fears of heavy rain and landslides in Mexico
Heavy rains could cause life-threatening flooding and landslides on Mexico’s Pacific Coast, the US National Hurricane Center warned.
Hurricane Polo has sent heavy rain and strong waves across Mexico’s Pacific coast, while Tropical Storm Nolo is approaching Hawaii with the potential for catastrophic flooding.
Early on Thursday, the hurricane was swirling about 130 miles (209 kilometres) south-southwest of the Mexican city of Zihuatanejo. It was moving northwest at 7mph (11kph) and forecast to turn west-northwest later in the day, taking it further out to sea, before turning northwest on Saturday.
Polo was forecast to maintain Category 5 strength as it moves along Mexico’s coast over the next few days.
While the eye and the strongest winds were expected to remain at sea, the heavy rains could cause life-threatening flooding and landslides, warned the US National Hurricane Center in Miami.
A hurricane watch was issued for Hawaii county and disaster preparations are under way because Tropical Storm Nolo could hit the island on Friday or Saturday, warned the National Weather Service.
John Bravender, a weather service warning coordination meteorologist, said during a news conference on Wednesday afternoon that the tropical storm could develop into a major hurricane.
Hawaii County Mayor Kimo Alameda told residents in a video message that they should start preparing for the storm. He urged them to put together emergency kits with food, water and medications, as well as trim vegetation and clear drains.
“This is a very serious situation,” he said. “We do believe that the rain is going to come. It’s coming already.”
Governor Josh Green’s office said public schools and state and county offices across Hawaii’s Big Island will close on Thursday and Friday, while Maui County will shut them on Friday ahead of the threat of heavy rain, winds and flooding.

NIZHNY NOVGOROD, September 24. /TASS/. Russian vessels with a capacity exceeding 500 metric tons are being equipped with orbital constellations from the Gonets Satellite System company (a subsidiary of Roscosmos state corporation) to transmit location data for fishing vessels, said CEO of the company Andrey Manoylo.
As of January 1, 2026, the Russian fishing industry fully transitioned to using exclusively domestic orbital constellations.
"Since January of this year, <...> we have completely replaced the Inmarsat system on large-tonnage vessels over 500 metric tons. Currently, all large-tonnage vessels transmit and exchange information through the Gonets satellite system," the chief executive said at the Satcomrus-2026 exhibition.
According to an order of the Ministry of Agriculture, the use of UK Inmarsat satellite stations on vessels as technical monitoring tools was discontinued in Russia on January 1, 2026. Industry companies now use the Russian orbital constellations Gonets, Yamal, and Express to transmit vessel location data to the Federal Agency for Fisheries’ industry monitoring system. The new equipment regulation applies to vessels with a gross tonnage of more than 80 metric tons and a main engine power exceeding 55 kW.

Municipalities look to libraries to get kids reading
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:02:00 UTC
22:02:00 KST

Municipalities look to libraries to get kids reading
Estonian municipalities want to get kids reading more. One option may be for school and public libraries to team up more, making it easier for children to access books.
"The more they see books, the more they hold books in their hands and the more they see people reading books, the more likely they are to start reading themselves," said Narva Estonian State High School principal Irene Käosaar.
Reading, she added, also helps kids do better in school.
By law, libraries must be located in or near a school, but local governments can decide how exactly to organize library services. In Jõgeva, the local school and public libraries were merged seven years ago.
"They'll see a good place to study, meet up and enjoy culture," said Agne Vaalmäe, cultural adviser for the Association of Estonian Cities and Municipalities (ELVL). "And maybe they'll even start coming here on their own."
Just outside Tallinn, Rae Municipality has seen firsthand that location matters: its school and public library have operated together for about 20 years, making the library more accessible to young readers.
"If our library were still in the building where it was before, about a kilometer further away from the school, the number [of visitors] would be much, much smaller," said Rae Municipal Library director Ülle Siska.
"Kids today will only make a separate trip to the library when they really need to," she explained. "But when it's in the school building, it's all right there for them — and for the teachers too."
A trustworthy place
Experts caution, however, that combining libraries should not mean removing the librarian, as shelves of books alone likely won't actually get kids reading.
In an age of information overload and spreading artificial intelligence (AI), libraries are also taking on a bigger role as a trustworthy source of information and guidance.
"Finding reliable information is getting increasingly difficult," said Estonian Librarians' Association (ERÜ) board chair Kristi Veeber. "People need to be taught that the library is a trustworthy place they can turn to for help."
Updates to the Public Libraries Act are expected to provide a clearer framework for cooperation between school and public libraries in the near future.

Meeting of G7 Development Ministers in New York Development G7 Statement On : September 23rd 2026 The Minister Delegate for Francophonie, International Partnerships, and French Nationals Abroad, Ms. Eléonore Caroit, chaired a meeting of G7 Development Ministers on September 23, 2026, in New York, on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly. France, as G7 Presidency, chose to involve major emerging economies and regional partners in the work towards a more cohesive G7. The representatives from India, Brazil, the Republic of Korea and Egypt, as well as representatives from Nepal, the African Development Bank, the World Bank Group, and the United Nations Development Program, participated in the discussions. The meeting’s agenda focused on promoting the new approach based on mutually beneficial partnerships into the international development system, building on the work carried out at the Evian Summit (June 15-17, 2026), and also addressed the situation in Nepal. This meeting aimed to deepen the implementation of a renewed approach designed to move beyond the traditional development policies to achieve greater effectiveness and efficiency. The Ministers advocated for a more strategic use of official development assistance where it is most needed to support the most vulnerable countries, for promoting an ambitious reform agenda to streamline the international development architecture, as well as for supporting the sovereignty and resilience of partner countries. The discussions also addressed the mobilization of domestic public resources and of private capital in favour of development. They also addressed supporting concrete initiatives to mobilize private capital in partner countries, particularly in Africa. Following the Africa Forward Summit (May 11-12, 2026), several G7 members, including France, reaffirmed their support for the ATIDI (African Trade & Investment Development Insurance) initiative, which provides (political or credit) risks insurances through a guarantee mechanism. Regarding Nepal, following the devastating floods and landslides that occurred at the end of August, G7 Development Ministers reiterated their solidarity with the Nepalese people. They presented the response of G7 members to the urgent needs of the affected populations. Together, G7 members contribute a total of 69,4 M USD. The Ministers also supported the efforts of the World Bank, the Asian development Bank and the UNDP to prepare for the reconstruction of the affected areas. The Ministers reaffirmed their commitment to promoting cooperation in reconstruction efforts and to strengthening the resilience of countries vulnerable to disasters. They emphasized the importance of disaster risk reduction to strengthen the resilience of the most vulnerable countries, including through early warning systems for natural disasters and Earth observation capabilities, and highlighted the role of the CREWS (Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems) initiative. The G7 Development Ministers and partner countries will meet on October 16th in Bangkok, on the margins of the World Bank and International Monetary Fund's annual meetings, to discuss the progress of these initiatives.

Breadcrumb
Could Morocco be on the cusp of getting its first female prime minister?
Morocco could be on the verge of appointing its first female prime minister after Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri's party emerged victorious in parliamentary elections, putting the prominent politician among the leading contenders to head the next government.
The Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) won 97 seats in Wednesday’s election, according to preliminary results announced by the interior ministry, making it the largest party in Morocco's 395-seat House of Representatives.
It finished ahead of its outgoing coalition partners, the National Rally of Independents (RNI), which secured 66 seats, and the Istiqlal Party with 65.
The result has turned attention to Mansouri, one of Morocco’s most prominent female politicians and a leading figure in PAM.
If King Mohammed VI appoints her to lead the next government, the 50-year-old would become the first woman to serve as Morocco's prime minister and only the second woman to head a government in the Arab world, after Tunisia's Najla Bouden.
Could Mansouri become prime minister?
Under Article 47 of Morocco's constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the political party that comes first in elections to the House of Representatives.
That means the next prime minister should come from PAM, but it does not automatically mean the job goes to the party’s leader.
Mansouri is among the names being discussed for the post, alongside other senior PAM figures.
One potential rival is Fouzi Lekjaa, Morocco’s budget minister and president of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation, who joined PAM ahead of the election.
Another name floated in Moroccan media is Mohamed Mehdi Bensaid, who served as youth, culture and communications minister in the outgoing government.
The decision ultimately rests with King Mohammed VI.
PAM will also have to negotiate a coalition after falling well short of the 198 seats needed for an outright parliamentary majority.
Its outgoing coalition partners could provide the numbers. PAM, the RNI and Istiqlal together secured 228 seats according to the preliminary results, although the shape of the next governing coalition has yet to be determined.
Who is Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri?
Born in Marrakech in 1976, Mansouri trained as a lawyer before entering politics following PAM's establishment in 2008.
She rose to national prominence the following year when she became mayor of Marrakech, the first woman to hold the position.
Mansouri returned to the mayoralty following the 2021 elections and was appointed minister of national territorial planning, urban planning, housing and city policy in the government of outgoing Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
She further strengthened her position within PAM in 2024 when she took a leading role in the party's collective leadership.
Her party's victory has now placed her within reach of Morocco’s most senior government post.
Mansouri has sought to present herself as a politician whose career has been built through party politics and local government rather than her gender.
She has also rejected descriptions of herself as an "iron woman", previously describing herself instead as a “free activist”.
What happened in Morocco’s election?
PAM emerged as the largest party with 97 seats, gaining 10 compared with the previous parliament.
The RNI, which led the outgoing government, fell to 66 seats, while Istiqlal secured 65.
The Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) staged one of the election's biggest comebacks, winning 54 seats after securing just 13 in the 2021 election.
The PJD had led Morocco’s government for a decade before suffering a dramatic electoral collapse five years ago.
Its campaign this year included strong opposition to Morocco’s deepening ties with Israel, an issue that has generated considerable public anger since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza.
Morocco normalised relations with Israel in 2020 as part of the US-brokered Abraham Accords, when the PJD itself was leading the government.
The election also took place against a backdrop of economic and social discontent, including high youth unemployment and the aftermath of Gen Z-led protests.
Turnout stood at just 38 percent, the lowest level recorded in a Moroccan parliamentary election since 2007.

Parents’ genetic traits might indirectly influence a child’s risk for anxiety and depression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:00:27 UTC
22:00:27 KST

A child’s risk of developing anxiety and depression is influenced not only by the genes they inherit, but also by the genetic traits their parents possess. A large study published in Nature Mental Health found that a mother’s genetic likelihood for smoking and a father’s genetic propensity for general well-being help predict a child’s mental health outcomes over time. These results illustrate how a parent’s DNA can shape a child’s environment, creating indirect genetic pathways that affect youth emotional development.
Depression and anxiety are categorized as internalizing problems, which involve directing distress inward. These conditions often take root during childhood and adolescence. Researchers wanted to understand exactly how much of a child’s mental health risk comes from their own biology versus the environment their parents create. Disentangling these two factors is exceptionally difficult because biological parents provide both the home environment and the DNA of their offspring.
Scientists refer to the influence of a parent’s genes on a child’s environment as an indirect genetic effect, or genetic nurture. For instance, if a parent has a high genetic likelihood for depression, that biological trait might influence their parenting style or the emotional stability of the household. The child might then develop anxiety or depression as a reaction to that environment, rather than purely because they inherited the specific genes for those conditions.
Researchers led by Razieh Chegeni, a psychologist at the University of Oslo in Norway, conducted the research to separate these tangled pathways. By looking at a broad spectrum of genetic scores across whole families, the team sought to map how different genetic traits in parents and children combine to influence mental health risk. They were specifically interested in seeing how these patterns change as children grow from middle childhood into adolescence.
To investigate this, the researchers analyzed data from 9,314 parent and child trios, classifying it as a large study. The participants were part of the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study. The team utilized 90 polygenic scores to assess the genetic propensities of the mothers, fathers, and children. A polygenic score is a tool that estimates a person’s genetic likelihood for a specific trait based on thousands of tiny variations across their DNA.
The researchers calculated polygenic scores for a variety of traits beyond just mental health. These included body mass index, intelligence, attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), smoking habits, and cognitive skills. They then used an advanced statistical technique to sort through these highly correlated variables. This allowed them to identify which combinations of genetic scores best predicted the child’s symptoms of depression and anxiety at age 8 and again at age 14.
When looking at depression at age 8, parental genetics played a heavy role. A mother’s genetic likelihood for having multiple sexual partners or experiencing depression was linked to higher depressive symptoms in the child. The researchers note that these maternal genetic traits might act as proxies for a more unpredictable home environment or reduced emotional availability, which can negatively affect a young child.
As the children reached age 14, their own genetic traits became more influential in shaping their mental health. The child’s own polygenic scores for cognitive skills and ADHD emerged as prominent risk factors for depression in adolescence. A high genetic liability for ADHD often involves challenges with emotional regulation and impulse control, which can naturally elevate the risk of developing depressive symptoms as teenagers navigate complex social environments.
Throughout both developmental stages, a father’s genetic likelihood for general well-being acted as a consistent protective factor against depression. A father with a genetic disposition toward positive psychological traits may contribute to a more resilient and supportive family environment. Unsurprisingly, the child’s own genetic propensity for well-being also insulated them against depressive symptoms at both age 8 and age 14.
For anxiety, the predictive patterns looked slightly different. The mother’s genetic likelihood for smoking cigarettes was the strongest indirect risk factor for the child’s anxiety at both assessed ages. The researchers suggest this might reflect how genetic tendencies toward stress regulation difficulties in mothers can create a sustained environmental vulnerability for the child.
The child’s own polygenic score for well-being provided the strongest protective effect against anxiety across both time points. In contrast to its effect on depression, a child’s genetic liability for ADHD was associated with protection against anxiety. The researchers explain that this aligns with previous studies showing that temperaments with high novelty-seeking and low harm-avoidance are often linked to lower anxiety levels.
The study also examined how the genetic traits of family members might interact with one another. They found that shared genetic likelihoods between both parents for certain cognitive and non-cognitive skills were associated with higher depressive symptoms in their offspring. This highlights how shared traits between partners might compound to create specific family dynamics that influence a child’s emotional health.
Despite the large study size, the total variance in mental health symptoms explained by the polygenic scores was small. The models explained a maximum of 2.7 percent of the variance in depression and 1.2 percent of the variance in anxiety. This small explanatory power means that current polygenic scores are scientific tools for understanding broad population trends, rather than practical clinical tests for predicting a specific person’s future mental health.
The genetic data originated primarily from people of European descent in Norway. Broadening this research across different global populations and ancestries is required to see if these developmental patterns apply to humans universally. Additionally, the genetic scores used for the children were calculated based on adult data, which might not perfectly match how those genetic pathways express themselves during the earlier stages of childhood.
Finally, the researchers note that these associations are observational. The correlations do not confirm that the genetic factors directly cause the specific mental health outcomes, as other unmeasured environmental variables could be at play. Future research will need to incorporate direct observations of parenting styles alongside genetic data to build a more complete picture of how nature and nurture shape youth mental health.
The study, “Direct and indirect parental genetic effects on offspring susceptibility to internalizing problems across development,” was authored by Razieh Chegeni, Ragnhild Bang Nes, Rosa Cheesman, Ziada Ayorech, Eivind Ystrøm, and Espen Røysamb.

‘You can’t just bet everything on exports’: as its gas runs out, is Bolivia doomed to repeat history?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:00:18 UTC
22:00:18 KST

Once hailed as the “energy heart of South America”, Bolivia’s economy was buoyed up by a fossil gas boom from 2006 to 2014. At its height, then-president Evo Morales commissioned a gleaming presidential skyscraper and installed the world’s longest urban cable car network in La Paz, the seat of government.
Flush with cash, the country grew its GDP, expanded social programmes and halved poverty rates. But then commodity prices plummeted and gas reserves started to dry up, bringing Bolivia’s “economic miracle” crashing down. Inflation – once the region’s lowest – has soared.
In the markets of La Paz, some imported staples have now doubled in price. “Because prices are so high, people are buying less and switching to the cheapest options,” says Felipa Huanca, who sells vegetables at the city’s bustling Rodríguez market. “Wages just aren’t keeping up.”
Bolivia’s decades-long reliance on gas is driving the crisis. A failure to discover new fields, coupled with costly subsidies and capital flight, has pushed the economy into a tailspin. Though more sustainable alternatives exist, powerful extractive lobbies continue to impede progress towards a more diversified and sustainable model.
The roots of the crisis trace back to 2006, when Morales took control of Bolivia’s hydrocarbons sector and renegotiated contracts with foreign companies. The move coincided with high global fuel prices and brought an economic windfall to one of the poorest nations in the Americas.
But rather than investing in industrialisation or developing value-added exports, successive governments funnelled the profits into heavy state spending, costly fuel subsidies and maintaining a fixed currency exchange rate pegged to the US dollar.
“We failed to take advantage of a historic opportunity that brought in immense revenue,” says Luis Fernando Romero, the former head of an association of economists in southern Bolivia.
The country fell into a classic rentier state model – common for hydrocarbon-rich nations – where state revenues depend on exporting raw natural resources rather than building domestic industries.
“If you compare other petrol states like Qatar and Norway, it’s not the fact of having a large and state-owned hydrocarbon industry that determines your fate,” says Andrés Arauz, a former chief operating officer of the Central Bank of Ecuador and a senior research fellow at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, a thinktank. “It’s whether the private sector development, diversification, domestic market and poverty alleviation efforts are accompanying that.”
In Bolivia, those parallel investments never materialised.
Experts say sustained prosperity would have required investment in core economic pillars: steel and aluminium plants, agriculture, education and healthcare. Diversifying revenue away from a single commodity was equally essential.
While some economists blame hydrocarbon nationalisation for Bolivia’s decline, Arauz notes that the failure to regulate offshore capital is often ignored. “It’s not that poor people have a little bit more money,” he says, referencing the macroeconomic stability that state hydrocarbon control brought. “The bigger factor is that rich people are taking their money out and that there is no response from the domestic elites in establishing an industrial economy.”
Bolivian elites hold an estimated $10bn (£7.4bn) offshore – an eighth of the country’s GDP – which Arauz says is an underestimate.
After the 2014 commodity crash, Bolivia’s foreign reserves dwindled due to heavy fuel subsidies and its dollar peg, which wasn’t ended until earlier this year. Production fell as gas reserves went unexploited, but the government sustained subsidies and the peg, printing money to cover deficits.
The boliviano’s exchange-rate fix boosted cheap imports and consumer power but hurt local industry by fostering import reliance. Carlos Arze, a Cedla hydrocarbons expert, notes that cheap imports eroded productive sectors, requiring protection from Asian competition. Cheap dollars also grew the informal labour sector to 84% in 2024 – Latin America’s highest.
Dollar shortages and a parallel exchange rate still discourage industry. “Speculating on the exchange rate can be more profitable than legitimate business,” says Arauz.
Foreign investors remain wary, says Romero, due to Bolivia’s complexity, technological hurdles, and dollar shortages. A $1.9bn IMF loan in July mostly services debt or adds reserves, not economic diversification.
In December, the government cut fuel subsidies with little support for the vulnerable. After austerity and agroindustry-favouring land reforms, protesters called for President Rodrigo Paz’s resignation. The government then announced that the state hydrocarbons firm will now focus on exploration, extraction, and refining.
As gasfields run dry – with estimates that Bolivia will become a net fossil gas importer by about 2030 – the growing goldmining and agroindustry sectors are becoming the country’s next frontiers in an export-oriented rentier model. “It’s a repeating story of natural resource dependence,” says Arze, the hydrocarbons expert.
Yet in Bolivia’s Amazonian lowlands, Indigenous and peasant communities have long practised an alternative economic model. For generations, they have gathered wild fruits and nuts such as açaí, cacao and Brazil nuts. Known as non-timber forest products, these plants thrive naturally without clearcutting, forming the foundation of sustainable “bioeconomies” that generate income while leaving forests intact.
Unlike industrial soya plantations or environmentally destructive gold dredging, these harvests directly benefit thousands of people in local communities. “Each dollar you invest benefits a lot of different people,” says Vincent Vos, a biologist who has lived and worked in the Bolivian Amazon since 2002.
Bolivia exported £145m worth of Brazil nuts in 2024, double the value of its timber sector. In 2025, gold exports were reportedly worth £890m, though far more was trafficked illegally.
While these alternative economies “are still not near what you get from mining or soya”, says Vos, combining sustainable forest harvesting with tourism and carbon sequestration programmes could help them grow. Also key is long-term sustainability. “You can harvest soya for about 10 years and then your land is destroyed,” he says. “But when you harvest Brazil nuts, you can do it until eternity.”
Yet scaling these green alternatives faces major political barriers. Mining and agroindustrial lobbies hold increasing power over a government that has sidelined environmental policy. “Cacao and açaí don’t have any power whatsoever compared to that,” Vos says.
Arauz also cautions against dependence on exporting yet another commodity. “To just continue exporting raw materials – whether they are more niche-based or even fair trade-based – is not enough to transform a national economy,” he says. “You can’t just bet everything on export markets without consciously and proactively transforming domestic ones.”
For Rosmery Vega, another vendor at La Paz’s Rodríguez market, Bolivia’s economic decline is simple. “Our politicians are to blame – they’ve failed to manage this country,” she says. “They’re financially comfortable, but it’s us ordinary people who suffer.”

This year’s El Niño just broke a record months before it’s expected to peak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Warnings of an El Niño unlike any other are starting to become reality.
For months, scientists have cautioned that the natural climate pattern could grow into a record-breaking beast, releasing extraordinary amounts of heat from the ocean and fueling droughts, floods, heat waves and severe storms. Now, a traditional strength measurement of El Niño, called the Oceanic Niño Index, indicates that the pattern has reached an intensity unseen in recorded history.
On September 21, the daily sea surface temperature in the region where El Niño develops — the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean — reached 3.08 degrees Celsius warmer than the 1991 to 2020 average. That’s more extreme than any other El Niño ever recorded.
Hotter water
Since El Niño emerged in June, the daily average sea surface temperature has climbed extraordinarily high in the heart of the Pacific Ocean region where El Niño develops. On September 21, it reached 3.08 degrees Celsius above both the 1991 to 2020 average (coarse dashed line) and the 1982 to 2010 average (fine dashed line). Prior to this month, the most extreme anomaly on record was 3.02 degrees Celsius, set by an El Niño in November 2015.
“It has been a remarkable event,” says Nathaniel Johnson, a climate scientist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory in Princeton, N.J. What’s more, the El Niño will probably grow even stronger, Johnson says. “We’re probably going to reach our peak within the next few months.”
The oceanic heat released by the phenomenon could contribute to an increase in global land temperatures of about 1.2 degrees Celsius over the coming months, leading to over 450,000 additional heat-related deaths by February 2027, researchers from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago report.
NOAA has yet to declare this event the strongest on record. It uses a rolling three-month-average anomaly, rather than the daily anomaly, in calculations of an El Niño’s strength. And it’s shifted to a new method for measuring El Niño strength, called the Relative Oceanic Niño index, which better represents the phenomenon’s ability to sway weather globally. By that measurement, the current El Niño has yet to surpass the strength of the one in 1997 and 1998.
But that record is on track to be broken soon, the latest seasonal forecast from NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center suggests. To understand what’s driving this historic El Niño and its potential impact, Science News spoke with Johnson, who is part of the team that produces the forecasts, and Nathan Lenssen, a climate scientist at the National Center of Atmospheric Research in Boulder, Colo. The conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
SN: How much of this El Niño’s strength has been fueled by human-caused climate change?
Johnson: It’s really an unanswered question. If we look at the historical record, we have been seeing more rapid swings between El Niño and La Niña [which is the other extreme phase of the El Niño Southern Oscillation that generally has the opposite effect on weather patterns]. There’s some evidence from simulations that increasing greenhouse gas emissions leads to more of those extreme swings. But there’s not yet a scientific consensus on how climate change is impacting El Niño, especially an extreme El Niño like this one.
Lenssen: It’s a matter of debate how much we can directly attribute to climate change. But due to the warming of the planet, there is more energy in the oceans now, and El Niños are when the ocean releases some of that heat into the atmosphere.
SN: What are the most predictable and unpredictable impacts of this El Niño?
Johnson: We see a lot of the most predictable impacts in the tropical regions, as that’s where El Niño itself develops. We’ve already seen this suppressed Atlantic hurricane season and enhanced Pacific hurricane season, and we’ve also seen droughts in Central America. We also tend to see droughts over northern South America and the Amazon, and a weakening of the Indian monsoon.
As we get into late fall, we typically see more impacts a little farther from the equator. For instance, over the southern part of the United States we tend to see rainier conditions, whereas it’s typically drier than normal over the Pacific Northwest and warmer than average over the northern United States and Canada.
Lenssen: An important detail is that just because this El Niño is so powerful, that doesn’t necessarily mean we’re more confident about these impacts. The global warming of the oceans has made some of the historical mid-latitude impacts less likely, so there’s a kind of twist there. For example, the El Niño in 2023 and 2024 didn’t lead to as much wet weather in California as expected, and some research has shown that was due to other warming ocean patterns. That clouds the picture a little.
SN: How long could this El Niño last?
Johnson: El Niños typically last just a year, so we’ll probably see it weaken after winter and be over by spring or early summer. But when we have big El Niño like this, we’re more likely to see a shift in the following year to La Niña [which can also have global impacts on weather]. So that’s definitely something we’ll be keeping our eye on.
Lenssen: It’s possible that this event could be followed by a double La Niña, which is when we get back-to-back events separated by a brief period of neutral conditions. That happened in 2016 and 2017, after the strong El Niño of 2014 and 2015.
SN: Aside from its strength, what sets this event apart from others in the past?
Johnson: We’ve seen such a dramatic change in the equatorial Pacific Ocean over the course of the year. The transition has been very rapid, from a La Niña last winter to a very strong El Niño in less than a year. That might be the fastest transition that we’ve seen.
SN: Is there any sort of silver lining here?
Lenssen: Though more work is needed to understand this, some research suggests that future El Niños may actually become more predictable as the world continues to warm. That could potentially give us months of additional lead time to prepare for the impacts, which would be great.

Zelensky: No 'Anchorage agreements' in negotiations

Zelensky appears on cocaine seized in Russia (VIDEO)
Unknown

Zelensky appears on cocaine seized in Russia (VIDEO)
Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) has seized 311 kg of cocaine in Moscow Region, with some of the haul featuring images of Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky. One suspect has been detained on suspicion of helping organize a supply route from Latin America to the EU.
The FSB said its officers caught the suspect while he was transporting the drugs. In a video shared by the agency, the man’s car could be seen loaded with about a dozen heavy duty bags filled with cocaine bricks.
During the examination of the packages, about nine of the bricks were revealed to have a photo of Zelensky with dollar signs for eyes. The agency has not offered any explanations as to why the Ukrainian leader’s photograph appeared on the cocaine packages.
However, Zelensky’s image has increasingly been associated with cocaine use. His former press secretary Yulia Mendel recently confirmed to Tucker Carlson that the Ukrainian leader’s drug use is “an open secret” in Kiev. Russian officials have also long accused Zelensky and other Ukrainian elites of being addicts.
The detained man is an unemployed Russian citizen born in 2001, according to the FSB. It described him as an active member of an organized group that arranged large drug sales through the dark web without meeting buyers in person.
The agency said the group’s international supply route brought cocaine from Latin America through Russia for eventual sale in EU countries.
Investigators have opened a criminal case against the suspect on charges of attempted large-scale drug trafficking. A court has ordered him held in custody while the investigation continues, the FSB said.
In commentary shared by the agency, Aleksandr Yevtushenko, a dean at Kuban State University, said international drug traffickers have increasingly used Russia as a transit route. He described cocaine arriving from Latin America by sea in containers carrying goods such as bananas and fish before being moved overland toward the EU.
The latest bust follows several major cocaine seizures in Russia in recent years. In July, the FSB said officers found more than half a ton concealed inside frozen tuna imported from Ecuador. Before that, in September 2025, the agency also announced the discovery of a record 1.5 tons of the narcotic hidden in a cargo of bananas at a St. Petersburg port.
Тhe UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) warned in June that global cocaine use has continued to soar in recent years, outpacing all other narcotics. Its illegal production skyrocketed to a record 4,000 tons in 2024, more than four times the level recorded a decade earlier.

Swiss firm Kühne+Nagel to shed light on Nazi past

Swiss firm Kühne+Nagel to shed light on Nazi past
Kühne+Nagel, a Swiss logistics firm with German roots, intends to shed full light on its activities during the Second World War, particularly its links with the Nazis.
The Schwyz-based company has confirmed statements to this effect made by its chair, Jörg Wolle.
“There is no doubt that we need to address this issue. I believe this would be in keeping with Kühne’s wishes,” Wolle told the German-language magazine Bilanz. The details of this project and start date have yet to be determined.
The board of directors will consider the matter in the near future, a spokesperson told the AWP business news agency.
More
With no heirs, Kühne’s Swiss foundation gets $49 billion fortune
The focus is expected to be on the company’s role in the expropriation of property belonging to Jews. Adolf Maass, a Jewish partner at Kühne+Nagel, was forced to relinquish his 45% stake in the company in 1933.
Maass was subsequently deported by the Nazi regime to the Auschwitz concentration camp, from which he never returned.
During this period, Kühne+Nagel is also said to have been involved in the transport of movable property confiscated from Jews who were fleeing or had been deported. These activities are said to have been carried out under the direction of Alfred Kühne, the father of Klaus-Michael Kühne, the long-standing majority shareholder who recently passed away.
During his lifetime, Klaus-Michael Kühne had opposed an in-depth historical investigation into the company’s history during the Nazi era. According to Bilanz, he was particularly unwilling to fund an expert report that would have taken a critical look at his father’s role.
Founded by August Kühne and Friedrich Nagel in 1890 in Bremen, in the German state of Lower Saxony, the company began by transporting coffee, cocoa, wool, cotton and cereals. It now describes itself as a “global logistics player”.
Kühne+Nagel’s presence in Switzerland dates back to 1975, when the group opened a branch in the canton Schwyz municipality of Pfäffikon. In 1992, the head office was moved to Schindellegi, in the same canton. It has remained there ever since.

Tunisia fuel strike highlights growing economic and political anger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:54:47 UTC
21:54:47 KST

Tunisia fuel strike highlights growing economic and political anger
A 48-hour strike by fuel transport workers in Tunis exacerbates public frustration amid worsening public services and a deepening economic crisis.
Fuel transport workers in Tunis have launched a 48-hour strike to demand better working conditions, wage increases, the disbursement of previously agreed allowances from 2019 and the settlement of social security dues.
Al Jazeera correspondent Saifeddine Bouallegue reported that the strike, organised by the General Federation of Oil and Chemicals and lasting until Thursday, prompted citizens to rush to petrol stations, threatening widespread paralysis in a country that relies almost entirely on trucks for fuel distribution. Khaled Bettin, general manager of the national oil distributor Agil, confirmed that fuel remains available but urged a swift resolution to the strike to avoid further disruptions.
Worsening public services
The union action coincides with mounting public anger across Tunisia over recurrent electricity and water outages, rising prices and medicine shortages. More than five years after President Kais Saied suspended parliament and began ruling by decree, old grievances are resurfacing as the space for civil society and political dissent narrows significantly.
Experts suggested the fuel strike is a symptom of a much broader macroeconomic crisis, characterised by inflation, eroded purchasing power and the state’s inability to secure external funding.
Kholoud Toumi, a Tunisian economist, told Al Jazeera that the current situation is the result of overlapping internal and external pressures.
“The global economy suffers from an economic crisis and fluctuations in oil and energy prices globally, and this reflects directly on the import bill as well as the economic needs for hard currency,” Toumi told Al Jazeera. “Tunisia suffers from a crisis in providing hard currency, and this reflects on the external balance.”
Toumi warned of the severe consequences of the transport stoppage.
“This strike came for its main reason, which is the decline in purchasing power and the rise in inflation,” Toumi noted. “The fuel sector is considered one of the sensitive sectors, so a two-day strike will have disastrous results on the Tunisian economy. Any disruption in transport, production and supply raises the cost of activity.”
She also noted that the government’s failure to secure foreign funds has forced a reliance on domestic borrowing, which has negatively impacted investment and consumption.
Deep structural reforms
The broader economic crisis has reignited debates over reforms that international financial institutions have pushed. Toumi described those reforms as a “medical prescription” the International Monetary Fund had issued but Tunisia’s government had failed to implement so far. The economist said the primary obstacle was opposition from the country’s main trade union, the Tunisian General Labour Union, better known by its French acronym, UGTT. The General Federation of Oil and Chemicals, which is leading the transport strike, is affiliated with the UGTT.
However, some analysts framed the current crisis as a legacy of long-term mismanagement and ongoing union disputes rather than recent policy failures.
Souhaib al-Mazriqi, a political analyst, told Al Jazeera that the fuel strike stems directly from a conflict between the labour union and the employers union.
“The labour union accuses the employers union of reneging on the demands and agreements that were made in 2019,” al-Mazriqi said. “The situation, which we can term as economically and socially constrained, was the result of successive government policies.”
Demands for accountability
Other observers rejected blaming the previous decade for the current public service collapse, pointing directly to the current administration’s monopolisation of power.
Ahmed al-Ghiloufi, a political analyst, told Al Jazeera that the government must bear full responsibility for the mounting public anger and lack of transparency.
“The fuel sector is the tip of the iceberg of a general and comprehensive crisis,” al-Ghiloufi said, citing statistics from the Tunisian Forum for Economic and Social Rights showing that Tunisia in 2026 has witnessed the most protests in a decade. “Those who want to escape responsibility by throwing the ball to previous decades are running away from their responsibility. There is one ruler who rules the country, and he must bear the responsibility.”
Al-Ghiloufi also questioned the economic data released by the government and its crackdown on the political opposition.
“If we rely on what the government says, I say that governments of this type never give you the correct numbers,” he said. “We live in a closed system that has no transparency and no initiative.”
“The major issue is that the current regime does not allow dialogue and considers itself an absolute and sole delegate over the future and fate of this people and does not accept any partnership,” al-Ghiloufi concluded.

Milan exhibition explores the enduring bond between Salvador Dalí and fashion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:54:09 UTC
21:54:09 KST

A new exhibition at Milan’s Palazzo Reale explores the Dalí’s love affair with fashion, from his collaborations with Elsa Schiaparelli in the 1930s to the designers still borrowing from his surreal visual world today.
Italy’s fashion capital is celebrating the enduring and surprisingly underexplored relationship between Salvador Dalí and fashion with a major new exhibition.
Featuring more than 200 objects, the show at Milan’s Palazzo Reale brings together artworks, garments, photographs and archival material, to explore how the weird and wonderful Spanish artist drew inspiration from fashion and how generations of designers have drawn inspiration from the master of Surrealism.
“The relationship with Dalí and fashion goes right through his work. When you start looking at his work again, it's incredible. You sort of see it everywhere,” says Judith Clark, one of the exhibition’s curators.
"You see it in its kind of fashion's transformational power that, of course, he was so interested in, the art of transformation, the art of shock, the art of disguise, and it goes on, and it goes on and you find that the words associated with his work can be applied to fashion,” she adds.
Dalí’s relationship with fashion dates back to the 1930s, when he collaborated with designers including Elsa Schiaparelli.
“Fashion draws inspiration from Dalí, and it still does today, and this is a particularly interesting aspect highlighted in the exhibition. Yet Dalí himself, by the mid-1930s, was working alongside renowned fashion designers like Elsa Schiaparelli and inevitably drew inspiration from fashion,” says exhibition curator Laura Bartolomé.
One such example of this collaboration is Schiaparelli's famous shoe hat which was inspired by an image of Dalí with a woman's shoe balanced on his head. Dalí then sketched the idea for Schiaparelli, who transformed it into an actual high-heeled shoe-shaped hat.
“His paintings and artworks became fashion, but the reverse was also true: fashion found its way into his paintings and the Surrealist objects of the era,” explains Clark.
The exhibition explores this exchange through Dalí’s fascination with mannequins, clothing and the human body, alongside creations by contemporary designers including Daniel Roseberry for Schiaparelli, and Maria Grazia Chiuri and Jonathan Anderson for Dior.
The exhibition does not follow a chronological sequence. It takes visitors on a broader journey, bringing artworks and garments into dialogue and revealing the connections between Dalí’s visual universe and fashion, and vice versa.
“On display are Daniel Roseberry’s most recent creations for Schiaparelli, as well as those by Maria Grazia Chiuri and Jonathan Anderson for Dior,” Bartolomé says.
“This was a challenge, but also a unique opportunity to link Dalí not only to the most renowned names in 20th-century fashion history but also to his enduring influence on the creative directors and designers of such celebrated fashion houses today,” she concludes.
“Dalí and Fashion” runs at Milan’s Palazzo Reale until 31 January 2027.

Ukraine has changed the rules for electricity disconnections over unpaid bills: what consumers will no longer have to pay for
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:51:50 EEST
21:51:50 KST

Ukraine has changed the rules for electricity disconnections over unpaid bills: what consumers will no longer have to pay for
Kyiv • UNN
Consumers will not have to pay for disconnection if the debt is below half the subsistence minimum or if the procedure was violated. The new prices will take effect on October 1, 2026.
The National Energy and Utilities Regulatory Commission has updated the Rules of the Retail Electricity Market. The changes are aimed at strengthening the protection of consumers’ rights during the termination and restoration of electricity supply. This was reported by the NEURC, according to UNN.
Details
In particular, household consumers will not have to reimburse the costs of disconnection and reconnection if, at the time the warning was served, their electricity debt amounted to less than half of the subsistence minimum for able-bodied persons.
This guarantee also applies in cases where, after the disconnection, the operator clarifies the data based on the meter’s actual readings and it turns out that the real debt was below the established threshold. In that case, all costs will be borne by the system operator
In addition, consumers will not have to pay for these services if they were disconnected in violation of the established procedure.
The regulator has also introduced uniform approaches to pricing. Where technically possible, operators are required to choose the least complicated and cheapest method of carrying out the work, while the cost of services may not exceed the maximum amount calculated under the new rules. Companies must publish the relevant lists and prices on their own websites.
The disconnection procedure will become more transparent: after the work is completed, specialists will be required to draw up an act recording the time and method of disconnection, the EIC code, and the meter readings. One copy must be left with the consumer or sent within three business days if the consumer was not at home.
At the same time, the time limits for restoring power have been clarified: after the violations are remedied, electricity must be restored within three business days in cities and five business days in villages.
The resolution enters into force on the day following its official publication on the NEURC website, while the new mechanism for determining the cost of services will take effect on October 1, 2026.

Highways agency Rijkswaterstaat has imposed a one-way system on the IJssel river in the east of the country because of falling river levels.
From Friday morning barges and boats travelling from Arnhem to Zutphen will have to take a detour of up to 300km.
Rijkswaterstaat said the water channel in the river was too shallow to allow ships to pass each other.
The summer drought has brought the flow in the major Dutch rivers down to unprecedented levels, with the Rhine down to 600 cubic metres a second at Lobith, the point where it enters the Netherlands from Germany.
Koninklijke Binnnenvaart Nederland, which represents inland waterway users, said it was a further blow for a sector that had already been forced to adopt limits on its activities.
Spokesman Andries de Weerd told NOS: “We’ve been taking half or even one-third loads, and now we’re having take the long route round, so unfortunately the costs are going to go up a little.”

Finance Watch warns of online tactics designed to influence retail investors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:48:58 UTC
21:48:58 KST

Online design tactics can influence consumers and retail investors, including minors, to make decisions that may not be in their best interests, while making information about potential risks less prominent, Finance Watch has warned.
Influencers giving advice without adequate financial knowledge, trendy investment lists, pre-selected investment amounts and countdowns designed to create a sense of urgency, and prominent ‘buy’ buttons appearing on the screen are some of the common tactics identified by the non-profit organisation Finance Watch in a report about addictive and misleading online design patterns that it says can be detrimental to consumers and retail investors.
As retail investing becomes more accessible through social media platforms, civil society organisations and policymakers are increasingly looking at ways to protect people online, particularly vulnerable groups such as minors.
The organisation analysed the websites and apps of 24 banks, neobanks and trading platforms, as well as 59 financial influencers, known as ‘finfluencers’, on social media across Germany, Spain, Czechia and Hungary.
The report, published on Tuesday, identified repeated design patterns that Finance Watch says can steer investment choices or obscure information about product risks, including for minors.
"Potential returns were often emphasised, while information about risks was placed in less visible or collapsible sections," the report says, while calling on EU policymakers to introduce new legislation to restrict or ban such practices.
"The upcoming Digital Fairness Act is an opportunity to clean up, so that consumers choices reflect their needs and appetite for risk, not the profit interests of platforms and influencers," Finance Watch senior officer Peter Norwood said in a press statement.
The European Commission is expected to present the Digital Fairness Act before the end of the year, with the proposed legislation aimed at protecting consumers from potentially unfair or manipulative online practices.
The organisation also recommends tighter regulation of the activity of ‘finfluencers’, and calls for a ban on their promotion of retail investment products.
“On social media, finance influencers broadcast to vast audiences without credentials or demonstrable competence,” Finance Watch wrote in the report.
“Financial education is too important to become a disguise for advertising or unqualified advice,” the organisation added.
The European Union is also focusing on increasing financial literacy in the bloc, as limited financial knowledge has been identified as one of the obstacles to making Europe more competitive globally.
The European Commission is promoting a range of initiatives to help people develop financial skills, such as events and exchanges with stakeholders, while helping national authorities to organise initiatives on the ground.
According to a 2023 Eurobarometer survey, only 18% of EU citizens reported having a high level of financial literacy, potentially leaving some consumers less equipped to navigate financial products and services and identify risks, including online.
