The unexpected result points to a hidden cellular role that could help explain why people respond differently to certain leukemia treatments.
- Share:
For more than seven decades, doctors have used the drug 6-thioguanine (6-TG) to treat leukemia. Its effects in patients are well documented, but researchers are still working to understand the molecular details that determine why some cells are killed by the drug while others manage to withstand it.
A team at the CeMM Research Center for Molecular Medicine of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working with scientists at the University of Oxford, the Weizmann Institute of Science and the University of Dundee, has now identified an unexpected factor in that response: a protein called NUDT5.
The finding follows a recent discovery from the Kubicek and Huber laboratories (Science, 2025). That earlier work showed that NUDT5 has an important role inside cells that does not depend on its usual enzymatic activity. Rather than functioning only as a catalyst that drives chemical reactions, NUDT5 can also act as a molecular scaffold that helps organize cellular metabolism.
That unusual function appears to matter for how cells respond to 6-TG.
"We initially expected that NUDT5 would influence 6-TG through its enzymatic activity," says co-first author Tuan-Anh Nguyen from CeMM. "Instead, we found that inhibiting the enzyme had little effect. What mattered was whether the protein itself was present."
Removing NUDT5 Changes the Drug Response
Many drugs that target enzymes are designed to block the chemical reactions those enzymes perform. The researchers wanted to know whether suppressing NUDT5 in this way would also change the effects of 6-TG.
To test that idea, they used an emerging strategy known as targeted protein degradation. Instead of merely blocking a protein's activity, this method causes the cell to eliminate the protein altogether.
"We developed a cell-based platform to accelerate the discovery of NUDT5 degraders. This platform helped guide the medicinal chemistry efforts that ultimately produced dNUDT5, our most active degrader," said Anne-Sophie Marques, a first author of the paper whose work at Oxford contributed to the findings.
A medicinal chemistry program led by the Huber laboratory at the University of Oxford produced a collection of highly selective NUDT5 degraders. The researchers also created matched control compounds that could bind to NUDT5 without causing the protein to be destroyed.
They then compared the effects of these molecules with conventional NUDT5 inhibitors.
The difference was clear. Blocking NUDT5's enzymatic activity did not meaningfully change how cells responded to 6-TG. Removing NUDT5 from the cells, however, protected them from the toxic effects of the drug. Genetic experiments led to the same conclusion.
"Chemical degraders give us a way to separate what a protein does as an enzyme from what it does as a physical presence in the cell," says Professor Kilian Huber, Centre for Medicines Discovery at the University of Oxford and co-corresponding author of the study. "In this case, that distinction was decisive: removing NUDT5 revealed biology that conventional inhibitors missed."
A Hidden Function Beyond Enzyme Activity
The results indicate that NUDT5 affects sensitivity to thiopurine drugs through a mechanism that does not depend on its catalytic activity. In other words, studying what the enzyme chemically does is not enough to explain its influence on 6-TG.
"As the results came in, it became immediately clear that the dNUDT5 was protecting cells from 6-thioguanine toxicity in a dose-dependent manner. That was an incredibly exciting moment," said Ludwig Bauer, a first author of the paper.
The researchers also discovered an intriguing connection between NUDT5 and another protein called NUDT15, which is already known to affect how patients respond to thiopurine drugs.
The two proteins appear to have opposing effects.
Loss of NUDT15 makes cells more sensitive to 6-TG. Reducing NUDT5, by contrast, makes cells more resistant to the treatment. The findings suggest that the proteins influence thiopurine response through different mechanisms that can push cells in opposite directions.
"Our results show that proteins can have important biological functions that are completely independent of their enzymatic activity," says corresponding author Stefan Kubicek, Principal Investigator at CeMM. "By removing NUDT5 rather than simply inhibiting it, we were able to uncover a hidden layer of biology that helps determine how cells respond to a clinically important drug."
A New Window Into Leukemia Drug Response
The findings do not immediately lead to a new treatment, but they reveal an unexpected mechanism that helps control the effects of a long-used leukemia drug.
By showing that NUDT5 influences 6-TG through a non-catalytic function, the research could help scientists better understand why responses to thiopurine treatment can differ. It also demonstrates how targeted protein degradation can expose biological functions that may remain invisible when researchers rely only on traditional enzyme inhibitors.
This work was supported by the European Research Council (ERC) under the European Union's Horizon 2020 research and innovation program, the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the Vienna Science and Technology Fund (WWTF), the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions Postdoctoral Fellowships program, the Innovative Medicines Initiative 2 Joint Undertaking (IMI2 JU), the Wellcome Trust, Merck Sharp & Dohme Corp. and Janssen Pharmaceutica NV.

Will Banque Misr UAE branches takeover end US sanctions crisis?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:47:17 UTC
21:47:17 KST

Breadcrumb
Will the takeover of Banque Misr UAE branches end the crisis from US sanctions?
The predicament surrounding Banque Misr's branches in the UAE entered a new phase on Tuesday, 22 September, after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the Dubai branch "will be closed", following US allegations that around $1.8 billion was processed in transactions linked to Iranian entities.
The US escalation has placed Banque Misr in a crisis that goes beyond suspending dollar transactions or cutting correspondent banking relationships from 1 October, according to the deadline set by the US Treasury Department.
On Tuesday when Banque Misr and the National Bank of Egypt said in a joint statement that the Central Bank of the UAE had issued preliminary approval for the National Bank of Egypt's request to acquire Banque Misr's branches in the UAE.
A confirmation followed from senior Egyptian sources to The New Arab that the government was moving quickly to put alternatives in place to manage the crisis.
The sources said a delegation from the Central Bank of Egypt and the Foreign Ministry would travel to the UAE in the coming hours to meet officials and relevant parties to discuss the repercussions of the decision to close Banque Misr's five branches.
The delegation would also discuss the operational procedures that would follow until the end of the current month, as well as notifying customers of the branches before the decision is implemented from 1 October.
Takeover of Banque Misr branches
In an exclusive interview with The New Arab, former Banque Misr deputy chairwoman Sahar El-Damaty said the announcement of the closure meant that the decision had already been taken.
She explained that the US Treasury secretary had given Banque Misr 30 days to respond to questions concerning transactions by the bank's branches with institutions and individuals affiliated with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. However, the deadline had not expired when the decision was initially announced.
She said that Bessent had spoken before Congress about a week ago during a hearing, before later announcing that the branch would be closed, and the closure was announced on Monday evening, 21 September, before the deadline expired.
Damaty explained that the decision meant the US side had evidence of financing passing through some companies that Washington considers fronts for Iran and its sanctioned institutions.
She stressed that banks normally carry out all the required procedures to verify customers' identities and the documents submitted to them. However, she quickly pointed out, they cannot necessarily know whether a company or certain individuals are transferring money to entities affiliated with people or institutions with a military nature in Iran unless they have an intelligence service investigating the activities of companies.
This is usually carried out by central banks in cooperation with intelligence agencies, something that was not available to Banque Misr's branches in the UAE.
Damaty also explained that the amount involved in the US decision, $1.8 billion, does not represent a large sum compared with what a country such as Iran, with millions of residents, could purchase, and the import and arms deals it concludes are worth tens of billions of dollars.
She stressed that the existence of financial transactions through a bank with a country or companies does not necessarily mean the bank itself was involved, explaining that responsibility could relate to employees or other parties.
Damaty said that Banque Misr has five branches in the UAE, questioning the size of these branches and the impact of their closure on the bank.
At the same time, she stressed the need to respect US sanctions, confirming that dealing with sanctions had always been handled with great caution when she served as deputy chairwoman of Banque Misr and that the necessary measures should have been taken at the time.
She noted that bank employees work in the UAE under existing procedures and oversight, questioning the role of the Central Bank of the UAE in monitoring the transactions in question and that UAE banks operating in Egypt are subject to the supervision of the Central Bank of Egypt, while Egyptian banks operating in the UAE are subject to the supervision of the Central Bank of the UAE.
Money laundering in the UAE
Damaty also discussed money laundering in the UAE, noting that the UAE had faced a problem in this area and had recently resolved it.
She questioned whether it had taken measures at the time to close entities that held funds linked to the issue, and said that the presence of people of Iranian origin in the UAE does not mean that dealings with them should be closed. Rather, transactions involving the purchase or financing of military or non-military equipment and other operations that may not be permitted should be examined.
She also question the importance of the Central Bank of the UAE moving to close Banque Misr's branch in the UAE, as one of the branches operating under its jurisdiction, laws and direct supervision.
Damaty stressed that the decision to close Banque Misr's branches in the UAE, according to what the US side announced, does not mean the closure of Banque Misr itself, as closing five branches does not mean closing the entire bank.
She explained that the issue concerns the closure of the branch, rather than simply suspending dollar transactions or the "SWIFT" system, noting that Banque Misr in the UAE deals in various major currencies.
She further said that closing the branch in this way, if implemented, would represent a severe penalty because it would mean halting all branch operations, rather than merely suspending its dollar activities.
She expected that the branch's activities could be limited to transactions in the UAE dirham, noting that there are UAE banks that could carry out the same transactions.
She added that transfers made by Banque Misr could be conducted in other currencies, including the UAE dirham, Chinese yuan and Egyptian pound.
Regarding the impact of the decision on remittances by Egyptians in the UAE, Damaty said there are other banks that Egyptians can use such as the National Bank of Egypt in the UAE, although it is smaller than Banque Misr.
Damaty said dealing with the United States on such issues is "very difficult", and that matters could change through negotiations and political channels.
She said the Central Bank of the UAE and the Central Bank of Egypt are the two parties capable of resolving the issue because they have been involved in the matter since the first day.
She added that the penalty itself remains unclear in terms of its duration and nature, as the announcement of the closure did not specify whether it was final or for a set period.
Banks' public image
Banking and investment expert Rashad Abdo told The New Arab that Egypt would not lose much from a banking perspective because Banque Misr has a large number of branches inside and outside Egypt.
He said the more important issue was its external image before public opinion, amid talk of dealing with the Iranian regime and allegations of money laundering.
He added that the most that could happen would be the punishment of the branch manager and its employees.
However, Egypt should begin implementing the decision and consider possible alternatives, he said.
He pointed to the possibility of reaching an agreement with the UAE government for a branch of another bank, such as the National Bank of Egypt, to perform the same role for Banque Misr customers in the UAE.
The bank would have to comply with the directives and take into account all matters related to the decision, which he said was reflected in the preliminary approval of this approach.
Abdo explained that Banque Misr's branch in the UAE is subject to the Central Bank of the UAE.
He noted that UAE authorities said they monitor and inspect transactions and, following the US position, announced that they would send a committee to conduct further inspections and examinations, informing Egypt and the US side.
Noting this was the first time such an incident had occurred, he explained that the United States has its own controls and rules and implements what it considers necessary to impose its dominance.
He added that the US had begun a naval blockade of Iran and that the blockade would also become aerial.
Arguing that the US power is based primarily on its currency, as the dollar is the currency in which oil and minerals are sold globally, strengthening its influence, Abdo also opined this was why Washington was concerned about moves towards creating an alternative currency for the BRICS group, particularly as the group expands, a step that Washington strongly fears.

Yemeni Houthis Set Up Missile and Drone Production Using Chinese Components – Bloomberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:47:13 UTC
21:47:13 KST

Yemeni Houthis have established missile and drone production using equipment and components of Chinese origin that are entering Yemen as commercial goods and dual-use items.
This is reported by Bloomberg, which analyzed intercepted cargo, customs documents, and UN reports, and spoke with Yemeni officials and experts.
The publication describes these shipments as part of a network supporting the Houthis’ military-industrial capabilities.
During a detailed inspection in July 2026, phenolic resin—a heat-resistant material that can be used in missile production—was found in one of the containers, along with tail fins and other parts resembling ballistic missile components.
Subsequently, three more containers linked to the same supply network were inspected at the port of Aden. They were found to contain what appeared to be missile body components, guidance systems, launch equipment, CNC machine tools, and twin-cylinder engines suitable for use in unmanned aerial vehicles.
The head of the port department of the counterterrorism unit stated that the components had been deliberately distributed among four containers, making them difficult to detect. In his assessment, the seized parts collectively constituted the components of a nearly complete missile assembly.
The cargo also included earthmoving and ventilation equipment, which, according to Yemeni security officials, could be used in the construction of underground infrastructure.
At the same time, a significant portion of the discovered products is dual-use and can be legally used in the civilian industry. Bloomberg notes that there is no evidence that the Chinese manufacturers were aware of the products’ end user.
Experts interviewed by the publication note that the availability of Chinese engines, electronics, flight controllers, GPS modules, servo drives, and composite materials makes it possible to procure a significant portion of the components needed for the production of attack drones through regular commercial channels.
Previously, the Houthis relied heavily on shipments of finished weapons from Iran. In July 2025, Yemeni forces intercepted a large shipment of weapons bound for the group, which included missiles and other systems of Iranian origin.
However, the supply model subsequently began to change: instead of exclusively receiving ready-made weapons, the Houthis began to receive components, equipment, and materials that allow them to assemble missiles and drones directly in Yemen. It is precisely this trend that is confirmed by the shipments of Chinese components and industrial equipment described by Bloomberg.
The results of their development of in-house drone systems are already becoming apparent on the battlefield. In August 2026, Militarnyi reported that the Houthis had struck a Saudi M1A2S Abrams tank with munitions dropped from a UAV.
At the same time, the group is expanding its control over strategic areas of the country. In September, the Houthis captured the port of Mocha near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, so the growth of their ability to independently produce missiles and drones is becoming increasingly important for the safety of shipping in the Red Sea.

The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the rebel group at the center of Ethiopia's 2020-2022 war, said Wednesday that it had launched an attack against the Ethiopian army in the country's north.
In a statement, the TPLF-led Tigray regional government said federal forces had launched an attack on Wednesday and that its forces had been ordered to enter what it described as a “defensive” war.
The group also claimed that federal forces had launched a large-scale offensive from several directions, using infantry and mechanized units as well as drones and other air assets.
Local media reported clashes between federal forces and TPLF-affiliated fighters in parts of the Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions.
Getachew Reda, a former head of Tigray's interim administration who now serves as a federal government adviser, accused the TPLF leadership of launching a large-scale attack on government positions in Afar and Amhara.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie said his country had exercised “immense restraint” despite what he described as interference by “adversarial elements.”

Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to Mekelle, Axum and Shire in the Tigray region from Wednesday, citing the security situation.
The African Union called for restraint as military tensions increased, saying the Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, signed in November 2022, remains the foundation of the peace process.
The United Nations also expressed concern over the deteriorating situation.
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged the parties to de-escalate tensions and return to dialogue under the 2022 Pretoria agreement.
The TPLF and Ethiopia's federal government fought a two-year war that began in November 2020. The conflict, which was centered in Tigray and drew in forces from neighboring regions, is estimated to have killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
The war ended with the Pretoria agreement, which halted major fighting but left several issues unresolved, including the status of disputed areas in western Tigray, the return of displaced people and the disarmament of TPLF forces.
The TPLF, which dominated Ethiopia's political system for decades before Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power in 2018, has remained a major political and military force in Tigray.
Last week, seven armed and political groups from different parts of Ethiopia, including the TPLF, announced that they had formed an alliance to coordinate their opposition to the federal government led by Abiy.

====================================================================================================

Trump finally gets his Greenland deal, but what actually changes from a similar 1951 pact?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:43:12 UTC
21:43:12 KST

US President Donald Trump has wanted Greenland for years, repeatedly threatening to take the autonomous Danish territory, even by force, if needed.
He first expressed interest in acquiring the island in 2019 and, during his second term, escalated his rhetoric, at times refusing to rule out military or economic force to bring it under US control.
Polling shows an overwhelming majority of Greenlanders have rejected the idea.
Despite that, Trump continued to push the issue, and on Friday, he said that the US had finally reached an agreement with Denmark and Greenland, giving Washington “permanent control” over security and “all other needs” on the island.
The arrangement would cost the US nothing and have an “Infinite Life”, while barring US adversaries from establishing bases, stationing military personnel or making sensitive investments in Greenland without American approval, the president added.
But the deal Trump is presenting as a sweeping expansion of US power falls short of his earlier demand to “take Greenland”, according to experts.
The Danish and Greenlandic governments have framed the agreement differently. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it preserves the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, while recognising Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
Greenland Prime Minister Jens Frederik Nielsen called it a “win win win agreement”.
The agreement appears to be a compromise between three different perspectives, according to Hasan Akintug, researcher at the Centre for Nordic Studies, University of Helsinki.
“On the American side there seems to be a desire to exercise unrestricted sovereignty on the island in the domains of security and defence policy. From the Danish perspective, the agreement maintains that Greenland is a part of the Kingdom of Denmark,” Akintug tells TRT World.
“From the Greenlandic perspective, the new agreement also explicitly refers to Greenland as a factor in international politics and a potential independent state within this agreement. The preamble of the agreement is particularly important in terms of understanding the different interests of the three actors involved.”
“There are elements that are appealing to all sides, and it would not be surprising if each would actively attempt to frame the agreement as a victory from their own point of view,” Akintug adds.
The agreement was signed Tuesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Its terms allow Washington to “modernise and expand” its activities at Pituffik Space Base and establish defence areas at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and Mestersvig in the east.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio described it as a deal that “permanently and completely” addresses Washington’s national security concerns.
That leaves a basic question: how much of what the US side is calling “permanent control” is actually new?
The US already has broad military rights
Washington has already had extensive military access to Greenland since the 1951 Defence of Greenland Agreement with Denmark.
The treaty allows the US to establish and operate defence areas agreed with Denmark under NATO defence plans.
Where Washington is responsible for a defence area, it can construct, install, maintain and operate military facilities, station personnel, store supplies and control the movement of ships, aircraft and vehicles within the area.
US forces also have free access between defence areas through Greenland, including by land, air and sea, while US aircraft can fly over and land across Greenland subject to agreed limitations.
The agreement also gives the US exclusive jurisdiction over defence areas for which it is responsible, while explicitly preserving Danish sovereignty over them.
The arrangement was updated in 2004, when Greenland’s home rule government became a party to the agreement. The amendment also provided for new defence areas and updated the framework for US military activities on the island.
In other words, Washington has had a legal framework for maintaining a substantial military presence in Greenland since the early Cold War. During the Cold War, the US maintained 17 military installations and more than 10,000 personnel on the island. Today, Pituffik Space Base is the only US military installation there.
The word “permanent” is also less transformative than President Trump’s language suggests.
According to Akintug, the 1951 agreement also did not have an explicit termination clause.
However, he notes that Article XI of the 1951 agreement implicitly acknowledges the possibility of termination, referring to the removal of US facilities and equipment “at any time before the termination of this Agreement or within a reasonable time thereafter.”
“The 2026 agreement mentions that there is no ‘end date’ and that it can only be amended by mutual agreement. It also mentions that an independent Greenlandic state commits to remaining part of NATO and would take over defence-related responsibilities from the Danish government,” Akintug says.
“This could be seen as a restriction of Greenland’s defence policy options and, consequently, its sovereignty, should it become independent,” he says.
It is not clear what practical implications the ‘no end date’ clause will have or what would happen to the agreement if the parties later decided to terminate it, Akintug adds.
What is new?
The new agreement does add something tangible: a framework for expanding the US military presence beyond its existing installation at Pituffik.
The accord allows Washington to establish defence areas at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and Mestersvig in the east, while also permitting additional defence areas and stronger US military operations or facilities elsewhere on the island.
The agreement also places clearer limits on potential rival military activity. No non-NATO country can establish its own manned or unmanned military installations in Greenland or maintain a persistent military presence unless the signatories agree otherwise.
However, Akintug says no publicly available information indicates that any non-NATO country is actively attempting to establish a military presence in Greenland.
“Regarding sensitive investments, the US has not previously hesitated to express its discomfort with certain investments (such as Chinese investments in airports and telecommunications) in either autonomous territory (Greenland and the Faroe Islands) in the Kingdom of Denmark.”
“It is not clear if the new agreement will cause a major shift in US policy in this regard. Perhaps it could be seen as an explicit acknowledgement of existing practice,” he adds.
Emphasis on NATO
Greenland sits between North America and Europe and has long been strategically important for monitoring the Arctic and North Atlantic.
The agreement puts US military access to Greenland within a broader NATO security framework, with the signatories saying they share an interest in US access to defend Greenland, the NATO area and the American continent.
Greenland itself is a party to the new arrangement. If Greenland eventually becomes independent, the agreement says it can remain in force provided Greenland remains in NATO and assumes Denmark’s rights and obligations under the deal.
The agreement therefore creates a long-term framework for US military access regardless of whether Greenland’s constitutional relationship with Denmark changes in the future.
The agreement’s emphasis on NATO also needs to be understood in the context of Greenland’s existing relationship with the alliance, according to Akintug.
“The Greenlandic government in its 2024 strategy clearly defined Greenland as a part of the ‘Western Alliance’ and opinion polls from 2024 also showed that 65% of interviewees had a positive view of NATO, with 31% having a neutral view and only 4% viewing NATO negatively,” Akintug says.
“The emphasis on NATO is somewhat surprising considering the current US administration’s general rhetoric. It is also important in light of a shift in Canadian foreign policy, with Ottawa taking a more NATO oriented approach to its Arctic territory after decades of skepticism.”
“It is very difficult, if not impossible, to predict what the broader implications are for the Nordic countries. But considering the new orientation of Sweden and Finland within NATO, the other Nordic countries are likely to welcome a stabilisation on the US-Denmark-Greenland axis,” he adds.

Navy wraps up major drill amid warnings to Greece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:43:00 UTC
21:43:00 KST

A Turkish Navy aircraft releases countermeasure flares during the Denizkurdu-I naval exercise. (AA Photo)
The Turkish Navy wraps up a large-scale military exercise on Sept. 25 involving 100 naval vessels, 50 aircraft and 14,000 personnel across the Black Sea, Aegean and eastern Mediterranean, as Ankara has warned Greece against steps it says could undermine regional stability.
The exercise, dubbed “Denizkurdu-I” (Sea Wolf-I), involved frigates, corvettes, fast attack craft and other naval assets. Units conducted operational readiness training and live-fire exercises across a maritime area stretching from the Black Sea through the Marmara and Aegean seas to the eastern Mediterranean.
A key event was a distinguished observer day aboard the Turkish navy’s flagship TCG Anadolu in the eastern Mediterranean on Sept. 24. The Defense Ministry also held its weekly press briefing aboard the amphibious assault ship.
The exercise took place amid renewed tensions between Türkiye and Greece over longstanding disputes in the Aegean, including maritime boundaries and the military status of Greek islands near the Turkish coast.
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’ recent visit to Meis, also known as Kastellorizo, drew a sharp reaction from Ankara after he toured military facilities on the island, which Türkiye says has a demilitarized status under international treaties.
Asked about recent developments in the eastern Mediterranean, Turkish defense officials said the ministry was closely monitoring military activity on Cyprus, including what it described as the continued arming of the island’s Greek Cypriot administration and its military cooperation with third countries.
The ministry said such moves could undermine the “sensitive balance” and security environment on the island and would not contribute to confidence-building, peace or stability.
“Türkiye, as a guarantor country, will continue to take the necessary measures, as it has in the past, today and in the future, in cooperation with the authorities of Turkish Cyprus to protect the security, peace and welfare of the Turkish Cypriot people,” the ministry said.
The ministry said Ankara expected Athens to avoid actions that could harm peace and stability in the region and to comply with its treaty obligations.
“Türkiye will continue its constructive approach in favor of good neighborly relations and dialogue in the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean, while resolutely protecting its rights and interests under international law and taking necessary measures for the security of our country,” it said.
The ministry also addressed a planned undersea electricity cable linking the divided island with Greece and Israel, reiterating Türkiye’s claims to maritime rights and interests in the eastern Mediterranean.
It cited a 2019 maritime boundaries memorandum with Libya and the continental shelf boundaries Türkiye submitted to the United Nations in 2020 as the legal framework for its position.
The ministry said activities such as laying cables or pipelines and conducting scientific research in areas it considers part of its continental shelf must be coordinated with Türkiye in advance under international law.
“Unauthorized activities that disregard our country’s rights and interests are not permitted,” it said, adding that authorities were closely monitoring developments and taking necessary measures.
The Sea Wolf exercises are held twice a year in two phases, Denizkurdu-I and Denizkurdu-II, and rank among the Turkish Armed Forces’ largest maritime drills.

Takaichi’s Pre-emptive Diplomacy: What Japan Needs From the Trump-Xi Summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:43:00 UTC
21:43:00 KST

When Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae sat down with U.S. President Donald Trump in New York on September 22, the timing itself was the message. Chinese President Xi Jinping would arrive in Washington, D.C. the next day for state visit to Washington and his second summit with Trump this year. Takaichi said afterward that holding the talks at such a moment demonstrated the strength of the Japan-U.S. alliance. But the most important audience may have been Trump himself.
Tokyo’s anxiety is not hard to understand. Trump personally greeted Xi on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, an unusually warm welcome for a visiting foreign leader. Xi, for his part, struck a conciliatory tone upon arrival, declaring in a written statement that China and the United States “should be partners, not rivals.”
The hospitality will continue at the White House, with an elaborate welcoming ceremony and a state dinner. But expectations for substantive breakthroughs remain low. Washington and Beijing still face deep divisions over trade, artificial intelligence, Taiwan, and other issues.
With U.S. midterm elections about six weeks away, Trump has strong incentives to secure tangible economic results from China. Just before the summit, Washington and Beijing agreed to extend their trade truce by another two months, until January 10, postponing additional tariffs and export restrictions. The agreement reduces the immediate risk of renewed confrontation while giving both sides more time to negotiate.
For Tokyo, however, one concern stands above the economic bargaining: Taiwan.
China strongly opposes U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, while Trump has described such sales as a bargaining chip. Xi could use Trump’s desire for a broader economic deal to press Washington to continue delaying arms sales to the island. That has fueled concern in Tokyo that Taiwan could become part of a wider bargain between Washington and Beijing.
For Japan, Taiwan is a critical security issue. Japan’s southwestern islands lie close to Taiwan, and Takaichi’s remarks in the Diet last November that a Chinese use of force against Taiwan could constitute a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan triggered a sustained Chinese pressure campaign against Tokyo. Any significant weakening of U.S. support for Taiwan could therefore have direct implications for Japan’s security and for deterrence across the Western Pacific.
That made Takaichi’s meeting with Trump more than a routine alliance check-in. According to the Japanese government, the two leaders discussed the economy, issues related to China (including economic security, AI , semiconductors, and critical minerals), and North Korea, and exchanged views on China with the Trump-Xi summit specifically in mind. Takaichi also said Japan hoped stable China-U.S. relations would contribute to international stability.
Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu, who attended the Takaichi-Trump meeting, told NHK ahead of the Trump-Xi summit that he believed Washington’s position on Taiwan remained unchanged from the leaders’ previous summit in May. Motegi said he believed Japan and the United States shared an understanding on this point.
Whether or not that is the case will become clearer only after Trump’s talks with Xi – particularly in how Washington handles Taiwan.
Takaichi’s U.N. General Assembly speech on the same day as her meeting with Trump illustrated the other side of her China diplomacy. She declared that the “stable post-Cold War era” was over and warned that the international order based on the rule of law was facing serious challenges. She explicitly named Russia over its invasion of Ukraine and North Korea over its nuclear and missile programs. Yet she did not mention China by name, saying instead that unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion must not be tolerated anywhere in the world.
The omission was notable after months of deteriorating China-Japan relations. It suggests that while Takaichi wants Washington to remain firm in the face of Chinese pressure, Tokyo is also seeking to prevent a further deterioration in its own relationship with Beijing.
That approach fits the broader diplomatic environment surrounding the Trump-Xi meeting. Despite fierce competition over trade, technology, and AI, both Washington and Beijing appear interested, at least for now, in managing their rivalry rather than allowing it to spiral into another confrontation. Xi’s message that the two countries should be “partners, not rivals,” and the extension of the trade truce both point in that direction.
For Japan, stable China-U.S. relations are desirable. But stability achieved through a bargain that changes Washington’s approach to Taiwan would present a very different calculation for Tokyo.
Takaichi made Japan’s concerns clear before Xi arrived in Washington. The Trump-Xi summit will show whether those concerns figure in Trump’s calculations – and whether his pursuit of deals with Beijing changes the strategic environment Japan must navigate.

Germany news: Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid

Germany news: Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Thursday, September 24, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
University of Münster inaugurates faculty of Islamic theology
The University of Münster inaugurated Germany's first-ever faculty of Islamic theology on Thursday evening.
This gives Islam the same status as the university's dedicated Catholic and Protestant faculties of theology.
The new faculty's founding dean, Mouhanad Khorchide, pledged it would pursue an "Islamic theology with and for Europe."
He stressed that the new faculty would be a place of academic inquiry and remain independent.
"A faculty is not a pulpit; preaching takes place in the mosque," Khorchide said.
Gonca Türkeli-Dehnert,North Rhine-Westphalia's State Secretary for Culture and Science, said that "Islamic theology should have a firm place at state-run German universities."
Hundreds of people attended the inauguration on Thursday night, including faith leaders from Christianity and Judaism, as well as international delegates.
The university's rector, Johannes Wessels, said the new Islamic theology faculty would join its Catholic and Protestant counterparts to form a "Theology Campus" which he envisioned as "a hotspot for interfaith discourse."
Rhineland-Palatinate to chair Conference of Minister-Presidents for another year
The German state of Rhineland-Palatinate will retain the chairmanship of the Conference of Minister-Presidents for another year. This decision was made unanimously by the heads of government of the federal states, according to a statement from the State Chancellery in Mainz.
Saxony-Anhalt was due to take over the chairmanship in October. However, following the election victory of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in that state, Saxony-Anhalt's premier, Sven Schulze, wrote to his Rhineland-Palatinate's counterpart, Gordon Schnieder (both CDU), on 8 September to inform him of his intention to decline the scheduled chairmanship of the state council beginning in October.
The rest of the rotation of presidencies remains unchanged, according to the statement. This means that Schleswig-Holstein will assume the presidency in October 2027, as originally planned. State legislative elections will be held there in April of next year.
The Conference of Minister Presidents is an informal coordinating body through which the states coordinate with each other and with the federal government. Rhineland-Palatinate has held the presidency since October 2025.
The chair of the Conference significantly influences setting the agenda, preparing for meetings, conducting negotiations, and communicating issues to the public. The chair coordinates and moderates meetings of state leaders.
Far-left German activist Lina E. freed again after refusing to testify
A German woman convicted of attacking far-right activists will be released from detention following a ruling by the Federal Constitutional Court.
A court spokeswoman confirmed that the woman, identified only as Lina E. due to German privacy laws, will be released pending a final decision.
Lina E. was originally sentenced to five years and three months in prison in May 2023 for serious assault and forming a criminal association. She and her accomplices were accused of carrying out several attacks against suspected members of far-right groups in the eastern states of Saxony and Thuringia between 2018 and 2020.
Her conviction sparked outrage among left-wing activists and led to riots in several cities across Germany, most notably in Leipzig.
After serving two-thirds of her sentence, she was released on probation in May in a ruling by the Federal Court of Justice.
However, in June, she was jailed for six months by a Dresden court after refusing to testify in a case involving the far-left Antifa-Ost group.
German Defense Ministry declines comment on reported CIA drone warning
A German Defense Ministry spokesperson declined to comment on media reports that the CIA had warned of potential Russian drone attacks targeting Spain, France and Italy.
Asked by DW what the warning means for Germany, the spokesperson said the ministry generally does not comment on media reports. However, the spokesperson said European Union (EU) and NATO members routinely share intelligence through bilateral channels, EU operations and NATO's integrated air and missile defense framework.
German military units and institutions also contribute on an ongoing basis to creating a shared situational picture, the spokesperson added.
Citing a source close to the Lithuanian Ministry of Defense, Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that the US intelligence agency has warned Russia is preparing to carry out drone strikes in Europe targeting France, Spain and Italy from the sea.
It comes in the wake of a string of drone incidents near sensitive sites elsewhere in Europe, including Belgium, Germany and Denmark.
IN DEPTH: Could Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?
The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election partly on the promise to implement the city's 2021 expropriation referendum to address the city's rent crisis. But can it really happen?
German business confidence up in September — Ifo
The monthly business climate index put out by the Ifo economic research institute has risen 1.1 points to 89.9 points, the highest level in more than three years.
The index, Germany's most important economic barometer, has been rising constantly over the past five months, indicating that the country is slowly returning to economic health after years of struggle.
The business optimism comes despite an energy price shock that has pushed fuel costs to record highs.
"The German economy continues its recovery," said Ifo president Clemens Fuest.
The gauge of business expectations accompanying the index rose to 90.4 from 89.1 in August, while companies also gave a rosier assessment of their current situation than the month before, improving to 89.5 to 88.5 points.
Ifo said, however, that the automotive sector was still in "difficult terrain."
The index is based on a monthly survey of 9,000 companies.
The news from Ifo comes as the country's five leading economic institutes presented a joint fall forecast raising 2026 GDP growth expectations to 1.3% from 0.6%.
105-year-old suspected Nazi POW guard under investigation
German prosecutors said on Thursday that they were investigating a 105-year-old man over crimes that might have been committed during his alleged time as a guard at a Nazi prisoner-of-war camp during World War II.
In a statement seen by the AFP news agency, they said the man was "thought to have been a guard at the prisoner-of-war camp Stalag 326 VI K" in the Senne region of western Germany.
The man is "accused of being an accessory to multiple murders through his activities there," the statement said.
The Stalag 326 VI K camp held between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by US troops, according to the memorial at the site.
Some 30,000 Soviet POWs are believed to have died at the camp.
The age of the suspect is a reminder that time is running out to prosecute people who committed crimes as part of Germany's Nazi regime.
In April 2025, for example, an alleged former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp near Berlin died before he could face trial on charges of complicity in the murder of more than 3,300 people.
Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid
Berlin has confirmed reports that it is withdrawing its bid to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics.
The decision means that only Munich and the western Rhine/Ruhr region are still in the running as potential hosts, with Hamburg having pulled out in May after failing to win support at a referendum.
The withdrawal comes after the socialist Left Party's victory in Berlin's elections on Sunday. The party's lead candidate and potential mayor, Elif Eralp, said she did not support Berlin's bid.
The current mayor, Kai Wegner of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), told reporters: "Today is a sad day for Berlin, because the Olympic and Paralympic Games would have been a tremendous opportunity."
"When Ms. Eralp stated that the bid was effectively off the table ... the leading sports associations made it clear: We cannot give you our approval under these circumstances," he said, adding: "I deeply regret this."
Kaweh Niroomand, the volleyball manager who led the Berlin bid, said, "We simply could not offer the political stability required."
On Saturday, the German Olympic Committee (DOSB) is to choose a preferred region as part of a bid to the International Olympic Committee to host one of the 2036, 2040 and 2044 Summer Games.
The Summer Olympics have been held twice on German soil.
Berlin hosted the Games in 1936 in then Nazi-ruled Germany and Munich, then as part of West Germany, was the site of the 1972 Games.
IN DEPTH: Top economic think tanks raise 2026 GDP growth forecasts
Economic experts predicted on Thursday that German GDP will double to 1.3% this year. They also warned of difficulties ahead.
You can read more about their forecasts for Germany's economic future in the next few years in this article: Germany: Economic institutes double growth forecast for 2026
Planned intelligence reforms trigger heated Bundestag debate
The German parliament has held its first debate on government plans to give intelligence agencies more power as national security is threatened by new dangers at home and from abroad.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told parliamentarians that the planned reforms would turn Germany's intelligence agencies — the BND (Bundesnachrichtendienst), in charge of international intelligence, and the BfV (Bundesamt für Verfassungschutz), responsible for domestic intelligence — into "true secret services."
He said the agencies would no longer just gather information on threats but be equipped to provide "real defense against dangers, attacks and terror."
Under the plans, the agencies would receive more power to collect, save and automatically evaluate data, as well as permission to react to sabotage or hacking attacks with counterattacks.
Intelligence reforms under fire
Various parliamentarians voiced concerns about the reform's implications in what was sometimes a heated discussion.
Konstantin von Notz from the Green Party said he recognized the need to "update" the powers of the agencies in view of the growing threat from Russia.
But, he said, "the excessive plans for domestic intelligence activities" needed to be trimmed or the the reforms would not survive an appeal to the Constitutional Court.
He said the government needed to take the interests of people professionally entrusted with confidential information much more into consideration, especially psychotherapists.
Clara Bünger of the socialist Left Party accused the government of breaking down the distinction between intelligence agencies and the police that had been a lesson learned "from the crimes of the German fascists."
The far-right politician Gottfried Curio from the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party was strongest in his criticism, saying the government wanted to create a "Stasi 2.0," a reference to the secret service in former communist East Germany.
The reforms would bring about "more than a total surveillance state," he said.
Bundestag set for organ donation debate
The Bundestag will discuss two separate cross-party proposals on Thursday to increase the number of human organs donated for often life-saving transplant operations.
One proposal upholds Germany's current system, under which people who wish to donate organs must actively give permission.
Advocates of the proposal say that the shortfall of donated organs can be remedied by campaigns calling on adults to take part and making it easier to register the desire to donate.
The other proposal calls for an opt-out scheme under which organs can be removed postmortem from anyone who has not expressly rejected being an organ donor.
Backers of this proposal say that although surveys show that most people in Germany are willing to donate their organs, very few actually document this wish.
They also cite statistics showing that countries with opt-out schemes have more donations, with Germany lagging behind in international comparisons.
Altogether 254 of the 630 members of the Bundestag have signed on to the opt-out scheme, and 58 have backed the first proposal to maintain the current national system.
The Bundestag last voted on the issue in 2020, with a majority supporting the opt-in model, even though an opt-out proposal had more signees then, too.
France, Spain and the Netherlands are examples of European countries that have opt-out models in place.

And the university in Münster is to open a faculty of Islamic theology — the first in the country — that will have an equal status with the Catholic and Protestant faculties there.
All this comes amid a bit of good news for the German economy, which experts say will grow twice as much this year as previously forecast.

The Ministry of Finance confirmed that it is working on the issue of taxing aircraft leasing
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:41:30 EEST
21:41:30 KST

The Ministry of Finance confirmed that it is working on the issue of taxing aircraft leasing
Kyiv • UNN
The Ministry of Finance is working on the taxation of lease payments to non-residents for aircraft and helicopters.
The Ministry of Finance of Ukraine is reviewing the issue of taxing leasing or rental payments for providing aircraft for use to non-residents. This is stated in the Finance Ministry's response to a request from UNN.
Why did the problem with aircraft leasing arise?
As UNN previously reported, since 2024 the Bureau of Economic Security has begun interpreting aircraft leasing operations involving non-residents of Ukraine as the use of equipment. According to the investigators' version, Ukrainian air carriers were supposed to pay royalties for the rental of airplanes and helicopters. Based on this approach, the BES opened criminal proceedings against at least five air carriers, including MAU, "Constanta Airlines," "Windrose," H3Operations, and "Skyline Express." According to UNN, another airline — "Urga" — may also figure in a similar case.
The criminal cases were opened despite the fact that almost all air carriers had successfully undergone tax audits, and the tax authorities had raised leasing-related objections against only one company.
Representatives of the aviation industry insist that the problem arose because of an ambiguous interpretation of the legislation and that it requires the development of a unified state approach.
Earlier, in response to a request from UNN, the Ministry of Finance reported that the taxation of aircraft leasing operations is carried out in accordance with the Tax Code and Ukraine's international treaties. At the same time, the Tax Code of Ukraine does not provide for the possibility of taxing aircraft leasing as royalties.
Therefore, representatives of the aviation industry call the Bureau's approach to interpreting aircraft leasing, without changes to the tax legislation, pressure that could destroy the entire passenger and freight transportation industry. According to data from the State Register of Civil Aircraft of Ukraine, 86% of Ukrainian companies' aircraft fleet is leased.
To resolve the situation, the issue of aircraft leasing was submitted for consideration by the tax committee of the Public Council under the Ministry of Finance. Following the first meeting, it was decided to initiate the establishment of a working group at the Finance Ministry, which is to develop a draft general tax consultation on the taxation of leasing payments made to non-residents.
The Finance Ministry is already reviewing the issue of aircraft leasing
The Finance Ministry reported that the working group on this issue has not yet been established. However, the ministry has begun reviewing the taxation of operations involving the leasing of airplanes and helicopters from non-residents.
At the same time, the Finance Ministry is reviewing an issue concerning not the regulation of the leasing market in general, but the application of the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine and Ukraine's international treaties on the avoidance of double taxation to income received by non-residents in the form of leasing or rental payments for providing aircraft for use
The ministry plans to prepare a general tax consultation that will become a unified approach to the taxation of the relevant operations.
According to the Finance Ministry, consideration of issues concerning the application of Ukraine's international treaties on the avoidance of double taxation to income received by non-residents is coordinated by the Department of International Taxation. The application of the provisions of the Tax Code of Ukraine to aircraft leasing is coordinated by the Department of Tax Policy.

Morocco’s elections: Fragmentation, disengagement and PJD’s major comeback
PAM leads as the PJD quadruples its seats and turnout hits its second-lowest level under King Mohammed VI.
Morocco’s parliamentary elections have reshaped the balance between the country’s main parties amid sharply lower turnout.
According to provisional results, the Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) emerged from Wednesday’s voting as the largest party with 97 seats, up from 87 in 2021.
The National Rally of Independents (RNI), which led the government after the last election, fell from 102 seats to 66.
The Istiqlal Party dropped from 81 to 65 seats while the Justice and Development Party (PJD) staged a striking comeback, rising from just 13 seats to 54.
The remaining seats were distributed among several other parties.
Only 38,08 percent of registered voters turned out, compared with 50,86 percent in 2021. The figure was also below the 42,27 percent recorded in 2016.
Morocco has seen considerable social and political mobilisation in recent years, including protests involving younger Moroccans over employment, healthcare, education and living costs. The elections, therefore, were held against a backdrop in which political and social grievances have been expressed outside the ballot box as well as through parties and elections.
A major reshuffling of the governing party balance
The three parties that formed the outgoing government did not emerge from the elections with the same parliamentary weight.
Apart from PAM, which gained 10 seats, RNI shed 36 seats and Istiqlal lost 16.
The three parties remain among the main forces in parliament, but their relative weight has changed substantially since 2021.
RNI was the largest party after the 2021 elections and went on to lead the government. Five years later, PAM has moved into first place in the provisional results while RNI and Istiqlal are separated by just one seat.
PAM’s 97 seats put it at the starting point of the government formation process. Under Article 47 of Morocco’s Constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the political party that comes first in elections for the House of Representatives.
That gives PAM the first position in the process, but it does not give the party a parliamentary majority. A majority in the 395-member House requires at least 198 seats.
According to the provisional figures, PAM, RNI and Istiqlal could renew their three-party coalition without bringing in another party.
Together they hold 228 of the 395 seats, comfortably above the 198 needed for a majority. Whether tensions exposed during the campaign can be put aside is a separate question.
PAM and RNI spent the campaign trading accusations despite having governed together for five years. Their disagreements became part of the electoral contest itself, alongside the competition over the government’s record and the parties’ respective programmes.
The possibility of another coalition between the two parties was also questioned during the campaign.
Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri, PAM’s national coordinator, said that if RNI came first, she personally would not want to join another government led by the party. She stressed that the final decision on post-election alliances would belong to PAM’s National Council.
Mohamed Mehdi Bensaid, another senior PAM figure, also ruled out a renewed coalition with RNI if the latter finished first.
The dispute between the two parties was not limited to coalition politics. RNI accused PAM of trying to recruit its local figures and elected officials before the elections while PAM responded by pointing to defections to RNI before the 2021 elections.
With PAM now first and RNI second, those tensions will form part of the backdrop to coalition negotiations.
The PJD’s comeback
The PJD’s comeback is the other major change in the new parliament.
Its collapse in 2021 was dramatic. After winning 125 seats in 2016, the party was reduced to just 13 five years later.
It has now returned with 54 seats.
That puts the PJD among the four largest parties in the new parliament although it remains well below its 2016 result.
The PJD’s relationship with PAM makes the question of its possible role particularly relevant.
The two parties have long been political opponents. PJD leaders have accused PAM of being created in large part to counter the PJD and limit its political rise.
That criticism resurfaced after Fouzi Lekjaa joined PAM. Former PJD head of government and current party leader Abdelilah Benkirane has argued that Lekjaa’s arrival was intended to counter the PJD. That is Benkirane’s political interpretation rather than an established fact.
Lekjaa is now a senior PAM figure after joining the party’s Political Bureau. He was already a prominent public figure through his leadership of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation, which he has headed since 2014, and through his role as minister delegate in charge of the budget in the outgoing government, a post he held as a nonpartisan minister before joining PAM.
His move into party politics has brought a high-profile figure from football and government into the centre of electoral politics. His entry into PAM has also made him one of the figures being discussed in connection with the next government.
Abdellah Bouanou, one of the PJD’s leading parliamentary figures, has described his relationship with Lekjaa as a good, professional, human relationship despite the political divide between their parties.
Together, PAM, RNI, Istiqlal and the PJD hold 282 seats. Whether the PJD remains in opposition or becomes part of a future governing arrangement will depend on the negotiations that follow.
The turnout question
The reasons for nonparticipation are not uniform, and the election figures alone do not establish why individual voters stayed away from polling stations.
The 2026 figure is the second-lowest turnout recorded in parliamentary elections since King Mohammed VI succeeded his father, Hassan II, in 1999 after the 37 percent recorded in 2007.
Possible explanations for nonparticipation discussed in Morocco include dissatisfaction with established parties, economic concerns and perceptions about the effectiveness of electoral politics. These factors may differ across regions and age groups.
Regional figures underline that point. Participation was much higher in some southern regions, reaching 77 percent in Laayoune-Sakia El Hamra and 61 percent in Dakhla-Oued Ed-Dahab.
The numbers leave two questions: Which parties can assemble the next governing majority, and what explains the decision of most registered voters not to take part?
The first will be decided through coalition negotiations. The second will require looking beyond the seat totals.

Water levels in eastern Switzerland fall to record low
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:39:55 UTC
21:39:55 KST

Water levels in eastern Switzerland fall to record low
Water levels in lakes across eastern Switzerland have fallen to a record low. Lakes Untersee and Zurich have never recorded lower water levels.
The drought, which has persisted for months, is particularly evident on the Untersee, the western part of Lake Constance.
Boats have been aground in many places throughout the summer. There has clearly been a shortage of water in the harbour at Mannenbach-Salenstein since June.
More
How heatwaves are changing Switzerland’s major lakes
On Wednesday, the water level in the Untersee fell four centimetres below the lowest level ever recorded, which was on January 14, 1949. Water levels have been measured at this point since 1885.
Water bodies in canton Thurgau are generally at historically low levels and in some cases, they have dried up completely. According to forecasts, the situation is set to worsen further in the coming weeks.
Extreme drought
The water level of Lake Walen currently stands at 418.18 metres above sea level. The measuring station there has never recorded a lower reading in the month of September. However, this water level is not an all-time record.
According to federal hydrological data, the water level of Lake Walen was 26 centimetres lower on 14 February 1949.
Due to the prolonged low water level, very little water is flowing from Lake Walen into the Linth, the main tributary of Lake Zurich.
Lake Constance, too, is mainly lacking water from its most important tributary. Although this international body of water has around 200 tributaries, it is particularly dependent on the Rhine.
Accounting for around 62% of its water supply, the river is by far the most important source. However, according to data from the Federal Office for the Environment, the area between Chur and the Rhine’s confluence with Lake Constance is one of the regions experiencing extreme drought this year.
The drought this year is worse than in 2003 and 2018, according to canton St Gallen’s website. This has been caused by a second consecutive winter with little snow and intense summer heatwaves.
As no significant rainfall is expected until the end of September, this is likely to be the sixth consecutive month with below-average rainfall.
In the summer two years ago, the situation was quite different, particularly on the Untersee. Following days of rainfall, the highest flood alert level was in force around Lake Constance in June 2024.
In various towns on the Untersee, lakeside promenades, car parks and garden restaurants were submerged. Attempts were made to hold back the lake water using mobile dyke systems – hoses filled with water.

RSPP calls for unified approach to protecting industrial sites from drone attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:36:50 UTC
21:36:50 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Unified approaches are needed to protect industrial facilities from drone and missile attacks, with requirements continuously adjusted to changes in warfare technologies, President of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP) Alexander Shokhin told reporters.
"Everything is changing very rapidly. At the beginning of this year, no one imagined that attacks could be carried out on such a massive scale. Protective netting and some form of kinetic counter-drone systems were considered a sufficient level of protection. That could have served as a standard, but now, to put it mildly, it is already yesterday’s approach, both literally and figuratively. So, what is needed is a mechanism such as Manturov’s subcommission (the subcommission on ensuring the uninterrupted operation of individual sectors of the economy, chaired by Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov - TASS), which would continuously adjust these requirements," Shokhin said.
According to him, developing unified approaches to protection against aerial attacks is also necessary for implementing the presidential decree on measures to ensure the security of critical infrastructure facilities, which provides for the possibility of placing the property of companies that have failed to adequately protect critical infrastructure facilities from drone attacks under temporary administration.
"Because, again, when it comes to placing assets under external administration, it is unclear what constitutes adequate protection and what constitutes timely restoration of a facility. This essentially has to be handled on a case-by-case basis as well; there can be no fixed criteria here. The main thing is to prevent the lack of transparency from being abused," Shokhin said.
Companies’ spending on protection
According to Shokhin, businesses’ spending on financing air defense systems and installing protective structures will increase. "Protecting facilities does not provide a 100% guarantee that there will be no damage in the future. The situation is constantly changing in terms of technology and the use of artificial intelligence. In some areas we are ahead, while in others we have to catch up. So, spending will probably continue to rise. But it is still lower than the potential losses and damage. Therefore, even without being pushed, businesses are naturally interested in putting effective protection in place," Shokhin said.

RFE/RL says the prospective destination is Alabuga, a plant producing drones used against Ukraine. Arab Centre in Washington examines shifting US Palestine policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:34:08 UTC
21:34:08 KST

Breadcrumb
Arab Centre in Washington examines shifts in US policy toward Palestine and its future
US support for Israel is fuelling wars in the Middle East and obstructing prospects for peace, political scientist Ian Lustick warned at the Arab Centre Washington DC's third annual conference on Palestine, arguing that the region’s crises are increasingly rooted in US domestic politics.
Lustick, a professor of political science at the University of Pennsylvania, said at the conference on Wednesday that the influence of pro-Israel lobbying groups over Washington had helped ensure continued US backing for Israel even as its policies became increasingly extreme.
"Support for Israel hinders peace, fuels wars and drags America into them, diverting our attention from the threats posed by China and Russia elsewhere," Lustick said.
"Quite simply, the biggest problem in the Middle East today, or one of the biggest, is an internal American political problem."
Speaking during a session moderated by Yousef Munir, head of the Palestine and Israel Program at the Arab Centre, Lustick argued that lobbying groups supporting Israel wield significant influence over US politicians and foreign policy.
The conference, titled Shifting Tides: Palestine, US Elections, and Pathways Forward, was organised by the Arab Center Washington DC as its Third Annual Palestine Conference and held at the National Press Club in Washington, DC, on Wednesday.
It brought together academics, analysts and advocates to examine developments in Palestine, shifts in US policy towards Palestine and Israel, and whether changing American public opinion could ultimately translate into changes in Washington's policy.
Lustick is the co-author with Eli Clifton of The Israel Lobby, America in the Grip of a Foreign Power. Speaking separately to The New Arab, he described the situation facing Palestinians as one of "frustration and horror", while criticising the disregard of political leaders for events on the ground.
"What is infuriating is the disregard of those in power for what is happening, despite the situation on the ground and what we hear about Israeli objectives aimed at emptying the land of as many Palestinians as possible through killing, repression and impoverishment," he said.
Lustick argued that fundamental change for Palestinians living under Israeli control would be impossible without challenging the influence of the Israel lobby over US policy.
"We treat Israel as if it were a crazy state, and the Israel lobby's remarkable success in ensuring there is no divergence between the positions of the United States and Israel, regardless of how extreme Israeli policies become, has strongly contributed to turning Tel Aviv into a rogue regime and an internationally isolated state," he said.
He argued that unconditional US backing had also shaped Israeli domestic politics by convincing voters that Washington would continue to protect Israel from accountability regardless of the policies pursued by its leaders.
Lustick also rejected the viability of the two-state solution, describing it as a "safe political option" for Democrats and Republicans that allowed politicians to avoid confronting the question of Palestinian democratic rights.
"We should not abandon the struggle to end the occupation. The occupation must end, but it will not end through regional agreements or military withdrawals. It will end through democratic transformation," he said.
He instead advocated a one-state framework centred on equality and democratic rights.
Can shifting US opinion change policy?
Lustick's intervention came as speakers at the conference examined whether growing support for Palestinian rights in the United States could translate into changes in Washington's longstanding policies towards Israel.
Opening the conference, Arab Centre Washington DC executive director Tamara Kharroub pointed to recent opinion polling showing declining support for Israel and growing opposition to US military aid.
She said at least 55% of Americans now believe military assistance to Israel should either be reduced or stopped, while Israel's net approval rating had fallen sharply over the past eight years.
"The support for Palestine that was once considered an electoral liability has now become part of a successful coalition," Kharroub said.
She argued that the significance of the 2026 US midterm elections would extend beyond how many pro-Palestinian candidates enter Congress.
"The importance of the 2026 elections should not be measured only by the number of candidates who reach Congress but also by the emergence of political constituencies and voters for whom the Palestinian issue is a decisive factor in choosing their candidate," she said.
Kharroub said Palestine had increasingly become connected in the US political debate to civil liberties, freedom of expression, lobbying, the use of taxpayers' money and international law.
"The balance has changed today, and the question now is, can this shift in public opinion and political activism become a fundamental change in US foreign policy?" she said.
Gaza suffering becoming 'permanent reality'
Other sessions focused on conditions facing Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
Jihad Abu Salem, executive director of the Gaza Genocide Centre, said Palestinian suffering was being transformed from an emergency into a "permanent and painful reality" nearly a year after the ceasefire.
"The killing has not stopped. More than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire began," he said.
He said nearly 11,000 buildings had been destroyed during the same period, bringing the proportion of damaged buildings in Gaza to more than 82 percent, while much of the population continued to live in tents, damaged buildings or temporary shelters.
Yara Asi, an assistant professor at the University of Central Florida's College of Global Health and Management, meanwhile highlighted escalating settler violence in the occupied West Bank.
She said more than 1,600 settler attacks against Palestinians had been recorded between January and mid-September this year, citing figures from the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.
Omar Rahman, a researcher at the Middle East Council on Global Affairs, criticised the political framework created by the Oslo agreements, arguing that it had left the Palestinian leadership dependent on Western funding while weakening links between the Palestine Liberation Organisation and Palestinian communities abroad.
Calls to turn public opinion into political pressure
The conference concluded with discussions about how changing attitudes towards Israel could be converted into concrete US policy.
Participants called for Palestinian rights to remain a political priority and for campaigners to connect the issue with human rights, freedom of expression, domestic spending and the economic costs of US involvement in foreign wars.
They also called for continued efforts in Congress to halt weapons shipments to Israel, even where legislation has little immediate prospect of passing, as a way of building a congressional bloc capable of influencing future administrations.
Daniel Levy, president of the US/Middle East Project, argued that greater pressure could also be applied over Israeli settlements, including by examining the banks and financial institutions involved in financing them.
Participants also called for normalising proposals for sanctions on Israel and an end to US arms sales, while looking towards the 2028 presidential election as another opportunity to turn changing public opinion into political pressure.
The central question running through the conference was whether the increasingly visible shift in American attitudes towards Israel and Palestine can ultimately break through in Washington and produce a corresponding change in US policy.
