Taiwan health insurance premiums expected to remain unchanged next year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:00:54 UTC
21:00:54 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The National Health Insurance premium rate is unlikely to rise next year if wages go up and the government provides additional funding, Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said Thursday.
CNA reported that the 2027 National Health Insurance global budget will reach about NT$1.04 trillion (US$32.7 billion), topping NT$1 trillion for the first time. The budget will grow by 5.5%, the upper end of the government-approved range.
Shih expects higher minimum wages, public-sector salaries, and wages in other industries to increase revenue from regular insurance premiums. Supplemental premiums and NT$60 billion in additional government funding are also expected to strengthen the system's finances.
The health ministry estimates reserves will equal about 2.3 months of spending by the end of 2027 under those conditions. That would allow the regular premium rate to remain unchanged, per Yahoo News.
The budget covers hospitals, clinics, dental care, and traditional Chinese medicine. Representatives of the four sectors and premium payers agreed on the 5.5% growth rate, per Liberty Times.
The increase will add about NT$55 billion to National Health Insurance spending from this year. It is the third consecutive year that the system has adopted the upper end of the projected growth range, per UDN.
Addressing concerns that much of the annual budget negotiation is settled before the formal meeting, Shih defended advance discussions as necessary for efficiency. Trying to resolve every issue in one meeting would make the process more difficult, he added.

Taiwan PCB output to top NT$1 trillion on AI boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:00:52 UTC
21:00:52 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The PCB industry is expected to post combined domestic and overseas output of NT$1.14 trillion (US$35.83 billion) this year, the Taiwan Printed Circuit Association said Thursday.
Q2 output reached NT$279.1 billion, up 27.9% from a year earlier, while first-half output rose 23.9% to NT$524.7 billion, per CNA. The TPCA said output this year has been stronger than in the previous two years.
The association said demand for AI servers, high-speed networking equipment, and memory is boosting demand for high-end PCBs, including IC substrates, high-layer-count boards, and high-density interconnect boards. Tight supplies of high-end materials and rising raw material costs have also pushed PCB prices higher.
The TPCA expects combined output to rise 24.5% year on year in the second half to NT$611.8 billion, according to UDN. Growing AI applications and emerging uses such as AI glasses and satellite communications are expected to support demand.
The industry still faces risks from rising component costs, tight supplies of key materials, geopolitical tensions, and uncertainty over returns on AI infrastructure investments, the TPCA said. Changes in supply and demand could also affect growth in the second half.
Despite the risks, the association expects AI infrastructure investment to continue expanding. Continued shortages of high-end materials are expected to support PCB prices and shipment volumes, it added.

Personal hardship and online isolation predict support for white nationalism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:00:25 UTC
21:00:25 KST

About 5 percent of white American adults express support for the core ideas of the white nationalist movement, with rates rising to over 13 percent among young white men. The research indicates that personal hardships and isolated online social lives predict this support, rather than changing local racial demographics. The findings were published in Nature.
White nationalism is an ideology based on the belief that white people are under threat in the United States and that the white race must ensure its survival. According to this worldview, white people should hold more political and economic power than other groups, maintain a demographic majority, and treat white culture as superior to all other cultures. The movement operates through informal online networks, paramilitary groups, and public rallies. Until recently, public opinion researchers had not directly measured how many Americans explicitly endorse these exact principles.
Previous research has shown that white Americans hold distinct in-group racial identities, which sets the stage for understanding their political behavior. For instance, a 2019 study showed that many white Americans possess a strong sense of white racial solidarity. Other studies have explored what might cause these group-based attitudes to turn hostile.
A 2014 study indicated that learning about the country’s growing non-white population tends to make white Americans feel threatened and adopt more conservative views. Additionally, a study covered by PsyPost in 2020 found that people holding extreme white identitarian attitudes tend to score lower in personality traits related to politeness and openness to new experiences.
“We observed white nationalist ideas becoming more visible in American public life—in marches and rallies, on the internet and social media, and even in election campaigns,” Patrick J. Egan, a professor of politics and public policy and director of the Berkley Institute for Civil Discourse & Civic Solutions at New York University, told PsyPost.
“That led us to wonder the extent to which white nationalism appeals to the broader public, and who is most likely to support it,” Egan explained. “It turned out no academic study had directly measured support for the white nationalist movement before, and so we decided to investigate these questions ourselves.”
Egan and his colleagues suspected that explicit support for white nationalism might actually be driven by personal economic hardship or online radicalization, rather than local demographic changes. They also wanted to measure support directly by providing respondents with an accurate definition of the movement, reducing the chance that people would misunderstand the label.
To explore this, the researchers conducted three national surveys of non-Hispanic white adults in the United States. In the first study, conducted in 2021, the team surveyed 3,227 people using an online panel matched to national demographics. To test whether people truly understood what white nationalism meant, the researchers ran an experiment. Half of the participants were asked if they supported the movement, while the other half were given a short, factual description of its core beliefs about white power and cultural superiority before being asked the same question.
Providing the definition increased expressed support from 3.8 percent to 7.6 percent. When people were informed about the movement’s actual goals, their answers aligned more closely with their other racial attitudes, such as their sense of white identity and their opposition to minority groups holding power. This suggests that some white Americans agree with the movement’s ideas but are unfamiliar with the term white nationalism until it is explained to them.
Using the fully informed responses, the researchers then looked for demographic predictors. They found that support for white nationalism was 15 percentage points higher among people without a high school diploma compared to those with postgraduate degrees. It was also higher among conservatives, Republicans, frequent church attenders, people who believe in political conspiracies, and those who feel disconnected from politics entirely.
The researchers then tested the competing theories about what drives these beliefs. They found evidence supporting the idea that social and economic strain plays a role. People who had experienced three or more personal hardships in the past year, such as job loss or divorce, were 4 percentage points more likely to support white nationalism than those who experienced none. Living in a county with high levels of social distress, measured by poverty and unemployment rates, also predicted higher support.
However, the researchers found no evidence that changing local demographics drive white nationalist support. Living in a county with a large non-white population or a rapidly shrinking white population was not associated with endorsing the movement. The researchers note that these findings challenge the common assumption that everyday exposure to racial diversity fuels white nationalist grievance.
“One finding that is somewhat unexpected is that white people living in areas that are becoming more racially diverse were not more likely to support white nationalism,” Egan said. “This is in contrast to what we would expect from status-threat theories, which hold that demographic change can spark backlash and resentment.”
“Of course, we don’t have causal evidence in either direction here: our null findings regarding status threat may in part stem from suppressor bias introduced by whites’ residential sorting into preferred ethnoracial environments,” he added. In other words, if white Americans who dislike diversity simply move to neighborhoods that match their preferred racial makeup, it could mask the true relationship between demographic changes and nationalist views.
The study also explored the role of the internet. General social media use did not predict support for white nationalism. Instead, the nature of a person’s social ties mattered. Support was 13 percentage points higher among respondents who said all three of their closest friends were people they only knew online, compared to those whose closest friends were all known in real life.
In 2024, the researchers conducted a second study to confirm these patterns using a probability-based sample of 2,114 non-Hispanic white adults. This method is generally considered more accurate for estimating how common a belief is in the general population. This second survey replicated the main demographic findings, including the strong link between lower education, lower income, and higher support for white nationalism.
Based on this second sample, the researchers estimated that 4.9 percent of white American adults support the white nationalist movement once its tenets are explained to them. Support was highest among young men. The data showed that 13.5 percent of white men aged 18 to 29 endorsed the movement. The researchers noted that young men today spend vast amounts of time online and face unique social and economic challenges, potentially making them more receptive to grievance narratives.
A third survey, involving 2,548 white adults in late 2024 and early 2025, was designed to rule out statistical errors. The researchers tested whether respondents were just clicking a button to agree with whatever the survey asked, a phenomenon known as acquiescence bias. They also checked if asking about racial attitudes earlier in the survey primed people to express more extreme views. The results held up against these checks, confirming that the measurement of white nationalist support was robust.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that exposing white Americans to news about a growing non-white population did not actually increase their feelings of racial threat or worsen their attitudes toward minorities. The new study builds on this by showing that even real-world, local demographic trends fail to predict explicit support for white nationalism.
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relies on observational data taken at specific points in time, meaning it cannot strictly determine cause and effect. Unmeasured factors, such as underlying personality traits or mental health challenges, might make someone more likely to experience personal hardships and also more susceptible to extreme political views.
The connection between online friendships and white nationalism is also complex. While isolated people might fall into online extremism, it is equally possible that holding extreme, unconventional political views makes it difficult for someone to maintain offline friendships. This dynamic could force individuals to seek out like-minded communities entirely on the internet.
Finally, the researchers noted that their study focuses strictly on ideological agreement rather than behavior. “We want to emphasize that we are only asking about endorsement of white nationalist views,” Egan noted. “We do not measure organizational affiliation with the white nationalist movement, nor do we measure support for its tactics.”
“We hope that researchers—whether that be ourselves, or other scholars—use our measure on future surveys to determine whether support for white nationalism is changing over time,” Egan said. “This will help us know if the rising visibility of white nationalism in the US is being accompanied by rising support for its ideas in the mass public.”
The study, “Predictors and prevalence of support for white nationalism in the United States,” was authored by Patrick J. Egan, James Bisbee, and Joshua A. Tucker.

Zelensky had already addressed the prospect of talks in Moscow on Jan. 30. He said a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin there was “impossible” and publicly invited Putin to Kyiv instead.
“I invite him publicly, if he dares, of course,” Zelensky said at the time.
He added that Ukraine was serious about ending the war and would consider a leaders’ meeting in a format that could produce results. But Moscow and Belarus, he said, were unacceptable venues because Russia was waging war against Ukraine and Belarus was its partner in those actions.
“But if someone doesn’t want to meet but can’t bring themselves to say so directly for some reason, that’s when these invitations to Moscow come up. It’s clear what’s going on,” Zelensky added.
Against that backdrop, on Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov claimed that Zelensky had not rejected Russia’s invitation.
“Zelensky has not refused to come to Moscow. At least, I haven’t heard that,” Peskov said, according to Russian state news agency TASS.

Do any coffee-flavoured drinks come close to the real thing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:00:16 UTC
21:00:16 KST

My family has benefited hugely from charities that support healthcare, so it is with extra zeal that I’ll be drinking coffee with a slice of cake tomorrow to mark this year’s Macmillan Coffee Morning. In anticipation, I’ve been tasting some coffee-flavoured drinks.
I should preface this by saying that, when it comes to coffee, I am a creature of habit and, almost 30 years into my relationship with the stuff, I know what I like: short-ish, strong, preferably made in a moka pot and only a tiny splash of milk. I’m less faithful to brands, though I do rate Union’s House Roast, which is bold, crowdpleasing, not too bitter and sold in most big supermarkets. Much as my partner has tried to seduce me to the trendy charms of filter coffee, this leopard can’t seem to change her spots.
So imagine my feelings when I lined up the cast of products to taste for this column. Canned lattes! Coffee-flavoured protein drinks! Instant coffee 2.0! I’ll start with the first group, because the market is now teeming with examples (many of them in extra-unsustainable packaging). All the big players are there – Starbucks, Nescafé, Califia Farms – and all with the three-quarters (or more) milk to one quarter (or less) coffee ratio typical of a latte. The difference is that these drinks all have added sugar or sweeteners, thereby turning your morning coffee into a liquid pudding. If they contain dairy milk, it tends to be UHT (not a taste I like), although some use lactose-free or plant-based milks. The best of the bunch was Grind’s Iced Vanilla Oat Latte: less milk (57%), more coffee (40%) and less sugar, too.
As far as I could tell, Emmi’s Caffe Latte High Protein is no higher in protein than any of the rest, so it strikes me that the brand may simply be jumping on what’s becoming a rather hackneyed bandwagon catering to a health-anxious and possibly appetite-suppressed crowd. Yfood’s This Is Food, meanwhile, made me quickly wonder: “Is it?” This ready-to-drink, coffee-flavoured “complete meal” with 30g protein per bottle and more than 20 ingredients is a sorry substitute for a food, and it certainly isn’t coffee.
Cold brew – that is, coffee that has been steeped in cold water for an extended period for a softer, more naturally sweet result – takes a fair while to make, so I can see the point in buying it off the shelf: Tesco and Nescafé both make inoffensive unsweetened cold-brew concentrates that are a good option for an Indian summer. And, much to my surprise, I rather enjoyed the next-gen flavoured instant coffees by Little’s and Beanies, especially the former’s glazed cinnamon number. But as much as Union from my moka? Come off it.
Four coffee drinks worth your attention
Grind Iced Vanilla Oat Latte £2.25 (250ml) Ocado. The best example of this dubious genre: a not-too-sweet, good-quality cold brew blended with oat milk.
Tesco Finest Cold Brew Coffee £4.50 (500ml). A cold brew concentrate to which you just add water. Would be nice with a slice of citrus.
Little’s Glazed Cinnamon £4 (50g) Ocado. The doughnut vibes are more in the aroma than the taste, but it’s a scent that could seduce non-coffee drinkers.
Union House Roast £7.50 (200g) Ocado. You can’t beat a home brew, and this balanced, slightly chocolatey all-rounder is my food shop stalwart.

Taiwan’s quiet push into Chinese studies in Naples
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:00:15 UTC
21:00:15 KST

Inside the Hall of Mirrors at Palazzo Corigliano in Italy‘s Naples, a quiet but meaningful agreement was signed Sept. 4.
Weng Chih-tsung (翁誌聰), acting director-general of Taiwan’s National Central Library, and Roberto Tottoli, rector of the University of Naples “L’Orientale,” inked a partnership creating Italy’s third Taiwan Resource Center for Chinese Studies. It looked like routine academic diplomacy. It was not.
L’Orientale is no ordinary university. Founded in 1732 by missionary Matteo Ripa, it is the oldest school of Sinology in Europe, teaching Mandarin since 1724 — decades before most Western nations had ever heard the word.
Its prestige in Chinese studies is unmatched on the continent. That is precisely why Taiwan wanted this signature.
Since 2007, L’Orientale has also hosted a Confucius Institute, established jointly with Shanghai International Studies University under China’s state-run Confucius Institute network. L’Orientale’s own rector, Roberto Tottoli, serves as its president, while SISU’s director, Li Yansong, sits as co-president.
Cultural reach
So, the very same historic halls that teach Chinese language under Beijing-linked sponsorship now also host Taiwan’s own cultural outreach.
This is not accidental. In the US, 104 of the 118 Confucius Institutes that once operated there have closed, according to a 2022 report by the National Association of Scholars.
They were accused by critics, including the Heritage Foundation, of functioning as instruments of Chinese Communist Party influence and academic censorship on topics like Tibet or the Cultural Revolution. Sweden became the first European country to shut down its last Confucius classroom in 2020. Universities across Europe have grown wary too.
Taiwan saw the opening and moved. Since 2021, its Overseas Community Affairs Council has built a network of Taiwan Centers for Mandarin Learning, reaching 93 sites worldwide by mid-2026.
The majority are in the US, with three in Italy. Unlike Confucius Institutes, instructors answer to no foreign government, and they teach traditional characters, the script still used in Taiwan, not the simplified system promoted by Beijing.
OCAC Minister Hsu Chia-ching (徐佳青) recently put it plainly: Taiwan’s Mandarin education “can’t stay confined” to old diaspora circles, it must reach the wider world. The message is strategic as much as cultural: language as a bridge, but also as a quiet declaration of identity.
Choosing sides
What Naples received was concrete, not symbolic alone.
The National Central Library, now connected to 58 partner institutions worldwide, delivered 248 volumes on Chinese and Taiwanese studies, with annual expansions, digital archives, research databases, and two precious facsimiles, including one of the Diamond Sutra. L’Orientale joins Ca’ Foscari University of Venice and Sapienza University of Rome, both partners since 2018, completing a trio considered Italy’s leading centers for Chinese studies.
Taiwan is not asking Italian universities to choose sides outright. However, by building resource centers inside the very institutions that still host Confucius Institutes, Taipei is offering something Beijing’s model increasingly struggles to provide: transparency, academic independence, and a living connection to a functioning, pluralistic Chinese-speaking democracy.
It is cultural diplomacy at its most effective, patient, precise, and quietly winning ground Beijing can no longer hold.
Naples did not close its Confucius Institute on Sept. 4 but instead opened a second door — the one built in Taipei, not Beijing. In the long, patient competition for how the world learns to read, write, and understand Chinese, that door matters.

Exclusive: The Admiral Who Must Prevent War With China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

In the summer of 1986, when he was a college student in Pennsylvania, Samuel Paparo took his future wife Maureen to watch Top Gun.
Many young Americans emerged from theaters across the country with a new hero: the brash, daring, risk-taking Maverick, played by Tom Cruise, who became an avatar of American power at the twilight of the Cold War. But Paparo took away a different lesson.
“The hero of the movie is supposed to be Maverick, but the hero of the movie is actually Iceman,” Paparo tells TIME, referring to the main character’s rival at the elite Navy pilot training school. “Maverick’s got all the personal charisma, but Iceman is fastidious, quiet. He’s the hard-working guy that does the right thing, that doesn’t do flashy, dangerous stuff for its own sake.”
Paparo had already passed the Navy’s entrance exams when he went into the theater that day, and joined the next year. His career would precisely mirror the fictional Iceman’s: He attended the Navy Fighter Weapons School, also known as TOPGUN; became a fighter pilot; then a four-star admiral; and eventually commanded the Pacific Fleet. But Paparo would go further, taking the helm of the U.S. Pacific Command, the nation’s oldest and largest geographic combatant command, which covers about half of the earth’s surface.
Few Americans will have heard of Admiral Paparo, and that suits him fine. “If I do my job right, history will never know my name,” he says in his office at the headquarters of the U.S. Pacific Command in Hawaii, on a hill overlooking Pearl Harbor, in late July. But his role places him at an inflection point, as American dominance in the Pacific faces its most serious challenge since World War II.
His command is designed to be the immovable object that blocks the unstoppable force of China’s expansionist ambitions in the region. And those ambitions have been stated clearly: Beijing has vowed to bring Taiwan, the self-ruling island that has been politically separate from the mainland since China’s civil war ended in 1949, under its control—by force if necessary. China’s President Xi Jinping has described unification as “a historical inevitability.”
Paparo’s job, in its simplest terms, is the projection of American power. His most important mission is to deter a Chinese invasion of Taiwan, an event that would challenge the very foundations of a global system underpinned by American hegemony. That the outlines of this mission stay the same regardless of which party or President is in the White House speaks to the importance of his role. The force Paparo builds and the plans he puts in place last for decades, and could determine to whom the next century belongs.
The public face of American military power is, of course, the Commander in Chief. The public voice emanates from the Oval Office and the podium in the White House press briefing room. But behind that power sits commanders like Paparo, overseeing the often hidden and awesome infrastructure that backs up that public face and voice—his command oversees some 400,000 military and civilian personnel, a Pacific Fleet of some 200 ships, including five aircraft carrier strike groups, and more than 1,000 aircraft. He marshals that power in distant oceans, islands, and military bases that most Americans will never see or even think about.
With President Donald Trump set to meet Thursday with China’s Xi for their third face-to-face summit since he returned to office, the cameras are trained on the White House; reporters will parse each utterance by the two leaders to divine whether the two powers are heading toward cooperation or conflict. It is Paparo’s job to ensure that whatever happens when the leaders talk, U.S. power remains pre-eminent—and that if somehow in the future conflict breaks out, it comes out on top. He must hold to that approach even as wars elsewhere consume the munitions and resources he may need, and upheaval at the Pentagon raises the stakes of pushing back.
“I’m almost quoting Sun Tzu when I say winning without fighting is the acme of skill,” he says, referencing the Chinese military strategist who wrote The Art of War. “Mission success for me is not to fight and win a war; it’s to provide a deterrent capability so that we never go to war in the first place.”
Paparo, 61, speaks deliberately and in a low voice, smiling often. But when conversation turns serious, so does his expression—his brows become furrowed, and he stares into the middle distance to summon his words. “We don’t seek to become great wartime leaders,” he says. “We seek to be great peacetime deterrers.”
What if deterrence doesn’t work? The U.S. emerged from World War II with its dominance of the Pacific unquestioned, but that may now be changing. Over the past few decades, as China has transformed into the world’s second largest economy, it has been engaged in a historic military buildup. China’s defense spending has increased 13-fold over the past three decades, and it now spends more on defense than the next 22 Indo-Pacific countries combined, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), a bipartisan Washington, D.C.–based think tank. It has made rapid technological advances in artificial intelligence and fielded several generations of fighter jets. Its navy has grown from a coastal force into something capable of projecting global power, and by hull count it is now the largest in the world.
Brian Hart, deputy director of the China Power Project at CSIS, describes it as a “comprehensive, across-the-board modernization effort,” one that has changed the calculus for every power in the Pacific. The People’s Liberation Army, he tells TIME, has “significantly transformed the balance of power.”
Paparo need only look out his office window at the turquoise waters of Pearl Harbor to be reminded of the last time U.S. supremacy in the Pacific was truly tested. He describes China’s buildup as “historic” and “an exponential increase in military power, and more specifically, in power projection capability.”
“Twenty-five years ago the People’s Liberation Army Navy was about 37 warships, and today it’s 12 times that,” he says. “Just in the last 18 months they’ve delivered two cruisers, eight destroyers, eight frigates, an aircraft carrier, 11 submarines, four amphibious ships, and four long-range combat logistics ships.” He is particularly concerned by China’s advances in space and missile development and the rapid expansion of its nuclear arsenal. “They’re moving toward world reach,” he says.
For all of its global ambitions, much of China’s military development has been pursued with one target in mind. U.S. intelligence assesses that China’s Xi has ordered his military to be capable of seizing Taiwan by force by 2027, the centenary of the People’s Liberation Army. The intelligence community’s annual threat assessment, released in March, suggests no invasion is currently planned for next year, but by then, the pieces Xi needs to do so will likely be in place.
If there appears to be a path to capturing Taiwan without using force, Xi insists he would prefer to take it. Presidential elections in Taiwan in January 2028 may provide some clarity in that regard: China’s old rival, the Kuomintang, is increasingly amenable to negotiations with Beijing. If the political party wins in 2028, the likelihood of an invasion may decrease. If Taiwan’s President Lai Ching-te, a fierce opponent of China’s sovereignty claims, wins reelection, Hart says, “Beijing could significantly ramp up pressure on Taiwan.”
Paparo’s job is to convince Xi that the costs of military action will be too much to bear, regardless of what is happening politically on the island. By act of Congress, the U.S. is obliged to sell Taiwan the weapons it needs for its own defense; while it does not require the U.S. to defend the island directly, the commitment could go further to include direct conflict with China. He describes his mission as a delicate balancing act between ensuring that his counterparts know American capabilities well enough to understand the risks of engaging, and protecting its necessary secrets and strategy. “It’s demonstrating credible combat power, demonstrating capability and will, but keeping the crown jewels of the nation that are going to deliver combat success opaque to your counterparts, so that they can’t build a counter for it,” he says.
Paparo describes the strategy as deterrence by denial. “It’s a way of expressing that we’re not seeking the overthrow of the Communist Party,” he says. “It’s just that you should know that where America’s direct vital interests are involved, there’s a high probability of denying your aggression.”
This theory of deterrence operates on a grand, geopolitical scale, and in much smaller interactions. Paparo recounts a confrontation with a Chinese counterpart over what he describes as an “unsafe” encounter in June 2023 during a transit of the Taiwan Strait in which a Chinese Luyang destroyer cut across the bow of an American ship.
In the ensuing back-and-forth, Paparo told his counterpart that he had been in command at the watch center for the engagement and had video showing that their version of events was not true. He offered to share it, then let the matter rest.
“I’m not going to impugn his own character in it. He’s representing his country. He’s in uniform, and you know, if we do have a fight, him and I might have to shake hands at the end and agree to go to our separate sides,” he says.
In that moment, Paparo chose a diplomatic approach. He does, however, have a more direct plan to deter a Chinese attack on Taiwan. It is based on a term he uses to describe the environment Chinese forces would walk into if they took military action: “Hellscape.”
The strategy has been partly inspired by Ukraine’s defense against Russian invasion, and its ability to halt Moscow’s advances by turning the front lines of that conflict into a no-man’s-land patrolled by killer drones. Paparo would aim to saturate the Taiwan Strait with cheap, mass-produced precision drones, along with more conventional high-tech missile power, to deny China the ability to land an amphibious assault, or at least significantly delay it.
“We’ve seen that assault warfare, whether that is an amphibious assault, an airborne assault, has become a much more costly human endeavor,” he says. “In the ways that Ukraine is about a 600-mile-by-30-mile hellscape of drone warfare, I seek to put those principles at work to deter an armed invasion.”
He continues: “Putting 21st century technological change to work for the United States of America is what that’s about. We need not gain air or maritime superiority of a space; we need only deny its use to aggressors.”
Direct American involvement in a conflict over Taiwan is by no means assured. Paparo is tasked with building a force to confront China, but the President will decide how to respond. “The highest ideals of American civil-military relations are such that policy is king,” he says.
Who would win that conflict is something that is fiercely debated. A 2023 CSIS war game found that the U.S. and its allies defeated a Chinese amphibious invasion of Taiwan in most scenarios, but the costs to the U.S. were substantial: two aircraft carriers, dozens of ships, and hundreds of aircraft, the heaviest American losses since World War II. Those war games were run before the war in Iran depleted U.S. missile stocks.
“I am confident in our ability to prevail,” Paparo says. “What I am working toward is the margin by which we do, and that margin expresses itself in lives, capability, money, and time. I want to drive that bill down to zero.”
An enormous map of the Indo-Pacific theater lines the wall of Paparo’s office. His desk overlooks a large room adorned with historical Pacific artifacts and gifts given to the admiral and his predecessors: a five-star flag that belonged to General Douglas MacArthur; a barometer gifted to Admiral Harry Harris Jr., who led the command from 2015 to 2018, by China’s Ministry of National Defense. Closer to his desk is a large computer screen showing the positions of every vessel under his command. As he toggles through the ships on the screen to demonstrate the scale of his fleet, he pauses somewhere near the Indian Ocean to press home a point: His command is not merely preparing for war; it is fighting one. “The Iranian frigate was sunk by us,” he says. He is referring to an incident in March, when the U.S.S. Charlotte submarine torpedoed and sank the Iranian navy frigate IRIS Dena in the Indian Ocean as it was returning to Iran from India, where it had taken part in an international exercise. More than 100 Iranian sailors were killed. Paparo’s forces have also helped enforce a blockade of Iran’s coastline and support logistics for the war.
That the U.S. Pacific Command is fighting one war on one side of the world while preparing for another 6,000 miles away in the Taiwan Strait is a measure of its scale. As he stands in front of his map, Paparo sweeps his arm down the Western seaboard, along the coast to Southern California, and across the central Pacific, pointing out an array of U.S. territories and possessions. These places may seem like distant lands to many Americans. To Paparo, they are as much a part of the U.S. as New York or California. To see the Pacific in this way is to understand the meaning behind this projection of power: it’s not just for the protection of an important strategic partner in Taiwan; it is for the protection of the U.S. itself. “There’s no more Pacific a country in the world than the United States of America,” he says.
It’s not just about Taiwan and China, either. The North Koreans, he says, “are seeking a nuclear deterrent” and want to present the world with a “fait accompli.” The Russians “have increased their air, missile, and maritime capabilities.”
Much of the job is managing friends rather than enemies. The Pentagon has called on Paparo to mediate between allies at odds with one another, and he says there is nothing new in that. Those military-to-military relationships, he adds, “tend to be an anchor that attenuates the ups and downs of policy disagreements among political leaders ... but it always respects the national policy of our civilian leadership.”
Few conflicts in the world today do not brush up against the Indo-Pacific theater or impact it in some way. The Iran war and U.S. support for Ukraine have placed severe strain on the resources available to all commands, causing a depletion in the stockpiles for missile defense like the Patriot and THAAD systems, and in long-range ground attack missiles, according to the Pentagon and CSIS estimates.
In May, a planned $14 billion arms package for Taiwan was put under review in part to preserve munitions for the Iran war. Experts have warned it may take years to replenish those stocks, a timeline that could affect the calculus of China and Russia.
Those shortages are no secret, but it’s a perilous time to be out of step with the White House and the Pentagon. At least 20 top military leaders, including generals and admirals, have been fired or left their positions since Pete Hegseth became Secretary of Defense at the start of the second Trump Administration. The turmoil culminated in the late August resignation of Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who reportedly left his role after clashing with Hegseth over the firings of senior generals and the Secretary’s alleged stymieing of Army modernization efforts in the midst of a U.S. war against Iran.
Hegseth has characterized those departures as part of a campaign to undo what he saw as the promotion of “woke” leadership. In a speech in September 2025 in Quantico, Va., to the military’s generals and admirals, all of whom were required to attend, Hegseth criticized the promotion of leaders for what he described as “the wrong reasons, based on their race, based on gender quotas, based on historic so-called firsts.” Paparo was visible in the front row of that gathering, his expression giving nothing away.
He has been careful in his public remarks about the impact the war in Iran has had on the readiness of his command. When questioned in the Senate about how prolonged conflict could impinge on his mission, Paparo conceded only that “there are finite limits to the magazine, and I have all the faith in the world that they’re being employed judiciously.”
In private, he appears to have been more candid. Paparo’s name emerged recently in a Washington Post report on a classified assessment, along with other combatant commanders, in which he is said to have objected to the continued use of an aircraft carrier strike group and destroyers for the war in Iran. He was also named in a New York Times report as one of several “private interlocutors” who had been offering “unvarnished” views of the Iran war to Vice President JD Vance. Vance’s team declined to comment on the report.
Ward Carroll, a Navy veteran who flew in F-14s and a friend of Paparo’s for many years, says the admiral’s circumspection is part of his character. “He doesn’t want headlines,” he says. “He’s not out there like some other folks have been, saying Epic Fury was a huge mistake. He may say it in private ... but he’s certainly not going to say it to the media or allow it to be leaked.” Paparo excels, Carroll says, by choosing not to “wade into the food fight that is modern-day media and politics at all.” A spokesperson for Pacific Command declined to comment on Paparo’s private conversations about the Iran war.
When TIME asks Paparo about the potential impact of Ukraine and Iran, he is again cautious, pivoting to the lessons the U.S. is learning from both: namely the rapid deployment of drones in Ukraine and of AI-enabled operations in Iran, which were used to select and recommend targets for the U.S. military.
“The nature of an operation in the Pacific would be to counter an amphibious invasion. Well, we’ve just not used a lot of anti-ship weapons—we still maintain robust inventories of those,” he says. “And so, while I’m not going to whistle past the problem of the expenditure of munitions, it is our job to charge into the learning, and for us to get better.”
If there is a permanence to America’s projection of power in the Pacific, it can also be found in Paparo’s own family. His father Samuel Paparo Sr., who died in February, served four years in the Marine Corps before becoming a shipworker at the Philadelphia Naval Shipyard. There he helped refit the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Kitty Hawk and repair the U.S.S. John F. Kennedy. The younger Paparo would later fly from both. “He was really proud of that,” he says of his father. His grandfather was a Seabee, serving in one of the Navy’s construction battalions across the Pacific during World War II, in Bora Bora, Guam, and other islands. He died when Paparo was 13, but he left behind an old wooden scrapbook he had built with pictures from the war and all the places he had been. A young Paparo would pick it up from time to time and leaf through it. “I don’t think he imagined his grandson to be here in command,” he says.
His mother washed hair in a South Philadelphia barbershop and later worked a makeup counter in a department store. “Neither my father nor his father finished high school. In fact, nobody in my family before me had ever had a university education,” he says. He would later attend Villanova, the Catholic college also attended by the first American Pontiff, Pope Leo XIV. “We make Popes and admirals,” he says of his alma mater.
He joined TOPGUN, whose exacting culture left a lasting impression. “What the school confers is attention to detail, dedication to execution, dedication to getting better, and being introspective and running to your own problems, of seeking the perfect flight that you’ll never get,” he adds. He flew F-14, F-15, and F/A-18 jets, and clocked more than 6,000 flight hours and 1,100 carrier landings. He says he initially aimed to serve as long as his father. “Serving for four years was intentional, and serving for 40 was a blessing,” he adds.
Paparo’s time leading the Pacific Command is historic not just for the opponent he faces, but also because it coincides with a rapid and dramatic change in the nature of warfare. On one wall of his office hangs a reprint of a TIME cover from May 18, 1942, depicting Admiral Chester Nimitz, the naval commander who led the U.S. to victory over Japan at sea in the Pacific war. Nimitz took command of the Pacific Fleet in December 1941, also at a time of great technological change.
After Pearl Harbor, and under Nimitz’s watch, the battleship would be eclipsed by the aircraft carrier. Amphibious warfare would be revolutionized and directed under a single commander. And then there was the kamikaze—organized suicide attacks by aircraft flown by Japanese pilots—and their foreshadowing of the questions posed by the advancement of unmanned aerial drones in warfare today. “He adapted to change, including the unknown,” Paparo says of Nimitz. “That’s the greatest leadership model I can think of.”
Paparo hopes that he never has to fight the war he has spent so long preparing for, that his plans go untested and passed on to the next commander. In the meantime, he will continue with the quiet work. “Mine is not a heroic story,” he says. “Heroism is service that happens at the unforgiving hour. The best service prevents the unforgiving hour.”

‘Peace remains only a promise’ for millions in eastern DR Congo, General Assembly hears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘Peace remains only a promise’ for millions in eastern DR Congo, General Assembly hears
The Prime Minister of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) cautioned against growing global demand for “blood-stained minerals” in the rush to net-zero, in her speech to the UN General Assembly.
Against a backdrop of decades of violent insecurity and mass displacement in the resource-rich eastern region of the vast country – where a deadly Ebola outbreak is also spreading – Judith Suminwa insisted on Wednesday that few other situations “illustrate so painfully the gap between international commitments and [people’s] lived reality”.
“We cannot build a decarbonized economy through blood-stained minerals,” she said. “And we will not bring about a just transition by reproducing a greenwashed version of our past dependencies.”
Speaking to leaders gathered at UN headquarters in New York, she maintained that the DRC “continues to face a war of aggression led by Rwanda through its proxy the AFC/M23” (Alliance Fleuve Congo/M23 Movement). Other armed groups, particularly the Allied Defense Forces (ADF) and CODECO are exacerbating the humanitarian crisis.
Elusive peace
The Prime Minister pointed to several developments that have opened up prospects for an end to violence, such as the peace agreement signed in Washington, DC, in June 2025, between the DRC and Rwanda.
She noted, however, that “for millions of Congolese, this peace remains only a promise”.
She said UN Security Resolution 2773 (2025) “has laid out an unambiguous path” in its call for an effective cessation of hostilities, the withdrawal of Rwandan forces from Congolese territory and restoration of State authority, among other measures.
“But we don't need new texts to replace those that have already been adopted,” she said.
Repatriation of FDLR fighters
Ms. Suminwa also addressed issues surrounding the Democratic Forces for the Freedom of Rwanda (FDLR), a largely ethnic Hutu armed group, recalling that a protocol signed in May provides for the disarmament and demobilization of its combatants.
Earlier this month, the UN peacekeeping mission in the DRC, known as MONUSCO, supported the repatriation of 120 people associated with the group, which she called “a first testament to the protocol's implementation”.
A just transition and jobs
The Prime Minister pointed to rising demand for copper, cobalt, lithium, nickel and other critical minerals, including to power the energy transition and expansion of digital and AI infrastructure.
She said the DRC is at the heart of the transition, being the largest global producer of cobalt - used in making lithium batteries and digital equipment, for example - and a major producer of copper.
“It would be both unjust and dangerous for added value, jobs, know-how, and technologies to remain concentrated far away from the communities that are making these changes possible,” she warned.
She said that the DRC “rejects the old model that limits producer countries to crude extraction while processing, research, technology, and the bulk of the profits are concentrated elsewhere”.
Going forward, the country wants to join African and international partners to build “competitive regional businesses that create jobs, skills, and shared prosperity”.

Palestinian existence under threat, Abbas tells UN, warning of ‘another Nakba’
Israeli policies now threaten “the very life and existence of the Palestinian people on their homeland”, Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas told the UN General Assembly on Thursday, urging the world not to allow “another Nakba”.
Mr. Abbas addressed the Assembly’s annual debate via pre-recorded video after his delegation was, for the second consecutive year, denied the visas needed to travel to the US – measures he called unlawful and a breach of the United States’ obligations as host country.
He called on the US administration to reverse such measures and “return to the language of dialogue and mutual respect.”
He said Palestinians in Gaza were being subjected to killing, destruction, starvation, attempted forced displacement and a “a war of genocide”, while in the West Bank settlement expansion was accelerating.
He added that East Jerusalem was being isolated and settler terrorism was escalating under the occupation forces. Moreover, crimes of land theft, home demolitions, roadblocks and incursions continue.
‘Not separate events’
What is happening in Gaza and in the West Bank and East Jerusalem “are not separate events”, he said, but “part of a malicious colonial plan” to make Palestinian life harder and drive people to forced departure from their land.
“For how long will some States continue to remain silent about Israel, or supply it with the weapons it uses against our people?” he asked.
Mr. Abbas said he had welcomed President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan as well as the Security Council resolution 2803, which endorsed the plan and called on all parties to implement it, but had not seen any of it materialize on the ground.
With one year left of a transitional period due to end in 2027, he called for the second phase to be implemented without further delay, leading to the reunification of Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, under “one State, one government, one law and a single legitimate authority over arms”.
He warned against the Israeli E1 Settlement Plan, which he said would cut East Jerusalem off from the rest of Palestine, and called for implementation of Security Council Resolution 2334 on halting settlement activity.
He also called for continued support for the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA), saying there was “no alternative to the agency” while the refugee question remains unresolved, and demanded the release of more than $6 billion in Palestinian funds withheld by Israel.
‘Honored our commitments’
A year after the General Assembly endorsed the New York Declaration, which seeks to resolve the Israeli-Palestinian conflict through a two-State solution, Mr. Abbas said, “we have honored our commitments”, citing reforms to public finance, social protection and school curricula in cooperation with the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO).
Legislative elections will be held on 28 November, he said, followed by renewal of the Palestinian National Council and presidential elections.
“We want a democratic Palestinian state that respects the rule of law and human rights – an unarmed state living in security and peace alongside the State of Israel,” he said.
He thanked the 160 states that have recognized the State of Palestine, urged the others to follow and called for full UN membership.
“We will not leave our homeland. We will not accept displacement. We will not allow anyone to decide our future on our behalf,” he said.

World News in Brief, ‘New intensity’ to Russian attacks on Ukraine, Yemen, Gaza and Colombia updates

World News in Brief: ‘New intensity’ to Russian attacks on Ukraine, Yemen, Gaza and Colombia updates
Russian armed forces have carried out repeated attacks across Ukraine over the past several days, killing and injuring civilians and damaging homes, hospitals, shops and workplaces, UN human rights monitors said on Thursday.
The attacks have involved ballistic and cruise missiles, drones and guided aerial bombs. Between 1 and 24 September, the Mission recorded at least 200 civilians killed and 1,234 injured – figures expected to rise as verification continues.
Vegetable warehouse hit
In the latest strike on Thursday, Russian forces hit a vegetable sorting facility on a farm in Stara Hnylytsia, Kharkiv region, killing seven civilians and injuring 12 others, local authorities said. All were reportedly farm workers sorting vegetables at the time.
“Workers have been killed while sorting vegetables. Families have been caught beneath the rubble of their homes,” said Danielle Bell, head of the Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, citing hits on shopping centres, pharmacies, food warehouses and fuel stations.
“This is 48 hours in Ukraine, and it comes after months of mounting civilian casualties.”
Kyiv saw civilian casualties on 16 of the first 24 days of September, the highest monthly frequency since the full-scale invasion began.
Odesa has also faced repeated attacks, while Ukraine has stepped up strikes on Russian territory, where local authorities report growing civilian casualties.
Yemen’s people have suffered enough, warns Türk
Amid ongoing fighting in Yemen between Government forces and Houthi rebels, UN human rights chief Volker Türk highlighted the “appalling” civilian toll on Thursday.
In a statement urging all sides to halt the violence, the High Commissioner for Human Rights said around 125,000 people have been uprooted from their homes, many forced to flee for their lives.
OHCHR spokesperson Jeremy Laurence called for an end to the escalation, urged respect for and protection of civilians and civilian infrastructure, and said humanitarian assistance should reach “all those who need it”.
“The people of Yemen cannot withstand another full-scale conflict,” he said.
Since the start of August, OHCHR has documented the killing of 32 civilians, including 15 children and three women.
Houthi offensive
The emergency follows the Iran-backed Houthi fighters’ rapid advance down Yemen’s western coast to the Bab el-Mandeb, clashing with Saudi-backed Yemeni Government forces.
International human rights law prohibits targeting civilians, whose protection must be the overriding priority, Mr. Türk said.
OHCHR also demanded the immediate release of 73 UN staff members, and others, arbitrarily detained by the Houthis – also known as “Ansar Allah” – some for many years. “Their ongoing detention…is intolerable and unacceptable,” Mr. Türk said, adding that he feared for their safety amid the renewed fighting.
Gaza’s economic collapse has wiped out decades of development
War has hollowed out Gaza’s economy to such an extent that people now earn just 58 cents a day, the UN Trade and Development agency (UNCTAD) said on Thursday.
In its annual report on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, the agency said 92 per cent of Gaza’s businesses are now damaged or destroyed.
Hundreds of thousands of jobs have been lost since 2023, and unemployment is “unprecedented”, with more than nine in 10 working-age adults now out of work.
“The military operation has gutted nearly every business,” said Mutasim Elagraa, UN Trade and Development Coordinator, speaking in Geneva.
“That means productive capacity is wiped out, while the entire population is displaced and condemned to multidimensional poverty.”
Basic needs go unmet
“By multidimensional poverty, I mean not just income poverty. It’s also a lack of proper shelter, and a lack of access to basic services like health, education and sanitation.”
Housing has sustained more damage than any other sector, the report found, as a result of the war sparked by Hamas-led terror attacks on Israel in October 2023. Rebuilding homes alone will cost an estimated $19 billion, Mr. Elagraa said.
According to President Trump’s Board of Peace, around $71 billion will be needed over the next decade to rebuild Gaza.
Colombia’s new drug-trafficking laws reinforce ‘systemic racism’, say rights experts
Colombia’s renewed efforts to combat drug traffickers risk reinforcing systemic racism against people of African descent, independent rights experts reporting to the UN Human Rights Council warned on Thursday.
The warning follows the Colombian Government’s announcement that it intends to take a more forceful response to armed groups and drug gangs, including more arrests and law enforcement operations. After taking office in August, the Government also announced renewed efforts to eradicate illegal crops, including by spraying herbicide from aircraft.
Clashes continue
It is 10 years since the Government and the FARC-EP armed opposition reached a UN-backed peace deal aimed at ending decades of conflict, though clashes between security forces and drug gangs continue across the country.
The UN International Independent Expert Mechanism to Advance Racial Justice and Equality in Law Enforcement warned that “predominantly punitive, militarised…approaches have failed to restore peace”, adding that security-led programmes have had a “disproportionate impact on Afro-Colombian communities, particularly in territories affected by armed violence, illicit economies and limited State presence”.
After visiting Colombia earlier this year, the independent experts, who are not UN staff, maintained that people of African descent continue to suffer “deeply rooted” systemic racism in law enforcement and criminal justice institutions.
Racial stereotypes linking people of African descent with criminality continue to influence police encounters, disciplinary sanctions, and access to justice and effective remedy, they said.

Scientists find two tiny new snails with shells that close like doors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:59:43 UTC
20:59:43 KST

Scientists find two tiny new snails with shells that close like doors
- Date:
- September 24, 2026
- Source:
- Pensoft Publishers
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered two tiny new snail species in Montenegro, showing that even Europe still holds animals unknown to science. One lives in the threatened Komarnica Canyon, where a proposed hydropower reservoir could destroy habitat before its full biodiversity is understood.
- Share:
Two newly identified snail species have expanded the known diversity of European land snails. The species, Cochlostoma komarnica and Cochlostoma dobrido, are described in a new study published in the open-access Biodiversity Data Journal.
Neither species has an English common name yet. Both are small, with cone-shaped shells measuring about 6 mm in length, and they live on limestone rocks where they feed on algae and lichens.
They also have several unusual features. Unlike most land snails, their eyes are positioned along the sides of the head rather than at the tips of eye stalks. They also carry a circular disk attached to the tail that can seal the shell opening like a door when the animal retreats inside.
New Species Found in Montenegro's Mountains
The snails were discovered during expeditions organized by Taxon Expeditions, an initiative that allows members of the public to take part in genuine scientific fieldwork.
Between 2018 and 2025, expeditions in Montenegro were carried out through a partnership involving Taxon Expeditions, the non-profit Taxon Foundation, and local collaborators from the Montenegrin Ecologists Society.
The field teams brought together international researchers, citizen scientists, local students, and conservationists to investigate the biodiversity of Durmitor National Park and Komarnica Canyon.
Researchers encountered the snails at several locations while working in the region's rugged mountain terrain. However, it was not immediately clear that they represented species unknown to science. That became evident only after the animals were dissected and genetically analysed in the field laboratory.
Named After the Places Where They Were Found
The expedition team chose the names during a vote held at camp.
"Cochlostoma dobrido," was named after the Dobri Do Plateau, located among the peaks of Durmitor National Park. "Cochlostoma komarnica," takes its name from the stunning but unprotected Komarnica Canyon, which lies south of Durmitor.
"I was amazed that it is still possible to discover new animal species in Europe," says musician Janine Buisman from The Netherlands, who participated in one of the expeditions and later became a co-author of the paper.
Biologist Jovana Đokić of the Montenegrin Ecologists Society (MES), another author of the study, says the canyons, mountains, and gorges of this part of the Balkans contain extensive biodiversity that remains poorly explored, with many species potentially still waiting to be documented.
Komarnica Canyon Faces a Hydropower Threat
Đokić says that makes plans affecting Komarnica Canyon especially concerning.
"It is all the more worrying that the Komarnica Canyon is targeted to be flooded by a hydropower dam and reservoir. This will destroy this wild river canyon and all the biodiversity in it, including many species still unknown to science."
- Jovana Đokić
The proposed development has helped make Komarnica Canyon a major focus of organized biodiversity surveys. Researchers and conservation groups are documenting its wildlife in an effort to build a scientific case for protecting the area.
MES is calling for Komarnica Canyon to become part of the UNESCO World Heritage site of Durmitor and for plans for the hydropower project to be abandoned.
"Hydropower is neither green nor sustainable energy when it destroys a unique ecosystem like this," says Đokić.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Pensoft Publishers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Menno Schilthuizen, Rob Boomsma, Sofie Faes, Marije Jousma, Janine Buisman, Dirk-H. Lankenau, Sotiris Kountouras, Marlijn van den Broek, Elisabeth Hemelaar, Jeroen Noomen, Rick de Vries, Giulia Lopatriello, Antonina Rita Limongi, Simone Maestri, Panche Kamchev, Siebe van Manen, Mohd Zacaery Khalik, Massimo Delledonne, Jovana Đokić, Andrijana Mićanović, Jelena Popović, Iva Njunjić, Enrico Zallot. Two new Cochlostoma species from the Durmitor and Komarnica regions of northern Montenegro (Caenogastropoda, Cochlostomatidae). Biodiversity Data Journal, 2026; 14 DOI: 10.3897/BDJ.14.e196955

Experimental project releases 30,000 mosquitoes in Lisbon that do not bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:59:24 UTC
20:59:24 KST

Thirty thousand sterile male mosquitoes will be released on Thursday in Alvalade, Lisbon, in a final trial to curb the Asian tiger mosquito, which spreads dengue, zika and yellow fever.
Lisbon will release 30,000 mosquitoes this Thursday. Yes, you read that right, but rest assured, they don't bite.
They are sterile male Asian tiger mosquitoes belonging to the species 'Aedes albopictus' and will be released in the Lisbon parish of Alvalade. They are part of anexperimental project whose ultimate aim is to reduce the population of the Asian tiger mosquito, because of its implications for public health.
The project focuses on the Asian tiger mosquito because of its implications for public health, as it can transmit diseases such as dengue, Zika and yellow fever, with the risk arising if the mosquito bites an infected person and subsequently passes the pathogen on to another person.
This is not the first time this has been done. In total, 60,000 mosquitoes have already been released in Portugal and this will be the last release of this type of insect.
Speaking to the Lusa news agency, Afonso Moreira, a public health doctor at the Francisco George Public Health Unit of the Santa Maria Local Health Unit, explained that these mosquitoes were sterilised using a proven and safe technique.
"When we release them into areas where there is a population of this mosquito, they will essentially compete with the male mosquitoes that are already there, the wild mosquitoes," said the project leader.
The aim is to assess whether this competition reduces the species' reproduction, given that mating with sterile males does not produce offspring. And since only females need blood, reducing the number of wild males and the opportunities for reproduction would help control the number of mosquitoes of this species that can bite humans.
However, the researcher stressed that in this first phase the main objective is to understand how the released specimens behave, particularly their ability to disperse and survive in the intervention area.
If the results of the first stage are positive, further progress in the research is expected in May, with a comparative study between areas where the mosquito has been released and areas where it is being controlled.
Speaking to Lusa, Afonso Moreira stressed that the release of sterile mosquitoes is only one of the control measures, and argued that it remains essential to continue eliminating the places where this species breeds.

Details

Delhi High Court dismisses YouTuber Ajeet Bharti’s anticipatory bail plea in caste remarks case
NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court on Thursday refused to grant anticipatory bail to YouTuber Ajeet Bharti in a case over alleged casteist and derogatory remarks against Nagina MP Chandrashekhar Azad, holding that the plea was not maintainable.Justice Saurabh Banerjee dismissed Bharti’s pre-arrest bail plea, saying a case under the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act was prima facie made out against him. The court also noted the statutory bar on granting anticipatory bail under the Act."In view of the fact that a case under the provisions of the SC/ST Act is prima facie made out against the applicant and considering the statutory bar (on grant of bail) under the SC/ST Act, the present petition seeking grant of anticipatory bail is dismissed being not maintainable," the judge said while pronouncing the verdict.
The high court had reserved its order on September 16 after hearing arguments from Bharti's counsel, the Delhi Police and Azad.Bharti had moved the high court after a Delhi trial court rejected his anticipatory bail plea on September 7. The trial court had found that the material before it prima facie disclosed the ingredients of an offence under the SC/ST Act and that the statutory bar on pre-arrest bail applied.
Bharti's counsel argued before the high court that the SC/ST Act was not attracted because there was no intentional insult or humiliation. He said the remarks should be considered in the context in which they were made.His lawyer also argued that Bharti had not used any casteist slur and had made the remarks during an exchange on social media after what he described as serious provocation involving a family member.The Delhi Police opposed the plea, arguing that the words allegedly used by Bharti directly insulted a particular caste. The prosecutor said the remarks were made on a social media platform and not in a closed setting, and contended that the ingredients required to attract the SC/ST Act were present.Azad's lawyer also opposed the anticipatory bail plea, describing the alleged remarks as derogatory and intentional.
Azad, the Bhim Army chief, had complained to the Delhi Police that Bharti made caste-based, abusive, derogatory and humiliating statements against him, members of the Scheduled Caste community and B R Ambedkar on social media.The FIR was registered under provisions of the SC/ST Act, the Information Technology Act and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS).The case relates to remarks allegedly made by Bharti during a programme on social media. The complaint was registered at Delhi's North Avenue police station.Bharti had challenged the September 7 trial court order, arguing that the allegations did not make out an offence under the SC/ST Act and that custodial interrogation was not required since the material forming the basis of the case was already available in the public domain.The trial court had said its observations were limited to deciding the anticipatory bail plea and did not amount to an opinion on the merits of the case.

"His heart couldn't take the stress": 65-year-old man dies in shelter during attack on Kyiv
A 65-year-old man died in one of the underground pedestrian crossings in the Solomianskyi district during the attack on Kyiv. A few minutes after the explosions, he lost consciousness and began to struggle to breathe.
Source: hromadske, a Ukrainian independent media outlet
Details: Viktor lived alone and went to a shelter every time there was an attack.
Hromadske journalist Denys Bulavin witnessed the man's death. He said Viktor had brought his own chair into the underground crossing. A few minutes after the explosions, he lost consciousness, began struggling to breathe and his face quickly turned blue. Medics who arrived at the scene pronounced him dead.
"When he lost consciousness, his phone fell out of his hands. The screen was showing tracking of what aerial asset was flying and where," Bulavin wrote.
The man who died was 65-year-old Viktor Yerko, originally from Chernihiv Oblast. His daughter Anna Venedyktova said he worked in construction his whole life. When he retired, he kept on working anyway.
"The best dad and grandad. He was so happy when his grandson was born. He'd come to see us all the time, bringing whole bags of presents. My son knew his grandad until he was three, but when the full-scale war started we had to leave, so we barely saw each other for almost five years," Anna says.
Despite this, the family always stayed in touch: Anna wrote to her father every day to check he was okay. But today, she learned he died. She was only told it happened in an underground crossing – the rest of the details Anna saw in the news.
"His heart couldn't take the stress. He lived alone and went to the shelter every single time. But sadly, it didn't save him. We love him so much. His grandson Marko will never get to hug his grandad again," Anna says.
Viktor has also left behind a son and a granddaughter.

EU electric car registrations jump nearly 63% as Chinese brands gain ground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:55:41 UTC
20:55:41 KST

New electric car sales jumped by nearly two-thirds in August 2026 compared to their levels last year as fuel prices hit fresh records in the European Union. But German carmakers struggle to benefit from a broader recovery of the EU car market.
New electric car registrations soared in the EU in August, against a backdrop of rising fuel prices and geopolitical uncertainty.
Battery electric car registrations rose 62.7% from a year earlier, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA). Their share of all new EU car registrations climbed from 17.8% to 27.7% over the same period.
The increase also boosted the wider market. New car sales across the 27 EU countries rose 4.5% in August from a year earlier and were up 5.3% in the first eight months of 2026 compared with the same period last year.
According to an EY analysis, two factors helped drive the growth: subsidies for electric cars and an extra working day in many countries compared with last August.
Constantin M. Gall, global aerospace, defence and mobility industry practice leader at EY, warned against seeing the increase as a sign of a wider recovery. “The upward trend in the European new car market is primarily driven by subsidies for e-mobility,” he said, adding that EV sales could fall sharply if the subsidies end.
Across the EU, plug-in hybrid registrations increased by nearly 11% compared with last August, while hybrid electric registrations rose by more than 2%. The latter category remained the most popular powertrain, accounting for about a third of new car registrations in August and 36.6% in the first eight months of 2026.
Year-to-date, battery electric and petrol cars each accounted for 21.7%.
Germany led EU electric car sales in August, with nearly 69,000 new EVs, followed by France with more than 36,000. Denmark came next with nearly 13,900, ahead of Belgium and the Netherlands. The fastest growth was in Estonia (up 278%) and Slovenia (up 266%), although those increases represented 174 and 1,651 cars respectively.
EU fuel prices hit fresh records in the week beginning 21 September, according to the European Commission. Average petrol prices reached €2.092 a litre, while diesel rose to €2.226 a litre. Both were the highest in the Commission’s series, which began in 2005. ECB experts expect diesel refining margins, rather than pump prices, to peak in October. They made that forecast before the US began examining a possible partial or full ban on diesel exports.
Chinese-owned car groups gain ground
Chinese-owned car groups are gaining a share of the EU market as European manufacturers face fierce competition, US tariffs and the cost of switching to electric vehicles.
Sales by the five Chinese-owned groups listed by ACEA rose by about 71% in August from a year earlier. Their combined share of the overall new car market climbed from 6.6% to 10.8% — roughly one in nine new cars sold in the EU. The figure includes brands with European roots, such as Volvo Cars, which ACEA counts within Geely Group.
Among the fastest-growing manufacturers were Leapmotor (up 211%), Chery (201%), BYD (129%) and Geely Group (24%). Tesla, the US carmaker, grew by 53%. These figures cover all cars sold by each manufacturer, not EVs alone.
German car groups lost ground. Combined sales by Volkswagen Group, BMW Group and Mercedes-Benz fell 1.1%, while their share of the EU market declined from 41.3% to 39.1%.
“Current subsidy measures in European countries are disproportionately benefiting Chinese manufacturers and Tesla, which offer highly competitive models — particularly in the low- and mid-price segments — along with often attractive financing terms,” Gall said. He expects Chinese manufacturers to keep gaining a share of the market, especially in lower-priced segments and southern Europe.
European carmakers may need to tighten their belts
EY warns that August’s growth may not last if subsidies end. Gall also pointed to weak economic growth, high oil prices and geopolitical uncertainty as reasons buyers may put off purchasing a new car. He urged manufacturers to prepare for more difficult years and rising price pressure.
There is another pressure on prices: a recent report covered by Euronews argued that proposed “Made in Europe” battery rules could add about €2,100 to the cost of an electric car. That could make it harder for European manufacturers to offer cheaper models, even as competition grows.

Zelensky said Ukrainian forces had learned to intercept Russian cruise missiles and drones and were developing ways to counter jet-powered Shahed attack drones.
“We are already seeing good results,” he said. “But against ballistic missiles, only Patriot interceptors work for now, and they are needed practically every day.”
The two officials discussed Ukraine’s current interceptor requirements and ways its partners could assemble a winter support package.
Zelensky thanked Rutte for his readiness to seek solutions, adding that stronger air defenses were also important for NATO members amid what he described as Russia’s continuing threats to expand its aggression.
Kremlin Says Too Early to Discuss Putin’s G20 Trip After Welcoming US Invitation
Ukraine intercepted approximately 60% of the ballistic missiles launched during the latest Russian attack, Zelensky said earlier on Thursday.
He acknowledged, however, that interception rates during previous attacks had fallen as low as 10%, while some barrages ended with no ballistic missiles intercepted.
“It’s not because someone lacks experience. Someone lacks missiles,” Zelensky said.
Three waves hit Kyiv
The Russian assault killed two people and injured at least six in Kyiv, according to city authorities.
Missile debris damaged a private house, a 16-story apartment building and an eight-story nonresidential building in the Dniprovskyi district.
In the Podilskyi district, debris damaged the facade and windows of a maternity hospital and set vehicles on fire in a nearby parking lot. A diagnostic center and several warehouses were also damaged.
No patients or medical workers inside the maternity hospital were reported injured.
The ballistic missile assault followed a major Russian drone attack on Kyiv on Wednesday that killed two people, injured dozens and damaged businesses, gas stations and transport infrastructure.
European allies of Ukraine were struggling to find enough Patriot missiles before winter because of limited stocks and competing defense requirements.
Most PAC-3 interceptors capable of engaging ballistic missiles are manufactured in the United States, making Washington central to efforts to replenish Ukraine’s air defenses.
