Why Yemen's Houthis are so difficult to fight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:49:19 UTC
20:49:19 KST

Breadcrumb
From insurgents to regional force: Why Yemen's Houthis are so difficult to fight
On 10 September, Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, captured the Red Sea port city of Mocha during a major offensive against Yemeni government-aligned forces.
The group then advanced south, reportedly reaching the coastal town of Dhubab on 11 September, before moving against strategic islands near the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, including Mayun, also known as Perim, and the Hanish Islands.
These gains have strengthened Houthi control along Yemen’s western coast and near the southern entrance to the Red Sea, threatening shipping on the wider Suez–Red Sea route, which carries about 12% of global trade and a significant share of global oil and LNG.
The offensive is part of a broader campaign that began in July, intensified in August, and peaked in September, including a Houthi naval blockade targeting Saudi-linked vessels and renewed attacks on Saudi oil facilities.
In September, Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline was also hit by drones launched from Iraq.
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognised government and allied factions have so far struggled to stop the Houthi advance.
Saudi forces have provided air support against Houthi positions and reinforcements, while Yemeni government forces and allied groups continue ground operations.
Meanwhile, the Houthis have pushed from the Red Sea coast toward strategic positions in the Kahboub Mountains in Taiz and Lahj, triggering heavy clashes over high ground overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
The Houthis have learned from years of war
The struggle to halt the Houthi offensive reveals how the Iran-aligned group has refined its military capabilities and tactics over years of conflict to expand its territorial and political leverage while advancing an agenda broadly aligned with Tehran. The offensive is also deepening Yemen’s role in wider regional tensions involving the US and Iran.
The Houthis, a Zaydi Shia Islamist movement, were formed in northern Yemen in the 1990s, emerging as a major political and military force in September 2014, when they captured Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, effectively splitting the country and triggering a civil war against the internationally recognised government and allied forces.
In 2015, a Saudi-led coalition of Gulf and other Arab states intervened militarily in support of the government. A UN-brokered truce in April 2022 temporarily reduced major combat operations.
The Houthis’ military strategy and tactics have evolved significantly over time. Their early insurgency relied on guerrilla tactics, mountain terrain, tribal networks, local alliances, and captured weapons.
With Iranian training and technical support, and assistance from Hezbollah, the Houthis developed increasingly sophisticated ballistic and cruise missiles, UAVs, and anti-ship capabilities, which gradually allowed them to strike targets in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and across the Red Sea.
This has led them to evolve into a regional force capable of targeting military, oil, and maritime interests beyond Yemen.
Their latest operations have also become more coordinated. The group, whose fighters are estimated to number up to 350,000, tends to attack using a combination of missiles, drones, artillery, and mobile ground forces.
The Houthi assault on Yemen’s western coast earlier this month, for example, suggests a shift toward smaller assault units that attack specific targets from multiple directions, according to Mohammed al-Basha, analyst and founder of risk advisory Basha Report.
“This approach makes them harder to target with airstrikes and allows them to maintain pressure on government forces,” he told The New Arab, adding that Houthi operations combining drone and missile strikes show growing firepower and ammunition capacity.
The latest escalation also highlighted the role of information warfare. The Houthis have allegedly used social media and digital platforms to put out propaganda and disinformation.
They were accused of using an AI-generated voice deepfake of Tareq Saleh, commander of the National Resistance Forces and nephew of former president Ali Abdullah Saleh, to send out a false withdrawal message, potentially causing confusion and lowering morale.
“The Houthis understand these forces really well and know that Tareq Saleh’s forces on the Red Sea coast are not trusted by the local people,” Michael Knights, head of research at New York-based strategic advisory Horizon Engage, told The New Arab. He explained that the Houthis effectively used SMS, email, and WhatsApp to flood Yemeni commanders with confusing messages.
“They also know that the Saudi forces are not particularly trusted by the Tariq forces, which makes it very easy for them to exploit the gap.”
A fragmented coalition struggles to respond
Internal divisions within the anti-Houthi coalition seem to have translated into poor coordination, making the Houthis more difficult to counter.
While the Houthis appear to have a more cohesive command structure, the anti-Houthi coalition remains divided, with Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) backing rival Yemeni factions.
In December 2025, tensions boiled over when Saudi-led forces struck a UAE-linked shipment at Mukalla, which Riyadh said was destined for UAE-backed separatists. Yemen’s Saudi-backed authorities then demanded the withdrawal of UAE forces.
“It’s impossible to bring them to work together because each of these groups has different political agendas,” Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group, told The New Arab.
“There are also many issues related to military coordination, which have weakened the government and prevented it from mounting a strong resistance when the Houthis move toward any of their fronts.”
Internal divisions have, as a result, left Saudi Arabia without a unified, effective Yemeni ground partner.
RANE's Middle East and North Africa analyst Freddy Khoueiry told The New Arab that “airpower can destroy infrastructure and slow advances, but historically it has struggled to translate that into durable territorial gains without a capable ground force”.
This, coupled with weaknesses in the Saudi-led command structure and an intelligence failure to detect the Houthi buildup, has "likely contributed to the rapid collapse along the Red Sea coast".
Yemen’s geography is also a factor to take into account. The Houthis benefit from the country’s mountainous terrain, which means airstrikes have limited impact.
But at the same time, local forces have taken advantage of the same terrain to hold off Houthi attacks. This week, government and local forces in Taiz reportedly held strategic positions and slowed the Houthi advance.
Saudi Arabia is also struggling to secure external direct military support. The US said it won’t join the conflict for now, while Turkey and Pakistan, part of the Mecca agreement with the Kingdom, have yet to provide military assistance.
Riyadh has sought air-defence support from Egypt. The UK has agreed to provide defensive air-to-air refuelling.
Basha doesn’t rule out US intervention but said Washington’s reluctance reflects its existing commitments in the Iran war and concerns over diverting resources to Yemen.
“The Houthis appear to understand this risk,” he told The New Arab. “Their strategic communications have been carefully calibrated to avoid directly threatening American interests and to reduce the likelihood of US intervention.”
US President Donald Trump said earlier this month that the Houthis had contacted the US and “don’t want to fight us,” adding that they were “letting most ships go through,” while excluding Saudi-linked shipping.
Houthi control of Bab al-Mandeb adds a further layer to the US-Iran war. It potentially gives the Houthis leverage over a key strategic chokepoint while advancing their own agenda, and it could give Iran an additional pressure point alongside tensions over the Strait of Hormuz.
Fatima Abo Alasrar, a researcher and founder of The Ideology Machine, a publication on authoritarian information systems, said the Houthi campaign could serve a broader Iranian strategy of raising economic costs for Saudi Arabia and the US by disrupting oil and trade.
With Iran constrained by sanctions, its allies can disrupt rivals’ energy flows and create pressure for negotiations.
“The Houthi strategy is to drive a wedge between Washington and Saudi Arabia, leaving Saudi Arabia exposed while offering not to attack the US,” she said, noting that Tehran employed a similar coercive approach in 2018, when former President Hassan Rouhani warned that if Iran could not export oil, “no one else” in the region would be able to either.
“If that weakens Saudi Arabia and erodes trust in Washington, the Gulf security architecture begins to shake,” she told The New Arab.
The Houthis’ growing regional role has prompted Iran to become more vocal in its support. Nagi said the Iranians “are no longer supporting the Houthis from behind the scenes”.
Despite developing some military autonomy, the Houthis “remain heavily reliant on Iran for key components of their missile, air-defence and anti-ship systems,” Knight explained.
And despite being part of the ‘Axis of Resistance’, the Houthis still pursue their own priorities. Khoueiry argued they have incentives to calibrate escalation independently rather than automatically joining every stage of the US-Iran conflict.
“Houthis are more likely to complicate the wider war than fundamentally change its military balance,” he said.
Dario Sabaghi is a freelance journalist interested in human rights

Israel threatens more land grabs in Syria, says territory 'ours forever'
Israel’s far-right defence minister threatened on Wednesday to seize and permanently retain more Syrian territory, as he rejected demands from Damascus for Israeli forces to withdraw from land occupied since the fall of Bashar al-Assad.
Responding to Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who this week renewed calls for Israel to withdraw from occupied Syrian territory, Israel Katz warned that any future Israeli seizure of Syrian land would be permanent.
"If our forces or the territory of the State of Israel is attacked from Syria, we will have no choice but to act and respond. Any area we seize this time will remain ours forever, in accordance with the laws of war," Katz said.
The threat comes nearly two years after Israel exploited the collapse of Assad’s regime in December 2024 to send troops beyond the Golan Heights and across the 1974 disengagement line.
Israeli forces seized the UN-patrolled buffer zone and positions on the Syrian side of Mount Hermon, expanding Israel’s occupation of Syrian territory and bringing its troops closer to Damascus.
Israel has sought to justify its continued military presence in southern Syria on security grounds. Damascus, however, has repeatedly said it does not seek war with Israel and has pushed for a diplomatic resolution requiring Israeli forces to withdraw.
Negotiations between the two sides, which began last year, have so far failed to secure an Israeli withdrawal.
"We will not allow Syria to become a threat to the State of Israel, and we will do whatever is necessary to prevent that," Katz said.
Sharaa has demanded that Israeli forces return to the positions they held before 8 December 2024, when Assad’s regime fell, and Israeli troops crossed the disengagement line.
In an address to the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, Sharaa reaffirmed Syrian sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights and said Israel's annexation measures were "null and void" under UN Security Council Resolution 497.
The UN continues to regard the Golan Heights as Syrian territory under Israeli occupation. Israel captured the territory in 1967 and unilaterally annexed it in 1981, a move rejected by the UN Security Council.
Sharaa also accused Israel of carrying out nearly 500 air and artillery strikes against Syria, more than 1,200 incursions and around 300 arrests and detentions of Syrians since Assad’s fall.
He said the attacks threatened Syria’s stability and ran counter to the position of much of the international community.
Sharaa reaffirmed Syria’s commitment to the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and called on Israel to withdraw from the territory it seized following Assad's overthrow.
He also rejected Israeli attempts to impose a fait accompli through military force, saying the continuing attacks and incursions undermined regional security and stability.
Katz responded by declaring that the occupied Golan Heights were "an integral, eternal part of Israel" and ruling out an Israeli withdrawal from Mount Hermon or the buffer zone.
"We will not withdraw from Mount Hermon and the security zone," Katz said.
He claimed Syria had violated the 1974 agreement by becoming "an Iranian base and a threat to Israel and its borders" under Assad.
Katz said Israeli forces would remain on Mount Hermon and in the occupied buffer zone "as long as there is a jihadist threat" along the border, including what he described as threats from Syrian government forces and other Islamist groups.
Iran and Iran-backed militias fought alongside Assad’s forces during Syria’s civil war, while Israel carried out thousands of strikes against Syrian, Iranian and allied targets.
Following Assad’s fall, Islamist-led rebels headed by Sharaa rose to power in Damascus.
Despite Israel’s continued occupation, strikes and incursions, Sharaa has repeatedly said Syria does not seek conflict with neighbouring states and wants to focus on rebuilding the country after more than a decade of devastating war.
He reiterated that position this week, saying there remained an opportunity for a "just peace" that protected the rights of all sides.
Israel also maintains forces on Lebanese territory and has expanded settlements and military control across the occupied West Bank. Its military continues to occupy much of the Gaza Strip.

Labour regains lead as Nigel Farage’s Reform slips in YouGov model
- Labour leads with 241 seats in YouGov's latest poll, gaining nearly 100 seats from last year, but still short of a majority in a hung Parliament.
- Reform UK drops to 123 seats amid donation scandals, while Conservatives and smaller parties like SNP and Plaid Cymru improve their positions.
- The poll shows a tight three-way race with many marginal seats, highlighting the impact of tactical voting and shifting British multi-party politics.
AI generated
LONDON – Labour would win the most seats if a British general election were held tomorrow, according to a detailed poll that gives Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s outfit a boost ahead of its annual conference and reflects a drop in support for Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.
The governing party would win 241 of the 650 seats in the House of Commons, compared to 130 for the main opposition Conservative Party and 123 for Reform, according to YouGov’s survey, its first in-depth survey since Burnham came to power in July.
While that’s well down on the 411 seats Labour won in the 2024 general election, it’s almost 100 seats more than YouGov’s poll a year ago showed.
The results bolster Labour heading into its conference, which starts on Sept 27 in Liverpool, showing the potential electoral benefit stemming from its decision to depose Keir Starmer as leader and premier just two years after he secured a massive majority.
It also highlights how support for Reform has come off the boil amid increasing scrutiny over political donations to the insurgent party.
It’s a stark contrast from 2025’s conference, when YouGov projected Labour would shed two-thirds of its seats in a historic defeat, including those of most Cabinet ministers.
If the latest survey were to pan out, Labour would be the largest party in a hung Parliament, dependent on other parties to form a government.
Even if they formed an alliance with the Liberal Democrats – who YouGov projects would win 71 seats – they would be short of an outright majority.
YouGov sampled 14,000 respondents between Aug 23 and Sept 18 in a so-called multilevel regression and post-stratification poll, known as MRP, which models seat-by-seat results.
The Times reported the poll earlier.
Allies of the prime minister have said he’s not planning to call a snap general election, and YouGov’s survey highlights why: he would lose his majority.
Despite a so-called Burnham Bounce, the pollster found Labour would still only win 24 per cent of the vote – the party’s lowest share since 1918.
The 241 seats it’s projected to win would fall short of its losing tally in the 2017 and 2010 elections.
YouGov warned of “uncertainty” due to the closeness of constituency modelling.
In aggregate, it put Reform on 22 per cent and the Tories on 21 per cent, putting the gap between the three parties within the margin of error.
Proponents have argued a fresh election would allow Burnham to win his own mandate, free of the promises of the party’s last election manifesto, while catching Reform on the back foot, as the populist outfit fights off scandals and before it can benefit from two record-breaking donations totalling £72 million (S$121.88 million) that it received earlier in September.
Reform has denied any wrongdoing in its fundraising activities.
YouGov’s survey also showed how tight it is between the parties as Britain moves away from the Labour-Tory duopoly of the past century and embraces multi-party politics.
More than a third of seats would be decided on margins of less than five points, including 82 projected Reform wins, making Farage’s outfit particularly vulnerable to tactical voting, according to the pollster.
“A small shift in national sentiment or a modest and plausible level of tactical switching could dramatically change seat numbers,” Rob Ford, a political scientist at the University of Manchester, said in a post on Bluesky.
Separate polling from YouGov shows that a growing proportion of voters are willing to vote tactically against Reform.
That reinforces the results of July’s Manchester mayoral election, when left-wing voters whose first choice was knocked out in the first round of voting were more likely to support Labour in the second round than right-wing voters were to rally around Reform.
Reform currently has only 8 Members of Parliament – having won five in the 2024 general election before welcoming Conservative defectors into the fold.
YouGov’s survey suggested the former Tories Robert Jenrick (Reform’s Treasury spokesman), Suella Braverman and Danny Kruger would all lose their seats to their former party.
There are nevertheless opportunities for Reform, which currently trails Labour by less than five percentage points in 45 seats.
In a similar number of seats, Farage’s party would beat Labour if it could win all of the votes going to Rupert Lowe’s far-right Restore party.
Lowe himself won a seat for Reform in 2024 before being ejected from the party and setting up his own.
YouGov’s survey also suggests the Conservatives have begun the job of fixing their relationship with the electorate under Kemi Badenoch’s leadership.
A year ago, YouGov’s MRP poll had them winning just 45 seats to be just the fourth biggest party in Parliament.
Their new tally of 130 would be a small advance on the 121 seats they won in 2024, albeit well below the 365 they won in 2019.
The latest survey put the Scottish National Party on 40 seats, up from just 9 in 2024, with the Welsh nationalists of Plaid Cymru almost quadrupling their presence to 15 seats.
The Greens would more than double their small representation in Parliament to 9 seats, while failing to make the breakthrough that seemed possible when the left-wing party was higher in the polls earlier in 2026. BLOOMBERG

Poland says Starlink fire was sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:47:56 UTC
20:47:56 KST

The fire at a Starlink ground station near Warsaw on Wednesday night was an act of sabotage and part of hybrid warfare against Poland, Digital Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said Thursday morning.
“[This was] sabotage and an attempt to disrupt the operation of a vital station that is crucial for the security and continuity of internet services in Ukraine,” Gawkowski told state broadcaster TVP Info, stopping short of blaming Russia for the incident directly.
“It’s about actions aimed at shutting down the internet and disrupting the functioning of basic services. These may concern the supply of water, gas or electricity, as well as the financial system,” Gawkowski added.
Advertisement
The fire broke out in the village of Wola Krobowska, 50 kilometers south of Warsaw. It didn’t cause significant damage and there were no injuries. Poland’s counterintelligence agency, ABW, and the police are investigating the incident.
Operated by the state-owned telecoms company Exatel, the station links Starlink satellites to terrestrial internet networks. Together with a station in Kaunas, Lithuania, it serves Central European users as well as Ukraine, Polish media reported.
The minister has previously warned that Poland faces some 2,000–3,000 cyberattacks on its infrastructure daily.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned last week that NATO, Ukrainian and Polish intelligence assessments point to Russian plans to step up hybrid attacks on countries supporting Kyiv, including Poland, in the coming months.
Tusk also said Moscow would mask such strikes as accidents to undermine NATO’s willingness to respond collectively.
Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski urged Moscow to end the war at the U.N. Security Council Wednesday, citing the West’s economic superiority over Russia.
“You can still kill a lot of people, but you cannot win. You can stop this imperial war of choice at any time,” Sikorski said.

UNGA: Netanyahu, Abbas to speak as Middle East dominates day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:46:00 UTC
20:46:00 KST

UNGA: Gaza dominates agenda as Abbas, Netanyahu speak
Published September 22, 2026last updated September 24, 2026
What you need to know
- Israel's Prime Minister said attacking Iran was one of his 'easiest' decisions, as he had no real choice
- Many representatives walked out of the UN General Assembly ahead of Benjamin Netanyahu's speech
- Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas earlier urged nations to support the two-state solution, and sharply criticized Israel and the US
- The UK will host a meeting on the future of the Gaza Strip, while Saudi Arabia and Norway have called a ministerial meeting to discuss the implementation of the so-called two-state solution
- Beyond the Middle East, day 3 of the UNGA will address the problem that rising sea levels pose for low-lying islands and coastal regions
Read below for all the top headlines, videos and analyses on the 81 UN General Assembly from September 22-28, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
Netanyahu calls genocide allegations 'the greatest lie of the century'
The Israeli prime minister said allegations of genocide in Gaza leveled at Israel by various world leaders or groups were false.
"It will take time for the world to acknowledge what is so plain to see. That Hamas used Palestinian civilians as human shields. That it used hospitals, schools, mosques as terrorist command posts. That it sold much of the food we let into Gaza," Netanyahu alleged.
"And while Hamas did everything possible to keep Palestinians in harm's way — often at gunpoint — Israel did everything possible to get them out of harm's way," he said, listing measures like warnings to civilians.
"I want to ask you a question: what genocidal regime gives a million polio vaccinations to the enemy's population? What genocidal regime enables the distribution of 2 million tons of food into Gaza? Accusing Israel of genocide is the greatest lie of the century," he said.
He also called out New York's "antisemitic" mayor, Zohran Mamdani, as one of the people spreading this message. He said that since Mamdani's election "many Jews no longer feel safe in New York."
Netanyahu said the "simple truth" was not that Israel committed genocide but that it prevented one, saying "that's exactly what Mr. Mamdani's Hamas buddies would have done to us if we had not stopped them."
Netanyahu says he 'drew a red line' on same podium 14 years ago
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began his speech with a reference to his notorious General Assembly appearance in 2012, when he stood with illustrated graphics depicting how near to creating a nuclear bomb he thought Iran was.
"Ladies and gentlemen, 14 years ago I stood on this podium and I drew a red line," he said. "I vowed to prevent Iran's murderous dictatorship from developing atomic bombs. Nuclear weapons that could destroy the state of Israel, nuclear weapons that could threaten the whole world. That's exactly what we did."
Netanyahu said that while it was "very hard" to devastate Iran's nuclear facilities, he said it was "one of the easiest decisions" he'd had to make as prime minister, "because if we hadn't done it, we'd all be dead."
Iran contends that its nuclear program was for peaceful purposes like electricity generation, a claim that Israel and the US dispute.
Netanyahu also referred to Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa's call for Israel to pull back its forces in the Golan Heights border area, addressing al-Sharaa and saying "you should know that the Jews have been in the Golan Heights since the days of Moses," referring to the Old Testament prophet thought to have lived more than 3,000 years ago.
Delegates leave the chamber in large group as Netanyahu enters
As Israeli Prime Minster Benjamin Netanyahu's turn to speak at the UN General Assembly came, a large number of delegates from various countries stood up and left the chamber to cheers and jeering.
Only after repeated appeals for calm was it possible for him to begin his address.
"Before I begin, just a quick announcement: if there any other moral cowards who have not yet left this hall, please do so now. Thank you very much," Netanyahu said.
He returned to the issue of the walkout later when discussing his decision to target Iran and its nuclear capabilities.
"Now do you want to hear the ultimate irony? In defending itself, Israel is also defending many of the countries whose delegates just left this hall. In fact, I want you to know that many of their leaders even thank us privately for taking out Iran's nukes," he claimed, saying "it's hard to imagine more mind-blowing hypocrisy."
Protesters had also gathered outside the building in New York ahead of Netanyahu's address. Some were arrested by police. A Democratic nominee for New York's 10th congressional district in November's midterm elections, Brad Lander, also joined the demonstrators, albeit wearing a suit and tie rather than a slogan-laden T-shirt.
READ: Nigeria and US sign mining deal
On the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Nigeria and the United States agreed to increase American investiment in the West African nation's mining sector.
Nigeria's Minister for Solid Minerals Dele Alake announced the deal on Thursday, a day after he signed the framework deal with US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau.
"Nigeria cannot remain a source of raw materials while others capture most of the value. We want more local processing, quality jobs, stronger skills and greater opportunities for Nigerian businesses," Alake said.
Read more about the US-Nigeria mining agreement.
Abbas calls for saving two-state solution and Palestinian self-determination
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas used his remarks to implore nations to support the two-state solution, saying his people seek a non-militarized, democratic Palestinian state that can exist alongside Israel in peace.
He said the first step to preserving the idea of such a solution is to protect the lands upon which a future Palestinian state would be based, as well as protecting those people who have lived upon them for generations.
Abbas underscored the fact that the Palestinian people would not be displaced by "military occupation, nor settlement expansion, annexation, nor settler terrorism."
He further said that "no lasting security can be built upon the occupation of another people and the denial of its legitimate rights," adding that the Palestinians have their own plans for an independent state and emphasizing the need to end the Israeli occupation in order to negotiate a solution.
This plan, Abbas said, is based on protecting Palestinians from displacement, preserving their lands, democratically renewing political institutions and building a new sovereign Palestinian state — with east Jerusalem as its capital.
All of this, he said, would be carried out with a "commitment to international law" and the right to exercise self-determination with the aim of achieving security and peace with Israel to, "pave the way to regional integration, cooperation, prosperity and security for everyone."
Abbas concluded his remarks by thanking those 160 nations whom he said have recognized Palestinian statehood, calling for its inclusion in the United Nations.
Palestinian leader Abbas blasts US and Israel in General Assembly
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas, addressing those gathered at the UNGA via video because the US State Department refused to allow the Palestinian delegation into the country, has rejected Washington's approach as "unlawful and punitive."
Abbas described the denial of visas as a US failure to live up to its responsibility as the host nation of the international body.
Abbas quickly pivoted to blast Israel's "genocidal war" in Gaza, as well as the sanctioned "ethnic cleansing" perpetrated by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank.
Saying that Israeli violations of international law put the two-state solution at grave risk, Abbas described the situation in Gaza, the West Bank and east Jerusalem as part of a "malicious colonial scheme" and warned of a "new Nakba."
He also referenced attacks on Muslim and Christian religious sites by radical Jews as having the potential to transform the current security situation into a wider religiously fueled conflict.
Not only Middle East, rising sea level threat also on slate for day 3 meetings
Beyond AI and the headline-grabbing conflict in the Middle East, the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday will discuss another pressing issue that impacts the world’s citizens — rising sea levels.
A high-level meeting is slated to begin at 10:00 a.m. (1400 GMT) on Thursday as swelling seas redraw coastlines and pose existential risks for islanders and those who live in low-lying areas near the shores of the world's oceans and seas.
The UN says nearly 900 million people live in such areas, adding that another one million could be impacted by mid-century.
Rising sea levels, says the UN, threaten not only land but also livelihoods and even the existence of entire nations. In the words of UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, "Rising seas are sinking futures."
Israeli and Palestinian leaders set to address UNGA on day 3
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas are both expected to address members of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) on Thursday, with the issue of the Middle East writ large on the day 3 agenda.
Netanyahu, who is increasingly unpopular at home and abroad, will not meet with US officials or Arab leaders during his stay. His office cited a "tight schedule" as the reason, listing as many as nine meetings during his visit, including with the presidents of Argentina and Bolivia, the vice president of Colombia and the prime minister of Papua New Guinea.
The increasingly isolated Israeli leader's Palestinian counterpart, President Mahmoud Abbas, will also address the General Assembly. Abbas, however, will do so via video, as the US State Department refused to issue him an entry visa.
The broader subjects of Gaza's future and Palestinian statehood will also be topics of discussion. The UK will convene a meeting on Gaza's current and future status, and Saudi Arabia and Norway will host a ministerial meeting to hash out plans for the implementation of the so-called "two-state solution."
That's a wrap on Day 2 of the UNGA
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blamed Russian President Vladimir Putin for the ongoing war between the countries, calling him "patient zero."
The Ukrainian leader also announced new defense deals with Finland and Australia.
Elsewhere, Syrian leader Ahmed al-Sharaa called for the Israeli occupation of the Golan Heights to end, saying the territory belongs to Syria.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also addressed Israel, calling for what he described as the "genocide" in Gaza to stop.
This comes ahead of a speech by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the UN General Assembly on Thursday.
'Too much power in too few hands' — AI leaders warn about technology dangers
Besides world leaders, top bosses at AI companies also addressed the UN about dangers concerning artificial intelligence.
AI executives spoke to the UN Security Council and urged international cooperation on the hotly debated technology.
Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI, highlighted two big risks with AI.
"First, we could lose control of the future to AI. The risk is that it moves so fast that people can no longer follow what's happening or intervene when needed," he said, adding that such a scenario would be "terrible."
Second, he said AI systems "could concentrate too much power in too few hands." "No one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their worldview on everyone else."
Anthropic boss Dario Amodei used the platform to call for a ban on the use of AI in the development of biological weapons, describing AI as the most crucial global security issue facing the world.
"If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," he said.
Amodei also urged global standards for testing new AI models.
Spain PM Pedro Sanchez calls for reforming the UN Security Council
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchezcalled for reforming the UN Security Council so that "all of the regions in the world" would be fairly represented.
Sanchez quoted the UN Charter, saying "no country should be a judge in its own case, no matter how powerful they are."
The Spanish leader continued to condemn the "genocide that (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu is still perpetrating in Gaza," while pointing to Madrid's sanctions against Russia as an example of his government's willingness to take action against countries whose conduct violates the UN Charter.
Ebola outbreak 'major' test for country, Congo's PM tells UNGA
Congolese Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka described the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo as a "major test" for the country.
"For the DRC, fighting this epidemic is an absolute priority. After having contained 16 previous outbreaks, the DRC is mobilizing recognized scientific and operational expertise. And thanks to national mobilization and the support of our
partners, the response has recently begun producing tangible results," she told the UN General Assembly.
As of 22 September 2026, Congo reported a total of 7, 773 confirmed cases, including 3,759 related deaths. A total of 839 patients are hospitalized in isolation.
Venezuela to hold elections, Rodriguez tells UNGA
Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, delivered her first address to the UN General Assembly since coming to power, promising her country would hold elections when the nation's people determine the "right moment."
"I want to make this very clear at this General Assembly: there will be elections in Venezuela," Rodriguez said, adding that her country "has initiated the process of democratic transformation for its rebirth" following two blows this year.
First, "strangulation of its internal political life and the heightened confrontation with the United States" and second, the earthquakes on June 24 that caused the deaths of more than 6,500 people.
Rodriguez took power after the US toppled the then-president Nicolas Maduro in January.
Rodríguez briefly met US President Donald Trump at the UN General Assembly as well.
Ukrainian foreign minister met with Iranian delegation on the sidelines of UNGA
DW's US Correspondent Misha Komadovsky reported that the Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Sybiah earlier in the day told a UN Security Council meeting that Ukraine was ready for an immediate and complete ceasefire without preconditions, if Moscow did too.
German FM calls on Iran to end Hormuz blockage
In a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul called on Iran to end its closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
"It is up to Iran to engage constructively in negotiations and to loosen its stranglehold," Wadephul told journalists ahead of the meeting.
Wadephul also urged Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi to engage seriously and credibly in sustainable negotiations with the US and neighboring states in the region, sources in the German delegation were cited by the DPA news agency as saying.
"There must now be an overall willingness to compromise in order to bring about a solution to the deadlocked conflict in the region," Wadephul was quoted as saying.
He stressed the readiness of Germany and the so-called E3, which also includes France and the United Kingdom, to support mediation efforts.
Wadephul also stressed in the talks the need for Iran and militias it supports in the region, namely Yemen's Houthi rebels, to halt attacks on civilian ships. He added that Berlin expects free transit through the Strait of Hormuz to be restored immediately, stressing the rejection of any fees for passage through the critical waterway.
"Not only the Gulf States, but large parts of Asia, Africa and also Europe are suffering under this blockade," Wadephul said.
He added that Germany welcomes renewed talks between the US and Iran on the sidelines of the General Assembly, adding that he planned to speak to his counterparts from Jordan, Pakistan, Iraq and Oman.

What to cook when summer meets autumn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:45:16 UTC
20:45:16 KST

The weather in London can’t quite make up its mind. You leave the house in the morning and immediately wish you’d brought gloves, but by lunchtime you’re carrying your jacket under your arm, and by dinner you’re closing the windows again. Summer hasn’t exactly gone, but winter has started sending little reminders that it knows where we live.
We love this time of year. The air feels fresh from the occasional shower, the days are still long enough to make something of, the light is perhaps the most beautiful it will be all year, and, for cycling, it is perfect. There are days when London seems to contain two seasons at once: summer in a sunny spot at lunchtime, winter the moment the sun disappears.
For the cook, however, this time of year can be confusing. A bowl of cold salad no longer feels quite enough, but we’re not yet ready for the great pots of soup, beans and stews that will soon take up permanent residence on the hob. We want something cooked, but not necessarily piping hot; substantial, but still bright. Food that acknowledges the chill in the evening without surrendering completely to it.
Our solution is to live in the territory between salad and supper. Roast vegetables, grains, rice and pasta are particularly good here: dishes that can be eaten warm from the oven or sit happily on the table until everyone is ready to eat, with plenty of lemon, herbs, vinegar, chilli or yoghurt to keep things lively. Rachel Roddy’s rice salad with red peppers, celery, herbs and egg is exactly that sort of thing, especially eaten at room temperature rather than fridge-cold. Rukmini Iyer’s roast red pepper orecchiette with pistachios and ricotta takes the last of the peppers somewhere warmer without turning them into winter food, while another Rachel dish, fusilli with roast squash, gorgonzola and sage, pushes us a little farther into autumn. Nigel Slater’s braised aubergines, courgettes, preserved lemon and olives are perhaps even better at room temperature than hot, which is exactly where we want to be. Then there’s Yotam Ottolenghi’s aubergine and red pepper pahi with fenugreek and curry-leaf oil, which has that combination we crave now: something cooked and substantial, but also sweet, sour and spicy. Finally, and staying with Yotam, his black rice with fennel and butternut squash feels made for this time of year: roast vegetables, rice, chilli and a sharp dressing.
This is how we want to eat now, with one foot in each season. A tray comes out of the oven, something sharp gets squeezed over it, a handful of herbs goes on top, and dinner can wait while we take one last bike ride before dark. In the coming months, the days will get shorter and colder, and our food will get darker and browner, so we will take this opportunity to get as much colour and zest as possible out of every meal.
Our month in food
Local heroes | Our new favourite London street is Grove Lane in Camberwell. Turn down it from Camberwell Church Street and you will first see Lala Books, surely London’s most charismatic bookshop thanks to the consistently excellent selection, the coffee and the neighbourhood feel. A few shops down is Theo’s pizzeria, which we have long loved, while even further down the road is the glorious Kerfield Arms, which offers some of the best food in the city right now, including an incredible Sunday lunch and what has to be the best lunch deal in town: a plate and a glass of wine for £15. They even have a Michelin star.
Happy place | Wildflowers is a restaurant nestled in a Pimlico back yard and it’s easy to miss – but it really shouldn’t be, because it’s where we want to spend every birthday and anniversary for the foreseeable future. The menu is very seasonal, so we will spend the next 12 months praying they’ll bring back the heavenly sweetcorn and truffle agnolotti.
Go west | We are heading back to the US – and before you ask, no, it’s not just to get more of Trader Joe’s pickle mustard, though we certainly will stock up. Instead, we’re setting out on the west-coast leg of our book tour, so if you’re reading this and are in the area, do come say hi! And if you have any recommendations – and we mean food recs, obviously – do drop us a line.

spell of unsettled weather tomorrow. However, the sun will
return for the weekend, with highs 2-4°C above the seasonal
average, according to Tedici, head meteorologist and media
spokesperson for iLMeteo.it.
                                    
                                       
				"In the coming hours," he states, "we will see a partial
increase in cloud cover over the Alps and Tyrrhenian regions,
with light scattered showers developing later on Thursday in the
northeastern mountains and over Sardinia.
                                    
                                       
				A cool air mass moving down from Central Europe will reach Italy
overnight between Thursday and Friday."
Local showers are forecast for the Northeast, with more
widespread rain expected along the central Adriatic coast.
                                    
                                       
				On Friday, this brief unsettled spell will affect the Adriatic
regions, Lazio, and the South (excluding Sardinia), accompanied
by generally stronger winds. Sunny weather returns for the
weekend.
                                    
                                       
				On Saturday, lingering showers will affect only Calabria and
Sicily, with skies clearing significantly by the afternoon.
                                    
                                       
				Stable conditions will prevail across the country on Sunday,
September 27: overnight lows will see a temporary, slight drop,
while daytime highs will rise widely, reaching 27-28°C in
central regions.

daytime temperatures 2-4°C above the seasonal average.

Courthouses to establish units against digital crime, disinformation

Justice Minister Akın Gürlek (AA Photo)
Türkiye’s Justice Ministry is establishing specialized units at courthouses to monitor digital crime, protect citizens from harmful online content and combat criminal disinformation, Justice Minister Akın Gürlek has announced.
The new “Digital Environment Security and Disinformation Combat Bureaus” will be established at the offices of chief public prosecutors in 175 judicial centers across the country, Gürlek said on social media.
Under the new system, specialized prosecutors will closely monitor criminal content and activities encouraging crime on digital platforms, with the aim of speeding up the identification of suspects and the launch of judicial proceedings.
Gürlek said the measures would strengthen the judiciary’s capacity to respond to digital content targeting children and young people with crime, violence or abuse, as well as material threatening citizens’ privacy, personal rights and security.
The new units will also improve coordination among public institutions in addressing criminal disinformation activities intended to deliberately mislead the public or undermine social peace and public order.

Gal Gadot gives prize money to Israeli group behind 'babies in ovens' hoax
Israeli actress Gal Gadot has donated part of a $3 million prize to a Jewish rescue group whose leader and members were behind the false claim that babies were put in ovens during the 7 October 2023 attacks.
Gadot won the prize money, which will be given to two dozen non-profits in Israel, after being named the 2026 Genesis Prize, known in the country as the "Jewish Nobel".
Part of the money will be given to the United Hatzalah volunteer rescue service, whose workers and founder were the source of several unevidenced claims repeated by advocates of Israel's brutal war on Gaza, which has killed over 70,000 Palestinians.
United Hatzalah President Eli Beer claimed to have witnessed the aftermath of babies burned in ovens by Palestinian fighters - an assertion he related to the Republican Jewish Convention in Las Vegas shortly after the 7 October attacks.
Beer also made other claims about alleged atrocities, which have never been proven and are now widely considered to have been false.
"The soldiers sliced open the stomach of a pregnant mother, took out the baby, and stabbed the little tiny baby in front of her and then shot her in front of her family," he told the convention, in remarks which were circulated by international media outlets.
Beer also said he had seen beheaded children.
"I saw little kids who were beheaded. We didn’t know which head belonged to which kid,” he said, amid similar claims made by Israeli figures about Hamas beheading 40 babies.
Beer told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency (JTA) that he had heard the stories from two of United Hatzalah's rescue workers.
Asher Moskowitz, a United Hatzalah first responder, was quoted at the time telling international media outlets that he had personally seen the remains of a baby who had been baked to death.
“They took the baby and put it, literally, in a kitchen oven,” Moskowitz said.
The atrocity claims came at a time when Israel was inviting foreign journalists to some of the attack sites, and holding screenings about the attacks to press their narrative. The atrocity claims were repeated, often uncritically, by Western journalists, some of whom later retracted their comments.
Another organisation which will receive money from Gadot's prize is Bshvil Hamachar, described by the Genesis Foundation as "Israel's leading nonprofit organisation dedicated to the mental health and well-being of Israeli combat veterans and reservists, helping them and their families cope with war trauma through transformative journeys in nature".
Gadot has served in the Israeli military herself, including during Israel's 2006 war on Lebanon.
Following the 7 October attacks, Gadot encouraged her social media followers to "stand with Israel".

Netanyahu's 'humiliating' UN visit reflect growing Israeli isolation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:42:00 UTC
20:42:00 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived in New York Thursday for a whirlwind, less-than-eight-hour visit to the UNGA, highlighting Israel's deepening diplomatic isolation amid ongoing wars on Gaza and Lebanon, and expanding illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.
In stark contrast to his week-long trip last year, Netanyahu’s compressed schedule included no meetings with U.S. President Donald Trump, key American political figures, or leaders from major Western European allies.
The lack of top-level U.S. engagement reflects increasingly strained ties between Israel and its traditional international partners ahead of Israel's Oct. 27 general election.
A planned meeting in New York with billionaire Elon Musk was also canceled, leaving the Israeli leader without any high-profile U.S. engagements on his agenda.
Israel's former ambassador to Washington, Michael Oren, said he could not recall a time when an Israeli prime minister visited the U.S. without meeting the president, describing this as a blow for Netanyahu ahead of Israel's Oct. 27 general election.
"It's a campaign speech. Now it would be much better if that campaign speech were accompanied by a meeting with the president, or another world leader, or at least the secretary of state, but apparently it's not," said Michael Oren, a former Israeli ambassador to Washington.
"I don't recall a time when the prime minister came to the United States and didn't meet with the president ... So I'm sure that he was disappointed by that."
Alon Liel, a retired ambassador and former director general of Israel's Foreign Ministry, offered an even harsher assessment of the prime minister's brief stopover.
"Never before has there been such a humiliating visit to the UN for an Israeli prime minister," Liel said.
"Netanyahu can meet with Argentine and Greek leaders, but he cannot meet with any American politician or official. That means not only Europeans, but Americans are running away from him too," he added.
"I think this is the big blow; because the U.S. is the only country in the world where Netanyahu could go. Now he has fallen into a situation where he does not feel comfortable even in the U.S., unable to even stay overnight in New York," he said.
Liel added that Netanyahu is behaving "like a persona non grata even in the U.S." during an extraordinary period of international pressure.
Two Israeli officials confirmed Netanyahu would spend under eight hours in New York before flying back to Israel. His office defended the schedule, stating that numerous world leaders had requested bilateral meetings, but the prime minister could accommodate only a limited number due to time constraints and the need to return before the onset of the Jewish holiday of Sukkot.
According to his office, Netanyahu's itinerary features meetings with the presidents of Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay, Panama, and Ethiopia; the vice president of Colombia; and the prime ministers of Greece, Slovenia, and Papua New Guinea. Conspicuously absent were officials from Washington or European powers like Britain and France.
The absence of a meeting with Trump comes despite the two leaders jointly launching a war on Iran in February. While Trump has met with Netanyahu eight times during his second presidential term – most recently in July – cracks emerged in the alliance as Washington sought an exit strategy. An interim U.S.-Iran agreement signed in June drew sharp opposition from Israel before unraveling weeks later.
Public backing for Israel in the U.S. has dropped significantly since the former launched a genocidal war on Gaza following the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas incursion.
Domestically, Netanyahu faces severe political headwinds, with opinion polls indicating he could lose the upcoming election as his national security standing remains damaged by the Oct. 7 breach.
Diplomatic friction with European capitals has deepened over military actions in Gaza and Lebanon, as well as Israel's push to activate the controversial E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank.
The development plan aims to sever occupied East Jerusalem from the West Bank while dividing the northern and southern sections of the Palestinian territory, drawing sharp condemnation from London and other European governments.
In response, 12 Western nations – including Britain, France, and Canada – announced or implemented sanctions against illegal Jewish settlements in the West Bank. Washington offered only a muted response to the Western sanctions, further signaling Tel Aviv's waning diplomatic shield.
Israel responded aggressively to London’s measures. Israeli authorities ordered the closure of Britain’s consulate serving Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem, expelled British representatives in Kiryat Gat, terminated participation in training programs for Palestinian Authority security forces and barred 12 British citizens, mostly members of parliament, from entering the country.
"Compared to before Oct. 7, 2023, we are in a much weaker position internationally, including in the Middle East," Liel emphasized, highlighting how international isolation has intensified since last year's U.N. assembly, when several Western nations moved toward recognizing a Palestinian state.
"This is definitely not a normal visit. It is not normal in terms of the political objections against him, the speeches made against Israel at the U.N.," he said.

Global bond sell-off piles new pressure on UK borrowing costs before budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:41:08 UTC
20:41:08 KST

Oil prices lurched upwards again on Thursday, creating a growing headache for UK policymakers ahead of John Healey’s budget next month.
While Healey has been keen to present an upbeat picture of the UK’s economic prospects, Treasury sources concede the sharp jump in oil and gas prices means they have “less room” than a month ago.
Officials are working “at pace” on a range of possible options for supporting consumers, particularly if high prices persist, feeding through into a sharp rise in the quarterly energy price cap in January.
But any package is expected to fall far short of the costly across-the-board subsidies announced by Liz Truss in 2022, with the Treasury mindful of the measures already taken, including Andy Burnham’s VAT cut on electricity bills.
Options are believed to include shifting more green subsidies into general taxation, echoing the approach taken by Rachel Reeves, or targeting help at the poorest households – though some officials are sceptical about how effectively this can be achieved.
The price of a barrel of Brent crude was up almost 5% at $108 on Thursday after reports of more military clashes between Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces.
Donald Trump has given little indication of how, or when, the wider US-Israeli war on Iran could be brought to a close, despite the impact on gasoline prices in the US before crucial midterm elections.
Senior UK government figures are also increasingly concerned about the prospect of interest rate rises, which could push up the cost of a mortgage just as Burnham has promised voters “breathing space”.
After leaving interest rates on hold at 3.75% last week, the Bank of England said it expected the energy price cap to rise by as much as 24% in the new year.
The Bank’s chief economist, Clare Lombardelli, said in a speech on Thursday that the longer oil prices remained elevated as a result of the war, the more likely it was that rates would have to rise.
“The longer higher energy prices persist, the greater the risk that indirect effects build and that inflation expectations, wage bargaining and price-setting behaviour begin to adjust in response,” she told an economic conference in Warsaw, Poland. “On that basis, policy is increasingly likely to need to tighten if elevated energy prices persist, absent clear evidence of disinflation or weaker activity.”
Lombardelli’s warning was echoed by another member of the Bank’s monetary policy committee, the deputy governor Sarah Breeden, who told a conference at Imperial College London: “The larger and longer the shock, the more likely it is that we’ll see the material second-round effects that policy needs to respond [to].”
Expectations of higher inflation and interest rates caused by rising energy prices are a key factor driving the global selloff in government bond markets – raising the cost of borrowing for the UK, alongside other economies.
The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds, known as gilts, rose to 5.39% on Thursday, approaching the 19-year high set last week.
Higher interest rates raise the upfront cost of government investment and feed through into Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts of whether the chancellor is on course to meet Labour’s fiscal rules.
Analysts believe recent increases in yields have wiped out more than half of the £24bn “headroom” against the rules that Reeves had built up at the time of the spring statement in March.
Healey has repeatedly promised to meet the rules with a “buffer against uncertainty” but this is widely expected to be significantly lower than £24bn. Rebuilding it to that level would be likely to require large tax increases or spending cuts, but Treasury sources insist the budget will be narrowly focused.
Investors across the main markets have been ditching bonds in recent weeks in a wave of selling, as the conflict in the Middle East rumbles on. As the bond sell-off continued to worsen on Thursday, yields on 10-year US treasury bonds surged to 5.17%, the highest level since 2007.
Alongside higher inflation, investors appear to be concerned about the risks of uncontrolled US government spending. Some analysts also suggest large-scale bond issuance by AI firms is undermining demand for treasuries.

Türkiye, Iraq agree to clear Sinjar of PKK
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:41:06 UTC
20:41:06 KST

President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi met in New York on Sept. 23. (AA Photo)
Türkiye and Iraq have agreed to end the presence of PKK in the strategic province of Sinjar, according to a joint statement that seeks to deepen security cooperation between the neighbors.
The joint statement was released after the meeting between President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi in New York on Sept. 23. It was the second meeting of the two leaders in three months.
The statement said Turkish and Iraqi authorities addressed all aspects of the strategic relations between the two countries and agreed to deepen their security cooperation.
“In this context, they agreed to fully restore state authority in Sinjar and eliminate the presence of illegal foreign armed elements,” read the statement.
“In light of progress achieved by these security measures implemented by Iraq, Turkish forces will gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zilkan base to the Federal Government of Iraq in accordance with the agreed mechanism and timetable.”
Although the statement did not specify which elements are concerned, it is well known that the PKK terror group has long been using Sinjar as a corridor between Syria and Iraq.
Baghdad had declared PKK as an illegal organization and banned all its activities in 2024. Türkiye and Iraq have also signed a comprehensive security cooperation in August 2024 that stipulates the former’s training of the Iraqi security forces against terrorism and other organized crime.
HH Türkiye to evacuate Bashiqa
According to the statement, Iraqi authorities’ success in disarming PKK in Sinjar and reinstating state authority will gradually trigger the evacuation of Turkish troops from the Bashiqa base near Mosul.
The presence of the Turkish Armed Forces (TSK) at the base started in 2015 in line with an agreement with the Kurdistan Regional Government for the training of the local forces in their fight against ISIL.
The Iraqi government at that time slammed Türkiye for violating its sovereign rights for unilaterally deploying troops.
After Türkiye and Iraq launched a new era in ties in 2022, they deepened their security ties and agreed to turn the Bashiqa base a joint military facility under the control of the Iraqi army.
The agreement reached in New York will pave the way for the complete evacuation of the Turkish troops from northern Iraq. Ankara and Baghdad have also developed an intelligence sharing mechanism to coordinate the latter’s efforts in Sinjar.
HH Deal in line with anti-terror bid
The timing of the Ankara-Baghdad deal is also important as the former has advanced the implementation of its “terror-free Türkiye” project that requires the disarmament and dissolution of PKK.
As PKK’s members and its senior brass as well as other facilities are in Iraq, the cooperation between Ankara and Baghdad is inevitable for the success of the process.
Clearing Sinjar of PKK and cutting its supply routes from Syria are considered to be important developments for the creation of a “terror-free region,” according to Ankara.

The Backstory: When EC disagreements went public, from Seshan to Lavasa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:40:54 UTC
20:40:54 KST

From TN Seshan’s battle over the Election Commission’s structure to Ashok Lavasa’s dissent in 2019, the poll panel has seen internal disagreements emerge into the public domain.
NEW DELHI: The Election Commission is facing a fresh political storm over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise, with the opposition demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation following a report in The Indian Express on differences within the poll panel over the exercise.According to the report, Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had objected at least 14 times over 10 months to SIR-related decisions, including those concerning voter deletions and electoral roll data. The report has brought into focus a question that has surfaced at different points in the Election Commission's history: what happens when members of the poll panel disagree over how it should exercise its powers?
There have been two prominent instances when such differences moved beyond the commission's internal proceedings and became matters of public and judicial scrutiny. In the 1990s, Chief Election Commissioner TN Seshan challenged the creation of a multi-member Election Commission and the appointment of two Election Commissioners alongside him. In 2019, Election Commissioner Ashok Lavasa publicly dissented from the majority view on complaints alleging Model Code of Conduct violations by senior political leaders.
When Seshan challenged other Election Commissioners
TN Seshan was appointed Chief Election Commissioner in December 1990 and became known for his strict enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct and his assertion of the Election Commission's constitutional powers.
The structure of the commission changed in October 1993, when the government moved to make the poll panel a three-member body.
On October 1, 1993, the President promulgated an ordinance providing for two Election Commissioners in addition to the CEC. On the same day, MS Gill and GVG Krishnamurthy were appointed as Election Commissioners. Seshan challenged the move in the Supreme Court, alleging that the appointments were intended to dilute his authority and "sideline" him. The government defended the move, maintaining that the Constitution permitted a multi-member Election Commission.The dispute soon spilled beyond the courtroom. The Supreme Court's eventual judgment recorded "unpleasant exchanges" between Seshan and Krishnamurthy at a meeting in October 1993, noting that allegations and counter-allegations had been made by the two commissioners. Gill later spoke publicly about the strained relationship, recalling his attempts to establish contact with Seshan after the appointments."The CEC, however, acted as if we don't exist," Gill famously said in 1995.Seshan approached the Supreme Court on October 26, 1993, challenging the ordinance and the appointments. The case raised a larger constitutional question: could the Chief Election Commissioner exercise overriding authority in a commission that now had two other members, or were all three meant to function collectively?
1995 verdict: CEC not above other ECs
The constitutional battle ended with a Supreme Court Constitution Bench judgment on July 14, 1995, which upheld the law providing for a multi-member Election Commission as well as the appointments of Gill and Krishnamurthy.The court rejected the proposition that the CEC's view would automatically prevail over those of the other Election Commissioners. "If the CEC is considered to be a superior in the sense that his word is final, he would render the ECs non-functional or ornamental," the court observed.The judgment also commented on the personal friction that had accompanied the constitutional dispute. "It is a pity they did not try to work as a team," the court said, adding that "suspicion and distrust got the better of them", while expressing the hope that the commissioners would work with mutual respect and confidence.The verdict thus established the framework for the functioning of a multi-member Election Commission, making clear that the CEC could not treat the other Election Commissioners as subordinate members whose views could simply be overridden.
2019: Lavasa's dissent
More than two decades later, another disagreement within the Election Commission became public during the 2019 Lok Sabha elections. The commission then comprised CEC Sunil Arora and Election Commissioners Ashok Lavasa and Sushil Chandra, with Lavasa disagreeing with the majority view in several complaints alleging Model Code violations by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then BJP president Amit Shah.The majority gave PM Modi and Shah clean chits in the complaints, while Lavasa wanted his dissenting views to be recorded and included in the commission's orders. The disagreement subsequently became a dispute over whether a minority opinion should form part of the final order issued by the poll panel.
Ashok Lavasa resigned before he was made CEC.
Lavasa eventually informed Arora that he would stay away from proceedings concerning MCC complaints. In a letter, he said his minority decisions were being "suppressed" in a manner contrary to conventions followed by multi-member statutory bodies and wrote: "In the present circumstances, I am left with no option but to keep away from such proceedings."
'We are not clones': Sunil Arora
The dispute became public during the election campaign, prompting then CEC Sunil Arora to respond. On May 18, 2019, Arora said the three members of the Commission were not expected to agree on every issue."The three members of ECI are not expected to be template or clones of each other," Arora said, describing the controversy as "unsavoury and avoidable". He also noted that differences of opinion had existed within the Commission in the past.
The full Commission subsequently discussed how dissent should be recorded. Lavasa's demand that minority views be made part of the final MCC orders was not accepted. Instead, the commission decided that the views of all members would be recorded in its proceedings, while the final order would reflect the majority decision.
On August 18, 2020, Lavasa resigned as Election Commissioner after being appointed vice-president of the Asian Development Bank. He had joined the Election Commission in January 2018 and still had more than two years left in his tenure. He was also next in line to become Chief Election Commissioner.The Election Commission formally bid farewell to Lavasa later that month, with Arora saying the ECI's loss was the Asian Development Bank's gain.
News desk journalist, digital, at The Times of India, with a focus on Indian politics. Over a decade of chasing stories, taming headlines and arguing with commas like they're part of the opposition. Tracks elections, policy pivots, party drama and the fine print of power, where every word can tilt the narrative. Believes good journalism is clarity under pressure, ideally filed before the next breaking alert crashes in. Powered by deadlines, context, sharp edits and a steady supply of strong tea.

Russia Prepares Sea-Launched Drone Attacks on Mediterranean NATO

According to the Spanish newspaper, US intelligence services have gathered information about alleged Kremlin plans for further escalation and shared it with several European governments.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“They will use drones concealed inside shipping containers and launched from the sea; it is not difficult at all,” said a source close to Lithuania’s Ministry of Defense, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
According to El Mundo, the governments of Spain, France, and Italy have been informed about the reported plans.

The drone is approximately two meters long, has a wingspan of about 2.5 meters, weighs up to 18 kilograms, and can reach speeds of around 160 kilometers per hour, according to the report.
Its maximum reported range is approximately 600 kilometers, although the actual distance depends on factors including payload and weather conditions. El Mundo reported that commercial vessels could potentially carry several Gerbera drones, which are easier to launch than larger Shahed or Geran-type attack drones.
If launched from a vessel positioned 200 to 300 kilometers offshore, a Gerbera could reach the coast in roughly one hour and 15 minutes to two hours, depending on its speed. While its relatively small payload would limit the scale of physical destruction, the report said such a drone could potentially start fires, damage exposed infrastructure, or temporarily disrupt operations at ports or airports.
The reported plans come amid broader concerns over Russian hybrid operations against European countries supporting Ukraine. Russia has generally operated below what security experts describe as the threshold of direct military conflict with NATO, while European governments have accused Moscow of involvement in sabotage and other hybrid activities. El Mundo noted that recent drone incidents have heightened concerns that such operations could be used to test European defenses and gauge NATO countries’ responses.
Concerns over possible further escalation have also been raised elsewhere in Europe. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that countries supporting Ukraine, including Poland, could face Russian hybrid attacks involving drones and missiles in the coming months.
Tusk said there was a risk that drones or missiles could enter the territory of one or more NATO countries along the alliance’s eastern flank and potentially cause damage, with such incidents subsequently portrayed as accidental.

Russia recruiting up to 25,000 North Koreans to assemble drones: What the data shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:40:45 UTC
20:40:45 KST

Pyongyang, which supports Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, has helped staff and arm its forces. The UN says up to 25,000 North Koreans assemble drones in Russia, with most of their pay seized by Kim Jong-un's regime.
According to a report by the UN Security Council's Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team (MSMT), between 15,000 and 30,000 North Korean workers were present in Russia at the end of 2025.
Up to 1,000 of them were employed at strategically important facilities, including defence plants, steelworks and shipbuilding capacities.
The Ukrainian outlet "Ukrainska Pravda" also confirmed that up to 25,000 North Korean citizens are working on drone production in the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan, where Russian versions of Iran's Shahed drone are assembled.
Radio Liberty cites similar data, noting that North Koreans are registered as "students" in order to bypass UN sanctions that prohibit the use of DPRK labour abroad.
In 2025 Russia issued more than 36,400 visas to North Korean citizens, of which 35,800 were student visas.
Where North Koreans work
Workers from North Korea are now reportedly spread across Russia, from traditional employment regions in the Far East (Vladivostok, Khabarovsk and Sakhalin) to newer destinations such as Moscow, Saint Petersburg and Irkutsk.
Tatarstan has become the main centre of their employment, in particular the Alabuga special economic zone, which features in most investigations as a key hub for assembling strike drones.
It is here, according to Current Time and Radio Liberty, that North Korean workers staff assembly lines producing drones used by Russia to attack Ukrainian cities and infrastructure.
Sanctions evasion scheme
Although UN Security Council sanctions have banned the export of North Korean labour since 2017, Moscow and Pyongyang have built an entire ecosystem for circumventing these restrictions, the MSMT report notes.
North Koreans are being registered en masse on student and tourist visas, which allows their real status to be concealed and their work at Russian companies to be legalised.
According to reports, Russian legislation was amended to create legal loopholes that enabled "students" to receive income officially.
The report also describes cases in which Russian universities were bribed to arrange fictitious study programmes, as well as the role of intermediaries from third countries, including Belarus, which help organise entry and distribute the workforce.
This points to a systemic scheme that allows Pyongyang to earn millions of dollars and enables Russia to plug labour shortages in strategic industries.
Control and confiscated wages
According to MSMT, the working conditions of North Korean labourers in Russia remain extremely harsh and are fully controlled by the Pyongyang authorities.
The average annual income of such workers is around $7,500 (€6,593), but almost all of this is seized by Pyongyang.
The report notes that in 2025 alone North Korea received up to 800 million dollars from the labour of its citizens abroad. These funds, the report stresses, are channelled into financing the country's nuclear and missile programme.
The workers in effect live under constant surveillance by DPRK security services: their movements are strictly restricted, contact with Russian citizens is forbidden, and they are housed in closed dormitories to which outsiders have no access.
Human-rights activists describe these conditions as "slavery", citing the absence of freedom, isolation and the people's complete dependence on the regime. These findings are reported (source in Russian) by "Radio Liberty" (RFE/RL) and "Current Time", which underline the systematic exploitation of North Korean citizens at Russian enterprises.
Juche ideology at the service of Moscow's imperial ambitions
In October 2024, intelligence services in South Korea, the United States and Ukraine began reporting that thousands of Pyongyang's soldiers were being sent to Russia.
At the BRICS summit that same month, Russian President Vladimir Putin acknowledged the presence of North Koreans, but did not specify the purpose of their deployment.
Russian military officials later confirmed that North Koreans were being used to help counter Ukraine's successful incursion into the Kursk region, which began in August 2024.
Kim's regime subsequently established large-scale deliveries of arms and ammunition to Russia: artillery shells, ballistic missiles, small arms and artillery systems, and also sent military instructors.
The money Pyongyang receives is spent on purchasing more powerful weapons, a massive housing and industrial construction programme and, experts believe, on developing its nuclear programme, where Moscow may also be providing expert advice.
Why is Russia using North Korean labour?
Russia is facing an acute labour shortage because of its war against Ukraine and mobilisation.
North Koreans have become one means of filling staff gaps at defence-industry plants, especially in the drone sector, which requires large numbers of low-paid workers.
German international broadcaster Deutsche Welle notes that cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang intensified after Kim Jong Un's visit to Russia and agreements to expand military and industrial cooperation.
But the use of North Korean labour at Russian defence plants has sparked concern:
- The United States, South Korea and Japan see this as a violation of UN sanctions;
- human-rights organisations highlight the exploitation of people and the funding of North Korea's nuclear programmes;
- experts warn that the cooperation boosts the military potential of both countries.
What this means for the war in Ukraine
Russia launches hundreds of drones against Ukrainian territory every day. Moscow is now banking on mass production of cheap UAVs that can operate in swarms and overwhelm Ukrainian air defences.
The use of more powerful, faster jet-powered drones is also expanding, and countering them is particularly challenging.
The large-scale production of drones, in which North Korean workers are involved, directly increases the intensity of these attacks.

Gulf nations keep oil flowing amid Iran war, but it’s getting costly

Gulf nations keep oil flowing amid Iran war, but it’s getting costly
Despite the Strait of Hormuz blockade and other attacks, oil exporters and the US military have found workarounds, but they may not be sustainable
When Iran shut down the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the war, choking off sea passage for some 15 million barrels of oil a day, many feared that prices would skyrocket, cratering the world economy.
Instead, nearly seven months on, oil is expensive but not exorbitant, and analysts say there is enough oil available to meet current global needs, even as the higher prices cause political problems for US President Donald Trump and others.
That’s because Saudi Arabia and other Gulf producers quickly found alternative routes and reached for unused pipeline capacity. When Iran and its militant allies targeted those, the oil exporters and the US military found still other ways – workarounds for the workarounds – in an often clandestine game of whack-a-mole.
With oil now at around US$100 a barrel – higher than before the war but not as bad as feared – Iran has diminished leverage, while a US naval blockade and tightened sanctions smother its own economy.

Russian Drone and Missile Barrage Damages Kyiv Maternity Hospital and Odesa Medical Facility
Russian forces launched a massive missile and drone strike across Ukraine on September 24, killing at least two people in Kyiv and damaging medical facilities in the capital and Odesa, despite Ukrainian air defenses intercepting over 200 drones and seven advanced missiles.
Russian forces launched a large-scale overnight assault on Ukraine, deploying a mix of anti-ship and ballistic missiles alongside a swarm of 282 strike drones, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on September 24.
Ukrainian air defense systems successfully intercepted a significant portion of the complex barrage, neutralizing four Zircon cruise missiles, three ballistic missiles, one S8000 “Banderol” jet-powered loitering munition, and 219 unmanned aerial vehicles.
