Press review: US, NATO hamper nuclear dialogue as US gains partial control of Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. The United States and the North Atlantic Alliance hinder efforts toward restoring the nuclear dialogue, while the US-Iran dialogue appears stalled, despite a recent meeting between the two countries. Meanwhile, US leader Donald Trump secures partial control over Greenland. These stories topped Thursday's newspaper headlines across Russia.
Izvestia: US, NATO hamper efforts to restore nuclear dialogue
Seven months into the expiration of the New START Treaty in February, the global security system is facing new threats. Russian Permanent Representative to the United Nations Office and other international organizations in Geneva Gennady Gatilov told Izvestia that France and Britain have begun an opaque buildup of their strategic arsenals, disregarding their own principles of transparency in the nuclear sphere. The destabilizing practice of holding joint NATO-led nuclear missions is being expanded further, and "some new schemes of deterrence" that heighten nuclear non-proliferation risks are being introduced, he said.
Earlier, US Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said that the United States possesses orbital weapons for space control. The Western media said his remark could imply electronic warfare systems rather than kinetic weapons. Outer space is a sphere covered by the Golden Dome, a proposed US multilayered anti-missile defense initiative, Dmitry Stefanovich, research fellow at the Center for International Security at the Primakov Institute of World Economy and International Relations of the Russian Academy of Sciences (IMEMO), emphasized.
He views the likelihood of talks about a new agreement in the nuclear sphere as low, even as the number of challenging issues that require compromises has increased, the expert stressed.
Pavel Anisimov, deputy director of the International Relations and Political Science Institute at Russian State University for the Humanities, said the parties could soon attempt to agree on at least temporary limitations or channels to prevent a crisis. Now that the US has obtained orbital weapons, nuclear arms control can no longer be discussed separately from anti-missile issues, space and high-precision non-nuclear weapons, he argued.
Meanwhile, contacts at various levels between Russia and the United States are ongoing, and the two leaders regularly exchange phone calls. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio held a meeting in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly High-level Week in New York. However, no dialogue on strategic stability is currently underway, and whether it will be resumed depends on whether Washington acknowledges the need to improve relations with Russia, Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said.
Izvestia: US-Iran dialogue stalled, despite contacts at UNGA
The meeting between Iranian and US officials at the UN General Assembly is unlikely to end the confrontation between the two countries, experts interviewed by Izvestia said as they warned about escalation risks instead, even as US President Donald Trump described the three-hour talks as "very good." The US leader himself was absent from the meeting as he refused to tone down harsh rhetoric toward Tehran, saying that a deal could be made and threatening to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic. However, Tehran is standing its ground: the Iranian side said it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz as soon as the US lifts its naval blockade, unblocks frozen assets, pays compensation, and ends the war "on all fronts."
The US-Iran meeting on the sidelines of the UNGA was the first after the June ceasefire completely collapsed. The US team of negotiators included special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi represented Iran. At that, the two countries’ diplomats did not communicate directly, and Qatari officials acted as mediators as they moved between the two delegations during the day.
Experts interviewed by Izvestia do not expect any breakthrough from the New York meetings. The contacts themselves were positive, as they could help ease tensions for a while, Yelena Suponina, an expert in Oriental studies, said. However, she continued, one should not expect any lasting settlement amid the deep mutual mistrust and fundamental differences between the two countries.
Each side pursues its own pragmatic goals in this round of talks, with Tehran, for one, seeking to demonstrate readiness for dialogue, Igor Pshenichnikov, a political analyst, said. The talks could also help Trump to demonstrate to the US electorate at least minimal progress on the foreign policy track before the congressional midterms.
There is no chance of an actual settlement right now, another political analyst, Alexander Kargin, said. According to him, the points of the Islamabad memorandum, signed last summer, were basically never implemented, except for the brief reopening of the Hormuz Strait for purely pragmatic purposes: Tehran needed to resume oil exports and Washington sought to bring fuel prices down. Transit is blocked again, and the two sides are waiting to see who will be first to make concessions.
According to Pshenichnikov, Trump cannot get out of the conflict, as this would mean capitulation for the White House. However, he cannot continue the protracted campaign either. Since Tehran's conditions remain unacceptable to the United States, the confrontation may flare up with renewed vigor and escalate to a large-scale regional crisis after the November election, the analyst warned.
Kommersant: US gets partial control of Greenland
At a ceremony on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly session in New York on September 22, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed an agreement on defense cooperation that will allow the Americans to expand their military presence on this strategically important Danish island and make it almost inaccessible to non-Western countries. Even as Greenland remains an autonomous Danish territory, the document gives such broad powers to the US that a case could easily be made for its partial control of the island.
Among other things, the US will get the right to modernize and expand the Pituffik space base, formerly known as Thule, and build two new facilities in Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig. Besides, the agreement provides a legal opportunity to accelerate the deployment of additional military bases there.
Alexander Yermakov, researcher with the Center for International Security at the Russian Academy of Sciences’ Institute of World Economy and International Relations, explained in a column for Kommersant that the US decided to resume expanding its military activities on the island after their gradual reduction there peaked in the 1950s-early 1960s.
Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig will likely host patrol aircraft and drones for monitoring the northern Atlantic Ocean and the Arctic, even as other activities, including the deployment of offensive arms or anti-missile systems, cannot be ruled out either, the expert argued. It’s hard to predict for now but it is a matter of modernizing space surveillance systems as the US base there has primarily served this purpose over the past few decades.
As regards the Pittufik space base, a line in the new agreement reads that the sides agree to deploy elements of the new generation Golden Dome missile defense system currently being built on Trump’s orders there. "This could perhaps imply anti-missile deployments as a radar modernization would hardly require a separate article in the agreement," Yermakov argued.
"It would be useful for the US to set up a permanent base for patrol flights and long-range UAVS there to monitor the Northern Sea Route and the broader Arctic and deploy infrastructure for more frequent and longer deployment of fighter jets in order to provide air defense purposes on the island and approaches to the United States," the expert concluded.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: Trump seeks to pave way for new meeting with North Korea’s Kim
US President Donald Trump held a meeting with his South Korean counterpart, Lee Jae-myung, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York. As the US leader wished, he and Lee mostly discussed $350 billion in proposed South Korean investment in the US economy in exchange for lower tariffs on South Korean exports. Among other issues, the two leaders discussed the potential resumption of Trump’s contacts with North Korea’s Kim Jong Un.
Besides, the Trump-Lee meeting discussed fuel supplies to nuclear-powered submarines and South Korea’s push to secure US agreement to transfer wartime operational control to Seoul. Even as no combat has been conducted on the Korean Peninsula since 1953, the US maintains an 18,000-strong military contingent in South Korea that would form the backbone of an allied group of forces should war break out again. This does not sit well with the government led by the Democratic party which came to power in 2025 as it seeks to appeal to nationalist sentiments in society.
Alexander Vorontsov, head of the Korea and Mongolia Department at the Oriental Studies Institute under the Russian Academy of Sciences, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta in an interview that this was a long-standing issue. "Under the US-South Korea agreement signed in the 1950s, the US should hold the core war-fighting command of a combined US-South Korean force. Under a South Korean government led by Democrats, as is the case now, they say that this infringes upon the country’s sovereignty. <…> Therefore, they seek the transfer of operational command over their forces to South Korea. The Americans were previously skeptical of this idea. On the contrary, Trump takes a different view as he believes that allies should pay the US more for their defense and, whenever possible, defend themselves independently. Given this stance, he is more constructive toward South Korea’s ambitions."
Lee also hinted that Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping scheduled for September 24 could contribute to improving South Korea’s relations with China.
Also, Lee told Trump that he expected the US leader to help him restore ties with North Korea. Trump agreed to help as he also said he had established a good relationship with North Korea’s Kim. There has been no confirmation that Trump-Kim relations have been established indeed. There was only a statement from the US president that he would agree to meet with the North Korean leader and that he looked forward to such a meeting. If work toward this goal is underway indeed, a partial transfer of control over the joint US-South Korean battlegroup to Seoul could be part of the effort to create positive conditions for a meeting with Kim.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Moscow might need new mega-tall skyscraper
There are 2,594 buildings over 200 meters tall globally, including 256 supertalls of 300 meters or more, Oleg Bogdan, the creative director of Genpro architects, said at a discussion hosted by the Moscow State University of Civil Engineering. As many as 222 cities across 52 countries have at least one skyscraper of more than 200 meters. Burj Khalifa in Dubai is the world’s tallest at 828 meters, but it will soon lose that status as Saudi Arabia should build Jeddah Tower at 1,008 meters in 2028.
Russia appears to be an outsider against this background. The 462-m tall Lakhta Center in St. Petersburg is Europe’s tallest, and the Federation East tower in Moscow City, which is 373.7 meters tall, is second-tallest. Moscow is among the top ten global cities for buildings over 300 meters.
Moscow is currently building more skyscrapers than all European capitals combined, Vasily Solomin, the creator of the Neboskryoby (Skyscrapers) channel on Telegram, said. Almost as many towers as there already are is currently being built in Moscow City, meaning the number of skyscrapers in the business center will double in the next two to three years. And even more skyscrapers are being erected outside that area in the Russian capital.
The growing number of skyscrapers in and around Moscow City even distorts the silhouette of the business quarter and may deprive it of its postcard appearance, Filipp Nikandrov, chief architect at Gorproekt, argued. To prevent this, the capital needs a new mega-tall building, or a taller flagship building rising to 800-900 meters.
Projects are no longer being developed solely for PR, the expert said, as economic viability is increasingly being considered. In 2025, 114 skyscraper projects, or a record high, were put on hold worldwide. Only projects with genuine demand for commercial space survive, Bogdan explained.
TASS is not responsible for the material quoted in these press reviews

Why No One Wants to Date Tech Bros
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Engaged in a flirtatious conversation at a bar in Manhattan, 23-year-old Gary stood with a Guinness in hand as he explained to a woman why he took an engineering job at Palantir, the data analytics company cofounded by Alex Karp and Peter Thiel. Raking in a $250,000 salary would allow him to help pay off his parents’ mounting medical bills, he explained.
Gary wasn’t met with sympathy. Medical debt, the woman told him, was “not an excuse to work somewhere like that.” She was referring, of course, to Palantir’s controversial work with governments, including the US and Israel, which use the company’s surveillance tools for law enforcement and military operations.
Since joining the tech company in 2025, Gary has noticed that naming his employer prompts brutal reactions from prospective paramours. One woman, he says, called him the devil; another asked how he lives with himself. “Sometimes people would just straight up stop talking to me,” he says.
Recently, Gary’s buddies requested he not mention Palantir on their nights out together so as to not tank the whole group’s chances of getting laid. “I get nervous now. I don’t bring it up,” he says. (Gary, along with the other daters in this piece, have been given pseudonyms to protect against professional, if not romantic, repercussions.)
Gary has resorted to saying he works in AI. “Even that gets some pretty bad responses sometimes,” he says. His Hinge profile doesn’t mention his employer. And sometimes he makes up stories out of thin air to justify working for Palantir—like that line about the medical debt. His parents don’t have any, nor are they ill.
The bachelors of Palantir aren’t the only tech bros dealing with the industry’s fall from grace. Take 29-year-old James, who lives in San Francisco and works at Tesla. Earlier this year, on his third date with a woman he met on Raya, she asked whether he’d voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 election. A self-described “moderate liberal or moderate progressive” who “always votes blue and always will, probably,” James was offended. “I was like, ‘Are you kidding me? Did I really give that off?’” She replied, “You work for Tesla, so I just need to check.”
James says skepticism of his politics has “come up repeatedly” in his dating life. “If I don’t immediately say that I don’t like Elon Musk, people think that I’m conservative, which is generally not something that people like in San Francisco,” he says.
Once seen as a groundbreaking leader in sustainability and a quirky futurist, Musk—recently crowned the world’s first trillionaire—is better known these days for his record-breaking donation to Trump’s 2024 campaign, being the brain behind DOGE, the dismantling of Twitter, an apparent Nazi salute, frequent ketamine use, racist tweets, and something of a breeding kink.
Long gone is the cliché of the optimistic tech guy in flip-flops and a ratty old hoodie. The tech industry is now seen as the locus of unchecked power. Meta created an environment where Russian bots could influence elections and designed features that foster social media addiction among teens. Amazon, which has been widely accused of unfair labor practices and of generating a staggering amount of waste, has aided in the collapse of small, independent businesses, while a glowed-up Jeff Bezos has become a poster child for extreme wealth inequality. More recently, the AI industry is being widely maligned over claims that it’s exacerbating job loss, pollution, and a critical-thinking crisis.
Amy Laurent, the founder of a high-end matchmaking company, has a front-row seat to the way Big Tech’s moral failings are causing problems for single, rank-and-file tech bros. Turns out their cushy paychecks often aren’t enough of an upside anymore.
“I think 10 years ago, saying you worked in tech was more about innovation, ambition, intelligence,” says Laurent. Now, many people charge Big Tech with “causing the breakdown of society,” whether they’re worried about “AI, job displacement, wealth inequality, privacy and surveillance, content moderation, or political influence.”
Laurent says that when she pitches her tech-employed male clients to women, she acknowledges their hesitation right off the bat: “Listen, I have a great guy to tell you about. He’s such a good match for you. Now hear me out: He’s in tech.” The justifications are a new feature of her work.
Jessica Engle, a family and marriage therapist, has noticed that men in tech worry about being perceived as red-pilled. Recently, one of her clients expressed concern about having his Apple Watch visible in his dating profile photos. He wondered whether the gadget “would make him look like a tech bro” and whether it might signal a “very particular kind of toxic masculinity that we’re seeing more and more in the news.”
Engle’s client wasn’t wrong to worry. Mira, a 29-year-old Bay Area resident, says she perceives a career in tech as a possible “right-wing flag” or a sign that someone might be “manosphere-coded” or libertarian.
When 28-year-old Helen was an undergraduate at Stanford from 2016 to 2020, she viewed men in tech as guys who “stay up late and maybe have bad hygiene.” But her feelings toward them have gotten even worse over time as she’s questioned the industry’s overall impact.
Helen’s family is from the Tigray region of Ethiopia, whose population, beginning in 2020, was subjected to a prolonged period of human rights abuses. “When I started thinking about questions around genocide and the technology that kills or tracks or excludes,” Helen says, “I realized that the things these people are building are secretly, or under the surface, really nefarious, and I could not personally be with someone who is a puzzle piece in that tapestry.”
Helen herself has worked in tech. Soon after graduating from college, she accepted a job at Grammarly. But after about a year, she went to work for a mutual-aid platform and now is employed at an impact investing firm funding technology for underserved communities. Similarly, Sasha, a 31-year-old Oakland resident, had a brief stint working in AI before heading to a sustainability-focused tech company, where she is now chief of staff. In dating, when she meets someone who works or wants to work in AI, she wonders, “Does that mean that we have the same values in terms of climate and sustainability and thinking about human rights?”
Even if they do, she adds, “then the issue I have is there’s clearly this cognitive dissonance happening between what you’re working on and what you care about, which I have a really hard time accepting.”
James, the Tesla employee, confesses that he embodies plenty of tech bro stereotypes that might work against him, including “paying too much in rent” (or “just generally gentrifying”), ordering most of his meals on DoorDash (“I suck at cooking”), and not “really contributing to the culture of the city that much.”
“I really fit the mold so much that it’s sort of like, I have to at least be self-aware of it,” James says.
The pushback James gets IRL makes him wonder how much more happens behind screens. “There’s less visible rejection because you kind of get prefiltered out,” he says. “If I were to write on the dating app that I work at Tesla, I think it would just cut a lot of people right away.” His experience seems to bear this out. On his Hinge profile, he disclosed his place of work; on Raya he decided against it. He says he’s had more success on Raya.
In fact, about four months after joining Raya, he met someone. His new girlfriend had recently moved to the Bay Area for medical school and, before dating James, had managed to stay insulated from tech culture. “I was talking to my now girlfriend, and she was like, ‘Yeah, I feel like I’ve gotten lucky. I didn’t really know what the tech bro stereotype is.’”
“I was like, ‘Thank God. I don’t think I would have made it if you did.’”

Waymo offers new incentives for commuters on public transit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Waymo offers new incentives for commuters on public transit
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Waymo customers in San Francisco will soon be able to earn credit toward future rides when they use one of the robotaxis to connect to public transit.
Alphabet-owned Waymo introduced its transit rewards program Tuesday. It will start in Northern California and expand to other cities. Waymo employees will be the first to access the program.
To earn ride credit, or Waymo Cash, customers will have to link their Visa card to the Waymo app and use it to take an autonomous trip and public transit within two hours of each other. For each connected trip on public transit, riders will earn $2.85 in Waymo Cash, which is the cost of transit fare in San Francisco.
Students who commute to college by bus and train often experience delays and safety threats. But they don’t have to deal with the high costs of driving.
“Access to transit is really something that transit agencies need to put focus on,” said Henriette Cornet, co-director of the Autonomous Vehicles and the City Initiative at the University of San Francisco, who has done research on autonomy and public transit. “In the Bay Area, rail is solid and we have very good bus rides, but for some neighborhoods it’s very hard to access that first point of transit.”
The rewards program applies to all 27 Bay Area transit agencies that accept Visa tap-to-pay. San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie launched a tap-to-pay option throughout the Muni transit system last year.
“Public transit networks and shared autonomous vehicles are part of a complementary mobility ecosystem,” Waymo said in its announcement.
Waymo announced today it received approval from California regulators to expand its service area across 18 counties, including the cities of San Diego and Sacramento.
The move to incentivize the use of public transit could broaden the appeal of Mountain View-based Waymo, which has been offering rides to the public in San Francisco since 2024.
The white Jaguar I-Paces, equipped with sensors and cameras, have become a common site on the hilly streets of the city and beyond.
Waymo also recently launched its newest vehicle, a blue van dubbed the Ojai.
The transit rewards program also helps position Waymo as a collaborator with public transit rather than a competitor.
“It’s a way for them to to show a willingness to integrate within cities and to be more complementary rather than replacing,” Cornet said.
It could help the company’s reputation in the city, which took a hit after a robotaxi struck and killed a neighborhood cat last year.
Local officials have also raised concerns about Waymo affecting the availability of human driver jobs.
L.A. Metro asked the Legislature for $379 million for Olympics-related capital projects, and got just $20 million.
“San José has always believed innovation should make everyday life work better,” said San José Mayor Matt Mahan in a statement. “This partnership does exactly that by using new technology to strengthen public transit, not replace it, making regional travel more seamless and giving people more ways to get where they need to go.”
According to Waymo, recent surveys show that more than 50% of Waymo customers use public transit in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Phoenix.
“We’re proud to invest directly in this connectivity to make everyday commutes easier and more affordable,” the company said.

Australia calls for 'absolute consensus' on Pacific military group
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:59:47 UTC
18:59:47 KST

Pacific defence ministers call for consensus on military response group
In short:
Pacific defence ministers are taking a cautious approach to expanding the Pacific Response Group, a military force.
Although ministers previously agreed to consider giving it a broader role in responding to civil unrest, they have put the brakes on, not wanting to be rushed.
What's next?
Australia's defence chief says any change must have "absolute consensus" among Pacific countries.
Pacific defence ministers have signalled they will not rush to expand the remit of a new military response group, with Australia's defence chief saying there must be "absolute consensus" about how it evolves.
The South Pacific Defence Ministers' Meeting (SPDMM) — which draws in Australia, Chile, Fiji, France, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and Tonga — has wrapped up in Fiji.
On top of the agenda was the Pacific Response Group (PRG), which was formed in 2024 as part of a push from Australia and several other governments to develop a more coordinated response to natural disasters in the region.
Last year, the ministers endorsed a move to broaden the mandate of the PRG so it can also conduct "stabilisation operations" for Pacific nations that request military help to deal with civil unrest.
And in May this year, senior Pacific military officers endorsed a push for a new regional treaty that would govern how deployments take place, recommending Pacific leaders kickstart negotiations on a framework that would make it easier to rapidly send personnel to countries grappling with crises.
But while there is enthusiasm for the idea, it is also politically sensitive.
That is partly because the PRG can easily be seen as part of a broader push by Australia and its allies to block China from the security space, and partly because it will have to grapple with fraught questions around what legal immunity is offered to personnel deployed to other countries.
Some Pacific nations are also dealing with internal political issues — for example, Fiji is embroiled in an intense domestic debate on constitutional reform, and is likely to go to the polls before February next year.
On top of that, Pacific bureaucracies have also struggled to keep pace with the push for rapid change within the PRG just a couple of years after it was established.
When Pacific leaders met in Palau, they did not agree to kickstart negotiations on the treaty, signalling that they wanted to move more slowly on the issue.
And this afternoon, SPDMM defence ministers released a communique saying they had told senior military officers that the framework had to "consider the privileges and immunities relevant to HADR [humanitarian and disaster relief] and any future PRG stabilisation function".
The ministers also said they had agreed to take a "phased approach" to expanding the PRG's mandate, "recognising the importance of first consolidating and enhancing the PRG's humanitarian assistance and disaster relief [HADR] capabilities" before working to "include stabilisation operations".
Australian Defence Force chief Admiral Mark Hammond, who represented Australia at the meeting along with Assistant Defence Minister Peter Khalil, told the ABC that the group "must pay due respect to sovereign constitutional processes" and there had to be an "absolute consensus of an overlap with respect to national interest".
"We still need some time to work things through their constitutional processes and some of the nations at the table are on the cusp of national elections, some have only recently elected them or had a cabinet reshuffle, so these take time to bed down," Mr Hammond said.
But Admiral Hammond told the ABC there was still rock-solid support for the PRG at a "macro level" because it embodied the idea of Pacific-led security.
"When you look at the Pacific Response Group and the number of nations that are present in that, and you see that arriving as an initial response force to one of our Pacific Island nations, there will be representatives from that nation, in the PRG, that will be able to speak to the local issues, to help us cut through bureaucracy and to interpret their national interest into individual language that enables us to get on, deliver and support," he said.
One Pacific government representative, who requested anonymity to speak frankly, said there was not any "opposition" to the PRG, which they said was largely seen as a "great idea."
But they said some of the questions around immunity and sovereignty, as well as the geopolitical backdrop, could be "a little bit sensitive".
"Everyone wants to take this slowly and carefully and get this right,"
Pacific security expert Anna Powles from Massey University said it was "not surprising that securing regional consensus is proving challenging".
"Some countries are suggesting the process has been rushed and have questions about where the agreement will sit within the regional security architecture," she said.
"It could be useful to locate the framework under the Biketawa Declaration, which has the credibility and the tested mechanisms to support regionally led responses."
The seven countries represented at SPDMM also expressed "grave concern" over China's ballistic missile test earlier this year, using much stronger language than was adopted at the Pacific Island Forum (PIF) leaders' meeting in Palau earlier this month.
"Ministers highlighted that the manner in which this activity was conducted risked undermining PIF leaders' declaration of the Blue Pacific Continent as an Ocean of Peace," they said.
"It also undermined leaders' call to engage with the Blue Pacific Continent in a manner that honours the Pacific Way, respects national sovereignty and supports national and Pacific-led approaches."

2026-09-24

Ukraine’s disgraced former Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko has moved to Austria, the media outlet Ukrainska Pravda reported late on Sept. 23.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from Kravchenko and will publish his response once it is received.
Kravchenko was fired by parliament on Sept. 15 amid a major corruption investigation.
He left Ukraine on Sept. 14, under the pretext of an official trip to a conference in Paris. But the organizers told the Kyiv Independent that they had not expected him to attend, strengthening the suspicions that the trip was a fig leaf for fleeing Ukraine to avoid potential charges.
Ukrainska Pravda cited records from Austria’s Central Register of Residents.
According to the register, Kravchenko and his wife are registered on 7 Jordangasse, apartment No. 12, in downtown Vienna.
Apartment No. 12 at 7 Jordangasse is the office of CS Corporate Services GmbH, a company that provides registered addresses to Austrian limited liability companies, secretarial services, management services, and the sale of shelf companies that are already incorporated and ready to be transferred to a new owner, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
There is speculation in the media that Kravchenko may apply for political asylum in Austria.
Austria does not generally extradite Ukrainian citizens, and several former Ukrainian officials live there.
Kravchenko's personal office was searched by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau in early September as part of a large-scale corruption investigation into an alleged scam call center protection racket run from the Prosecutor General's Office.
Within the investigation, a top prosecutor described as a “confidant” of Kravchenko was charged. Publicly revealed evidence hints at Kravchenko being implicated, and he submitted his resignation on Sept. 7.
Kravchenko left Ukraine on Sept. 14 and simultaneously approved charges against the head of the anti-corruption agency investigating him.
The charges against Semen Kryvonos, head of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau, and an unnamed “close associate” of Oleksandr Klymenko, chief of the Special Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), were seen by many as a petty vendetta rather than pursuit of justice.
The charges were canceled by the Prosecutor General's Office late on Sept. 14, and Kravchenko was dismissed by parliament the next day.
On Sept. 17, President Volodymyr Zelensky appointed Anton Kovalsky, chief prosecutor of Khmelnytsky Oblast, as acting prosecutor general.
Media reports suggest Kovalsky could ultimately be appointed prosecutor general, rather than merely serving in an acting capacity.

Ukrainian Defense Forces strike two Russian radars, drone launch site

Ukrainian Defense Forces strike two Russian radars, drone launch site
According to Ukrinform, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Facebook.
In temporarily occupied Donetsk, a site used to store, prepare and launch attack drones was struck. Hitting such facilities is one of the priority areas of combat operations by the Defense Forces.
In temporarily occupied settlements of Chekhohrad (formerly Novohrodivka) and Yakymivka in the Zaporizhzhia region, 35N6 Kasta and P-18 radar stations were struck.
The 35N6 Kasta is a Russian mobile all-round surveillance radar designed to detect aerial targets, including those flying at extremely low altitudes, and transmit data to air defense systems.
The P-18 is a mobile long-range early-warning radar operating in the meter wavelength range that was developed during the Soviet era. It is designed to detect aerial targets, determine their coordinates (azimuth and range), and transmit data to users. It is operated by the Russian military as an early-warning asset for air defense.
In temporarily occupied Velyka Bilozerka in the Zaporizhzhia region, a fuel and lubricants depot of Russian forces was struck.
As reported by Ukrinform, Ukrainian Defense Forces units also struck Russian UAV command posts, a drone depot of the Rubicon unit, and other facilities of the Russian invading forces.

Gelderland to impose nitrogen limits on farms despite BBB split
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:54:58 UTC
18:54:58 KST

Gelderland to impose nitrogen limits on farms despite BBB split
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Gelderland has become the first province to restrict farming in “buffer zones” around nature reserves to bring down nitrogen compound emissions.
The provincial assembly voted to draw a 500-metre cordon around the Veluwe and three other vulnerable areas, in anticipation of nationwide restrictions that the government is drawing up.
New livestock farms and extensions to existing ones will be banned within the buffer zones from this year.
Other limitations will be phased in over the next 10 years, including a ban on synthetic fertiliser, restrictions on gas consumption and an obligation to make cattle sheds more energy efficient.
The plans have divided the parties in the agricultural province, which has the highest levels of ammonia pollution in the Netherlands.
They were drawn up by Ans Mol, executive member for the farmers’ party BBB, who said that doing nothing would mean “very big risks” for the sector. But seven of the BBB’s 12 assembly members voted against the plan.
Farmers’ protests
Coalition partners VVD, CDA, ChristenUnie and the SGP all backed the measures, which were also supported by the opposition parties GroenLinks, PvdA and D66.
Farmers picketed the provincial assembly building in Arnhem at the weekend to protest against nitrogen restrictions, arguing that they were not supported by evidence and deprived farmers of a future.
The provincial plans have been announced while the government in The Hague is still drawing up its own schedule of measures to bring down nitrogen pollution so that major housebuilding and infrastructure projects can go ahead.
Chris Backes, professor of environmental law at Utrecht University, has warned that some provinces will have to bring in their own measures to prevent the government using the “emergency brake” of a 5% to 10% reduction in heads of cattle.
Farmers are also facing legal action from environmental campaign groups such as Mobilisation for the Environment (MOB), which has petitioned regional courts to cancel the licences for 130 farm businesses.
All construction projects have to obtain a nature permit which shows they comply with environmental regulations, including European limits on nitrogen compound emissions around Natura-2000 conservation areas.

No synagogues, but signs of fishing 20,000 years ago in northern Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:54:38 UTC
18:54:38 KST

There is a handwritten sign on the bank of the Jordan River in northern Israel. It is designed to both intrigue and deter: "Benot Yaakov Bridge archaeological excavation. Here we are looking for bones and tools of early humans (about 660,000 years). We haven't found any gold and there are no dinosaurs."
The sign is positioned for the people boating down the river can see it. During our visit to the archaeological site, dozens of kayaks passed the bridge, but actually the excavation is a kilometer north of where we were sitting. Gonen Sharon of Tel Hai University excavated just by the bridge for several years, but now his attentions have moved to a bit south.
Like gold prospectors in California, the excavators, including about ten students, dig through and sift the riverbank soil, searching for bone fragments and tiny artifacts from ancient cultures.
We knew the people in the Hula Valley were fishing at the same spoty on the shore for more than 10,000 years, mostly net fishing. Sharon shows us a stone with a narrow "waist." Its length is no more than eight centimeters. Clearly he delights in the find. As he recently reported with colleagues, the prehistoric fisherfolk used limestone weights to weigh down fishing nets as long as 15,000 years ago by the Gesher, and as much as 20,000 years ago at Lake Kinneret. There, at the site called Ohalo II, archaeologists not only found net sinkers but a strand of plant fiber string.
The layers now excavated at the Jordan River Steps, at the Jordan River's outflow south of the Hula Valley, record people present on the shore of what had once been Lake Hula for thousands of years. The earliest excavated layer at this spot, by carbon-14 dating, is about 20,000 years old. The latest is Neolithic, about 10,000 years ago.
Note that there are older layers beneath all that which remain to be excavated.
The period Sharon describes spans 20,000 to 10,000 years ago. To grasp the immense stretch of time unfolding before us on the riverbank, he adds with a smile: "King David probably lived only about 3,000 years ago, and his story already blends legend with reality, making it very difficult for us to know what is true and what is fabricated. Imagine how much harder it is for us to determine clear and definitive things about much older periods."
Inexhaustible bounty
The fishers who sat on what is now the Jordan River, enjoying the cool water on a hot day just like us, didn't know their ancestors who used the same technology, but it seems they preserved a tradition of selecting the most suitable stones for weights. According to Sharon, a development in weight technology can be observed.
Over time, the frequency of stones shaped with indentations better suited to being tied increased. But the selection of stones of similar size, shape and weight is a connecting thread between cultures separated by thousands of years. The discovery of concentrations of weights suggests specific areas where nets were maintained, perhaps where weights were replaced, or where a net was left and not retrieved.
Net fishing was just one of the techniques used at the site. The fishers also carved hooks from bones and used fish traps, catching among others silver carp and common carp. Jordan tilapia and Galilee tilapia, and catfish.
Analysis of fish teeth found at sites along the Jordan River reveal that the lake also harbored giant barbel, a carp that could grow to more than two meters in length. Fish bone analysis indicated that the lake also contained trout (known more commonly as rainbow trout) which have gone extinct or nearly so in nature here, but are bred in local fish farms.
These fishers weren't the earliest inhabitants. Naama Goren-Inbar of the Hebrew University is a world-renowned expert in the study of the dawn of humanity, excavated in the area of the bridge area for years. Gesher Benot Yaakov features the signs of deliberately nurtured fire a million years ago, and one thing that distinguishes the boggy sites along the river is the exceptional preservation of plant material, allowing us to know what the valley's vegetation was like almost a million years ago – and what the hominins, existing hundreds of thousands of years before our species emerged, ate, which included plants, and apparently animals from elephants to horses and bears to swine.
During the 10,000 years documented in the site's layers, the Northern Hemisphere was transitioning from Last Glacial Maximum to the interglacial period, in which we live today. The maximum peaked about 23,000 years ago, and mean global average temperatures then were 9 to 5 degrees Celsius lower than today, an enormous difference. Here there were no glaciers, but in any case, by 10,000 years ago the climate along the Jordan River was just like it is today (excluding global warming).
The period between 20,000 to 10,000 years ago is called the Epipaleolithic. Its end marks the transition from hunting and gathering societies to agricultural societies.
At the start of the Epipaleolithic, everybody lived in small nomadic groups of hunter-gatherers. There were no permanent settlements. By the end, as the Neolithic began, there was a shift to an economy based on agriculture and domestication, essentially leading to the world as we know it today.
The site studied by the Jordan River became a fishing site during the Epipaleolithic. The people didn't live there, they came to fish.
"We clearly see a development in fishing technology. The hooks represent this best. We found 20 hooks, each looking different – the barbs, the size, the way the line is tied. Some of the hooks are very small, and we are still researching which fish they were suitable for. We also found small weights with a groove around them, allowing a rope to be tied so the hook would sink in the water," Sharon says. "In total, we currently have about 20 hooks and 10 weights."
The giant carp were identified by teeth, not bones. Sharon assumes they were caught with nets, not hooks. How were they cooked? "Some were roasted over fire, and others were preserved with salt or dried. The knowledge was passed down from generation to generation," Sharon answers. There was a high level of resource utilization and sophistication here. The diet was diverse and included meat and fish." (Giant carp are long since extinct here.)
However, once people settled down, it wouldn't take long to use up an area's resources – how long, 20 years? 30? "After that, there is no choice but to develop agriculture, on land and in water. A permanent resident can't just get up and move… At this point, one can understand the importance of location. River resources are inexhaustible. More fish will always arrive," Sharon points out.
Swamp plants also regenerate quickly, and migratory birds come every year, he adds. "One of the things we are learning here is that water resources, in particular, may have enabled the first permanent settlements."
King David wasn't here
At this point, Sharon takes a deep breath. The conversation turns to a topic dear to his heart: the struggle of prehistorians to gain the recognition and assistance received by archaeologists excavating later periods.
"The sites along the Jordan River are among the most important in the world. There is preservation and findings here that exist nowhere else," he says. "We have a major problem in Israel with presenting prehistoric sites… Some people in Israel say the world is 5,700 years old. From their perspective, I am researching events that occurred before the creation of the world and talking about things like technology, evolution and human development, in periods when, in their opinion, there was no world… The feeling in Israel is sometimes that if it's not directly related to King David, no one is interested."
Yet this site by the Jordan River is more important than Jerusalem, he argues. "Jerusalem matters only to Christians, Muslims and Jews. This site is important to all of humanity. It documents the exit from Africa, the cultural evolution of humans and the technology they used."
Here, we have the earliest evidence of fire beyond Africa all the way to the fishing 10,000 years ago, when agriculture began. "Anywhere else in the world, this place would become a pilgrimage site," he claims. Not here. "See for yourself. Boats pass by, some colliding with the stream banks and destroying the layers. There are construction works, farming, cows going down to the water. At Einan [nearby] are the oldest houses in the world, and nothing is being done about it. If I had found a synagogue here – everything would look different."
We fell silent. A dinghy sailed down the stream, its occupants cheerfully waving at us. We waved back. One of them asked, "What did you find?" Sharon replied, "Just bones."
Roast fresh fish
The conversation about roasted fresh fish whetted the appetite. We drove to Iskander, a restaurant that operates at the site from which the boats we saw depart. On the way, I dreamed of fresh fish, trout or tilapia, in the best local tradition of thousands of years. I envisioned a whole fish, beautifully prepared, with rice, tahini and some fresh vegetables. At Iskander, even before we sat down, it became clear that it was time to wake up from my dreams. First, it's a meat restaurant. The waitress pointed to the vegetarian dishes on the menu and said the fish appeared there. With tiredness-induced naivete, I asked, "Is it local?" The waitress looked at me suspiciously and said, "It's salmon."
Salmon is a local fish, in Norway. Is there no other fish? "No. That's what we have, but there are skewers, chicken or lamb."
We thanked her and left. We settled for hummus at a local joint but the question of the fish our ancient ancestors ate continued to occupy me.
From a publication by the Agriculture Ministry and the Fish Breeders Organization, I learned that in an average week, a person in Israel eats about 350 grams of fish; each year, an Israeli resident eats about 18-19 kilograms of fish, a quarter of which is fresh. The most popular fish in Israel are tilapia and salmon. Far behind them are sea bream and carp.
Salmon is imported from aquaculture farms in Norway and Chile and in fact, 90 percent of the fish eaten in Israel are imported. Each year, 150,000 tons of fish are imported into the country, most frozen. Only 15,000 tons of fish come from local production: aquaculture (14,500 tons) and the rest from fishing in the Mediterranean Sea and Lake Kinneret.
If one appreciates the ancient tradition highlighted by Sharon's research to find successors in the Galilee, then it is worth noting the recent news that a new restaurant opened in Kibbutz Ein Gev. Its menu features only fish from Lake Kinneret: tilapia, Kinneret bleak (a freshwater fish that grows only in Lake Kinneret), mullet and silver carp.
Erik Melamed, the entrepreneur who opened the restaurant, says: "We advocate sustainability and local agriculture; we fish using environmentally friendly ecological methods. We do not approach breeding areas or shallow waters, we return small fish to the water, and we only catch what we need. There is a treasure here that has not been used for many years because no one fished in Lake Kinneret, and now we are here to make it accessible to everyone."

Esra Tekin
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Iran is misreading the US political system if it believes the November midterm elections could restrict President Donald Trump’s ability to act against Tehran, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday.
“I think the Iranians are under this illusion that Democrats are going to win in November, and the president will no longer be able to do things against them,” Rubio told reporters in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Rubio said Tehran appeared not to understand the division of powers in the US, arguing that while Congress plays an important role, the president retains extensive authority over national security matters.
“When it comes to the national security of our country, when it comes to the imposition of both sanctions and the use of military force, the president has extraordinary powers,” he said, pointing to Trump’s constitutional role as commander-in-chief.
His remarks came one day after Trump said he believed Washington would reach an agreement with Iran following the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump told the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, claiming Iranian leaders were waiting to see how his Republican Party performed in the vote.
Rubio said the outcome of the elections would not change Trump’s approach, describing Iran’s nuclear program as a national security issue rather than a matter of domestic politics.
“For him, the Iranian issue is not a political issue,” he said.
Rubio argued that US presidents and most countries had agreed for nearly five decades that Iran must not acquire a nuclear weapon but had repeatedly failed to take sufficient action.
Trump, he said, was prepared to act despite the associated costs because the consequences of failing to prevent a nuclear-armed Iran would be “substantially higher,” particularly for future generations.

Our auspicious programmes are not determined according to the English date. They are determined according to the Indian calendar and Indian dates.”

Summits for all diplomatic seasons: how the US has set the stage for Xi Jinping
From informal walk-and-talks to a state dinner, Chinese leader’s past meetings reveal the roles of personal rapport and official diplomacy
Xi’s first US visit as president: a shirtsleeves summit
In June 2013, just months after assuming the presidency, Xi travelled to the United States following a tour of Latin America.
According to then US president Barack Obama, “Our decision to meet so early [in Xi’s term] signifies the importance of the US-China relationship.”
Instead of heading to the diplomatic protocol-heavy capital of Washington, Xi’s historic first meeting with Obama took place at the Annenberg Retreat at Sunnylands, a 200-acre (81-hectare) estate in Rancho Mirage, California.
Originally built as a winter haven by publishers and philanthropists Walter and Leonore Annenberg – close friends of former US president Dwight Eisenhower – the estate holds a unique place in American history as a secluded sanctuary that has often hosted political heavyweights.

The Takeaway: UN General Assembly debate Day 2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:50:37 UTC
18:50:37 KST

The Takeaway: UN General Assembly debate Day 2
This edition of UN News's The Takeaway recaps key highlghts at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, including focus on the war in Ukraine and a renewed push by African countries for Security Council reform.
Conflicts test the UN’s ability to deliver peace
Why it matters: World leaders offered sharply different assessments of the United Nations as conflicts, geopolitical tensions and economic shocks increasingly extend beyond national borders.
- Argentina’s President Javier Milei accused the UN of failing to guarantee collective security.
- Czechia’s President Petr Pavel described the Organization as indispensable, particularly as a forum for dialogue between adversaries.
- Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called for renewed nuclear non-proliferation efforts and strict regulation of AI.
War in Ukraine poses a major test
The big picture: Leaders warned that Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine threatens regional security, global food supplies and contravenes the principles of the UN Charter.
- Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had lost nearly 250,000 troops on the battlefield between January and August this year.
- Estonia’s President Alar Karis called the aggression “one of the biggest tests for the UN’s relevance”, pointing to attacks on Black Sea ports and the resulting threat to global food security.
- Latvia’s President Edgars Rinkēvičs stressed the risk of regional instability: “What happens in Ukraine does not stay in Ukraine.”
Distant conflicts bring local consequences
Reality check: Leaders from several regions described how wars and instability affect countries far from the fighting.
- The President of the Dominican Republic, Luis Abinader stressed that conflicts in Europe and the Middle East directly affect food and energy prices in his country.
- He also warned that criminal networks controlling territory and trafficking arms and people in Haiti threaten regional peace and security.
- Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian condemned attacks on his country and accused the international community of applying double standards to Iran’s nuclear activities and Israel’s nuclear capabilities and actions in Gaza.
- Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo presented opposing accounts of the conflict in eastern DRC, where Rwanda-backed M23 fighters have seized and held key cities such as Goma and Bukavu, while both emphasized the need for progress towards peace.
From conflict and division to recovery
One bright spot: Some leaders highlighted efforts to move beyond years of destruction, displacement and political division.
- Syria’s President Ahmad Al-Sharaa declared that “Syria is rising”, pointing to reconstruction, transitional justice and the return of 3.5 million refugees and internally displaced persons.
- Libya’s Presidential Council President Mohamed Al-Menfi called for a unified, sovereign State and for the Mediterranean to become a bridge for development, trade, investment and security.
- Saida Mirziyoyeva of Uzbekistan said that Central Asian countries had begun to see one another as partners rather than as sources of threat.
- Cyprus President Nikos Christodoulides called for substantive negotiations on the island’s future within a UN-agreed framework.
Africa renews its call for Security Council reform
What was said: African leaders again argued that the Security Council no longer reflects current global realities.
- Kenya’s President William Ruto noted that Africa’s 54 countries represent almost one quarter of UN membership but have no permanent Council seat.
- “That imbalance might have reflected the world of 1945; it does not reflect the world of today,” he said.
- King Mswati III of Eswatini called for fair African representation and greater international support for African-led peace and stability initiatives. You can follow all of Thursday's big speeches on our live meetings coverage page right here

South Korea Approves Development of New AShM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:50:21 UTC
18:50:21 KST

South Korea has approved a development and procurement strategy for the new Ship-to-Ship Missile-II anti-ship missile (AShM).
The decision was made during a meeting of the Defense Project Promotion Committee, Naval News reports.
The missile development program is scheduled to run from 2028 to 2039, with a total budget estimated at $1.1 billion. Development is planned for 2028–2033, with mass production set to begin in 2034. The main platforms for the missile will be the future KDDX Batch-I and Batch-II destroyers.
The project’s main goal is to double the engagement range against surface targets compared with the standard Haeseong (SSM-700K C-Star) AShM, which has a range of 150–180 km. The new subsonic missile is expected to have an operational range of approximately 300–360 km.
The missile will feature a low-observable airframe and a turbofan engine instead of the turbojet engine used on Haeseong missiles.
The Agency for Defense Development (ADD) will serve as the lead developer, while South Korean defense companies will be involved in producing prototypes.
The increase in the missile’s range is a response to the growing threat from neighboring navies and North Korea’s ongoing naval modernization, which includes the construction of 5,000-ton destroyers of the Choe Hyon and Kang Kon classes.

Spain's Sanchez urges UNSC reform, slams Israel's Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:49:00 UTC
18:49:00 KST

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on Wednesday called for reforming the U.N. Security Council to ensure fair representation for all regions and abolishing the permanent members' veto power.
"We need to reform the Security Council so that all of the regions in the world have fair representation, and so that we can do away with the right of veto of the permanent members," Sanchez said, addressing the U.N. General Assembly.
Because as the U.N. Charter sets out, "no country should be a judge in its own case, no matter how powerful they are," he added.
He warned that the principles underpinning the international system were increasingly being challenged.
Peace, sustainability and equal opportunities are "being attacked" by political actors and governments seeking to take the world back to a "dark past," he said.
"I don't need to point them out. We all know who they are and what their modus operandi is."
Sanchez also outlined Spain's actions in response to conflicts, saying Madrid had done "everything possible" to oppose actions running counter to the U.N. Charter.
He cited sanctions against Russia as well as an arms embargo on the Israeli government.
He also reiterated Spain's "unequivocal" condemnation of the "genocide that (Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu is still perpetrating in Gaza."
Sanchez argued that multilateralism remains the best way to manage global interdependence and called for renewed trust in the U.N. and efforts to strengthen the organization.
The Spanish leader accused forces hostile to multilateralism of deliberately seeking to weaken international institutions, describing what he called a "planned and coordinated demolition attempt."
He said such actors first question international rules, then break them, cut contributions to multilateral organizations and obstruct their work before portraying them as ineffective.
"They start by questioning the rules, then they break them, knowing well that nobody will dare to hold them accountable. They cut their contributions to multilateral bodies like this one (the U.N.)." he said.
"They obstruct these organizations' ability to act, so then write them off as useless entities that we can do without," he added.
Despite those pressures, Sanchez urged countries to "ramp up our trust" in the U.N. and strengthen the organization so that it can play "the same key role it played last century." However, he acknowledged that such strengthening would "not be easy."
Turning to the U.N.'s leadership, Sanchez called for the next secretary-general to be a woman from Latin America, noting that all nine people to hold the post have been men.
"The time has come for a woman from Latin America to become United Nations Secretary-General," he said, describing it as a "historic debt that we must settle."
Sanchez also addressed the irregular migration crisis in the Spanish city of Ceuta, saying Spain would resist the temptation to "turn migrants into the enemy" or break the law and would instead respond while respecting human rights.
"Spain does not choose the easy route," he said. "We always choose the fairest route, and I also want to recognize that the world knows this."
Around 72,000 people irregularly crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on July 30-31, according to the Spanish government’s official estimate.
According to the latest government estimates, more than 3,000 migrants, including several hundred minors, are still living on the streets of Spain's North African enclave.
While temporary accommodation facilities have been established, authorities say up to 200 people voluntarily return to Morocco each day.

Ukraine grain output could drop 12 mln tonnes in 2027 on reduced acreage – Kernel CEO

Kernel agricultural holding CEO Yevhen Osypov expects Ukraine's grain production to decline by 12 million tonnes next year in a stress scenario, due to a possible reduction in acreage by farmers if a solution to resume exports is not found within the next six months, an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent reports.
"It is difficult to make such forecasts today. We hope that some solution will be found within the next six months. If a physical solution is not found, then objectively the planted areas will be reduced. In such a stress scenario, we estimated this as an underproduction of 12 million tonnes of grain next year," he said at the Forbes Ukraine Economic Resilience Forum in Kyiv on Wednesday.
According to Osypov, with the seaports closed, Ukraine will be able to export only about 20 million tonnes out of the 50 million tonnes of agricultural products required, or 40% of the necessary volume, meaning companies have to shift to other business models.
"Based on our own experience within the most recent corridors, efficiency was about 50%, which is insufficient, so new routes need to be sought. Because for business now, this is a matter of building a new business model. In other words, the old business model does not work there. Therefore, for our part, we are focusing on processing and exporting processed products," Osypov said.
According to him, under its new business model, Kernel is focusing on exporting smaller volumes of products with higher added value, while retaining the ability to purchase oilseeds from Ukrainian farmers, settle payments with them and export processed products.
Osypov also added that at present, due to restrictions related to security and logistics, as well as external factors, it cannot be expected that the Danube ports will be able to handle the volumes of cargo that Ukraine had in 2022-2023.
As reported, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), in its September report, raised its estimate of wheat production in Ukraine this year by 0.6 million tonnes from its August forecast, to 26 million tonnes, due to record yields. It also raised its estimate for other grains, excluding wheat and corn, by 0.5 million tonnes, to 7.29 million tonnes, while maintaining its corn production forecast at 31.8 million tonnes. Thus, the USDA estimates Ukraine's total grain production this year at 65.09 million tonnes.

BEIJING, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese-Egyptian joint archaeological mission has uncovered the remains of two sacred lakes at the Montu Temple precinct in Luxor, Egypt, the National Cultural Heritage Administration said Thursday.
The discovery marks the first layout of double sacred lakes within a single ancient Egyptian temple precinct, the administration said at a meeting on the progress of major archaeological projects.
Located in northern Luxor, the Montu Temple precinct is an important part of the Karnak Temple Complex and dates back more than 3,000 years.
Since 2018, a joint archaeological team comprising researchers from the Institute of Archaeology of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences and Egypt's Supreme Council of Antiquities under the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities has conducted systematic archaeological surveys and excavations at the site.
By 2026, the team had excavated an area of about 2,300 square meters.
During the latest work, archaeologists identified a previously unknown southern sacred lake covering more than 50 square meters. Together with the northern sacred lake, the discovery forms a distinctive layout of two sacred lakes within the same temple precinct.
The discovery provides important clues for studying the rituals and functions of the Montu Temple, according to the administration.
Since its founding in 2018, this collaborative team has been conducting excavations and research at the Montu Temple, making a series of important discoveries that has gradually uncovered the secrets of this ancient Egyptian site.
Beyond the Montu Temple, Chinese archaeologists are also actively engaged in sites across Egypt, including Luxor, Cairo and Alexandria, and cultural exchanges between China and Egypt have expanded into various fields. ■

Ocean drones deployed to monitor Southern Ocean carbon uptake
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:47:55 CST
18:47:55 KST

CANBERRA, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- A new fleet of uncrewed surface vehicles (USVs) has been deployed from Australia's Hobart to monitor the Southern Ocean and improve understanding of how much carbon dioxide (CO2) from the atmosphere is absorbed by the ocean surface.
The USVs will be deployed every quarter over five years to circumnavigate Antarctica, operating in the challenging conditions of the Southern Ocean, according to a statement released Thursday by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization (CSIRO), Australia's national science agency.
The USVs are autonomous mobile research platforms, powered by wind and solar energy, and will operate in remote waters for months at a time, recording data in real time to better understand ocean carbon sinks, the statement said.
Each deployment is expected to cover about 22,000 km in the Southern Ocean, specifically to acquire data in seasons and regions where ship traffic is limited, said CSIRO Principal Research Scientist Elizabeth Shadwick.
The project is an international collaboration involving CSIRO, the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, South Africa's Southern Ocean Carbon-Climate Observatory, among other partners.
Ocean sinks store about a third of the CO2 absorbed from the atmosphere each year, with the Southern Ocean accounting for 40 percent of global ocean CO2 uptake, according to CSIRO.
The USVs will collect continuous atmospheric and oceanographic observations, including atmospheric CO2, wind, temperature, sea surface temperature, salinity, dissolved oxygen and seawater CO2, it said, adding that the research will contribute to the annual Global Carbon Budget, which quantifies sources and sinks of CO2 emissions. ■

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- The International Conference on Combating Online Scams (ICCOS) concluded in Cambodia on Thursday with the adoption of the Phnom Penh Declaration, cementing a global commitment to disrupting criminal networks and eradicating online fraud.
The two-day conference drew representatives from governments, law enforcement agencies, international organizations, financial institutions, tech and telecom firms, and think tanks across more than 20 countries.
The declaration established 11 commitments to strengthen international cooperation against online scam networks and the transnational criminal activities associated with them.
"The commitments cover coordinated enforcement, disruption of illegal financial flows, asset recovery, victim protection, and measures to dismantle scam compounds and associated infrastructure," said a press release issued at the conclusion of the conference.
Cambodian Deputy Prime Minister Neth Savoeun, who serves as vice chairman of the country's Commission on Combating Online Scams, said that the declaration provides a vital roadmap for unified action.
"The fight against online scams cannot be successfully achieved by any single nation; it requires international cooperation at all levels," he said during the closing ceremony.
He added that as the host nation, Cambodia expects further endorsements of the Phnom Penh Declaration from additional countries and global bodies in the coming days.
Path Kosal, a secretary of state at the Office of the Council of Ministers and an ICCOS organizing committee member, echoed the call for solidarity in his closing summary report.
"The core message of this conference is clear: online scams have evolved into a severe transnational crime and a governance challenge. No single country, institution, or sector can tackle this cross-border threat alone," he said.
"Therefore, timely, effective, and collective actions require both stronger national capacity and stronger regional and global cooperation," he added. ■

Russian oil helping India weather Iran energy shock – Russian deputy FM

Russian oil helping India weather Iran energy shock – Russian deputy FM
Russian crude supplies helped cushion India from an oil-supply shock after the conflict in the Middle East disrupted energy flows through the Strait of Hormuz, showing Moscow’s reliability as an energy partner, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko has said. 
Rudenko’s statement comes amid renewed scrutiny on India’s Russian oil purchases, and after Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky called for choking off Russia’s oil trade under a new US sanctions law. 
Indian refiners turned heavily to Russian crude after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which used to handle roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies. 
The scale of the shift was most visible in March, when India’s Russian crude imports nearly doubled from the previous month to 2.25 million barrels per day (bpd) and accounted for half of its oil purchases. 
Gulf shipments to India simultaneously plunged 61% to 1.18 million bpd. Existing arrangements between Moscow and New Delhi helped “significantly mitigate” the consequences of disruptions to global energy trade, Rudenko told Russian news outlet NEWS.ru on Wednesday.
It showed Moscow could meet demand from its partners even in difficult geopolitical conditions, he added.
Good to meet @SecRubio of the US #UNHighLevelWeek
Reiterated India’s interests and concerns with regard to SRIA. Also discussed the Gulf and Ukraine situations.
🇮🇳 🇺🇸 pic.twitter.com/163YRVlMZG
Meanwhile, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar, who is in New York to attend the United Nations General Assembly meeting, raised New Delhi’s concerns about the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday. 
The law gives US President Donald Trump the authority to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top buyers of Russian oil and gas. India’s Russian oil purchases have eased from record summer levels as other supplies recovered, but Moscow remains India’s largest crude supplier.
Russian shipments stood at about 2.1 million bpd in August, and are tracking at around 1.9 million bpd in September, according to preliminary data from commodity analytics firm Kpler. India has maintained that securing affordable and dependable energy for its 1.4 billion people requires multiple suppliers, and warned against restrictions that could distort or constrict global energy markets.
Russia’s energy cooperation with India extends beyond oil. Rudenko pointed to the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant in southern India built in collaboration with Russia and said another site will soon be allocated for a Russian-designed nuclear facility.

Canada’s First CF-35A Lightning II Takes Flight for the First Time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:45:35 UTC
18:45:35 KST

A CF-35A Lightning II fighter jet, intended for the Royal Canadian Air Force, has made its maiden flight.
The F-35 Lightning II’s press service reported this on X.
The aircraft, bearing serial number AR-1, took off on September 23, 2026, from Naval Air Station Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth in Texas, where Lockheed Martin’s production facility is located.
Canadian identification markings have already been applied to the fighter jet. The air intakes feature the bilingual RCAF–ARC designation, and the tail bears a low-visibility Canadian flag.
As part of the Canadian Air Force, the aircraft will be designated CF-35A, marking the first use of a two-digit designation for a Canadian aircraft since the introduction of the new designation format in the 1960s.
Canada’s CF-35As are set to replace the CF-188 Hornet fleet, which will continue to carry out missions for NORAD and NATO until its retirement in 2032.
Canada joined the F-35 program in 2002 as a Tier 3 partner, but did not make the final decision to select the F-35A to replace its CF-188 Hornet fighters until 2022. In January 2023, the Canadian government signed an agreement to purchase 88 aircraft.
Officially, the entire fleet was expected to achieve full operational capability by 2032–2034. The F-35A was selected over Sweden’s Saab Gripen E to replace the aging CF-188 Hornet.
The situation changed after Donald Trump returned to power and a trade war began. On March 14, 2025, just days after taking office as prime minister, Mark Carney ordered a review of the decision to purchase 88 F-35As.
In May 2026, Canada’s Department of National Defence said that the review was ongoing and a final decision would be announced later. At the same time, preparations to receive the F-35 are continuing.
Canada initially approved the purchase of the first batch of 16 aircraft. The first eight F-35As are expected to arrive at Luke Air Force Base, Arizona, in 2026–2027 for Canadian pilot training, while the first aircraft are scheduled to arrive in Canada in 2028.
The main alternative to the F-35 remains Saab’s Gripen fighter proposal. A mixed fleet combining the F-35 and Gripen E is also being considered.
The first Canadian F-35As are expected to be delivered this year, while the future of the entire program depends on the Canadian government’s decision following its review.

Meta unveils lightweight VR glasses and camera-free AI glasses at Connect 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:45:15 UTC
18:45:15 KST

Meta unveils lightweight VR glasses and camera-free AI glasses at Connect 2026
Meta has revealed slimline VR glasses for immersive entertainment on the go and an audio-only, camera-free version of its Ray-Ban glasses as the latest additions to its expanding product portfolio.
Announced by CEO Mark Zuckerberg last night at the technology company's annual Connect conference, the Meta VR Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses expand its market-leading range of eyewear and headsets.
The Meta VR Glasses represent the bigger breakthrough, bringing virtual-reality gaming, 3D movies and other immersive digital experiences into a form factor only slightly larger than an ordinary pair of glasses.
This allows them to be worn for longer than current headsets and carried on the daily commute, as people might do with a pair of over-ear headphones.
Meta says it achieved the lightweight construction by splitting the architecture into two: the glasses, weighing about 100 grams, plus an attached "puck" that clips onto a pocket or bag and handles the processing.
Also key are the glasses' ultra-compact pancake lenses, which are about the size of a Scrabble tile and are fixed within a soft mesh structure on the inside of the frames.
The wearer manually shifts these lenses to sit directly in front of their eye, filling everything but their peripheral view with a 5K display.
This micro-OLED display offers angular resolution of 37 pixels per degree – more than Meta's current market-leading Quest VR headsets and enough to deliver crisp text and rich imagery.
The Meta VR Glasses can be used to play games or watch entertainment from the Meta Quest platform, including movies recorded in or converted to 3D. There are also new immersive formats that Meta is pioneering, like "immersive sports" streamed in ultra-high definition from the edge of the playing field at live events.
Users navigate the operating system using their eyes, voice and natural hand gestures like swiping and pinching, without having to use controllers – in some cases even to play entire games.
Meta also envisions the VR Glasses being used for work. Using full-colour passthrough – the view of the world in front of the glasses that's captured through its outward-facing cameras – wearers can turn any table surface into a keyboard and touchpad and surround themselves with multiple virtual screens from their Mac or PC.
The VR Glasses will deliver up to three hours of continuous media playback from the battery on the puck. Meta expects to put the device on sale in spring 2027.
Unlike the rest of Meta's eyewear offering, the VR glasses are not intended to be worn all the time or to be used primarily for AI assistance, although the company's new Muse AI will be built-in.
The use of Meta's AI glasses out on the street has earned them the nickname of "pervert glasses", due to various documented incidents of men using the barely visible camera to covertly film women.
Surveillance concerns were also amplified after a Swedish news investigation revealed that videos captured by wearers' cameras – including highly sensitive ones where they were nude or having sex – were being streamed to subcontractors in Kenya.
The pushback against these aspects of the technology may be a driver behind Meta's other key new product launch at Connect, the Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses.
Developed with long-term partners EssilorLuxottica, these glasses lack the controversial camera of other Meta models, as well as the small screen of the Meta Ray-Ban Displays, launched this time last year.
Their functionality is more limited, letting users listen to audio through small open‑ear directional speakers built into the frame and interact by voice with Meta's AI assistant.
The slimmer feature set has allowed Meta to introduce new slimmer styles like the partially wire-frame Ray-Ban Clubmaster. The glasses' 12-hour battery life and 43-gram weight also mean they can more easily be worn all day.
In addition to the new products, Meta revealed the Gen 3 version of its Ray-Ban Meta glasses, with three new frame silhouettes, and several new versions of the cheaper Meta Glasses, launched just three months ago, including one with pop star Lisa, whose influence is partly responsible for the Labubu craze.
The keynote presentation also detailed the expanding capabilities of its Muse "personal AI agent", which was first revealed two weeks ago and which the company will be adding to all of its glasses. At the end, there was a quick sneak peek at a new Tamagotchi-like Muse Charm gadget.
Meta has established itself as the dominant player in the small but growing market for AI glasses, accounting for 94 per cent of display-less AI glasses shipped in the first half of 2026, according to tracking by Counterpoint Research.
By the end of the year, it will have more than 100 different styles available in its Ray-Ban, Oakley and own-brand collections.
