Venus May Have Devoured Its Moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

Venus has nearly the same mass, size, and structure as Earth, which has led astronomers to believe it should have a moon, but it doesn’t. It is technically possible that a moon never formed, but scientists have also come up with several scenarios to describe how Venus could have lost its satellite.
One previously presented hypothesis is that Venus’ moon was destroyed by a collision with some massive celestial body. But a recent study by researchers at the University of California, Riverside, suggests a different course of events. It posits that instead of being obliterated by some catastrophic external force, the moon was slowly pulled in by Venus’ gravity and plodding rotation until it fragmented and was completely swallowed.
“Venus didn’t require a catastrophe to arrive at what we can see today,” Steven Kane, an astrophysicist and the paper’s lead author, explained in a press release. “It turns out the gravity of the planet itself combined with the rate at which it spins naturally caused the moon to collapse on top of it.”
A planet’s rotation can either push or pull on its satellites, depending on its speed. The rotation can cause variations in gravitational strength. This is why our moon isn’t in any danger of being eaten. In fact—because our 24-hour days are rather fast in a planetary sense—our moon is currently drifting away from Earth at a rate of about 1.5 inches per year.
And when astronomers say Venus spins slowly, they really mean it. The time it takes for Venus to complete one rotation is 243 Earth days. That’s longer than Venus’ year and makes the bright planet the slowest spinner in our solar system. This protracted rotation, combined with the planet’s gravity, means that even if a moon existed, it would not be pushed outward but would instead be dragged inward.
To verify this mechanism, Kane and his research team built a computer model simulating gravitational interactions between celestial bodies. After verifying the model’s accuracy by faithfully recreating the evolution of Earth’s moon, they ran simulations varying several factors including the time it takes Venus to complete one rotation and the mass of a hypothetical moon, ranging anywhere from 0.01 to 10 times that of Earth’s natural satellite.
The outcomes showed that the moon’s fate depended on Venus’ rotation speed, the lunar mass, and the shape of its orbit. Under many conditions, the satellite spiraled inward, eventually breaking apart and succumbing to the planet’s gravity. “When I made this discovery, I was shocked,” Kane recalled. “I thought surely the broad range of scenarios I was exploring would lead to a variety of results. But it all went pretty much in the same direction.”
In a few instances—such as when the researchers artificially sped up the planet’s rotation to once every 10 to 12 hours and the moon had a mass comparable to that of Earth’s—the simulations indicated a moon could survive for up to 4.5 billion years. But that’s little more than an interesting test of the model. It’s an extremely unlikely reality given our planetary neighbor’s current lethargic speed.
This study does not, however, prove that Venus once had a moon, and finding physical evidence of its existence will not be easy. Venus’ surface is geologically young, the number of craters indicating that top layer of rock is just a few hundred million years old. The planet itself formed at the same time as the rest of our solar system, some 4.6 billion years ago, but extreme amounts of volcanic and tectonic activity have essentially remodeled the surface.
If any evidence of a moon exists, it’s been paved over and may lie deep underground. Seismological surveys penetrating far into the Earth have provided evidence of our moon’s formation—anomalous structures pointing to a massive impact. If similar measurements could be conducted on Venus, it’s possible that traces of a moon that was once absorbed might be found.
The moon’s fate could also provide clues to solving another long-standing mystery: whether Venus once had an environment capable of supporting life. Swallowing a moon would have imparted enormous energy and angular momentum to the planet, which could significantly shift its rotation, geology, and climate—altering the course of the planet’s evolution.
This is not limited to Venus. Scientists seeking to identify habitable worlds among exoplanets have often considered the presence of a moon as a factor influencing habitability. However, it remains unclear whether a large moon is essential for the existence of life.
“My feeling is there are benefits to having a moon, but it isn’t required for habitability,” Kane said. “The moon has definitely changed the way Earth has evolved through time, but we don’t fully know how important that role is.”
This finding that planets with slower rotation speeds are less likely to retain a moon offers a new perspective in the search for Earth-like exoplanets. Even if very Earth-like planets are located, if their rotation speeds are not fast enough, they might come to devour their moons.
This story originally appeared on WIRED Japan and has been translated from Japanese.

Tactical voting at next election could push Reform into fourth place, poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:14:54 UTC
18:14:54 KST

Progressive voters could push Reform UK into fourth place and put Labour within touching distance of a majority if tactical voting is widespread at the next election, a major poll has found.
Andy Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage, the results suggest.
The poll of more than 8,000 voters, shared with the Guardian, suggests a widespread openness to voting tactically. It also shows the prime minister’s most successful electoral strategy would be to unite the centre and left bloc of voters, while the right remains split.
It would be a marked contrast to the tactics of Keir Starmer’s Labour before the 2024 general election, when the party tried to attract more conservative older voters. Such a tactic would be likely to unsettle some in Labour, given the same strategy was deployed for Ed Miliband’s failed bid in 2015, albeit before Reform’s arrival as a major electoral force.
The poll on the eve of Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool shows a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham’s Labour and will encourage those in the party who are thinking of gambling on an early election while Reform’s ratings are ebbing and while leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.
Twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right since April.
The previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, was conducted by Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees in Burnham’s first month as prime minister.
It suggests Labour would be the largest party in parliament if an election took place today, on 272 seats, a four-point lead. This would mean achieving 42% of parliamentary seats with 28% of the vote.
Reform would become the official opposition on 153. This represents 24% of seats – the same as its vote share. The Conservatives would fall to third place with 85.
Two hundred seats are tight marginals decided by under five points, meaning a two- to three-point swing could move about 100 seats that are likely to decide a future election. But in a sign of the volatility of the polls, a far higher percentage of voters are open to tactical voting in those seats when they cite their preferred party.
If voters are prepared to switch to one of the two frontrunners in their seats, rather than their preferred party, then Reform UK’s seat count would fall dramatically, favouring Labour and the Conservatives.
About 18% of voters who live in a seat where tactical voting would make a substantial difference say they are willing to do so but are not yet doing so. If those voters decided to vote tactically, Reform UK would be reduced to 62 seats, giving Labour 319 – six short of a majority.
Of the 91 seats where Reform would cease to be the most likely winner, 46 would go to the Conservatives and 43 to Labour. The projection is unlikely to be exact at this stage in the electoral cycle.
Reform’s chances of winning fell by more than 50 points in 59 seats. Among these are the Wrekin, Torridge and Tavistock, and North West Cambridgeshire – all of which have Reform as the most likely leader under the “normal” assumptions but lose out to the Conservatives under a scenario with more tactical voting.
In 2024, the now-chancellor, John Healey, held Rawmarsh and Conisbrough with 49% of the vote, with Reform in second place on 28.6%. The base modelling of the MRP indicates that Reform could win a tight race in the seat, with a 51% chance, but this plummets if tactical voting increases, with a 76% chance of Labour holding the seat in this scenario.
In Bassetlaw, Reform could lose even as its own vote share rises from 35% to 40%, because tactical voting would lift Labour further – from 32% to 40%. The Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and Greens would lose supporters if this switching took place. The forecast estimates that the winner would shift from Reform, with a 77% chance, to Labour, with a 58% chance.
Newark, held by the Conservative-turned-Reform MP Robert Jenrick, is forecast to flip to the Conservatives under both scenarios, although under heavier tactical voting the chance of a Conservative win increases from 68% to more than 99% should Labour backers vote Conservative to stop him.
Damian Lyons Lowe, Survation’s chief executive, said: “Estimating tactical voting is a complex consideration, but the mechanics here are simple. Four in 10 voters are currently backing a party that can’t finish in the top two where they live and are willing to vote tactically.
“But when we ask whether they would lend their vote to the stronger local contender in a two-horse race, around half said yes. That gap – worth some 18 points of the national electorate – is an enormous untapped reservoir for parties looking to squeeze voters.
“Should these voters act as they say, our model shows Reform falling from second place to fourth, losing around 90 seats, despite its own vote share actually going up. Reform-leaning Conservatives will consolidate too. Reform doesn’t collapse; it risks being outnumbered, seat by seat, by voters coordinating around whoever is best placed locally on the left and right.”
The prediction is also complicated by the sheer number of seats Labour won in 2024 from the Conservatives where the party has been polling as low as third over the past year. Progressive voters living in seats such as Labour-held Southend would be unlikely to opt to vote for the Conservatives, even if they were technically the best placed to beat Reform at the next election, showing the limitations of predictions around tactical voting.
The poll also suggests Labour is gaining considerable numbers of voters back from other leftwing parties, but not from Reform. The share of Labour’s lost 2024 voters going to the Greens, Liberal Democrats, Plaid Cymru or the Scottish National party has fallen from 60% to 46%; but on the right, of those lost to Reform or the Tories, it has fallen from 27% to 24%.
Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, said the polling indicated a far more optimistic public mood than before the Labour conference last year, but there was also significant expectation that Burnham needed to deliver.
“There are signs of optimism and even hope, but what has not changed is the way voters are crying out for bold action, fast,” she said. “The results show a huge amount of common ground between voters, especially when it comes to the cost of living. Voters who have moved in different directions since the general election two years ago are united by the fact that action on the cost of living crisis will have the single biggest bearing on their future vote.”

80 years and still steaming: A milestone year for the world’s last seagoing paddle steamer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:14:10 UTC
18:14:10 KST

This October, the Waverley paddle steamer is marking its 80th anniversary with cruises along London’s iconic River Thames.
Your next cruise on London’s iconic River Thames could be aboard the world’s last seagoing paddle steam vessel – The Waverley. And, should you board this October, you could be celebrating its decades-long maritime history, too.
Next month, tourists will have the chance to step aboard The Waverley as it marks 80 years since its launch in October 1946.
Powered by a 2,100 horsepower steam engine, the Waverley takes its name from the eponymous novels by Scottish author Sir Walter Scott. A series of more than two dozen, the "Waverley Novels" unpacked different phases of Scottish history and dealt with themes such as visions of the future.
"Reaching 80 years is a remarkable achievement for any vessel, but for Waverley it represents far more than a milestone," Paul Semple, General Manager of Waverley Excursions, told Euronews Travel.
"Her story began on the Clyde on 2 October 1946, when she was launched at the Pointhouse Yard in Partick, Glasgow. Eighty years later, she remains in service and continues to give people the opportunity to experience the unique sight, sound and atmosphere of a traditional paddle steamer."
After decades of commercial service, her working life came to an end in 1974 when she was gifted to the Paddle Steamer Preservation Society for £1, but her story didn’t end there. She was brought back into service with the establishment of the Waverley Steam Navigation Co. Ltd. charity as a tourist attraction.
Since 1975, and after being fully restored to her original 1940s style, the Waverley has carried more than six million passengers, cruising across various UK destinations during the day, afternoon and evening.
A recent independent Economic Impact Assessment found that this has contributed £11.6 million (€13.5 million) to the British economy.
80 years and counting
The UK capital is the destination of her special birthday sailing on 2 October as she is set to depart from London Tower Pier. There will be live entertainment onboard, too, including performances from the Bel Canto Vintage Sisters – a jazz trio bringing the sounds of 1940s jazz and swing to the 21st-century.
For £47 (€54.67), passengers get a one-way ticket from London Tower Pier to Gravesend in Kent. This riverside town is the location of Gad’s Hill Place, home of English writer Charles Dickens, where he penned titles such as Great Expectations, which can be visited on select days.
Travellers will also be able to board cruises to and from Southend-on-Sea, with the London-bound route passing iconic landmarks like the O2 Arena, Canary Wharf and Tower Bridge.
Meanwhile, a £81 (€95) return ticket gives passengers the chance to see three Second World War-era forts built in the Thames estuaries: Shivering Sands, Red Sands and Knock John. The full day itinerary departs at 9:30 am and returns at 9:00 pm.
"The remarkable thing about Waverley is that, 80 years after her launch, she continues to sail and attract new generations of passengers," Semple said.
"Reaching this anniversary is a significant achievement, and we are delighted to be able to celebrate it onboard with the passengers, supporters and volunteers who have played such an important part in keeping Waverley sailing."
Other cruises this season will depart from English towns including Southampton, Swanage, Yarmouth, and Portsmouth Harbour, as well as further afield in Scotland from Dunoon, Glasgow, Greenrock, Kilcreggan, Blairmore and Largs.

Russian attacks kill at least 16, injure 59 across Ukraine as Kyiv hit by waves of drones, ballistic missiles

Two people were killed and eight others injured in Kyiv, where Russian ballistic missiles struck the capital in three waves overnight. Residential buildings, a maternity hospital, energy, and logistics infrastructure were among the sites damaged, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
"Every such attack happens because pressure on the aggressor has still not become total, and Russia believes it can continue relying on ballistic terror," Zelensky said. "We need ballistic missile interceptors to protect lives."
Russia launched 282 attack drones of various types overnight, including jet-powered drones, as well as Zircon anti-ship missiles and Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 ballistic missiles, the Air Force said. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 227 aerial targets, including 219 drones, four Zircon missiles, three ballistic missiles, and one Banderol munition. Strikes were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations.
In Donetsk Oblast, eight people were killed and 19 others injured in Russian attacks over the past day, regional Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Five people were killed in Oleksandrivka, two in Kramatorsk, and one in Sloviansk.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed six people and injured 12 others over the past day, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Among the attacks, Russia struck an agricultural enterprise in Stara Hnylytsia, where 12 people were injured, according to the Governor.
In Sumy Oblast, nine people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, local authorities said. Russian forces carried out nearly 60 attacks against 22 settlements.
In Odesa Oblast, two people were injured in a mass combined Russian attack that damaged a hospital, a school, residential buildings, a shopping center, warehouses, and other civilian infrastructure, regional Governor Oleh Kiper said.
In Kherson Oblast, two people were injured as Russian forces attacked critical infrastructure as well as residential areas, local authorities said. Two apartment buildings, a house and gas pipelines were damaged.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, six people were injured in Russian attacks on the Zaporizhzhia district, Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out 690 strikes against 55 settlements across the region over the past day.
Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast injured one person over the past day, regional authorities said. Russian forces attacked three districts more than 10 times with drones and artillery.

“Ukrainians understand that this winter may be very hard for us, but in response, we will have no other choice but to make it painful for Russia as well,” Zelensky said.

The phrase “General Winter” traditionally describes the severe weather that helped Russia repel invading armies. Zelensky turned the metaphor around to warn that attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure could provoke intensified strikes against the energy resources financing Moscow’s war.
Kyiv ties retaliation to Russian attacks
Zelensky presented the warning as conditional retaliation rather than an unconditional campaign against Russian energy infrastructure.
He said Ukraine had not chosen the war and was fighting because its people had chosen “not to die.” The president called for concrete de-escalation measures before winter but argued that Kyiv could not be expected to exercise restraint while Russia continued targeting civilian utilities.
Russia Sanctions Lifted for Two Oligarchs
Zelensky also said Ukraine’s strikes were aimed not at oil, fuel, or ports for their own sake, but at Russia’s ability to finance and continue the invasion.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, storage facilities, and export infrastructure with long-range drones. Kyiv considers such facilities legitimate military targets because they supply Russian forces and generate revenue for the Kremlin’s war effort.
Proposed energy truce remains uncertain
Zelensky’s warning came one day after talks with US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Previously Zelensky told Trump Ukraine was prepared to stop attacking Russian refineries if Moscow reciprocated by ending strikes on Ukraine’s electricity, heating, and water infrastructure.
“We are ready for an energy ceasefire,” Zelensky said after the meeting. “You don’t attack these, and we will not attack these.”
Trump had announced on Sept. 14 that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy facilities. However, neither side subsequently published formal terms, a list of protected sites, or a mechanism for monitoring alleged violations.
Kyiv has insisted that any pause must be reciprocal and cover every type of Russian attack against Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Zelensky has also said Moscow must clearly identify which Russian facilities it wants protected and accept equivalent restrictions concerning Ukrainian electricity and gas supplies.
Another winter battle over energy
Russia has repeatedly attempted to cripple Ukraine’s electricity and heating systems during the coldest months of the war, launching waves of missiles and drones against power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has expanded its ability to strike refineries and other energy facilities deep inside Russia. The attacks have disrupted fuel production and increased the economic cost of Moscow’s invasion.
Zelensky’s UN speech suggested that Kyiv would intensify that strategy if Russia launches another winter campaign against Ukrainian utilities.
He stressed that de-escalation remained possible, but only if Moscow stopped trying to use cold weather and the destruction of civilian infrastructure as weapons.
“General Winter,” Zelensky warned, may no longer fight exclusively for Russia.

‘Source of anxiety’: Pakistan cracks down before march to free Imran Khan

‘Source of anxiety’: Pakistan cracks down before march to free Imran Khan
The government has blocked highways to the capital and set up container barriers in preparation for the PTI protest, which seeks ex-PM Imran Khan’s release from jail.
Islamabad, Pakistan — The motorway linking Pakistan’s capital with Peshawar, about 180km (110 miles) to the northwest, has been closed to all traffic until further notice, according to a police notification.
So have the highway towards Dera Ismail Khan, the Hazara motorway and the Grand Trunk Road at Attock.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Pakistan ex-PM Imran Khan’s family accuses gov’t of defying hospital order
- list 2 of 4‘Where’s the humanity?’: Imran Khan’s sons fear for jailed ex-Pakistan PM
- list 3 of 4Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan’s sisters arrested before planned PTI march
- list 4 of 4Pakistan seals roads to Islamabad before protests for Imran Khan’s release
Each carries traffic between Islamabad and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the province governed by the party of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan, whose supporters plan to march on the capital on Sunday, September 27, demanding his release.
The motorway from Lahore, about 375km (235 miles) to the southeast, remains open.
Inside Islamabad, workers have welded shipping containers together and filled them with gravel and sand so they cannot be pushed aside. Several schools and colleges have been told to shut so police brought in from Punjab and Sindh can be housed there.
Police expect the march to draw between 20,000 and 25,000 people, according to local media reports.
While two of the country’s main opposition parties announced marches on the capital this month, only Khan’s Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) has faced measures on this scale.
Jamaat-e-Islami (JI), a religious party, also set out for Islamabad last week to protest against rising fuel prices. On Monday, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif telephoned its leader, Hafiz Naeemur Rehman, and by Tuesday afternoon JI had postponed its march, pending a meeting between the two men.
PTI leaders have received no such call.
Instead, Khan’s three sisters, all over the age of 65, have been detained in Lahore and at least six of the party’s legislators in Islamabad, all under a 1960 public order law that allows preventive detention without charge.
PTI says the true figure of those arrested is higher, and that one lawmaker taken from the parliament lodges has not been traced since.
Khan has been in prison since August 2023 and remains Pakistan’s most prominent opposition figure. But his party enters the final stretch before the protest weakened, with no major demonstration outside Khyber Pakhtunkhwa since November 2024, by its own account.
Yet, say analysts, the Pakistani government appears to be treating the protest march as a far bigger threat than a regular political event would warrant.
“While this is undoubtedly a difficult moment for PTI, it is equally exposing the government’s own frustration,” Habib Akram, a Lahore-based political analyst, told Al Jazeera.
“In fact, the government’s conduct suggests something more. It isn’t just afraid of this protest; it has turned this protest into a matter of its own survival.”
A capital behind containers
More than 2,000 containers have been placed across Islamabad and at Attock Bridge, the main crossing between Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Punjab, according to media reports, with 19,000 police officers on their way from Punjab and Sindh, and thousands more deployed at Attock.
Dawn, the country’s leading English-language newspaper, said in an editorial that the government appeared to be preparing “not for a political event but an invasion”.
Talal Chaudhry, the junior interior minister, rejected the suggestion that the government was shutting down the capital itself.
“Normal life in Islamabad is continuing. Hospitals, offices and essential services are functioning. The containers and security arrangements are precautionary measures, not a shutdown,” he told Al Jazeera.
Rana Ihsaan Afzal, a coordinator to the prime minister and a government spokesperson, was more candid.
“In trying to counter the rhetoric PTI has adopted, we do have to take certain measures, and yes, those measures carry their own consequences too, but we have to look at the bigger picture,” he told Al Jazeera.
It is all being mounted during one of the deadliest weeks for Pakistan’s security forces this year.
An attack on a police compound in Kohat, in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, killed more than 20 people on September 18, and six soldiers were killed in a gunfight in nearby Hangu two days later.
Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi set those losses against the march in Lahore on Monday.
“The situation in KP [Khyber Pakhtunkhwa] over the past 10 days is before everyone. There was a suicide attack on a mosque, and two or three other attacks. Our captain was killed, our soldiers were killed, our policemen were killed, and these people are preparing to storm a city,” he said.
The government’s case
Government ministers have seized on a remark by Junaid Akbar, PTI’s chief in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, who said protesters would turn Islamabad into Somnath, a Hindu temple in India sacked by Mehmood of Ghazni, an 11th-century invader, to try to paint the upcoming protest as a major law and order threat.
“Peaceful people do not leave their homes carrying nail-studded sticks,” Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said in Kohat on Monday.
But the PTI’s Sohail Afridi, the chief minister of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, who will lead the September 27 march, answered Tarar in Peshawar on Monday.
“We will go there on nothing but two hands and two feet. There will be nothing else in our hands,” he said.
In a September 18 judgement, the Islamabad High Court ruled that no party could block roads into the capital, and barred provincial governments from using state resources for the march.
Days later came the arrests of Imran Khan’s sisters. Aleema Khan was detained in Lahore on Sunday, and her sisters, Uzma Khan and Noreen Niazi, were taken in a predawn raid on their homes the next day, according to a family statement on September 22.
The Lahore High Court has reserved its decision on whether a petition challenging Aleema’s detention is admissible, after the family’s lawyer argued that the order was issued after the arrest.
Chaudhry said the sisters faced several cases, had led confrontational protests in the past, and were being held as a preventive measure.
PTI says the arrests reach far wider, listing five members of the National Assembly, a senator, provincial legislators and more than 1,500 workers.
“We were peaceful, we are peaceful, and we will remain peaceful. We are being punished for being peaceful,” Gohar Ali Khan, the PTI chairman, said in Peshawar on Monday, noting that four women from Khan’s family, including his wife Bushra Bibi, are now in jail.
‘Long march’ vs ‘permanent plan of action’
But Interior Minister Naqvi suggested that the government is bracing for a confrontation.
“I think this time we will draw up a permanent plan of action. We will not go halfway,” Naqvi said in Lahore on Monday, adding that the matter would be settled “once and for all”.
What he ruled out was a long sit-in of the kind PTI has staged before.
“This time, it will not happen that they come, and the country is shut down for 10 or 20 days. That possibility does not exist,” he said.
Afridi has signalled that he has exactly that in mind.
“The long march is not a T20, it will be a Test match,” he said on Monday, a reference to cricket’s five-day format.
If Naqvi’s comments sound ominous, they also carry a history with them.
On May 9, 2023, after Imran Khan was briefly arrested, his supporters attacked military installations across the country, including burning down a senior commander’s official residence in Lahore. That led to a major crackdown on the PTI’s supporters and leaders, with hundreds placed under arrest for days, and party leaders pressured to leave the group.
Then, on November 26, 2024, a PTI march on Islamabad ended in an overnight crackdown by security forces, in which the party says at least 12 of its supporters were killed. The government denies that, and says four security personnel died — even though Al Jazeera met families of some of the PTI supporters killed.
A contested mandate
PTI was stripped of its electoral symbol before the February 2024 general election, forcing its candidates to run as independents.
They still won 93 seats, more than any other party, but could not form a coalition, and the Pakistan Muslim League – Nawaz took power with other major parties.
A Commonwealth observer group, in its report on the polls released a year later, found that decisions by key institutions had “consistently limited the ability of one particular party” to contest the vote, in a reference to the PTI.
While the Election Commission of Pakistan rejected allegations of rigging, two and a half years on, the popularity scale remains tilted in favour of PTI.
Bilal Gilani, executive director of the pollster Gallup Pakistan, said its unpublished Public Opinion Pulse surveys showed a landscape broadly similar to 2024.
“PTI continues to lead nationally, but faces strong competition from PML-N in Punjab and PPP in Sindh,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that Khan remained the country’s most popular leader.
For Akram, that unresolved argument — over the lack of legitimacy of the 2024 election in the eyes of Pakistanis — is what keeps the pressure on.
“You can hold as much power as you want, but that question never fully goes away. It continues to haunt you, and it continues to be a source of anxiety for the government,” Akram said.
The ‘hard state’
In March 2025, army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir, who now also serves as Pakistan’s chief of defence forces, told a parliamentary security committee that the country must stop acting as a “soft state”.
“How long will we continue to sacrifice countless lives in a manner of a soft state?” he asked, according to state broadcaster PTV.
For Ahmed Ijaz, an Islamabad-based political analyst, the response to the September 27 march is a response to that thinking, rather than the PTI’s strength.
“Behind that confidence lies the thinking of a hard state, one that has decided no one will be granted an unconditional right to protest going forward,” he said.
Akram, however, said that a different factor might also be worrying the government and the military behind it.
The war in the Middle East has pushed petrol to 393.75 rupees ($1.42) a litre ($5.37 per gallon), up about 51 rupees ($0.18) since the start of September. That is what Jamaat-e-Islami was marching against, and it has warned that it will resume its march in October if the prime minister offers no relief.
Akram said the government’s real worry is multiple issues of antigovernment anger — price rises and Imran Khan’s continued incarceration — coming together.
“That merging could then pull other groups out onto the streets too, and that is precisely what worries the government,” he said.

US intelligence warns Europe of possible Russian drone attacks: Report

The CIA has warned several European governments of a possible Russian drone operation against Spain, France, or Italy, Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported late Wednesday, citing sources familiar with the alert.
The newspaper said the potential operation could involve Gerbera drones concealed aboard merchant ships and launched from the Mediterranean Sea. A source close to Lithuania’s Defense Ministry told El Mundo that launching the drones from a ship would be relatively straightforward.
According to the report, officials in Lithuania have information about the type of drone that could be used, while the governments of Spain, France, and Italy have been informed of a possible operation against one of these countries.
The report said several defense analysts were aware of a detailed CIA report that had circulated among European governments.
The Gerbera has a reported maximum range of 600 kilometers (373 miles), depending on its payload and conditions, the newspaper said. Launched from 200-300 km (124-186 mi) offshore, such a drone could potentially damage exposed equipment or temporarily disrupt operations at a port or airport, it added.
El Mundo linked the warning to CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s Aug. 25 visit to Moscow. It also cited reports by The Wall Street Journal and Politico that Ratcliffe had warned Russia against attacks or provocations targeting NATO.
The reported intelligence warning and the alleged Russian plans have not been independently confirmed.

Chinese shipments fueling Iran's weapons programs despite US sanctions - report
The report puts Chinese support for Iran at the center of President Xi Jinping's Washington visit this week, a summit President Trump has said will also cover trade, artificial intelligence and Taiwan
A Wall Street Journal investigation found Chinese suppliers sent around 1,300 shipments of dual-use components to Iran's defense ministry in the first half of 2026, sustaining Tehran's drone and missile programs even as Washington pressed Beijing over its support for Iran. The findings come as President Xi Jinping visits Washington this week for a summit with President Trump covering trade, AI safety and Taiwan.
Iranian customs records reviewed by the Journal, covering January 2025 through June 2026, listed thousands of shipments to Iran's defense ministry, including GPS devices, electric motors and aircraft engine parts, many citing a tariff exemption for defense imports.
Data showed one shipment of electronics components used in drone and missile guidance systems arrived in Tehran on the same day the US and Iran signed a 60-day truce in June. More than a dozen additional shipments worth over $6 million in drone-usable parts followed two days later.
China has become the only major buyer of Iranian oil despite US sanctions, providing billions of dollars to Tehran this year through Chinese front companies and banks that route transactions using China's currency to evade US oversight, according to US officials cited by the Journal. Satellite imagery from Chinese entities has also been linked by US officials to an Iranian strike that killed three American troops.
Suggested articles
The Journal reported that President Trump has told top officials that preserving relations with Xi is a priority, leading senior officials to downplay Chinese support for Iran ahead of the summit. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told lawmakers that China was enabling Iran "at different levels," while Trump said he trusted Xi's assurances that China would not supply Iran with weapons.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Chinese assistance had not changed the war's trajectory.
Despite hundreds of US sanctions, including the late-August "Operation Economic Outcast," no major Chinese companies have been targeted. Roughly four million barrels of Iranian oil reportedly reached China in the week after the program launched.
Senator Elissa Slotkin urged Trump to make Chinese support for Iran a "centerpiece" of his talks with Xi, while Beijing has denied wrongdoing, saying it maintains strict export controls and opposes unilateral US sanctions.

Oil keeps flowing, but cost of Gulf workarounds mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:10:03 UTC
18:10:03 KST

A boy stands with his bicycle on a beach overlooking commercial vessels anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Sept 7, 2026. (AP Photo)
When Iran shut down the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the war, choking off sea passage for some 15 million barrels of oil a day, many feared that prices would skyrocket, cratering the world economy.
Instead, nearly seven months on, oil is expensive but not exorbitant, and analysts say the supply is pretty much sufficient to meet current global needs, even as the higher prices cause political problems for U.S. President Donald Trump and others.
That’s because Saudi Arabia and other Gulf producers quickly found alternative routes and reached for unused pipeline capacity. When Iran and its militant allies targeted those, the oil exporters and the U.S. military found others — workarounds for the workarounds — in an often clandestine game of whack-a-mole.
With oil now at around $100 a barrel — higher than before the war but not as bad as feared — Iran has diminished leverage, while a U.S. naval blockade and tightened sanctions smother its own economy.
But the workarounds are expensive and may not be sustainable. The drawing down of existing commercial oil stocks — especially by China — has also helped keep prices in check, but cannot continue indefinitely.
Iran began attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz in response to the U.S.-Israeli bombardment that started the war. In response, the Saudis turned to their East-West pipeline that carries oil to their Red Sea port of Yanbu.
From there, tankers headed out through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait toward Asia. Likewise, the United Arab Emirates used its pipeline cutting across neighboring Oman to Fujairah — a route that skirts the strait.
Both pipelines had spare capacity, and the UAE’s state oil company ADNOC and Saudi Aramco used it to keep exports from collapsing completely during the first weeks of the war.
Meanwhile, some oil leaked out of the Strait of Hormuz. In May, ship operators willing to risk Iranian attack started taking advantage of a U.S.-supervised route near Oman, defying Iran’s demands to use its own vetted route. They shuttled back and forth at night with location systems and mobile phones turned off, and offloaded to tankers waiting outside the strait. Flows from Kuwait, Iraq, and the UAE started to rise again.
But Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen disrupted the Yanbu workaround in July by declaring a blockade of Saudi oil shipments, threatening the Bab el-Mandeb — a repeat of the Hormuz disruption.
Then the East-West pipeline was attacked earlier this month and forced to shut down, potentially for weeks.
With oil loading halted at Yanbu from Sept. 11, the Saudis shifted again, joining other Gulf producers sending oil through the U.S.-guided corridor in the Strait of Hormuz.
Analysts estimate some 6 million barrels of oil per day or more have been passing through the Strait of Hormuz on the dark shuttle route on average — some 40 percent or more of prewar flows.
Rahul Choudhary, vice president of upstream research at energy data firm Rystad Energy, did the math as follows: with 6 million or 7 million barrels per day now flowing through the southern route, plus 2 million barrels through the pipeline to Fujairah, fully 8 million or so of the blocked 15 million barrels per day from before the war have been restored.
But wait: about 3.5 million barrels per day are being drawn down from the globe’s abundant oil inventories. Meanwhile, demand has fallen by perhaps another 5 million barrels per day, due to the higher price and sluggish economic growth in key markets. Add in 500,000 to 700,000 barrels per day from other suppliers such as the U.S., and that pretty much evens out the global oil market.
“Our take is that the market is very tightly balanced,” Choudhary said. “That is why you are not seeing exceptionally high prices for crude; they are still in the $100 range, and they have not touched $140-$150 per barrel — which could have been the case if there was a deficit of 5-6 million barrels.”
The workarounds are time-consuming and expensive.
Sending oil to Asia through the Suez Canal instead of the Red Sea can add as much as a month to the voyage. Meanwhile the Hormuz shuttle trade involves expensive tankers waiting at least a day and a half in the Gulf of Oman for the ship-to-ship transfer.
The demand for supertankers has sent charter rates — normally $30,000 to $50,000 per day — through the roof. Spot charter rates for Hormuz transits reached $1 million per day on Sept. 11, according to maritime data company Windward, equivalent to roughly $26 per barrel. That means shipping is a quarter of the cost, instead of the usual 1 percent to 3 percent.
And markets are braced for further disruption. The attack on the East-West pipeline has shown pipelines can be vulnerable. Iran could try to disrupt the US route through the Strait of Hormuz or target areas near the Omani coast where the ship-to-ship transfers are taking place.

We need to talk: Greek PM says efforts to return Parthenon Marbles must be revived
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:09:58 UTC
18:09:58 KST

Talks on the future of the Parthenon Marbles appear to have reached an impasse according to new reports, as Greece's Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis renews diplomatic efforts for all sides to resume stalled negotiations.
Discussions between Britain and Greece over the return of the Parthenon Sculptures have apparently reached a dead-end.
According to reports in The Telegraph, talks have effectively been broken off with Athens expressing its strong disappointment over the lack of progress. At present no negotiations are under way and there appears to be no plan for their resumption, the British paper adds.
However, the Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis has penned an article for The Guardian in which he argues forcefully for a return to the talks table, making the permanent reunification of the Sculptures in Athens his key condition.
Greece revived negotiations with the British Museum in 2021, as part of its effort to secure the return of the archaeological sculptures that were taken to Britain in the early 19th century.
The latest intervention by Mitsotakis in The Guardian takes on particular significance, coming in the wake of the British Museum's suggestion that the agreement on the loan of the Bayeux Tapestry could serve as a possible model for the Parthenon Sculptures as well.
Mitsotakis: "We cannot borrow parts of our own monument"
In his article, the Greek prime minister rejects any comparison between the two cases. He notes that the Bayeux Tapestry remains a single work of art, which France lent to Britain and which is to be returned to its country of origin.
By contrast, he argues that the Parthenon Sculptures are parts of a single monument which were removed and scattered between London and Athens.
According to the Greek position, therefore, the issue is not only about the possession or ownership of the works, but about restoring the "physical, aesthetic and conceptual integrity" of the monument.
Mitsotakis stresses that the surviving Sculptures should be displayed together and at the same time maintain a visual relationship with the Parthenon, pointing out that the Acropolis Museum was designed precisely with that prospect in mind.
As he reiterates, Athens cannot accept any agreement that would require Greece to recognise the British Museum's ownership of the Sculptures or to treat them as works that Greece is "borrowing".
The deadlock over a long-term loan
This issue lies precisely at the heart of the disagreement. The British Museum argues that, under the current legal framework, it can lend the Sculptures but cannot permanently transfer them. A loan agreement would require, according to the British side, recognition of the museum's ownership.
The Greek side rejects this condition and insists on the permanent reunification of the Sculptures with the other parts of the monument in Athens.
Mitsotakis notes that his government has held "detailed discussions" in recent years with the British Museum's leadership on how reunification could be achieved.
For that reason, he says, he was surprised by the museum's recent proposal to use the agreement on the Bayeux Tapestry as a template for the Sculptures.
The Greek position on the Bayeux Tapestry
The comparison between the two works is a central argument for the Greek prime minister. The nearly 70-metre-long Tapestry narrates, as a single work, the events leading up to the Norman conquest of England, the Battle of Hastings and the death of Harold.
Mitsotakis argues that it is precisely this unity that allows the viewer to grasp the story it tells. In the same way, the Parthenon Sculptures were created as integral parts of a single architectural and artistic ensemble.
The Greek argument is that no one would consider it reasonable to cut up the Bayeux Tapestry and exhibit one part of it in London and the rest in France. Athens maintains that the Parthenon Sculptures should be treated in the same way.
"It is not about emptying museums"
The Greek prime minister also seeks to distinguish Greece's claim from a broader demand for the mass return of objects from major museums.
He argues that the Parthenon case is unique, because "what is at stake is not simply a change in the custody of an archaeological object, but the restoration of the unity of a monument of global significance."
Greece, he adds, hopes that the reunification of the Sculptures will become the starting point for broader cultural cooperation with Britain, opening up new opportunities for exhibitions, scientific research, conservation of works and exchanges between Greek and British museums.
In his article, Mitsotakis also cites a poll published last year, according to which a majority of Britons support the return of the Sculptures to Greece.
He pays particular attention to the 72% who, according to the same survey, agreed that the Sculptures are better understood as part of a single entity together with the Parthenon.
UNESCO and the row over ownership
Greece's claim to the Sculptures has also been restated within UNESCO, where the Intergovernmental Committee has repeatedly called on the United Kingdom to engage in dialogue with Greece.
The British government and the British Museum maintain that Thomas Bruce, 7th Earl of Elgin, obtained a lawful permit from the Ottoman authorities to remove the works from the Parthenon. Greece disputes that there was any valid permit that could justify their removal.
In 2024, Turkey intervened in the debate, expressing support for the Greek position. Turkish representatives at UNESCO said that research in the Ottoman archives had found no evidence documenting the existence of the contested "firman".
The "political will" Athens is calling for
Concluding his article, Mitsotakis argues that the reunification of the Sculptures could serve as a new model of cultural cooperation between Greece and Britain.
He also refers to a statement by Andy Burnham from 2023, before he became mayor of Manchester, in favour of the return of the Sculptures "without conditions".
The prime minister finally links the issue to the Parthenon's longstanding symbolic association with democracy. He argues that restoring the unity of a monument so closely tied to the birth of democracy could send a broader message of cultural cooperation.
Athens, he concludes, declares itself ready to move forward. What is now required, according to the prime minister, is the political will for the decisive step: the reunification of the Parthenon Sculptures and the transformation of a long-running dispute into a new relationship of cultural cooperation between Greece and Britain.

Trump’s push for ‘superintelligence’ finds no support from AI makers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:09:31 UTC
18:09:31 KST

Hasan Huseyin Ozdemir, Dogukan Gurel and Emir Yildirim
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
US President Donald Trump’s proposal to rename artificial intelligence (AI) “superintelligence” during the UN General Assembly has not found support from AI developers, including those based in the US.
While the tech world is debating whether to slow down AI development due to the many risks involved, Trump wants to rename the technology entirely.
Leading figures from the sector called for slowing down the development of AI, but Trump argued such restrictions would give China a significant edge as the US lags behind.
“The use of the word artificial makes intelligence fake,” Trump said during his speech on Tuesday, explaining his reasoning for renaming the technology. “It is not fake. It’s actually amazing.”
Widely used applications preferred to define themselves as advanced algorithmic systems or simply “artificial intelligence,” arguing that the term “superintelligence” cannot replace the already widespread term.
ChatGPT developer OpenAI said the term “artificial intelligence” is unlikely to disappear any time soon, but if systems with truly superhuman capabilities were to emerge, the term “superintelligence” could become an umbrella term for such advanced models rather than replacing the existing terminology.
Grok maker xAI, billionaire Elon Musk’s company, also said it is unlikely that the term will be replaced.
Claude developer Anthropic said it is unlikely that the term “artificial intelligence” will be phased out of general use, but “superintelligence” could find its way into official statements from Washington.
Google’s AI, Gemini, echoed Claude’s sentiments, saying that the term “superintelligence” might enter political terminology to denote a specific stage in technology development.
China’s DeepSeek also said that neither would the term “artificial intelligence” disappear nor would “superintelligence” replace it, noting that the two terms refer to distinct categories in computer science and the industry and that a political statement cannot simply alter the existing terminology.
AI models generally noted that the concept of superintelligence is more likely to describe a much more advanced stage of AI development or political discourse than to completely replace the term currently in use.
Meanwhile, Türkiye favors taking joint steps in AI discussions.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said at the UN General Assembly that controlling AI has become increasingly difficult, urging the creation of a common international legal framework for the technology.

Australia Condemns ‘Unacceptable’ OpenAI Breach of Government Health Portal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:08:54 UTC
18:08:54 KST

An OpenAI agent hacked into an Australian government health database in June, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed Wednesday, amid concerns from world leaders and artificial intelligence firms about the industry’s rapid, unregulated expansion.
Albanese said the AI agent had accessed public and non-public files in the statistics reporting service portal for Australia’s universal health insurance scheme, Medicare, in June. OpenAI, however, only notified the government of the breach 84 days later—through an email sent to the public mailbox.
“No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing,” Albanese said in a press conference in New York, where he attended the U.N. General Assembly. “Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable.”
An OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement that during a recent review, they identified activity involving “several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation.” Its AI models then “took actions we did not intend.”
The breach follows a string of incidents where AI models have gone rogue, prompting debate about whether the world is ready to deal with such security risks stemming from its swift development.
Read More: The AI Tipping Point
Albanese said he had a “very frank” phone call with Altman about the breach, and the Prime Minister claimed the OpenAI CEO “has acknowledged their issues with protocols.”
The Prime Minister then said Australian intelligence authorities will help conduct a “forensic investigation” to look into whether other government systems were affected. A task force will also review the incident, and the Australian government will seek advice on whether any offenses were committed and if the incident should be referred to the federal police.
The AI agent-led hack comes just as OpenAI CEO Sam Altman himself warned leaders present at the U.N. Security Council about the risks AI systems pose with their increasing capabilities and autonomy: “They could move faster than our institutions, concentrate power in too few hands, or make decisions that people no longer understand or control.”
What happened?
On June 18, OpenAI’s research team used an internal model that accessed the Medicare statistics website, as it looks into public medical spending, according to Albanese. Katy Gallagher, the Minister for Government Services, said the website is “most often used by researchers and academics who get that aggregated data about benefit statistics, prescribing statistics, to use in their own research,” and clarified that it is “not in any way related to Medicare in terms of claims, payments, processing, individual information.”
But OpenAI hadn’t been aware of the potential breach until August, when it was reviewing “misaligned model activity”—or activity that deviates from the user’s intent.
Albanese said that after encountering security blocks, the agent “found a way around those blocks—didn't accept no for an answer” to get the information it wanted.
OpenAI notified Services Australia, which delivers the federal government’s social services, on Sept. 10. It wasn’t until Sept. 17 that Gallagher had been advised of the breach, and it reached Albanese over the weekend. Albanese criticized how Australia received a mere email from OpenAI, and how delayed the notification was despite the security risk.
The Prime Minister added three other Australian government websites may have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Victorian Department of Health, though Minister for Defense Richard Marles later said in a Thursday press briefing that the interactions with agents in these three sites were “entirely normal” and only included public information.
The NSW bureau said it was aware of a vulnerability that could allow access to a crime mapping tool, but asserted that the concerned dataset has no personal information such as names, dates of birth, personal addresses, or other identifiable information about people. There’s also no evidence that a breach has already occurred.
Marles added that while the impact of the Medicare statistics portal breach is “relatively minor,” a non-human agent’s ability to access a government website unauthorized represents “a very serious incident.”
Shocking, yet predictable, says Albanese
Several high-profile incidents of AI agents going rogue preceded the Australian government breach.
In July, OpenAI announced that, during a cybersecurity test, its agents infiltrated the AI company Hugging Face. Nonprofit research laboratory Transluce also reported other incidents of OpenAI systems’ unsuccessful hacking attempts, including a digital library at the University of New Mexico and a platform visualizing U.S. government data in May. Independent researchers also discovered that rogue OpenAI agents took over a German website, transforming it into a message board for other AI agents.
But it’s not only OpenAI: during testing by the U.K.’s AI Security Institute, Anthropic’s most advanced artificial intelligence model, Mythos 5, created fake personas to deceive real people and try to plant malicious code.
“It was a shock that it occurred, because it was real and serious,” Albanese said of the Australian government website hack. “But it also, I think, was something that had been predicted, including by the AI companies themselves.”
TIME has a licensing and technology agreement with OpenAI. Salesforce, where TIME owner Marc Benioff is CEO, is an investor in Anthropic.

Faces of Oct. 7: The battle for memory is not over - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:07:52 UTC
18:07:52 KST

There are portraits you can never look at the same way twice.
In September 2024, when we opened the Faces of October 7th exhibition in Jerusalem, one unbearable question hovered over some of the faces on display: Would they come home?
Two years have passed. The faces remain the same, but beside some of them, a new chapter has been written. Some returned from captivity alive and are now relearning what freedom means.
Others were brought home to Israel for burial, to the families who had waited for them. Some families continue to live with an endless absence, while new stories of courage and sacrifice have become part of Israel’s painful mosaic.
Between the exhibition we presented in 2024 and the one we are opening now, it is not just the words beside the portraits that have changed. We, too, have changed.
The story of these portraits began with a spur-of-the-moment decision. On October 6, 2023, graffiti artist Benzi Brofman was invited to paint live at the Unity Festival in Re’im. Abandoning his original plan, he decided to return home that day rather than stay for Shabbat. Hours later, the place where he had stood and painted became part of the site of the deadliest massacre in Israel’s history.
Once he recovered from the initial shock, Benzi did what he knew best: he painted. He set aside his commercial work and began creating, voluntarily and in collaboration with the families, portraits of those murdered, hostages, and fallen IDF soldiers. In each portrait, he captured a direct, piercing gaze that is impossible to avoid.
The portraits on display represent the full spectrum of our October 7 story: hostages who returned alive and those brought home for burial, young people who went to dance at the Nova festival and never returned, families murdered in their homes, civilians killed while trying to save others, fallen IDF soldiers, and innocent civilians.
Behind every portrait is an entire world. A person who loved, laughed, dreamed, and made plans for the following day. A family that still wakes each morning to a reality it did not choose.
The war that began on October 7 did not remain within Israel’s borders. Its reverberations reached university campuses, newsrooms, parliaments, and social media platforms around the world. Alongside the war on the ground, another front opened: a battle over facts, over memory, and over the Israeli peoples’ very right to tell the world what happened to them.
We have watched denial, conspiracy theories, and disinformation spread like wildfire.
Victims have been asked to prove their pain, images have been stripped of context, and terrorist organizations have been treated by many as credible sources. Before families had even begun to process the disaster, they were forced to watch the world cast doubt on their stories.
Actively remembering
At StandWithUs, we confront this reality every day. Around the world, our staff works with students, youth, educators, communities, and leaders. We research and refute false information, develop educational resources, bring personal testimony to audiences, and give supporters of Israel the knowledge and tools they need to speak out based on facts.
Israel advocacy is not an attempt to erase complexity, nor does it require agreement with every decision made in Israel. It is a basic insistence that any discussion begins with the truth, and that even amid political disagreement, we do not lose the ability to see human beings.
The exhibition connects the portraits with personal stories, video, interactive installations, and a virtual reality experience. Above all, it asks us to stop, for even just a moment, and resist the urge to move on.
Memory is not passive. To remember is to look, to listen, and to tell. It is to ensure that even when the world’s attention shifts to the next crisis, the people of October 7 do not become a footnote.
I invite the public to visit the exhibition, look them in the eyes, and leave with a renewed commitment to telling their stories. The struggle for truth and memory is not taking place only overseas. It begins here, with each and every one of us.
The Faces of October 7th exhibition will be on display from September 23 to October 8 at the StandWithUs Katz Education Center, 2 George Washington St., Jerusalem. For details and registration, visit the exhibition website: www.standwithuscenter.com/facesofoctober7
The writer is the associate director of StandWithUs Israel.

Iran receives Chinese intelligence, military-linked components to bolster drone program - report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:07:32 UTC
18:07:32 KST

Iran is receiving substantial support from China, including the provision of intelligence and electronic components for military purposes, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.
According to WSJ, citing Iranian customs data, China has shipped around 1,300 shipments to Iran's defense ministry containing "dual-use" components and chemical compounds that could be used for drones, missile guidance systems, and ballistic missiles.
The WSJ also cited US officials as saying that Chinese banks and front companies had assisted Iran in avoiding US sanctions, providing billions of dollars to the regime.
Iranian officials did not respond to WSJ requests for comment.
Trump reluctant to jeopardize relationship with Xi Jinping
US President Donald Trump has been reluctant to confront China's aid to Iran, the WSJ reported.
According to people familiar with the discussions, Trump said that a top priority was maintaining a good relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping ahead of the United Nations General Assembly.
Michigan Democrat Sen. Elissa Slotkin confronted Trump over this in a letter sent on Friday, which the WSJ saw.
Ellis urged Trump to focus on China's aid to Iran during his talks with Xi.
"There is now a large and growing body of evidence that Chinese companies are helping Iran target and kill American troops, keep Iran’s drone and missile programs alive, and sustain Iran’s economy,” she wrote.
A US Treasury spokesperson told the WSJ that the Trump administration "has repeatedly targeted malign Iran-related activity that exploits or transits China’s jurisdiction and will continue to do so."
Iran receives satellite imagery of US base from China
Earlier this month, the WSJ revealed that Iran had obtained high-resolution satellite imagery of a US base in Jordan from Chinese sources before launching the missile attack that killed three American soldiers in July.
The WSJ reported that Washington has drawn a direct line between the Chinese-sourced imagery and the July 17 strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, but did not confirm direct involvement from the Chinese government.
Iran has also used a barter-like arrangement to bypass sanctions on its oil sales and buy billions of dollars’ worth of goods from China, including military gear, two senior Iranian sources and three other people familiar with the matter told Reuters earlier this month.
The secretive trade mechanism, in which Iranian oil is exchanged for credits for Chinese imports, has provided a financial lifeline for Tehran in recent years as the United States stepped up economic and military pressure over its nuclear program, according to the sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity.
In July, Reuters reported that Iran was expected to receive within weeks a first shipment out of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers, as it rebuilds its defenses amid war with the United States.
The purchase, valued at $60-70 million, is one of Tehran's largest-known efforts to strengthen its short-range air defenses since the outbreak of its war with the US and Israel, which exposed gaps in Iran's ability to protect military sites and strategic infrastructure.

EXPLAINER – Washington summit: What will define this Trump-Xi encounter?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:07:06 UTC
18:07:06 KST

- 'The most notable aspect of the summit may be the positive visuals that emerge from it,' expert Ryan Hass tells Anadolu
- AI takes center stage as risks are discussed
 
Can Donald Trump and Xi Jinping turn a fragile US-China thaw into a more stable relationship?
The answer may hinge on trade, rare earths, artificial intelligence and a series of geopolitical flashpoints when the two leaders meet Thursday.
The meeting will be the second face-to-face encounter between the two leaders this year, following Trump's visit to Beijing in May, and Xi's first state visit to Washington in more than a decade.
Breaking with his usual practice of hosting foreign leaders at the White House, Trump went to Joint Base Andrews near Washington with first lady Melania Trump to meet Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, as they stepped off the plane.
Thursday's schedule opens with an official welcome and a troop review at the White House, after which the two leaders will hold talks behind closed doors, followed by a state dinner where prominent US tech figures, among them Nvidia chief Jensen Huang and Elon Musk, are on the guest list.
For Ryan Hass, director of the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution and a former White House official on China, the optics may be the main story.
"Both leaders are interested in projecting an image of a positive and productive relationship. The most notable aspect of the summit may be the positive visuals that emerge from it," Hass told Anadolu.
Kyle Chan, a fellow at the same center who studies Chinese technology and industrial policy, was more cautious.
"I have low expectations for the summit," Chan told Anadolu.
Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, shared that view.
"The meeting is unlikely to produce any breakthroughs," Wyne told Anadolu. "Its major objective will be to preserve a tactical thaw between the world's two foremost powers."
Beijing's official framing is broader.
Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said China is willing to work with the US to enrich what Beijing calls a relationship of "constructive strategic stability," strengthen dialogue and properly manage differences.
The phrase was adopted as a new description of ties after the leaders met in Beijing in May.
 
Trade truce extended, bigger deal uncertain
The summit’s most pressing economic question was settled shortly after Xi’s plane touched down.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that Washington and Beijing had agreed to extend until Jan. 10 the trade truce reached after Trump’s meeting with Xi in Busan, South Korea, last October.
The announcement came after Bessent met Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in Washington, following preparatory talks in New York on Sunday.
Under the Busan deal, Washington lowered fentanyl-related tariffs and suspended higher reciprocal duties, while Beijing loosened export curbs on critical minerals. The pause had been due to expire on Nov. 10.
Bessent said Beijing had fallen short on some commitments and that Washington wants fuller implementation in the coming months. He said it remained unclear whether the sides would reach a broader deal or simply extend the current one.
Bessent also signaled that more announcements could come from the Chinese side in the coming days, including purchases of US farm products and possible deals in financial services.
Another sticking point is rare earths.
The US has pressed China to ensure supplies of rare earths and other critical minerals used in industries ranging from automobiles and electronics to aerospace and defense. 
 
Beijing, which processes about 90% of the world’s rare earths, has sought greater access to US technology and urged Washington to ease restrictions on Chinese companies.
China imposed export controls on seven categories of rare earths and related magnets in April 2025. It later announced broader restrictions, which were suspended for one year under the Busan arrangement.
US officials have repeatedly said Chinese performance on restoring reliable flows has fallen short of expectations.
According to Chinese customs data, rare earth magnet exports to the US fell 21% in August from July.
 
AI: From rivalry to hotline?
Artificial intelligence has moved to the top of the agenda. 
The two countries are the world's leading AI powers and see the technology as central to economic and military strength.
At the same time, both governments have begun exploring whether they can communicate about the risks created by sophisticated AI systems.
Trump and Xi discussed potential consultations on AI during their May meeting, but a formal mechanism was not established at the time.
Hass expects both leaders to acknowledge the importance of keeping channels open on AI safety, but does not expect “concrete outcomes beyond that."
Chan, meanwhile, said the risks posed by AI systems could create an incentive for Washington and Beijing to maintain communication despite their broader differences.
"In general, there's actually growing motivation for both countries to work together due to the escalating risks from AI, especially around cyber capabilities and autonomous systems."
Bessent said the US and China had agreed to set up a hotline to notify each other of AI safety incidents, although Beijing has not publicly confirmed the arrangement.
Chan noted that Congress has several bills ready to tighten restrictions on chips and chipmaking equipment sold to China. "The question is whether Trump might try to intervene in this process," he said.
 
Geopolitical flashpoints
Taiwan, the self-governing island that Beijing considers part of its territory, is expected to be among the most delicate subjects.
After the May summit, the US paused a record $14 billion arms package for Taiwan.
Trump described arms sales to the island claimed by China as a "very good negotiating chip."
 
The summit also takes place against the backdrop of the US war in Iran, which began on Feb. 28.
The conflict has direct implications for China because of the country's energy needs and its reliance on Middle Eastern oil. Chinese officials have recently said Beijing is prepared to play a constructive role in efforts to resolve the conflict.
Hass said Trump might want to briefly address the issue. "Trump will not want to ask Xi for assistance in dealing with Iran, and Xi will be reluctant to offer any assistance in exercising influence over Iran to lay down its arms."
He also expects Ukraine and North Korea to feature in the leaders' broader discussions.
Beyond specific deals, analysts say the larger question is whether the meeting keeps the current calm intact.
The visit comes weeks before US midterm elections.
"Both leaders recognize the benefit of buying time and space to reduce vulnerabilities to each other," Hass added. "Whether they will be able to act in self-interest to extend that period of calm will be a key question from the summit."

Vistry Group, one of Britain’s biggest housebuilders, has cut its annual profit expectations after half-year losses ballooned as it grappled with a £600m pile of unsold homes.
Adam Daniel, the new chief executive of the Bovis Homes and Countryside owner, insisted “the issues can be fixed” as he set out a detailed turnaround plan that involves pulling out of private sales in south-east England and slimming operations to turn Vistry into a more focused, 12,000-homes-a-year builder.
Further job losses loom, however, after Vistry announced new cost savings of £50m, on top of a £25m voluntary redundancy programme and hiring freeze earlier this year. It said it reduced its workforce to 4,150 at the end of July, with 350 people leaving since the summer, according to PA. The company is closing some regional offices, moving from 25 to 12 regions.
Vistry reported a loss before tax of £661.3m for the first six months of the year, versus a profit of £40.9m the year before, dragged back by a £475m writedown and a £73m provision for building safety works.
For the year as a whole, it now expects to post an adjusted profit before tax of £165m, after making an adjusted loss of £83.3m in the first half, far worse than expected.
The company completed 6,304 homes, down by 8% from a year earlier. After resorting to steep discounts to sell a £600m pile of houses, it is now left with £220m of unsold properties. In July it said the average discount offered to homebuyers was 7.1%. Half-year revenues fell by 9% to £1.7bn while Vistry’s debt jumped from £293.1m to £468.8m.
Vistry blamed “disappointing summer sales of private homes” and withdrawals or renegotiation of deals to build affordable homes. It has also been hit by cost inflation of 3% to 4% as a result of the Iran war, which has driven fuel prices sharply higher.
In August, the company received £350m funding from the government to construct 3,000 affordable homes, the largest slice awarded under the £39bn social and affordable homes programme, and it is one of 33 strategic partners that take part. Vistry said it had already started building those homes.
Daniels, who took the helm in April, laid out measures such as reducing the land bank from 51,000 to 36,000 plots and a reorganisation of the business, simplification of product range, brands and operating processes, and greater exposure to the north, Midlands and west of England.
Daniels said: “We have made substantial progress in refocusing the business and delivering on our immediate priority to improve cash generation. In parallel, we have now completed an extensive review of our business and operating model including how best to position the group for future success.”
The Vistry share price plunged more than 8% in early trading.
Victoria Scholar, the head of investment at Interactive Investor, said: “The housebuilder has been faced with macro headwinds from this year’s energy shock leading to cost pressures, weaker affordability and consumer confidence amid the higher-for-longer interest rate backdrop.
“Shares had already had a painful run lately, shedding close to 60% year-to-date before this morning’s further sharp slide, underscoring the challenges at hand for its boss and the need for a drastic turnaround.”
