"It's time Norway realises that we also need to change" says Line Ramstad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:00:39 UTC
18:00:39 KST

"It's time Norway realises that we also need to change" says Line Ramstad
As a wealthy nation, Norway has a responsibility to tackle climate change by developing a nature-first approach to designing buildings, Oslo Architecture Triennale director Line Ramstad tells Dezeen in this interview.
At this year's Oslo Architecture Triennale, built environment professionals and the general public gathered at Oslo's Sofienberg Church to discover architects' visions for prioritising nature through materials, design and planning.
Ramstad believes this discussion is long overdue.
"For a long time, we have needed to put nature first, but we are coming to a point where we can no longer close our eyes to it because otherwise there will be no future," she told Dezeen. "We need to take into consideration our position in the building industry and our ability to see solutions."
"Our green way of doing things is not really green"
Ramstad, a landscape architect from Norway, argued that the construction industry's current sustainability goals aren't doing enough to reduce carbon emissions and that a more circular, holistic approach to design is essential.
"We have started to talk about climate in our projects and our businesses, but we have tried to solve it within the system that created them, and more of the same doesn't solve anything," she said.
"Our green way of doing things is not really green. We lack the holistic thinking around this."
Norway in particular needs to confront its contribution to global warming, said Ramstad. She hopes that this year's Oslo Architecture Triennale will draw greater attention to the work required to mitigate the effects of climate change.
"Norway is a wonderful place to live – it's a rich country, but there's not that much willingness to change because things are going okay," said Ramstad.
"Having the triennale here is important for Norway to discuss internally what can be done – how can we shift our linear society to a circular one? Are there examples? Yes. Do we act within the system in a way that creates change? No."
"It's an important topic everywhere, but it's especially important here because we don't feel the consequences [of climate change] as directly as other places in the world," she continued. "It's time Norway realises that we also need to change."
One project presented at the triennale exhibition that tackles Oslo's natural and built landscapes is General Plan 2.0 by Sigrid Legernes Teigen and Greta Gleisner Birkeland. It criticises years of building over historic waterways, which has contributed to increased flooding, and proposes a city plan that grows alongside the water.
"It's impressive what Sigrid and Greta have done," said Ramstad. "When rivers and wetlands become something we can build on, that's crazy."
"That's not putting nature first, and nature's natural forces will work against us, so what if we work with nature and plan our cities accordingly?"
Ramstad credits her fierce advocacy for designing with, not against, nature to her upbringing on a farm and her grandmother, who was a feminist and environmentalist.
In 2009, Ramstad founded non-profit architecture group Gyaw Gyaw and spent 15 years living on the Myanmar-Thailand border constructing buildings with local communities. It was here that her understanding of the effects of altering natural landscapes for construction crystallised.
"The results of our actions are so clear there," said Ramstad. "We built with local colleagues who have this closeness to what they're doing that we have lost a little here."
"Moving back to Norway was challenging after years of living in my jungle bubble."
"I have always had a sustainable approach, but coming back and meeting the reality in Norway, I was a little bit like, oh my God, we've gone far away in just 15 years," she continued. "We removed ourselves a lot from what my grandparents used to do."
"This triennale has made me more hopeful"
Although Ramstad's ambition of a nature-first future in the built environment sounds like a utopian dream, the work collected in the triennale has left her optimistic that this could one day be a more commonplace reality.
But, she acknowledged that systemic change in the industry is needed for architects' ecological proposals to become built projects.
"Working with this exhibition and this triennale has made me more hopeful than I was before because there is a great movement into thinking more holistically and circularly," said Ramstad.
"Architects are very concerned about [putting nature first], but when the system around an architect is not, it requires a lot for that office to implement a change by themselves."
"I hope that conversations here can inspire people to at least try, to get someone on board, see good examples and think, 'They did it there, so we can do it here'. We will make it, step by step."
The photography is by Julie Hrncinova of Abrakadabra unless stated.
Oslo Architecture Triennale takes place from 17 September to 1 October at Sofienberg Church in Oslo, Norway. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Clan leader in Paris sentenced to eight years over child pickpocketing gangs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:00:13 UTC
18:00:13 KST

A clan leader who sent gangs of child pickpockets to target tourists in the Paris Métro and popular attractions such as Disneyland Paris has been jailed for human trafficking.
Roberto Hamidovic, 48, likened to Fagin, Charles Dickens’s notorious criminal boss, ran a network of child thieves, mostly girls, some as young as 10, who brought in an average of €25,000 (£21,500) a day, according to police.
If the terrorised youngsters failed to hand over enough money, they would be beaten, burned or sexually abused, the Paris court heard.
While Hamidovic, the patriarch of a Roma family of Bosnian origins, and the adult family members lived a “life of luxury” – enjoying designer clothes, five-star hotels, expensive restaurants and cars, and flashing their cash at casinos – the girls were put up in budget hotels or dilapidated squats.
Seven members of what detectives called the Hamidovic clan – four men and three women – were on trial for human trafficking, organised theft, corruption of minors, money laundering and criminal association as part of what detectives say is an international pickpocket network spanning several European countries. All denied the charges.
The court sentenced Hamidovic to the maximum eight years in prison and a €500,000 (£430,000) fine; his wife, Lejla, was given a six-year prison sentence and €300,000 fine. Two of the couple’s sons, a nephew and two female relatives were given between five- and seven-year prison sentences and fines. All were told they would be extradited and banned from entering France on their release.
For detectives who have been investigating the Hamidovic network for decades there was a grim sense of deja vu. In 2010, French police arrested Roberto Hamidovic’s uncle Fehmi, 58, who already had a conviction for people trafficking in Austria, along with his two sons near Rome and a dozen other clan members in the south of France and Italy. At the time, Paris’s judicial police chief, Christian Flaesch, said: “It feels like we have broken up a completely medieval structure.”
After Fehmi Hamidovic was convicted in 2013 and sentenced to seven years in prison, his nephew Roberto took control of the clan, believed to be responsible for up to 75% of thefts in the Paris Métro. In court, however, Roberto Hamidovic claimed he was a secondhand car dealer earning between €2,000 and €5,000 a month.
Alice Guillet, the public prosector, put forward a different story. She said the Hamidovic family used minors “to ensure a kind of impunity”. The pickpockets were told to tell police they were 12 years old – a year below the age of criminal responsibility in France – forcing police to release them. She described the girls’ daily lives as particularly “challenging and painful”.
They were “children without roots, without a future, whose parents sometimes don’t even know their birth date”, she added.
A pre-trial investigation by Le Monde revealed that Hamidovic’s son Roberto Hamidovic Jr, 22, nicknamed Gony, oversaw the pickpocket gangs on behalf of his father – booking taxis to transport them to various sites around Paris.
Investigators said groups of six to nine youngsters were sent each day at Disneyland Paris, Charles de Gaulle airport and the Métro and told to target foreign tourists. At Disneyland they would mingle with crowds gathered for the evening parades.
They would also hang around bank cash machines, wait for customers to put in their pin numbers, then surround them and steal the money and their wallets.
Hamidovic and his wife are believed to have amassed an estimated €2m, much of which is reportedly hidden abroad. The couple spent part of their time in the Adriatic seaside resort of Pula in Croatia.
His son, Roberto Jr, one of 13 siblings, grew up in Rome in the care of a grandmother and moved to France at the age of 14. Like his brothers and sisters he did not attend school regularly. Most family members are unable to read or write. He and his wife, Alessandra, have a three-year-old son called Al Capone who is being raised by a nanny in Bosnia, Le Monde reported. The paper said Hamidovic Jr told detectives he did not drink but they discovered he had spent €1,420 on two bottles of champagne at a Paris nightclub to celebrate his brother Goran’s release from prison.
Guillet described the network as a grim cycle. The exploited children sent out to steal became exploiters in turn when becoming adults.
“During this trial, the issue of determinism arose, an issue that is glaringly obvious from the very first line of the case file,” Guillet said, pointing out that the seven accused had themselves been forced to steal for their parents during their childhood.
“What chance did they have of not putting the younger children to work in turn as soon as they were old enough?” Guillet added. “The chances were slim, if not nonexistent. They went from being victims to perpetrators … we have to stop this defeatism and fatalism.”
Guillet said the only way to challenge the impunity with which the Hamidovics continued to operate through three generations, in defiance of previous convictions of family members, was to impose long prison sentences followed by extradition from France.
“In the face of such a system, the only tool is severity. This sends a message,” she said.
After the sentencing, Emperatriz Aguirre, Roberto Hamidovic’s lawyer, said: “The sentences are too severe because they relate to the crime of human trafficking for which there was no tangible evidence.”
Many of the dozens of children used as pickpockets, who were not called to give evidence in order to protect their identities, disappeared after the seven were arrested or were taken by social services and placed in foster homes. Almost half of them are believed to have since run away.

Scientists Detect Radio Signals from an Exoplanet for the First Time in History
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

Approximately 63 light-years from Earth lies a planetary system so young that it's less than 1 percent as old as our solar system. It is called Beta Pictoris, and—as far as astronomers have confirmed—it consists of a star more massive than the sun, three giant planets, and a huge disk of dust and debris.
The middle planet in the system, Beta Pictoris b, is a gas giant several times more massive than Jupiter. Being a gas giant, it likely does not have a solid surface on which to “land,” and at just a few tens of millions of years old, it can be considered a newborn planet in astronomical terms. It’s also one of the most extensively studied exoplanets through direct observation. Its youth keeps it hot and bright, and its distance from the star—similar to that between our sun and Saturn—makes it possible to distinguish from the star with sufficiently powerful telescopes.
Now, a new study from researchers at Harvard and the University of Oregon claims that Beta Pictoris b is the source of something that has never before been unequivocally detected on another world: radio emissions.
Recorded by the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa, the signal is likely of natural origin, as in no, it’s not aliens. The authors are quick to note this from the outset of their preprint. And while the study has not yet been peer-reviewed, the authors present sizable evidence to support their interpretation that the source of the broadcast is intense magnetic activity.
The characteristics of the radio waves match theoretical predictions for magnetic fields generated by young, massive planets. Charged particles can become trapped in the planet’s powerful magnetic field, and as the planet rotates, these particles can accelerate and release energy in the form of radio waves. In a sense, this phenomenon—known as an auroral radio emission—is the planet’s magnetosphere “shouting” into space.
The team detected several of these calls and, for the first time, managed to pinpoint their origin directly to an exoplanet—something scientists have been trying to achieve for years.
Astronomers have come close to this achievement a few times in recent years, such as in 2023, when bursts of radio waves were detected in the YZ Ceti system. The signals appeared to repeat in sync with one planet’s orbit. However, researchers could not rule out the possibility that those emissions were simply caused by the star’s magnetic activity.
The Beta Pictoris system also holds a special place in the history of astronomy. In 1984, Beta Pictoris became the first star around which a disk of dust and debris was directly photographed. That image suggested planet-forming processes might be taking place there, though at that time astronomers were unable to confirm the existence of any planets.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Russian strikes claimed the lives of 8 people and injured more than 20; Nova Poshta was affected — consequences by region
Kyiv • UNN
Russian attacks on September 24 killed six farm workers in the Kharkiv region and two people in Kyiv. Civilian facilities were damaged in several regions.
In Ukraine, 8 people are now known to have been killed as a result of Russian strikes overnight and on the morning of September 24—people in Kharkiv region were sorting vegetables at a farm, while in Kyiv people tried to hide from the enemy’s ballistic attack; at least 20 more people were injured. In the capital region, Nova Poshta branches and a depot were damaged. This was reported by Interior Minister Ivan Vygivskyi and Nova Poshta, UNN writes.
Which regions were attacked by Russia
Kharkiv region
"Six agricultural enterprise workers were killed as a result of the morning Russian strike on Kharkiv region. At the time of the attack, they were sorting vegetables. My condolences to their families and loved ones. Twelve people were injured and are receiving all necessary medical assistance," Vygivskyi said on social media.
According to him, rescuers and police investigators are working at the scene.
Kyiv and Kyiv region
"In Kyiv, more than 50 civilian facilities were damaged as a result of the overnight shelling—residential buildings, post offices, a maternity hospital, and a textile enterprise," the Interior Minister said.
Nova Poshta clarified that "as a result of enemy strikes on Kyiv region overnight on September 24, Nova Poshta branch No. 6 was destroyed and the company's sorting depot in Kyiv was damaged."
"None of the employees was injured. Some of the cargo was destroyed. We are already moving the surviving parcels to another location. The response operation is ongoing," the company said.
Nova Poshta said it had already deployed backup logistics to minimize possible delivery delays and would compensate customers for the declared value of shipments destroyed as a result of the attack.
Vygivskyi confirmed that as a result of Russia's attack, "two people were killed—a woman who was walking to a shelter and a man who was waiting out the Russian attack in an underground passage." "Eight more people were injured, including a police officer who arrived to help the victims. Two people are in serious condition," the Interior Minister said.
The Kyiv Regional Military Administration reported that Russian attacks on the region continued throughout the day and night; Russia attacked with strike drones and ballistic missiles. "In Bucha district, five private houses and a car were damaged. One person, born in 1945, was also injured. She was diagnosed with an acute stress reaction. A fire broke out in the house and was promptly extinguished by rescuers. The necessary medical assistance was provided at the scene. In Fastiv district, one vehicle was damaged. In Boryspil district, a private house was damaged," the post said.
Overall, according to the available data, another 8 facilities were damaged in Kyiv region.
According to the Interior Minister, Zhytomyr, Mykolaiv, and Odesa regions were also under attack overnight.
Odesa region
In Odesa region, according to a report by Regional Military Administration head Oleh Kiper, a hospital, a gymnasium, residential buildings, a shopping center, warehouses, and other civilian facilities came under attack. "As a result of the attack, a 10-story non-residential building, a shopping center that had previously been attacked, the roof of a city hospital branch, and food warehouses were damaged. The glazing of the gymnasium and residential buildings was shattered, and cars were damaged. Two people were injured. All relevant services are working at the sites of the strikes. The injured are receiving medical assistance. Law enforcement officers are documenting yet another Russian war crime," Oleh Kiper emphasized.

In Bilhorod-Dnistrovskyi district, windows were shattered in three private residential buildings. Repeated air-raid alerts complicated the rescuers' work," the post said.
Western regions

In Khmelnytskyi, according to the head of the Khmelnytskyi Regional Military Administration, Serhii Tiurin, a hit on a residential high-rise building was recorded as a result of the Russian attack. As a result of the attack, a hit on a residential high-rise building in the regional center has been reported," the official said.

Germany seeks wider 'Made with Europe' rules, setting up clash with France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:59:14 UTC
17:59:14 KST

Berlin wants the EU’s “Made with Europe” rules opened to trade partners, challenging France’s push to reserve public contracts for European-made goods.
The German government has called on the EU to open its planned "Made with Europe" rules to countries outside the bloc, according to a position paper obtained by Euronews, setting it up for a collision course with France.
Berlin is leading the push for a more open-market approach to the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), a draft EU law that would restrict public procurement — government contracts for goods such as steel, batteries and electric vehicles — to products and companies meeting minimum EU production requirements.
Where the Commission's original text favours "Made in Europe", Berlin wants "Made with Europe": rather than requiring goods to be made in the EU, it wants the origin rules opened up to the bloc's trade partners, as long as those countries offer the same access to European companies in return.
"Germany rejects protectionism and discrimination. In times of geopolitical and geoeconomic challenges, the EU relies on close partnerships — particularly its global network of free trade agreements — to enhance resilience and competitiveness," reads the position paper.
Opposing visions
The document was circulated ahead of Thursday's Competitiveness Council in Brussels, where EU industry ministers discussed industrial policy.
The initiative highlights the divide between Berlin's open-market approach and Paris's push to use public contracts to support European companies as they struggle with the so-called China 2.0 shock.
The same strategic divide extends beyond industrial policy to defence.
"The EU must remain a reliable partner for its free trade partners and uphold its legal obligations, compatible with the EU's international obligations," the document says.
Berlin wants the EU origin rules extended to countries that have signed the WTO Agreement on Government Procurement, under which members open public contracts to each other's companies, as well as countries with a free trade agreement or customs union with the EU.
Germany argues that this would encourage partner countries to pursue ambitious trade agreements and open their own markets to European companies.
Berlin also argues that allowing more bidders into EU public procurement would drive down costs and improve quality for public authorities.
However, Berlin wants the EU to be able to react quickly if a partner country stops offering reciprocal access, through an "opt-out" mechanism allowing it to be excluded from the scheme.
Reciprocity
"This ensures a level playing field on a reciprocal basis and creates an incentive to keep markets open to one another," the paper argues, adding that the Commission should first try to resolve any dispute through existing settlement mechanisms.
"If a partner country is under an obligation to treat EU companies equally (national treatment) in public procurement or in relation to support measures, and if these obligations are not met, access to EU procurement markets and support programmes should also be withheld," it continues.
Berlin backs a recent compromise brokered by Ireland, which holds the rotating EU Council presidency, to task the Commission with adding or removing third countries from the scheme via secondary legislation, but wants clearer criteria for how those decisions are made.
"To determine, without red tape, whether certain products from specific countries fall under the 'Made with EU' approach, the European Commission should draw up a product-specific list of countries or tools," the document adds.
Such a list would give businesses and public authorities clarity over which products meet the origin rules, rather than requiring them to carry out their own checks.
Berlin argues that this approach would also better serve one of the IAA's main goals: diversifying supply chains and reducing dependence on critical inputs, such as batteries, that the EU cannot yet produce at sufficient scale.
Adverse undermining
Germany also warns against what it calls "adverse undermining," a scenario in which a third country sets up production in one of the EU's partner countries specifically to exploit that partner's more favourable origin rules, entrenching the very dependencies the law is meant to reduce.
The concern reflects a wider fear in Brussels that Chinese companies could relocate parts of their production to countries such as Morocco to sidestep EU restrictions.
Germany proposes a two-stage response.
First, the Commission would run a preliminary assessment based on indicators rather than automatic triggers, such as a rise in imports from a partner country, increased foreign direct investment, or greater participation by foreign bidders in tenders.
Second, the Commission would be empowered to request evidence on short notice, impose strict compliance checks, and exclude specific companies or entire countries from the origin rules.
The German paper also proposes shifting the burden of proof onto the company or country under investigation in some cases, making it easier for the Commission to enforce the rules.

Activists denounce reported visa conditions
The reported visa decision has drawn criticism from Sudanese activists and journalists, who have questioned whether access to the UN should be linked to negotiations over the conflict.
One X user, @Atifazhri, criticised the US move by pointing to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ability to obtain a US visa despite being wanted by the International Criminal Court on allegations of war crimes in Gaza.
“The issue is double standards – when visas become instruments of political coercion against a sovereign state while far more serious cases are treated differently,” the user wrote, adding that international law and justice should not be applied selectively.
The comments reflect growing criticism in Sudan over the reported visa conditions, while the US has not publicly confirmed that Burhan’s visa was formally made conditional on accepting the ceasefire.
Washington presses for ceasefire
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio described efforts to mediate an end to Sudan’s war as frustrating, saying the parties had repeatedly agreed to commitments before backing away when they believed they could gain an advantage.
“We’ve had people agree to things, sign to things, and the commitments are never met,” Rubio told reporters in New York.
The conflict erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between Sudan’s army and the paramilitary RSF. It has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

Britain's largest banks make first interbank transactions using tokenised deposits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:55:48 UTC
17:55:48 KST

Britain's largest banks have completed what the industry describes as the first transactions anywhere using tokenised deposits to move money between one another, a milestone for a blockchain-based form of bank money that the Bank of England favours over privately issued stablecoins.
Pounds held in ordinary bank accounts have moved between rival lenders on blockchain rails for the first time.
Lloyds, NatWest and Barclays carried out two remortgage transactions using tokenised deposits, while a group of three banks including HSBC ran a customer-to-customer payment simulating an online marketplace purchase, industry body UK Finance announced on Thursday.
A tokenised deposit is a normal bank deposit recorded on a blockchain rather than on a bank's internal ledger. It keeps the same legal status and protections as money already sitting in an account, but can settle instantly and be programmed to move only when certain conditions are met.
The trials showed how that works in practice.
In the remortgages, funds were released between banks automatically once the property transfer was confirmed. In the marketplace test, the buyer's money was held and paid to the seller only after delivery was verified, though no real goods changed hands.
The significance lies in the word interbank.
Banks have experimented with blockchain for more than a decade, but each built its own system, leaving them unable to transact with one another. The pilot, known as the "Great British Tokenised Deposit" project and launched last year, links them together.
Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds, Monzo, NatWest, Nationwide and Santander are all taking part as it also carries official backing.
The Bank of England has said it would rather banks innovate with tokenised deposits than with stablecoins, which are crypto tokens usually pegged to the US dollar and issued by private companies outside the banking system.
Participating lenders now plan to set up a company and a governing rulebook, and aim to issue three digital bonds in the first quarter of 2027 that would be traded and settled using tokenised deposits.
A week of major developments for tokenisation in Europe
The UK milestone caps a week in which Europe's approach to digital money has come into sharper focus.
On Monday, the Eurosystem launched Pontes, allowing banks to settle trades in tokenised assets using central bank money, with 13 institutions ready to use it immediately.
The ECB also said it would invest some of its own funds in tokenised securities through this new system.
A day later, Europe's central banks published their response to the review of the EU's crypto rulebook, MiCA, calling for a wider ban on interest payments on stablecoins and new powers to curb tokens pegged to foreign currencies such as the US dollar.
The common thread is a preference for money issued by regulated banks and central banks over privately issued stablecoins.
London and Frankfurt are pursuing different tools, but both are betting that the future of tokenised finance should run on familiar forms of money rather than on tokens controlled by crypto firms.

Liberia is squandering the moral authority it claims at the UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:55:17 UTC
17:55:17 KST

Liberia is squandering the moral authority it claims at the UN
Its deal to take deportees is the latest in a long history of unequal agreements with the US.
For the past nine months, Liberia has used its experiences of prolonged armed conflict to serve as a principled voice in United Nations debates about the humanitarian consequences of a number of the most intractable geopolitical crises – from Gaza and Sudan to Ukraine and Iran.
Yet, hidden beneath this virtuous veneer lies a troubling contradiction. As my country prepares to assume the rotating presidency of the UN Security Council (UNSC) in December as a non-permanent member, it is flouting our Constitution and contravening UN conventions by hosting deportees expelled from the United States.
A year before its current charm offensive across the Atlantic – where a delegation led by the president is now courting American lawmakers in Washington and broadcasting its peace and security agenda at UN General Assembly convenings in New York – Liberia signed an agreement on September 10, 2025 with the Trump administration to accommodate an undisclosed number of third-country nationals deported from the US.
Since January 2025, the Trump administration has struck deportation agreements with 35 countries, almost a third of them in Africa, to receive foreigners whose US immigration statuses range from regularised (and legal) to protected from removal. Liberia’s cooperation is one of the largest and has proved particularly controversial.
Late last month, the first 20 of an expected 1,200 deportees arrived in a widely reported – and condemned – handover at Roberts International Airport (RIA). In a dramatic turn of events, the six who refused to disembark were whisked off to Equatorial Guinea under opaque terms. For those still in Liberia, it is equally unclear who they are, why they were deported, where they will reside, whether they are free to leave, and what legal standing they possess.
Although the agreement between Monrovia and Washington is skimpy on the details, it remains politically fraught, ethically suspect and illegal. Deportations without due process, and involving cruel and inhumane treatment, contravene principles within the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Consenting to host third-country nationals without legislative approval breaches Article 34(f) of Liberia’s Constitution.
Several deportees who landed at RIA on August 20 said they had been detained in the US without due process, contrary to articles 8 and 10 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, which guarantee the right to an “effective remedy” and a “fair and public hearing” before an independent court or tribunal. They also said they had been chained during the flight to Liberia, treatment that may violate Article 5, which states that “no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment”.
Other UN agreements which may have been flouted include the 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees, the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment, and the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which both Liberia and the US are parties.
On the home front, Liberia’s Constitution states plainly that any “treaties, conventions and such other international agreements negotiated or signed on behalf of the Republic” must be ratified by the National Legislature. Our Legislature neither deliberated on nor approved the agreement to host third-country nationals, which was unilaterally authorised by the executive. On that basis, implementing the agreement without legislative approval is unconstitutional.
By accepting mostly Black and brown deportees under such questionable arrangements, Liberia is complicit in executing “make America white again”-era expulsions that would shame its founding mothers and fathers who fled 19th-century chattel slavery and racial discrimination in the US. This small West African country – once a 21st-century poster child for post-war stability – has undercut any credibility it might wield in UNSC deliberations going forward. So, what exactly do Liberian policymakers in the executive branch of government hope to gain?
What’s in It for Liberia?
As a scholar who researches migration to/from/within Liberia, I was naturally curious about the terms, conditions and implications of Liberia’s bilateral agreement with the US. An official press release issued two days before the first batch of deportees was expected turned my curiosity into suspicion. It spins the agreement as a “humanitarian” arrangement for the “dignified, safe and orderly transfer” of non-criminals removed from the US. It also claims that although Liberia had “not demanded or received any compensation or promise of reward”, “support” would be available for managing the programme and strengthening migration management.
The word “support” deliberately muddles the truth. Why would a low-income country agree to host up to 1,200 third-country nationals without monetary incentives when the Trump administration previously paid five foreign governments more than $32m collectively to accept roughly 300 deportees? Nothing added up, so I went looking for answers.
I encountered evasion at every turn. The minister of foreign affairs said she could not share the agreement with me because it was “at the level of the National Security Council”. Instead, she forwarded me the press release I had already read – and doubted – as a consolation. The president’s national security adviser feigned ignorance. The National Security Agency director admitted he had the agreement and would get back to me. I am still awaiting his response. And Liberia’s then minister of justice, who has since assumed the role of acting minister of defence, declared haughtily that the agreement remained classified because it was entered into with a “foreign country”.
Despite these policymakers’ lack of transparency, I discovered the agreement hidden in plain sight on the US State Department website. It raised alarm not only because of what it says, but also because of what it leaves out, particularly the legitimacy of expelling third-country nationals whose protection claims in the US are pending, as well as rewarding a foreign government [Liberia] for facilitating this. If The New York Times’ August 21 story is anything to go by, Trump administration officials agreed to pay Liberia $5m for accepting deportees. Not only does this contradict claims of receiving no “compensation or promise of reward”, but remuneration also violates Article 34(f) of Liberia’s Constitution because it was not approved by the National Legislature.
Other questions loom. How was the $5m negotiated and by whom? What exactly does funding cover? How are resources being channelled if not through Liberia’s budget? Who manages the money? How are expenses monitored and reported? These questions are particularly salient because, if New York Times compensation figures are accurate, the amount allocated for Liberia is significantly less than what other governments have collected for accepting fewer deportees. Rwanda, for example, received $7.5m to accept just seven people.
A century of bad deals
My country has a long track record of signing dubious deals with the US. Most recently, the US-Liberia Bilateral Health Cooperation Memorandum of Understanding was signed last December. In exchange for more than $124m in planned “assistance” from the Trump administration, Liberia handed over access to its citizens’ health data without our permission. Similar aid pacts have been rejected or resisted by several other African governments. Although Liberia’s government has never publicly released the memorandum of understanding, one could argue that it too violates Article 34(f) of the Constitution since legislative approval was not granted.
Exactly a century ago – in 1926 – Liberia finalised another agreement with the US that undermined its sovereignty. Heavily indebted and desperate to ward off French and British colonisers, it accepted under duress a $5m loan from the Finance Corporation of America, a private subsidiary of US-based Firestone Tyre and Rubber Company. This was in exchange for signing a 99-year lease of 404,700 hectares (one million acres), enabling Firestone to extract unprocessed rubber at a measly six cents per acre. Loan terms authorised the US president to appoint Americans as administrators of Liberia’s finances, and forbade Liberia from borrowing without Firestone’s written consent. This set into motion an enduring legacy of US resource extraction from which Liberia has never recovered.
If Liberia is to assume its rightful place as Africa’s first independent Black republic – and a post-war “success story” at that – it must cancel bilateral agreements with the US that weaken its autonomy, violate national laws and erode citizens’ trust. It must actively pursue “positive peace”, the absence of structural violence, in the corridors of power both at home and abroad.

EBRD cuts Ukraine growth outlook to 1.5% for 2026, 2.5% for 2027
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:55:06 EEST
17:55:06 KST

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) has downgraded its forecast for Ukraine's real GDP growth to 1.5% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2027 due to Russian strikes on Black Sea ports and vessels, whereas in early June of this year, it had projected growth of 2.2% and 4%, respectively.
"Ukraine's macroeconomic outlook has weakened materially, with the economy shifting from slow recovery to near stagnation amid an escalation in Russian air attacks," according to the EBRD's Regional Economic Prospects (REP) report published on Thursday.
According to the report, downside risks are stemming from any prolonged disruption to Black Sea shipping, renewed Russian attacks on energy infrastructure and wider external financing gaps.
Real GDP contracted by 0.6% year on year in the first quarter of 2026, the EBRD said. As for the second quarter, it cites preliminary data from Ukraine's State Statistics Service indicating GDP growth of 0.6%, although the Service has since revised its estimate downward to 0.4%.
"While defence production, public spending and resilient services supported activity, damaged energy infrastructure, labour shortages, weak confidence and renewed logistics bottlenecks constrained growth," the EBRD said.
The bank added that inflation accelerated to 7.7% in July, reflecting higher fuel and energy costs, exchange-rate pass-through, labour-market pressures and wider supply disruptions, prompting the central bank to raise the policy rate to 15.5% (based on August results, inflation rose to 8.1%, while the National Bank raised the key policy rate to 16%).
The goods trade deficit widened sharply as energy and defence imports increased, while export capacity was hit by renewed Russian attacks on Black Sea ports, civilian shipping and transport infrastructure, the EBRD said.
"Alternative land and river routes can mitigate, but not replace, the lost deep-sea shipping capacity, while low Danube water levels, strikes on Danube infrastructure and rolling-stock shortages add further constraints," the bank said.
The EBRD said that Ukraine held more gas in storage in mid-2026 than at any point since 2022.
As for the impact on the global markets, the EBRD said that Russia and Ukraine together account for about a quarter of world wheat exports. A prolonged disruption to exports may significantly raise food prices and intensify inflationary pressures.
"Rerouting grain by land or rivers is expensive and logistically challenging. Low water levels in the Danube have also limited the main alternative route for Ukraine's exports," the bank said.
As reported, due to destruction in the industrial and trade sectors and deteriorating business expectations, the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) has lowered its real GDP growth forecast for this year to 1.1–1.2%, down from the 1.8% estimate made in late July.
In its 2027–2029 Budget Resolution, the Ukrainian government projected GDP growth of 1.6% for this year, with acceleration to 4.5% in 2027 and 5.3% in 2028. However, the government's draft state budget for 2027 is based on a pessimistic scenario of 1.3% GDP growth. Regarding the current year, the government initially forecast growth of 2.4%, later revising it to 1.6%; the Ministry of Economy now acknowledges the possibility that the forecast could be downgraded further to 0.5%.

Netherlands to build anti-drone laser with Australia’s EOS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:53:23 UTC
17:53:23 KST

- Dutch State Secretary for Defense Derk Boswijk signed a letter of intent with Australia's EOS to develop its high-energy laser into a counter-drone weapon.
- EOS intends to develop and produce the laser in the Netherlands, and the Dutch plan to buy several systems if development succeeds.
The Netherlands plans to turn an Australian-designed laser into a working weapon against drones and build it on Dutch soil, the Dutch Ministry of Defense said Thursday.
State Secretary for Defense Derk Boswijk signed a letter of intent this week with Electro Optic Systems (EOS), the Canberra-based maker of the Apollo high-energy laser.
The ministry and EOS intend to develop the laser into a complete weapon system and study whether a production site can be set up in the Netherlands, supplied by a Dutch-led European supply chain. EOS intends, in principle, to carry out both development and production in the Netherlands, which would become the company’s European base. If development succeeds, the Netherlands plans to buy several of the systems. The ministry did not say how many, what they would cost or when a purchase decision is due.
A high-energy laser converts electrical power into a concentrated beam that burns through or disables its target. Each engagement uses electricity instead of a missile or shell, so the weapon does not run short of ammunition as long as it has power and cooling. The ministry said that could make the laser more effective and cheaper to use than missile-based air defense.
EOS markets Apollo against drones ranging from small quadcopters to military aircraft weighing up to about 600 kg (1,320 pounds), and says the beam can also blind their sensors from a distance. Manufacturer information cited by Defence Watch puts Apollo’s output at roughly 50 to 150 kilowatts. The system can be installed in a standard shipping container or on a vehicle. EOS says Apollo contains no U.S.-controlled technology subject to American export rules and that it can hand over full technology to customers who want to build it themselves.
The Netherlands already has one Apollo on order. In 2025, EOS announced a €71.4 million ($81.4 million) export contract for a 100 kW-class laser for a European NATO member, and it later identified the buyer as the Netherlands, calling it the world’s first export order for a laser weapon of that class.
EOS chief executive Andreas Schwer said in June that the Dutch system was due for delivery around 2028, but that the company was ahead of schedule and could ship the first components as early as mid-2027. EOS opened a factory in Singapore this year to build its lasers, and Schwer said he expected many customers to push for local production.
EOS is also in final talks with an unnamed Middle Eastern customer on a 300 kW version of Apollo, about three times the power of the Dutch system. Schwer said the buyer wants that output to shoot down rockets, artillery shells and missiles as well as drones.
Britain is on a similar path with DragonFire, a laser weapon for Royal Navy warships. QinetiQ holds a £67 million contract to deliver the lasers, which are expected to be fitted to ships as early as 2027.

Wave of AI videos showing far-right protests in Europe spreads online
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:52:21 UTC
17:52:21 KST

A mass of AI-generated videos of protests across Europe has emerged on TikTok, which experts say aims to "amplify societal polarisation".
A series of AI-generated videos showing thousands of people protesting in a range of European cities against immigration, the state of the country, the current government, or for nationalist values has been doing the rounds on TikTok.
The videos analysed were published in the past four months, with some gathering more than 300,000 views.
The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, has identified this kind of content targeting users in Portugal, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, and the UK, with many appearing to believe what the videos showed.
However, none of the protests depicted in these specific videos is real, yet they use tactics to try and fool users into thinking otherwise.
To begin with, many of the videos pose as legitimate news outlets.
For example, one of the videos appears to show a Portuguese journalist working for the state-owned media RTP, as seen by the logo on her microphone, while the graphics embedded into the video itself resemble those of the Portuguese private media channel SIC Notícias.
Her location is also off: in real life, the Tagus River flows where the building she is standing in is depicted.
The Cube also reached out to RTP, which told us that the journalist in the AI-generated video did not work for them, and that they have no connection whatsoever with the video in question shared on TikTok.
Despite the vague reasons behind these alleged protests, such as those expressing anger at "the state of the country", some messages in the videos have connections with far-right parties. This is the case in some German videos that The Cube team has encountered, which contain captions in support of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Some also contain comments from TikTok users who evoke these parties, asking them to step up and fix issues such as migration. Some of the figures called upon include André Ventura, of the Portuguese far-right party Chega; the French National Rally; and Germany's Alice Weidel, from the AfD.
Most of the videos end by asking the audience to engage with their content by sharing their opinions about the protests or the name of the city they are watching from.
Experts claim that the primary purpose of the mass production of these types of videos is to manipulate public perception and amplify societal polarisation across Europe, posing severe risks to democratic discourse.
"Audiences engage with these videos primarily because synthetic imagery taps directly into pre-existing political anxieties and cultural grievances," Bruna Martins dos Santos from WITNESS, a global organisation that examines the impact of emerging technologies, especially generative AI and deepfakes, told The Cube.
Familiar misinformation tactics
All of these videos use three common misinformation techniques: emotional language, AI-generated content and polarisation.
Most of these tactics serve as engagement bait, according to Martins dos Santos.
"Topics like immigration, nationalism, and societal decline evoke strong emotional responses," she said. "This effect is especially pronounced on short-form video platforms where visual impact and emotional resonance precede context, leading viewers to process the spectacle — the crowd size, flags, and chanting — long before questioning its authenticity."
Additionally, social media recommendation algorithms amplify this dynamic by pushing provocative visual content to users most likely to resonate with it.
Using AI to produce this content makes the production cheap and scalable, effectively driving views, follower counts, and interaction metrics, Martins dos Santos said.
Why is this kind of content available?
The videos have been labelled as AI by TikTok itself. The platform claims that it bans AI-generated content that is "misleading about matters of public importance" or violates its misinformation guidelines.
In fact, it goes further: "Unlabeled content may be removed, restricted, or labelled by our team, depending on the harm it could cause."
Some videos, however, seem to slip through.
"The fact that these videos remain online can mean a policy violation of TikTok's own rules, but also highlight a failure in the platform's detection tools' capacity," said Martins dos Santos.
Moreover, under the European Digital Services Act, it must also take effective measures against content that could negatively affect "civic discourse and electoral processes".
"While the continued presence of these videos does not automatically establish a policy breach, it raises critical questions about the effectiveness of TikTok's detection mechanisms, labelling standards, and recommender algorithms," Santos said.
TikTok did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Real protests have gripped Europe in recent weeks
While the AI-generated videos show fabricated protests that did not take place, there have been widespread demonstrations across Europe recently for a range of issues.
Perhaps the most high-profile has been the protests in Spain in response to the Ceuta crisis, which saw an estimated 80,000 people breach the border between Morocco and the north African Spanish territory.
The majority of the migrants have since returned, but estimates say that up to 13,000 of them could still be in Ceuta, prompting protests in response to the government's handling of the crisis.
In Germany meanwhile, demonstrations erupted in opposition to the AfD party after it won a landslide victory in a state election earlier in September.
Thousands in Switzerland, on the other hand, recently marched to protest government inaction in the face of global warming.

What we know about CIA warning of Russian drone threat to southern Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:52:07 UTC
17:52:07 KST

The US has warned southern states of a possible Moscow attack that would see Russia fire 600 km-range drones from commercial ships at Spain, France and Italy. We examine what is known and how the threat is mounting.
US intelligence services have shared a report with several European countries pointing to a possible Russian operation using drones against targets in Spain, France or Italy, according to Spanish media.
The information was first revealed by journalist Xavier Colás — a former Russia correspondent — in the Spanish newspaper El Mundo. It traces the origin of the alert to CIA director John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow last August, and sets out a very specific attack scenario: drones launched from merchant vessels disguised as ordinary commercial traffic.
The Gerbera, a cheap and hard-to-detect weapon
According to information gathered by anonymous sources in Lithuania's Ministry of Defence, and reported by El Mundo, the device in question would be the Gerbera, a small Russian drone (barely two metres long and weighing 18 kilos) capable of travelling up to 600 kilometres at around 160 km/h.
Its limited explosive payload — between four and five kilos — is not intended to cause mass destruction, but to have a symbolic and disruptive effect: temporarily shutting down an airport, starting a fire, or demonstrating that Moscow can strike at Europe's rear without having to cross any land border.
This method is not just a distant hypothesis. The Kremlin has already tested launching drones from maritime platforms. Only last February, a Swedish naval unit detected a drone taking off from a Russian intelligence vessel in the Öresund Strait. Add to this the precedent set by the armed-drone attack at Leipzig airport in Germany, which Berlin attributes to Russian intelligence, and the episode of 19 unarmed drones flying over Polish airspace a year ago.
Why southern Europe, and not only the eastern flank
The Kremlin's logic, according to analysts consulted by the Spanish newspaper, is driven not by geographical proximity but by political vulnerability. British expert Keir Giles, a specialist in Russian military strategy, argues that Moscow will look for "the weakest point in Europe", explicitly naming countries such as Spain, which lack integrated air defence systems suited to this type of threat.
This idea ties directly into a warning issued months ago by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte: a Russian missile would take barely ten minutes longer to reach Madrid than to reach Warsaw. Rutte sought to dismantle the perception that southern Europe lies outside the "eastern flank" and is therefore beyond the radius of risk posed by the war that Russia launched against Ukraine in 2022, which threatens the entire continent.
Intimidation using drones launched from the Mediterranean, slower but just as symbolic, fits that same message: distance is no longer a guarantee of security for any European country.
Spain, France and Italy also share another risk factor highlighted in the investigation: all three will hold elections in 2027 and have political forces capable of capitalising on the social fatigue generated by years of war in Ukraine (despite Trump's stated desire to end the conflict before winter) — something that Vladimir Putin's government could try to exploit with a low-cost action and high media impact.
Italy’s Defence Minister, Guido Crosetto, has posted a message on X asking people not to "add fuel to the fire": "It serves no one and is completely unsubstantiated the alarm raised this morning by a Spanish newspaper suggesting possible attacks on Italy, Spain and France by Russian ships and drones. We are already living in difficult and "tense" times, and it does nobody any good to add fuel to the fire," said the politician.
Sánchez, defence spending and tension with Washington
The report comes at a particularly delicate moment for Spain in security terms. Pedro Sánchez's government has been reluctant to raise defence spending to the new threshold demanded by NATO, a stance that has led to open tension with Donald Trump and to an almost broken bilateral relationship. One of the latest examples was seen at the UN General Assembly, where Sánchez refused to attend the reception hosted by Trump in New York.
In this context, an intelligence alert of this kind adds further pressure on Moncloa: the lack of investment in air-defence and anti-missile systems is a weak point laid bare just as the perception of a direct threat to Spanish soil grows.
The Russian diaspora and asset ties on the Costa del Sol
The debate about Spain's exposure to Russian interests is not limited to the military sphere. For years, various journalistic investigations have documented the presence of assets linked to circles around the Kremlin along the Andalusian coast. Among the best-known cases is that of Liudmila Ocheretnaya — formerly Liudmila Putina — Vladimir Putin's ex-wife, who together with her current husband, Artur Ocheretny, came to own two luxury homes in the Lomas del Rey complex (Marbella) worth 2.2 million euros.
Those reports at the time already pointed to an urgent sale of those properties for fear of being included on the European Union sanctions list, after the United Kingdom had already sanctioned her.
Subsequent journalistic investigations have continued to document the web of companies and foundations linked to Ocheretny and his circle, keeping alive the question of the real extent of Russian economic interests, direct or indirect, on Spanish territory. There has been no recent public confirmation that the properties were in fact sold, nor of Ocheretnaya's current residence status on the Costa del Sol.
A threat Europe can no longer treat as distant
The report cited by El Mundo itself recalls that Moscow has for months been operating "below the threshold of war", combining isolated acts of sabotage with tests of reaction such as those carried out in Poland or Germany.
What is new now is that, according to the CIA, this pattern of escalation could spread to the Mediterranean, shattering the false sense of distance that for years has protected countries such as Spain, at least in the collective imagination. As Rutte sums it up, in today's Europe a difference of ten minutes no longer separates a safe country from one at risk.

Drug cartels attempt to establish major cocaine transit hub in Russia — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:51:16 UTC
17:51:16 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. International drug cartels are making significant efforts to establish a foothold in Russia, seeking to turn the country into a major transit hub for cocaine shipments from Latin America to the European Union, according to Alexander Yevtushenko, Dean of the Department of History, Sociology, and International Relations at Kuban State University. His remarks were released by the Public Relations Center of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB).
The FSB previously reported the arrest in the Moscow Region of a man involved in organizing drug shipments from Latin America to EU countries. He was apprehended in the act, with 311 kilograms of cocaine seized from him.
"Recently, international drug cartels have been drawing Russia into their criminal activities. Our country is becoming a major hub and transit zone, forming part of the illicit cocaine trafficking system," Yevtushenko said.
According to the expert, cocaine enters Russia from Latin America by sea through ports before being transported to major cities such as Moscow and St. Petersburg. Shipments are concealed in containers intended for food products, including bananas and fish.
"From there, it is essentially transported overland to European Union countries. The scale of this activity is staggering," Yevtushenko said.
He cited several recent seizures as evidence of the scale of the trafficking. In September 2025, authorities confiscated a 1.5-ton shipment of cocaine, while in July 2026, a 500-kilogram shipment was seized in St. Petersburg.
"All this indicates that the activities of drug traffickers in Russia are indeed reaching an industrial scale, and, unfortunately, an increasing number of our people are becoming involved in them," the expert said.
He added that traffickers use various covert communication and data-transfer channels, including the dark web, to facilitate their operations. Despite these measures, he said, the schemes are being uncovered by the FSB and other law enforcement agencies.

Interior Minister Çiftçi instructed police chiefs on school safety. (AA Photo)
Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi has instructed newly appointed provincial police chiefs to strengthen school security and take preventive measures before threats reach school gates, following a shooting that injured 11 students in the western province of Manisa.
Speaking at a meeting for newly appointed police chiefs, Çiftçi said judicial and administrative proceedings into the attack were being conducted meticulously.
Çiftçi issued 10 directives to police chiefs, beginning with mapping the security and risk profile of their provinces and closely monitoring high-risk areas. He called for a firm response to groups targeting children and young people and urged police to address crime both on the streets and in the digital sphere, including illegal betting, online fraud and criminal networks operating through social media.
He said each school should undergo an individual risk assessment covering its surroundings, student routes, abandoned buildings, parks and suspicious activity. Police should closely monitor access to firearms, peer bullying, threats and violent behavior, including threats made online, while strengthening coordination between cybercrime, intelligence and operational units.
Police chiefs were also instructed to maintain regular contact with school administrators, families, local officials and businesses, increase school liaison officers and reinforce patrols and visible police presence where necessary.
“Measures must be taken before danger reaches the school gate,” Çiftçi said, adding that school security should no longer be treated as a routine public-order issue.
The directives followed a shooting outside İnci Üzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in Turgutlu on Sept. 22. A ninth-grade student opened fire with a hunting rifle, injuring 11 students, three of whom were reported to be in critical condition. Çiftçi said the school had been classified as a first-degree high-risk school.

BJP’s Bengal spending outpaces Congress’ five-state total

Erdoğan noted that achieving a transition to a circular economy means strengthening sustainable development, expanding recycling, improving waste management and turning toward renewable energy sources.
“We see zero waste as a key to achieving all of this. Because zero waste is not merely a waste-management approach that individuals incorporate into their daily lives. Zero waste means redesigning our production and consumption models and redefining our relationship with nature,” she said, stressing the need for new economic models to transform the entire system from production to consumption.
She urged establishing “an order in which people who adopt zero waste in their lives are supported by the right systems.”
The first lady noted that the world still has a window of opportunity to combat the climate crisis and build a sustainable future.
“I believe that Zero Waste, which we launched in Türkiye in 2017 and which has now become a global movement, is a transformative force in making the most of this opportunity,” she said.
“With the right steps we take together, I hope we can make a new beginning — one in which we protect our resources rather than consume them and create value instead of waste,” she added.

US judge blocks Trump’s White House ban on CNN, MS NOW, and Politico
Trump-nominated judge rules that outlets are likely to succeed in claim they were denied due process.
A United States judge has blocked President Donald Trump’s ban on three news outlets from the White House, ordering his administration to immediately restore their access pending a later court hearing.
Issuing a temporary restraining order early on Thursday, US District Judge Timothy J Kelly said CNN, MS NOW and Politico were likely to prevail in their legal challenge to Trump’s ban on several grounds, including that it violated their due process rights.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Gaza watches Israel’s elections with fear and antipathy

- list 3 of 4UN funding cuts hit refugees at Cox’s Bazar settlement
- list 4 of 4China vs US: Who is winning the AI race, in four charts
Kelly said the outlets had made a convincing case that they were stripped of their credentials without due process and were likely to suffer “irreparable harm” in the absence of the temporary order.
Kelly, who was nominated by Trump during his first term in 2017, also found there was a public interest in blocking the ban “given the importance of the free press”.
Rejecting the Trump administration’s claim that the outlets had been barred to protect national security, Kelly said the government’s argument lacked “factual support”.
“Defendants offer no declarations or other support – classified or unclassified – explaining how any of the reporting they identified in their letters to Plaintiffs damaged the national security,” Kelly said in the ruling.
Kelly ruled that the Trump administration should “immediately return, reinstate, and restore” the outlets’ access to the White House.
Kelly imposed the injunction for 14 days, pending further proceedings.
Theodore Boutrous, the lawyer representing the outlets, welcomed the ruling as a vindication of the “freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law”.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump later claimed in a news conference that the outlets produced “negative news” and sought to “diminish” his administration and the Republican Party.
CNN, Politico and MS NOW on Monday announced they had jointly filed a lawsuit seeking to overturn the ban, arguing it violated their free speech and due process rights.

India Lays Keel of First NGMV Missile Boat to Replace Veer Ships
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:40:59 UTC
17:40:59 KST

On September 18, India held the keel-laying ceremony for the lead NGMV (Next Generation Missile Vessel) missile boat for the Indian Navy.
The ceremony took place at Cochin Shipyard Limited (CSL), the facility reported.
According to Naval News, the main armament of the NGMV boats will be BrahMos anti-ship missiles housed in two twin-canister slanted launchers in the bow of the vessel.
To defend against aerial threats, the boats will be equipped with the VL-SRSAM SAM system, a 76 mm SRGM gun, and aft CIWS.
The primary radar will be a multifunctional X-band radar from Bharat Electronics Limited, with a target detection range of up to 200 km.
Each boat will be powered by a main propulsion system comprising a single GE Aerospace LM2500 gas turbine, which will be assembled under license by Indian company HAL.
The turbine will drive three large Kamewa waterjets from Norwegian company Kongsberg Maritime, with a contract for 18 units signed in April.
Delivery of the lead missile boat to the customer is scheduled for early 2027.
The new 1,500-tonne ships are intended to replace the aging Veer-class missile boats, which have been in service since the 20th century.
In July, India held the launch ceremony for the seventh ASW SWC (Anti-Submarine Warfare Shallow Water Craft) coastal anti-submarine warfare vessel.
The newly built craft was named INS Machilipatnam after the historic port city in Andhra Pradesh state.
The Indian Navy also planned to begin construction of four to five surface ships and submarines in 2026.

Netanyahu takes UN stage with one eye on Israel’s election

Netanyahu takes UN stage with one eye on Israel’s election
As criticism of Israel intensifies, Israeli PM Netanyahu heads to the UN with his own political future in focus.
When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu takes to his feet at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York later on Thursday, he does so at a critical point in both his political career and in his country’s long and fractious relationship with the international body.
Israel has faced repeated accusations of genocide at the UN, as well as systematic war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Those criticisms continue to shape the country’s fractious relationship with the body.
Recommended Stories

“The UN is playing host to a war criminal,” said Sonya Meyerson-Knox from Jewish Voice for Peace, a New York based group protesting against the Israeli premier. “Solidarity with Palestinian freedom has never been greater, and here in the US we are demanding with one voice: Stop arming Israel.”
For Netanyahu, appearing in front of the UNGA for the 15th time, the stakes have rarely been higher.
Addressing a domestic Israeli audience that polls show to be losing faith in him and his Likud party in the run-up to crucial elections later this year, Netanyahu has already pitched himself as Israel’s primary voice on the international stage.
Nevertheless, analysts say Netanyahu’s address could prove a pivotal moment domestically, amplified by international criticism of Israel and expected to dominate headlines and be carried live across the country’s television networks.
“This is a regular fixture for him,” former Israeli consul general in New York and ex-government adviser, Alon Pinkas, told Al Jazeera. “It’s his way of being seen in Israel as standing up against the world and of telling members that he will never give up or surrender. He’s also turned the event into some kind of national holiday in Israel, with everyone sitting down to watch the address on television. He’s brainwashed people in Israel into believing his speech is somehow an announcement of policy, stated in defiance of the [rest of the world] who don’t believe a word he says.”
A history of hostility
Israeli leaders have long framed their stance towards the UN as one of defiance in the face of hostility. The UN has long been a platform for critics of Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestinian land and repeated attacks on its neighbours. It has included attempts to censure Israel over what UN investigators have described as apartheid in the West Bank, as well as accusations of genocide and pogroms across the occupied Palestinian territory since October 2023.
There have been numerous UNGA resolutions criticising Israel’s conduct – nearly all dismissed by Israeli lawmakers as evidence of institutional bias – culminating in Israel declaring UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres persona non grata and severely restricting the operations of the UN’s agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.
“Generally speaking, many Israelis tend to see the UN as anti-Israeli,” Nimrod Goren, the president of the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies, Mitvim, said.
Against that background, criticism from New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani – already cast as anti-Israel in the Israeli press – has drawn greater public attention to the event. Underscoring the sense of hostility towards Israel are stories within the country’s media suggesting that Netanyahu’s visit to New York has been curtailed due to unspecified security concerns, with the Israeli premier expected to fly out of New York on the same day as his arrival.
In response, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, who has repeatedly accused the organisation of waging “diplomatic terrorism” against the state, called for Mamdani’s arrest for what he said was the mayor’s incitement against New York’s Jewish community before Netanyahu’s visit.
“Netanyahu is going into his UNGA speech with not one but both eyes focused firmly on the upcoming Israeli election,” Goren said. “The speech is usually treated in Israel as a major event, receiving broad coverage and dominating the news cycle. Netanyahu will likely try to leverage this to bolster his image as a close ally of the US and to talk up the threat posed by Iran.”
US backing
Some have interpreted US President Donald Trump’s apparent lack of availability to meet Netanyahu during this trip as a sign of waning support. But US backing for Israel at the UN has remained steadfast since the October 7 attack and has contributed to growing frustration within the UN over what they see as Israel’s ability to resist international censure.
Alongside the creation of the Board of Peace, which shifted significant responsibility for Gaza’s future from the UN to the Trump-founded organisation, Washington has repeatedly used its veto at the UN Security Council (UNSC) to shield Israel from resolutions it opposes. The US has vetoed at least six UNSC resolutions on Gaza since October 2023, most of them demanding an immediate ceasefire.
“There seems to be genuine frustration within the UN General Assembly over the body’s failure to play a significant political role in Gaza and the West Bank, but also in its failure to protect its own staff and agencies,” Chatham House Associate Fellow Zizette Darkazally, who previously worked with the UN, said.
“However, it’s worth remembering the context the UN operates within in the occupied territories and the important humanitarian role it plays. The UN continues to get aid and medical support into Gaza and the West Bank, which are both areas where Israel has absolute control over access,” she said. “It’s also worth remembering that the UN is only as strong as the commitment of its member states.
“That, combined with a system of veto that’s more than 80 years old, has left the organisation weaker now than it had ever been,” she said of the confrontations between the UN and Israel. “And we’re seeing the effects of that, not just in Palestine, but in Yemen, Sudan and Iran, where the UN is playing next to no political role.”

Employer representative Chiu I-che (邱一徹) said many small- and medium-sized businesses, traditional manufacturers, and service companies still face weak demand and higher material, energy, and labor costs. He urged the committee to focus more on inflation and what different industries can afford, per Economic Daily News.

L3Harris wins $876 million for Growler radar jammer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:38:52 UTC
17:38:52 KST

- The U.S. Navy added $876.4 million to L3Harris' Next Generation Jammer Low Band contract for the EA-18G Growler, with work running through fiscal 2031.
- The Royal Australian Air Force obligated $23 million at award, compared with $3.65 million from the U.S. Navy.
The U.S. Navy has added $876.4 million to L3Harris Technologies’ contract for the Next Generation Jammer Low Band, a radar-jamming pod for the EA-18G Growler electronic attack jet flown by the U.S. Navy and the Royal Australian Air Force, the U.S. Department of War announced.
The award is a modification to the $587.4 million contract Naval Air Systems Command gave L3Harris in August 2024 to take the jammer through engineering and manufacturing development, the final stage before production. The new money is larger than that original award.
It pays for continued development of the pod, tooling, equipment and labor needed to build it, and delivery of test pods for system demonstration. It also covers additional cybersecurity work, along with logistics, testing and software support for both air forces. Work is scheduled to finish in fiscal 2031.
The modification is undefinitized, meaning the Navy authorized the work before the final terms and price were agreed. It is a cost-plus-incentive-fee deal, which reimburses L3Harris’s costs and pays a fee tied to performance targets. The Navy did not compete it.
Australia is putting in more money up front than the United States. At the time of award, the Navy obligated $3.65 million in fiscal 2026 research and development funds, while the Royal Australian Air Force contributed $23 million in cooperative funds.
Most of the work, 43%, will take place at L3Harris’s facility in Salt Lake City. The rest is spread across sites in Alabama, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Colorado, California, New York and Texas, with 3.4% performed in Australia.
The Growler is a modified F/A-18F Super Hornet built to jam and disrupt enemy radars and communications, clearing a path for other aircraft. Its main jamming system has long been the AN/ALQ-99 pod, first fielded in the 1970s. The Navy is replacing it with a family of Next Generation Jammer pods, each covering a different part of the radio spectrum.
RTX’s Raytheon builds the mid-band pod, the AN/ALQ-249, which already flies with the fleet. L3Harris’s low-band pod targets lower-frequency search radars. Those radars track targets less precisely than higher-frequency systems, but they can spot aircraft at long range and cue long-range missiles toward them.
L3Harris says the pod will let Growler crews suppress enemy air defenses with high-power jamming from standoff ranges, keeping the aircraft farther from the threats they are attacking.
Suppliers are already delivering hardware. In July, CPI Aerostructures of Edgewood, New York, received a $13.6 million contract from L3Harris to build pod structures for operational prototypes that will go to the Navy for fleet assessment and to extra test units for airworthiness and design checks. The company said it had delivered its first test article. Honeywell Aerospace joined the program in June 2025, and Marotta Controls announced contracts to support it this month.
