Burmese Refugees in Thailand Face Fresh Deportation Threat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:43:00 UTC
13:43:00 KST

In April of 2026, 23-year-old Nway became scared of the dark for the first time in her life. She would lie awake at night, jumping at the noise of a car engine humming past the house she shared with her single mother, anxious that she could be dragged from her bed as she slept.
Her fear of the dark was not unfounded. As a Burmese political activist who had spent the last four years of her life in prison until April of this year, she was a high-profile target for forced conscription into the Myanmar military, which seized power in a coup in 2021. The military, which now fully controls only around 20 percent of the country’s territory, has conscripted over 30,000 young people since February 2024 in a bid to strengthen their struggling forces.
Since then, young people have been grabbed from the street, their workplaces, and their homes, after which they are reportedly deployed to the frontlines and used as “cannon fodder and human shields.” Nway said that her cousin was abducted by the authorities while drinking with friends by the river in Yangon one evening in 2024. He returned home earlier this year to share that “everyone except him had died; he was the one and only lucky man.”
Nway’s previous activism meant that when she was released from prison, she was targeted by the police, who would sit outside her home and visit her mother weekly to tell her, “if you don’t give us money, she will be listed.” Concerned for her daughter’s safety, Nway’s mother instead paid the authorities for her to fly safely to Thailand. Nway found a community of Burmese refugees and activists in the northern city of Chiang Mai, many of whom had similarly been targeted for conscription before fleeing the country.
Since the military coup, thousands of young refugees like Nway have started to rebuild their lives in Thailand, following in the footsteps of past generations of refugees and exiles. But harassment and arrests from Thai police and a deportation law approved in August continue to threaten their security. The new legal framework has been developed for “administering deportation issues speedily and effectively” in the absence of pre-existing “concrete guidelines.” According to civil society organizations, the new laws are already a source of concern for refugees in Thailand.
When Nway arrived in northern Thailand, she was reunited with Pho Thar, another activist and photojournalist whom she had known at university. Both had been held in separate facilities in Yangon’s Insein Prison for years, reuniting only once they had left the country. Pho Thar has already secured his migrant worker’s card, known as a “pink card,” which is the most accessible way for Myanmar nationals to gain legal residency, and Nway is in the process of securing her own.
Nway and Pho Thar are comfortable sharing their stories and names because they know they can never return to Myanmar. For Nway, this is because an outstanding legal case ensures she will be arrested and likely conscripted. Pho Thar, who has already been arrested four times by the Burmese authorities, believes he will be killed if he returns. Sitting outside a Burmese-owned restaurant on the edge of the city, he cracks his shoulder, a permanent injury sustained during his last arrest.
When Pho Thar was released from prison in November 2025, he knew he was listed for conscription and left Yangon within five days, travelling to Karen State where friends in the People’s Defense Forces helped him cross the border.
Pho Thar decided to travel straight to Chiang Mai when he entered Thailand because he believed the risk of staying in the border city of Mae Sot without documentation would be too high. Almost half of the nearly 4 million Myanmar nationals living in Thailand are undocumented and they face regular harassment, extortion, and threats of deportation from the Thai authorities. A 2025 report by Human Rights Watch (HRW) identified that police bribes had become so prevalent in Mae Sot that they referred to Myanmar nationals as “walking ATMs.”
Fear of the authorities and deportation has ruled the lives of several young Burmese refugees who agreed to speak to The Diplomat on condition of anonymity.
One 22-year-old Burmese refugee, Aung*, said that as an undocumented migrant, he found work in a garment factory where he is paid only 150 baht a day – the equivalent of around $4.50 and below minimum wage – and receives one day off per month. Despite his exhaustion, he is grateful for the layer of protection this workplace provides from the police. “I’m always afraid of the Thai police so I rarely go out to the town, I always stay in my factory,” he said.
In Myanmar, the parents of young people who have fled the country continue to pay bribes to Burmese authorities so their other children are not conscripted instead. Aung said that until August 2026, his mother continued to pay for him. “If I was deported to Myanmar, I would be taken to the frontlines and I will never go back home,” he said. “I face difficulty in Mae Sot so I always miss my home. I want to go back, but it is not possible.”
Thirty-five-year-old music producer Kyaw* also said that his mother, who recently recovered from breast cancer, continues to pay monthly bribes for her three children who have fled the country. He is still waiting for his documents in Mae Sot, and similarly knows that if he was deported he would be forced to join what he calls the “one-way troops” that are sent to the frontlines. He decided to leave Yangon when he went to the smoking area near his workplace and witnessed several young colleagues being kidnapped by military personnel during a work break.
Having already paid a 14-million-kyat bribe – over $6,600 – after being arbitrarily arrested and threatened with conscription, Kyaw started the long journey to the border. “I didn’t want to serve in the military because it’s just a civil war,” he said. “Since moving to Thailand, I have to start from zero but if I don’t have anything to eat I don’t care; I will sing a song for the revolution.”
Elsa, who fled to Mae Sot in 2023 with her family, said that they had to wait until 2025 for them to receive their migrant worker’s cards. She reported that they did not leave their home for four months between April and August in 2024 due to increased patrols and arrests by the authorities. She now works in an office but said that “it is a difficult life.”
Since Thai immigration laws do not recognize Myanmar nationals as refugees, and Thailand has not signed the 1951 Refugee Convention, the paths to residency are limited and refugees rely on a broker to navigate the application process for a worker’s card. Interviewees in HRW’s report confirmed that it was unclear exactly what the fees they were paying brokers were being used for in the application process.
In late August, new deportation regulations were approved by the Thai government, which facilitate the prompt deportation of “undesirable” foreigners. Civil society organizations have criticized this legislation, calling for it to include safeguards protecting refugees from deportation. As it stands, while the legislation acknowledges decisions around deportation should account for Thailand’s “relevant international obligations” there is no mention of non-refoulement, which would prevent refugees or asylum seekers from being sent back to any country where they could face persecution or serious harm.
Two foreign nationals have already been deported under the new legal framework. Thanida Piyachot, a human rights specialist at the advocacy group Fortify Rights, said that “the Thai government’s enactment of regulations that can directly affect people’s rights without a thorough review is already deeply concerning. Now, with the enforcement of this fast-track deportation process, serious questions remain about how decisions will be made in practice when there are no clear standards of safeguards.”
Tanyakorn Thippayapokin, the policy, advocacy, and communications coordinator at Asylum Access Thailand, added that it’s very likely the law will be used to extort, harass, and deport Burmese nationals because it is written “very broadly to target anyone staying illegally in the country.”
The Coalition for the Rights of Refugees and Stateless Persons, which includes Fortify Rights and Asylum Access, has called for the government to promptly review the regulations with civil society organizations to address gaps that could put refugees at risk of forced returns and have a standard operating procedure that aligns with principles of non-refoulement.
For the undocumented refugees who are waiting for their migrant worker’s card applications to be processed, this law adds to their concerns about being deported to Myanmar and forcibly recruited. Everyone interviewed by The Diplomat believed that deportation would result in them being conscripted against their will and likely dying on the frontlines, a risk that does not appear to have been considered under this new legal framework, according to civil society organizations.
Piyachot argued that the new law is already impacting the security of undocumented Burmese migrants. “It is creating fear among refugee communities. I believe [the authorities] can use this law to threaten them, and worsen the corruption and extortion,” she said.
Meanwhile, Nway is trying to start a new life in Chiang Mai, alongside Pho Thar. Now she is in Thailand, she says she “doesn’t expect a lot. I really want to go back to my country because it’s where my childhood memories are, but it’s impossible.”
Instead, she says she wants a simple life. “I don’t want to worry again about what will happen at night, like in Yangon,” Nway said. “I want to sleep peacefully.”
*Some names have been changed to preserve respondents’ anonymity.

IDF probe: Paga troops never drilled for large-scale assault before 18 were killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:42:34 UTC
13:42:34 KST

The inquiry, which was also presented to the IDF chief of staff, was conducted by Col. Uri Ron, Lt. Col. (res.) Tzachi Aroati and other members of the investigative team. Over 10 months, they collected testimony, radio recordings, video footage and material from other investigations.
Its conclusion was unequivocal: the IDF failed in its defensive mission. It did not prevent the Paga outpost from falling or stop terrorists from breaking through toward Kibbutz Be’eri.
The inquiry found that the outcome reflected a systemic failure to prepare for a large-scale surprise attack and to fulfill the military’s responsibility to defend the sector.
Eighteen commanders and soldiers were killed in the fighting across the area, 22 were wounded and two additional soldiers were abducted to the Gaza Strip.
At the tactical level, the company combat team from the Golani Brigade’s 13th Battalion was not sufficiently prepared for the mission, the inquiry found. The deficiencies included combat equipment, the operational readiness of fighting positions and the outpost’s infrastructure.
The prevailing operational concept before October 7 focused largely on dealing with disturbances along the Gaza border fence. As a result, troops had not adequately prepared or trained for a scenario involving a large-scale enemy raid.
When the attack began, Hamas struck intelligence-gathering systems in the sector and disabled assets that could have given the defenders a significant advantage.
Key commanders were also killed during the first hours of the fighting, including the outpost commander and the mortar platoon sergeant, severely affecting command and control. The company commander was unable to reach the sector.
The inquiry also found that most Israeli Air Force strikes during the battle were not sufficiently effective because of coordination gaps between aircraft and troops on the ground.
The battle begins
The timeline reconstructed by the inquiry shows that troops carried out the required dawn readiness procedure on the morning of October 7.
At 6:29 a.m., as massive rocket fire began, soldiers moved into the fortified dining hall, which had been designated as an assembly point.
Tanks dispatched to positions along the border immediately moved to engage the attackers. A tank commanded by Staff Sgt. Shay Levinson killed 10 terrorists, according to the inquiry, but tanks were then struck by anti-tank missiles and by an explosive dropped from a drone.
The commander of one tank was abducted. A tracker stationed at the nearby Sahaf outpost was killed and was later classified as a fallen soldier whose body had been abducted.
At 6:55 a.m., nine terrorists entered the Paga outpost through the armored vehicle gate and split into squads that attacked the mortar compound and entrances to the post.
Troops at the mortar position fought the terrorists at close range, killing four of them, but suffered heavy casualties.
The outpost commander took command of the battle, reinforced defensive positions and continued fighting despite a severe shortage of weapons and equipment.
At 7:49 a.m., he left with several soldiers to retrieve a LAW anti-tank weapon in an effort to neutralize a terrorist positioned in a pillbox. Under grenade attacks and gunfire from the nearby hill, soldiers were killed and wounded.
Rescue attempt fails
At 9:34 a.m., troops attempted to evacuate the wounded from the dining hall using a Namer armored personnel carrier.
The attempt failed after a terrorist attached an explosive device to the vehicle’s rear door. A malfunction in one of the firing ports prevented the soldiers inside from neutralizing him.
At 10:35 a.m., the outpost commander and his radio operator were killed while advancing toward the main gate and engaging terrorists.
With the company commander’s approval, the platoon sergeant disengaged with some of the surviving soldiers and linked up with a Namer in nearby orchards.
Those who remained inside the dining hall fortified its entrances and continued fighting.
At about 1 p.m., terrorists set fires on both sides of the building, filling the fortified dining hall with smoke.
Five soldiers made the decision to leave through the burning kitchen and engage the terrorists outside. All five were killed in the fighting.
Rescue forces from the IDF’s counterterrorism school and Golani officers reached the outpost only between 4:20 p.m. and 4:50 p.m. They cleared the compound and evacuated the wounded and the dead.
Later that evening, an anti-tank missile was fired at the evacuation convoy, killing another soldier.
‘A different outcome was expected’
The inquiry concluded that, based on the circumstances that existed that Saturday morning, IDF forces should have been capable of producing a different outcome and defeating the terrorists who raided the outposts.
The troops’ level of preparedness, it found, did not match the defensive mission assigned to them.
Alongside the systemic failures, however, the inquiry highlighted what it described as exceptional acts of bravery, comradeship and determination to engage the enemy by junior commanders and soldiers.
They continued fighting in what the investigators described as an extraordinarily difficult, at times nearly impossible, operational reality.

OpenAI agent hacked Australia government portal: PM Albanese
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:42:00 UTC
13:42:00 KST

OpenAI agent hacked Australia government portal: PM Albanese
September 24, 2026
An OpenAI agent infiltrated an Australian government health data portal, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Thursday, in what is the first known instance of an artificial intelligence hack of a government system.
Albanese said the breach occurred in June when an autonomous OpenAI program accessed both "public and non-public" files on the statistics reporting portal of Medicare — Australia's publicly funded universal health insurance scheme.
The available evidence did not indicate a broader network compromise, Albanese said, adding, "Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable."
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman to express Australia's "extreme concern" over the incident.
OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, said in a statement that it spotted the breach while carrying out an "extensive review" of its AI tools, adding that "our models took actions we did not intend".
Altman had earlier on Wednesday addressed the UN Security Council, apprising the risks AI poses as the world faces the technology's development.
What did Australia's Albanese say about the OpenAI breach?
Albanese told reporters that OpenAI informed Australia about the breach only on September 10, three months after the incident, through an email sent to a public mailbox.
The Australian leader said he expressed his "disappointment" to Altman that it took OpenAI "way too long to inform the government" on what occurred.
Albanese also deemed the nature of the notification "unacceptable."
The prime minister announced that a probe into the security breach would determine whether OpenAI could face criminal charges.
He added that the investigation would also examine how the breach went past Australia's security agencies, which were unaware of it before OpenAI notified them.
How did the breach take place?
The breach occurred as OpenAI ran training exercises to rate the performance of AI models.
Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher said OpenAI asked the model to search the internet for data showing how much Australia's government spent on medicine.
She said the portal had since been closed and the data moved to more secure systems.
Albanese said no personal information is believed to have been accessed during the incident.
"I think OpenAI know that they need to have better protocols in place. And they're one of the businesses that themselves have warned of the risks which are there," Albanese said.
What has OpenAI said?
OpenAI said in its statement that it discovered the rogue activity in an August review.
"During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation," it said.
The San Francisco-based company added that it had found no evidence of Australian patient records being accessed.
Australia's Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles called the breach "fundamentally unacceptable."
"It was not sitting behind a particularly high fence. This AI agent scaled the fence ... and the point is it was unintended. It wasn't asked to. That's our concern here," Marles said.
In July, OpenAI disclosed that its advanced AI model went rogue during a security test and carried out a dayslong hacking spree into the Hugging Face AI technology digital repository.
Days later, rival company Anthropic announced that three separate versions of its AI broke out of cybertesting environments and hacked three firms.

WELLINGTON, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- The New Zealand government is providing 150,000 NZ dollars (85,217 U.S. dollars) in one-off funding to six accredited wildlife care facilities to support bird flu surveillance and response, ministers said Thursday.

Conservation Minister Tama Potaka said in a statement that the facilities were important partners in protecting native species and helping authorities understand emerging threats such as bird flu.
Biosecurity Minister Andrew Hoggard said the facilities were an important part of New Zealand's bird flu surveillance through existing contracts with the Ministry for Primary Industries (MPI).
"Early detection will be critical to limiting the impact on industries, wildlife and communities if bird flu spreads beyond individual wild birds," Hoggard was quoted as saying.
The funding would allow the facilities to strengthen biosecurity protocols, purchase equipment or increase their capacity to care for sick or injured native birds, he said, adding that MPI has also offered wider support, including equipment and practical information. ■

Asian Games | Feature: Age no barrier to Asian Games glory
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
12:41:23 CST
13:41:23 KST

by sportswriter Cao Yibo, Sun Zhe and Lin Deren
NAGOYA, Japan, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Nasser Al-Attiyah does not look, or shoot, like a man of 55.
The Qatari, who claimed his sixth Dakar Rally title barely eight months ago, teamed up with two compatriots on Wednesday to win gold in the men's skeet team event at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, his third gold and sixth medal across nine Asian Games spanning 32 years.
"To start from the Hiroshima Asian Games and to come back here again, and today for our team to win two gold medals, is really amazing," he said. Al-Attiyah described his performance as "one of the highest scores in the field," despite having only about two months to prepare between rally races.
Al-Attiyah is far from alone among the older competitors at these Games. At Nagoya City General Gymnasium this week, 51-year-old Uzbek vaulter Oksana Chusovitina, known to fans simply as "Chuso," was competing at her seventh Asian Games, a run stretching back to Hiroshima 1994, the same edition where Al-Attiyah made his debut.
At Aichi-Nagoya 2026, Chusovitina qualified fourth for the vault final with a score of 13.266, adding another chapter to a career that has already brought her two golds, four silvers and two bronzes since 1994.
Chusovitina's longevity, however, has never been only about medals. In 2002, her three-year-old son Alisher was diagnosed with leukemia, and she turned gymnastics into a lifeline, competing wherever prize money and support were available.
Her son had recovered by the time she won vault silver at Beijing 2008. Rather than step away, she chose to keep competing, through Tokyo 2020 at 46 and an injury-forced absence from Paris 2024, before returning at 50 to win World Cup gold in Baku.
Asked in Nagoya, inevitably, when she might retire, she shot back with a grin: "What, don't you want to see me anymore?" With Los Angeles 2028 in her sights, she is not ruling out a ninth Olympics.
The same refusal to be counted out defines Nosheen Aslam's Asian Games debut. At 55, the Pakistani table tennis player was the oldest competitor in the women's team event in Nagoya, sharing a roster with a 15-year-old teammate and facing opponents decades younger.
She took up the sport 12 years ago, already a mother of three, and often trains at night after cooking, working and caring for her children. "Every time I play, I feel happy and forget the worries of my life," she said. "Age is just a number."
Her results in Nagoya did not go her way, but she left already looking ahead to next April's South Asian Games. "Maybe I can play for another two or three years," she said, before adding with a smile: "Maybe next time my performance will be better."
China also has its own example of longevity. Wan Antao, a 41-year-old shooter, is making his Asian Games debut as the oldest member of an 815-strong Chinese delegation whose average age is 24.
At the opposite end of that same delegation is its youngest athlete, nearly three decades his junior: 12-year-old skateboarder Cao Shiqi.
The Beijing native discovered the sport by chance at a shopping mall at age four, balancing on a demonstration board before she could properly ride a bike. She has spent this year making progress in her specialty, park, an event in which competitors perform tricks in pool-like courses up to 4.5 meters deep.
The seventh-grader won the junior title at the Asian Skateboarding Championships in April and the national title in July, bouncing back after a fall at China's National Games last November left her in tears.
Her coaches have been careful not to make results the sole focus. For a 12-year-old, her family says, simply experiencing the atmosphere of a major Games matters more than a place on the podium, with the Olympics a longer-term target.
Youth is making itself felt well beyond the Chinese team.
Should eleven-year-old Kurihara Yuki, a fifth-grader from Tokyo, medal in Nagoya in Esports, he would break the record for the youngest medalist in Asian Games history, currently held by a 12-year-old Indonesian skateboarder who took bronze at Jakarta 2018.
No teenager at the Games has made a bigger impact than 13-year-old Chinese swimmer Yu Zidi. Making her Asian Games debut, she broke the Games record to win the women's 200m butterfly, then broke the Asian record in the 200m individual medley two days later, edging compatriot and defending champion Yu Yiting in one of the closest races of the meet.
On Wednesday, she added a third gold in the 400m individual medley, finishing nearly four seconds clear of the field. "It's the final 50 meters, so I just told myself not to hold anything back," she said of her closing kick.
Out of the pool, she is unmistakably 13, calling her parents from training camps and insisting people remember she is "just a kid" her age. In the water, she sounds like anything but a novice: "Even when I'm very tired, I have to keep training. When I feel I can't hold on, I still have to keep going."
From Yu at 13 to Chusovitina at 51, from Al-Attiyah's three decades of elite competition to a fifth-grader's rise through the ranks of a video game, the Asian Games have shown that high-level sport does not belong to any single age group.
What connects them is not the number of years behind them, but a determination not to let age decide when their time in competition is over. ■

PAM party leads Morocco’s legislative elections with 97 seats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:29:47 UTC
13:29:47 KST

Diyar Guldogan and Ikram Kouachi
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Morocco’s Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) emerged as the leading party in the country’s legislative elections, securing 97 seats, according to results announced by the Interior Ministry.
 
Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit announced the preliminary official results at a news conference in the capital Rabat early Thursday.
 
Laftit said voting across the country took place under “normal conditions, except for isolated cases,” which he did not specify, that “did not affect the electoral process.”
 
The National Rally of Independents (RNI) followed PAM with 66 seats, while the Istiqlal Party won 65 seats.
 
The Justice and Development Party (PJD) placed fourth with 54 seats.
 
The Popular Movement won 29 seats, followed by the Socialist Union of Popular Forces with 26, the Party of Progress and Socialism with 19 and the Constitutional Union with 17.
 
The Left Alliance and Social Democratic Movement each won eight seats, while the Democratic Forces Front and Insaf Party each secured two seats. The New Democrats and Unity and Democracy parties each won one seat.
 
The results determine the composition of Morocco’s 395-member House of Representatives.
 
Under the country’s constitutional system, the king appoints the head of government from the party that wins the largest number of seats.
 
The ministry said voter turnout stood at 38.02% nationwide, down from 50.18% in the 2021 legislative elections.
 
According to official data, the number of voters registered on the electoral rolls stood at 15,801,162.
 
A party needs at least 198 seats for a majority in the House, opening the way for consultations to form a governing majority following the announcement of the results.
 
In the 2021 elections, RNI topped the results with 102 seats, followed by PAM with 86 and Istiqlal with 81.
 
RNI leader Aziz Akhannouch currently heads a coalition government that also includes PAM and Istiqlal.
 
The next government will face political, economic, and social issues, as well as projects related to Morocco’s preparations to co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup.

Taiwan airlines ride AI boom in North American cargo market

04:13:59 UTC

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Demand for AI servers and semiconductor equipment is driving a surge in high-tech air cargo between Asia and North America.
China Airlines expects its cargo revenue to grow about 40% to 50% this year, while EVA Air said large AI equipment is driving demand for charter flights and reserved cargo space, per CNA. Starlux Airlines, which currently relies mainly on passenger aircraft for cargo, is also benefiting from rising high-tech shipments.
The global AI boom and investment in data centers have increased demand for servers, semiconductor equipment, and related components. The shipments are often high-value and time-sensitive, with larger equipment requiring dedicated freighters or reserved cargo capacity, according to CNA.
China Airlines Americas cargo head Lo Pao-jen (羅保仁) said the surge became noticeable after AI infrastructure investment expanded in 2024, per CNA. AI servers and other IT products have become major cargo sources, while semiconductor demand has also increased shipments of related manufacturing equipment from the US, he explained.
Lo said higher fuel costs following the outbreak of fighting in the Middle East in February have been offset by strong AI-related demand, keeping freight rates at reasonable levels. He said China Airlines operates more than 40 freighter flights a week in North America, with the region accounting for more than 60% of its cargo revenue.
EVA Air President Sun Chia-ming (孫嘉明) said in June that AI-related cargo accounted for about 40% to 50% of the airline’s cargo business, while North America generated about 70% of cargo revenue. He added that the company plans to expand its freighter fleet from nine aircraft to 12 by 2028.
Starlux, which has no dedicated freighters yet, has seen cargo revenue rise 41% year on year to NT$713 million (US$22.39 million) in May and NT$672 million in August and has ordered 10 Airbus A350F freighters, with deliveries potentially delayed until 2028.
The surge in air cargo comes as AI demand continues to drive exports. August exports hit a record NT$2.62 trillion, up 41% year on year, with electronic components and information, communications, and audiovisual products among the strongest performers, according to the Ministry of Finance.

Taiwan environment ministry to expand list of hazardous air pollutants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:13:30 UTC
13:13:30 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The Ministry of Environment announced plans Wednesday to add 31 hazardous air pollutants to its regulated list, expanding the number of substances subject to controls to 104.
The amended list includes specialized solvents and chemicals used in precision manufacturing that have mutagenic, reproductively toxic, or highly bioaccumulative properties, according to a press release. On the list is benzo[a]pyrene (BaP), a common carcinogen at the center of a food safety scandal in July.
The ministry said it will establish emission standards for the newly listed pollutants and consider imposing air pollution fees based on their environmental impact.
Existing regulations cover heavy metals such as lead and mercury, as well as certain volatile organic compounds including benzene and trichloroethylene.
To amend the list, the ministry reviewed regulatory lists in the US, Germany, Japan and South Korea, as well as hazard assessments by the WHO, the International Agency for Research on Cancer, and the EU.
The government is seeking to tighten overall air quality rules, with the ministry announcing Monday amendments to the Indoor Air Quality Management Act targeting indoor facilities used by young children and older adults.
Huang Wei-ming (黃偉鳴), director-general of the ministry’s Department of Atmospheric Environment, said the ministry hopes to establish standards for indoor air quality monitoring by the end of the year.
Chou Nan-chun (周南君), chair of the Taiwan Indoor Environment Quality Management Association, said people in Taiwan spend more than 80% of their time indoors and that a science-based management system is critical to addressing risks such as extreme heat and emerging infectious diseases.
Deputy Environment Minister Hsieh Yen-ru (謝燕儒) said Taiwan has a high rate of air-conditioner use, but keeping windows closed while running air conditioning for long periods of time means indoor air quality needs greater attention.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan wrapped up his four-day visit to the US on Wednesday.
Erdogan arrived Sunday in New York to address the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
The president and first lady Emine Erdogan were welcomed at John F. Kennedy International Airport by Türkiye’s Permanent Representative to the UN Ambassador Ahmet Yildiz, Türkiye’s Ambassador to the US Sedat Onal and Türkiye’s Consul General in New York Muhittin Ahmet Yazal.
On Monday, Erdogan met with his Vietnamese counterpart To Lam at the Turkish House, or Turkevi Center, where they addressed bilateral relations as well as regional and global issues.
Welcoming Vietnam’s positive response to Türkiye’s proposal to elevate bilateral relations to the level of a strategic partnership, Erdogan said Ankara is working to further expand cooperation with Vietnam in many fields, particularly in investment, trade and the defense industry.
Erdogan met separately with Mohamed al-Menfi, chairman of the Libyan Presidential Council, at the Turkish House.
Discussing bilateral relations between Türkiye and Libya and regional issues, he stressed that Türkiye continues its efforts to preserve stability in Libya.
Kuwaiti Crown Prince Sheikh Sabah Khaled Al-Hamad Al-Sabah was also among the leaders that Erdogan met Monday at the Turkish House, where they discussed bilateral ties and regional developments.
Erdogan also received Kosovo Prime Minister Albin Kurti at the Turkish House, where the president reaffirmed that Türkiye’s support for Kosovo in attaining its "rightful place" in the international community will continue, adding that Türkiye also supports dialogue among the Balkan countries.
The Turkish president also held a closed-door meeting with Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam at the same venue, saying that Türkiye is making efforts to achieve lasting peace and stability in Lebanon and highlighting the need for an international initiative to supersede the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon. (UNIFIL).
He also met with Georgia's Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze. Bilateral relations as well as regional and global matters were on the agenda, with Erdogan highlighting the importance of sustained solidarity between the two countries at the international level, adding that making the most effective use of the Türkiye-Georgia-Azerbaijan cooperation mechanisms would also benefit the countries.
Erdogan delivered a speech Monday at the “100 Years of Friendship: Türkiye–United States of America” event.
"The conflicts, wars and crises we face in our region and around the world require Türkiye and the United States to maintain close dialogue," he said, adding the two countries are achieving "favorable outcomes" on a number of issues with global implications, particularly in the Middle East as well as in Africa and Asia.
Ankara is determined to sustain and intensify its efforts in the coming period, he added.
"At this point, I would like to emphasize: We can never consider our strategic relationship with the United States separately from our economic and trade ties, nor do we."
Despite global economic and political fluctuations, Erdogan said the bilateral trade volume has doubled over the past 10 years.
"Our bilateral trade, which exceeded $38 billion in 2025, reached $28 billion in the first eight months of this year. It appears that by the end of the year, we will surpass the 2025 figure, reaching $40 billion. I consider the $100 billion trade target we set together with (US) President (Donald) Trump to be highly realistic and achievable."
He also said that Türkiye is ready to further the cooperation with the US in the areas of energy, including nuclear and liquefied natural gas (LNG), civil aviation and advanced technology.
"It is obligatory to advance the defense industry, which is traditionally one of the strongest areas of our partnership, both bilaterally and within NATO," he said.
Erdogan on Tuesday urged countries that have not yet recognized the state of Palestine to review their position.
Addressing the 81st session of the General Assembly, he said Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' absence from the assembly hall was an injustice to Palestinians that "wounds consciences."
"I wish to reiterate that even though Mr. Abbas cannot be present here in person, we will, just as we did last year, continue to serve as the voice of the free and sovereign State of Palestine and to proclaim the struggle of the Palestinian people to the world from this podium.
"Hereby, I once again call upon all countries that have not yet recognized the State of Palestine to reconsider their decision," he said.
Turning to the Gaza Strip, Erdogan said that over the past three years, 74,000 Palestinians have fallen victim to Israel’s "state terrorism."
“Gaza today is not merely the world’s largest graveyard for children. It is also the territory with the highest rate of child amputees in the world. Gaza is the most inhumane and most shameful concentration camp of our time," he stressed.
Erdogan called on countries to "exert greater pressure" on Israel for the reconstruction of Gaza "without delay."
The president also reiterated his call that the UN Security Council must "absolutely" be reformed in accordance with the principle that “the world is bigger than five.”
After his speech, Erdogan met with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres. During the meeting, Erdogan said they have worked closely with Guterres, whose term of office is nearing its end, on a wide range of issues concerning global peace and security.
Erdogan also met with Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. During the meeting, Erdogan said that Israel continues to refrain from taking steps toward peace in Gaza and that it is important for the international community to exert "strong pressure" to hinder Israeli aggression in the region.
The Turkish leader also had his first face-to-face meeting with newly elected UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the UN, where they discussed bilateral relations as well as regional and global issues. Erdogan said that relations between Türkiye and the UK are growing stronger in every field and that he believes cooperation will be further advanced through steps to be taken in many areas, particularly the defense industry and trade.
Erdogan also separately met with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, Poland's President Karol Nawrocki, Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye to discuss bilateral relations as well as regional and global issues.
US President Donald Trump met with Erdogan and the leaders of Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) member states at the UN headquarters.
The meeting was attended by Türkiye along with leaders or foreign ministers from the GCC member states of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman as well as Egypt, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon.
Trump recalled that he had met with countries from the region on the sidelines of the UN a year ago, when they took important steps on Gaza and worked to bring the crisis in the region to an end.
Turning to Erdogan as he spoke about the process, he said: “Exactly one year ago, many of us met here on the sidelines of the United Nations to discuss how we could end the bloody war in Gaza, and almost the same people were here, including my friend right over here from Türkiye. He’s a tough cookie. Don’t mess around with him. He’s a fantastic guy.”
Trump said the leaders gathered around the table had worked hard to stop the bloodshed in Gaza and that those countries were now prepared to make significant contributions to the reconstruction of the enclave.
Later, Erdogan attended a reception Tuesday hosted by Trump in honor of UN General Assembly delegates.
On Wednesday, addressing a meeting with representatives of the Turkish-American business community in New York, Erdogan said: “As we approach the 100th anniversary of our diplomatic relations, our strategic cooperation with the US is developing in all areas.”
Voicing his belief that 2027 will be a stronger year in terms of disinflation, Erdogan drew attention to the highly positive situation in fiscal discipline and added that structural transformation has been placed at the center of the program, since it is efficiency that actually matters.
"We wish to reflect the harmony we have achieved in our political relations, in our economic and trade ties as well. In fact, we possess very significant potential in this regard. Through our joint efforts, we have recently concluded important agreements in energy, aviation and other critical sectors," he said.
Stressing that the US is Türkiye's top LNG supplier, Erdogan said Ankara aims to expand this cooperation to the entire energy field, including nuclear.
Türkiye will host the UN Climate Change Conference, or COP31, in Antalya from Nov. 9-20, with efforts underway to make the summit an event where decisions on climate change are translated into action, Erdogan said Wednesday.
Erdogan made the remarks at a high-level climate meeting convened by Guterres.
“Last year, you will remember, I stated here that Türkiye was bidding to host COP31. This year, we will hold COP31 in Antalya from Nov. 9-20, 2026,” he said.
He said Türkiye is working to ensure that the gathering focuses on implementing decisions taken on climate change.
“Any proposal that fails to align our climate targets with social and economic realities will be doomed to failure. Steps aimed at enhancing countries’ prosperity need to be shaped in accordance with their own circumstances, capabilities and development priorities
"Given the ongoing inequalities in access to financing and technology, it is not realistic to expect all countries to make progress at the same pace. We can make a fair transition permanent to the extent that we manage to cultivate a strong connection between climate targets and development and prosperity."
Erdogan met with his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the Turkish House to discuss bilateral relations, the Russia-Ukraine war and regional developments.
During the meeting, he said that Türkiye is always ready to do its utmost to ensure that the war concludes with a lasting peace and that efforts to revitalize direct negotiations will continue.
Erdogan also stressed the need to take steps to ensure navigational safety in the Black Sea, saying there could be no justification for attacks on commercial vessels.
The president also told Zelenskyy that it is necessary to take steps regarding the safety of navigation in the Black Sea, that attacks on commercial vessels are "unjustifiable," and that Türkiye expects responsible behavior from the parties involved.
Erdogan said that Ankara would continue efforts to strengthen relations with Ukraine, emphasizing that increased cooperation in areas including energy, mining and the defense industry would benefit both countries.
Erdogan and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi agreed Wednesday to deepen security cooperation between Ankara and Baghdad at their meeting in New York.
"In this context, they agreed to fully restore state authority in Sinjar and eliminate the presence of illegal foreign armed elements. In light of the progress achieved by these security measures implemented by Iraq, Turkish forces will gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zilkan base to the Federal Government of Iraq in accordance with the agreed mechanism and timetable," said a joint statement.
The parties also reached a consensus on expanding bilateral trade and investment, ensuring the immediate implementation of the agreements signed, and accelerating joint strategic projects, particularly the Development Road Project.
Separately, Erdogan also received Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan at the Turkish House, where they addressed contacts between Türkiye and Armenia as well as regional and global issues.
Stating that Türkiye supports the normalization process with Armenia in the areas of bilateral trade and transportation, Erdogan emphasized the importance of maintaining the positive momentum in bilateral relations. The president expressed Türkiye’s satisfaction with the reciprocal steps that Azerbaijan and Armenia are taking in the peace process.
Addressing a gathering of Turks and brotherly communities in New York on Wednesday, Erdogan said that Muslims should be allowed to integrate into the societies where they live without being expected to abandon their language, culture or roots.
“Unfortunately, there are problems in many parts of the world, particularly in Europe. Muslims are expected not to integrate but to assimilate. We say ‘yes’ to integration and ‘no’ to every form of assimilation,” Erdogan said.
He called for stronger representation of Turkish Americans in politics, business, academia, culture and the arts, saying individual achievements should develop into strong institutions and lasting structures that can be passed from one generation to another.
Erdogan said stronger communities can help combat anti-Muslim sentiment, xenophobia and discrimination.
The president also addressed the upcoming US midterm elections, urging citizens to exercise their democratic rights and make their voices heard.
“I call on all our citizens to exercise their democratic rights in the upcoming midterm elections. It is very, very important that you reflect your will at the ballot box at the highest level,” he said.

WATCH Catholic priests and nuns make Gaza ‘genocide’ march to Vatican
Around 150 Catholic priests, bishops, friars, and nuns have marched to the Vatican as part of a procession through Rome demanding an end to what they describe as Israel’s “genocide” in Gaza.
The group stopped near St. Peter’s Square before continuing to the Palestinian and Lebanese embassies and ending outside the headquarters of Italian arms manufacturer Leonardo.
Participants carried olive branches and posters depicting the Madonna holding an emaciated child with the words “Christ Died in Gaza.” They also carried a large white banner bearing the names of hundreds of Palestinian and Lebanese children killed in Israeli airstrikes.
Outside Leonardo, which has supplied weapons and military equipment to Israel, Italian Archbishop Franco Moscone called for international arrest warrants targeting arms-industry executives. Moscone has previously compared Israel’s conduct in Gaza to Nazi methods and urged European countries to consider withdrawing recognition of Israel.
Tuesday’s event was organized by Priests Against Genocide, an international Catholic network established last year. The group said clergy from eight countries took part, including South Africa, England, Ireland, Germany, the US, and Spain.
The network has taken a more categorical position than the Holy See. The late Pope Francis called for an investigation into whether Israel’s actions in Gaza met the legal definition of genocide, while his successor, Leo XIV, has said the Vatican is not prepared to make such a determination.
A UN commission of inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, citing killings, serious bodily and mental harm, deliberately destructive living conditions, and measures intended to prevent births. A separate case brought by South Africa remains before the International Court of Justice, which has yet to issue a final judgment.
Israel strongly rejects the genocide allegation, saying it targets militants and seeks to minimize civilian casualties while accusing Hamas of operating in densely populated areas.
Israel launched its offensive in Gaza following the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, which killed around 1,200 Israelis, mostly civilians. Gaza health authorities say more than 73,000 Palestinians have since been killed, nearly half of them women and children.

China is holding sensitive F-35 parts diverted to Hong Kong: Sources
- China has taken possession of sensitive F-35 stealth aircraft parts diverted to Hong Kong during shipment from Australia to the US, raising security concerns amid a high-profile state visit.
- The parts, coated with radar-absorbing material and supplied by Lockheed Martin, were unexpectedly rerouted via South Korea and Hong Kong; the reasons for diversion remain unclear.
- US authorities and Congress are investigating the incident, with the Pentagon working to retrieve the parts and prevent future occurrences, highlighting espionage risks and geopolitical tensions.
AI generated
WASHINGTON/HONG KONG – The Chinese government has taken possession of potentially sensitive F-35 stealth aircraft parts that were inexplicably diverted to Hong Kong while being sent to the US from Australia, people briefed on the incident said.
UPS was shipping a cockpit canopy and weapons-bay door from an Australian military F-35 that was being sent to the US for inspection and possible repair or disposal in late May, according to the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private matters.
Both parts, supplied by Lockheed Martin, were coated with radar-absorbing material that enhances their stealth capabilities, two of the people said.
The plane stopped in South Korea en route to the US and from there, it was routed to Hong Kong, said one of the sources.
It is not clear why the plane stopped in South Korea or why it was diverted to Hong Kong, or whether the parts were intentionally diverted or by mistake.
The Chinese government later took possession of the parts but so far has not returned them, two of the people said.
A Chinese embassy spokesman declined immediate comment on Sept 24.
Disclosure of the incident comes at a politically sensitive time for the two countries, with Chinese President Xi Jinping arriving in the US on the evening of Sept 23 for a state visit hosted by President Donald Trump.
At least two congressional committees are investigating how the parts fell into Chinese hands.
China’s possession of the parts, the stop in South Korea and the fact that UPS was used to transport them had not been previously reported.
Politico reported earlier that the parts had been unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong.
“The juxtaposition is hard to miss,” Senator Elissa Slotkin, a Michigan Democrat, said on Bloomberg Television. “The Chinese are holding some of our most sensitive technology and we are rolling out the red carpet for their president.”
Slotkin said she had not received a briefing on the issue.
“When it comes to intelligence and military issues, China is a competitor and an adversary. They are always seeking information about our military equipment; sensitive information.”
China has for years targeted the F-35 in its espionage efforts.
Concerns that China could learn valuable intelligence about the jet were one reason why a US bid to sell F-35s to the United Arab Emirates, announced in Trump’s first term, later collapsed.
Members of Congress have also raised concerns that plans to sell the F-35 to Saudi Arabia could risk exposing cutting-edge US military technology to China.
The Pentagon said it was working to retrieve the parts.
Officials are aware of “a shipment issue of unserviceable F-35 components”, a statement from the Pentagon said.
“We are actively working with US authorities and industry partners to retrieve these components, investigate the incident and place safeguards to avoid a future occurrence.”
The F-35 is one of the world’s most advanced fighter jets and some 20 countries have purchased the aircraft, including South Korea, Japan, Singapore and Australia. It has flown numerous missions against Iran.
Australia is the Indo-Pacific inventory hub for parts and maintenance of F-35s flown by allies in Asia.
“It’s always best when your adversaries have to guess at your capabilities,” said J.J. Gertler, a former aviation analyst for the Congressional Research Service who is now director of The Defence Concepts Organization. “You never want to hand them evidence.”
UPS disclosed the incident to the State Department’s Directorate of Defence Trade Controls, which enforces export control laws, out of an abundance of caution.
Company spokesman Malcolm Berkley declined to comment.
Australian Defence Minister Richard Marles told reporters on Sept 22 that his country is examining “everything that has occurred at the Australian end”. “The point I would make here is that we are confident about the way in which we’ve engaged with the programme and through the US’ prime contractor, Lockheed.”
Lockheed Martin said in a statement that the US Department of Defense picked the transportation options and “we select the carrier that aligns with those government-mandated parameters”.
Lockheed Martin did not disclose which carrier shipped the parts but said the company is working closely with it “to develop and implement preventive measures to strengthen our collective oversight and prevent recurrence”.
During a closed Senate Armed Services Committee F-35 hearing on June 23, Defense Department officials expressed their hope that the components would be returned, according to people familiar with the exchange.
The diversion is being reviewed by two House congressional panels – House Foreign Affairs and Armed Services. Armed Services Committee spokesperson Heather Vaughan said the “committee is aware of this issue and we’ve received multiple briefings on it”.
The Senate Armed Services air-land sub-committee also “is aware of the reports and is currently looking into the matter”, said spokesman Dave Vasquez. BLOOMBERG

Building reuse defines shortlist for Scotland's best building

Building reuse defines shortlist for Scotland's best building
The conversion of a Victorian hospital is one of three reuse projects that make up the shortlist for the 2026 RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland award.
Designed by Bennetts Associates, the former hospital building now houses a mix of teaching spaces for the University of Edinburgh, including a 450-seat auditorium.
It is vying for the title of Scotland's best new building alongside a restored pool pavilion in Aberdeenshire by Studio Octopi and a public library housed in a dilapidated building in Paisley by Collective Architecture.
The Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) has awarded the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award annually since 2002.
RIAS said this year's shortlist represents "imaginative reuse and restoration of existing, historic buildings, demonstrating how architects can bring new life to existing buildings and places through a thoughtful, sustainable and inclusive approach to design".
"All three tap into important, current conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse across three very different contexts," said RIAS president Libby Heathcote.
Located in the Scottish capital, the Edinburgh Futures Institute by Bennetts Associates houses teaching and social facilities for the University of Edinburgh within a Category A-listed Victorian hospital.
The jury said it was shortlisted in recognition of how its architect "preserved the integrity of the historic building yet created a modern, welcoming, clever, and stimulating place that people want to work in and return to".
The Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture was selected for demonstrating "how underused high street buildings can be revitalised into inspirational spaces for learning and connection".
It involved converting a dilapidated building in Paisley's town centre into a welcoming community space that feels both contemporary and a part of the urban fabric.
The final project is the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion – an existing Art Deco structure in Aberdeenshire faithfully restored by Studio Octopi.
It was designed as part of a wider project focused on breathing life back into the outdoor pools and hailed by the jury for showing how "sensitive design can revive a historic site while embracing contemporary use”.
This year's jury for the 2026 RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland award consisted of president Heathcote alongside Purcell chairman Elizabeth Smith and The Business editor Kenny Kemp.
The winner will be announced on 26 November. In the lead-up to the event, RIAS is hosting a live discussion on 8 October with the three shortlisted practices for "a deeper look at the projects that are in the running".
Last year's award was given to John McAslan + Partners for its restoration of the Burrell Collection museum in Glasgow.
Previous winners include a remote house by Ann Nisbet Studio and a small office and cafe by Moxon Architects.

Outgoing UN chief makes final climate push at New York summit

Outgoing UN chief makes final climate push at New York summit
- Outgoing UN chief Antonio Guterres called renewable energy "unstoppable" and urged countries to set clear plans to quit fossil fuels, highlighting the urgent need to cut emissions and avoid climate catastrophe.
- Germany issued a road map to quit fossil fuels, joining France and the Netherlands, while global leaders at the summit discussed balancing climate goals with economic and social realities ahead of COP31.
- Guterres stressed increasing climate financing for developing countries and expanding early warning systems by 2027, with a focus on electrification and climate justice for vulnerable nations like Nepal.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Outgoing UN chief Antonio Guterres on Sept 23 hailed the “unstoppable” rise of renewable energy and urged countries to develop firm plans to quit fossil fuels in his final climate meeting at the world organisation’s New York headquarters.
Speaking a day after denouncing “Big Oil” for treating the atmosphere like an “open sewer”, the 77-year-old secretary-general used his opening speech to sound a note of hope.
“Renewables are the cheapest, fastest and most secure source of new electricity almost everywhere,” he said. “Clean energy has gone from alternative to unstoppable.”
He called on countries to lift their emissions-cutting targets and release concrete plans to quit fossil fuels – a cause given a boost by Germany, Europe’s biggest economy, which issued its road map hours before Guterres’ swansong address as a summit convener.
Germany is the third country to do so, after France and the Netherlands.
“We are the first generation with the tools to end the fossil fuel age – and the last who can avert climate catastrophe,” Guterres concluded.
He made climate change a defining issue of his nine-year tenure, which ends on Dec 31, and was hailed by Rachel Cleetus from the non-profit Union of Concerned Scientists as “an extraordinary climate champion” for consistently elevating the voices of the most vulnerable.
The stakes are clearer than ever as the impacts of climate change surge around the world – from heatwaves and wildfires in Europe to catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet triggered by a glacier collapse.
Extreme weather events are set to worsen, with a strengthening El Nino cycle that has already tied a record for intensity months from its peak.
And the world is set to shoot past – at least temporarily – 1.5 deg C of warming. Scientists say temperature increases above that level will bring on worse climate-linked catastrophes.
Turkey tempers expectations
Guterres’ remarks at the summit, called the High-level Event on Climate Action and the Just Transition, were followed by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
The two countries are co-hosting COP31 climate talks in Antalya in November in an unusual arrangement, with Australia running the talks but Turkey holding the event and rallying support for voluntary pledges.
“Action is not optional,” said Albanese, touting the fact that during the height of the last Australian summer, half of the power for the grid came from renewables.
Yet, his climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, is travelling to India and Saudi Arabia this week for talks on strengthening Australia’s oil supplies.
Erdogan followed and appeared to temper expectations about the degree of ambition at COP31.
“Any proposal that fails to reconcile our climate objectives with social and economic realities will be doomed to fail,” he said.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband pledged an investment of £330 million (S$559 million) in the Global Environment Facility, a financial mechanism to support global goals for nature, climate and pollution.
“It’s a little disappointing that there weren’t more commitments and more announcements here,” Cosima Cassel from climate change think-tank E3G told AFP, though she praised Germany’s road map.
Emissions cuts, financing, electrification
Guterres asked leaders to accelerate the greening of their economies and mobilise climate financing for developing countries, and said life-saving early warning systems must extend to every person on earth by 2027.
Momentum is also gathering for electrification: switching combustion-based systems, like in heating and vehicles, to electricity.
Turkey has advanced a “35x35” target to increase electricity’s share of global energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035. However, it has not specified that the electricity should be generated by renewables, which are key to tackling climate change.
Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal of Nepal, where more than 1,400 have died and thousands more remain missing after a devastating Aug 26 flood, said “such tragedies are not isolated events; they are symptoms of global crisis, a crisis Nepal did not create”.
“At this point, we’re asking for what we call climate justice,” he said. AFP

Spiraling Up: 6 Projects Using Spiral Ramps for Vertical Movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

In most architectural projects, vertical circulation is expressed as a purely functional element, tucked away behind fire-rated doors or an elevator core. However, sometimes architects also use spirals when trying to resolve site elevation changes. Given the right scale, these elements allow for a more artistic formal expression that serves both utilitarian and aesthetic purposes without relying on mechanical lifts or stairwells. Structural systems like cantilevered steel trusses and reinforced concrete decks allow these spiral elements to extend outward as sheltered entry canopies or wind around open central atriums. Functionally, these circulation paths may be expressed in several ways: as stairs like the Itamaraty Palace in Brasilia, or as ramps, which can offer the possibility to reduce mobility barriers for visitors. In both cases, the spiral can provide smooth transitions across varied floor levels while maintaining an unobstructed line-of-sight throughout the program.
In this curated collection, we explore how architects adopt the spiral geometry primarily to solve complex circulation and site transition challenges without resorting to abrupt vertical stair cores or mechanical lifts. In some of the projects that involve large public and commercial interventions, the spiral continuous ramp operates with an accessibility-compliant slope that bridges significant elevation changes while maintaining fluid movement. In other projects, these spiral ramps project outward into the urban landscape, turning an exterior entry threshold into an architectural promenade that also contributes to the overall formal expression of the building. Finally, for some projects, the spiral ramp forms the building itself, becoming not just the circulation space but also part of the functional interior spaces within the program.

- The inquest found turbulence caused cardiac failure, clarifying initial reports of congestive heart failure.
- Kitchen’s wife sued SIA for damages due to her injuries, while investigations noted pilots acted appropriately and weather radar missed the turbulence threat.
AI generated
A British man who died on board turbulence-hit Singapore Airlines (SIA) Flight SQ321 in 2024 had suffered a cardiac arrest, an inquest was told, reported British media. He was earlier said to have died of congestive heart failure.
Geoff Kitchen, 73, was the only fatality in the incident, which occurred as the Singapore-bound flight from London’s Heathrow Airport flew over south-west Myanmar on May 21, 2024. The incident left 72 passengers injured, including Kitchen’s wife Linda, who had spinal fractures.
At an inquest at Avon Coroners’ Court on the afternoon of Sept 23, the court’s assistant coroner, Peter Harrowing, was quoted by The Independent as saying: “At first blush, one might consider natural causes being an appropriate cause of death. That does not take account of the events that occurred of the severe turbulence to which Geoff was subjected.
“I shall record that Geoffrey Kitchen died of cardiac failure as a result of the aircraft for which he was a passenger encountering severe turbulence.”
An initial post-mortem examination held in Thailand, where the plane had been diverted for an emergency landing, found that Kitchen, a retired insurance professional, had died of congestive heart failure.
While Kitchen had undergone an operation to fit stents to his right coronary artery in April 2019, his doctor said a review in October that year found he had returned to “normal exercise capacity”.
The Independent also quoted Harrowing as saying that Kitchen was found not to be experiencing any problems, following a review in 2023 for ischaemic heart disease.
Edward Sheffield, who performed an additional post-mortem examination in Bristol, gave Kitchen’s cause of death as cardiac failure due to coronary artery atheroma and the physiological effects of turbulence.
According to the BBC, he told the inquest on Sept 23: “I am satisfied that it was the physiological effect of the aircraft turbulence which precipitated the cardiac arrest and ultimately, Geoff’s demise.”
When contacted, SIA said it is unable to comment on matters before the court.
The inquest also heard a statement by Kitchen’s wife, 74, who said Kitchen had pressed her to the side during the incident, which caused injury to her back. She also had a head wound, which was “bleeding profusely”.
She said Kitchen fell onto her lap before passengers helped move him back into his chair, where his head “flopped forward”. She was later moved across the aisle to be treated for the head wound while cardiopulmonary resuscitation was carried out on her husband.
She was taken to intensive care in Bangkok before she was airlifted after 10 days back to Bristol, where she spent another week in hospital.
The BBC reported in August that she was suing SIA for damages to help her access specialist support for her broken back.
Anthe Korelidou, a specialist aviation lawyer representing Kitchen, said: “While it’s more than two years since Geoff’s death, Linda and the rest of her family continue to have a number of questions and concerns about what happened and if more could have been done to prevent their injuries.
“All Linda wants is for the most thorough investigations to be conducted. The issuing of High Court proceedings is a major milestone in being able to provide Geoff’s loved ones with the answers they deserve.”
According to the BBC, the couple had flown out of Heathrow for a six-week holiday to Singapore, Indonesia and Australia.
The Transport Safety Investigation Bureau, in its final report detailing its investigation findings, said on May 19 that inclement weather had not been detected by the weather radar on board.
The pilots did not observe any clouds in their immediate flight path prior to the incident either, and the bureau noted that their actions were “understandable and appropriate for the situation”.

More REM sleep linked to lower risk of 83 diseases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
03:58:30 UTC
12:58:30 KST

More REM sleep linked to lower risk of 83 diseases
Tracking sleep in more than 95,000 people revealed striking links between sleep patterns and long-term health.
- Date:
- September 23, 2026
- Source:
- PLOS
- Summary:
- A large study tracking more than 95,000 people suggests that how you sleep may be linked to your risk of developing dozens of diseases. People who spent more time in REM sleep had lower risks of 83 conditions, including dementia, heart failure, and Parkinson’s disease, while more deep sleep was associated with lower risks of conditions such as type 2 diabetes and major depression.
- Share:
Greater amounts of REM and deep sleep were associated with lower risks of dozens of diseases, and less than 5 hours of total sleep was associated with high risks of disease, according to a new study published September 17th in the open access journal PLOS Medicine by Shengzhi Sun of Capital Medical University, China, and colleagues.
Sleep quantity and quality is a priority of China’s National Health Commission and a focus in China more broadly. The most recent 2026 China Sleep Health White Paper finds that while the average surveyed Chinese person sleeps 6.97 hours per night, 23 percent sleep less than 6 hours per night. The same report notes that only 26 percent of respondents reported a consistent sleep schedule, and that disturbances to sleep have increased over time. Understanding how sleep patterns are linked to disease risk is therefore of great relevance to Chinese citizens.
There remains limited understanding of how sleep stages and other real-world sleep patterns relate to health outcomes. In part, that is because self-reported sleep measures often show poor correlation with objective assessments, making it difficult to capture real-world sleep patterns.
In the new study, researchers analyzed data from 95,559 UK Biobank participants who wore wrist accelerometers for seven consecutive days and nights. The researchers used a deep-learning algorithm to calculate sleep stages (REM, deep, and light sleep), total sleep duration, wakefulness after sleep onset, and night-to-night sleep irregularity. Participants were followed for a median of 8.9 years, and health records were available to test for associations with more than 1,000 disease outcomes.
Greater REM sleep (per interquartile range, 47.6 minutes) was associated with a lower risk of 83 diseases, including heart failure (hazard ratio 0.74), dementia (hazard ratio 0.54), and Parkinson’s disease (hazard ratio 0.20), while greater deep sleep was linked to lower risk of 7 conditions, including type 2 diabetes and major depressive disorder. Greater sleep irregularity and wakefulness after sleep onset were each linked to higher risk of several conditions, including anxiety and substance use disorders. Total sleep duration showed a non-linear relationship with disease risk for many conditions, with the lowest risk concentrated in a 6-to-8-hour window; people sleeping less than 5 hours faced the most elevated clinical vulnerability, with an increased risk of 37 conditions. However, as an observational study, this research cannot establish that sleep patterns directly cause disease risk.
“The findings provide additional evidence supporting the role of a 6-8 hours’ sleep duration as a health safeguard for middle-aged and older adults, likely attributable to more favorable distributions of sleep stages,” the authors say. “Maintaining a sleep duration of 6-8 hours can effectively reduce the risk of multiple diseases, providing new insights for health promotion and preventive practice.”
The authors add, “Phenome-wide association analysis identified 156 significant associations between sleep patterns and incident diseases after Bonferroni correction.”
“Sleep duration exhibited significant non-linear associations with 86 disease phenotypes, with the minimum-risk duration for the majority of these conditions (69 phenotypes) precisely concentrated within a 6-8 hour window.”
This work was supported by the National Science Fund for Distinguished Young Scholars (82025031 to RC), the Key Program of the National Natural Science Foundation of China (82230109 to RC), the Beijing Outstanding Young Scientist Program (JWZQ20240101024 to RC), and the Young Beijing Scholars Project, the Chinese Institutes for Medical Research, Beijing (CX23YZ01 to RC). The funders had no role in study design, data collection and analysis, decision to publish, or preparation of the manuscript.
Story Source:
Materials provided by PLOS. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Jingsong Luo, Ruiyi Liu, Jie Yin, Wangnan Cao, Shengzhi Sun, Rui Chen. Accelerometer-derived real-world sleep stages and risk of incident diseases: A UK Biobank cohort study and phenome-wide association analysis. PLOS Medicine, 2026; 23 (9): e1005213 DOI: 10.1371/journal.pmed.1005213

Last week, Trump signed the bill called "Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026," named after deceased South Carolina Republican US Senator Lindsey Graham.
The bill passed by the US Congress paved the way for increased economic pressure on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine that began in early 2022.
Rubio and Jaishankar "discussed sanctions that could be leveled against states that engage economically with Russia and Iran," the State Department said in a statement after their meeting in New York.
Jaishankar wrote on X he "reiterated India's interests and concerns with regard to SRIA."
India has previously told Washington that new measures to levy tariffs over the purchase of Russian oil could impact bilateral ties.
The bill requires Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods imported into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas as well as any country that knowingly made new purchases of oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.
India is among the biggest buyers of Russian oil. After Russia invaded Ukraine, India sharply increased purchases of discounted Russian crude. The stepped-up purchases were partly the reason Trump imposed tariffs of as much as 50% on Indian goods in August 2025, among the steepest levied on any country.
In February, Trump rolled back those duties, citing what he said was India's commitment to halt Russian oil purchases. But New Delhi only briefly reduced purchases from Russia in early 2026. They have since jumped, especially since the supply shock that followed the US-Israeli war on Iran.
India says its large population and growing economy need affordable energy supplies. Indian analysts say India's purchases of Russian oil were not financing the war on Ukraine but helping stabilize global supplies and keeping domestic prices in check. REUTERS

China's FAST telescope discovers over 1,300 pulsars in decade of operation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
11:52:25 CST
12:52:25 KST

GUIYANG, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST) has identified more than 1,300 pulsars over the past decade, outnumbering the total pulsar discoveries made by all other international telescopes over the same period, according to an academic conference that opened on Wednesday.
Set to mark its 10th anniversary on Friday, FAST has driven a historic leap for China's radio astronomy over the past decade. Boasting enhanced observational capabilities, the telescope, located in southwest China's Guizhou Province, has continuously expanded humanity's understanding of the universe.
"Ten years of dedicated work has secured China's leading position in global radio astronomy," said FAST chief engineer Jiang Peng, also deputy director of the National Astronomical Observatories of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Noting that FAST has steadily fulfilled the goal of yielding early, abundant and high-quality scientific outcomes, Jiang said the telescope is striving to produce landmark major achievements.
FAST has made fruitful breakthroughs in engineering technology, frontier scientific research and practical application. Technological innovations including upgraded measurement and control systems, domestically manufactured steel cables and high-performance receivers have guaranteed the telescope's stable and efficient operation.
As one of the world's most vital astronomical observation facilities, FAST has achieved a series of internationally influential findings in key research fields covering pulsars, neutral hydrogen galaxies, fast radio bursts and gravitational waves.
Based on FAST's observational results, researchers have published 13 papers in top-tier journals Science and Nature. Its key achievements have been twice listed among Science's Top 10 scientific breakthroughs, once among Nature's Top 10 scientific discoveries, and ten times among China's Top 10 scientific and technological advances. ■
