US Democrat senator urges Trump to press Xi over China-Iran ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:51:22 UTC
07:51:22 KST

Breadcrumb
US Democratic senator urges Trump to press Xi over China-Iran ties
US Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen urged President Donald Trump on Wednesday to press Chinese President Xi Jinping over Beijing's support for Iran, accusing Chinese companies of providing Tehran with economic and military assistance.
The senior Democrat said Trump should use an upcoming summit with Xi to demand action against Chinese firms accused of supplying Iran with satellite imagery and components used in its missile and drone programmes, as well as helping Tehran circumvent sanctions on its oil exports.
Speaking in the Senate, Shaheen cited reports that Iran obtained high-resolution satellite imagery of a US base in Jordan from Chinese entities before carrying out a missile attack that killed three American soldiers and wounded four others.
She also pointed to China's role as the leading buyer of Iranian oil, saying around 90% of Iran's oil exports go to the country, providing Tehran with billions of dollars in revenue and a "critical economic lifeline".
Chinese and Hong Kong-based companies have also supplied components used in Iranian ballistic missiles and drones, Shaheen said.
"If we want to bring this war to an end, we need to cut off the outside support that allows Iran to keep fighting, and that starts with China," she told the Senate.
Shaheen called on Trump to "use his leverage" with Xi to stop Chinese companies from providing satellite imagery, missile and drone components and access to markets for sanctioned Iranian oil.
She also urged the Trump administration to step up enforcement of existing sanctions against Chinese entities accused of helping Iran.
"And if China doesn't stop, Congress should impose additional consequences," she said.
Shaheen linked China's relationship with Iran to its continued purchases of Russian energy, arguing that Beijing was helping finance conflicts involving both Tehran and Moscow, despite the US, alongside Israel, starting the war on Iran.
She said Trump should consider using powers contained in recently enacted legislation targeting Russia to impose penalties on Chinese buyers of Russian energy.
China was "the top funder of the war in Ukraine, as well as being one of the top funders of the war in Iran", Shaheen said.
Shaheen's call for tougher pressure on China comes despite broad public opposition to the US war with Iran, particularly among Democrats.
A Pew Research Center poll conducted in March found 59% of Americans believed the US had made the wrong decision in using military force against Iran, while 61% disapproved of Trump's handling of the conflict.
Opposition was especially strong among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, 88% of whom said the decision to use force was wrong and 90% of whom disapproved of Trump's handling of the war.
More recent Reuters/Ipsos polling has also found support for Trump's handling of the conflict remains weak, with only 34% approving of his strikes on Iran.

Live updates: Trump welcomes Xi to Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:49:00 UTC
07:49:00 KST

Trump and Xi hold US-China talks in Oval Office
Published September 24, 2026last updated September 24, 2026
What you need to know
- Donald Trump welcomed his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, to the White House
- This is Xi's first state visit to the US in a decade
- Trade, AI, Taiwan, Ukraine and Iran are key issues to be discussed
Follow along here for live updates on Xi's state visit to the US:
Melania Trump, Madame Peng head to Asian art museum
First Lady Melania Trump and Xi's wife Peng Liyuan left their husbands behind to tour one of the largest Asian art museums in the US.
The visit to the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art in Washington was supposed to celebrate cultural ties between the US and China.
Both wives are known for their focus on soft power and cultural issues, one is a former fashion model and the other a soprano.
A choir of young school children from the Hope Chinese School sang to the duo as they toured the building, singing famous Chinese folk songs including "Song and Smile" and "Jasmine Flower."
It's the first public meeting between the two spouses in nearly a decade, since a 2017 encounter in Beijing. A crowd had gathered on the sidewalk across from the museum, some waving Chinese and American flags.
Trump says the pair had a 'great meeting,' takes Xi inside presidential helicopter
Trump's first comments to reporters after the talks were brief in the extreme.
In response to shouted questions as he took Xi to board the Marine One presidential helicopter for a brief tour, he told reporters, "We had a great meeting."
Images from the meeting showed that Chinese Vice Premier Hi Lifeng and Foreign Minister Wang Yi attended at least part of the talks, as did US Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Xi left the White House after the meeting, but will be back later for the state dinner.
Xi tells Trump China's position on Taiwan and territory is 'crystal clear'
China's Xinhua news agency is reporting comments it says Xi Jinping relayed to Donald Trump during their talks in the Oval Office.
Xi said he hoped the United States would continue to oppose "Taiwan independence" and handle the question of Taiwan with "prudence," according to Xinhua.
He reportedly told the US president that China's position on safeguarding its national unity and territorial integrity was "crystal clear."
The US holds a complicated position when it comes to Taiwan. On the one hand, it is the small island nation's most important security guarantor. However, it has no formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan and does not recognize it as an independent country as part of its adherence to the so-called "one China" principle Beijing insists upon from all partners.
Xi also reportedly told Trump that China would support the US and Iran returning to negotiations "as soon as possible" as their naval standoff in the Persian Gulf drags well past the six-month mark.
WATCH: How US, China could end the AI race
As concerns grow over the rapid advance of artificial intelligence, experts are warning that the global race between the United States and China to develop ever more powerful AI systems could outpace safety measures.
DW explores fears over cybersecurity threats, autonomous AI behavior and even bioterrorism, while explaining why both Washington and Beijing see AI as a strategic priority.
With calls mounting for international oversight, what stance will US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping adopt?
CNN, MS NOW, Politico journalists are back at White House
Hours after a federal judge ordered Trump to lift the ban, US news outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico announced that they had been granted access to the White House.
Trump and Xi begin talks in Oval Office
After delivering their opening remarks and reviewing the military troops in the Rose Garden, Trump and Xi proceeded to the Oval Office for discussions.
Other US and Chinese officials joined them.
China to send two pandas to Atlanta zoo, Xi says
Speaking at the White House, Xi Jinping announced that a pair of pandas will soon make their home at Zoo Atlanta.
This isn't the first time Chinese pandas have been sent to a U.S. zoo. It's also an example of what's known as "panda diplomacy." Through this program, China lends the animals to select zoos around the world.
Xi also revealed that Beijing plans to invite 100,000 young Americans to visit China for cultural exchange and study over the next five years.
Xi thanks Trump for 'warm hospitality,' seeks to 'expand cooperation'
China's President Xi Jinping in turn thanked Donald Trump for his "warm hospitality," after the US president last night went to greet the Chinese leader and their wife on the tarmac at the airfeld.
In his opening remarks, as rendered by his interpreter, Xi said he was visiting the US to "carry on our friendship, expand cooperation and promote well-being of both our peoples."
He said that both the US and China were great countries with great people.
"I'm very glad to pay a state visit to your beautiful country, the United States of America," Xi said. "Thank you President Trump and Mrs. Trump for the warm hospitality that you have extended to me and my wife."
Trump touts 'truly great friendship' with China's Xi, seeks more 'balanced' trade relationship
The US president told reporters he was "proud" of the US-China relationship.
"From the time of my first election in 2016, President Xi and I have forged a friendship, a truly great friendship, actually, built on mutual respect and the vital interests of our people," Trump said.
He said that he and Xi would continue working together for a better future, while also hailing the "tremendous strides" he said had been made on issues facing the two countries.
Trump said that security, technology and artificial intelligence were likely to feature in Thursday's talks.
He said that US and Chinese officials were working to encourage a "more balanced" trading relationship between the two countries, including new market access for American farmers and ranchers.
Famously, Donald Trump tends to define "balance" in trade as not having an import surplus or trade deficit with a trading partner — a goal that can be particularly ambitious, bordering on impossible, when doing business with export giant China.
Why is AI regulation in such sharp focus amid the visit?
With frozen tariff talks and moving deadlines, continued tensions over Taiwan and the Pacific region more generally, war in Iran, Ukraine, and much of Africa, you'd be forgiven for thinking that questions of hardware, software, bits and bytes would be far from the minds of the world's two most powerful politicians.
However, more and more examples of AI agents bending or breaking the rules they were given — coupled with increasing concern from the very people developing the models — have thrust the issue to the forefront of the public eye.
At the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, various AI executives urged the UN Security Council and international governments to address some of the dangers concerning the technology.
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said there was a risk "we could lose control of the future to AI," because of its ability to move at such a rapid pace making human oversight difficult or impossible. He also said the systems could "concentrate too much power in too few hands."
Anthropic's boss Dario Amodei called for global standards for testing new AI models.
Compounding this, early on Thursday, Australia's Prime Minister Antony Albanese said that an Open AI agent had hacked Australia's public health data portal in June. It's the first known instance of AI hacking a government system, which is not necessarily to say it is the first.
OpenAI said in response that its models "took actions we did not intend," in by no means the first case of its kind.
The US and China are seen as the two leading AI-developing nations, and have broadly advocated more of a hands-off approach to regulation than countries with less financial incentive to have tech companies on a long leash.
Trump, First Lady welcome Xi, Madame Peng at White House
China's President Xi Jinping and his wife have arrived at the White House to begin Thursday's talks.
They were greeted by US President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump outside the South Portico of the White House late on Thursday morning.
Trump, Xi set for talks and a state dinner on Thursday
Welcome back as police and security staff in Washington gear up for an even higher-profile day than usual on Thursday.
Talks between leaders of the US and China on Thursday are set to culminate in a state dinner at the White House this evening, attended by various tech executives.
US President Donald Trump told his online acolytes that a "big day with President Xi of China" beckoned in his first social media utterance on Thursday.
He said that artificial intelligence or machine learning would "be a big topic of discussion."
But, mirroring his comments at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he wanted to "leave it exactly where it is."
He said that the US' "guardrail" for AI was its own Department of Justice, implying little interest in international or cooperative efforts to guard against any potential risks.
"That is China's position also," Trump asserted, though Xi Jinping is expected to deliver remarks of his own later.
Meanwhile, early morning reports from Washington suggest the White House was yet to react to the overnight court order demanding that it allow reporters from CNN, MSNOW and Politico back into the building, at least temporarily pending closer evalution of the case.
We're pausing our coverage for now
The main summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping is scheduled for Thursday.
There's a state dinner as well in the evening, with both leaders expected to deliver speeches.
Top US tech executives are expected to attend the dinner, suggesting that artificial intelligence will be a big topic of discussion.
China, US should be 'partners rather than rivals' — Xi
Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for cooperation with the US, Beijing's state news agency Xinhua reported.
"Our two countries should be partners rather than rivals," Xi said in a written statement published by Xinhua.
"The Chinese and US peoples have enjoyed long-standing friendly exchanges, and our interests are deeply intertwined," Xi added.
Xi was welcomed in Washington with a red carpet and military flyover.
In remarks published by Xinhua, Xi also said he looked forward to "in-depth exchanges" with Trump on "major issues concerning our bilateral relations and the global situation."
Trump wants Hong Kong's Jimmy Lai to be freed from prison — report
Chinese President Xi Jinping has arrived in Washington to a rare planeside welcome from his US counterpart, Donald Trump.
As Xi walked down a long red carpet on the airport tarmac, a White House spokesperson said that Trump believes Hong Kongdemocracy advocate Jimmy Lai should be released from prison and "wants to see that happen," the DPA news agency reported.
"The United States urges the authorities to grant Mr. Lai humanitarian parole," DPA quoted the spokesperson as saying.
Lai, a 78-year-old media tycoon, was sentenced to 20 years in prison earlier in the year under the National Security Law that China imposed in 2020 following massive pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong.
At a congressional hearing in Washington last week, Lai's son, Sebastien, repeated his appeal for his father's release.
Trump raised the issue of Lai's release when he met Xi in Beijing in May, but the US leader said the Chinese president told him Lai's case "would be a tough one."
On Tuesday, US outlet Politico reported that British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has asked Trump to discuss the release of Lai, who is a British citizen, with Xi.

Compounding this, early on Thursday, Australia's Prime Minister Antony Albanese said that an Open AI agent had hacked Australia's public health data portal in June. It's the first known instance of AI hacking a government system, which is not necessarily to say it is the first.
OpenAI said in response that its models "took actions we did not intend," in by no means the first case of its kind.
The US and China are seen as the two leading AI-developing nations, and have broadly advocated more of a hands-off approach to regulation than countries with less financial incentive to have tech companies on a long leash.
Trump, First Lady welcome Xi, Madame Peng at White House
China's President Xi Jinping and his wife have arrived at the White House to begin Thursday's talks.
They were greeted by US President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump outside the South Portico of the White House late on Thursday morning.
Trump, Xi set for talks and a state dinner on Thursday
Welcome back as police and security staff in Washington gear up for an even higher-profile day than usual on Thursday.
Talks between leaders of the US and China on Thursday are set to culminate in a state dinner at the White House this evening, attended by various tech executives.
US President Donald Trump told his online acolytes that a "big day with President Xi of China" beckoned in his first social media utterance on Thursday.
He said that artificial intelligence or machine learning would "be a big topic of discussion."
But, mirroring his comments at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday, Trump said he wanted to "leave it exactly where it is."
He said that the US' "guardrail" for AI was its own Department of Justice, implying little interest in international or cooperative efforts to guard against any potential risks.
"That is China's position also," Trump asserted, though Xi Jinping is expected to deliver remarks of his own later.
Meanwhile, early morning reports from Washington suggest the White House was yet to react to the overnight court order demanding that it allow reporters from CNN, MSNOW and Politico back into the building, at least temporarily pending closer evalution of the case.
We're pausing our coverage for now
The main summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping is scheduled for Thursday.
There's a state dinner as well in the evening, with both leaders expected to deliver speeches.
Top US tech executives are expected to attend the dinner, suggesting that artificial intelligence will be a big topic of discussion.
China, US should be 'partners rather than rivals' — Xi
Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for cooperation with the US, Beijing's state news agency Xinhua reported.
"Our two countries should be partners rather than rivals," Xi said in a written statement published by Xinhua.
"The Chinese and US peoples have enjoyed long-standing friendly exchanges, and our interests are deeply intertwined," Xi added.
Xi was welcomed in Washington with a red carpet and military flyover.
In remarks published by Xinhua, Xi also said he looked forward to "in-depth exchanges" with Trump on "major issues concerning our bilateral relations and the global situation."
Trump wants Hong Kong's Jimmy Lai to be freed from prison — report
Chinese President Xi Jinping has arrived in Washington to a rare planeside welcome from his US counterpart, Donald Trump.
As Xi walked down a long red carpet on the airport tarmac, a White House spokesperson said that Trump believes Hong Kongdemocracy advocate Jimmy Lai should be released from prison and "wants to see that happen," the DPA news agency reported.
"The United States urges the authorities to grant Mr. Lai humanitarian parole," DPA quoted the spokesperson as saying.
Lai, a 78-year-old media tycoon, was sentenced to 20 years in prison earlier in the year under the National Security Law that China imposed in 2020 following massive pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong.
At a congressional hearing in Washington last week, Lai's son, Sebastien, repeated his appeal for his father's release.
Trump raised the issue of Lai's release when he met Xi in Beijing in May, but the US leader said the Chinese president told him Lai's case "would be a tough one."

Chinese press-on nails showcased at Milan Fashion Week
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
06:35:34 CST
07:35:34 KST

MILAN, Italy, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese press-on nails were showcased in Milan on Wednesday during Milan Fashion Week, arousing the interest of visitors.
At a special event dedicated to Chinese nail art and crystal products, manufacturers from Donghai county in China's Jiangsu province presented designs combining crystal embellishments with traditional techniques such as filigree and hand-painting.
Press-on nails are pre-decorated artificial nails attached by adhesive, allowing wearers to easily switch styles for different outfits, occasions or moods.
This year marks the 10th anniversary of Donghai's designation as a World Craft City for Crystal by the World Crafts Council. The Donghai region has recently become a leading center for handmade press-on nails, successfully incorporating crystals and Chinese cultural elements into its designs. Its established e-commerce networks and logistics services have helped local brands easily reach overseas consumers.
Various styles have been displayed during the event. An Italian model showcased translucent, green-gradient nails adorned with green tourmaline, while another set combined hand-painting, color gradients and three-dimensional detailing to evoke Song Dynasty porcelain and traditional Chinese gardens. These designs incorporating Eastern aesthetic elements appealed to many Italian buyers who expressed interest in adding them to their collections.
Visitors gathered around the exhibition area, looking closely at the intricate patterns before trying them on and posing for photographs. Models also demonstrated how different nail designs could perfectly complement various fashion looks.
The showcase served as a platform for Donghai to pursue cultural co-creation and industry-wide collaboration, reinforcing mutually beneficial economic ties between China and Italy. Participants of the event expressed their anticipation for deeper cooperation in design research, brand development and market channels.
According to figures presented at the event, Donghai's crystal trade exceeded 60 billion yuan (about 8.94 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, while sales of handmade press-on nails reached 15 billion yuan (about 2.24 billion U.S. dollars). ■

Can the US and China verify an AI deal? Start-ups are starting to build the tools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:34:38 UTC
07:34:38 KST

Can the US and China verify an AI deal? Start-ups are starting to build the tools
Researchers are developing technology to monitor AI development without relying on trust between Washington and Beijing
There are growing calls for Washington and Beijing to agree to slow down development of artificial intelligence. But even if they wanted to do so, how could they verify that the other side would do the same?
A group of researchers and start-ups is developing technology intended to make this a possibility, without relying on trust alone. Their proposed tools would allow third parties and governments to check some claims about how AI models are being trained or used – possibly without needing access to the AI models and infrastructure themselves.
This work is drawing attention ahead of Thursday’s meeting in Washington between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, at which AI is expected to be a topic of discussion. Still, advocates of the technology, known as “AI verification”, acknowledge that much work still needs to be done before the technology could be relied upon to monitor the vast computing facilities used to develop advanced AI.
Nonetheless, they argue that a recent surge in interest from both policymakers and industry is likely to rapidly accelerate progress in the field.

Trump welcomes China's Xi on tarmac for US visit

Rabia İclal Turan
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
US President Donald Trump welcomed Chinese President Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington on Wednesday as Xi arrived for a three-day state visit to the US capital, marking the beginning of talks focused on bilateral relations and a range of economic and technological issues.
 
Trump and Xi stood side by side at the end of a red carpet with US and Chinese flags behind them as a US Air Force band played the two national anthems and cannons fired.
 
Two B-1 bombers flew over the airbase as the Chinese leader was greeted by Trump.
 
Trump later told reporters at the White House that the White House ballroom construction project was ahead of schedule and that he wished it had been completed in time for Thursday’s state dinner for Xi.
 
When asked if he would discuss Iran during Xi’s visit, he responded: “I’ll be talking about that and many other subjects, but it’s all coming along, including that."
 
Asked whether he agreed with his counterterrorism director’s characterization of fentanyl trafficking from China as “war by other means,” Trump said the situation was “not good,” while pointing to the tariffs and other penalties imposed on China.
 
Xi, for his part, said China and the US should be partners, not rivals, according to the state-run Xinhua News Agency.
 
“Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand, and the two countries can contribute to each other's success, thereby benefiting the wider world,” he said in a statement marking his arrival.
 
China and the US should work in the same direction, promote a stable relationship featuring cooperation as the mainstay, moderate competition, manageable differences, and promises of peace, Xi said.
 
He emphasized that the world is developing and times are changing, but the historical logic of peaceful coexistence between China and the US and the general expectations of the international community for the two countries have not changed.
 
Xi said he looks forward to having in-depth exchanges with Trump on major issues concerning bilateral relations and the world situation, constantly enriching the connotation of the constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability and expanding the space for exchanges and cooperation in various fields between the two countries.
 
Trump is scheduled to host Xi and first lady Peng Liyuan at the White House on Thursday for a state arrival ceremony followed by a military review in the Rose Garden and a bilateral meeting between the two leaders.
 
Trump and first lady Melania Trump will also host Xi and Peng for a state dinner Thursday evening in the East Room, while the two couples are scheduled to meet again at the White House on Friday before the Chinese president's departure.
 
Trump said Friday that his meeting with Xi would include “a lot of different deals,” saying they would have a “very good meeting.”
 
He also said the US and China “get along very well,” while pointing to tariffs imposed on Chinese goods.
 
Trump said tariffs had previously reached 145% before being reduced, describing that level as “really hurting them badly.”
 
Trade, rare earth minerals and artificial intelligence are among the issues expected to feature in the talks, according to US officials.
 
Several prominent US business leaders are expected at Thursday's state dinner, including Jeff Bezos, Elon Musk, Sundar Pichai, Michael Dell, Jensen Huang, Sam Altman, Jane Fraser and Tim Cook, according to a senior US official.
 
Xi's visit marks his first state visit to Washington in more than a decade.

Kwasniewski: Anti-Ukrainian rhetoric unlikely to unite Poland’s right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:30:00 UTC
07:30:00 KST

Kwasniewski: Anti-Ukrainian rhetoric unlikely to unite Poland’s right
The former Polish President said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
Asked how the results of Poland’s parliamentary elections in autumn 2027 could affect relations with Kyiv if the government configuration changes, Kwasniewski said the situation could develop in different ways.
“It may change, or it may not. The outcome will not necessarily be exactly what is being predicted today (a possible victory for right-wing forces – ed.). But if we look at the current polls, there is one certainty: Tusk’s party will most likely win these elections. The other question is whether it will have a majority?” Kwasniewski noted.
The former Polish President allowed for the possibility of a right-wing coalition involving Jaroslaw Kaczynski (Law and Justice party – ed.), Mateusz Morawiecki (Development Plus), Slawomir Mentzen (Confederation), and Grzegorz Braun (Confederation of the Polish Crown), although he described such a coalition as “extremely difficult” to form.
In his view, anti-Ukrainian rhetoric is unlikely to become the glue holding such a political alliance together.
“Being anti-Ukrainian today means being pro-Russian, and that is already impossible to reconcile with Polish interests. Anyone who opposes Ukraine is de facto agreeing with Russia’s dictate regarding Ukraine and therefore takes a pro-Russian position,” Kwasniewski stressed.
In his opinion, the left and liberals could still win next year’s parliamentary elections in Poland.
“There is a whole year ahead. But it needs to be used very actively, including by speaking openly about the strategic importance of Polish-Ukrainian relations. For example, talking about how good it is for Poland that one million or more Ukrainians want to work, live here and strengthen our economy,” Kwasniewski stressed.
Assessing the policy of incumbent Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk toward Ukraine, Kwasniewski said he had no doubts about Tusk’s pro-Ukrainian stance and experience.
“Unlike some other European politicians, Tusk certainly has no illusions about Putin. In this sense, Tusk is a very serious partner for Ukraine. Of course, in practice, some things could have been done better. But today, in my opinion, he is someone who correctly assesses the importance of Polish-Ukrainian relations,” the former Polish President concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, former Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski believes that incumbent President Karol Nawrocki has yet to move beyond his former role as head of Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) on issues related to Ukraine, and that his passivity in this area is not in Poland’s interest.

Russian ballistic missiles rock Kyiv as air defenses engaged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:28:54 UTC
07:28:54 KST

Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv kills 2, injures 8 after day of drone strikes
Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Two people were killed and 8 others were injured as Russian ballistic missile explosions rocked Kyiv overnight on Sept. 24.
At the same time missiles were battering the capital, President Volodymyr Zelensky was meeting with members of the U.S. Congress, discussing the recently passed Lindsey Graham law while attending the U.N. General Assembly. 
"Right now, the United States has an opportunity to respond strongly," Zelensky wrote on X. "We need ballistic missile interceptors to protect lives. Sanctions against Russia and those helping it make money must be implemented."
Yaroslav Yurchyshyn, a lawmaker from the opposition Holos party, told the Kyiv Independent he believed the timing of the attack was deliberate.
"Russia is clearly trying to influence the positions of the U.S. and Ukraine and push us to accept its terms, which would effectively amount to capitulation. It is also trying to pressure the U.S. ahead of the elections so that Washington puts even more pressure on us," Yurchyshyn said.
He argued that the appropriate response would be for the U.S. and its partners to provide greater support to Ukraine and tighten sanctions against Russia.
Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the Ukrainian parliament's Foreign Policy and Interparliamentary Cooperation Committee, told the Kyiv Independent that Russia routinely uses provocations and strikes to test how the U.S. and its allies will respond.
Merezhko said Moscow may see Trump as increasingly focused on Iran and the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, creating what he described as an opportunity for Putin to escalate without facing a strong response from Washington.
"Russia acts in a very primitive way. They carry out a provocation, for example, and watch the reaction. If there is no reaction, they intensify their attacks," Merezhko said.
"They see that there is no reaction from Trump. Putin believes that Trump is busy now and has no time for Ukraine... Putin is using this," he added.
Russia launched 282 attack drones of various types overnight, including jet-powered drones, as well as Zircon anti-ship missiles and Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 ballistic missiles, according to the Air Force.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down 227 aerial targets, including 219 drones, four Zircon missiles, three ballistic missiles, and one Banderol munition. Strikes were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at 10 locations.
"We had three waves of ballistic attacks. Today in Kyiv, 60% of the ballistic missiles were shot down," Zelensky told reporters at a press conference in New York on Sept. 24. "It is important. We would like more to be shot down, but today it was 60%, not 10% and not zero."
Zelensky added that there had been attacks earlier this year in which Ukraine intercepted none of the incoming ballistic missiles, attributing this to shortages of interceptor missiles.
"Russia has shifted to effectively round-the-clock attacks on Kyiv, Kharkiv, Dnipro, Odesa and other major Ukrainian cities," Ukraine's ambassador to the U.K. and former commander-in-chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi said.
"They are using everything they can. Old and new Shaheds are effectively going straight from the production line to Ukraine, while ballistic missiles are being stockpiled for nights like tonight," he said.
"For years, Russia has continued to receive imported components that allow it not only to continue, but also to increase its weapons production," Zaluzhnyi added. "The world must finally stop this. Otherwise, tomorrow it may fly not only at Ukraine."
Loud explosions were first heard in the city center of Ukraine's capital at around 1:00 a.m. local time, Editor-in-Chief Olga Rudenko said.
Ukraine's Air Force also warned that a ballistic missile was headed toward Kyiv after an air raid alert had been declared in Kyiv at 12:59 a.m.
"I got woken up by the sound of an explosion, slept through the air raid alert. When I checked my phone, I saw alerts for incoming missiles and went to my hallway as a series of explosions blasted out, one of them set off car alarms near my flat," War Editor Chris York said.
Then another ballistic missile was headed toward Ukraine's capital at 1:27 a.m., the Air Force said.
"It was quiet for about 30 minutes until another wave of ballistic missiles came in, I counted eight explosions," York said.
A third wave of ballistic missile explosions rocked the city again at around 1:52 a.m. local time, he added.
Updates from authorities
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that paramedics were headed to sites in the city's Solomyanskyi, Svyatoshynskyi, and Podilskyi districts as Russian missiles continued to target the city.
In the Dniprovskyi district, debris fell into a residential building courtyard, where there could be people trapped under rubble, he said. Debris also fell onto an administrative building in the district.
"In the Podilskyi district, debris fell on a parking lot near a medical facility. Several cars caught fire. Emergency services are en route," Klitschko said.
Kyiv City Maternity Hospital No. 2 was partially damaged in the attack, with windows and doors on the first through fifth floors damaged, as well as windows in the laundry and boiler room, Kyiv's Health Department said. No patients or medical staff were injured, as they were sheltering during the attack.
At 2:05 a.m., during the height of the attack, a baby boy was born in the hospital's shelter, where medical staff continued providing care.
"Even on such a terrible night, life goes on," Tetiana Mostepan, head of Kyiv's Health Department, said. "Our medical staff remain with patients under any circumstances and do everything possible to ensure that care is provided on time."
Although there were no casualties in the maternity hospital, one person was killed in a nearby parking lot, Klitschko said, adding that a medical diagnostic center was also damaged.
The attack also destroyed the production facility of Ukrainian jewellery business Dukachi, the company told the Kyiv Independent.
"When we arrived, we saw two groups of firefighters and realized that our premises were burning," co-founders Ana and Liza Knyzhenko said. "When we ran up, we saw a wall of fire. We understood that this was the end, that it was hell, and that nothing had survived."
The company said the building was effectively destroyed, with only some walls and partitions remaining. Equipment, furniture, and stock inside were burned, leaving the facility unusable and forcing the business to rebuild its production from scratch.
Dukachi said the loss was particularly difficult for a small business that had spent eight years building up the production facility. "We don't have programs or resources that would allow us to recover quickly. Everything will have to be rebuilt at our own expense, and that is very expensive and will take a long time," the co-founders said.
Russia regularly strikes civilian infrastructure and cities across Ukraine in fatal missile and drone attacks.
The prior day, on Sept. 23, a series of deadly Russian drone strikes on Kyiv killed two people and injured at least 43 others during the morning.
Railway infrastructure, residential buildings, and a historic market were damaged in the Russian attack.
On Sept. 22, Russian jet-powered drones struck Kyiv, injuring at least eight people and hitting sites across several districts of the capital, authorities said.

After split verdict, SC refers law on EC appointment to larger bench; decision comes amid row over EC functioning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:27:46 UTC
07:27:46 KST

SC: Constitution bench should deal with case to prevent delay
NEW DELHI: On a day when Election Commission found itself under the scanner, a two-judge bench of Supreme Court gave a split verdict on whether the issue of validity of the law on appointment of CEC/ECs be referred to a constitution bench, but later agreed to refer the case to a larger bench for the sake of early adjudication of the contentious issue.Validity of several provisions of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 has been challenged on the ground that the law gives the executive "overwhelming" power to appoint its nominee as election commissioner, as the selection panel composed of the PM, a Cabinet minister and the leader of the opposition is designed to give govt a 2:1 majority. The petitioners contended that EC's independence would be compromised in this process.The 2023 law was framed to replace an SC verdict which had directed that selection be done by a committee of the PM, CJI and leader of the opposition until Parliament determined the composition by passing a law. "Speaking in one voice would have better served institutional cohesion. Unfortunately, the court is divided in its opinion," a bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and S C Sharma said.
The hearing in the case went on for five days and at the fag end of proceedings, the Centre had sought referral of the case to a constitution bench.
SC: Constitution bench should deal with case to prevent delay
Noting that appointment of CEC/ECs was being litigated for last 11 years in SC after a petition was filed in 2015, the bench decided that the case should not be referred to a three-judge bench, which is the normal procedure, but to a constitution bench to settle the issue once and for all. It reasoned that a decision by a three-judge bench would be of little worth and only delay adjudication of the significant issue(s) that these writ petitions raise."Thus, we direct that the papers be placed before the CJI for considering the desirability of constituting a constitution bench of such number of judges to decide the question of vires of Sec 7 and the other provisions of Act," the bench said.The bench expressed hope that the case would be given priority as the issues raised were of "foundational importance to the democratic fabric of the country and its citizenry"."Petitioners seem to be justified in expressing their anxiety that references to five-judge benches remain unresolved for years. If statistics are any guide, none can say with any reasonable degree of certainty when long-pending references will get resolved. Undisputedly, this is an area of grave concern and the inordinate delay in resolution of the references is itself a source of institutional embarrassment which all stakeholders ought to strive to avoid. Self-introspection, indeed, is required," it said.
"We, thus, take this opportunity of requesting the Chief Justice to also explore the necessity of constituting a permanent five-judge bench to decide pure constitutional issues. This is not something novel that we are saying. It has been opined time and again by responsible citizens and we simply endorse their opinion. Given that resolving constitutional issues is the primary task of judges of this court, that must remain its core priority.
Pendency of references for far too long, any period between five and 20 years or more, does not reflect well on the institution. It is time that the institution addresses the issue with the urgency and promptitude it deserves," the bench said.

Austrian president's 'war crimes' accusation against Israel sparks diplomatic rift
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:26:25 UTC
07:26:25 KST

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen sharply criticized Israel during a visit to New York, accusing it of committing war crimes. Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar responded forcefully, drawing criticism from Israeli diplomatic officials in Jerusalem who expressed unease over the severity of his response.
The crisis between Israel and Austria erupted after Van der Bellen held a joint news conference on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly with Chancellor Christian Stocker and Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger. During the news conference, Van der Bellen said that "illegal settlements in the West Bank territories have accelerated, and this is violence against the Palestinian population there." The Austrian president went on to say that these were acts that "fall under the definition of war crimes."
He added that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government was moving into "dangerous territory" that would not pay off in the long run. However, he stressed that his remarks did not call Israel's right to exist into question and that the country's citizens as a whole should not be held responsible for their government's policies.
Foreign Minister Sa'ar responded sharply, writing on X that the Austrian president should "be ashamed." He invoked Austria's past — a country associated with some of the gravest crimes against humanity and the Jewish people — and said the Austrian president dared to level a false accusation against the Jewish state as it fights a jihadist axis seeking its destruction. Later in his response, Sa'ar described the president's remarks as "vile nonsense," while also making clear that Austrian citizens should not be held responsible for their president's comments.
While Israel's official response focused on attacking Van der Bellen, senior Israeli diplomatic officials in Jerusalem expressed unease over the severity of Sa'ar's remarks toward the president of a friendly country.
"We have reached the point where we are reprimanding the president of Austria — one of our friendliest countries in Europe," the officials said. "You can't lash out like this at the president of a friendly country. There is a way to voice criticism."
The chancellor distances himself
A senior Israeli official familiar with Israel-Europe relations elaborated on the issue, describing an ongoing decline in Austria's standing as a vocal ally of Israel. Until about two years ago, he said, Austria was among Israel's five friendliest countries in the European Union. Today, following changes in the government, that support remains but is less prominent and vocal. He said the Austrian president operates relatively independently of his government, accounting for some of the friction.
The official also criticized Israeli diplomacy itself, arguing that in recent years Israel has been working — too successfully, in his view — to alienate not only adversaries but also friends, based on the belief that it can manage on its own even at the cost of isolation. He warned that this trend was bringing Israel closer to a point at which sanctions and serious diplomatic measures against it could begin, a situation Israel wants to avoid.
Oskar Deutsch, president of the Jewish Community of Austria, also responded, though in a more measured tone than Sa'ar. He said Van der Bellen is a true friend of Israel and the Jewish community, which is precisely why his remarks were so serious: The president spoke of "war crimes" and placed responsibility solely on one side, without mentioning the existential threat posed by Palestinian terrorist organizations, Iran and its proxies, the attacks on Israelis or the declared aspiration to destroy the Jews.
Deutsch said genuine diplomacy requires a comprehensive view of the conflict, while presenting one-sided accusations as facts gives legitimacy to those who already "knew" in advance who was to blame.
Deutsch noted that since Oct. 7, 2023, Austria has experienced a wave of antisemitic incidents. Of the 1,532 incidents documented in 2025 by Austria's antisemitism reporting center, more than three-quarters had a connection to Israel — the most common form of antisemitism in the country today.
It is important to note that the Austrian chancellor's office also distanced itself from the president's remarks.
"Because of its history, Austria bears a special responsibility toward the State of Israel. Israel's right to exist is not in question. Equally, the binding nature of international law is not in question for us. Determining whether the law has been violated is the task of the courts."

Netanyahu's transit through French airspace 'consistent' with international law despite ICC warrant, says France

Esra Taşkın
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
France said Thursday that allowing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s plane to transit its airspace did not contradict international law, despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant for him.
Speaking to reporters, Foreign Ministry Pascal Confavreux argued that allowing Netanyahu's plane to travel through French airspace was "fully in accordance with international law."
Mentioning how France had allowed this before, Confavreux said the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC, does not impose an "obligation" on member states on the transit through their airspace of a state aircraft carrying a passenger who is subject to an arrest warrant.
Turning to the Middle East, Confavreux said the 1974 Agreement on Disengagement between Israel and Syria is still valid and that France has called on all parties, including Israel, to comply with it.
Also reaffirming France's support for the UN Disengagement Observer Force, a UN peacekeeping mission tasked with maintaining the ceasefire between Israel and Syria, he stressed that France expects "an end to all military deployments" in the buffer zone between the two countries.
Any military deployment in the area violates the 1974 agreement, he noted.
Earlier Thursday, the plane carrying Netanyahu to the US to attend the UN General Assembly used the airspace of Greece, Italy, and France despite the arrest warrant for him issued by the International Criminal Court.
According to flight-tracking website Flightradar24, his plane left Israel early Thursday for the US to attend the UN General Assembly and crossed the airspace of European countries that are members of the International Criminal Court.
All three countries are parties to the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC, and are generally required to cooperate with the court's requests to arrest and surrender wanted individuals found on their territory.

Gaza flotilla activist 'near death' on Tunisia hunger strike
Tunisian Gaza flotilla activist Wael Naouar is in a "very critical" condition after more than a month on hunger strike in prison, according to a leading human rights figure, as protests grow over his detention.
Naouar, a veteran political activist who took part in an attempt to break Israel's siege of Gaza last year, has been refusing food while demanding that financial misconduct charges against him and three other detained activists be dropped.
Bassem Trifi, president of the Tunisian League for Human Rights, warned that Naouar's health had seriously deteriorated.
He is "in a very critical health condition and on the verge of death," Trifi said.
Naouar was detained in March alongside three other organisers involved with the Global Sumud Flotilla on charges of money laundering and misusing donated funds. All four deny the allegations.
Tunisian authorities say the case is part of a judicial and financial investigation and deny that the prosecution is politically motivated.
Naouar's lawyers, however, say he and the other activists have been targeted because of their activism and popularity.
A prison spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Reuters about Naouar's condition.
Naouar was among activists who sailed from Tunisia last year as part of the Global Sumud Flotilla, an international initiative that sought to deliver humanitarian aid to Gaza by sea and challenge Israel's blockade of the Palestinian territory.
The flotilla, which also included Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, was intercepted by Israeli forces.
Footage of Naouar confronting Israeli soldiers during the interception subsequently circulated widely online.
His detention has prompted protests in Tunis, including a demonstration last week that ended with 14 arrests.
"He is on hunger strike, and the authorities are doing nothing," Tunisian artist Mounir Troudi said during the protest.
Naouar's mother, Hamida Dridi, said the detention had devastated his family.
"I don't understand why they arrested him. My son did nothing wrong," she told Reuters from the family home.
"The laughter is gone. The atmosphere in our family is gone," she added.
Naouar's case comes amid mounting criticism of President Kais Saied's government over its treatment of political opponents, journalists and activists.
Critics say the space for political dissent has narrowed significantly since Saied suspended parliament and began concentrating power in the presidency in 2021.
Saied has rejected accusations of authoritarianism and political interference in prosecutions, maintaining that freedoms are protected, the judiciary is independent and no one is above the law.
Naouar's brother, Nabil, said the family would hold the president and justice ministry responsible if anything happened to him.
The Tunisian prime minister's office did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment.

EC faultlines have a long history, dating back to 1989
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:19:02 UTC
07:19:02 KST

NEW DELHI: It is not the first time that the fault lines within the Election Commission are out in the open. The trend started from the time it became a multi-member body in 1989.Two election commissioners S S Dhanoa and V S Seigell were appointed in October 1989 and joined the poll body then led by chief election commissioner (CEC) R V S Peri Sastri. Though Sastri never publicly spoke about it, it is widely believed that the new arrangement was perceived by him as a dilution in power. By January 1990, the appointment of the two commissioners was rescinded and the EC reverted to being a single—member body.In 1993, with T N Seshan as an all-powerful CEC, the commission was once again made a multi-member body with the appointment of election commissioners M S Gill and G V G Krishnamurthy. What followed was a running feud between Seshan on the one hand and Gill and Krishnamurthy on the other. Seshan viewed the appointments as a direct assault on the independence of his office and completely refused to recognize the two new commissioners. He refused to share official documents with Gill and Krishnamurthy, barred them from attending critical meetings, and would not allocate them any office work. He openly ridiculed the election commissioners in interviews, even referring to them as “two donkeys in my office”.
Interestingly, it was on Seshan’s plea challenging the govt’s decision to make EC a multi-member body that the Supreme Court had, in 1995, ruled that the election commissioners and CEC were equal in status, power and decision-making authority and that the CEC was only “first among equals”.The other internal feud in EC to recall would be one between then CEC N Gopalaswami and election commissioner Navin Chawla between 2006 and 2009. Months before he was to step down upon the end of his tenure, Gopalaswami wrote to the President of India recommending the removal of Chawla on grounds of a pro-Congress bias. In his note to the President, Gopalaswami alleged that Chawla was passing on details of EC’s meetings to senior Congress leaders, often taking “toilet breaks” during commission meetings to do so. Gopalaswami’s recommendation was however turned down by the Manmohan Singh govt and Chawla succeeded him as CEC.During the 2019 general election, the differences between then CEC Sunil Arora and then election commissioner Ashok Lavasa came to the fore, with media reports alleging that he had dissented in cases relating to complaints of alleged model code of conduct violations by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and then BJP president Amit Shah, but was overruled without the commission making his dissent noted public. EC put out a clarification that dissent notes were only made public in quasi-judicial orders passed by EC.
Lavasa resigned on August 18, 2020, two years short of his tenure, and joined the Manila-headquartered Asian Development Bank (ADB) as its Vice-President.
Arun Goyal was the last election commissioner to quit in the middle of his term. Though he had cited personal reasons in his resignation dated March 9, 2024, it was widely speculated that he was not on the best of terms with the then chief election commissioner Rajiv Kumar.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in India’s neighbourhood.

Trump greets China’s Xi in rare airport welcome to kick off three-day state visit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:01:08 UTC
07:01:08 KST

Xi says China and US should be ‘partners rather than rivals’, kicking off three-day state visit
- Donald Trump personally greeted Chinese leader Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews, marking the first such US airport welcome for a Chinese leader in six decades.
- The rare gesture highlights Trump's respect towards Xi and aims to set a positive tone for their three-day state visit amid ongoing trade tensions.
- Despite the warm welcome, significant breakthroughs are unlikely due to deep divisions on trade, Taiwan, AI, and recent sensitive incidents involving military equipment.
AI generated
BEIJING/WASHINGTON – Chinese President Xi Jinping urged cooperation with the United States, Beijing’s state media reported, hours after being greeted in Washington on the evening of Sept 23 US time by President Donald Trump.
“Our two countries should be partners rather than rivals,” Xi said in written remarks published by state news agency Xinhua, adding that “the Chinese and US peoples have enjoyed longstanding friendly exchanges, and our interests are deeply intertwined”.
The comments came ahead of closely watched talks between Trump and Xi, who shook hands on a red carpet after the Chinese leader’s arrival in the US capital.
Thorny discussion topics are expected to include trade, technological competition – particularly in artificial intelligence – and Beijing’s diplomatic and economic support for Tehran.
Xi said that he was looking “forward to in-depth exchanges with President Trump on major issues concerning our bilateral relations and the global situation”, Xinhua reported.
The countries should “work towards each other to foster a stable relationship characterised by cooperation as the mainstay, competition within bounds, manageable differences and peaceful prospects”, Xi said.
And in a nod to Trump’s signature political slogan, he said that “the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and the goal of making America great again can fully go hand in hand”.
He added that the two sides should “chart a correct path for two major powers” to get along, Xinhua reported.
“I am confident we can achieve this,” said Xi. “I believe that with the joint efforts of both sides, this visit will yield fruitful results, enhance the well-being of our two peoples and bring new hope for world peace.”
He was treated to a rare personal airport welcome by Trump on Sept 23, kicking off a pomp-filled state visit aimed at smoothing superpower tensions on everything from AI to trade to Iran.
Trump and First Lady Melania shook hands with Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan after the Chinese President descended from his plane at Joint Base Andrews, a US military airfield outside Washington.
Trump, wearing a long coat and gloves, and Xi then stood side by side on the tarmac as a military band played national anthems.
A noisy flyover by two B-1 bombers clearly jolted Trump, who grimaced at the roar of jets, while his Chinese guest stood by impassively.
Trump brushed off the fact that Xi had not given him a similar airport welcome when he visited Beijing in May.
“I thought it was a great little meeting, a great greeting, and I think they appreciate it,” Trump told reporters at the White House after welcoming Xi.
The personal airport greeting – a courtesy Trump was notably denied when he visited Beijing in May – begins three days of pageantry that will include another flyover and a state banquet at the White House on Sept 24.
Six F-22 fighter jets and six F-16s were lined up on the tarmac in an apparent display of military might as US officials literally rolled out the red carpet for the Chinese leader.
But expectations of any breakthroughs are low. Analysts say the main aim of the lavish spectacle is to maintain a fragile diplomatic and trade truce between the world’s biggest economies.
Xi was accompanied by his right-hand man Cai Qi and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, among others, according to Chinese state media.
There were no Chinese chief executives in Xi’s delegation, two sources told AFP, despite the fact that top US tech bosses including the leaders of major AI companies are set to attend the Sept 24 White House state banquet.
Xi’s visit will wrap up on the morning of Sept 25 when the two presidential couples have tea at the White House and then visit the National Archives, home to the US Declaration of Independence.
The Iran war will be on the agenda, Trump confirmed on Sept 23, despite having earlier played down reports that Beijing was supplying Tehran with intelligence as the conflict drags on.
“I’ll be talking about that and many other subjects – but it’s all coming along well, including that,” Trump said when an AFP reporter asked if he would bring up Iran.
Trade war truce extended
When the two leaders sit down for their highly anticipated talks on Sept 24, they will be confronting a host of thorny issues led by fears – boosted by warnings from tech CEOs – that artificial intelligence risks wiping out humanity.
But with China and the US racing for AI supremacy there are few expectations of any deal to regulate the rapidly advancing technology.
Preliminary talks on Sept 20 between US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng included discussion of creating a communication channel for AI concerns.
There was one success on Sept 23, when after further talks, Bessent announced an extension of a truce in the simmering trade war between the world’s two biggest economies.
The “economic detente” will now extend beyond its Nov 10 deadline to Jan 10, Bessent said.
Jonathan Czin of the Brookings Institution told AFP that expectations were low for any concrete results from the meeting, but “I think there will be some extension of the gentleman’s agreement”.
Analysts said that China had meanwhile begun to look past Trump, whose second term ends in early 2029, and is in many ways playing for time and using the truce to consolidate its position.
Criticism from China hawks
Trump’s five-star welcome for Xi has drawn criticism from China hawks within his own party, especially amid reports that Beijing supplied Iran with intelligence for attacks on US troops.
“Our commander-in-chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator,” said Republican Senator Roger Wicker, chairman of the powerful Senate Armed Services Committee.
Trump, however, has played down the need to bring up the allegations of Chinese help for Iran, justifying it on the grounds that both Beijing and Washington spy on each other.
For Trump, Xi’s visit is also a chance to focus on pageantry instead of problems at home, where the Iran war’s effect on fuel prices has sent his approval rating plummeting to historic lows ahead of midterm elections in November.
American presidents very rarely travel to the airport to greet foreign leaders, although Trump welcomed Russian President Vladimir Putin off his plane in Alaska in 2025.
The last such welcomes at Andrews – apart from papal visits – are believed to be John F. Kennedy’s welcome for British prime minister Harold Macmillan in 1962, and Dwight D. Eisenhower’s for Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in 1959. AFP

====================================================================================================

'Real and imminent' risks – UNSC hosts 'one of Godfathers of AI', tech bosses in high-level briefing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:00:39 UTC
07:00:39 KST

UN Security Council, New York — It was no ordinary session at the United Nations Security Council (UNSC).
One of the "Godfathers of artificial intelligence", several top executives from leading AI firms, and council members lifted the discussion on AI risks from a technical debate into the council's core mandate of maintaining international security and setting rules.
The last time the UNSC held a dedicated meeting and briefing on AI was on July 18, 2023, under the UK presidency. Since then, frontier AI models have advanced rapidly, prompting researchers and industry executives alike to warn that unchecked and unregulated technological developments could pose catastrophic risks to humanity within years.
Following these warnings, the UNSC convened on Wednesday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly to focus specifically on the risks of losing control over increasingly capable frontier systems.
Yoshua Bengio, widely known as one of the foundational figures of AI and co-chair of the UN Scientific Advisory Panel on AI, set the tone for the session: "The dangers from AI technology are real and imminent."
Addressing the high-level session presided over by France, Bengio warned: "This council faces an unprecedented threat, one that none of its members would choose, that none can contain alone, and that does not respect the borders we defend."
Bengio noted that leading developers of advanced systems acknowledge the catastrophic risks involved yet lack conclusive technical solutions.
He cited recent incidents involving autonomous AI agents circumventing containment protocols, executing coordinated cyberattacks, and altering outputs to conceal deceptive behaviour. "They took actions that would be crimes if committed by a human," Bengio told the UNSC members.
Heightened concerns were recently sparked when Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, resigned while publicly criticising major labs for accelerating "self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives". Shortly thereafter, a senior safety researcher at Anthropic warned of significant risks that unaligned AI could lead to existential threats within 10 years.
These warnings prompted Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei to publish an essay arguing that organisations developing frontier general-purpose AI and large-scale foundation models should moderate the speed of capability development while urging countries to offer guardrails.
Wednesday's briefing also took place amid intense rivalry between the US and China. US President Donald Trump has resisted domestic curbs on the technology, citing competitive pressure from Beijing, and dismissed concerns over systemic AI risks as "hoax" during his address to the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.
Democratisation of technology
Presenting their evaluations and recommendations, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman, Anthropic CEO Amodei, and Hugging Face co-founder Clement Delangue warned of uncontrollable AI systems, stressed the necessity of measured pacing, and highlighted the importance of technological democratisation.
All three were signatories to a 2023 multilateral statement advocating that mitigating existential risks from AI be treated as an urgent global priority, comparable to the threats posed by pandemics and nuclear conflict.
Amodei outlined two major near-term risks: deliberate misuse and loss of control over frontier models. He observed that the consequences are "global in scale" and that "if managed poorly, AI could be risk to humanity as a whole."
Altman largely agreed with Bengio’s assessment, and warned against losing control of the future to AI "if it advances so fast that people can no longer follow what is happening or intervene."
Altman added that the concentration of frontier AI capabilities among a narrow group of actors creates profound vulnerabilities, emphasising that no individual, corporation, or state should monopolise powerful models to dictate terms globally.
Delangue of the Hugging Face argued the biggest risk is not powerful AI itself but uneven access: attackers vs. defenders, a handful of labs vs. everyone else, and a few countries vs. the rest of the world.
He cited a July incident in which OpenAI agents breached its systems; the company defended itself using open-source models, including a Chinese one, because closed US tools were more restricted.
At the time OpenAI described the episode as "evidence that, without proper safeguards, highly capable AI agents are now able to work around technical controls, collaborate through unapproved channels, and take dangerous actions that no human directed".
At the UNSC, Altman presented two distinct options, calling AI as a "new Renaissance of creativity and discovery" that expands human agency, or a "new Industrial Revolution of upheaval."
He advocated a "middle path between blind optimism and doomerism."
UNSC member states share concerns
The AI lab bosses advocated for human control on AI and alignment, international standards and cooperation, willingness to slow down, and licensing and accountability.
Bengio recommended treating frontier AI more like nuclear energy, aviation, or medicine — licensing, liability insurance, and mandatory incident reporting.
Altman said, "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone", and Amodei warned that "No leader, no company and no nation can manage this alone."
Member states, including Pakistan, Somalia, Denmark, and France, also shared their concerns and recommendations.
Pakistan's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar noted that AI's impact is already clear in international peace and stability and that it is shaping a new chapter of modern warfare as a "force multiplier."
Dar made several recommendations and said Pakistan takes the call to pace frontier development seriously.
Denmark’s Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said the unprecedented speed of AI innovation and its application bring new risks and opportunities for international peace and security. However, he stressed the need for "safeguards to ensure AI systems remain safe, secure and trustworthy."
France, Somalia and other members also voiced similar concerns.
Permanent UNSC members, China and US, were also expected to speak. Both countries are divided on how AI should be governed and framed. However, they both agree that they won’t slow down their own AI models.
Meanwhile, the UNSC briefing comes as bilateral US–China AI dialogue is being discussed around the current meetings between leaders of the US and China in Washington DC amid both countries’ diverging views on who should regulate and set the rules.

Alzheimer’s proteins predict early brain shrinkage before dementia symptoms appear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:00:30 UTC
07:00:30 KST

An analysis of the AMYPAD Prognostic and Natural History Study data found that, in older individuals with preserved cognition, amyloid-beta accumulation in the brain can predict future brain atrophy. In women, the association was stronger for predicting atrophy of the temporal region of the brain. It was also stronger in the frontal and lateral-temporal regions as well as the hippocampus in carriers of at least one version (allele) of the APOE-ε4 gene, a gene associated with increased risk of Alzheimer’s disease. The paper was published in NeuroImage: Clinical.
As people reach advanced age, their memory, attention, and mental processing speed tend to gradually worsen. This is a normal part of aging. However, in some people these changes can be more severe, indicating that some type of dementia or neurodegenerative disease might be developing.
Alzheimer’s disease is the most common cause of dementia. It gradually disrupts memory, reasoning, language, and the ability to function independently. Other forms of dementia, such as vascular dementia, Lewy body dementia, and frontotemporal dementia, produce similar symptoms but arise from partly different biological processes.
One of the hallmark features of Alzheimer’s disease is the accumulation of amyloid-beta protein into plaques between brain cells. Another important change is the buildup of abnormal tau protein inside neurons, which is closely associated with neuronal damage and brain atrophy. These pathological processes can begin many years before noticeable cognitive symptoms appear.
Study author Leonard Pieperhoff and his colleagues wanted to explore the influence of global accumulation levels of amyloid-beta in the brain on regional brain atrophy. To do this, they examined regional changes in brain volume and thickness in a large research sample composed of older adults without dementia.
They also explored whether the relationship between amyloid-beta accumulation and subsequent brain atrophy depends on an individual’s sex and on whether the person is a carrier of the APOE-ε4 gene. APOE-ε4 is a gene variant that increases a person’s genetic risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease. People with this gene variant also tend to develop Alzheimer’s disease earlier in life.
These researchers analyzed data from the Amyloid Imaging to Prevent Alzheimer’s Disease (AMYPAD) Prognostic Natural History Study (PNHS). The study included 1,329 participants who were all required to have no history of dementia and be above 50 years of age at the start. Participants’ average age was 68.2 years. 56% were women. 40% had at least one version of the APOE-ε4 gene.
All participants completed magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET) imaging of their brains. A subgroup of 684 participants completed these scans at least once again in the years after the start. The median follow-up time for these scans was 3.4 years later.
Results showed that participants’ brain volumes generally shrank over time, suggesting that there was widespread atrophy of the brain due to aging-related factors. This effect was the most prominent in temporal and parietal regions of the brain as well as in the hippocampus and amygdala. Similar reductions were seen in cortical thickness, although the posterior and anterior cingulate cortices showed thickening over time.
Higher amyloid-beta concentrations were associated with lower volumes of multiple regions of the brain including the lateral-temporal lobes, precuneus, posterior cingulate, amygdala, and hippocampus. Cortical thickness of these regions was also associated with amyloid-beta concentrations in the same way.
Across time, higher amyloid-beta concentrations in the cortex were associated with widespread decrease of volume and thickness at follow-up scans, across different brain regions. The strongest effects were observed in the posterior cingulate, fusiform, and parahippocampal gyri, as well as the hippocampus and amygdala. Notably, atrophy in the fusiform gyrus was predicted by amyloid-beta independently of tau protein levels. This association was stronger in women when temporal regions of the brain were concerned. For carriers of at least one variant of the APOE-ε4 gene, these associations were stronger in frontal and lateral-temporal regions and the hippocampus.
“Our findings suggest that in older adults with mostly preserved cognition, baseline Aβ-PET [amyloid-beta concentrations assessed using PET] predicts future brain atrophy, with fusiform atrophy showing independence from tau pathology [accumulation of tau proteins in the brain] and Aβ-dependent atrophy being exacerbated in region-dependent manners in females and APOE-ε4 carriers. Regional cortical volume and thickness may serve as sensitive markers for early Aβ-related neurodegeneration and aid in stratifying risk in AD [Alzheimer’s disease] prevention trials,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the neural correlates of dementia and age-related brain atrophy. However, it should be noted that the design of the study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results.
The paper, “Amyloid PET predicts atrophy in older adults without dementia: Results from the AMYPAD Prognostic & Natural History study,” was authored by Leonard Pieperhoff, Luigi Lorenzini, Sophie Mastenbroek, Mario Tranfa, Mahnaz Shekari, Alle Meije Wink, Robin Wolz, Sylke Grootoonk, Craig Ritchie, Mercè Boada, Marta Marquié, Wiesje van der Flier, Rik Vandenberghe, Bernard J. Hanseeuw, Pablo Martínez-Lage, Pierre Payoux, Pieter Jelle Visser, Michael Schöll, Giovanni B. Frisoni, Andrew Stephens, Christopher Buckley, Gill Farrar, Frank Jessen, Oriol Grau-Rivera, Juan Domingo Gispert, David Vállez García, Henk Mutsaerts, Frederik Barkhof, and Lyduine E. Collij, on behalf of the AMYPAD consortium.

Integrity Initiative: UK-funded network framed dissent as Russian disinformation for years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:48:28 UTC
06:48:28 KST

Integrity Initiative: UK-funded network framed dissent as Russian disinformation for years
A sprawling network of media influence “clusters” has existed in NATO member states for years, seeking to portray voices opposing the policies of the military bloc and the EU as Russian propaganda, RT America’s Ben Swann and independent investigative journalist Elizabeth Lane have learnt.
Founded in 2015, soon after the Western-backed coup in Kiev, the so-called Integrity Initiative program was designed to counter what it called Russia’s disinformation. It was run by the UK Foreign Office-funded Institute for Statecraft – an organization posing as an independent charity that was founded by Christopher Donnelly, a former adviser to a NATO secretary general, and Daniel Lafayeedney, a former Special Air Service officer.
The definition of ‘Russian propaganda’ developed by the organization, which received funding not just from London but also from the NATO-linked Atlantic Council, was so broad that it virtually included any criticism of NATO and the EU.
“They are not really after Russian disinformation,” Lane said. “They targeted independent journalists. And that’s very clear in their own communications.”
For the Integrity Initiative, Russian disinformation was “any position that is counter to the NATO position,” according to Swann.
Among the most prominent targets of the Integrity Initiative were former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and retired Spanish Army colonel Pedro Banos, who lost his appointment as director of national security in the Spanish government in 2018 amid a concerted campaign portraying him as a Russian asset.
The campaigns were focused on “killing the image” of any dissenter to the point where their political careers were ruined, Lane explained. “If you assassinate their image, no one wants to be associated to that person. And that’s what happened with Pedro Banos. That’s what happened with Jeremy Corbyn.”
The network established “clusters” of politicians and journalists it treated like “assets” in virtually all NATO nations, with many of them often unaware that they were part of a media influence network, according to Lane. “They are just given the script and they legit trust the story and they run the story and turns out they are part of the propaganda,” she said.
The Integrity Initiative came into the spotlight in 2018 when hackers, claiming to be linked to the Anonymous collective, leaked a trove of documents revealing the scale of its operations. The revelations led to an investigation into the Institute for Statecraft’s activities by the Scottish charity regulator OSCR, which concluded in 2019 that the organization was violating charity rules.
The institute then formally announced that it was terminating its involvement with the Integrity Initiative in 2019 but continued to operate until August 2023, when it was dissolved several months after being declared an “undesired organization” by the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office over what officials called “aggressive militarist rhetoric” and a “discreditation campaign” against the Russian authorities.

AI leaders urge caution at UN, with Anthropic chief pledging to slow down

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
